items.abstract: Abstract The rise of antibiotic resistance, particularly among pathogens such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus , necessitates innovative antibacterial strategies. Here we introduce FibriLysins, a class of engineered enzymes combining staphylokinase and endolysin, which dismantle fibrin-encapsulated multicellular staphylococcal communities, including biofilms and staphylococcal abscess communities (SACs). We characterized diverse staphylokinases, developing a library of 27 FibriLysins, with a 78% positive hit rate. The lead variant, FL-028, has significant antibacterial activity against prevalent clinical S. aureus isolates. In vitro, FL-028 reduced bacterial counts in SACs by 3.4 log and in biofilms by 2.3 log. In vivo, FL-028 exhibits superior efficacy in a mouse model of bone fracture-related infection, outperforming vancomycin by 1 log and eliminating SAC presence in tissues. FL-028 shows no adverse effects on bone healing, as confirmed by histological examination, mechanical testing and micro-computed tomography analyses. These preclinical findings highlight the potential of FibriLysins as a robust and safe therapeutic approach against difficult-to-treat staphylococcal infections.

items.abstract: Abstract Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses viraemia in people with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), but HIV provirus persists indefinitely in CD4-expressing cells. Cells containing active provirus express viral proteins and have been successfully targeted using broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs). In contrast, cells containing latent provirus cannot be specifically targeted without latency reactivation. Meaningful depletion of the latent HIV or simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) reservoirs has not been demonstrated except with cytotoxic conditioning for bone-marrow transplantation. Here we show that both the active and latent SIV reservoirs can be eliminated from infant macaques via profound but transient depletion of cells that express CCR5 using a single shot of CCR5/CD3 bispecific antibody. Neonatal rhesus macaques were infected with SIVmac251, then treated with ART beginning at 1 week after infection, followed by treatment with either a CCR5/CD3-bispecific or a CD4-specific antibody, both of which depleted target cells and accelerated the decline in plasma viraemia. Upon ART cessation, while rebound occurred quickly in all animals treated with ART alone, most animals treated with CCR5/CD3 bispecific antibody remained aviraemic for >3 months. Several remained aviraemic to the end of follow-up and efforts to detect replication-competent virus were unsuccessful. Our results show that bispecific antibody treatment achieves meaningful depletion of the replication-competent SIV reservoir and supports the possibility that clinically meaningful depletion of the HIV reservoir might be achievable for recently infected individuals.

Lynx reintroduction from a bottlenecked source exposes a lethal genetic defect
items.abstract: Abstract Conservation programmes worldwide use reintroductions and translocations as management tools to support endangered species. However, such efforts often result in small and isolated populations that face genetic challenges associated with reduced gene flow and inbreeding. Inbreeding depression is a well-known risk in such programmes, as increased homozygosity can expose recessive deleterious alleles, compromise fitness and threaten population persistence. Yet, no causal variant for a lethal disease has previously been identified in a wild population. Here we combine long-term health and population data with genomic analyses to identify a recessive loss-of-function allele causing lethal organ mineralization in young Eurasian lynx ( Lynx lynx ) from a reintroduced population in Switzerland. Spatio-temporal analyses revealed that the allele was introduced from one of the source populations and increased in frequency through founder effects and inbreeding. Our findings establish the first direct link between reintroduction history and a lethal genetic disease in the wild, illustrating how population genetic processes interact to shape the fate of a recessive deleterious allele and emphasize the vulnerability of small, isolated populations following reintroduction.

items.title: Egg mimicry leaves its mark on mitochondria

items.abstract: Abstract Amid the global biodiversity crisis, there is high demand for spatially explicit biodiversity indicators. Global models that quantify human impacts on biodiversity provide important insights for conservation, but systematic testing of predictive performance has been lacking. Here, when evaluating alpha- and beta-diversity models using representative global data, we find that, despite land-use impacts in line with previous research, there is a challenging gap between effect size inference and local prediction. The results show that mixed models with study attributes as random effects, common in biodiversity meta-analysis and indicators, exhibit low predictive accuracy, driven by reliance on highly averaged fixed effects. Ecologically structured models that replace study random effects with biome, realm and taxonomic parameters show improved but still modest results in sampled contexts. Further, performance when extending predictions to other contexts remains low, related to distribution shifts in environmental conditions and biodiversity responses. Our results highlight a tension between high-resolution predictor availability and the granularity at which biodiversity responses can be reliably estimated. While models are essential for informed conservation efforts, their applicability is fundamentally constrained by current data availability, which includes geographic and taxonomic biases. Countries with extensive data can build higher-fidelity national indicators, but accelerated and systematic data collection is needed to support data-poor regions with localized, actionable biodiversity insights.

items.abstract: Abstract The Clarion–Clipperton Zone (CCZ) is the focal region for imminent deep-sea nodule mining, with over 1.1 million square kilometres already under exploration licence. Although the International Seabed Authority has designated Areas of Particular Environmental Interest (APEIs) to protect regional biodiversity from mining impacts, there has been no formal assessment of whether this network functions as a coherent connected system. Here we use Lagrangian dispersal modelling and network analysis to provide a region-wide assessment of modelled larval connectivity across the CCZ and show that simulated larval exchange among APEIs is extremely limited. Under physically driven near-bed dispersal and reasonable pelagic larval dispersal times of 19–69 days, fewer than 0.02% of particles reach another APEI, with inter-APEI gaps exceeding modelled dispersal capacity. CCZ-wide dispersal is structured into four semi-isolated connectivity communities, and under mining disturbance when self-supply is removed from Areas of Mining Interest, unprotected non-mining areas emerge as the dominant modelled source of replenishment. Strategic corridor additions increase inter-APEI dispersal 406-fold and nearly doubles modelled replenishment from protected areas under disturbance, providing a reproducible, connectivity-informed evidence base for conservation design ahead of commercial mining.

items.abstract: Abstract Non-ribosomal peptides play important roles in microbial ecology and medicine, for example as toxins and antibiotics such as penicillin. Like ordinary proteins, non-ribosomal peptides are subject to evolutionary change, which is driven by rampant recombinations of their synthetases. The evolutionary dynamics and causes of non-ribosomal peptide diversification are not well understood, because recombinations complicate phylogenetic analysis and statistical tests for natural selection and drift. Here we study the non-ribosomal GameXPeptides, which entomopathogenic bacteria use to kill their insect prey. We use recombination-aware phylogenetics, ancestral sequence reconstruction and statistical analysis of historical recombination patterns to retrace the evolution of GameXPeptides. This uncovers dozens of new GameXPeptides, including striking patterns of structural convergence. We provide statistical and experimental evidence that this diversity is shaped by selection, but also that GameXPeptides experience substantial genetic drift and biased recombination rates that limit the space of accessible peptide variants. Our work illuminates the complex interplay of adaptive and non-adaptive evolutionary forces acting on some of the most versatile chemical weapons in nature.

Plasma proteomics identifies insulin resistance signatures predictive of cardiometabolic disease risk
items.abstract: Abstract Insulin resistance drives cardiometabolic disease, yet its molecular signatures and tissue origins remain incompletely characterized. Here we define a circulating protein signature that enables scalable assessment of insulin sensitivity. We applied multiworkflow proteomics to plasma from 161 individuals spanning the insulin sensitivity spectrum defined by the hyperinsulinaemic–euglycaemic clamp and identified 488 proteins associated with insulin sensitivity, capturing contributions from liver, adipose tissue and immune cells. A subset of these proteins shifted towards a more insulin-sensitive profile following an exercise intervention in men. We further developed a model combining 13 proteins, including IGFBP1, LEP, GDF15, PON3 and LDLR, with clinical variables (sex, HbA1c and the triglyceride-to-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio) to predict insulin sensitivity ( R 2 = 0.67). In ~20,000 UK Biobank participants, the model outperformed the triglyceride-to-high-density lipoprotein cholesterol ratio in predicting type 2 diabetes (concordance index, 0.86 versus 0.74) and, unlike HbA1c, predicted hepatic, renal, cardiovascular and respiratory disease. In an independent cohort of 1,700 individuals, the model also showed greater predictive utility than fasting insulin resistance indices, including the homeostatic model assessment of insulin resistance. Together, these findings establish a tissue-resolved plasma proteomic framework for characterizing insulin resistance and provide a scalable approach to precision cardiometabolic risk stratification.

Whole-blood NAD levels track cardiovascular disease but not chronological age
items.abstract: Abstract The extent to which whole-blood NAD levels are altered in human disease or ageing remains controversial. Here we conducted 1,340 measurements in 1,068 adults, and found that whole-blood NAD levels do not decline with age in healthy individuals; they remain stable in males and increase in females, but are reduced in chronic diseases, specifically cardiovascular disease and hypertension. These findings indicate that whole-blood NAD levels track cardiovascular disease rather than chronological age. As this research was not designed to investigate causality, these data do not provide direct evidence that NAD supplementation may serve as a treatment for cardiovascular disease or hypertension.

Aging disrupts sleep-driven brain fluid flow
The aging human brain exhibits reduced hemodynamic and cerebrospinal fluid flow waves during sleep
items.abstract: Abstract Aging reduces the quality and quantity of sleep, and sleep disruption is predictive of neurodegeneration and cognitive decline. Sleep loss could affect brain health through disruption of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulation, which is important for brain homeostasis. In young adults, large CSF flow waves appear during non-rapid eye movement sleep; however, whether sleep-dependent brain fluid physiology changes in aging is not known. Here we imaged large-scale CSF flow and hemodynamics in young (18–39 years) and older (60–84 years) adults during nighttime sleep. Sleep-dependent CSF flow was reduced in older adults, and was linked to reduced EEG slow wave power, decreased global hemodynamic oscillations and gray matter atrophy. Using sensory and vasoactive stimuli to drive CSF flow, we found that both neural and cerebrovascular changes contributed to this disruption. These results demonstrate reduced CSF flow during sleep in human aging, before disease onset, and identify parallel neural and hemodynamic mechanisms contributing to this decline.

Deep and quantitative proteomic profiling of low-volume mouse serum in a cross-sectional analysis of aging
items.abstract: Abstract Assessing and validating circulating biomarkers is essential for developing preclinical measures of biological aging in mice. However, comprehensive serum proteomics are limited by technical challenges and low sample volumes. Here we present a quantitative nanoparticle-based enrichment workflow coupled with data-independent acquisition mass spectrometry for deep proteomic profiling of low-volume mouse serum. This approach increased proteomic coverage by 3–6-fold with median coefficient of variation <10%. In 30 mice aged 12, 24 and 30 months, we uncovered 3,992 protein groups from 20 µl of serum and revealed age- and sex-specific changes, and capturing senescence-associated circulating proteins. With 1 µl additional serum,the proximity extension assay quantified 43 cytokines not detected by mass spectrometry. Comparison with plasma proteomics from the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging identified conserved age-associated circulating proteins, several of which were linked to frailty in humans, notably COL6A3. These results establish a scalable approach for discovering aging biomarkers in sample-limited mouse studies with translational relevance to human health.

Statins promote bone anabolism in estrogen deficiency by inducing osteogenic differentiation of skeletal stem/progenitor cells
items.abstract: Abstract Menopause-associated estrogen deficiency drives age-related bone loss in women. Statin use has been associated with higher bone mineral density in postmenopausal women, but whether menopause alters skeletal responses to statins remains unclear. Here, we show that statin use was associated with a slower annual decline in bone mineral density in postmenopausal women and that atorvastatin promotes bone anabolism specifically under estrogen-deficient conditions by inducing osteogenic differentiation of leptin receptor-expressing (LEPR + ) bone marrow stromal cells, which include skeletal stem/progenitor cells. Atorvastatin increases osteoblast formation by restricting RAC1 prenylation and enabling nuclear factor kappa B-mediated Oln transcription. Estrogen acts on the same LEPR + cells through estradiol–estrogen receptor-α signaling to promote Oln transcription. Thus, statins compensate for reduced estradiol–estrogen receptor-α signaling through a mechanistically distinct pathway. These findings reposition a major component of estrogen action to an earlier osteogenic stage and suggest broader implications for how statins influence stem/progenitor cell responsiveness beyond cholesterol management.

Mitsunobu reactions using iminophosphorane reagents
items.abstract: Abstract The Mitsunobu reaction is one of the most celebrated reactions in organic synthesis, enabling stereospecific C–O, C–N and C–S bond formation from abundant alcohol feedstocks. However, its widespread use is constrained by the need for explosive reagents, laborious product purification and a pronucleophile p K a window that precludes C–C bond formation. Here we disclose iminophosphoranes as a class of reagents for the Mitsunobu reaction that readily overcome these limitations. The key iminophosphorane reagent is rapidly and quantitively formed in situ from commercially available 1-azido-4-methoxybenzene and a trialkylphosphine, allowing the construction of C–O, C–N, C–S and, notably, C–C bonds from primary and secondary alcohol substrates with vastly simplified product purification. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the direct use of a solution of preformed iminophosphorane eliminates end-user azide handling altogether. The utility of the reaction was demonstrated through reaction scale-up and late-stage functionalization of pharmaceutically relevant compounds.

Stepwise and chemoselective installation of carbon substituents at silicon atoms via monobromination of hydrosilanes
items.abstract: Abstract Although organosilicon compounds containing different carbon substituents are ubiquitous in synthetic chemistry, their preparation is challenging. Laboratory synthesis commonly relies on the sequential substitution of tetrachlorosilane or tetraalkoxysilanes, producing complex mixtures that require demanding purification. This arises from limited control over nucleophilic substitution in functionalized silanes containing three or four (identical) leaving groups. Here we introduce an experimentally straightforward and reliable procedure for the preparation of both hetero- and homoleptic silanes using an overlooked monobromination of primary and secondary hydrosilanes. An equimolar amount of elemental bromine converts a Si–H bond into an Si–Br bond without ‘overbromination’. This step also shows exceptional functional-group tolerance to existing substituents at the silicon atom. Unsaturated moieties as well as heteroatom and heteroaryl groups are compatible. When performed in an iterative fashion, multihydrosilanes can be selectively converted into secondary, tertiary and quaternary silanes with two, three or four different carbon substituents in high yields. These functionalized silicon building blocks are relevant to synthetic chemistry as well as applied chemistry materials.

Quantitative measurement of viscosity in two-dimensional electron fluids
items.abstract: Electron hydrodynamics is an emerging framework that describes dynamics of interacting electron systems as conventional fluids. Although evidence for hydrodynamic-like transport has been reported in a variety of two-dimensional materials, precise quantitative measurement of the core parameter, electron viscosity, remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate that magnetoresistance in Corbino-shaped graphene devices offers a simultaneous ohmmeter and viscosometer capability, allowing us to disentangle the individual ohmic and viscous contributions to transport, even near viscous-ohmic crossover. In both monolayer and bilayer graphene, the effective electron-electron scattering rate scales linearly with temperature, deviating markedly from the T 2 dependence expected in conventional Fermi liquids. Instead, it is consistent with a recently identified tomographic fluid regime, theoretically predicted to be generic for two-dimensional electron systems.

items.title: Carbon dioxide and amorphous water ices in the debris disk around β Pictoris
items.abstract: The star β Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The outer disk is sufficiently far from the star that volatile molecules are expected to freeze into solid ices. We observed the β Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (<7% crystallinity) and carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) ice in both the 12 CO 2 and 13 CO 2 isotopologues. We infer that the CO 2 ice is intimately mixed with the water ice at a ratio of 1:10. This implies that the ices formed in cold conditions, likely in the interstellar medium. Frequent collisions within the debris disk are required to explain the observed uniform distribution of icy dust grains.

items.title:
Differentiation of stem-like CD4
                    <sup>+</sup>
                    T cells modulates early effector responses in colorectal cancer
items.abstract: Strategies to improve cancer immunotherapy have largely focused on the intratumor immunosuppressive microenvironment, whereas approaches to amplify peripheral T cells and promote tumor recruitment have not been thoroughly explored. Using imaging mass cytometry in patients with colorectal cancer (CRC), we observed T helper 1 (T H 1)–like immune architectures in mismatch repair–deficient tumors associated with response to anti–programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) immunotherapy. By contrast, mismatch repair–proficient (pMMR) tumors showed regulatory T–dominant spatial interactions. Clonal analyses revealed that stem-like CD4 + T cells differentiated into T H 1-like cells after PD-1 blockade. In pMMR CRC mouse models, combined OX40 agonist and PD-1 blockade suppressed tumor progression by expanding Il7r + early effector CD4 + intermediates in tumor-draining lymph nodes, promoting migration and connection with T H 1-like cells. This was accompanied by interferon-γ–dependent induction of immunostimulatory monocyte-macrophages and CD8 + effector T cells. These findings suggest that leveraging peripheral CD4 + T cell amplification may improve immunotherapy responses.

items.title: Giant elastoresistance in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
items.abstract: Strongly correlated and topological phases in moiré materials are exquisitely sensitive to lattice geometry at both atomic and superlattice length scales. Twist angle, pressure, and strain directly modify the lattice and thus act as highly effective tuning parameters. Here, we examined electrical transport in twisted bilayer graphene subjected to continuous uniaxial strain. Near the magic angle (≈1.1°), devices exhibited a pronounced elastoresistance that depended on band filling and temperature, with a gauge factor more than two orders of magnitude larger than that of conventional metals. In selected doping regimes, the elastoresistance exhibited a Curie-Weiss–like temperature divergence. We discuss possible microscopic origins, including nematic fluctuations and enhanced electronic entropy from fluctuating isospin moments. Our work establishes uniaxial strain as a versatile probe of correlated physics in a moiré material.

items.title:
Atmospheric O
                    <sub>2</sub>
                    reveals a strengthening ocean carbon sink and a stagnant net land sink since 1990
items.abstract: The global ocean and land biosphere absorb roughly half of fossil fuel carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. The temporal evolution of these sinks remains difficult to quantify owing to data sparsity. Leveraging 30+ years of atmospheric oxygen (O 2 ) and CO 2 observations, we find that the ocean carbon sink increased by 0.63 ± 0.19 petagrams of carbon per year per decade (Pg C year −1 decade −1 ) (a mean of 2.8 ± 0.4 Pg C year −1 ), accounting for 35% of fossil emissions between 1990 and 2019. The net land sink shows no robust trend (with a mean of 1.0 ± 0.5 Pg C year −1 , accounting for 13% of fossil emissions), despite large decadal variability. These results challenge many process-based model simulations of the land and ocean sinks, questioning their ability to accurately predict future climate states.

items.title: Limited genomic predictability of complex trait evolution despite genotype-phenotype stability
items.abstract: Whether genomic data can be used to effectively predict adaptation in natural populations is unknown. Here, we tested the efficacy of genomic prediction of complex trait evolution by monitoring genome-wide allele frequencies and pigmentation variation in genetically diverse populations of Drosophila melanogaster during evolution in both field mesocosms and a controlled, lab-based setting. At two points during trait evolution, we produced a high-powered, well-resolved genotype-phenotype map that exhibited marked stability across independent populations. Although we were able to use this map to correctly infer the direction of pigmentation evolution in both the lab and field settings, the particular loci responding to selection were largely unpredictable based on the direction of trait evolution itself. Our results hold implications for the promise, and limitations, of genomic prediction.

items.title: A trapped catalytic product acts as molecular glue for innate immune signalosome assembly
items.abstract: Innate immune systems of living organisms are essential for host defense. Central to these systems is the Toll/interleukin-1 receptor (TIR) domain, an evolutionarily conserved module. From antiphage systems in prokaryotes to innate immune systems in plants, TIR domains have catalytic activity. However, TIR domains within animal innate immune receptors, such as Toll-like receptors (TLRs), have been considered as scaffolds for adaptor recruitment. We report that the TLR4 TIR domain possesses an allosterically activated nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) hydrolase (NADase) activity that operates in a single-turnover manner. Its product, adenosine diphosphate ribose, is not released but entrapped as a “molecular glue,” stabilizing a composite catalytic pocket with adaptor TIR domain–containing adaptor protein (TIRAP) to nucleate signalosome assembly. This “produce-and-trap” mechanism represents a signaling mode that integrates enzymatic activity with adaptor function to drive downstream signaling.

items.title: Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants
items.abstract: Humans and many other animals live in interconnected social communities that are essential for survival and well-being. In principle, communities can persist despite changes in constituent members. However, gradually accumulating changes to membership could push systems past critical thresholds into alternate states, restructuring patterns of connectivity. Such changes can further affect systemic resilience against disturbance. We investigated social network dynamics for 443 wild female Asian elephants over 12 years by tracking community membership and structure. Following accumulated demographic turnover, networks fractured into smaller and more isolated communities. Connections changed not only owing to loss of members but also modifications in relationships among remaining individuals. This provides empirical evidence of a persistent state change in the social network of a long-lived terrestrial mammal following gradually accumulating demographic turnover.

items.title: Direct monitoring of breaching in deltaic submarine landslides
items.abstract: Submarine landslides threaten seabed infrastructure and trigger the transport of globally important amounts of sediment, carbon, and pollutants to deep-sea environments. However, fully submarine landslides have never been directly monitored in nature. Past hypotheses for their failure mechanism and dynamics therefore remain unvalidated for natural settings, including that prolonged upslope-migrating failures (breaching) occur in sandy seafloor environments. In this work, we present direct underwater monitoring of fully submarine landslides at Homathko Delta in western Canada that retrogress slowly upslope, indicating breaching-type failure. Their prolonged rather than instantaneous nature has important implications for the stress that seabed structures must be designed to withstand. Prolonged landslides also initiate sustained sediment flows (turbidity currents) that efficiently transport sediment, carbon, and pollutants further offshore.

items.title: Poisoned hunting weapons, megafauna, and plant use at a 125,000-year-old Arabian paleolakeshore
items.abstract: After the African origin of Homo sapiens , multiple dispersals radiated into Asia, yet the Saharo-Arabian archaeological record remains sparse. In this study, we report on ‘Uruq Aljelibah, a Middle Paleolithic site dated to ~125,000 years ago (marine isotope stage 5e) and located on the shore of Mundafan paleolake, Saudi Arabia. Levallois assemblages, refits, and megafaunal associations indicate in situ tool production and carcass processing. Stone tool residues, use-wear, and biomarkers reveal animal and plant processing, including palms, tubers, trees, and shrubs. Several points exhibit impact damage and poison residues (from Acokanthera schimperi ), indicating use as hafted weapon tips within composite hunting systems. Megafaunal remains include hippopotamus, buffalo, gazelle, ostrich, and camel, illuminating hominin use of freshwater and grassland ecosystems.

items.title: Climate aridity amplifies global riverine nitrate beyond human inputs
items.abstract: Nitrate pollution is widely perceived as a signature of human inputs. Here we show, with machine-learning reconstructed global maps, that climate aridity is also a dominant driver, systematically elevating nitrate concentrations across land-use gradients and creating unexpected hotspots beyond major agricultural and urban centers. Across ~2.9 million river segments worldwide, nitrate concentrations exceed ecological and health thresholds across ~33 and 2% of global land area, affecting ~5.6 billion (73%) and 0.5 billion (6%) people, respectively. Ecological threshold exceedance occurs mostly in headwaters, and about half of the health threshold exceedance occurs in middle-income countries and sparsely populated landscapes. These findings cast nitrate pollution as an aridity-amplified risk, suggesting that aridification may increase nitrate exposure even without additional human inputs. They call for regulatory standards that reflect risks across broad concentration ranges.

items.title: The genetic landscape of canine tumors: Insights from the Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA)
items.abstract: The Canine Cancer Genome Atlas (CCGA, https://caninecancergenomeatlas.org/ ) is an open, accessible comparative oncology resource that harmonizes whole-exome data across 10 canine tumor histotypes. It aggregates 667 tumor-normal pairs with curated single-nucleotide variants, insertions and deletions, structural variants, and copy number aberrations. Cohort-depth stratification distinguished primary, exploratory, and descriptive analyses. Selection analyses identified 39 cancer drivers, including recurrent TP53 , PIK3CA , PTEN , SETD2 , MAP3K14 , and FAT4 alterations; copy number events included MYC amplifications and PTEN deletions. Direct comparison with matched human cancers revealed conserved and species-enriched oncogenic mechanisms, pathways, and therapeutic contexts. The CCGA standardizes alignment, variant calling, and annotation through consensus pipelines and provides downloadable data and interactive analyses. This reusable framework advances precision veterinary oncology and strengthens translational bridges to human cancer, supporting comparative and translational research.

items.title:
TMEM184 proteins are Ca
                    <sup>2+</sup>
                    uptake transporters in lysosomes
items.abstract: Lysosomal Ca 2+ release from acidic stores is critical for lysosomal function, yet the molecular identity of the Ca 2+ uptake conduit has remained elusive. We used a Ca 2+ -imaging–based genetic screen of the lysosomal membrane proteome to identify TMEM184 family proteins as lysosomal Ca 2+ transporters (LyCaTs) essential for Ca 2+ uptake and refilling. TMEM184 selectively transported Ca 2+ while excluding monovalent cations. Loss of TMEM184B/C depleted lysosomal Ca 2+ stores, diminished Ca 2+ release, and disrupted lysosomal exocytosis, biogenesis, and membrane repair, thus phenocopying the release channel transient receptor potential mucolipin 1 (TRPML1) deficiency. Moreover, a human TMEM184B mutation associated with a neurodevelopmental disorder compromised lysosomal Ca 2+ transport, and Tmem184b -deficient mice exhibited profound motor impairment. Thus, TMEM184 constitutes the long-sought Ca 2+ uptake and refilling mechanism that governs lysosomal signaling and homeostasis.

items.title: Geodetic observations in West Antarctica reveal geodynamically consistent 3D mantle viscosity
items.abstract: The rapid ice loss in West Antarctica since the 1990s has led to substantial ice surface lowering, regional bedrock uplift, and gravity reduction, as measured by geodetic observations. The bedrock (crustal) motions and gravity changes result from glacial isostatic adjustment (GIA), a process controlled by Earth’s viscoelastic properties and deglaciation history. In this study, we present GIA models with geodynamically consistent three-dimensional mantle viscoelastic structures and reconstructed ice history for Antarctica from 1900 to 2020, which explain both the observed Global Navigation Satellite System crustal motions and Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment gravity changes in West Antarctica. This study demonstrates that a mantle rheology including a weak asthenosphere and temperature-dependent viscosity is consistent with both mantle convection at million-year timescales and ongoing decadal GIA occurring in West Antarctica.

items.title: ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering drive extracellular vesicle budding from cilia
items.abstract: Cilia-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) mediate cell-cell communication and remove signaling molecules from cilia. The Hedgehog receptor Smoothened (SMO) is selected for packaging into ciliary EVs by ubiquitin chains, but how cargo selection is coupled to EV budding remains unknown. In this work, working in mouse kidney cells, we found that the ubiquitin reader endosomal sorting complex required for transport–0 (ESCRT-0) orchestrates both cargo selection and EV biogenesis. Unlike the conventional ESCRT pathway, SMO secretion did not require the ESCRT-III membrane scission machinery. Instead, ESCRT-0 condensed at the ciliary tip, where it clustered ubiquitinated SMO to drive EV biogenesis. Disrupting ESCRT-0 condensation blocked SMO secretion, and combining forced recruitment of ESCRT-0 with optogenetic clustering of SMO was sufficient to reconstitute EV budding. Thus, ESCRT-0 condensation and cargo clustering constitute a minimal module for ESCRT-III–independent reverse-topology budding.

items.title: EDITOR’S NOTE on the Research Article “Mucus enhances gut homeostasis and oral tolerance by delivering immunoregulatory signals”
Tracking danger on the peaks
items.abstract: The Earth is warming, but not all regions are warming equally. In high mountain areas, temperatures are generally increasing by 1.5 to 2 times the global average, sometimes with devastating consequences. A small or gradual change in the mountain cryosphere—perhaps progressive thawing of frozen ground or a flood from a small glacial lake—can suddenly turn into a cascade of catastrophes with enormous ramifications. Monitoring systems for the cryosphere in high mountain areas have traditionally been designed to look at individual components and changes. What are the temperature and depth of the permafrost, or how much area is covered by snow, and what is the related avalanche danger? Many of the monitoring and warning systems were designed for historical patterns of snowfall or rainfall, and a river gauge may no longer be adequate if there is greater flow in the rainy season, or increased sediment that could damage the gauge.

items.title: A cellular atlas of the preinvasive breast cancer microenvironment
items.abstract: Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is the most common preinvasive breast cancer, however our knowledge of the DCIS tumor microenvironment (TME) remains limited. We constructed a comprehensive atlas of the TME in estrogen-receptor positive DCIS using fresh samples collected from normal breast tissues, DCIS and invasive breast cancers. We analyzed 854,911 cells from 159 patients by single cell RNA sequencing and 39 samples by spatial transcriptomics, which identified 9 cell types and 60 cell states. Our data shows remodeling of fibroblasts, vascular and basal cells that encircle the DCIS regions and immunosuppressive ducts that support the growth of the preinvasive cancer cells. This study delineates early alterations in the DCIS TME, including many changes that persist during invasive progression.

items.title: The cryosphere beyond a planetary safe operating space
items.abstract: The cryosphere plays a vital role in regulating planetary dynamics and habitability, yet it remains unclear whether its essential functions remain within a safe operating space (SOS) amid Anthropocene change. Here, we propose a cryosphere SOS and systematically evaluate its contributions to Earth system resilience using the planetary boundaries framework. Multiple lines of evidence indicate an accelerating and partly irreversible loss of cryospheric integrity, driven by amplifying feedbacks. Key cryospheric control variables either have left or are committed to departing from Holocene-like conditions. We conclude that the cryosphere has breached its SOS and is on a trajectory that locks in long-term risks for human societies and ecosystems. Safeguarding planetary resilience therefore requires explicit consideration of cryosphere change and its interactions across the Earth system.

items.title: Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome outbreak linked to cruise ship travel in April–May 2026
items.abstract: In April 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. ANDV genome sequences were obtained for 10 of the 13 identified cases during a cross-country investigation established to share initial raw data for joint analysis with reciprocal quality control. The genomic data, symptom onsets, and plausible contact patterns strongly support a tightly linked outbreak cluster compatible with a single or very few zoonotic spillover events prior to embarkment followed by human-to-human transmission onboard. The outbreak represents the international displacement of a virus already known to be capable, under specific conditions, to transmit among humans, and does not suggest emergence of a unusual viral strain.

items.title: Long-term local circulation of an Andes virus lineage in northern Patagonia is linked to the M/V Hondius outbreak
items.abstract: In 2026, a hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV) occurred on a cruise ship. Analyses revealed an unexpected relationship to an outbreak in Argentina in 2018. Retrospective investigation clarified the 2018 outbreak could involve person-to-person transmission and a common ANDV lineage spanned HPS cases from 2018 to 2025 in a geographically defined area in northern Patagonia, without widespread community transmission of ANDV. Route reconstruction for the index cases in the cruise ship outbreak identified geographically plausible exposures to viruses of this lineage in Argentina, but their timing was inconsistent with the expected ANDV incubation period. The infection source for the cruise ship outbreak cannot be resolved with current information, highlighting the need to expand viral surveillance in the ANDV endemic region.

items.title: Early epidemiological and spatial assessment of the Bundibugyo virus outbreak 2026
items.abstract: A Bundibugyo virus outbreak was first reported on May 15th, 2026 in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, with multiple cases reported across health zones during the early phase of the outbreak and suggestions of circulation weeks prior to detection. We pair highly resolved case and testing records with human mobility data to investigate the early outbreak dynamics of Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD). We show that human movement was a principle driver of early spatial expansion between May 10th and June 1st when the number of health zones and health areas reporting positive cases increased by 12 and 49, respectively. The early doubling time was estimated at ~10 days. Our work shows the rapid spatial expansion and growth of BVD with implications for intervention strategies.

items.title: Melting and resistivity of iron at Earth core conditions using pulsed Joule heating
items.abstract: The melting temperature and electrical resistivity of iron at high pressure are essential for understanding Earth’s core. Here we use a new high-pressure method – microsecond pulsed Joule heating in diamond anvil cells – to identify melting and measure resistivity of solid and liquid iron. More than 300 reproducible melting measurements indicate a surprisingly shallow melting curve, reaching 6 K/GPa and 4160 ± 80 K at 200 GPa. Extrapolating in pressure and iron alloy composition, and combining with our 76 μ Ω cm measurement of liquid iron’s resistivity, we infer a relatively cold core-mantle boundary (3430 K) with a low adiabatic outer core heat flow (9.8 TW). This suggests thermal convection alone could have powered the geodynamo prior to inner core formation and that today’s lowermost mantle is fully solid.

items.title: Quantum gases below 10 picokelvin in space
items.abstract: Ultracold atom platforms enable low temperatures and long free evolution times, which are crucial for fundamental physics tests and atom interferometry. The lowest equivalent temperature reported in such a system is 38 pK with a free expansion time of 2 s, achieved in atom-chip-based magnetic traps in microgravity. Optical dipole trap (ODT) systems offer better optical access and the flexibility to condense both magnetic and non-magnetic atoms, but have not been used to prepare quantum degenerate gases under microgravity conditions. Here we report an ODT-based Bose-Einstein condensate created aboard the China Space Station, containing 2.0 × 10 4 atoms, reaching an equivalent temperature of 9.7 − 2.7 + 3.2 pK with a free expansion time of 7.0 s. This record-low temperature could stimulate a new generation of ODT-based experiments in quantum simulation and precision measurements in space.

items.title: Equivalence of pseudogap and pairing energy in a cuprate high-temperature superconductor
items.abstract: The pseudogap stands out in the phase diagram of the cuprate high-temperature superconductors because its origin and relationship to superconductivity remain elusive. The origin of the pseudogap has been debated, with competing hypotheses attributing it to preformed electron pairs or local order, such as charge density waves. We present unambiguous evidence supporting the pairing scenario, using local shot-noise spectroscopy measurements in Bi 2 Sr 2 CaCu 2 O 8+δ . Our data demonstrate that the pseudogap energy coincides with the onset of electron pairing and is spatially heterogeneous with values reaching up to 70 milli–electron volts. Our results exclude a pure local order origin of the pseudogap, link the pseudogap to Cooper pair formation, and suggest that the limiting factor for higher critical temperature in cuprates is phase coherence.

items.title: Discovering molecular modulators with nanoswitch screening
items.abstract: Molecules that modulate protein-protein interactions, including through ternary complex formation, have been established as key therapeutics. Yet they can be challenging to discover, as standard screening approaches often lack throughput or fail to directly assay multibody interactions. We addressed this by combining DNA nanoswitch–based selection of nucleotide-encoded libraries with next-generation sequencing to create FIND (Functional Interaction–based Nanoswitch Discovery), which enables ultrahigh-throughput discovery of compounds that induce or increase protein-protein interactions. We demonstrate FIND by discovering nanobodies that stabilize the interaction between angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and the receptor-binding domain of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 and by discovering agonists of peroxisome proliferator–activated receptor gamma from a DNA-barcoded small-molecule library. By enabling rapid discovery of molecular modulators, FIND could lead to new therapeutics across many conditions.

items.title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
items.abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

items.title: Quantum gas microscopy of three-flavor Hubbard systems
items.abstract: Hubbard systems are paradigmatic realizations of strongly correlated many-body systems. Introducing additional species breaks the SU(2) symmetry of the Hubbard model and leads to a wide variety of new exotic quantum phases. Here, we extended quantum gas microscopy to three-flavor Fermi lattice gases in the Hubbard regime. Relying on site- and flavor-resolved detection, we studied the phase diagram of the three-flavor Hubbard model and found signatures of flavor-selective localization and selective pairing at temperatures down to the tunneling energy scale. Our measurements were then compared with numerical linked-cluster expansion calculations. Further increase of phase space density may enable the observation of a distinct pair Mott phase at half filling and shows a path toward the study of color superfluidity and other aspects of quantum chromodynamics.

items.title: Tumor metastasis co-opts liver hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression
items.abstract: Cancer-associated hematopoietic abnormalities contribute to systemic immunosuppression. However, whether tumors can initiate localized extramedullary hematopoiesis to suppress antitumor immunity remains unclear. In this study, we identify a distinct form of hepatic hematopoiesis driven by liver metastasis–associated hematopoietic stem cells (LM-HSCs). Liver metastases establish ectopic periportal hematopoietic niches that recruit bone marrow HSCs through Kupffer cell–dependent C-C motif chemokine receptor 1 (CCR1) signaling. Although LM-HSCs retain self-renewal and multipotency, cAMP response element–binding protein (CREB) activation skews their differentiation toward the myeloid lineage, particularly annexin A1–positive (ANXA1 + ) immature neutrophils. These neutrophils produce glucocorticoids, which activate glucocorticoid receptor signaling in a paracrine manner and induce immune checkpoint receptor expression and functional anergy in CD8 + T and natural killer cells. Collectively, these findings suggest that liver metastases reprograms hepatic hematopoiesis to promote immunosuppression.

items.title: Glacial abrupt transitions in ocean circulation were much slower than ice-core records imply
items.abstract: Dansgaard-Oeschger (DO) events during the last ice age are thought to reflect rapid shifts in the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC). Greenland ice cores suggest warming transitions within only a few decades—or even just over 10 years. Using precisely dated speleothem oxygen-isotope records from the Asian monsoon region, we have shown that the same DO warmings unfolded over more than a century. Isotope modeling revealed that Greenland records primarily capture a rapid atmospheric reorganization triggered by the initial sea-ice retreat in the northeastern North Atlantic, whereas the parallel AMOC recovery and hemispheric thermal adjustment proceeded much more slowly. These findings reveal that natural AMOC transitions evolved more slowly than the rapid North Greenland oxygen-isotope shifts would imply, thereby refining our understanding of “abruptness” during DO events.

items.title: Targeting hormone conversion through dietary fiber improves polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome
items.abstract: Excessive androgens serve as a primary driver for many phenotypic features of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Although dietary fiber has been shown to alleviate PMOS, its effects on androgen concentrations and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In a clinical trial, we demonstrated that a dietary fiber combination consisting of inulin, resistant starch, and β-glucan reduces androgen concentrations in patients’ plasma. Mechanistically, dietary fiber increased the abundance of Bacteroides xylanisolven s, which converts androstenedione into a nonandrogenic secondary hormone metabolite we named coproandrosterone, which is further metabolized by gut microbiota into dihydro-coproandrosterone. This metabolic pathway was validated in a mouse model. These findings highlight the potential of dietary fiber to alleviate PMOS by modulating androgen homeostasis through gut microbiota, offering insights for prebiotic and probiotic therapies.

items.title: When fat adapts: From physiological remodeling to disease
items.abstract: Adipose tissue undergoes extensive remodeling to adapt to changing physiological demands. This plasticity encompasses changes in adipocyte metabolism and number, extracellular matrix organization, vascularization, immune composition, and innervation. When coordinated, these processes preserve energy buffering, thermogenesis, endocrine function, and local tissue support. Pathological adipose tissue remodeling drives obesity-related complications and contributes to many diseases involving organ-associated adipose depots throughout the body. In cancer, tumor-associated fat can develop a metabolic and fibroinflammatory niche that promotes tumor growth and invasion, and remodeling of other depots can directly disrupt neighboring tissues. Recent studies have identified mesenchymal, immune, vascular, and adipocyte states that govern adaptive or pathological outcomes. These findings broaden therapeutic goals beyond reducing fat mass toward restoring adipogenesis, substrate turnover, thermogenic capacity, and tissue-niche function.

items.title: Direct evidence for psychoactive cannabis use 2800 years ago
items.abstract: Cannabis is the world’s most-used illicit psychoactive plant, yet direct prehistoric evidence for its consumption is rare. In this study, we present the earliest direct evidence of cannabis use: offerings of plant parts and chemical compounds in ancient human hair recovered from a monumental tomb in Siberia. The findings suggest that the plant was used for its psychoactive qualities across Eurasia, where specific wild populations might have had naturally higher active compound levels. We show that the practice of cannabis consumption dates back at least 2800 years, anchoring debates around contemporary usage and informing discussions on cannabis in medicine, public health, law, and industry.

items.title: Seafloor geodesy delineates fast megathrust relocking after the giant 2011 Tohoku earthquake
items.abstract: How and when the subduction megathrust recovers its locking state after a great earthquake is important to understanding earthquake-cycle physics and future hazards. Here we report the delineation of the relocking process after the 2011 magnitude 9 Tohoku earthquake with 14 years of postseismic seafloor geodetic observations. These data, combined with onshore geodetic observations, analyses of repeating earthquakes, and numerical modeling, reveal how the recovery of locking is interrupted by afterslip on the megathrust and accompanied by stress relaxation in the viscoelastic upper mantle. The results indicate that the megathrust has already arrived at a locking state today similar to that before the earthquake despite the ongoing stress relaxation. The acquired knowledge aids understanding of megathrust earthquake cycles at other subduction zones.

items.title: Stacked porous NiTi structure with low cost and ultrahigh fatigue life for elastocaloric cooling
items.abstract: Elastocaloric cooling (eC) uses shape memory alloys (SMAs) as energy-efficient, eco-friendly refrigerants. However, cost-effectively fabricating SMAs into fatigue-resistant, heat transfer–enhanced structures remains a key obstacle to commercialization of the eC technology. We introduce a “stamping and stacking” (S-S) method for producing porous, fatigue-resistant SMA structures. Honeycomb-like chips are stamped from nitinol (NiTi) thin sheets and then stacked into a layered tubular structure to increase heat exchange surface and at the same time avoid buckling and splitting failures encountered in existing SMA structures. The stacked structure endures >10 8 compression cycles and can deliver high specific cooling power of 3850 watts per kilogram. Our S-S method reduces fabrication costs by one order of magnitude compared with existing approaches, enabling mass production of eC refrigerant structures for commercial deployment.

items.title: The first 1000 days: Modeling language learning from individual children’s everyday speech
items.abstract: Children learn to understand and speak from the speech around them, yet how that everyday input shapes learning remains unresolved. Large language models show that language is learnable from data, but their scale and training conditions differ sharply from a child’s natural experience. We trained cognitively feasible, child-specific models on longitudinal home recordings from eight children across their first 1000 days of life. Each model learned incrementally from a single child’s ordered speech input without prior linguistic knowledge, developing phoneme-like and word-form representations that tracked each child’s learning pace. Learning was dependent on dense daily sampling and replay of recent input, indicating that both experience- and memory-related processes are necessary. These findings show that everyday experience contains sufficient structure for language learning and establish child-specific modeling for testing developmental theories.

items.title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
items.abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

items.title: Denoising the US Census: Succinct block hierarchical regression
items.abstract: The 2020 United States Census adopted differential privacy to protect individual confidentiality, adding calibrated noise to summary demographic measurements that are then reconciled into population tables. We developed BlueDown, a postprocessing algorithm that combines techniques from linear regression and constrained optimization while exploiting measurement structure for efficiency. On 2020 Census data, BlueDown reduced the error of groupings by race at the county level by 21 to 36% and of all county-level groupings by 9 to 58%; at the tract level, it reduced error of groupings by housing type by 38 to 61%. These gains came at no cost to confidentiality or computational efficiency and would improve the validity of research relying on this definitive dataset and analyses used to guide the distribution of more than $1.5 trillion in annual federal spending.

items.title: Expanding global access to GLP-1s: Challenges and opportunities
Obesity pharmacotherapies and cognition
items.abstract: Pharmacotherapies for obesity and type 2 diabetes are increasingly being evaluated for their effects on cognition and brain health. Evidence from preclinical models, observational cohorts, and clinical trials has intensified interest, but findings remain mixed. A central challenge is to determine whether potential cognitive effects arise from direct actions on neural circuits, indirect consequences of improved cardiometabolic health, or both. This Review examines the evidence across cardiometabolic disease, aging, and Alzheimer’s disease, focusing on glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)–based therapies and combination approaches that engage glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide, glucagon, and amylin pathways. We assess how receptor pharmacology, brain exposure, metabolic context, and disease stage shape cognitive outcomes and discuss how mechanistic clarity could guide therapies aimed at preserving or improving cognition.

items.title: Can artificial intelligence align with Indigenous science?
items.abstract: As the use of generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) increases, alarms are being raised about how the technology could replace human contribution, override human supervision, ignore ethical and technical guardrails, and cause increasingly irreparable harm to the environment. This creates potentially destructive outcomes for life on Earth. From a traditional Indigenous science perspective, such possibilities in themselves would be enough to immediately stop presently configured AI releases. In a Lakota context, science must ensure as little harm as possible is done to life. Therefore, AI as presently configured simply would not qualify to advance further from an ethical and scientific standpoint. Indigenous science asks something fundamentally different than what AI presently seeks to, or can, answer. But that does not mean that future forms of AI can never align with Indigenous science.

items.title: Pervasive patterns in bird songs resemble those in human speech and song and are independent of vocal learning
items.abstract: Bird songs are often described as analogs to human speech and songs, but expansive comparisons are necessary to determine analogy and mechanistic substrates. By analyzing global corpora consisting of 367 bird species (>74,500 vocal elements from ~5900 songs) within two clades of vocal learners (oscines and hummingbirds) and related nonlearners (suboscines and nightjars) and 52 human languages (>15,000 elements in >800 speech or song phrases), we revealed common patterns in bird songs that resemble prevalent patterns in human speech and song with variation in resemblance to speech or song. Vocal learning did not systematically affect acoustic patterning or similarity to human vocalizations. These data underscore the deep analogies between bird and human vocalizations and convergent motor mechanisms shaping communication.

items.title: Chiral altermagnon in MnTe
items.abstract: Altermagnetism has been recognized as a magnetic phase that bridges the properties of ferro- and antiferromagnetism. The momentum-dependent spin splitting observed in these materials reflects their distinctive symmetry characteristics, which also establish the conditions for chiral magnons to emerge. Here we provide direct experimental evidence for a chiral magnon in the altermagnetic candidate manganese telluride (MnTe) revealed by circular-dichroism resonant inelastic x-ray scattering. This mode, which we term chiral altermagnon, exhibits a distinct momentum dependence of its spin polarization consistent with the altermagnetic g -wave symmetry of MnTe. Our polarization-resolved data corroborate the existence of a discrete class of magnetic excitations, demonstrating how altermagnetic order shapes spin dynamics and paving the way for advances in spintronic and quantum technologies.

items.title: Rapid longitudinal flights cause time shifts and Sun compass error
items.abstract: Many animals use the Sun compass to guide their movement, sometimes over thousands of kilometers. Consistent use of the Sun compass relies on the endogenous clock to track the Sun’s arc, yet animals traveling east-west experience time shifts, potentially causing mismatches between their internal clock and local time. Using GPS, we reveal that Manx shearwaters ( Puffinus puffinus ) experience such shifts during homing flights, generating predictable errors in Sun compass orientation. Use of the Sun compass persists even when shearwaters have access to compass-independent cues during coast following. Our findings provide a new avenue for chronobiology research in the wild, suggesting that rapid longitudinal movements may affect other processes governed by the endogenous clock and that conserved chronobiological mechanisms impose substantial constraints on navigation.

items.title: The global geography of threats to freshwater biodiversity
items.abstract: Human activities are eroding biodiversity, especially in freshwater systems. Despite major advances in quantifying species vulnerability and threats, we still lack a crucial understanding of where threats are affecting freshwater species globally. Here, we produced a species-centered spatial assessment of threats, mapping the impact of 45 threats across 21,490 freshwater species of amphibians, fish, mammals, odonates, and reptiles. We found that species in highly developed and water-managed regions are strongly affected by multiple overlapping threats. Although threats vary across taxa and regions, increasing threat probabilities elevate extinction risk and population declines, with freshwater species experiencing greater threat intensity and distinct spatial patterns than terrestrial species. Our findings establish a spatially explicit baseline for targeting the most urgently needed freshwater conservation and management interventions.

items.title: Intrinsic gestational timing governs human cerebellar development after preterm birth
items.abstract: Intrinsic programs shape brain maturation; however, which of these programs are perturbed by prematurity as well as the molecular pathways involved remain unknown. The human cerebellum serves as a paradigm of extrauterine development—its accelerated growth and circuit formation align with the third trimester, a period disrupted by preterm delivery. Using multimodal datasets encompassing in vivo neuroimaging and neurodevelopmental outcomes with postmortem spatial-transcriptomic and histopathological profiling, we show that prematurity diverts the cerebellar developmental trajectory. Cerebellar growth and functional outcomes scaled with gestational age, despite modifying perinatal exposures. Spatially resolved developmental programs underlying macroscopic trajectories were marked by incomplete granule cell maturation and impaired Purkinje cell structural refinement, which indicate lineage-specific developmental asynchrony. Thus, prematurity constitutes biologically displaced maturation, in which infants of equivalent postmenstrual age occupy divergent developmental states.

items.title:
Altermagnetism revealed by polarized neutrons in MnF
                    <sub>2</sub>
items.abstract: Altermagnets are compensated magnets with symmetry-enforced spin split bands. Direct spectroscopic evidence for their existence has been reported in several materials. For example, inelastic neutron scattering (INS) has recently been used to witness a splitting of magnon bands in MnTe that is compatible with altermagnetism. Here, we present polarized INS results on MnF 2 showing that it is altermagnetic. Our data reveal a splitting coming from the long-range dipolar coupling. Furthermore, using a domain-biased sample, the data reveal a nonzero chirality in the neutron scattering cross section that reverses the sign between the two magnon modes. It is this feature that clearly demonstrates altermagnetism in MnF 2 . This finding highlights the potential for polarized INS to characterize altermagnets through its sensitivity to fine structure in magnon spectra.

items.title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival
items.abstract: Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich’s ataxia. By activating E3 ligases that evolved to safeguard cellular integrity, SPD expands the use of compound-induced protein degradation to complex pathologies of high unmet need.

items.title: Spatial coordination in the codevelopment of the human urogenital system during organogenesis
items.abstract: The human urogenital system originates from a common embryonic domain, yet the mechanisms guiding its spatiotemporal coordination remain understudied. Here, we combined high-resolution spatial transcriptomics with single-cell multiomics to profile human embryos from Carnegie stages 15 to 23, capturing the codevelopmental dynamics of the urogenital system. We revealed mesonephros- and adrenal primordium–derived signals that promote gonadal specification and enable efficient in vitro generation of cells resembling early gonadal lineages. We also uncovered a possible mesonephric origin of gonadal supporting cells through rete testis or ovarii linking the mesonephros. Finally, we delineate three transcriptionally distinct steroidogenic lineages differing in cholesterol sourcing, cortisol synthesis, and sex hormone production that together orchestrate sex differentiation. These findings deepen our understanding of urogenital system assembly and guide the exploration of coordinated multiorgan development.

items.title: A commensally regulated immune rheostat fine-tunes skin barrier fitness
items.abstract: At the skin’s surface, the epidermis must balance stem cell renewal with barrier maintenance to withstand environmental stress and shield against pathogens. In this study, we identify a microbial-immune-epithelial feedback mechanism that integrates environmental information into stem cell regulation in mice. Specifically, we show that Langerhans cells (LCs), an intraepithelial macrophage population, orchestrate this circuit by producing prostaglandin E 2 , which restrains stem cell proliferation, promotes epidermal differentiation, and maintains barrier integrity during homeostasis. Upon pathway disruption, stem cells become overactivated, hindering terminal differentiation and weakening barrier function. Upstream, LC activity is tuned by the local microbial environment in a rheostat-like fashion, coupling commensal sensing to stem cell dynamics. Our findings provide a general framework for how barrier tissues achieve adaptive homeostasis amid continual external fluctuations.

items.title: Genomic erosion across avifauna in a biodiversity hotspot sounds a conservation alarm
items.abstract: Loss of biodiversity can have a hidden dimension—the cryptic erosion of genetic diversity even in the face of apparent species resilience. We quantified changes in genetic diversity by comparing historical and modern genomes of 62 songbird species from the Gaoligong Mountains, a biodiversity hotspot in southwestern China. We identified genomic loss averaging between 43 and 49%; and, unexpectedly, common species were disproportionately affected. We argue that this loss was driven primarily by habitat fragmentation (and mitigated by dispersal ability) and show that it exceeds prior estimates and conservation policy thresholds. Species identified as having lost diversity continue to be listed as “Least Concern” on the International Union for Conservation of Nature’s Red List of Threatened Species, exposing a blind spot in extinction risk monitoring. We call for genomic metrics to be rapidly integrated into global conservation frameworks.

items.title: Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting
items.abstract: Continental rifting reflects the balance between tectonic forces and lithospheric strength, yet the mechanisms of breakup remain debated. Rapid rifting of the Gulf of California oblique rift (GOCOR) ~6 million to 8 million years ago is a key example; it may have resulted from the lithosphere responding to external kinematics or acceleration of long-lived extension. The dynamics of either scenario remain incompletely understood. In this study, we highlight that the rapid rifting of the GOCOR coincides with the initiation of Western Pacific double subduction. Using three-dimensional geodynamic models, we show that such subduction reorganization can transmit extensional stresses of ~5 to 15 megapascals across the Pacific plate, loading the GOCOR and the southern San Andreas fault. Subduction reorganization may represent the missing driver for the initiation of rapid GOCOR rifting within a preconditioned lithosphere and may be an overlooked tectonic force behind other rifting events.

items.title: Whole-body single-cell atlas of an adult vertebrate, Danionella cerebrum
items.abstract: A complete cell type transcriptome atlas of a vertebrate could promote understanding of animal cell type composition, organization, and evolution. The miniaturized, transparent, and regenerative teleost Danionella cerebrum brings whole-vertebrate single-cell profiling experiments within reach. We performed region-stratified single-cell RNA sequencing across the adult Danionella body and mapped cell types and gene expression at single-cell resolution using spatial transcriptomics. We delineated spatially distinct neural cell types on the basis of their regional gene expression signatures. The body-wide atlas elucidated cell types harboring adult molecular positional memory, uncovered paedomorphic features, and revealed conserved body-region and appendage-specification programs in adult connective tissue. Comparative analyses revealed conserved neural cell types, and regeneration datasets uncovered expression dynamics during telencephalon regeneration. This whole-vertebrate transcriptome atlas yields a comprehensive resource for myriad questions in biology and neuroscience.

items.title: Papaver self-incompatibility is controlled by two multiallelic idiomorphs
items.abstract: Self-incompatibility (SI) prevents self-fertilization through highly polymorphic genetic recognition at the S locus with multiple alleles. In Papaver rhoeas , the S determinants were previously identified as PrpS and PrsS . However, we found that PrpS-PrsS was absent in many S haplotypes. In this work, we report the identification of an alternative pair of polymorphic S genes, S locus oligopeptide transporter ( SOPT ) and S locus glycine-rich protein ( SGRP ), segregating at the S locus when PrpS-PrsS is absent. SOPT and SGRP display hallmark S determinant features and confer SI when heterologously expressed in Arabidopsis thaliana . Therefore, instead of having allelomorphs with homologous variants, the Papaver SI system is determined by two multiallelic idiomorphs sharing no obvious common ancestry. This discovery of a dual-idiomorph system reveals a distinct genetic basis for polymorphism, with implications for the evolution of allorecognition mechanisms.

items.title: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes
items.abstract: MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning–assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth–based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium). Experiments and modeling suggest semiconducting behavior and diverse magnetic states across this family. Together, these results expand the MXene family and demonstrate a data-driven strategy for accelerating materials discovery through sustainable methods.

items.title: The delocalized nature of chemical bonding at a catalytic metal surface
items.abstract: Adsorbate bonding at metal surfaces requires hybridization of localized molecular orbitals with delocalized electronic bands of the metal; hence, the electronic wave function involved in bonding may extend far beyond the adsorption site. We revealed the consequence of this delocalization by determining the distance over which structural variations of the metal surface influence the molecule-metal bond strength. Velocity-resolved kinetics provided adsorption energies for three molecules bound at atomic steps of platinum (Pt), each exhibiting bond-strength changes of up to 0.2 electron volts as the step-step distance varied over 100 angstroms. We observed molecule-specific behavior reflecting the hybridization of molecule-specific orbitals with symmetry-selected orbital bands of the metal that respond differently to structural modifications of the solid. We discuss implications of these observations for adsorption on Pt nanoparticles.

When AI takes away the thrill of discovery
items.abstract: “Pure math is being devastated or revolutionized, depending on your point of view.” So said Cornell professor Steven Strogatz after the artificial intelligence (AI) company OpenAI announced in early September a potential solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems that represent the highest goals for mathematical proofs. OpenAI’s solution involved unleashing an army of AI agents at a cost of millions of dollars in computing power, and it also certainly drew on decades of human effort in mathematics before it. Then a few weeks later, OpenAI posted 722 manuscripts describing progress on 372 mathematical problem families, and Google DeepMind published (in Science ) solutions from their own AI math system. These events are potentially exciting for those who long to know the answers to these problems as soon as possible, but they have also sent the world of mathematics reeling, and pose an even bigger question for all fields: Can the satisfaction of understanding ever replace the thrill of discovery?
