Whether SLSWs are altered in Parkinson’s disease (PD), and whether such alterations contribute to psychiatric or cognitive complications, remains unknown. In a cohort of 84 nondemented patients with PD and 30 healthy older adults, we found that SLSWs occurred more frequently in patients with PD. Hallucinatory traits in patients with PD were associated with higher SLSW amplitude, especially over frontocentral regions. Moreover, more prominent SLSWs were associated with poorer cognitive functions. We conclude that, whereas slow waves during sleep have positive physiological functions, exacerbated diurnal SLSWs may reflect responses related to PD neuropathology, at the cost of hallucinations and reduced cognitive function.

items.title: Dual inhibition of TNF-α and IL-1β signaling through BIG2 ameliorates osteoarthritis in mouse and primate models
items.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA), a leading cause of disability, is characterized by chronic low-grade inflammation and metabolic dysregulation in chondrocytes. TNF-α and IL-1β are key inflammatory drivers in OA pathogenesis, but clinical trials targeting them individually have been unsuccessful, highlighting the potential need for dual-targeting strategies. By screening a US Food and Drug Administration–approved drug library, we identified dabigatran, a thrombin inhibitor, as a potent dual suppressor of TNF-α and IL-1β signaling that restored chondrocyte metabolism. In preclinical OA models, including both mice and cynomolgus macaques, dabigatran attenuated cartilage degeneration, alleviated pain, and improved joint function. To elucidate the molecular mechanisms, we performed biochemical copurification coupled with mass spectrometry, identifying brefeldin A–inhibited guanine nucleotide–exchange protein 2 (BIG2) as a previously unknown dabigatran-binding target. Mechanistically, dabigatran binds to BIG2, promoting BIG2-dependent TNFR1 release to dampen TNF-α signaling while enhancing BIG2-mediated IL-1R1 degradation through the autophagy-lysosome pathway to limit IL-1β effects. These findings establish BIG2-mediated receptor trafficking and membrane dynamics as a regulatory node that concurrently inhibits TNF-α and IL-1β signaling, suggesting this pathway as a potential therapeutic strategy for OA.

items.title: Albumin-bound paclitaxel–induced stromal reprogramming drives resistance to neoadjuvant chemotherapy in patients with pancreatic cancer
items.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is a highly lethal malignancy for which neoadjuvant chemotherapy with albumin-bound paclitaxel combined with gemcitabine (AG) is a standard first-line approach for borderline resectable and locally advanced disease. However, secondary resistance to this regimen is common, and its underlying mechanisms remain poorly defined. In this study, we investigated how neoadjuvant AG therapy shapes the tumor stroma in PDAC. Single-cell transcriptomics of patient tumors revealed that AG treatment induces a phenotypic switch of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) from myofibroblastic (myCAF) to inflammatory (iCAF) states and identified a previously unrecognized TMEM100 + CAF subset enriched in nonresponders. Mechanistic studies showed that albumin-bound paclitaxel activates IL-2–STAT5 signaling to drive TMEM100 expression and that TMEM100 + CAFs promote chemoresistance through paracrine secretion of amphiregulin (AREG) and activation of tumor EGFR signaling. Genetic ablation of TMEM100 + CAFs in mouse models reversed CAF switching and enhanced the antitumor efficacy of AG therapy. These findings map chemotherapy-induced CAF plasticity, reveal a TMEM100-AREG axis of resistance, and highlight TMEM100 + CAFs as a promising target to sensitize PDAC to neoadjuvant treatment.

items.title: Osimertinib, platinum, and etoposide for patients with metastatic EGFR / TP53 / RB1 -mutant lung cancers at risk for histological transformation
items.abstract: Although EGFR inhibitors are highly effective for treating EGFR- mutant lung adenocarcinomas ( EGFR + LUADs), resistance inevitably emerges, with histologic transformation to small cell lung cancer (SCLC) representing a particularly aggressive mechanism. Our prospective trial enrolled patients with EGFR + LUAD at high risk of transformation ( TP53 / RB1 -deficient) and treated them with first-line osimertinib combined with platinum and etoposide. Despite the addition of SCLC-directed chemotherapy, nearly half of patients (5 of 11) underwent SCLC transformation, with median progression-free survival of 11 months and overall survival of 33 months. Genomic and single-cell transcriptomic profiling of patient samples revealed clinical and subclinical plasticity associated with TP53 / RB1 comutations, including histological transformation to SCLC, as well as mesenchymal and squamous histologies. These changes in plasticity were linked to progressive disruption of the RB pathway, leading to altered chromatin accessibility and induction of neuronal differentiation and epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition transcriptional programs, further intensified by osimertinib treatment. These findings provide insights into the role of plasticity in mediating drug tolerance.

items.title: Erratum for the Research Article “Preclinical and clinical evaluation of systemic danegaptide for the treatment of nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy”
Distinct tau PET dynamics in early versus late age-of-onset Alzheimer’s disease
items.abstract: Early-onset Alzheimer’s disease (EOAD) and late-onset AD (LOAD) differ in clinical presentations and rates of progression. We aimed to compare baseline and longitudinal tau positron emission tomography (PET) burden measured with 18 F-flortaucipir and its relationship with clinical variables in amyloid PET–positive, cognitively impaired participants from the Longitudinal Early-Onset Alzheimer’s Disease Study (EOAD; n = 390) and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (LOAD; n = 211). Participants with EOAD showed higher baseline tau PET burden, broader neuroanatomical involvement, and stronger associations of tau PET with amyloid PET and global cognition. Higher baseline tau PET burden in EOAD was independently validated in participants with EOAD from ADNI. Longitudinally, tau PET increased more rapidly in EOAD than in LOAD, independent of amyloid PET and clinical stage. We conclude that earlier age of onset in AD is linked to a more aggressive tauopathy, which in turn is a primary driver of clinical decline.

items.title: TWEAK signaling drives the transition from psoriasis to atopic dermatitis–like inflammation in paradoxical eczema
items.abstract: Targeted biologics have transformed the treatment of inflammatory skin diseases such as plaque psoriasis. However, some patients with psoriasis paradoxically develop eczematous skin reactions after therapy targeting tumor necrosis factor (TNF), interleukin-17 (IL-17), or IL-23. Although paradoxical eczema (PE) resembles atopic dermatitis (AD) clinically and histologically, the molecular mechanisms that drive its development remain poorly understood. Here, we generated high-resolution cellular and spatial maps of human skin using single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, immunohistochemistry, and in vitro assays, profiling lesional biopsies from patients with PE ( n = 8 donors), alongside healthy control, psoriasis, and AD skin ( n = 4 donors per group). In PE, we identified distinct transcriptional changes characterized by myeloid and T cell expansion and an altered keratinocyte phenotype shaped by TNF-like weak inducer of apoptosis (TWEAK; encoded by TNFSF12 ) signaling through its receptor TNFRSF12A , confirmed at the protein level by immunohistochemistry. To define the underlying mechanism, we stimulated immortalized (N-TERT) and primary human keratinocytes and found that TWEAK acted together with IL-13 to drive a T helper 2– and type I interferon–polarized epithelial program that partially recapitulated the keratinocyte signature of PE lesions. We validated key target genes by quantitative polymerase chain reaction in primary keratinocytes. In THP-1 cells and primary human CD14 + monocytes, anti-TNF treatment induced TWEAK expression, suggesting a compensatory inflammatory circuit. Together, these findings identify the TWEAK–IL-13 axis as a key driver of PE and suggest how cytokine blockade may reshape cutaneous immune responses.

items.title: Extended in vivo activity of VRC01 HIV-1 prophylaxis entails initial protective efficacy and subsequent breakthrough infections
items.abstract: The two parallel antibody-mediated prevention (AMP) efficacy trials evaluated whether intravenous infusion of the anti-CD4 binding site broadly neutralizing antibody VRC01 prevents HIV-1 acquisition. Here, we analyzed HIV-1 acquisition in AMP through the week 104 final study visit. Against viruses considered highly sensitive to VRC01 [80% inhibitory concentration (IC 80 ) < 1 microgram/milliliter], VRC01 prophylaxis maintained cumulative prevention efficacy of 66.3% (95% confidence interval: 32.4, 83.2%), suggesting that the antibody successfully blocked or cleared these infections. In the post–week 80 period (after the final dose at week 72), HIV diagnosis and resistance to VRC01 were more frequent and greater in the VRC01 groups versus placebo. For instance, more HIV diagnoses with viruses considered moderately sensitive or resistant to VRC01 (IC 80 ≥ 5 microgram/milliliter) were made in the VRC01 groups compared with placebo groups (11 versus 1). Plausibly, as in vivo VRC01 concentration waned, suppressed viruses—often evolving greater resistance because of selective pressure—emerged as detectable infections. Our findings suggest that, whereas single antibodies can block sensitive strains, multiple antibodies are likely required to prevent both viral escape and breakthrough infections.

items.title: Longitudinal remodeling of the tumor-immune microenvironment during regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer
items.abstract: Previous studies combining the multikinase inhibitor regorafenib with a PD-1 inhibitor showed promising activity in gastric cancer. We conducted a phase 1b/2 trial (NCT05394740) of first-line regorafenib, nivolumab, and chemotherapy in 30 patients with mismatch repair–proficient gastric cancer and investigated its impact on the tumor microenvironment. The primary end point was met; 22 of 30 patients showed objective tumor response (73%; 80% confidence interval, 60.3 to 83.8). Single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing were performed on biopsy samples at baseline, during treatment, and at disease progression. The combination treatment increased tumor antigen–reactive CD8 + T cells and M1-like proinflammatory macrophages and decreased immunosuppressive and tumor-promoting populations, including activated CCR8 + regulatory T cells, LRRC15 + cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), RGS5 + pericytes, and APLN + tip cells. At progression, LRRC15 + CAFs and APLN + tip cells remained reduced, activated CCR8 + regulatory T cells reexpanded, and additional treatment-resistant subsets emerged, including APOC1 + lipid-associated macrophages. In murine models of acquired resistance, therapeutic targeting of these suppressive immune cell populations with antibodies against CCR8 or TREM2 in combination with PD-1 blockade restored antitumor immunity. These findings demonstrate dynamic remodeling of the tumor microenvironment and suggest potential therapeutic targets.

items.title: A synthetic heparin oligosaccharide decouples anticoagulation from heparin-induced thrombocytopenia risk
items.abstract: Low–molecular weight heparin (LMWH) remains clinically indispensable for the prevention and treatment of thrombosis in cardiovascular surgery, hemodialysis, and other critical care settings. However, LMWH is constrained by heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and supply chain vulnerabilities of animal-derived sources. This study used chemoenzymatic synthesis to engineer homogeneous dodecasaccharide 12G-2, decoupling anticoagulant efficacy from HIT risk via dual structural modulation. Substitution with 2- O -sulfated glucuronic acid conferred conformational rigidity, and engineered sulfation attenuated platelet factor 4 (PF4) binding, whereas the antithrombin-binding domain remained intact. 12G-2 exhibited nanomolar anti–Factor Xa (FXa) activity in vitro, enoxaparin-equivalent venous antithrombotic efficacy, and superior arterial antithrombotic activity in murine thrombosis models, and it showed diminished PF4 binding, attenuated pathological β sheet formation, and minimal recognition by HIT-related antibodies in vitro. Both in vitro and in a murine tail-bleeding model, 12G-2 demonstrated high protamine reversibility, exceeding standard LMWH enoxaparin neutralization efficiency. In washed human platelets, 12G-2–PF4 complexes with the HIT-mimicking antibody KKO failed to induce integrin αIIbβ3 activation or P-selectin release and elicited minimal platelet spreading comparable to resting controls. Safety assessments in mice showed no hepatotoxicity at tested doses and low immunogenicity in a murine PF4-heparin immunization model. In PF4-heparin antibody–positive mice, 12G-2 attenuated platelet activation while exerting stronger FXa inhibition than enoxaparin. These findings established 12G-2 as an alternative to LMWH.

items.title: Cancer-specific T cell receptor discovery using 150,000 clinical genomics samples
items.abstract: T cell receptors (TCRs) can enable detection and elimination of cancer cells via recognition of cancer-specific peptides presented on human leukocyte antigen (HLA). We speculated that shared cancer antigens could be recognized by recurrent (“public”) TCRs, which might be identifiable using statistical methods. Here, we identified public TCRs against therapeutically relevant targets via computational analysis of large-scale bulk RNA sequencing data obtained from routine clinical genomics testing. Using data from ∼150,000 patient tumor samples, we identified TCR chains that were associated with well-known cancer antigens, including human papillomavirus, mutated KRAS, and CT83. We devised methods for pairing enriched TCR-α and TCR-β chain sequences and validated 44 TCRs across nine peptide-HLA targets for antigen recognition, including potent cytotoxic TCRs. Our results suggest that public anticancer TCRs are common and may represent a new source for the development of cancer therapeutics.

items.title: Erratum for the Research Article “CRISPR-engineered human brown-like adipocytes prevent diet-induced obesity and ameliorate metabolic syndrome in mice”
B cell subsets are associated with durable responses in distinct cancer types after immune checkpoint inhibition
items.abstract: B cells are a critical arm of the adaptive immune system. However, the impact of B cells and antibody responses on overall cancer survival remains understudied. Here, we report results from a prospective randomized phase 2 trial of 106 patients treated with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and identify that B cell antibody responses are associated with exceptional complete responses to ICI in certain cancer types. To further dissect the impact of B cell subtypes, we generated a comprehensive single-cell RNA sequencing database of intratumoral B cells in 12 tumor types from 152 patients. We found a context-dependent role for B cells, in which they are beneficial in certain cancer types and potentially unfavorable in others, with germinal center and memory B cells enriched in favorable prognosis cohorts and immunoglobulin A–positive plasma cells enriched in unfavorable prognosis cohorts. Depletion of B cells using rituximab in patients before surgery affected intratumoral T cell frequency and diversity. Furthermore, we show that B cells improve long-term overall survival even when T cell infiltrates are already high, indicating that a coordinated dual-arm T cell and B cell adaptive immune response is key to long-term tumor control. Overall, these results demonstrate that B cells and antibody responses in the proper context play an important role in durable complete responses in multiple tumor types.

items.title: MIF-CD74 orchestrates synovial macrophage metabolic-inflammatory reprogramming by ENO2 interaction to drive osteoarthritis pathogenesis
items.abstract: Synovitis is a central driver of osteoarthritis (OA) progression, yet the cellular and molecular mechanisms sustaining inflammatory circuits in the synovium remain incompletely understood. Through integrative analysis of time-resolved single-cell RNA sequencing in murine synovium and spatial transcriptomics of human OA tissues, we identified a pathogenic CD74 + macrophage subset that expands in OA and localizes at the synovial-cartilage interface. This subset exhibits a proinflammatory, nonclassical polarization and displays a metabolic dependency on glycolysis. Multiomics and mechanistic studies revealed that CD74 interacts with the glycolytic enzyme enolase 2 (ENO2). This interaction orchestrates a feed-forward signaling axis wherein CD74/ENO2 facilitates the nuclear translocation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-α (HIF-1α)/β-catenin dimers, which coactivate glycolytic and inflammatory gene programs, thereby sustaining a metabolically driven inflammatory state. Genetic ablation of CD74 in myeloid cells or its pharmacological blockade mitigated synovitis and cartilage degradation in murine OA models. To translate this axis therapeutically, we developed synovium-targeted cationic lipid nanoparticles decorated with MIF-mimetic peptides (PcLNPs) for the delivery of CD74 siRNA. Intra-articular administration of PcLNPs efficiently targeted CD74 + macrophages, attenuated their inflammatory and glycolytic phenotypes, and ameliorated murine OA progression in vivo. Our findings establish the CD74/ENO2/HIF-1α/β-catenin axis as a critical integrator of metabolic reprogramming and inflammation in OA synovitis and present a potential targeted nanotherapeutic strategy for disease modification.

items.title: T cell–mediated depletion of intratumoral regulatory T cells using a CCR8xCD3 T cell–engaging bispecific antibody (TCB) promotes antitumor immunity in preclinical mouse models
items.abstract: T cell–engaging bispecific antibodies (TCBs) have seen notable successes in hematologic malignancies, and emerging data demonstrate their potential for the treatment of solid tumors. Most oncology applications of TCBs have focused on targeting tumor cells via tumor-specific antigens; however, TCBs have been underutilized for strategic depletion of immunosuppressive cells in the TME. Regulatory T cells (T reg cells) play a crucial role in suppressing antitumor immune responses, making them an attractive target for immune-based therapies. T reg cells express several surface markers that can serve as potential targets for antibody-mediated depletion, including C-C chemokine receptor type 8 (CCR8), which is highly enriched on tumor-infiltrating T reg cells. Monoclonal antibody (mAb)–mediated T reg cell depletion relies on natural killer (NK) cells, which can be scarce in some solid tumors, whereas TCBs can broadly engage the T cell compartment by overwriting antigen specificity and redirecting potent T cell cytotoxicity against target cells. Here, we have developed a CCR8xCD3 TCB and show that it effectively depletes CCR8-expressing T reg cells in a T cell–mediated manner. CCR8xCD3 TCB led to the selective depletion of intratumoral T reg cells from human solid tumor samples in vitro and mediated inhibition of tumor growth in multiple syngeneic tumor models with variable levels of T cell infiltration alone or in combination with anti–PD-L1. In cynomolgus monkeys, CCR8xCD3 TCB was well tolerated without evidence of acute phase inflammation or cytokine release syndrome and led to effective and durable depletion of the CCR8-expressing subset of T reg cells.

items.title: Brain-sensing synNotch–CAR T cells enable precise targeting and clearance of diffuse midline glioma in multiple preclinical models
items.abstract: Diffuse midline glioma (DMG) is a lethal pediatric brain tumor with limited therapeutic options and a poor prognosis. The success of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy requires both improving T cell tumor infiltration and persistence and reducing the risk of on-target/off-tumor toxicity. Here, we adapted and advanced a brain-restricted CAR T cell platform previously validated in glioblastoma to address the anatomical and biological challenges of DMG. We engineered a T cell circuit in which a brain-specific synthetic Notch (synNotch) receptor recognizing brevican (BCAN) induced CAR expression against EphA2 or IL-13Rα2 (“B-SYNC”), thereby restricting CAR expression to the central nervous system (CNS). In immunodeficient DMG models, a single infusion of intravenous (iv) or intracerebroventricular (icv) B-SYNC circuit T cells led to tumor infiltration, sustained persistence, antitumor activity, and extended survival. An alternative BCAN-primed CAR targeting B7-H3 or IL-13Rα2 (“B-SYNC–B/I”) similarly improved therapeutic efficacy when delivered intravenously. However, icv administration triggered fatal neurotoxicity because of low-level B7-H3 expression in nontumor CNS regions, indicating that rapid CNS exposure via icv delivery can amplify off-tumor toxicity. In contrast, in an immunocompetent syngeneic DMG model, both iv and icv delivery of a murinized BCAN-gated B7-H3 CAR (mB-SYNC–B7-H3) achieved durable tumor clearance and resistance to rechallenge without any detectable neurotoxicity. Mechanistically, synNotch-primed CAR T cells exhibited reduced exhaustion, enhanced activation, and enrichment of naïve and stem cell memory–like subsets. These findings demonstrate that brain-sensing synNotch CAR T circuits represent a generalizable and translatable strategy for targeting multiple CNS malignancies, including DMG.

items.title: Keratinocyte-derived CHI3L2 reprograms phospholipid metabolism to promote skin inflammation in psoriasis
items.abstract: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disorder characterized by hyperproliferative keratinocytes and a dysregulated cytokine milieu, perpetuating a self-reinforcing inflammatory cycle. Despite the key involvement of keratinocytes in this pathogenic loop, the molecular pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. Here, we identify chitinase-like protein CHI3L2 as a key mediator. Elevated CHI3L2 levels were detected in serum and lesional skin from patients with psoriasis, predominantly in keratinocytes, as also verified by single-cell RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomic analyses. In vitro stimulation of keratinocytes with M5 cytokine cocktail (IL-17A, IL-22, oncostatin M, IL-1α, and TNF-α) increased CHI3L2 expression, demonstrating that CHI3L2 is inducible under inflammatory conditions. Transgenic mice expressing human CHI3L2 exhibited aggravated psoriasis-like phenotypes in both imiquimod- and mannan-induced psoriasis models, characterized by epidermal hyperplasia and scaling. To dissect the role of CHI3L2, we used recombinant protein injection, parabiosis, and bone marrow transplantation, identifying keratinocytes as the primary source of pathogenic CHI3L2. This was further confirmed by keratinocyte-specific CHI3L2 knockin mice. CHI3L2 functions in the HaCaT cell line and primary keratinocytes were investigated by recombinant CHI3L2 administration or CHI3L2 knockout. CHI3L2 disrupted phospholipid homeostasis, leading to altered inflammatory responses, proliferation, and differentiation of keratinocytes. CHI3L2 activated secretory phospholipase A2, elevating lysophosphatidylcholine, thereby establishing an autocrine loop perpetuating keratinocyte inflammation and reshaping the immune microenvironment. Therapeutic neutralization of CHI3L2 with antibodies or intervention of phospholipid pathway ameliorated skin inflammation in mouse psoriasis models. Our findings reveal CHI3L2 as an important regulator of keratinocyte-driven lipid remodeling and inflammation in psoriasis, highlighting potential as a therapeutic target.

items.title: Acute kidney injury as a systemic disease
items.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) affects ∼20% of hospitalized patients and is traditionally viewed as a transient complication of acute illness. Evidence suggests that AKI can initiate long-term renal and cardiovascular disease, even when kidney function appears to recover. Survivors of AKI face increased risks of CKD, heart failure, myocardial infarction, and premature mortality, yet post-AKI care remains poorly defined. We synthesize emerging mechanistic and clinical evidence linking AKI to systemic cardiorenal disease and discuss how biomarkers, imaging, and clinical risk prediction may enable identification of high-risk patients and support translational strategies to prevent progression to chronic disease.

items.title: Dengue virus controlled human challenge reveals that preexisting immunity shapes viral replication and broadly protective responses
items.abstract: Dengue is the canonical viral disease for which immune history is a determinant of protective versus pathogenic responses and immunogenicity. Yet, because of limitations in animal models and clinical presentation after peak viremia, how preinfection and early immune responses affect dengue outcome is not confirmed. We conducted a phase 1 clinical trial with 45 healthy adults to test whether secondary infection challenge with a heterotypic, full-length, attenuated virus increases viremia and immunogenicity compared with primary and tertiary infection. Viremia was associated with more, but still mild, clinical signs and symptoms, and secondary infection resulted in greater viremia, neutralizing antibodies, and protective T cell responses. However, those whose baseline antibodies most efficiently increased dengue virus replication in an in vitro assay experienced delayed inflammatory and adaptive immune activation, the highest viremia, strong acute immune responses, and waning of potent CD8 + T cells and antibodies. In contrast, higher baseline antibodies against the nonstructural protein 1 of multiple serotypes predicted early interferon and balanced immune activation, viremia control, and development of enduring, potent B and T cells, revealing how vaccines can induce broad, long-lasting protection. Last, individuals with potent and neutralizing antibodies and IFN-γ + T cells at baseline experienced minimal viral replication. Together, these findings demonstrate that controlled human challenge with dengue virus can delineate coordinated versus dysregulated acute immune responses and their effects on immunogenicity, informing therapeutic and vaccine strategies for dengue and other viral diseases.

items.title: The kinase inhibitor dabrafenib halts progression of cerebral cavernous malformations in a BRAF-independent manner
items.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) constitute the second most common type of intracranial vascular malformations. Cavernomas arise because of somatic or autosomal dominant inherited loss-of-function mutations in CCM genes, forming fragile mulberry-like malformed blood vessel structures that are prone to leak and break. Treatment is limited to surgical removal of solitary cavernomas, and because patients often present with multiple lesions, pharmacological alternatives to surgery are needed. We performed a high-throughput screen of 5200 bioactive molecules in programmed cell death 10 (PDCD10 or CCM3)–deficient mouse endothelial cells, coupled to automated image analysis. This screen identified dabrafenib, a clinically approved BRAF inhibitor, as a compound that restored cell-cell junctions and vascular barrier properties of CCM3-deficient endothelial cells. The potential translatability of dabrafenib was tested in acute and chronic CCM mouse models, where it reduced cerebral lesion burden and suppressed lesion permeability. Dabrafenib also rescued abnormal structural defects present in the developing retina vasculature in an acute CCM mouse model. Mechanistically, dabrafenib targeted extracellular regulated kinase (ERK)5–Krüppel-like factor (KLF)2/4 signaling and suppressed F-actin stress fiber formation in human brain endothelial cells, two potentially independent and central molecular processes involved in CCM pathology. Silencing BRAF did not prevent dabrafenib-induced KLF2/4 inhibition or restoration of cell-cell junctions, suggesting that its dual therapeutic outcome is independent of BRAF pathway inhibition. In conclusion, dabrafenib is a low–molecular weight compound that inhibits cavernoma pathogenesis, suggesting that CCMs could be treated with dabrafenib to block cavernoma growth and vascular leakage.

items.title: Single-nucleotide polymorphism–directed design of allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides for spinocerebellar ataxia type 3
items.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), also called Machado-Joseph disease, the most common form of autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia, is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in ATXN3 . The mutant protein is prone to aggregation and exerts toxic gain-of-function effects, whereas the wild-type protein has important neuroprotective roles as a deubiquitinase. Current treatment strategies for SCA3 lack specificity for the mutant allele. Identifying genetic variants such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in linkage with the pathogenic CAG expansion offers a promising avenue to develop allele-specific therapeutic interventions, like antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). To address this, we conducted allele-specific, targeted, multiplexed nanopore sequencing on 79 patients with SCA3 from Germany, UK, and Portugal. We identified almost 200 polymorphisms and grouped them into three haplotype blocks on the basis of linkage disequilibrium. These SNPs were strongly associated with the CAG expansion. Genotypic modeling of our subcohorts indicated that targeting only two SNPs from different blocks could enable allele-specific treatment of the majority of European patients with SCA3. We evaluated 17 candidate ASOs targeting SNPs from different haplotype blocks. Seven of these ASOs caused allele-preferential reduction of more than 65%. A single ASO application in two SCA3 iPSC-derived cortical neurons (AX1, AX2) achieved up to 90% reduction of mutant ATXN3. Toxicity assessments together with RNA sequencing analyses in AX1 did not indicate evidence of toxicity or widespread transcriptional perturbations. These findings highlight that characterizing heterozygosity rates offers valuable opportunities for selective ASO therapies. Our proof-of-principle targeting with ASOs demonstrates the feasibility of haplotype-informed allele-specific silencing in ATXN3 .

items.title: A fluorescent choline kinase alpha inhibitor for intraoperative molecular imaging during resection of canine NSCLC tumors
items.abstract: Choline kinase α (ChoKα) is a biomarker of lung cancer, is overexpressed in 60% of human pulmonary malignancies, and is associated with an aggressive phenotype and poor clinical outcome. Patients with lung cancer who undergo surgery have a recurrence rate of 30 to 50%, indicating a potential need for better tumor detection modalities. A near-infrared fluorescent ChoKα-targeting imaging agent, JAS239 (λ ex , λ em : 745, 775 nanometers), was developed for intraoperative identification of tumors, their margins, and local metastases. In lung cancer cells, JAS239 inhibited phosphocholine production, reduced viability in a dose-dependent manner, and accumulated in the cytoplasm where ChoKα is active. JAS239 had favorable pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics for imaging metastatic lung lesions in mice. In situ and ex vivo fluorescence imaging of primary lung tumors in a canine clinical trial showed distinct tumor identification and margin delineation with a tumor-to-background ratio of 5.0 ± 0.6 and a contrast-to-variance ratio of 2.0 ± 0.2 at 0.5 milligram/kilogram. Fluorescence imaging identified a clinically significant event where an occult lesion was found after primary tumor resection. Fluorescence imaging also identified a close surgical margin, which prompted further investigation. Immunohistochemistry for ChoKα showed overexpression in canine lung tumors proportional to tumor fluorescence. Ex vivo human tumor painting demonstrated preferential JAS239 localization with a tumor-to-background ratio of 1.5 ± 0.1 and a contrast-to-variance ratio of 0.9 ± 0.1. These studies establish JAS239 as a safe and effective imaging agent for intraoperative lung tumor detection, warranting further evaluation for human patients with lung cancer.

items.title:
Targeting ZIP12-mediated Zn
                    <sup>2+</sup>
                    signaling as a treatment for pulmonary hypertension
items.abstract: ZIP12, a membrane-bound zinc importer, is up-regulated in the remodeled pulmonary arterioles of patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Genetic deletion of its encoding gene, Slc39a12 , ameliorates the disease in rodent models. Here, we show that ZIP12 overexpression in human pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) increased intracellular labile Zn 2+ and promoted proliferation. ZIP12 siRNA knockdown attenuated pulmonary hypertension in rodent models. We developed a humanized anti-ZIP12 monoclonal antibody, APL-9796, that normalized intracellular Zn 2+ concentration, suppressed proliferation in fibroblasts derived from patients with PAH and PDGF-stimulated PASMCs, and reduced PDGF-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in PASMCs and contractility in PASMCs and engineered pulmonary artery tissues. APL-9796 showed dose-dependent efficacy in humanized Slc39a12 rats, improving cardiopulmonary parameters after induction of pulmonary hypertension and was well tolerated in phase 1 clinical studies. Transcriptomic profiling revealed modulation of several molecular pathways, including those involving AMPK, PPAR, and PI3K-Akt. ZIP12-driven labile Zn 2+ signaling underpins the pathogenesis of PAH. Targeting ZIP12 with APL-9796 offers a promising therapeutic strategy.

items.title: Graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis shapes T cell biology and immune reconstitution after hematopoietic cell transplant
items.abstract: Successful hematopoietic cell transplant requires immunosuppression to prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), a lethal, T cell–mediated complication. The phase 3 BMT CTN 1703 trial demonstrated superior GVHD-free/relapse-free survival for posttransplant cyclophosphamide (PT-Cy)–based GVHD prophylaxis versus tacrolimus/methotrexate (Tac/MTX), but the T cell biology underpinning these outcomes remains unknown. To determine this, 324 patients were coenrolled onto BMT CTN 1801 to investigate the distinct T cell immune reconstitution pathways of these regimens, including extensive evaluation of T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire, via sequencing of 2359 longitudinal samples and 180,432,350 T cells. Multimodal T cell analysis revealed that PT-Cy was associated with pan–T cell deletion followed by delayed T cell expansion from a smaller founder population compared with Tac/MTX. This created a T cell diversity bottleneck, leading to reduced TCR repertoire diversity for 2 years posttransplant. Reduced TCR diversity, more common in patients receiving PT-Cy, was linked to protection against chronic GVHD when patients were analyzed without regard to study arm. Leveraging donor- and host-specific TCR clonal analysis, we determined that PT-Cy–mediated T cell depletion also depleted pathogen-specific TCRs, rendering PT-Cy patients more likely to lack detectable graft-derived pathogen-specific TCRs early after transplant, which was associated with an increased risk of severe infection. This study reveals how distinct immunosuppression strategies uniquely remodel T cell immunity and shape divergent transplant outcomes.

items.title: Cas9 nickase–mediated contraction of CAG/CTG repeats is associated with phenotypic improvements in a Huntington’s disease mouse model
items.abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington’s disease (HD) patient–derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient–derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non–cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.

items.title: A 5 + 1 polyene scaffold that selectively recognizes ergosterol’s conjugated diene uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity
items.abstract: Amphotericin B remains the gold-standard therapy for invasive fungal infections, but its clinical utility is limited by toxicity arising from poor selectivity for fungal ergosterol over mammalian cholesterol, a challenge that decades of medicinal chemistry have failed to fully overcome. Here, we report mandimycin M16, a polyene macrolide engineered from a unique 5 + 1 polyene scaffold that uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity. Mandimycin M16 exhibited potent, broad-spectrum activity against 11 tested World Health Organization (WHO) priority fungal pathogens. Unlike amphotericin B, which binds cholesterol, M16 exhibited no detectable cholesterol binding and showed no detectable hemolysis, cytotoxicity, or nephrotoxicity at concentrations up to 128 micrograms per milliliter in vitro and after up to seven daily intravenous doses in mice. Mechanistic studies revealed that mandimycin M16 exerted rapid fungicidal activity through selective recognition of the conjugated C5–C8 diene system present in ergosterol but absent in cholesterol, a mode of sterol discrimination fundamentally different from classical polyenes. In multiple disseminated murine infection models, M16 outperformed liposomal amphotericin B at equivalent doses, achieving up to 3.4 log reduction in fungal burden and 100% survival without detectable renal injury by biomarkers or histopathology. These findings establish that the 5 + 1 polyene architecture enables complete sterol selectivity and molecularly uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity, providing a next-generation antifungal candidate for the treatment of invasive fungal infections.

items.title: Erratum for the Research Article “Systematic analysis of cellular cross-talk reveals a role for SEMA6D-TREM2 regulating microglial function in Alzheimer’s disease”
Autane: An autonomous crane for sustained port operations
items.abstract: Fully automated cranes are revolutionizing modern port operations by addressing labor shortages, improving precision, and enhancing safety. Toward this goal, we present the Autane (autonomous crane) system specifically developed for rubber tire gantry (RTG) cranes handling standardized containers in port yards, enabling autonomous safety-critical container grabbing, transport, and placement with high accuracy, adaptability, and efficiency. Autane overcomes the challenges of safe motion of large-scale cranes with centimeter-level precision requirements, providing long-distance high-precision perception. It uses multisensor fusion, real-time obstacle detection, and simultaneous localization and mapping to perceive the environment, identify container features, and dynamically adjust trajectories. By tightly coupling perception, planning, control, and operation and maintenance, Autane achieves safe and precise alignment, seamless interaction with transport vehicles, and robust execution of long-distance handling tasks. Deployed in multiple ports, Autane shows full-day operation and has autonomously handled more than 2 million 20-foot equivalent units. This work highlights the potential of fully autonomous RTG cranes to enable sustained, resilient, and low-intervention port automation.

items.title: Heavy metal acrobatics: Learning dynamic control for skid-steer loaders
items.abstract: Automation of heavy machinery offers the opportunity to improve productivity in mechanized industries such as construction, mining, and material handling. Yet, automation of such machines is challenged by their complex dynamics, in part because of hydraulic actuation that involves fluids, flexible elements, and nonlinear delays. A concomitant challenge is the size and weight of these machines, which can make experiments on the physical systems exceedingly dangerous. Here, we show that reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation, followed by transfer of the learned policies from simulation to reality, can successfully automate acrobatic maneuvers that push a heavy construction machine to the limits of its actuation and have only previously been accomplished by a small number of elite human operators in official world-record performances. We trained policies that perform autonomous acrobatic maneuvers on a John Deere 332G, an operational 5-tonne skid-steer loader. The policies can autonomously swing the machine up onto two wheels and, while balancing on two wheels, drive over rough terrain, trace out specified trajectories, spin around, and swing the bucket back and forth before landing it safely back onto four wheels. This work demonstrates that RL and sim-to-real transfer enable dynamic autonomous control of heavy machinery, directly contributing to greater automation in heavy equipment sectors.

items.title: Through human eyes: How perception and interaction shape humanoid robot acceptance
items.abstract: Robot acceptance is shaped by dynamic, multimodal interactions that influence trust, comfort, and behavioral intentions.

items.title: Bioinspired soft enteroscopic robot for intestinal locomotion, steering, and intervention
items.abstract: Diagnosing and treating small intestinal disorders such as bleeding, inflammatory bowel disease, and tumors present challenges because of limited access to this anatomical compartment. We present BIOSENTER, a bioinspired soft enteroscopic robot for deep procedures in the small intestine that addresses locomotion, steering, and intervention constraints of existing soft robotic systems. BIOSENTER features a hollow cylinder architecture comprising a linearly deformable soft pneumatic actuator as the body, two radially expandable soft pneumatic actuators wrapped with kirigami sleeves as the head and tail, a central hollow channel for accessory endoscopic tools, and a control box for navigation. Inspired by snake locomotion, the robotic body incorporates a fiber-reinforced actuator with four embedded inflatable chambers, enabling steering and axial expansion. The dynamic kirigami sleeves generate an anchoring force of ∼1.5 newtons on intestinal mucosa while requiring substantially less radial expansion than the corresponding nonkirigami configuration. A reinforced central channel supports tool passage for diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. The control box enables locomotion and steering at autonomous speeds of ∼100 millimeters per minute in vitro and ∼43 millimeters per minute in tissue-covered tubing. BIOSENTER successfully navigated the collapsed, tortuous small intestine for 2 meters in 11 minutes, with gentle forward pushing forces of 2.2 to 6.4 newtons in pig studies. In vivo pig studies demonstrated technical feasibility of tissue biopsy, localized fluid delivery as a model for future drug administration, and real-time visualization of the deep intestine, without macroscopic overdistention or visible tissue damage under the tested conditions.

items.title: The Mars 2020 OnBoard Planner: Increasing autonomy mission productivity of the Perseverance rover
items.abstract: Operators of planetary rovers, under strict energy and thermal constraints, face substantial challenges in maintaining high levels of rover productivity because of conservative ground-based planning and long communication latencies. In October 2023, to overcome these limits and increase science return, the Mars 2020 mission deployed OnBoard Planner into Perseverance rover operations. OnBoard Planner uses artificial intelligence constraint–based search to dynamically construct and modify activity schedules on board, adapting to real-time changes in rover state and martian environmental conditions. By replacing conservative ground predictions with real-time resource tracking, the system dynamically adjusts heating durations, reclaims unused schedule margin, and inserts opportunistic activities when extra resources become available. Here, we report on OnBoard Planner’s performance on Mars across more than 2 years of surface operations. The results demonstrate that OnBoard Planner increased discretionary rover activity by 10.5% overall while also improving the thermal and temporal conditions for certain types of scientific observations. Furthermore, the system achieved these productivity gains without increasing ground operations timelines. These findings are part of why OnBoard Planner has successfully become a standard part of Mars 2020 operations and demonstrate how dynamic onboard autonomy can enable resource-efficient operations for complex robotic systems in deep-space environments.

items.title: Robot autonomous agency by any other name
items.abstract: The humorous new science fiction novel Valet: A Novel philosophizes about robots gaining free will, but in real life, they may already have it.

items.title: Hearing the shape of an arena with spectral swarm robotics
items.abstract: Swarm robotics relies on robots with minimal sensing and computation that achieve self-organization at the level of the collective to address a variety of tasks. Yet, swarm robotics still struggles with global tasks that require understanding the broader spatial context in which robots operate, such as identifying the shape of the arena in which they are embedded. Here, we introduce spectral swarm robotics, a framework in which robots recover global spectral descriptors of the swarm’s geometric structure through strictly local interactions. To do so, robots emulate diffusion to locally estimate Laplacian spectral invariants, quantities normally obtained only through centralized computation. These spectral values serve as compact descriptors of the environment. In the present proof of concept, robots estimated the second Laplacian eigenvalue, λ 2 , and used it to classify arenas from a predefined set of shapes with distinct spectral signatures. We show that estimating a single eigenvalue is sufficient for one-shot classification among selected confined environments with distinct spectral signatures. We uncovered a scaling law linking swarm size (a global parameter) and interaction radius (a local parameter) that ensures robust estimation. We validated the approach experimentally on two distinct hardware platforms, Kilobots and Pogobots, achieving reliable classification of arena shapes under realistic noise and sparse connectivity conditions. Last, we discuss how locally recovering Laplacian spectral invariants opens avenues for swarm robotics in settings where producing efficient collective behaviors strongly depends on the global structure of the swarm.

items.title: Structural bias enables reliable sim-to-real transfer in reinforcement learning for robot swarms
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning offers a powerful framework for automatically generating control policies for robot swarms, yet its application to physical multirobot systems has been limited by the simulation-to-reality gap. Despite substantial advances in multiagent reinforcement learning, systematic demonstrations of gradient-based sim-to-real transfer to physical robot swarms remain scarce. Most work remains confined to simulation, and the few real-robot demonstrations lack evaluation across multiple runs and tasks. We show that this barrier can be overcome by embedding structural constraints into policy learning. We introduce attention-based counterfactual policy gradients for behavior selection in robot swarms (SwarmACB), a multiagent actor-critic method in which robots arbitrate among predefined behavior modules—reactive sensorimotor routines such as phototaxis or aggregation—rather than learning low-level motor commands. This architectural choice reduces the variance of learned solutions, which we argue mitigates overfitting to simulation artifacts. Through systematic evaluation on five collective missions using 20 physical e-puck robots (250 real-robot runs), we demonstrate that SwarmACB transfers successfully from simulation to reality, substantially outperforming continuous-action baselines. By progressively constraining policy architecture, perception, and model capacity, we show that smaller, structured policies transfer more reliably than large, unconstrained ones. These findings challenge the assumption that scale is necessary for successful transfer, suggesting instead that principled structural design enables reinforcement learning to produce control software for robot swarms that is both learned automatically and directly deployable in the physical world.

items.title: Reducing energy and air consumption in scuba diving with underwater exoskeletons
items.abstract: Assisting underwater locomotion with exoskeletons could reduce energy and air consumption during scuba diving.

items.title:
Click-Functionalizable
Tetrathiafulvalene-Tetrathiolate
Diradicaloids as Modular NIR-II Fluorophores
items.abstract: Abstract Near-infrared (NIR) emissive fluorophores are appealing for biological imaging and sensing applications, particularly in the lower-energy NIR-II region (1000–1700 nm). Compared to light in the visible and NIR-I regions, NIR-II light undergoes less absorption and scattering by biological tissues, enabling deeper tissue penetration and higher imaging resolution. Tetrathiafulvalene-tetrathiolate (TTFtt)-bridged bimetallic diradicaloid complexes exhibit bright NIR-II emission with high photoluminescence quantum yields (PLQYs) relative to other NIR-II fluorophores. These complexes are also particularly modular, as the capping ligands on the metal centers can be substituted to impart desired properties. Here, azide-functionalized bis(imino)acenaphthene (BIAN) capping ligands are introduced to leverage and expand this modularity. BIAN-capped TTFtt complexes exhibit chemical and photophysical properties comparable to previously reported TTFtt complexes. BIAN backbones functionalized with an azide group further enable Huisgen cycloaddition “click” chemistry for the attachment of diverse functional moieties while preserving the intrinsic NIR-II photophysical properties of the TTFtt core. As one example, a sulfonate-clicked TTFtt complex (1-C3) displays enhanced solubility and increased photoluminescence (PL) intensity in aqueous solutions compared to other TTFtt complexes. Notably, 1-C3 also exhibits pH-dependent PL intensity, suggesting its potential utility as an NIR-II-emitting pH sensor. Furthermore, the enhanced water solubility of 1-C3 enabled us to obtain in vivo gastrointestinal imaging in murine models. Overall, these results demonstrate the dramatically expanded modularity of TTFtt complexes through the use of clickable-BIAN ligands.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Bandedge-State-Limited
Single-Photon Emission from
Volumetric Quantum Design of 2D Colloidal Quantum Wells
items.abstract: Abstract Present-day solution-processable single-photon sources are dominated by three-dimensionally confined colloidal quantum emitters, yet their particle-to-particle variation in single-exciton properties limits reproducibility and scalability. Here, to avoid such heterogeneity, we demonstrate reliable room-temperature single-photon emission from atomically flat two-dimensional (2D) colloidal quantum wells (CQWs) with inherently uniform one-dimensional quantum confinement, despite their long-standing limitations of efficient multiexciton emission and pronounced exciton-surface susceptibility. We resolve these challenges through volumetric quantum design (VQD) of CQWs, yielding a highly localized, single bandedge state. This design laterally confines the bandedge excitonic domain within the exciton coherent area and vertically decouples it from surface states via a thick, strain-relieved quantum-barrier shell that preserves strong confinement, overcoming the daunting thickness-confinement trade-off in 2D CQWs. Statistical single-particle spectroscopy reveals that VQD-CQWs deliver near-blinking-free (on-time: &gt;99.5%) and fluence-insensitive antibunching (g(2)(0): ∼0.041), protected by a bandedge-state-filling bottleneck, together with linear polarization of up to 73% under cavity-free conditions, originating from synergistic transition-dipole and electric-field anisotropies. These advances establish 2D CQWs as a viable, homogeneous and scalable platform for quantum technologies.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Buried
Interfacial Transport Governs Oxide-Protected
Electrocatalysis
items.abstract: Abstract Protective overlayers are widely used to stabilize metal catalysts under harsh electrochemical conditions. Unlike graphene coatings, oxide overlayers introduce a buried metal-oxide interface that fundamentally reshapes reaction pathways by separating proton delivery from product release. Although proton transport through oxides has been extensively investigated, the fate of reaction products at buried interfaces remains unresolved; for example, H2-molecule vs H-atom pathways remain under debate in oxide-protected hydrogen evolution. Here, we revisit this buried interface using a microelectrochemical cell with well-defined model structures. Systematic measurements across nine metal-oxide heterostructures, combined with density functional theory calculations, reveal that product transport is governed by two sequential kinetic barriers: hydrogen spillover across the metal-oxide junction and hydrogen permeation through the oxide lattice. These coupled barriers determine whether reaction products are released, accumulate at buried interfaces, or induce interfacial failure. This work not only identifies superior Pt-TiO2 and Pd-TiO2 but also clarifies which step is impeded in Au-TiO2, Pt-SiO2, Pt-HfO2, Pd-SiO2, Pd-HfO2, Au-SiO2, and Au-HfO2 heterostructures. Guided by these model studies, we implement a TiO2 protection strategy in a proton-exchange-membrane water electrolyzer with remarkable durability. These findings provide a framework for constructing a complete proton-to-product route for buried interfaces, potentially resolving long-standing ambiguities in oxide-protected electrocatalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Expanding Chemical Space Enables Data–Driven
Structure–Activity Relationships in Cage Catalysis
items.abstract: Abstract Data-driven approaches are increasingly popular in catalysis, supplementing and even replacing traditional strategies that relied on empirical optimization. However, their application in the field of bioinspired cage catalysis remains largely unexplored, primarily due to the limited chemical space of known catalytically active cages. As a result, mechanistic insights are often obtained using computationally intensive DFT calculations on a handful of structurally similar cages. As chemical systems grow in complexity, this approach becomes impractical. Herein, we report a framework that significantly expedites the exploration of a much wider structural landscape while offering computational insights. This is made possible by a novel in situ experimental procedure─which circumvents the traditional time-consuming process of prepare, isolate, characterize, and test─coupled with data-driven methods to identify molecular features that govern activity. Using this approach, we experimentally explore 30 unique PdnL2n cages (n = 2–4) that mediate a nitro-aldol reaction with activities spanning over 4 orders of magnitude. Using this data set, a random forest model trained on molecular descriptors was developed to predict ΔG‡ (MAE of 0.4 kcal mol–1 and R2 = 0.9). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analysis highlighted geometric preorganization and electrostatic interactions within the cage as key determinants of catalytic efficiency. Moreover, DFT calculations on a selection of cages further validated these insights, indicating that meaningful mechanistic understanding can be achieved at significantly reduced computational cost. We anticipate that this integrated, screening, data-driven, mechanistic strategy will provide a blueprint workflow for understanding metal–organic cage reactivity and encourage the generation of more comprehensive structural data sets, ultimately enabling the rational design of improved catalytic architectures.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Regulating Functionalized
MXene Crystal-Field Splitting
toward Efficient Bifunctional Oxygen Electrocatalysis of Lithium–Oxygen
Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract MXenes offer fast conductive frameworks with abundant intrinsic active metal sites, making them promising cathode catalysts for lithium–oxygen batteries for addressing sluggish oxygen kinetics and severe cathode passivation. However, the predictive electronic descriptors for rationally regulating these intrinsic active sites remain elusive. Here, we demonstrate the implementation of crystal-field splitting engineering at Ti sites of Ti3C2-MXene to achieve bifunctional oxygen electrocatalysis. Through coordinated anionic and cationic modifications, we regulate the local coordination environment of Ti atoms, weakening crystal-field splitting and promoting electron delocalization within Ti3C2-MXene frameworks. X-ray absorption spectra reveal systematic shifts of Ti K-edge and contraction of the pre-edge splitting, consistent with weakened and distorted Ti ligand fields. This electronic rearrangement promotes an asymmetric Li2O2 adsorption configuration, thereby lowering the energy barriers for both ORR and OER. Consequently, the functionalized Cu–Ti3C2Br2 delivers a high discharge specific capacity of 11,662 mAh g–1 and reduces the initial charge overpotential by 50% compared with Ti3C2OF. This study indicates crystal-field splitting as a key descriptor governing oxygen electrocatalytic behavior in lithium–oxygen batteries.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Disrupting Hidden Antiaromaticity in N -Hydroxyphthalimide Reveals a Design Principle for Highly Reactive N -Oxyl Hydrogen Atom Transfer Mediators
items.abstract: Abstract N-hydroxyphthalimide (NHPI) and its corresponding N-oxyl radical, phthalimide N-oxyl (PINO), have long been used as mediators for hydrogen atom transfer (HAT), particularly in radical-mediated C–H oxidations. Although numerous NHPI/PINO derivatives have been developed, the absence of an intuitive model connecting scaffold structure to intrinsic HAT reactivity has left catalyst development largely empirical. Herein, we show that insertion of a heteroatom between one carbonyl group of the NHPI/PINO framework and the fused aryl ring substantially accelerates HAT in electrochemically driven oxidations, with rate enhancements of up to 36-fold for benzylic alcohol substrates. This enhanced reactivity correlates with significantly larger computed O–H bond dissociation enthalpies relative to NHPI (ΔBDEO–H = 6.5–8.1 kcal/mol), which increase the thermodynamic driving force for HAT by the corresponding N-oxyl radicals. NICS, NBO, and DFT-based structural analyses support a model in which previously overlooked antiaromatic destabilization within the five-membered imide motif weakens the O–H bond of NHPI and is relieved upon formation of PINO. Among the heteroatom-containing analogues examined, sulfur-containing N-hydroxythiobenzouracil (NHTBU) provided a favorable balance of high HAT reactivity and catalyst persistence, enabling the electrochemical oxidation of numerous substrates under mild conditions with activity superior to NHPI.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Proton-Coupled Electrostatic
Regulation of Anion Electrosorption
in Electric Double Layers
items.abstract: Abstract Electric double layers underpin electrochemical energy storage and modulate interfacial reactivity through the organization of ions and solvent molecules. However, regulating anion accumulation at compact aqueous interfaces while limiting parasitic water reactions remains challenging. Here, anodic polarization reconstructs oxygen-deficient TiO2–x into a depth-graded architecture comprising a rutile interior, a disordered interlayer, and a thin crystalline anatase surface. This architecture establishes an internal electric field that promotes subsurface proton accumulation, creating a responsive charge distribution that regulates anion electrosorption and moderates lateral anion interactions. The thin crystalline surface complements this electrostatic regulation by extending the accessible anodic operating range, combining enhanced interfacial charge storage with high-voltage aqueous operation. Symmetric aqueous supercapacitors sustain cycling over 3.0 V in neutral Na2SO4 for 45,000 cycles and over 2.7 V in natural seawater. These findings identify subsurface ionic chemistry as a design variable for regulating anion electrosorption at aqueous oxide interfaces.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Hydration Shell Structure and Water-Mediated Binding of Closo -Dodecaborates Probed by Raman Hydration-Shell Spectroscopy
items.abstract: Abstract The binding of closo-dodecaborates, B12X122– (where X = H, Cl, Br, I), to solutes and interfaces has widely been attributed to a water-mediated (super)chaotropic effect. The role of water, however, has so far been inferred only indirectly from thermodynamic measurements. Herein, we employ Raman hydration-shell spectroscopy in the OH stretch region to investigate B12X122– in aqueous solution. Specifically, we elucidate (i) the water structure in the hydration shell, (ii) its temperature dependence, and (iii) the water release upon superchaotropic binding. The hydration-shell spectra reveal that all dodecaborates give rise to a sharp Raman band close to 3600 cm–1. This feature is strongly blue-shifted compared to bulk water and represents weakly H-bonded, “almost dangling” OH groups in the hydration shell. Heating is found to blue-shift the hydration water resonance less than the bulk water resonance. Hydration and bulk water resonances thus become more similar at high temperature. This trend reflects a progressively reduced difference in hydrogen-bonding energy upon heating between hydration and bulk water, and is opposite to that of hydrophobic hydration. Furthermore, hydration difference spectra in the presence of the nonionic polymer hydroxypropyl cellulose (HPC) reveal that weakly H-bonded hydration water is released from B12X122– upon superchaotropic binding, together with more strongly H-bonded hydration water from the hydration shells of both B12X122– and HPC. These findings identify weakly bound hydration water, its weak temperature dependence, and its spontaneous release upon binding as molecular hallmarks of the superchaotropic behavior of B12X122–.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Antiaromaticity for
Through-Space Molecular Thermoelectricity
items.abstract: Abstract Charge transport in molecular junctions has largely relied on aromatic frameworks, where intramolecular π-delocalization stabilizes the electronic structure but inherently limits intermolecular electronic coupling. Here we show that antiaromatic Ni(II) norcorrole assemblies outperform their aromatic counterparts in thermally driven charge transport. This superior performance arises from strong intermolecular coupling, facilitated by the externalized electronic stabilization of antiaromatic building blocks. Such strong intermolecular coupling enables unusually thick molecular stacks within molecular junctions and yields Seebeck coefficients of up to 600 μV K–1, far exceeding those of the aromatic analogue. Quantum transport calculations reveal that π–π stacking in the antiaromatic assemblies shifts the HOMO transmission resonance closer to the Fermi level while progressively narrowing it, accounting for the substantial enhancement of the Seebeck coefficient while maintaining efficient long-range charge transport with a low tunneling attenuation coefficient. These findings establish antiaromaticity as a design principle for thermoelectric energy conversion based on collective intermolecular coupling rather than isolated molecular orbitals.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Zeolite Crystallization
via Seed-Mediated Chemical
Vapor Deposition
items.abstract: Abstract The demand for zeolites with specific, tailored characteristics is expected to further accelerate. For decades, however, zeolites have been predominantly synthesized by hydrothermal methods, in which tightly coupled sol–gel processes, nucleation, and crystal growth constrain property control and complicate device-oriented fabrication. Here we report the direct synthesis of zeolites by chemical vapor deposition (CVD), in which vapor-delivered precursors crystallize on preexisting zeolite seeds. Mechanistic investigations reveal that zeolite growth under CVD follows a fundamentally distinct pathway, where vapor-phase hydrolysis–condensation reactions are spatially decoupled from interfacial crystallization. This decoupling enables the maintenance of a controlled and steady supersaturation, offering a facile strategy for fabricating zeolite films with low dielectric constants and robust mechanical properties. The unique mechanism and operation mode of CVD bring zeolite crystallization into a manufacturing-relevant vapor-phase regime that could be extended to other zeolite types and deployed in diverse applications.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Electronic Polarization
of Covalent Organic Framework
Membranes for Precise Antibiotic Purification
items.abstract: Abstract Precise molecular separation is essential for pharmaceutical production and purification, yet existing sieving systems struggle to distinguish structurally similar molecules due to their predominant reliance on size exclusion. Herein, we fabricate a covalent organic framework (COF) membrane featuring fluorine-induced polarized nanochannels for fast organic solvent nanofiltration. The incorporation of fluorine atoms redistributes electron density along the pore walls, creating a polarized electrostatic environment while lowering surface energy. This unique pore environment promotes the uptake and transport of polar solvents, while enhancing separation selectivity by retarding highly polar solutes through polarity-dependent solute-framework interactions. Furthermore, the low surface energy imparted by the robust C–F bonds also reduces irreversible foulant adhesion and facilitates permeance recovery after cleaning. The resultant COF membrane achieves a molecular weight cutoff down to 350 Da and stable operation for over 550 h. Notably, it differentiates structurally related fluoroquinolone antibiotics according to their molecular polarity and delivers a favorable separation factor of 8.9 for norfloxacin over its synthetic intermediate piperazine. This work demonstrates that engineering pore-wall polarity in COF membranes provides a viable route to chemically regulated molecular recognition beyond size-based separation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Thiol-ene Radical Polymerizations of Regio - and Stereo -Isomers of a CO2-Derived δ-Lactone Leading to High Molar Mass Polythioethers
items.abstract: Abstract Thiol-ene radical polymerization of CO2-derived lactones containing α,δ-dienes offers a route to sustainable polythioethers with up to 20 wt % CO2. The direct product from CO2/1,3-butadiene telomerization is 3-ethylidene-6-vinyltetrahydro-2H-pyran-2-one ((E)EVP) whose α-alkylidene group causes poor reaction kinetics and nonquantitative alkene conversion with dithiols affording low molar mass polythioethers. Here, we use 3,6-divinyltetrahydro-2H-pyran-2-one (DVP) which was synthesized from the base-catalyzed contrathermodynamic α,β- to β,γ-photodeconjugation of EVP, resulting in the transformation of the α-alkylidene to an α-vinyl functional group. This subtle regio-isomerization was found to result in a 17-fold and 8-fold increase in the rate of α- and δ-ene consumption, respectively, owing to the relative stability of the intermediate carbon-centered radicals. Leveraging these rapid kinetics, high molar mass polythioethers (34 kDa) could be prepared via thiol-ene step-growth polymerization of DVP with 2,2’-(ethylenedioxy)diethanethiol. These molar masses are 10-fold higher than the upper limits obtained with the EVP-derived counterpart, and the polythioethers display mechanical performance suitable as a pressure sensitive adhesive.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: A Mirror-Image L-RNA Aptamer Targeting Hypoxia-Inducible Factor-1α Promoter G-Quadruplex Potentiates Tumor Radiotherapy In Vivo
items.abstract: Abstract The hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) coordinates the response of tumors to low oxygen by stimulating genes involved in metabolism and angiogenesis. HIF pathway activation is highly associated with tumor progression and radiotherapy resistance. Ligands that target this pathway are potential agents for the treatment of solid tumor malignancies. We developed an L-RNA aptamer, L-Apt5–4, targeting the HIF-1α promoter DNA G-quadruplex (dG4) via mirror-image SELEX. This L-RNA aptamer adopts a stem-loop secondary structure, binds HIF-1α dG4 with high affinity and specificity, and enters the nucleus to effectively downregulate HIF-1α and its downstream targets in cancer cells. By suppressing HIF-1α, L-Apt5–4 not only inhibits tumor cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, but also acts as a potent radiosensitizer, synergizing with radiotherapy to enhance cancer cell death. The combination therapy significantly suppresses tumor growth and metastasis while exhibiting excellent biosafety in vivo. Thus, L-Apt5–4 represents a novel HIF-1α-targeted therapeutic and radiosensitizer for combined cancer treatment.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Detecting Catalytically
Competent Surface-Bound Hydrogen
on Electrocatalysts with Weak Acids
items.abstract: Abstract The characterization of catalytically competent molecular metal-hydride intermediates distinguishes mechanistic possibilities in reductive molecular electrocatalysis. While surface-bound hydrogen is invoked in several heterogeneous electrocatalytic schemes, the synthetic and spectroscopic tools to establish catalytic competence in molecular systems are not readily translated to surfaces. Molecular systems offer uniform and well-defined active sites; however, surface systems consist of multiple possible binding sites. Here, we discover that the judicious choice of the proton donor enables the independent generation and characterization of catalytically competent surface-bound hydrogen using hydrogen evolution as a model reaction. Using dimethyl sulfoxide, a solvent where Brønsted acid pKa values are well-characterized, and Ag electrocatalysts, compatible with surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (SEIRAS), we find that acids with pKa values higher than the protonated solvent generate spectroscopic signatures consistent with the reductive formation of long-lived and linearly bound hydrogen. Conversely, stronger acids that protonate the solvent do not give rise to detectable surface-bound hydrogen, and instead, yield electrokinetic data consistent with hydrogen evolution proceeding via rate-limiting formation of the same linearly bound surface hydrogen. By independently generating the Ag-bound hydrogen with a weak, general acid and subsequently introducing a stronger acid that protonates the solvent, we show that the accumulated surface-bound hydrogen is catalytically competent for hydrogen production via specific-acid-coupled electron transfer. Our work demonstrates that catalytically competent surface-bound hydrogen intermediates in heterogeneous electrocatalysis can be detected and characterized through the strategic choice of the proton donor.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Structural and Electronic
Properties of Lead Halide
Perovskite Thin-Film Surfaces
items.abstract: Abstract Polycrystalline perovskite thin films are consistently associated with high-performance optoelectronic devices. The main challenges currently under the spotlight lie with the stability and reliability of these devices, requiring a better understanding of thin-film surfaces and interfaces. However, their consistent investigation is often very challenging. Given the soft nature of these materials, there is a struggle to directly assign the origin of the electronic features and correlate them to the chemical nature of the surfaces. Here, by exploiting a multimodal approach, we measure for the first time, at submicrometer scales, the diffraction patterns of the thin-film grain surface, which provide the material fingerprint and experimental evidence that the surface of such soft semiconductors is not as disordered as often claimed. Then, building on such knowledge, we move to ultraviolet photoemission spectroscopy, which provides information about the electronic structure of the first few nanometers of the thin-film surface. Having identified the structural nature of the surface, we are eventually able to unambiguously assign the origin of the photoemission spectra for a wide range of metal halide perovskites. In particular, metallic lead is identified to be the origin of the often-reported midgap photoemissive states, thus far assigned to deep electronic states within the halide perovskite semiconductor band gap. The chemical composition of the metal halides, the photodegradation of the perovskites under visible light, the quality of the precursors, and the actual stoichiometry of the thin film heavily define the presence of such states and elucidate the origin of carrier loss, photodegradation, and sample reproducibility in metal halide perovskite optoelectronics.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Correlative Multidimensional
Tracking and Modeling
Reveals Mechanical Regulation of Nanoparticle Endocytosis
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding nanoparticle–membrane interactions during endocytosis is critical for advancing nanomedicine. However, a comprehensive understanding of its dynamic complexity remains elusive, largely due to limitations in often oversimplified theoretical models and experimental challenges in correlating nanoparticle conformations and protein assemblies. To bridge this persistent theoretical–experimental divide, we developed an integrated approach combining multidimensional single-particle tracking with theoretical modeling for understanding clathrin-mediated endocytosis of rod-shaped nanoparticle cargos in live cells. Real-time tracking reveals a characteristic seesaw-like rotational motion of nanocargos that is temporally correlated with clathrin and dynamin recruitment, enabling the endocytic process to be classified into six distinct stages. Theoretical modeling, informed by these experimental observations, identifies orientation-dependent energy preferences arising from the interplay between membrane-associated effects and clathrin lattice elasticity, yielding orientation trends consistent with experimental observations. By focusing on this core structural framework, our work establishes a quantitative foundation for understanding how geometric and mechanical interactions govern the nanoparticle internalization. This correlative experimental and theoretical work is exemplary of the renewed efforts to establish closer connections between experimental evidence and theoretical modeling with higher biological complexity.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Planar-Chiral Metal
Clusters Direct Polarization-Responsive
Supercrystals
items.abstract: Abstract Chiral metal clusters are promising atomically precise building blocks for hierarchical chiral materials, but their programmed assembly into structurally resolved supercrystals with traceable chirality transfer remains challenging. Here, we show that planar-chiral Cu5 clusters can serve as symmetry-defined modules for constructing polarization-responsive supercrystals. Through single-site capping control and symmetry-matched linker-directed coordination assembly, the Cu5 unit is organized into monomeric, dimeric, trimeric, and helical crystalline architectures, thereby enabling chirality to be traced from discrete clusters to higher-order supercrystalline structures. Single-crystal analyses reveal how the planar chirality of the cluster is encoded locally and propagated through distinct, orientationally ordered packing sequences. Quantitative Mueller matrix measurements show architecture-dependent circular and linear optical responses, including circular and linear retardance, which correlate with the crystallographic orientation and packing sequence of the Cu5 units, particularly Cu···Cu bonding. This work establishes planar-chiral metal clusters as versatile, stereochemically programmable synthons, providing a quantitative framework that links cluster-level chirality, arrangement orientation, and macroscopic polarization-dependent optical responses. The strategy offers a novel modular route to structurally defined chiral supercrystals, in which optical polarization responses can be traced to atomically resolved anisotropic sequences of chiral cluster assembly.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Regio- and Diastereoselective
Thiol-ene Click Reaction
and Application for the Synthesis of Semicrystalline Polythioethers
items.abstract: Abstract Thiol-ene click is a powerful reaction for its high efficiency, functional-group tolerance, and operational simplicity, yet regio- and stereocontrol in radical thiol addition to internal alkenes as well as its potential use in the stereoselective synthesis of semicrystalline polymers has received much less attention. Here, we report a substrate-enabled, perfectly (&gt;99%) regio- and diastereoselective thiol-ene click reaction of a bicyclic lactone alkene, BiL=, with diverse thiols and its application in thiol-ene photopolymerization to regio- and stereoregular polythioethers (PTEs) with excellent thermomechanical and barrier properties.
