Here, we incorporate halogen and hydrogen bond donors into an easy-to-prepare organic cage molecule and demonstrate that this can bind anions at either or both of a halogen-bonding pocket and hydrogen-bonding pockets depending on the nature of the anions and the solvent. The halogen-bonding pocket comprising six bromopyridinium donors is a potent host for iodide anions and can selectively bind this guest in water as strongly as biological iodide binders (Ka = 43,000 M–1 measured by 1H NMR spectroscopy) with the exclusion of other halide anions. In DMSO/water mixtures, the hydrogen-bonding pockets are able to recognize chloride anions, resulting in the formation of mixed anion iodide/chloride complexes with an iodide bound in the center of the cage and chlorides in the peripheral binding sites. This demonstrates the exquisite selectivity afforded by halogen-bonding systems and reveals a general route to a range of supramolecular anion hosts that bind multiple guests in different locations.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Anti -Dihydroxylation-Enabled Dual-Resolution Profiling and Imaging of Fatty Acid C═C Bond Isomers
items.abstract: Abstract Lipids are essential for membrane structure, signaling, and stress adaptation. Their diverse biological roles are largely dictated by the presence of C═C bonds in unsaturated fatty acids (FAs), which vary in both position and geometry. However, unambiguous characterization and in situ mapping of these two structural features have remained longstanding analytical challenges. Here, we present a stereochemistry-preserved chemical derivatization strategy coupled with trapped ion mobility spectrometry-tandem MS (TIMS-MS/MS), enabling complete resolution of both FA C═C bond position and geometry within a single workflow. This approach facilitates rapid and quantitative profiling of dynamic cis–trans isomerization in bacteria under diverse stress conditions and, notably, reveals a previously unrecognized dose-dependent antibiotic adaptation mechanism in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a multidrug-resistant pathogen. To translate this strategy to spatially resolved analyses, we developed an in situ derivatization workflow for mass spectrometry imaging, which uncovers the spatial heterogeneity of FA isomers in proximally cocultured, clinically relevant polymicrobial pathogens. These findings highlight colony-specific spatial dynamics of cis and trans lipid isomers and suggest lipid-mediated metabolic interactions between co-occurring microbial species. Together, this integrated platform enables both quantitative and spatial interrogation of lipid isomerization, providing new opportunities to systematically investigate its roles in microbial physiology, pathogenesis, and beyond.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Photomediated Chromium-Catalyzed
Regio-, Diastereo-,
and Enantioselective Deoxygenative Coupling of Activated Allylic and
Propargylic Alcohols with Aldehydes
items.abstract: Abstract Chromium-catalyzed asymmetric Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi (NHK) reaction is a powerful tool for constructing synthetically valuable enantioenriched homoallylic alcohols and allenols. However, catalytic asymmetric NHK-type coupling of allylic or propargylic C–O electrophiles remains largely underdeveloped. Herein, we report a photomediated chromium-catalyzed deoxygenative coupling of activated allylic and propargylic alcohols with aldehydes, enabling the synthesis of a variety of chiral homoallylic alcohols with wide structural diversity and allenols. The reactions were performed under mild conditions, and a wide range of synthetically useful functional groups was found to be well tolerated. Importantly, this method provides a straightforward way for the construction of homoallylic alcohols bearing a chiral quaternary carbon center with high ee and dr. Furthermore, stereodivergent access to all four homoallylic alcohol stereoisomers is realized through orthogonal combinations of Z/E-configured allylic alcohols and R/S-configured ligands. Combined experimental and computational mechanistic studies provided insight into the key catalytic intermediate and the origin of stereocontrol.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Magnetic Resonance
Silent Activatable Probe with Massive
Signal Amplification for Rapid Detection of Inflammation-Associated
Fibrogenesis
items.abstract: Abstract Biomarker-specific molecular imaging is vital in precision medicine. However, a fundamental challenge of most molecular imaging methods is the difficulty of distinguishing specific molecular signal from nonspecific signal arising from the distribution of the molecular probe. This is even more pronounced in metabolically active organs such as the kidney and liver where the probe may concentrate prior to elimination. As a result, almost all molecular imaging relies on delayed imaging to achieve specificity, but this constrains clinical throughput and impedes rapid assessment of the diseased organ. Here, we report a magnetic resonance (MR) probe, Fe(II)-IAFP2, which combines 3 drivers of relaxivity enhancement to decouple disease specificity from probe distribution. Fe(II)-IAFP2 is MR-silent in its Fe(II) state, producing negligible MR signal even at high concentrations. In inflammatory, fibrogenic microenvironments common to many diseases, rapid oxidation to Fe(III) activates MR enhancement, while reversible aldehyde-mediated binding to remodeled extracellular matrix further amplifies relaxivity and promotes retention at the site of tissue injury. This dual activation–retention mechanism enables robust signal generation within minutes of administration. In mouse models of renal and liver fibrogenesis, Fe(II)-IAFP2 generated disease-associated MR contrast within minutes after intravenous administration. Together, this work demonstrates an effective strategy for rapid, activity-based molecular MR imaging through the combination of pathological activation and complementary tissue retention.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Double-Tethered Metallacyclobutadiene
Catalyst for
Cyclic Polymer Synthesis
items.abstract: Abstract The synthesis, characterization, and catalytic polymerization results of an unprecedented double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complex (4) are discussed. Complex 4 is active for the polymerization of acetylenes. Complex 4 polymerizes tert-butylacetylene to form cyclic poly(tert-butylacetylene). Evidence for a cyclic polymer topology comes from size exclusion chromatography (SEC) and intrinsic viscosity (η) measurements. This unusual reactivity of complex 4 toward a tert-alkylacetylene is attributed to its fluxional behavior, which arises from the double tethering of an yne-ol proligand (2) that facilitates monomer access and catalytic turnover. The preliminary scope of this complex design is demonstrated through modification of the yne-ol proligand, which afforded two additional double-tethered metallacyclobutadiene complexes 10 and 11 that are also catalytically active for polymerization.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Visible-Light-Driven
Dearomatization via Electrocyclic
Ring Expansion for Solar Energy Storage
items.abstract: Abstract Molecular solar thermal (MOST) energy storage compounds capture solar photon energy in the strained chemical bonds of metastable photoisomers and release it on demand as heat, yet simultaneously achieving visible-light absorption and high energy storage density has remained a persistent challenge. Here we introduce 9-aryl acridine N-oxides as MOST compounds based on visible-light-driven dearomative ring expansion. Irradiation at 470 nm, near the solar irradiance maximum at 482 nm, quantitatively converts these compounds to metastable 1,2-oxazepines, which thermally revert to the parent N-oxides and discharge the stored energy. The system achieves energy storage densities of up to 0.54 MJ/kg, comparable to Dewar anthracenes, while absorbing substantially more red-shifted light and offering nearly 3 orders of magnitude longer storage lifetimes of up to 1.4 years in the solid state. The thermal half-lives of the 1,2-oxazepines are tunable through para-substitution on the aryl ring and solvation, enabling up to a 1,300-fold reduction in half-life. Crucially, the 9-aryl substituent biases the transient oxaziridine intermediate toward selective reversion to the N-oxide over competing decomposition pathways, overcoming the limitations of other acridine N-oxides reported to date. This work establishes light-induced ring expansion as an effective strategy for MOST and expands the scope of viable MOST compounds.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Conjugate Chiral Carbon
Dots for Scalable Asymmetric
Photocatalysis in Flow
items.abstract: Abstract Carbon dots (CDs) have emerged as scalable, metal-free photocatalysts, but their use as conjugate organo-photocatalysts for enantioselective chemistry remains unexplored. Here, we covalently anchor a chiral imidazolidinone organocatalyst to amorphous, citric acid-derived CDs, giving a colloidal conjugate that acts as both photosensitizer and enantiodetermining component. This chiral CD material promotes the asymmetric radical α-alkylation of aldehydes in up to 84% yield and 93% e.e. Its semihomogeneous nature enables catalyst recovery by precipitation and reuse over five cycles with only minor loss in yield and e.e. The well-dispersed conjugate is also compatible with continuous photoflow, where Bayesian optimization in only 10 experiments enabled a gram-scale reaction in 80% yield and 91% e.e. This work establishes chiral conjugate CDs as a practical, recoverable platform for sustainable asymmetric photocatalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Molybdoenzyme Mediates
Carbon–Sulfur Bond
Making and Breaking in Ergothioneine Biosynthesis
items.abstract: Abstract The molybdopterin-dependent ergothioneine synthase (MES) from Caldithrix abyssi is the first molybdoenzyme known to catalyze the formation of carbon–sulfur bonds. To complete its catalytic cycle, this bifunctional enzyme desulfurates l-cysteine at a pyridoxal 5′-phosphate binding site and transfers the harvested sulfur atom (S0) to the molybdenum center of a bis-molybdopterin guanine dinucleotide cofactor more than 50 Å away. Subsequently, the sulfurated Mo-center transfers the labile sulfur atom onto the imidazole ring of Nα-trimethyl histidine (TMH). Combining experimental observations from cryo-electron microscopy, X-ray crystallography, X-ray absorption spectroscopy, sequence-activity correlation, and substrate-specificity studies, we delineate the structural basis for long-distance sulfur transfer via a persulfide relay, the identity of the imidazole sulfurating species, and key sequence motifs that are indispensable for activity. Furthermore, the reversibility of MES-mediated sulfurization of TMH under physiological conditions suggests that ergothioneine may serve as a soluble reservoir of oxidizing equivalents, supporting anaerobic metabolism in deep-branching bacteria such as C. abyssi.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
All-Visible Wavelength-Gated
Multistate Photochromic
AIEgen: High-Efficiency Photocyclizations in a Single Luminogenic
System
items.abstract: Abstract Synthetic photochromic molecules that enable noninvasive orthogonal control using distinct wavelengths of light are still in their infancy, yet ensuring the independence of photoreaction pathways and multiple addressable states in a single luminogenic system remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report an aggregation-induced emission (AIE) luminogen capable of undergoing wavelength-selective photocyclizations under visible-light irradiation, exhibiting a photorearrangement at 410 nm purple light and an oxidative photocyclization at 465 nm blue light to yield two stable yet distinct photochromic states. Experimental and theoretical results provide insight into the wavelength-dependent reaction pathways, as well as the corresponding synergistic mechanism of aromaticity, steric strain, and inductive effect in its photocyclizations. Eventually, a model information encryption system was developed to showcase its practical potential for all-visible-light-controlled multistate operations. This work thus offers both a viable strategy and a versatile structural motif for developing visible-light-controlled multistate luminogens and advanced multifunctional systems.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Decyanation, Dioxygenation,
and Oxidative Ring Contraction
Catalyzed by the DUF4243 Oxidase OzmD Rely on Ferric Oxygen Activation
items.abstract: Abstract Domain of unknown function 4243 (DUF4243) family proteins are an emerging class of nonheme mononuclear iron enzymes characterized by a distinctive iron-binding motif comprised of four histidine (His) and one Nε-carboxylysine (Kcx) residue. Although predominantly found in fungi, OzmD is the only characterized bacterial member. OzmD catalyzes oxidative rearrangement of an aminopyridone ring into a 1,3-oxazine moiety with concomitant cyanide elimination in the final step of oxazinomycin biosynthesis. Herein, the X-ray crystal structure of OzmD is solved, demonstrating the presence of a conserved 4-His-1-Kcx iron-binding motif similar to other DUF4243 family proteins. Biochemical characterization using a substrate analog carrying a hydroxypyridone ring reveals that OzmD also exhibits intrinsic dioxygenase activity, catalyzing a transformation analogous to those of fungal DUF4243 dioxygenases. Electron paramagnetic resonance and Mössbauer spectroscopic characterization of MinCC, a functionally equivalent homologue of OzmD, reveals that the as-isolated protein predominantly contains ferric iron, which can be reduced to the ferrous state upon binding with either the native substrate or the hydroxy analog under anaerobic conditions. These findings support a unified mechanism in which catalysis begins with single-electron transfer from the substrate to ferric iron, enabling molecular oxygen activation and formation of an alkylperoxide intermediate. Overall reaction mechanisms for substrates bearing aminopyridone and hydroxypyridone rings are proposed based on chemical precedents and computational analyses. These findings reveal that OzmD employs a distinctive FeIII-dependent path for oxygen activation in contrast to the classical FeII-dependent route used by most oxygenases and establish a functional connection between bacterial and fungal DUF4243 enzymes.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
An Experimental MOF-Polymer
Latent Space for Composite
Design
items.abstract: Abstract Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) have tremendous promise for filtration, catalysis, and sequestration, but they are limited by the polymer matrices in which they must be embedded to form functional composites. Here, we find an experimental approach in which composite performance can be predicted using a single MOF particle. In particular, we attach single MOF particles to atomic force microscope (AFM) probes and find that the forces between the MOF-tipped probe and polymer films can be transformed into an instructive low-dimensional descriptor of MOF-polymer interactions. This two-dimensional latent space provides direct measures of chemical compatibility as well as the work of adhesion and can be used to understand interfacial phenomena in MOF-polymer composites. For example, polymer intercalation is observed via X-ray scattering for MOF-polymer combinations with high chemical-compatibility latent-space variables. Bulk composite performance can also be predicted using the latent space values for cases where the MOF is held constant. For example, a simple linear model was trained to predict CO2 absorption into composites of UiO-66-NH2 based solely on the latent space variables. In addition to providing a rapid way to screen polymer matrices to complement a MOF chosen for its bulk properties, these results suggest that composite performance may be a separable function of bulk properties and the interfacial latent space. In this way, this transfer-learning approach can vastly accelerate the design and understanding of functional composites.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Tailoring Three-Dimensional
Porphyrin Hosts to Control
Fullerene Recognition and Charge-Separation
items.abstract: Abstract Porphyrin–fullerene assemblies are widely regarded as model systems in artificial photosynthesis. However, attaining precise structural control over both fullerene binding and charge-separation behavior within a single, rigid three-dimensional porphyrin host continues to be a significant challenge in supramolecular design. Dihydroanthracene- and triptycene-functionalized tetraarylporphyrins are shown here to act as biconcave aromatic hosts for C60, forming 1:1 and 1:2 complexes with association constants up to 104 to 105 M–1, as evidenced by 1H NMR and fluorescence titrations, and electrospray ionization mass spectrometry. Key in the host design is the porphyrin β,β-substitution that generates a well-defined and encapsulating environment for C60. Triptycenoporphyrins exhibit more geometrically confined C60 binding than their dihydroanthracene analogues, highlighting the critical role of topological control in C60 recognition. Despite identical binding strengths in nonpolar toluene and polar benzonitrile, the corresponding C60@triptycenoporphyrins display pronounced solvent-dependent excited-state behavior. Charge-separated states are generated more rapidly in benzonitrile yet attain significantly longer lifetimes in toluene, as revealed by steady-state and time-resolved spectroscopic measurements. These results demonstrate that tailoring rigid three-dimensional porphyrin frameworks enables simultaneous enhancement of C60 binding and fine control over charge-separation and -recombination dynamics, establishing this scaffold as a versatile platform for artificial photosynthetic systems that require long-lived charge-separation.

items.title:
Optical Access to a
Molecular Nuclear-Spin Register
in Catalytically Relevant Palladium(I) Complexes
items.abstract: Abstract Paramagnetic metal complexes are powerful tools in chemical catalysis and, increasingly, quantum information science, positioning them as ideal tools for quantum sensing within reactions themselves. However, this application requires an interface between spins and light in chemically relevant platforms. Here, we demonstrate that circularly polarized light can generate electron spin coherence in low-symmetry, catalytically relevant Pd(I) complexes. By measuring ultrafast changes in optical polarization with time-resolved Faraday rotation, we optically detect coherent superhyperfine interaction between the Pd(I)-centered electron spin and adjacent 31P nuclei from the ligand at ambient temperature in solution. The electronic origins of this behavior are attributed to excited-state orbital angular momentum through combined spectroscopic and computational analysis, and the optically measured coherence is benchmarked against pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance. Spin polarization is coherently exchanged between the electron spin and initially incoherent nuclear spins, constituting a rare example of optical access to a nuclear spin register in an ambient-temperature, solution-phase molecular system. Both reactivity and quantum spin function are mediated by the bisphosphine ligand; taken together with in situ detection of coherent Pd(I) spin dynamics directly in reaction mixtures, this work moves molecular qubits toward quantum sensing in chemical reactions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Unifying Polar and
Hydrophobic Models of Ice Recognition
by Antifreeze Glycoproteins
items.abstract: Abstract Antifreeze glycoproteins (AFGPs) enable polar organisms to survive at subzero temperatures by inhibiting ice growth through selective association with specific crystallographic planes. However, the molecular basis of this interaction and its remarkable selectivity remain incompletely understood, and both polar and hydrophobic binding models have been proposed. Here, we combine the synthesis of AFGP variants with high-resolution NMR spectroscopy, antifreeze activity measurements, and molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the molecular determinants of ice recognition. Minimally perturbative chemical modifications, including site-specific deuteration and fluorination, were used to probe the contributions of nonpolar and polar interactions while preserving the characteristic AFGP conformation. The combined structure–activity relationships and computational analyses support an integrative binding model that provides a unified and parsimonious interpretation of the experimental observations. Within this framework, our experimental evidence is consistent with the view that dispersive interactions involving peptide and carbohydrate methyl groups favor productive association with the ice surface, whereas carbohydrate hydroxyl groups, together with sugar- and backbone-associated water molecules, contribute polar interactions that promote selective and persistent binding. This model reconciles key aspects of previously proposed polar and hydrophobic descriptions and provides a molecular rationale for the characteristic plane selectivity of AFGPs and the conservation of specific sequence motifs. More broadly, our results highlight minimally perturbative isotopic substitution and fluorinated molecular editing as useful chemical strategies for probing weak dispersive contributions to complex molecular recognition processes while preserving native molecular architecture.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Solvent Cage Suppresses
Dynamically Induced Entropic
Pathways to Provide High Selectivity in Intramolecular Fe-Oxo Radical
Rebound Reactions
items.abstract: Abstract For homogeneous transition metal reactions, it is generally assumed that when intermediates are formed, they are sufficiently long-lived for the surrounding solvent cage to fully equilibrate prior to product formation. However, some transition metal reactions generate a highly reactive and transient intermediate for which product selectivity is not governed by subsequent competing transition states but rather by dynamic effects during descent from the transition state that forms the intermediate. In such reactions, solvent reorganization may be slow relative to product formation, which could significantly impact reaction pathway selectivity. Here, we demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage and explicit solute–solvent interactions in determining pathway selectivity for the ultrafast-evolving radical pair intermediate generated during (PDP)Fe-oxo-catalyzed intramolecular sp3 C–H functionalization. Quasiclassical reactive trajectories showed that with only a continuum solvent model a mixture of oxygen rebound/hydroxylation, desaturation, and direct carboxylate rebound products are formed due to dynamically driven, entropically favored wandering, which is inconsistent with experiments. In contrast, trajectories in explicit solvent reproduced the experimental product selectivity and demonstrated that solvent controls the nonstatistical, motion-driven selectivity by acting as a nonequilibrated solvent cage that restricts access to entropically favorable wandering configurations. The solvent effectively guides the radical pair intermediate toward one dominant product pathway. These results demonstrate the important role of the solvent cage in reactions involving highly transient intermediates where dynamic effects control selectivity.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Synergistic Interactions
Enable Superior Oxygen Evolution
Reaction Activity in Compositionally Complex Nanocrystal–Nanosheet
Hybrids
items.abstract: Abstract Thiospinel nanoparticles are promising catalytic materials due to their compositional tunability, electronic conductivity, and structural stability. While significant gains in catalysis have been made through material engineering, one continuously developing route is through the use of support materials to enhance performance. Here, we report a simple, scalable, low-temperature method to coproduce colloidal multimetal nanocrystals (&lt;20 nm in diameter) and In2S3-based nanosheets (&lt;1 nm thick), forming compositionally complex hybrid nanocrystal–nanosheet heterostructures in situ. The in situ-formed heterostructures demonstrate enhanced catalytic activity in the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in alkaline conditions; peak performance was achieved in heterostructures formed between (Ni,Co,Fe)3S4 nanocrystals and (In,Fe,Mn)2S3 nanosheets with overpotentials as low as 283 mV at 10 mA/cm2. Heterostructures can also be produced ex situ by introducing nanosheets, postsynthetically, to the nanocrystals, reducing the overpotential of (Ni,Co,Fe)3S4 nanocrystals from 362 mV to 312 mV with only a 5 wt % addition. This improvement highlights synergistic interactions in the heterostructures. These results suggest that an optimum nanosheet loading that maximizes effective nanocrystal–nanosheet interfacial coupling while preserving access to the Ni/Co-rich catalytic domains is the relevant design parameter. Our findings provide a low-temperature, colloidal route for synthesizing compositionally complex and highly uniform (&lt;15% dispersity) sulfide nanocrystals, nanosheets, or heterostructures of the two with tunable structures and enhanced electrocatalytic performance. To our knowledge, this is the first report of a compositionally complex hybrid material that is able to enhance performance when formed both in situ or ex situ and the use of In2S3 as a scaffold for a support material for enhancing OER performance.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Magneto-Optical Studies
on the Orbital Angular Momenta
and Spin–Orbit Coupling in the Excited Triplet States of Octahedral
Mo6 Clusters: Magnetic Circular Dichroism and Magnetic
Circularly Polarized Luminescence
items.abstract: Abstract The magneto-optical properties─magnetic circular dichroism (MCD) and magnetic circularly polarized luminescence (MCPL)─of octahedral hexanuclear [Mo6I8Y6]2– clusters (1, 2, and 3, possessing OPOPh2, N3, and CF3COO as the terminal Y ligands, respectively) were studied. In their MCD spectra, negative Faraday A terms corresponding to the S0 → Sn transitions were observed at ∼400 nm, reflecting the orbital angular momentum (OAM) and high symmetry of the molecular orbitals (MOs). In their highly concentrated solutions, positive Faraday A terms corresponding to the spin-forbidden S0 → Tn transitions were observed at ∼600 nm due to large spin–orbit coupling (SOC). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first direct observation of the spin-forbidden S0 → Tn transition in metal clusters by MCD. In their MCPL spectra, negative, strong phosphorescent MCPL signals (g ≈ 1.0 × 10–2 at 1.6 T) were observed at ∼690 nm, indicating that these Mo clusters are promising candidates for novel CPL materials. Time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations performed for the model cluster [Mo6I8Cl6]2– could reproduce UV–vis absorption and MCD spectroscopic properties. Especially, the MCD signals were evaluated by analyzing the SOC and the Zeeman effects of the OAM and spin angular momentum in the excited triplet state. TD-DFT gradient calculations indicated the geometrical distortion and stabilization of the lowest excited triplet [Mo6I8Cl6]2– and the destabilization of its Franck–Condon ground state, which explain the large red shift of phosphorescence. These results open new possibilities for understanding and functionalizing metal clusters.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Enantioselective Three-Component
Reductive Coupling
of Aldehydes, Amines, and Alkynes via Ligand-Enabled Cobalt/Photoredox
Dual Catalysis for Modular Synthesis of Allylic Amines
items.abstract: Abstract Here, we disclose a catalytic strategy that merges visible-light photoredox with cobalt catalysis to realize a previously elusive three-component enantioselective reductive coupling of readily available aldehydes, amines, and alkynes. This transformation provides a direct, step-economical route to high-value chiral allylic amines with broad substrate scope and high chemo-, regio-, and enantioselectivity, while overcoming long-standing challenges, including parasitic single-electron over-reduction, competitive aldehyde–alkyne coupling, and the inherent regioselectivity issues of unsymmetrical internal alkynes, and circumventing the moisture sensitivity and limited scope of pre-isolated imines. Central to this breakthrough is the rational design of a chiral phosphoramidite ligand featuring a tricyclic tetrahydrobenzoquinoline core, which avoids coordination saturation at cobalt and establishes a unique electronic “push–pull” synergy with a coordinated iodide anion. Mechanistic studies support an anion-promoted, single-ligand catalytic model wherein a high-spin cobaltacyclopentene intermediate serves as the key stereocontrol element. The monodentate, π-accepting phosphoramidite functions as a flexible electronic buffer, mitigating Pauli repulsion and dramatically lowering the oxidative cyclization barrier. The synthetic utility is demonstrated by late-stage functionalization of complex bioactive molecules and a concise synthesis of the antiplatelet drug prasugrel.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Mechanism-Guided Development
of Thioacetylene Probes
for Chemoproteomic Profiling of Cellular Protein Thiyl Radicals
items.abstract: Abstract Protein thiyl radicals are transient reactive intermediates involved in oxidative stress and enzymatic catalysis. However, their proteome-wide, site-resolved profiling in living cells remains challenging due to the lack of suitable tools. Here, we report chemoproteomic probes enabling covalent capture and site-resolved identification of protein thiyl radicals in living cells. Designed to leverage sulfur-mediated stabilization of a vinyl radical intermediate, our thioacetylene-based probes selectively capture cysteine thiyl radicals while minimizing cross-reactivity with nucleophilic thiolates and nonradical amino acid residues. In vitro validation and live-cell chemoproteomic analysis established radical-dependent labeling and site-resolved detection of protein thiyl radicals. Notably, the probes enabled site-specific mapping of thiyl radical-associated cysteine residues in live E. coli, including Cys439 of ribonucleotide reductase A (NrdA), a canonical enzymatic thiyl radical site. Expanded residue profiling further confirmed cysteine-predominant labeling and detected probe modification at established and putative glycyl radical residues in PflB, NrdD, and YjjI, suggesting that the platform may extend beyond thiyl radicals to other protein-centered radicals. Application of the probe under oxidative and nitrosative stress revealed condition-dependent changes in cellular protein radical-associated labeling, including decreased labeling at established glycyl radical residues and bidirectional changes in cysteine radical-associated labeling. Together, these findings establish thioacetylene probes as a platform for site-resolved mapping and comparative monitoring of endogenous protein-centered radicals in living cells.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Evolution of Interfacial
States Induced by Hydronium–Water
Ordering on Au(111)
items.abstract: Abstract Structured interfacial water can substantially modify charge transfer at solid–liquid interfaces, yet direct spectroscopic evidence for how water ordering reshapes interfacial electronic states remains scarce. Herein, using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), we identify parabolic interfacial states (IFSs) arising with the ordered water structures on Au(111), in striking contrast to the insulating nature of disordered water multilayers. Light exposure induces partial dissociation of H2O, and the resulting hydrated protons combine with residual H2O molecules to form ordered Eigen/Zundel-type hexagonal hydronium-water monolayers on Au(111) at 120–140 K. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations based on Eigen/Zundel-type motifs reproduce the experimentally observed IFSs and indicate that the states derive from the renormalized Au(111) Shockley surface state with a reduced effective mass at the water/gold interface. Annealing-driven transition from the Eigen-type to Zundel-type monolayers is evidenced by the distinct changes in the dispersions of the IFSs. These results establish a band-structure perspective for ordered water/metal interfaces and show that hydrated-proton-introduced excess electrons, when confined at a two-dimensional interface, can reshape the interfacial electronic landscape and charge transport.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Effect of Water on
Elementary Reactions in Solid-Acid
Catalyzed Reactions: Thermodynamics of Acid–Base Interactions
in H-ZSM-5
items.abstract: Abstract The influence of water on acid–base interactions in zeolites was quantified by measuring the enthalpy of pyridine adsorption on H-ZSM-5 with three Si/Al ratios (11.5, 40, and 140) in water using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC). This calorimetric study reconciles the liquid- and gas-phase energetics of acid–base interactions in a solvated, pore-filled zeolite through a Born–Haber cycle analysis. In water, the apparent adsorption enthalpy is about 150 kJ/mol less exothermic than the gas-phase value and becomes more exothermic as the Si/Al ratio increases, whereas the gas-phase enthalpy is near −200 kJ/mol and independent of the Si/Al ratio. Since the intrinsic acid strength of the framework does not vary with Si/Al ratio, this increasing apparent adsorption energy trend with increasing Si/Al ratio reflects the influence of solvation rather than acidity. Water stabilizes both the acidic proton and the pyridinium ion, and a fraction of this stabilization is lost when adsorbed pyridine displaces water from the acid site. By combining ITC data with vapor-phase water adsorption isotherms and differential scanning calorimetry to construct a Born–Haber cycle for each zeolite, the aqueous-phase enthalpies are quantitatively reconciled with their gas-phase counterparts, and their dependence on Si/Al ratio is traced to the different extents to which the initial and final states are solvated.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Electronic
Dynamics in Long Linear and Cyclic Polyynes
items.abstract: Abstract Carbyne─the one-dimensional sp-hybridized allotrope of carbon─has long been predicted to exhibit unique properties, yet its synthesis remains elusive. To probe its behavior, finite sp-carbon chains such as cumulenes and polyynes have been studied. While much has been established about the ground-state properties of cumulenes and polyynes, our understanding of their photophysical dynamics, which gives critical insight into how electronic relaxation, structural reorganization, and spin formation evolve, has focused almost exclusively on short, linear systems, with little consideration of topology. Here, we investigate long 48-carbon linear and cyclic polyynes in the liquid phase using steady-state and ultrafast, temperature- and polarization-resolved optical and vibrational spectroscopy. We find highly delocalized ground states in both topologies, with softened Peierls distortion and reduced bond-length alternation relative to shorter chains. In contrast, the excited state singlet dipole depolarization mechanism and subsequent intersystem crossing are strongly dependent on chain length and topology. As in shorter polyynes, transient infrared spectroscopy shows that photoexcitation of long linear polyynes induces a cumulene-like excited-state geometry; however, this structural rearrangement is weaker and shorter-lived than in shorter analogues. Comparison with shorter-chain trends and theoretical predictions shows that the Huang–Rhys factor remains far below the ideal infinite-chain value at 48 carbons, suggesting that vibronic coupling grows more slowly at long chain length than expected from simple extrapolation. Our results reveal how topology influences the largely backbone-dominated electronic dynamics of long polyynes and refine our understanding of finite sp-carbon systems at longer chain lengths than previously accessible with such time-resolved methods.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Dynamic
Nonlinear Effects in the Asymmetric Kinetic
Resolution Polymerization of Racemic Diazoacetates to One-Handed Helical
Polycarbenes
items.abstract: Abstract The asymmetric kinetic resolution polymerization (AKRP) of racemic diazoacetates mediated by a [Rh(cod)Cl]2/chiral amine dual catalyst system exhibits dynamic nonlinear effects (DNLEs) in the relative rate constant (Krel). The overall Krel increases nonlinearly with the monomer conversion during polymer chain propagation and reaches a plateau at a medium conversion. These DNLEs originate from synergistic chirality amplification between the catalytic chain end and the evolving helical conformation of the growing polymer chain. Under optimized conditions, Krel increases from 15 at 3% monomer conversion to ∼ 138 at 33% conversion, and then reaches a plateau. The steric bulk of both the pendant groups of monomers and the chiral amine ligand critically regulates the magnitude and evolution of DNLEs, and reducing this bulk leads to a pronounced decrease in Krel. Chain extension experiments using the preformed helical macroinitiators exhibited a constant Krel, confirming that a well-formed helical conformation maintains stable enantioselectivity for AKRP. Computational studies further revealed that, during chain propagation, decameric species with well-developed helical conformations exhibit more pronounced energy differences between the R- and S-enantiomers than the corresponding initial monomer-inserted species. These results suggest that the one-handed helical conformation is associated with the enhanced enantiomer recognition at the catalytic center. This study reveals DNLEs in AKRP in which enantioselectivity evolves nonlinearly during polymer chain propagation, highlighting a dynamic chiral amplification mechanism that can surpass the intrinsic selectivity of a static catalyst through the cooperative action of chiral chain ends and helical conformation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Zeolite-Confined
Triatomic Cu Oxides at Silanol Nests
as Hydrogen Transport Channels for H2 Production from Methanol
Steam Reforming
items.abstract: Abstract Cu-based catalysts offer high methanol steam reforming (MSR) activity but are limited by unstable Cu+–Cu0 interconversions due to the redox and sintering labilities of Cu. Herein, we developed a universal amino-functionalized “gripper” strategy for firmly and precisely anchoring atomically dispersed metals (e.g., Cu, Co, Ni) within Beta-zeolite. Triatomic Cu oxide (Cu3Ox) sites lower the methanol dehydrogenation activation barrier, and the synergistic interplay with adjacent OH groups from silanol nests accelerates H2 evolution and the MSR reaction. Spatially decoupling Cu-mediated methanol activation from silanol-driven H2 evolution at silanol nests as proton transport channels within the confining zeolite framework also effectively protected Cu from sintering, achieving a high specific activity of 951 molH2·molCu–1·h–1 and over 600 h of stability under continuous regeneration. This work provides a universal strategy for synthesizing atomically dispersed metal catalysts and a new design principle for maintaining the Cu structure during MSR.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Design and Evolution
of an Orthogonal HaloTag for
Multiplexed Labeling in Cells
items.abstract: Abstract The self-labeling protein HaloTag is used to install a wide variety of functional small molecules in cells and living organisms with exquisite specificity with respect to cell type and subcellular localization. HaloTag is a core part of many biotechnology-based tools for sensing, tracking, and manipulating biological systems with a high degree of spatial and temporal control. Due to the limitations of fluorescent proteins and other self-labeling proteins, most of these tools have historically been restricted to a single channel. In this work, we used structure-guided rational design and directed evolution to produce an orthogonal HaloTag protein called OrthoTag which reacts selectively with a modified chloroalkane substrate. OrthoTag retains many of HaloTag’s superior properties, and reaction rate measurements with purified proteins show OrthoTag and its substrate have 109-fold mutual orthogonality to HaloTag with respect to substrate concentration. We demonstrate the application of OrthoTag for multiplexed labeling experiments in mammalian cells with minimal optimization. Going forward, OrthoTag should be straightforward to incorporate into HaloTag-based systems to allow simultaneous measurement or manipulation of two biological targets or processes. The availability of multiple high-performance self-labeling proteins will enable the continued development of new multiplexed biotechnology methods.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Efficient Long-Wavelength
Through-Space Charge-Transfer
Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence in Conformationally Adaptive
Emitters without Conformational Locking
items.abstract: Abstract Through-space charge-transfer thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TSCT-TADF) emitters often employ conformationally constrained donor–acceptor architectures to control through-space electronic coupling, particularly for long-wavelength emission. Here, we report conformationally adaptive orange-to-red TSCT-TADF emitters based on an S-shaped donor−π–acceptor−π–donor framework composed of phenoxazine donors, xanthene linkers, and a dibenzo[a,j]phenazine acceptor. Structural and NMR analyses reveal substantial conformational mobility, while systematic conformational searches and excited-state calculations identify thermally accessible conformers with distinct donor–acceptor geometries and excited-state characteristics. Comparative studies with reference compounds and fragment-resolved transition-density analysis show that the xanthene linker primarily acts as a conformational regulator and that the low-energy CT states have predominant TSCT character with only minor linker involvement. Temperature-dependent early-time photoluminescence measurements reveal continuous spectral relaxation in fluid toluene that slows upon cooling and is absent in rigid Zeonex and mCBP hosts, providing strong evidence for structural relaxation following photoexcitation within a pre-existing conformational ensemble. The emitters exhibit orange-to-red TADF with reverse intersystem crossing rates on the order of 105–106 s–1. Organic light-emitting diodes employing these emitters show electroluminescence at 598–624 nm, external quantum efficiencies up to 14.9%, and limited efficiency roll-off over a broad luminance range. These results demonstrate that efficient long-wavelength TSCT-TADF can be realized without permanent conformational locking and establish a framework for understanding the interplay between ground-state conformational heterogeneity and excited-state structural relaxation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Photoresponsive Mechanically Interlocked [ a n]Daisy Chain Network
items.abstract: Abstract Muscle integrates molecular-machine motion with hierarchical structural organization, enabling it to sustain large deformations under physiological loads. Mechanically interlocked molecules offer a versatile platform to mimic such molecular-level motion, but efficiently translating it into macroscopic material performance, akin to muscle, remains challenging. Herein, we report a mechanically interlocked network (MIN) with [an]daisy chain backbone which can efficiently scale up the photoresponsive behavior of mechanical bonds, exhibiting intelligently tunable mechanical properties. In specific, photoresponsive unit of arylazopyrazole (AAP) is embedded onto the axis of each mechanical bond in the [an]daisy chain backbone. Ultraviolet light triggers the trans-to-cis (E/Z) isomerization of the AAP moieties, and when amplified through the [an]daisy chain backbone, it brings about significant changes in the material’s properties. On one hand, the E/Z isomerization significantly shortens the dimension of the [an]daisy chain framework, resulting in a notable increase in the material modulus (from 1.6 to 4.0 MPa). On the other hand, the cis configuration of AAP formed after the isomerization restricts the mobility of the mechanical bonds, resulting in a shorter elongation at break (from 343% to 272%). Our work presents an efficient method for amplifying mechanical bond responsiveness, providing a fresh perspective for the development of intelligent materials.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Tailoring Solid-State
Reaction Pathways for Bulk Fluorination
of Mn-Rich Rock-Salt Cathodes
items.abstract: Abstract Manganese-based cation-disordered rock-salt (DRX) cathodes offer high capacities without relying on cobalt and nickel, but maintaining that capacity over extended cycling often requires bulk fluorination. The challenge is that incorporating fluorine into Mn-rich DRX host structures is hindered by unfavorable thermodynamics and the stability of LiF, often necessitating elevated synthesis temperatures that promote severe lithium and fluorine volatilization. This study overcomes that limitation by manipulating the solid-state reaction pathway using unconventional Li6MnO4 and MnF2 precursors in a challenging Mn-rich model system (Li1.2Mn0.6Ti0.2O2–xFx). This precursor engineering strategy reshapes the thermodynamic landscape. Computational modeling and in situ X-ray diffraction reveal that by using reactive starting materials, we suppress the crystallization of less reactive intermediates, enabling bulk fluorination at a lower temperature. The resulting DRX retains both a high fluorine content and the lithium excess required for three-dimensional percolation, delivering improved electrochemical performance relative to material synthesized from conventional precursors.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Multiphase
Inorganic-Rich Interphases with Integrated
Li-Ion Capture-Transport Ability for High-Rate Lithium Metal Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Lithium metal batteries promise high-energy-density storage but are limited by unstable solid–electrolyte interphases, which couple poor passivation, sluggish Li+ transport, dendritic deposition, and safety risks. Herein, we report a multiphase inorganic-rich solid–electrolyte interphase (m-SEI) containing P- and Al-derived species including Li3P, LiAl5O8, Li3PO4, and Li2Al, which is formed from the in situ reaction between a flame-retardant aluminum diethyl hypophosphite (ADP) interlayer and lithium metal. This multicomponent inorganic SEI enables an integrated capture-transport mechanism by combining high Li+ affinity, facilitated desolvation, and low-barrier Li+ migration pathways in individual inorganic phases and their heterophase interfaces, thereby facilitating rapid Li+ interfacial migration. Its chemical inertness and high Young’s modulus of 17.14 GPa further suppress electrolyte decomposition and Li dendrite growth. As a result, the Li-metal batteries with m-SEI deliver an extended lifespan of 1000 h at a high current density of 4 mA cm–2. Li||NCM811 full cells with a high cathode loading (20 mg cm–2) and ultrathin Li foil (50 μm) retain 80% capacity after 250 cycles, while Li||NCM811 pouch cells retain 90% capacity after 500 cycles. This work establishes the capture-transport mechanism as an effective design principle for regulating Li+ interfacial dynamics and offers a practical interphase-engineering strategy for constructing ion-conductive and chemically protective interphases in durable lithium metal batteries.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Hydration-Dependent
Working-Surface Chemistry in Photocatalytic
Methane Coupling
items.abstract: Abstract Selective photocatalytic methane coupling requires directing methane-derived intermediates toward C–C bond formation while limiting their oxidation to CO2, yet how the reaction environment controls this competition through surface chemistry remains unclear. Water is ubiquitous in photocatalytic methane conversion, but its influence is commonly interpreted through specific chemical functions rather than through its broader effects on working-surface chemistry. Here, Au/ZnO is used as a compositionally defined, coupling-competent model catalyst to reveal how hydration regulates carbon transformation pathways by reshaping the working-surface chemistry. Systematic variation of water availability reveals three hydration-dependent catalytic regimes with markedly different product distributions. Moderate hydration increases the ethane production rate from 1590 to 8407 μmol g–1 h–1 and enables ethylene formation, whereas excessive hydration increases CO2 production and lowers C2 selectivity. In situ spectroscopies show that these catalytic regimes are accompanied by hydration-dependent changes in methane adsorption, methane-derived and coupling-related surface intermediates, and oxygen-deficient surface states within a reaction network involving both carbon- and oxygen-centered radical chemistry. Moderate hydration establishes surface conditions that favor C–C coupling and C2 hydrocarbon accumulation, whereas excessive hydration favors oxidized surface species and carbonate formation. These results identify hydration as a key determinant of the steady-state surface chemistry governing carbon partitioning between C–C coupling and oxidation during photocatalytic methane conversion.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Porphyrin-Driven Redox Tuning in Structurally Defined De Novo Heme Proteins
items.abstract: Abstract Designing redox proteins with predictable and tunable electron transfer properties is a major goal in de novo bioenergetics. Here we show that replacing heme B with a series of structurally conservative non-natural metalloporphyrins enables broad modulation of redox potentials over 400 mV in the de novo designed monoheme m4D2 and diheme 4D2 T19D. The non-natural porphyrins bind with high affinity and do not compromise either the heme binding site or global protein structure, as evidenced by X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy. We also report the native-like NMR structure of m4D2 loaded with the non-natural and symmetric iron 2,4-dimethyldeuteroporphyrin IX, confirming our modular approach to tetrahelical redox protein design. This work establishes a versatile platform for constructing tunable electron carriers for engineered bioenergetic pathways and bioelectronic applications.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Dynamic
Acidic Adsorbates Govern Fast Oxygen Incorporation
in Ceria through Interfacial Electrostatics
items.abstract: Abstract The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) is a key heterogeneous process underpinning energy conversion, catalytic, and sensing technologies. However, reported ORR kinetics at oxide surfaces often vary widely because surface chemistry evolves under operating conditions. Ceria-based fluorites have been proposed as protective layers to stabilize perovskite electrodes, but ORR kinetics are typically considered sluggish and reported values have large variability. Herein, we demonstrate that cathodic polarization triggers an unexpected activation in Gd-doped ceria (CGO) dense thin films at 500 °C, enabling oxygen incorporation rates that surpass state-of-the-art materials such as La0.5Sr0.5FeO3−δ and approach the performance of La0.6Sr0.4CoO3−δ. Operando near-ambient-pressure X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (NAP-XPS), supported by ex situ surface-sensitive tip-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (TERS), reveals that CGO surface activation coincides with a reversible, overpotential-dependent modulation of sulfate adsorbates. Integration of these measurements with nondilute space-charge modeling suggests that charged adsorbates dynamically tune the near-surface electrostatic potential and electron concentration, thereby controlling oxygen incorporation kinetics. These results support adsorbate-induced electrostatic effects as a key mechanism in ceria and show that ORR kinetics are dynamically set by surface chemistry under operation, rather than by intrinsic bulk defect chemistry alone.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Synthesis and Crystal
Structure of Bulk Methanetetrol
C(OH)4
items.abstract: Abstract Methanetetrol, C(OH)4 (orthocarbonic acid), is an elusive tethrahydroxymethane that, due to its rapid dissociation under ambient conditions, has never been synthesized in bulk. A recent study detected the formation of C(OH)4 molecules in the gas phase. Here, we show that C(OH)4 can be synthesized in a diamond anvil cell through the reaction between H2O and CO2 at 45(3) GPa and 50(3) GPa and temperatures &lt;1200(200) K. The crystal structure of C(OH)4 was determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction and corroborated by density-functional theory calculations together with Raman spectroscopy. It is composed of isolated [C(OH)4]-molecules linked by strong hydrogen bonds. Under high-pressure conditions, orthocarbonic and carbonic acids are denser than coexisting water ice phases, allowing them to segregate gravitationally and form stable reservoirs of oxidized carbon. These phases incorporate large amounts of carbon into their crystal structures as part of [CO4]4–- or [CO3]2–-building blocks. Because the amount of carbon that can be stored as CO2 in clathrates or filled-ices is significantly smaller, orthocarbonic and carbonic acids may provide a host mechanism for sequestering large carbon inventories in the icy mantles of water-rich exoplanets.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Programming Oxygen
Reduction Selectivity via Peroxo
Basicity: Acid-Controlled 2e–/4e– Reduction Switching at a Dicobalt Platform
items.abstract: Abstract Achieving switchable 2e–/4e– oxygen reduction selectivity within a single molecular catalyst remains an unmet challenge because the key metal–oxygen intermediate typically commits to one pathway. Herein, we demonstrate that this limitation can be overcome by elevating the basicity of the peroxo intermediate to a level where both proton-transfer (PT) and proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) manifolds become accessible, with the dominant pathway dictated solely by the external acid strength. A dicobalt μ-1,2-peroxo complex supported by an electron-rich macrocyclic poly-NHC ligand exhibits a computed pKa1 of ∼8.8, placing it in a unique thermodynamic window. Stoichiometric protonation bifurcates cleanly: strong acids (HClO4) trigger rapid diprotonation to release H2O2, whereas weak acids (Et3NHOTf) promote O–O bond cleavage to afford a μ-hydroxo complex. Under catalytic conditions, this dichotomy translates into complete selectivity switching─100% H2O2 with HClO4 versus 90% H2O with Et3NHOTf, accompanied by a switch in the rate-determining step from O2 binding to PCET (KIE = 1.60). Crucially, a structurally analogous but less basic peroxo complex predictably inverts the selectivity to H2O under identical conditions, providing a closed-loop validation of the basicity-selectivity relationship. These results establish intermediate basicity as a general, tunable design parameter for programming product selectivity in multielectron catalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Dye-Sensitization Enables
Visible-Light-Driven N–N
Bond Cleavage in a Dinuclear Rhenium Dinitrogen Complex
items.abstract: Abstract Conversion of μ-N2 complexes into nitrogenous compounds is one of the most important and challenging chemical transformations in N2 fixation. Although photochemical N2 splitting has been demonstrated, existing approaches predominantly rely on high-energy ultraviolet light that generally affords low efficiency and poor selectivity. Herein, we establish a visible-light-driven molecular photosensitization strategy that enables efficient and selective N–N bond cleavage in a dinuclear rhenium dinitrogen complex. Blue light excitation of the organic photosensitizer 4DPAIPN (2,4,5,6-tetrakis(diphenylamino)isophthalonitrile) is shown to initiate N–N scission to afford the corresponding rhenium nitride in 96% yield. Kinetic analysis of nanosecond transient absorption data through the Balzani-Scandola model indicates energy transfer from the photosensitizer to an acceptor state that lies approximately 2.31 eV above the ground state of the μ-N2-bridged dirhenium complex. This photosensitization strategy decouples light harvesting from N–N bond activation, eliminates the need for UV light, and shows broad applicability across different visible-light absorbing photosensitizers, including transition metal complexes and organic chromophores with long-lived, high-energy triplet excited-states. These findings establish dye-sensitization as a powerful strategy for visible-light-driven N–N bond cleavage for mechanistic study and the future realization of a photochemical pathway for nitrogen fixation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Unlocking Intrinsic
Chirality in Luminescent Copper
Clusters via Intramolecular Spatial Confinement
items.abstract: Abstract Most luminescent clusters that exhibit pronounced chiral signals typically rely on predesigned chiral ligands; however, stimulating the intrinsic chirality of clusters in the absence of exogenous asymmetric ligands remains a significant challenge. In this study, based on a series of structure-correlated Cu2 clusters, we demonstrate that intramolecular spatial confinement effectively induces distortions in flexible ligands, thereby imparting asymmetry to the cluster framework. This molecular asymmetry further determines the orientation of cluster entities during supramolecular assembly, thus enabling the modulation of chirality across this cluster series between inactive (“off”) and active (“on”) states. In addition, these structure-correlated Cu2 clusters display bright and tunable luminescence, allowing for the fabrication of uniform thin films that function as practical scintillation materials for high-resolution X-ray imaging. Collectively, this work provides a novel perspective for regulating the chiroptical properties of metal clusters through the activation of intramolecular spatial confinement and offers valuable insights into the fabrication of cluster-based nanomaterials with tailored photophysical performances.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Dynamic Metal Encapsulation in a Pt/TiO x system Regulated by Pt-Assisted TiO2 Amorphization
items.abstract: Abstract Strong metal–support interaction (SMSI) plays an important role in heterogeneous catalysis, but remains poorly understood, particularly on the origin of SMSI under an oxidative atmosphere. Hereby grand canonical structure exploration of over 4 million bulk PtTi alloys and Pt or PtTi-supported Ti oxide (TiOx) surface structure candidates, we resolve the Pt/TiOx system, a text-book example of SMSI, under both reductive and oxidative conditions: it experiences an encapsulation─deep encapsulation─decapsulation dynamic reconstruction under a sequence of H2 reduction─O2 oxidation─H2 plus O2 redox thermal treatment. The whole process was kinetically simulated by long-time (69 ns) molecular dynamics simulations, revealing in detail how a 3 nm Pt nanoparticle undergoes nonclassical SMSI under an oxidative and redox atmosphere. We find that Pt-assisted TiO2 amorphization is the key to the transition of various SMSI states at different conditions, which elevates Ti chemical potential via amorphization toward low-coordinated [TiO4]. Finally, explainable machine learning models were developed to predict nonclassical SMSI cases and clarify their rarity in nature.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Catalytic Interphases
Enable Sulfur Redox Catalysis
in All-Solid-State Lithium–Sulfur Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Weak solid–solid contact with limited chemical and transport continuity is a common bottleneck in solid-state batteries, particularly in all-solid-state lithium–sulfur batteries (ASSLSBs), where Li2S/S8 conversion requires catalytic acceleration but lacks a continuous solid-state catalytic pathway. Here, we propose an interphase catalysis strategy for solid–solid sulfur conversion by transforming discrete catalyst/reactant interfaces into a chemically integrated reaction interphase. WO3 is identified as a suitable oxide to construct such a metastable mixed-anion S–W–O catalytic interphase on Li2S based on the work-function difference between the metal oxide catalyst and Li2S/S8, which serves as a practical screening rationale for evaluating the relative tendency toward sulfur–oxygen coordination exchange. The interphase contains unsaturated W centers and a polarized electronic environment, enabling coupled electron/Li+ transport and dynamically regulating sulfur redox through coupled sulfur-species exchange. This integrated interphase further stabilizes cathode interfaces during repeated Li2S/S8 conversion. As a result, the optimized cathode sustains stable cycling over 15000 cycles at 10 C and a temperature of 60 °C. A record-high Li2S loading of 30 mg cm–2 with an areal capacity of 21.2 mAh cm–2 is also achieved, demonstrating interphase catalysis as an effective route to overcome solid-state sulfur-conversion limitations in practical ASSLSBs.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
X-Shaped Multichannel
Conjugation Enabled by
Excited-State Aromaticity
items.abstract: Abstract Molecular topology governs the photophysical properties of polycyclic π-conjugated systems by defining their effective conjugation pathways. Conventionally, linear π-extension is considered more effective than angular extension in increasing the effective conjugation length and narrowing the optical bandgap. Here we uncover an inverse topology–property relationship in π-extended dihydrophenazines (DHPs): linear extension unexpectedly blueshifts fluorescence, whereas angular extension produces pronounced redshifts. Transient spectroscopy, theoretical calculations and aromaticity analyses reveal that Baird aromaticity–driven planarization of the DHP core redistributes π-delocalization in the S1 state, causing linear fusion to disrupt global π-delocalization and shorten the effective conjugation length, while angular fusion promotes cooperative delocalization across the fused framework and extends it. Successive angular fusion progressively activates four structurally distinct π-extension branches through the shared Baird-aromatic DHP core, generating an X-shaped multichannel conjugation network. These findings reveal how excited-state aromaticity reprograms conjugation topology, offering new insights for controlling π-delocalization and emission.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Cationic Ionomer Coatings
Promote Anion Electroreduction:
Nitrate Reduction as a Model Reaction
items.abstract: Abstract Electrolysis technologies represent a promising pathway to valorize abundant feedstocks using renewable electricity. While ionomers serve critical roles as ion conductors and catalyst binders in electrolyzers, their impact on electrochemical transformations of ionic species remains poorly understood compared to extensively studied neutral-molecule conversions like water splitting and CO2 reduction. Herein, we use the electrochemical nitrate reduction reaction as a model transformation to investigate the influence of ionomer coatings in anion electroreduction reactions, which face fundamental challenges from electrostatic anion depletion near negatively polarized cathodes and premature desorption of anionic intermediates. We demonstrate that cationic ionomer coatings increase local nitrate concentration up to 10-fold compared to bulk electrolyte due to the interfacial Donnan potential. While prior studies have shown that ionomers can influence the local reaction microenvironment, this work provides, to the best of our knowledge, the first quantitative measurement of nitrate concentration within ionomer coatings as a function of charge density and its impact on catalysis. A 5-fold enhancement in ammonium partial current density was achieved with the ionomer bearing the highest charge density. Using in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS), we quantified enhanced local nitrate concentration (up to 1.1 M versus 0.1 M in bulk electrolyte), conversion, and supply with increasing charge density. This study establishes guiding principles for tuning ionomer charge identity and density to control interfacial ion concentrations in electrochemical transformations of dilute charged substrates.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Ion-Pair Receptors
Couple Cation Binding with Molecular
Electron Storage for Room-Temperature Birch-Type Reduction
items.abstract: Abstract The Birch reduction provides a powerful route to partially dearomatized products from aromatic precursors, but classical protocols rely on highly reactive solvated electrons generated from alkali metals in cryogenic liquid ammonia, offering limited molecular control over reducing equivalents. Here we show that ion-pair receptors couple Na+ binding with molecular electron storage within electron-deficient diimide-based π-frameworks. Reduction with sodium generates persistent sodium-associated radical-anion ion pairs in which the unpaired electron is delocalized predominantly over the π-accepting framework. Time-dependent UV–vis and EPR measurements establish persistence of the representative Na+·IP-4•– state in THF at room temperature under an inert atmosphere. Control experiments show that covalent integration of the Na+-binding and electron-accepting domains markedly enhances reduced-state persistence and productive electron transfer relative to the isolated components or their noncovalent combination. The resulting molecularly stored reducing equivalents enable room-temperature Birch-type reductions of polycyclic aromatic substrates in high yields using unprecedented catalytic receptor loadings. These results establish coupled cation binding and molecular electron storage as a supramolecular strategy for regulating highly reducing equivalents in solution-phase dearomatization chemistry.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
On-Resin P(V) Polyphosphorylation
of Serine, Threonine,
and Tyrosine
items.abstract: Abstract Protein phosphorylation is the most abundant post-translational modification (PTM) and plays a central role in regulating biological processes. Attaining discretely polyphosphorylated peptides is an open challenge. Their chemical synthesis relies on coupling of phosphorylated amino acid building blocks, which suffer from base-mediated elimination and incomplete couplings, or postsynthesis functionalization via a global phosphoramidite approach, which is prone to side reactions during oxidation. Herein, we developed an on-resin phosphorylation that utilizes a protected and activated phosphorus(V) species. This method gave ≥95% conversion for monophosphorylation of serine, threonine, and tyrosine and tolerated oxidation-sensitive methionine, cysteine, and tryptophan residues. Up to five phosphorylations were installed site-selectively, with superior performance to building block approaches, and it remained effective on sequences up to 83 residues. With an efficient method for site-selective polyphosphorylation established, the specificity of antibodies directed against phosphorylated variants of the oncoprotein MYC was evaluated. These antibodies are often used for evaluating the role of phosphorylation sites (phosphosites) in regulating MYC in cancer. Although all antibodies maintained selectivity for their specific phosphosite, binding varied upon additional phosphorylation sites around the epitope, underscoring the need for careful validation of antibodies to prevent misinterpretation. Overall, this strategy enables efficient access to complex, defined polyphosphorylated peptides for future investigations into the biological roles of phosphorylation sites on MYC, and provides a broadly applicable method for the synthesis of precisely (poly)phosphorylated peptides and proteins.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Mixed
Conducting Polymer with pH-Dependent Selectivity
for the Oxygen Reduction Reaction
items.abstract: Abstract Achieving 4-electron oxygen reduction with metal-free electrodes has remained a longstanding challenge. Here, we show that poly(benzimidazobenzophenanthroline) (BBL), an n-type ladder polymer, breaks this barrier through an electrocatalytic inner-sphere 2 + 2 series mechanism─a mode of reactivity unprecedented among organic mixed ionic-electronic conductors (OMIECs). Using pH-dependent rotating ring-disk voltammetry, we find that this series mechanism occurs over separate potential windows on BBL. At more positive potentials, an initial reduction wave correlated with electron polaron formation in BBL produces exclusively hydro(gen) peroxide across all pH values, followed by a second, pH-dependent wave for hydro(gen) peroxide reduction at more negative potentials. At pH 14.0, this second wave enables complete four-electron reduction of O2 (n ≈ 4) to OH–, driven by formation of a bipolaronic state in BBL. Decreasing the pH instead stabilizes a hydrogenated state in BBL incapable of O–O bond cleavage, reverting selectivity to n ≈ 2. These insights reveal that the coupling between ion selectivity during electrochemical ion-insertion and product selectivity during ORR catalysis shapes active-site structure and poisoning, establishing a new design principle in the emerging field of OMIEC electrocatalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
An Embedded Plasticization
Strategy for Flexible Thermally
Activated Delayed Fluorescence Polymers with High Luminance
items.abstract: Abstract Thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) polymers offer the theoretical advantage of achieving 100% internal quantum efficiency. Together with their solution processability, TADF polymers are promising candidates for flexible display technologies. However, emissive polymers that simultaneously combine efficient TADF emission with mechanical flexibility remain rare. Here, we report an embedded plasticized linker strategy for mechanically compliant TADF polymers. Polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based flexible segments are covalently incorporated into acridine–benzophenone–carbazole polymer backbones. This “TADF unit + plasticized linker” design preserves the donor–acceptor electronic structure required for delayed fluorescence while introducing flexibility into the emissive polymer framework. The resulting polymers exhibit small singlet–triplet energy gaps, clear delayed fluorescence, and favorable film deformability. The deformation behavior of the neat polymer films was evaluated on PDMS substrates under an applied substrate strain of 75%. Notably, the optimized rigid organic light-emitting diode (OLED) based on PIDC(2,7)-EO achieves a maximum external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 20.1% and a high luminance of 85 988 cd m–2. This luminance value is among the highest reported for polymer-based TADF OLEDs. Flexible OLEDs fabricated on flexible substrates further deliver a maximum EQE of 14.7%. These results demonstrate efficient electroluminescence from flexible device architectures. This work establishes embedded plasticized linkers as an effective molecular design strategy for high-performance mechanically flexible TADF polymers. This strategy provides a promising route toward next-generation flexible OLED technologies.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Tunable Aza-BODIPY
Photocatalysts for Near-Infrared
Metallaphotoredox Atom Transfer Radical Polymerization
items.abstract: Abstract The merger of photoredox and transition-metal catalysis has significantly advanced radical and redox transformations, yet its reliance on UV or visible light continues to limit applications in optically complex and spatially confined environments. Herein, we introduce a modular family of tetraaryl aza-boron-dipyrromethene (aza-BODIPY) organic photocatalysts (PCs) for near-infrared (NIR) metallaphotoredox atom transfer radical polymerization (ATRP). We systematically modulated peripheral electronics and core bromination, evaluating the dyes through quantum-chemical, electrochemical, and spectroscopic methods. This approach identified the key parameters governing catalytic performance: a delicate interplay between triplet-state accessibility, redox properties, and photostability. The optimized aza-BODIPY dye enables well-controlled ATRP of diverse acrylates and methacrylates at ultralow catalyst loadings, down to 5 ppm PC and 50 ppm copper complex. The system is further translated to open-air aqueous conditions, enabling rapid, high-throughput synthesis of water-soluble polymers in a 96-well plate format. Taking advantage of the enhanced penetration of NIR light, we demonstrate controlled polymerization through challenging physical barriers, including ex vivo tissue. Overall, this work defines design principles for far-red/NIR-absorbing aza-BODIPY PCs and expands the scope of NIR-mediated polymer synthesis to optically turbid, spatially restricted, and aqueous environments.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Confocal-Detection
Electrochemiluminescence Microscopy
for Three-Dimensional Imaging of Electrochemical Reaction Fields
items.abstract: Abstract Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) imaging is an important tool for visualizing electrochemical reactions and is generally performed by wide-field microscopy, which efficiently collects weak emission. The price of this high photon-collection efficiency, however, is that axial information is collapsed into a depth-integrated projection, preventing three-dimensional (3D) visualization. Confocal detection is attractive for 3D ECL imaging because it can distinguish emission from different focal planes, yet its application to ECL has not been systematically explored, mainly because of the limited photon output of ECL reactions. Here, we construct a confocal-detection ECL (CD-ECL) microscopy platform and identify three factors that make CD-ECL difficult: the low efficiency of ECL reactions, which limits photon generation; the optical trade-off between photon collection and spatiotemporal resolution; and the intrinsic instability of ECL reactions, which causes the emission intensity to change during confocal scanning. To address these problems, we first built a shared-objective configuration to compare confocal and wide-field ECL detection. We then optimized the ECL reaction conditions to increase photon generation, examined the trade-off between photon number and spatiotemporal resolution, and developed cyclic volumetric acquisition (CVA) to reduce the influence of temporal intensity variations. Under the optimized conditions, CD-ECL produced 3D images of emission around graphite-felt electrodes and followed the time-dependent evolution of the ECL reaction field. These results establish a confocal optical-detection route to 3D ECL imaging and provide a proof-of-concept basis for depth-dependent and time-resolved measurements under photon-limited conditions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Quantized Photocatalysis
Using Bandgap-Engineered
Metal Halide Perovskite Nanocrystals
items.abstract: Abstract Size quantization in semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) offers a convenient way to tune their bandgap and energy levels of conduction and valence bands. We have now employed a room-temperature synthesis of CsPbBr3 and CsPbI3 quantum dots, with sizes from 5 to 13.5 nm, to probe hole transfer to p-phenylenediamine and m-phenylenediamine. The apparent hole-transfer rate constants, as estimated from transient absorption spectroscopy measurements, indicate a strong dependence on QD size. The shift in the valence-band energy with decreasing QD size increases the driving force (−ΔG) for hole transfer. The apparent hole-transfer rate constants, which vary in the range of (1.5 ± 0.2) – (17.3 ± 0.6) × 1010 s–1 exhibit a dependence on the energy difference between the QD valence band energy and the oxidation potential of the hole acceptor. This dependence of the rate constants further establishes the normal and inverted regions, as expected from Marcus electron-transfer theory. The ability to modulate charge-transfer rate constants through size control paves the way for tailoring the performance of quantized photocatalytic systems.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Interfacial Electric
Field Dynamically Confined Enzyme
Self-Adaptation in Covalent Organic Framework Heterojunctions for
Photoenzymatic Catalysis
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial photoenzymatic synthesis systems based on 1,4-NADH-dependent enzymes are challenged by unclear interfacial interactions and limited stability. Inspired by the ordered assembly and Z-scheme electron transfer mechanism in natural photosynthesis, we constructed an enzyme self-adaptive covalent organic frameworks (COFs) immobilization platform featuring a built-in electric field and a targeted Z-scheme electron transfer pathway. The CT-COF@Py-COF served as a mechanical scaffold for in situ encapsulation of reductases at the heterojunction interface, where electrostatic interactions, π–π stacking, and the ensuing formation of an interfacial electric field (IEF) collectively facilitated enzyme encapsulation. Moreover, IEF drove the conformational self-adaptation of encapsulated reductases and promoted directional charge transfer across the Z-scheme heterojunction, which synergistically enhanced catalytic activity and operational stability. The IEF-integrated system, paired with various dehydrogenases, enabled the efficient synthesis of pharmaceutical precursors under visible light. In a continuous-flow reactor, the encapsulated dehydrogenase retained approximately 88% of its initial-cycle glycine-production activity after eight cycles and exhibited a 7.18-fold increase in lactate yield when coupled with light-driven 1,4-NADH regeneration.
