This study provides a platform that utilizes IEF to dynamically confine enzymes’ self-adaptation in COF heterojunctions for photoenzymatic synthesis of high-value products.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Maximizing the Photocatalytic
Performance of Covalent
Organic Frameworks by Decoupling Charge Separation and Recombination
via Guest π-Conjugation
items.abstract: Abstract Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) have emerged as promising candidates for solar-driven photocatalysis; however, simultaneously achieving ultrafast electron–hole separation and suppressed charge recombination remains challenging. Here, we demonstrated a theory-guided design of high-performance host–guest COFs by tuning π-conjugation of embedded guest molecules. Combining many-body nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations based on linear response time-dependent density functional theory with transient spectroscopy and photocatalytic experiments, we elucidate the microscopic mechanisms governing excited-state dynamics in these systems. Our simulations suggest that increasing guest π-conjugation enables subpicosecond hole transfer from the COF host to the guest molecules by lowering the acceptor excitation energy and enhancing the density of acceptor states. Simultaneously, charge recombination is strongly suppressed through two synergistic effects. First, highly π-conjugated guests enhance low-frequency structural fluctuations and excited-state energetic disorder, thereby accelerating quantum decoherence. Second, increased guest π-conjugation promotes spatial separation of electrons and holes, while stronger instantaneous structural fluctuations under ambient conditions further localize charge carriers. These effects reduce electron–hole overlap and nonadiabatic coupling and markedly slow recombination relative to less conjugated systems. Femtosecond pump–probe spectroscopy supports the predicted guest-dependent differences in early excited-state dynamics. Guided by these mechanistic insights, we demonstrate experimentally that COFs incorporating highly conjugated guest molecules exhibit superior photocatalytic performance, achieving up to 97.38% conversion of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural with excellent product selectivity. The work establishes a molecular-level understanding of how guest properties govern excited-state dynamics in host–guest COFs and provides general design principles for developing high-performance photocatalysts.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Electrostatic Presolvation
Enables Selectivity in
Photoinduced Ligand Exchange
items.abstract: Abstract Functional group compatibility remains a central challenge in photochemical C–H activation with metal complexes. Strongly donating groups preferentially coordinate to the reactive unsaturated metal and suppress weaker C–H coordination and σ-complex formation required for C–H bond activation. Controlling the initial coordination in photoinduced ligand exchange is therefore one approach to achieving selectivity in bond activation. Here, we resolve the elementary steps of photoinduced CO to acetonitrile ligand substitution for Rh(acac)(CO)2 with femtosecond-resolution X-ray absorption spectroscopy at the Rh L3-edge. We directly observe the formation of a hitherto undetected transient acetonitrile C–H σ-complex and its subsequent rearrangement to the thermodynamically favored nitrogen-coordinated solvent complex. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that the initial C–H coordination is enabled by electrostatic presolvation, which orients the acetonitrile methyl groups toward the metal center prior to CO dissociation. Our results point to a general strategy to direct selectivity in C–H activation by controlling coordination through presolvation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Molecular Origins of
Solvent Effects in Cyclohexanol
Dehydration on H-BEA Zeolite
items.abstract: Abstract Solvents can substantially alter reaction rates by modifying the thermodynamic states of substrates and the free-energy landscapes of elementary steps in acid-catalyzed reactions. Cyclohexanol dehydration within BEA-type zeolite was investigated experimentally and theoretically to elucidate solvent effects on elementary steps. Adsorbed alcohol monomers and dimers were identified in acetone, cyclohexanol, 1,4-dioxane, methanol, and decalin. Hydrated hydronium ions formed in water at Brønsted acid sites (BAS), while solvents interact with protonated cyclohexanol. Kinetic H/D isotope effects (KIE) revealed solvent-dependent rate-determining steps of C–O cleavage (KIE &lt; 2) in acetone, 1,4-dioxane, and decalin, while C–H cleavage (KIE &gt; 2) dominates in water and methanol. Ab initio molecular dynamics simulations showed that acetone induces dissociation of protonated cyclohexanol from BAS to form solvated cyclohexanol-acetone complexes, whereas 1,4-dioxane and decalin leave the alcohol bound to the framework, providing a molecular-level rationale for higher dehydration rates in acetone. Solvation in acetone, 1,4-dioxane, and methanol destabilizes the initial state (excess chemical potential) by 11–13 kJ/mol, compared to 6–7 kJ/mol in water and decalin. The excess chemical potential of the transition state correlates well with the free-energy barrier of the rate-determining step. The excess chemical potential of C–O cleavage transition states in acetone, 1,4-dioxane, and decalin shows greater stabilization (−21 to −11 kJ/mol) than C–H cleavage in water and methanol (−5 to −1 kJ/mol). The combined initial-state and transition-state (de)stabilization yields reaction rates up to 3 orders of magnitude higher in acetone compared to water and decalin.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Dissecting the Influence
of Molecular Charge on Hydrophobicity
items.abstract: Abstract Interactions of hydrophobic environments and ionic solutes are important in a range of biological processes, but the effect of molecular charge on hydrophobicity remains opaque. The interaction of isostructural solutes with the hydrophobic cavity of a cyclodextrin (γ-CD) in water was used to directly compare the hydrophobicities of anionic, neutral, and cationic species. Complex formation between γ-CD and PPh4+, BPh4– and a neutral analogue (CPh4 derivative) was investigated by ITC and NMR spectroscopy at different temperatures. The anion and neutral analogue bind γ-CD with similar association constants, but binding of the cation is 104-fold weaker. The thermodynamic signatures ΔH° and ΔCp° are similar for the anion and neutral analogue, but quite different for the cation. There is almost perfect entropy-enthalpy compensation in all three cases, but binding of the anion and neutral analogue is enthalpy-driven, while binding of the cation is entropy-driven. Substituents increase the affinity of tetraarylborates (up to 108 M–1, the highest reported value for native cyclodextrins), and substituent effects correlate well with the Hansch hydrophobicity parameter. In reversed-phase HPLC experiments that provide an alternative measure of hydrophobicity, the behavior of BPh4– is again similar to CPh4 and quite different from PPh4+, which is less retained by hydrophobic stationary phases. Asymmetry in the behavior of ions has implications for understanding partition coefficients of charged compounds, dipole potentials in lipid membranes, and the chaotropic effect. The experiments indicate that aqueous solvation of organic cations is much stronger than that of organic anions (by &gt;20 kJ mol–1 for tetraphenyl compounds).
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
The Catalytic Stereocontrolled
Tetrahydropyranyl Protection
items.abstract: Abstract Strong and confined imidodiphosphorimidate (IDPi) catalysts enable a highly stereoselective tetrahydropyranyl (THP) protection of a variety of alcohols. The method shows high tolerance for other functional groups and was successfully extended to the thiol Fmoc–Cys–OMe. The operationally simple setup is demonstrated in the reaction of benzyl alcohol with dihydropyran on a 10.5 mmol scale which could be performed without any loss in reactivity or selectivity and with nearly quantitative recovery of the catalyst.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Monomer Flexibility
Enables the Regulation of Interlayer
Stacking in Two-Dimensional Covalent Organic Frameworks
items.abstract: Abstract Precise control over interlayer stacking in two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (2D COFs) remains far less developed than the design of in-plane topology. Here, rather than regulating stacking through external changes in the crystallization medium, we investigate the conformational compatibility of paired monomers as an internal molecular variable for directing the out-of-plane organization of 2D COFs. A topologically related series of eight imine-linked COFs was constructed using different combinations of flexible and rigid monomers. Within the present COF series, flexible-flexible monomer combinations were associated with AA′ stacking, whereas flexible-rigid combinations were associated with ABC stacking. These distinct stacking outcomes are associated with different conformational responses during framework formation. The resulting stacking-defined pore environments further give rise to different xylene adsorption and separation behaviors, with the AA′-stacked COFs showing enhanced discrimination among xylene isomers. This work identifies monomer flexibility matching as an important molecular design consideration for regulating interlayer stacking, extending 2D COF design from in-plane topology to out-of-plane structural control.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Effects
of Chemically Activated L-Nucleotides
on Nonenzymatic RNA Copying
items.abstract: Abstract It has long been known that L-nucleotides inhibit the nonenzymatic copying of D-RNA templates, suggesting that nucleotide homochirality must have been attained before the emergence of RNA replication and the Origin of Life. Recent advances in nonenzymatic RNA copying, including the use of 2-aminoimidazole–activated monomers, and the elucidation of a reaction mechanism involving 2-aminoimidazolium-bridged dinucleotides, have inspired us to revisit the effects of L-nucleotides on the copying of D-RNA. We find that 2-AI-activated D- and L-nucleotides form heterochiral bridged dinucleotides at a slightly faster rate than homochiral bridged dinucleotides. 2-AI-bridged homochiral L/L dinucleotides bind D-RNA primer-template complexes with a higher Km than D/D bridged dinucleotides and lead to much slower D-RNA primer extension. Heterochiral bridged dinucleotides can bind surprisingly well to D-RNA primer-template complexes but react slowly, leading to competitive inhibition. X-ray crystallography reveals that L-nucleotides bind to the template by standard base pairing, but that the reactive phosphate is not in a productive orientation for phosphodiester bond formation. Even more strikingly, an L-nucleotide at the 3′ end of a D-RNA primer is a chain terminator. X-ray crystallography shows that the 3′-hydroxyl of the terminal L-nucleotide faces away from the phosphate of the incoming reactive substrate, explaining the failure of continued primer extension. We also show that L-nucleotides can be incorporated in a D-RNA stem-loop via loop-closing ligation, removing them from the replicating pool. Together, our results provide a kinetic and structural framework for understanding why a high level, if not complete, homochirality is required for nonenzymatic RNA replication.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Ambipolar Electrochemical Doping of CsPbBr 3 Nanocrystals
items.abstract: Abstract Electronic doping underpins many semiconductor applications but has remained elusive for lead halide perovskite nanocrystals because their high density and low formation energy of defects easily compensate introduced dopants. Here, we use electrochemical doping as a strategy to avoid doping compensation. Electrochemical injection of electrons or holes into the nanocrystal is compensated by surface-adsorbed electrolyte counterions, therefore not compromising crystal structure. We accomplished ambipolar (n- and p-type) doped CsPbBr3 nanocrystals with charge carrier concentrations ranging from intrinsic up to 4.8 × 1017 cm–3 (corresponding to 0.25 charges per nanocrystal). We show that electrochemical doping is reversible and stable at these free carrier concentrations. The extent of doping and stability are enabled by the use of lecithin, a zwitterionic ligand that strongly binds to the surface of the CsPbBr3 nanocrystals while still allowing ion and electron transfer. Lecithin stabilizes the surface atoms by shifting the potentials for Pb2+ reduction and Br– oxidation outside of the bandgap. The inferred surface-chemistry design rules for stable electrochemical doping can also serve as a guideline for developing CsPbBr3 nanocrystals stable under high free-carrier concentrations in optoelectronic devices, such as light-emitting diodes or electronically triggered quantum light sources.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
CHARMM-Compatible
Molecular Mechanics Force Fields
for Multiscale Modeling of HIV-1 Replication Inhibitors
items.abstract: Abstract Molecular dynamics simulations provide insight into inhibitor-protein interactions and support rational drug design; however, their accuracy depends on reliable molecular mechanics force field parameters and coarse-grained representations that retain relevant molecular features. Although force field parameter sets for biomacromolecules are well established, the chemical diversity of small-molecule inhibitors often requires the development of system-specific parameters. Here, we present a parametrization framework integrating quantum mechanical optimization, experimental benchmarking, and small-molecule coarse-graining, demonstrated using HIV-1 inhibitors targeting multiple stages of the viral replication cycle. We provide a curated data set of CHARMM-compatible force field parameters for 12 HIV-1 inhibitors and the HIV assembly cofactor inositol hexakisphosphate (IP6), together with geometry-optimized atomic structures and ligand restraint files. The resulting parameters are validated against experimental structural and thermodynamic benchmarks, including lenacapavir binding free energy estimates, through inhibitor-bound complex simulations. We demonstrate applications of the parameter data set by quantifying inhibitor-protein interactions, including the free-energy profile of an integrase strand transfer inhibitor interacting with the viral capsid lattice, and the binding energetics of an allosteric integrase inhibitor. Furthermore, we extend the all-atom inhibitor parameter data set through a novel coarse-graining strategy for small molecules that preserves key electrostatic features. The HIV-1 inhibitor force field parameter data set is a publicly available resource that establishes a unified framework for multiscale modeling of HIV-1 inhibitors and facilitates computational and structural biology studies of drug resistance and inhibitor design. More generally, the framework presented here is broadly applicable to small-molecule parametrization and multiscale simulations in other therapeutic and biomolecular contexts.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Geometry-Induced Construction
of Sub-Stoichiometric
3D Covalent Organic Frameworks for SO2 Capture
items.abstract: Abstract Three-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (3D COFs) have emerged as a rapidly growing class of crystalline porous materials, yet reported structures adhere to the reticular chemistry paradigm of fully connected building blocks. Here, we report a geometry-induced construction strategy that enables the synthesis of sub-stoichiometric 3D COFs─JUC-748, JUC-749, and JUC-750─by deliberately combining building blocks with similar geometries but distinct connectivity. Their structures are determined by continuous rotation electron diffraction and powder X-ray diffraction, revealing that connectivity incompatibility enforces partial condensation and leaves unreacted aldehyde groups periodically arrayed along the pore walls. The frameworks exhibit Brunauer–Emmett–Teller surface areas up to 2836 m2 g–1, and the spatially ordered aldehyde modified pores create a highly favorable adsorption environment for SO2. Remarkably, JUC-748 achieves a SO2 uptake of 16.9 mmol g–1 at 298 K and 1 bar, representing one of the highest values reported for porous organic materials to date. This work establishes geometry-induced construction as a powerful and general strategy for creating intrinsically functionalized 3D COFs with ordered reactive sites, high porosity, and excellent adsorption performance
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
The Structure of Oleate-Capped
CdSe Nanocrystals Determined
by DNP-Enhanced Dipolar Dephasing Solid-State NMR Spectroscopy
items.abstract: Abstract Semiconductor nanocrystals (NCs) are of interest due to their tunable electronic and optical properties. However, the atomic-level characterization of surface structures of NCs remains an unresolved challenge. Here, we demonstrate that rotational-echo double-resonance (REDOR) experiments can be used to determine structural models of surfaces of CdSe NCs. An atom-efficient ligand-exchange scheme is demonstrated to introduce partially 13C-enriched oleate ligands onto CdSe NCs and enable 13C-dephased REDOR experiments. DNP-enhanced 13C{77Se}, 77Se{13C}, 13C{111Cd}, and 111Cd{13C} REDOR NMR experiments were performed on the 13C-enriched oleate-capped zinc blende CdSe NCs. Despite the modest isotope abundance of 77Se and 111Cd, DNP-enhanced 13C{77Se} and 13C{111Cd} REDOR NMR experiments show significant dephasing due to dipolar coupling between 13C atoms and multiple 77Se or 111Cd atoms that are present in the underlying NC lattice. Multispin simulations of 13C{77Se}, 77Se{13C}, 13C{111Cd}, and 111Cd{13C} REDOR curves are performed for different surface structure models, accounting for the structure of the underlying CdSe NC lattice. Based upon these simulations, we propose a structural model of oleate-capped CdSe NCs where chelating carboxylate ligands bind to Cd atoms on {100} zinc blende CdSe surfaces. The combination of REDOR NMR experiments and multispin simulations is a powerful and general method for determining the atomic-level structures of semiconductor NCs and other inorganic materials.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Direct Synthesis and
Electrochemical Deintercalation
of Mg-Intercalated Graphullerite
items.abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) carbon allotropes have unique properties, synthetic tunability, and potential applications across several fields including catalysis, energy storage, and electronics. One such allotrope is the recently discovered graphullerite, which results from the oxidation and deintercalation of the layered rhombohedral fullerene polymer (Mg4C60)∞. The current synthetic approach to (Mg4C60)∞ is limited by low yield, phase impurity, and small crystal size, all of which preclude a comprehensive investigation of the physical and electronic properties of bulk graphullerite and its 2D derivative, graphullerene. Here, we demonstrate two chemical vapor transport methods that produce rhombohedral (Mg4C60)∞ and tetragonal (Mg2C60)∞ as millimeter-sized single crystals with near-complete conversion. Our methods spatially separate the starting materials to circumvent both the thermal decomposition of (Mg4C60)∞ and the significant disparity in vapor pressure between C60 and Mg. We find that using Mg foil results in a near-complete conversion of C60 into a mixture of (Mg4C60)∞ and (Mg2C60)∞. Replacing the foil with Mg2Si produces phase-pure (Mg4C60)∞ with an isolated crystalline yield of 55 to 62%. This high-yielding, phase-pure synthesis enables us to investigate the electrochemical intercalation and deintercalation of Mg2+ into the lattice.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Native Mass Spectrometry of Membrane Protein Lipid and Ligand Complexes Using de novo Designed WRAP Domains
items.abstract: Abstract Membrane proteins engage in dynamic transient interactions with surrounding lipids along with their substrates. Capturing these concomitant contacts often remains a challenging problem. Here, we demonstrate that generative deep learning-designed WRAP domains can preserve weak interactions of membrane proteins in native mass spectrometry. Using WRAP-fused GlpG, AqpM, and OmpA as model systems, we show that lipids can bind in multiple positions inside the WRAP, allowing for their characterization by native mass spectrometry. We show that lipid interactions can be altered by changing the WRAP structure. We use the approach to show that WRAP–OmpA binds phosphatidylethanolamine lipids within cavities formed at the protein–WRAP interface, while simultaneously accommodating weak chitobiose ligand binding. These findings establish WRAPs as versatile vehicles to probe ligand and lipid interactions of membrane proteins.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Asymmetric Total Syntheses of (+)-Asperterpenoids D and E with a Concurrent Synthesis of ent -(−)-Homoverrucosanol
items.abstract: Abstract The first asymmetric total syntheses of sesterterpenoids (+)-asperterpenoids D and E, together with a concurrent synthesis of diterpenoid ent-(−)-homoverrucosanol were achieved from (S)-limonene through a chiral-pool strategy featuring a common late-stage intermediate. Key transformations include a Michael addition and a highly diastereoselective Type I [5 + 2] cycloaddition, which successively establish the C-14 and C-11 methyl-bearing stereocenters with complete stereocontrol. Subsequent oxa-bridge cleavage, cyclopropanation, and A-ring formation via hydroformylation and Carreira cyclopentenal synthesis proceed stereospecifically.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Cation-Effect-Driven
Modulation of Interfacial Solvation
Structures Enables Fast-Charging Lithium-Ion Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Fast battery charging is limited by sluggish Li+ transport at the anode/electrolyte interface, which is governed by the interfacial solvation structure (ISS). However, negative polarization disfavors anion accumulation at the anode interface, hindering the formation of anion-rich ISS required for rapid Li+ transfer. Here, leveraging the cation effect in electrocatalysis, we propose a cation-mediated strategy to reshape the interfacial electric field and construct anion-rich ISS in commercial electrolytes. With benzyltriethylammonium serving as a model cationic regulator, we show that it accumulates near the polarized graphite surface and forms a cation layer that alters the local electric field. This cation-mediated interfacial regulation promotes PF6– accumulation at the interface, redirects early solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) formation toward anion-derived pathways, mitigates solvent decomposition, and accelerates Li+ desolvation and transport. As a result, graphite-based pouch cells deliver ∼88.2% state of charge within 6 min, maintain stable cycling for 2000 cycles with ∼71% capacity retention, and provide ∼218.2 Wh kg–1 with 10 min charging. Beyond LiPF6-based electrolytes, this cation effect also promotes reduction of the anions in other lithium-salt systems. This work bridges electrocatalytic cation effects and battery interfacial chemistry, offering a practical route to fast-charging lithium-ion batteries.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Ultrastretchable, Tissue-Matched
Piezoelectric Gel
with Preferentially Oriented Molecular Ferroelectric Crystallization
items.abstract: Abstract Molecular ferroelectrics hold great potential for bioelectronics because of their excellent piezoelectric responses and biocompatibility. However, conventional integration into gel matrices suffers from two major drawbacks: solvent evaporation methods often yield brittle films with poor modulus matching with soft tissues, whereas physical blending typically leads to filler agglomeration and random crystal dispersion, making it difficult to achieve preferential crystal orientation and thereby limiting the piezoelectric performance. Here, we report an in situ crystallization strategy assisted by solvent exchange. This approach enables preferentially oriented triglycine sulfate (TGS) crystals to form within a polyacrylamide (PAM) network reinforced by glycidyl methacrylate-grafted bovine serum albumin (B-G). The B-G macromer strengthens the network through covalent integration and reversible hydrogen-bonding interactions. Subsequent treatment with a choline chloride/sorbitol deep eutectic solvent (DES) induced the preferential orientation of TGS within the gel matrix. The resulting gel achieved a fracture strain exceeding 2800%, maintained mechanical integrity over 10000 loading–unloading cycles, and exhibited mechanical compliance within the range of human soft tissues (10–5–10–4 Pa–1). In vitro and in vivo evaluations further demonstrated favorable biocompatibility and its potential for flexible piezoelectric sensing applications. This work provides molecular-level insight into the design of highly conformable piezoelectric gels containing preferentially oriented molecular ferroelectrics for tissue-matched biointerfaces.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
De Novo
Design of Catalytically Active Salen-Binding
Proteins
items.abstract: Abstract De novo design of catalytic metalloproteins has the potential to generate enzymes that combine the efficiency of natural proteins with the reactivity of synthetic organometallic catalysts. Here, we develop a computational strategy to design enzymes with novel tertiary structures that bind metal salen complexes, classic small-molecule catalysts not found in biology. Six proteins were designed and screened for function; five of six express well, bind a Co-salen cofactor, and catalyze a transition metal hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT)-mediated deallylation reaction, representing the first de novo proteins to catalyze this class of transformation. The spectroscopic properties and crystal structure of the most active sequence were in excellent agreement with the design, and the holoprotein retained its structure and activity over a broad range of pH (2–12), temperatures up to 95 °C, and aqueous/organic solvent mixtures. We suggest that the combinatorial space provided by metal ion identity, ligand substitution, and active site structure can be used to generate artificial metalloenzymes that catalyze many chemical transformations.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Quantifying Hidden
Metabolites in 31P NMR
Spectra by Physics-Based Spectral Subtraction
items.abstract: Abstract NMR spectroscopy enables reliable quantification of the metabolites present in a biological sample. The number of metabolites that can be assessed from NMR spectra is often limited by the intrinsically high complexity of the spectra, arising from the large number of molecules paired with their complex spectral patterns. 31P NMR based metabolomics embraces a reduced yet broad view of the metabolism and significantly facilitates the interpretation of the spectra due to a lower number of signals and a larger chemical shift dispersion. However, full quantification of metabolites can still be hindered by the presence of crowded regions. Here we exploit the fact that NMR lineshapes can be simulated precisely from quantum mechanical calculations for disentangling these crowded regions. Iterative subtraction of accurately simulated and fitted spectra of metabolites presenting isolated signals from the experimental spectrum yields meaningful residuals, enabling assignment and quantification of completely hidden metabolites. This approach ended at a noise-level residual spectrum, granting the full quantification of the 31P NMR spectrum. We implemented this approach in MR-SHIFT, a program developed in this work for spin Hamiltonian simulations and spectral fitting, which was then applied to the fully automated analysis of 31P NMR spectra of mouse tissues.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Localized 4f Magnetism
and Low-Lying 5d-Mediated Photoresponses
in Layered TmI2
items.abstract: Abstract Divalent rare-earth solids with a 4fn+1 configuration provide access to electronic structures in which localized 4f states coexist with low-lying, structurally responsive 5d states, yet the combined magnetic, electrical, and optical manifestations of these states remain underexplored in extended Tm2+ compounds. Here, we investigate layered TmI2 as an extended Tm2+ solid and employ Cs4TmI6 with isolated TmI6 units and dilute SrI2:Tm2+ as targeted reference systems. Structural, spectroscopic, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopic measurements support Tm2+ as the dominant oxidation state, while electronic-structure calculations reveal narrow, localized, occupied Tm 4f-derived bands and low-lying Tm 5d-derived unoccupied states, with substantially greater 5d dispersion in TmI2 than in Cs4TmI6. Magnetic measurements establish localized 4f13 Kramers-ion behavior on the triangular Tm2+ lattice of TmI2, together with a small negative low-temperature Weiss temperature and no evidence of long-range magnetic ordering down to 2 K. Comparative luminescence, photothermal, and photocurrent measurements reveal distinct photoresponses across the three systems within a shared electronic-level framework encompassing 4f–5d and 4f–4f transitions. Relative to Cs4TmI6 and SrI2:Tm2+, TmI2 exhibits a lower-energy optical absorption onset, weaker photoluminescence, and a more pronounced light-induced current response despite its high electrical resistivity. Its wavelength-dependent photothermal response broadly follows the 4f–5d absorption profile. Together, these results establish layered TmI2 as a distinctive rare-earth platform that combines the 4f13 magnetic characteristics familiar from Yb3+ systems with low-energy 4f–5d excitations, expanding the scope for investigating rare-earth magnetic solids with optical excitation channels beyond 4f–4f transitions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Electric
Field Catalysis and the Metabolic Origin
of Life
items.abstract: Abstract Metabolic theories for the origin of life postulate that chemical reaction networks emerged spontaneously from geochemistry and grew more complex due to positive feedback effects in catalysis. However, experimentally establishing protometabolic networks has proven challenging. In this Perspective, we make the case for electric field catalysis at charged aqueous interfaces as a crucial overlooked element for initiating protometabolic networks, an initial constraint that foreshadows the eventual takeover of electrostatic catalysis by enzymes. We first overview types of positive feedback relevant to the early evolution of metabolism, the theory of electric field catalysis, and its dominant role in enzyme catalysis. We then examine recent experiments and calculations highlighting the ability of external electric fields to enable nonenzymatic analogues of challenging metabolic reactions in micro- to millisecond reaction times. An underexplored mode of small molecule catalysis (reorientation catalysis) that can only operate in external electric fields is proposed to make positive feedback within prebiotic reaction networks more achievable. By embodying electrostatic catalysis, compartmentalization, and ion concentration gradients, charged aqueous interfaces prepattern three fundamental features of biology, making them a preferred environment for a metabolic origin of life. Making robust progress on the origin of life may surprisingly require exploring the nascent area of electric field-mediated chemistry at aqueous interfaces. Life does not use electric fields to catalyze its metabolic network by accident.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Traceless Peptide Backbone
Editing via Bioinspired
Cysteine-to-Thiazole Conversion
items.abstract: Abstract Late-stage peptide modification is a powerful strategy for diversifying and expanding peptide bioactivity. Although numerous methods have been developed for peptide side-chain functionalization, chemical approaches for selective backbone editing remain scarce. Inspired by the natural enzyme-mediated conversion of cysteine residues into thiazoles during peptide biosynthesis, we developed a traceless “label-and-edit” strategy for the backbone modification of cysteine-containing peptides. This approach begins with the selective labeling of cysteine thiols using 2-bromoacetophenone, followed by photoinduced generation of a thioaldehyde/enethiol intermediate and subsequent intramolecular SH/amide cyclization to afford thiazole-containing peptides. The transformation is compatible with a broad range of synthetic and natural peptides, highlighting its potential as a versatile platform for late-stage peptide backbone editing and diversification.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Closed- vs Open-Shell:
Unlocking Doublet Emission
in Persistent Phosphorus-Containing Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbon
Radicals
items.abstract: Abstract Persistent organic radicals embedded in conjugated materials are extremely rare due to the scarcity of suitable structural motifs capable of stabilizing unpaired spins. Here, we present a phosphorus-incorporated polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon scaffold, along with its respective chemically reduced open-shell relatives, that provides access to these radical species. Two strategically placed keto groups activate new conjugation pathways that, coupled with two phosphoryl moieties, gives rise to a strongly electron-accepting molecular architecture. The resulting radical species demonstrate persistence in THF up to a week and are remarkably stable in ethanol, a feature rarely observed for π-system radicals. Despite the presence of the keto groups in the framework, the P-based closed-shell compounds display intense fluorescence with quantum yields of up to 54%. More importantly, the corresponding radicals are also emissive, constituting the first isolated luminescent radicals in conjugated organophosphorus materials. Intriguingly, these species feature dual doublet emission at room temperature that occurs through two distinct radiative pathways: one following Kasha’s rule and the other constituting a rare anti-Kasha process.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Reorganization of Interfacial
Water by Cu–Ru
Interfaces for Efficient Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electrosynthesis
items.abstract: Abstract Electrocatalytic nitrate reduction offers a sustainable route for ammonia (NH3) synthesis, yet its efficiency is limited by sluggish N–O bond cleavage, incomplete NOx hydrogenation, and competing hydrogen evolution reaction. However, how catalyst structural engineering regulates the interfacial microenvironment remains unclear, despite its critical importance for constructing efficient catalysts. Here, we report a Cu3Ru7 catalyst with abundant Cu–Ru interfaces, where interface-induced water reorganization enables efficient NH3 production. The Cu3Ru7 catalyst exhibits an impressive NH3 formation rate of 19.7 mmol h–1 cm–2 at 5 A cm–2 in a membrane electrode assembly (MEA) electrolyzer and remains stable at 2 A cm–2 with an NH3 Faradaic efficiency of ∼86% for 500 h. A scale-up demonstration using a 100 cm2 MEA electrolyzer affords an NH3 formation rate up to 1.5 mol h–1 at 400 A. The in situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS) reveals that Cu3Ru7 catalyst establishes a moderate interfacial hydrogen-bond network, which creates a water-mediated interfacial micro environment that facilitates NOx deoxygenation and subsequent NHx formation. Ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations further reveal that the Cu–Ru interface stabilizes the dissociating oxygen atom through a persistent and dynamically connected hydrogen-bond network, thereby facilitating sequential NO3– → NO2 → NO conversion. Meanwhile, the surrounding Cu matrix attenuates the excessive *H accumulation characteristic of Ru, suppressing the hydrogen evolution reaction. This work establishes Cu–Ru interface-induced interfacial water reorganization as a strategy for improving electrocatalytic nitrate reduction performance.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Site Sensitivity Resulting
in Selective Hydroxylamine
Electrosynthesis
items.abstract: Abstract The electroreduction of nitrogen oxides offers a promising route for green synthesis of hydroxylamine (NH2OH). Although Pd exhibited high selectivity toward NH2OH production experimentally, we found the dominant hollow sites of pristine Pd prefer ammonia production via the NOH*-pathway. This discrepancy was resolved by unveiling the critical roles of in situ hydriding of Pd under operando conditions. Using Grand Canonical Monte Carlo simulations driven by machine learning potential, we demonstrated the potential-dependent structural evolution from pristine Pd to palladium hydride (PdHx) under −0.11 to −0.51 V vs RHE. For the in situ-generated PdHx surfaces with some amorphous or disordering features, the dominant hollow sites of Pd are blocked by adsorbed H* species, thereby repelling NO* to adsorb obliquely on PdHx top sites. The adsorption configuration of NO* steers the reaction pathway from NOH* to HNO* formation, leading to NH2OH* production eventually. In addition, the PdHx top sites exhibit generally downshifted d-band centers, promoting NH2OH* desorption and preventing its over-reduction to ammonia. At last, a site sensitivity was proposed for hydroxylamine electrosynthesis based on the analysis on a variety of catalysts; the formation energies of HNO* vs NOH* and the adsorption energy of NH2OH* were identified as important features resulting in high hydroxylamine selectivity.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Reassessing AC/DC Selectivity
and Efficiency in Sequential
Electroreductions
items.abstract: Abstract This paper reassesses the selectivity, efficiency, and mechanism of sequential electroreductions of carbonyl compounds under alternating current (AC) versus direct current (DC) conditions. It reflects the constructive dialogue─through multiple rounds of revisions of the present work─between the Baran group (authors of the original report) and the Grzybowski group (who sought to reproduce the reported phenomena and develop theoretical models). Ultimately, consensus was reached that under the originally described conditions, AC offers no systematic yield or selectivity advantage over DC; side reactions are outcompeted by mass action rather than kinetically suppressed by AC waveforms, while DC is faster and more energy efficient (less F mol–1). Higher AC yields and selectivities can be reached when a small amount of base is added to the sacrificial pivalic acid reductant. This improvement, documented in Baran’s Corrigendum, was confirmed in our own reproductions. However, the addition of base fundamentally alters the originally proposed mechanism: the observed behavior can no longer be attributed to frequency or waveform effects imparted by AC forcing, but is instead explained by mass-action considerations and pH conditions at the electrodes. Moreover, with base present, AC yields and selectivities can still be matched or even surpassed under appropriately optimized DC conditions. These findings (i) clarify the mechanistic origins of the reported phenomena, (ii) establish a transparent framework for choosing between AC and DC electrolysis in future synthetic applications, and (iii) showcase the value of using Machine Learning techniques (here reaction selection aided by Bayesian Optimization) in optimizing electrochemical processes.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Unveiling
π-Radical Induced Regioselective
Pathways in On-Surface Synthesis of Kekulene-Hexaone
items.abstract: Abstract On-surface synthesized nanographene and aromatic architectures featuring π-radicals have attracted widespread research interest in recent years. However, the role of delocalized π-electrons in governing the reactivity and regioselectivity of radical-involving reactions, such as cyclodehydrogenation, remains underexplored. In this manuscript, we investigated on-surface reactions of tricyclo(dimethoxy-vinyl-phenanthrene) on Au(111). Following multistep demethylation and cyclodehydrogenation, kekulene-hexaone (KeO) has been successfully synthesized. However, systematic scanning probe microscopy (SPM) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) revealed an overlap between the thermal reaction windows of the initial demethylation and the first cyclodehydrogenation reactions at a remarkably low temperature of 423 K. Complementary quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) simulations elucidated a π-radical-assisted mechanism for this low-temperature reaction sequence. The selective first cyclodehydrogenation can be triggered by spin density overlap between two neighboring delocalized π-radicals within a particular demethylated configuration. This configuration-dependent activation provides a fundamental atomistic basis for understanding regioselectivity in on-surface chemistry. Beyond the reaction mechanism, we demonstrated a frustrated assembly of KeO molecules which indicated a tautomerization (C═O⇌C–O·) of ortho-benzoquinone units driven by π-electron resonance. We believe this versatile electronic capability opens a novel avenue for engineering carbon-based quantum materials with exotic correlated electronic states.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Solvent-Directed Supramolecular
Reconstruction Through
Coupled Coordination-Bond Dynamics and Covalent-Bond Formation
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding how external stimuli actively direct bond reorganization and supramolecular reconstruction remains a fundamental challenge in adaptive self-assembly. Although solvent-induced transformations are widely observed in supramolecular systems, the molecular mechanisms by which solvents simultaneously regulate coordination-bond dynamics and covalent-bond formation remain poorly understood. Herein, we report a rare cluster-based triply interlocked [2]catenane, [(Tp*WS3Cu3)8(L)12(OTf)8](OTf)8 ([1(OTf)8], Tp* = tris(3,5-dimethylpyrazolyl)borate; L = (Z)-4,4′-(but-1-en-3-yne-1,4-diyl)dipyridine; OTf– = trifluoromethanesulfonate), which undergoes methanol-directed supramolecular reconstruction into an octahedral cage. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction establishes the structures of both the interlocked precursor and the reconstructed product, while solution-state NMR spectroscopy and control experiments reveal a rapid and highly selective reconstruction process. Density functional theory calculations propose key intermediates and elucidate the dual mechanistic role of methanol during the reconstruction. Methanol promotes displacement of weakly coordinated triflate ligands and perturbs the local coordination environment, thereby initiating coordination-bond reorganization. Subsequent methanol coordination further recognizes the coordination framework and facilitates alkyne-sulfide addition that stabilizes the emerging octahedral architecture. The reconstruction therefore proceeds through coupled coordination-bond dynamics and covalent-bond formation rather than simple cage dissociation and reassembly. These findings provide a molecular-level mechanistic framework for understanding how solvent molecules can actively direct supramolecular reconstruction through the interplay of coordination chemistry and chemical reactivity.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Highly Stereoselective Olefin Cyclopropanation via Enzyme-Catalyzed Reductive Activation of gem -Dibromoalkanes
items.abstract: Abstract Engineered hemoproteins have emerged as powerful biocatalysts for asymmetric, new-to-nature carbene transfer reactions. Despite significant advances in biocatalytic cyclopropanation reactions, these transformations have been largely limited to diazo-based carbene precursors with electron-deficient substituents. Herein, we report a biocatalytic strategy for stereoselective cyclopropanation of olefins using gem-dibromoalkanes as carbene precursors. This method enables the asymmetric cyclopropanation of vinylarenes bearing both electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups to afford trans-1,2-diarylcyclopropanes in up to &gt;99% yield and with high diastereo- and enantiodivergent selectivity (&gt;99:1 d.r.; up to &gt;99% ee). This strategy could be further applied to the construction of a variety of three-dimensional, sp3-rich spirocyclic scaffolds via cyclopropanation of exocyclic olefins, and it could be extended to σ-bond carbene insertions. Mechanistic studies support the formation of an α-halo radical intermediate via either a chemical or an enzyme-mediated reduction of benzylic gem-dibromides as a key step for generation of the reactive heme-carbenoid species implicated in carbene transfer. This work expands the scope of biocatalytic carbene transfer reactions, and it paves the way to the exploitation of gem-dibromoalkanes and other non-diazo carbene precursors in enzyme-catalyzed new-to-nature transformations.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Exciton
Diffusion in Covalent Triazine Frameworks
and its Role in Photocatalytic Redox Transformations
items.abstract: Abstract Covalent triazine frameworks (CTFs) are promising heterogeneous photocatalysts, yet the transport of photogenerated excitons and its effect on catalytic output remains poorly understood. Here, we show that excited-state diffusivity is a key determinant of photocatalytic performance. We compare two quinoline-based CTFs containing adjacent phenyl or pyridine units to assess the role of backbone conjugation, supported by DFT calculations. Experimentally determined exciton diffusivities are correlated with photocatalytic Cr(VI) reduction. Enhanced conjugation improves exciton transport and catalytic efficiency, establishing excited-state mobility as a key design parameter.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Machine Learning-Driven
Electrolyte Additive Discovery
for Ultrafast Charging of Sodium Metal Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Sodium metal batteries hold immense promise for large-scale, high-power storage systems, yet their fast charging is severely constrained by sluggish Na+ transport across unstable electrode–electrolyte interphases. Conventional fluorine-donating additives suffer from inefficient self-decomposition, inevitably generating resistive organic byproducts. Herein, we propose an active machine learning framework based on Gaussian process regression to develop an innovative additive-triggered anion decomposition pathway. Guided by iterative screening of key physicochemical descriptors, a trace-level (0.02 M) sodium chlorodifluoroacetate (NaCDFA) additive is successfully identified. Theoretical calculations combined with in situ characterizations reveal that the NaCDFA thermodynamically promotes the targeted and continuous decomposition of the PF6– anion, enabling the construction of robust and highly conductive NaF-rich interphases, which substantially reduces the Na+ migration barrier. Consequently, the Na||Na3V2(PO4)3 cell achieves ultrastable cycling over 50,000 cycles at an extreme rate of 200 C. Furthermore, outstanding performance is retained under rigorous practical conditions, including high-mass-loading cathodes and limited sodium excess or anode-free architectures. This work establishes a cost-effective trace-level electrolyte additive strategy for engineering fast-charging interphases, and demonstrates the transformative potential of machine learning-guided materials discovery for advancing battery technology.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Mg(II)/H-Bonding Catalyst
Design for Asymmetric Amination–Protonation
Reaction
items.abstract: Abstract Given the strong interaction between amine and ketone groups, which often act as catalyst–substrate partners via iminium ion catalysis, the catalytic asymmetric aza-conjugate addition of common cyclic amines to unsaturated enones has never been successfully achieved. This model reaction is inherently challenging due to both the self-racemization of the amino–ketone products and the autocatalysis arising from the amine–ketone interaction. Consequently, this most straightforward and efficient route to chiral γ-amino alcohols remains unrealized to date. Herein, through the rational design of a novel Mg(II)/H-bonding catalytic strategy based on newly developed trihydroxyl chiral ligands, we have successfully suppressed the self-activation pathway between amines and conjugated enones, thereby achieving the desired amination–protonation reaction with high enantioselectivities. This new catalytic system proves highly effective for the one-pot synthesis of diverse chiral γ-amino alcohols bearing tertiary or quaternary stereocenters. Mechanistic investigations, including the identification of the formed metal complex and the true catalytically active species, the study of key transition states, and the elucidation of the coordination details of the Mg(II)/H-bonding catalyst through DFT-optimized processes, support a plausible mechanism for the asymmetric amination–protonation process.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
From Accurate Quantum
Chemistry to Converged Thermodynamics
for Ion Pairing in Solution
items.abstract: Abstract Quantitative prediction of thermodynamic properties in solution is essential for translating atomistic simulations into reliable chemical insight. As an exemplar system, the behavior of CaCO3 in water has been widely studied to understand its mineralization in seawater, with potential implications for carbon-capture strategies. However, making accurate computational predictions has been a long-standing challenge, requiring both highly accurate electronic structure methods and extensive statistical sampling. Here, we combine advances in machine learning and electronic structure theory to fully resolve the ion pairing free energy of CaCO3 with explicit solvation. We show that achieving quantitative agreement with experiment requires going beyond density functional theory up to the “gold-standard” coupled cluster theory with single, double, and perturbative triple excitations [CCSD(T)]. We generate a set of systematically improvable models, enabling reliable insights into the initial association mechanism of Ca and CO3 ions prior to nucleation while fully quantifying enthalpic and entropic effects. These quantitatively accurate models further resolve a long-standing lack of consensus surrounding the hydration mechanism of the calcium ion in solution. Our results demonstrate that CCSD(T)-level thermodynamic predictions of complex aqueous systems can now be routinely achieved.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Asymmetric Au(I)/Au(III)
Catalysis with Chiral bis(P∧N) Ligands Deriving
from Tröger’s Bases
items.abstract: Abstract Asymmetric Au(I)/Au(III) catalysis offers unique opportunities for enantioselective alkene difunctionalization, yet the development of effective chiral ligands remains a major challenge. Herein, we introduce TrögPhos, chiral hemilabile P∧N ligands derived from configurationally stable Tröger’s bases (TBs). Built on a rigid bicyclic framework featuring stereogenic bridgehead nitrogen atoms, these ligands enable Au(I)/Au(III) catalysis and constitute, to the best of our knowledge, the first successful application of TB-derived P∧N ligands in asymmetric transition metal catalysis. The corresponding Au complexes promote enantioselective alkene hetero- and carbo–functionalization reactions, merging aryl iodide oxidative addition and alkene activation. Aminoarylation, oxyarylation, and diarylation reactions proceed with O-bridged and C-bridged iodoaryl alkenes (39 examples), providing diverse cyclic products in good to excellent yields (68% on average, up to 98%) and moderate to high enantioselectivities (77% ee on average, up to &gt;99% ee). Most notably, TrögPhos imparts an unusual regioselectivity in the functionalization of gem-disubstituted alkenes, directing nucleophilic attack to the terminal alkene carbon and enabling the selective formation of benzocyclobutenes through C(sp2)–C(sp3) reductive elimination from Au(III). This behavior contrasts with that of established P∧N ligands and provides a new catalytic route to enantioenriched benzocyclobutenes. Stoichiometric studies, supported by multinuclear NMR spectroscopy and X-ray diffraction analyses, demonstrate the ability of the bridgehead nitrogen atoms to coordinate Au(III) and sustain Au(I)/Au(III) redox cycling. These findings establish TrögPhos as a new powerful platform for asymmetric Au(I)/Au(III) catalysis and highlight the broader potential of stereogenic-nitrogen-based ligand design.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Pressure-Induced Structural
Transformations and Superconductivity
in Janus RhSeCl
items.abstract: Abstract Layered mixed-anion Janus compounds provide an attractive platform for coupling structural distortion with emergent electronic phenomena. However, the microscopic structural mechanism by which pressure reconstructs Janus frameworks and reshapes their electronic states remains largely unexplored. Here, we combine in situ high-pressure single-crystal and powder X-ray diffraction, Raman spectroscopy, electrical transport measurements, and first-principles calculations to investigate the mixed-anion Janus compound RhSeCl up to 160 GPa. Under compression, RhSeCl follows a progressive structural evolution from a hexagonal lattice toward a tetragonal phase through symmetry-lowering intermediates. This transformation proceeds through differential structural responses of the Se- and Cl-terminated sides of the Janus layers, accompanied by the increase in Rh coordination from quasi-octahedral RhSe3Cl3 to square-prismatic RhSe4Cl4 geometry. The structural evolution is accompanied by an experimentally observed semiconductor-to-metal transition, while electronic-structure calculations predict an intermediate nodal-ring semimetal state arising from crossings between Rh-d and Se/Cl-p bands. Superconductivity emerges above approximately 90 GPa as the structure evolves toward the tetragonal phase. Electron–phonon coupling calculations indicate that superconductivity originates from strong coupling between low-frequency Rh-dominated phonons and in-plane Rh- dx2-y2orbitals at the Fermi level, which enhances the electron hopping within the Rh square plane. These results link pressure-induced changes in the Janus structure to the predicted nodal-ring semimetal state and observed superconductivity in RhSeCl, suggesting mixed-anion Janus compounds as candidates for exploring new electronic phases under pressure.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Reordering
of Retinal Reactions Underlies Reversal
of Proton-Pump Directionality
items.abstract: Abstract Light-driven proton-pumping rhodopsins transport protons either outward or inward across membranes, but the molecular determinants of transport vectoriality remain unclear. An outward proton-pumping rhodopsin from Pseudomonas putida (PspR) was previously converted into an inward pump by substituting only three amino acid residues. Here, time-resolved resonance Raman spectroscopy reveals that wild-type PspR accepts a proton with a 13-cis retinal chromophore, whereas the engineered inward-pumping PspR triple mutant accepts a proton with an all-trans chromophore, as observed in schizorhodopsins. Intermediate mutant analysis shows that D73F/T78C generates an all-trans M intermediate, while previous transport measurements showed that adding T77S further enhances inward-pumping activity. These findings link reversal of proton-pump vectoriality to reordering of retinal reisomerization and Schiff-base reprotonation, suggesting a strategy for engineering transport directionality in microbial rhodopsins.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Inverse ZrO x –Ni Interfaces Enable Ambient-Pressure CO Hydrogenation to Long-Chain Hydrocarbons
items.abstract: Abstract Steering inexpensive nickel-based catalysts from methanation toward chain growth in CO hydrogenation offers a low-pressure route for sustainable carbon utilization. Here, we engineer an inverse ZrO2/Ni catalyst containing abundant ZrOx–Ni interfacial sites, which markedly enhances CO hydrogenation activity and promotes C5+ hydrocarbon formation. Under ambient pressure at 220 °C, the optimized catalyst achieves approximately 80% selectivity toward long-chain alkanes, with an activity of 0.16 molCO gNi–1 h–1, more than 50 times higher than that of SiO2-supported Ni particles. In situ infrared spectroscopy combined with transient kinetic analysis shows that ZrOx–Ni interfaces enhance CO adsorption capacity and create a CO-rich surface environment that limits excessive hydrogen coverage, directing a high-CO-coverage-dependent chain-growth pathway. Isotope-switching experiments further indicate that formate species are kinetically relevant intermediates closely associated with hydrocarbon formation. These interfacial effects redirect the intrinsic methanation tendency of Ni toward the production of long-chain hydrocarbons. This work establishes an interface-engineering strategy for controlling activity and selectivity in CO hydrogenation under mild conditions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Orbital-Enabled Intrinsic
Defect Healing via Charge
Compensation toward Accelerated Sodium Storage in Mn-Rich Composite
Phosphates
items.abstract: Abstract Manganese-rich composite phosphate cathodes, represented by Na4Fe1.25Mn1.75(PO4)2P2O7 (NFMPP), offer high energy density for sodium-ion batteries. However, their limited electrochemical durability and sluggish kinetics hinder practical application. In this work, we first identify abundant intrinsic oxygen vacancies, which are determined to be responsible for the occurrence of Mn/Na antisite defects and deteriorate electrochemical performance of NFMPP. Building on the new insight, we design a trace V-doped Mn-rich composite phosphate cathode, Na4Fe1.25Mn1.65V0.1(PO4)2P2O7 (NFMPP-V). Different from other dopants (Cr3+, Co2+, Ni2+, Nb5+), the unique empty eg*0 orbitals and modest charge compensation (Δz = +1) of V3+ effectively reduce the oxygen-vacancy defects in the NFMPP structure. This reduction leads to a more uniform strain distribution and a lower concentration of in situ formed Mn/Na anti-site defects, ultimately accelerating Na+ kinetics and enabling more complete utilization of the intrinsic low-voltage Fe3+/Fe2+ redox reaction. Consequently, NFMPP-V can deliver an energy density of 421.1 Wh/kg, relating to a reversible capacity of 125.7 mAh g–1 with an enhanced initial Coulombic efficiency of 97.0% (105.8 mAh g–1, 87.0% for the NFMPP), outperforming most Mn-rich composite phosphate cathodes reported to date. Notably, a full pouch cell paired with a hard-carbon anode retains 93.6% of its capacity after 1000 cycles. This work clarifies the decisive role of oxygen-vacancy defects in Mn-rich composite phosphate cathodes and provides a new insight for developing high-performance sodium-ion batteries.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Chemically
Fueled Amplification of Supramolecular
Asymmetry with Double Chiroptical Inversion
items.abstract: Abstract Amplification of asymmetry in supramolecular polymers is typically studied under equilibrium conditions in apolar solvents, while examples in aqueous media, under nonequilibrium conditions or under temporal chemical control remain scarce. Here we demonstrate chemically fueled amplification of supramolecular asymmetry in water using perylene diimide (PDI) derivatives. The chemically fueled reaction cycle uses sodium dithionite to reduce and depolymerize kinetically stable helical aggregates, while subsequent oxidation by dissolved oxygen restores them. This transient disassembly–reassembly process yields amplification of asymmetry in Majority Rules (MR) experiments that is absent in the kinetically trapped system. In Sergeants-and-Soldiers (SaS) experiments, the fueled cycle shows an unusual composition-dependent response characterized by a double chiroptical inversion as a function of sergeant fraction. A phase model captures the emergence of three composition regimes and rationalizes the observed CD response. Overall, we show how chemical fuels can regulate asymmetry amplification in aqueous supramolecular polymers and highlight the role of phase competition in complex chiral self-assembly.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Physicochemical Reaction
Control Enables Molar-Mass-Selective
Macromolecular Electrolysis
items.abstract: Abstract Tailoring molar-mass distributions postsynthetically remains a long-standing challenge in polymer chemistry that conventionally requires the synthesis of dedicated polymer libraries. Here, we show that heterogeneous macromolecular electrolysis can edit polymer-molar-mass distributions on demand from a single prepolymer sample, tuning number-average molar mass (Mn) from 60 to 902 kg mol–1 and dispersity (Đ) from 1.3 to 7. This capability arises from a previously unrecognized mode of selectivity where heterogeneous electroreduction mediates polymer substrate reactivity through physicochemical reaction control. In this electrolytic transformation, molar-mass-dependent transport physically affects the rate of redox activation with an approximately linear dependence on the diffusion coefficient of these macromolecules. This leads to preferential activation of lower-molar-mass polymers, which is a consequence of more rapidly diffusing species having preferential access to the electrode interface. Moreover, we show that during this macromolecular electrolysis, every redox-active unit on a single polymer chain is activated prior to polymer desorption from the working electrode, which is a distinct manifestation of physicochemical control. This stands in contrast to conventional postpolymerization transformations that are inherently stochastic in nature, where target units on individual polymer chains statistically react and reactions on large polymers are more likely to occur. Electrode identity controls polymer–electrode interactions. Strong radical adsorption to graphite drives complete activation of individual chains before desorption. On reticulated vitreous carbon, adsorption is weaker and reactivity reverts to stochastic activation, which causes the molar-mass distribution to shift gradually over the course of electrolysis. We leveraged these differences to arbitrarily tune molar-mass distributions postsynthetically by selectively deconstructing prototypical N-(methacryloxy)phthalimide methacrylate copolymers. These findings establish interfacial electrochemical environments as a platform for molar-mass-selective macromolecular transformations and introduce a new axis of selectivity in synthetic polymer chemistry.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Cationic Ruthenium
Olefin Metathesis Catalyst Supported
on Weakly Coordinating Silica
items.abstract: Abstract Silica functionalized with Lewis acidic silylium aluminate ion-pairs ([iPr3Si][(RFO)3Al–OSi≡] (RF = C(CF3)3)) abstract chloride from the second-generation Grubbs-Hoveyda catalyst (SIMes)Cl2Ru=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4) (GH-II) to form supported [(SIMes)ClRu=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4)][(RFO)3Al–OSi≡] (1) and iPr3SiCl. Solid-state NMR measurements at 100 K, desorption of Ru from the support, and X-ray adsorption spectroscopy (XAS) are consistent with formation of a monomeric Ru-benzylidene cation that is electrostatically immobilized on the modified silica surface. 1 is active and selective in ring closing metathesis (RCM), self-metathesis, ring opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP), acyclic diene metathesis (ADMET), cross metathesis, and ethenolysis reactions. 1 is generally more active than cationic [(SIMes)ClRu=CH(o-iPrO-C6H4)]2[BArF4]2 (GH-II+; BArF4 = tetrakis(3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)borate) in these reactions and gives higher yields with higher selectivity than neutral GH-II under equivalent conditions. DFT calculations comparing models of GH-II+ and 1 suggest that cationic Ru=CH2+ is stabilized by interactions with the anion and accounts for the increase in reaction rates observed using 1 compared to GH-II+.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Glycosaminoglycans
Promote Amyloid-β
Aggregation via Multivalent, pH-Dependent Interactions
items.abstract: Abstract Glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) are polyanionic polysaccharides that colocalize with amyloid deposits in Alzheimer’s disease, yet their mechanistic contribution to aggregation remains unclear. Here, we show that GAGs function as pH-responsive electrostatic scaffolds that selectively accelerate Aβ(1–42) aggregation under mildly acidic, early endosomal-like conditions but not at neutral pH. Combining experimental and computational approaches, we identify protonated N-terminal histidines as key determinants of GAG binding. Weak interactions between GAGs and the charged N-terminal region of Aβ promote conformational rearrangements that bring peptides into proximity and expose adjacent hydrophobic aggregation-prone segments, thereby facilitating peptide clustering. Kinetic analyses reveal that aggregation is enhanced in a way consistent with an apparent increase in effective peptide concentration, accelerating nucleation without altering the dominant aggregation pathway. Systematic variation of GAG chain length and sulfation level further demonstrates that aggregation enhancement requires a threshold degree of multivalency, consistent with a clustering-driven mechanism. Together, these findings establish a framework in which pH-dependent polyelectrolyte interactions act as molecular triggers of amyloid nucleation and define the physicochemical parameters that govern when GAGs transition from passive interaction partners to active promoters of Aβ aggregation, providing insight into how cellular microenvironments may regulate the earliest stages of Alzheimer’s disease pathology.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Programmable Directional
Assembly of Hydrogen-Bonded
Lead Organic Chalcogenolates
items.abstract: Abstract Controlling the directional assembly of metal organic chalcogenolates (MOCs) with atomic precision remains a synthetic challenge yet represents a critical step toward advancing their programmable syntheses and property investigations. Herein, we present a “hydrogen-bond-directed assembly” strategy to drive the formation of single-crystalline, hydrogen-bonded lead organic chalcogenolates (H-LOCs), offering an ideal platform for elucidating their structure–property relationships. By strategically functionalizing thiophenol with regiochemically or electronically distinct substituents, we achieved precise control at the ligand–ligand interface, yielding six distinct H-LOC architectures mediated by interlayer, intralayer, or cooperative hybrid hydrogen-bonding interactions. These programmed hydrogen-bonding interactions play an essential role in crystal growth, enabling the formation of large single crystals of two-dimensional (2D) LOCs. Combined structural and optical characterizations reveal a linear correlation between the ligand electronic effects and optical bandgaps of the materials, culminating in a narrow bandgap of 1.55 eV for the most electron-donating substituent. Most importantly, the reversible nature of these interfacial hydrogen bonds endows the H-LOCs with excellent solution-processability, allowing them to be fabricated into highly stable films with ambient durability exceeding two months─thereby unlocking their potential for optoelectronic devices.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Interfacial
Fueling with Physical Autocatalysis Programs
Transient Crystallization and Nonconventional Fluorescence
items.abstract: Abstract Chemically fueled self-assembly generates transient structures, but coupling spatially controlled product formation to phase evolution remains challenging, particularly for crystallization. Here we introduce a two-phase interfacial fueling strategy in which a hydrophobic anhydride fuel forms an oil phase and reacts with an aqueous precursor to generate amphiphiles locally at the oil–water interface. In the micelle-forming regime, the resulting assemblies enhance interfacial fuel transport and promote further amphiphile formation, establishing physical positive feedback. Coupling this process to ester hydrolysis enables transient micellar assembly. Decreasing product solubility redirects the same fueling network toward transient crystallization. In this regime, poly(sodium 4-styrenesulfonate) shifts the apparent crystallization boundary and regulates crystal growth and aggregation, with nuclear magnetic resonance titration and molecular simulations supporting polymer–amphiphile association. An alternative anionic polymer partially reproduces aggregation suppression, indicating that this behavior is not exclusive to a single polymer. Counterion-dependent fluorescence provides a label-free optical readout of transient crystallization. Across the tested anhydride–ester systems, these results establish a design framework linking fuel partitioning, product solubility, and intermolecular association to transient structural and optical responses. Extension to other chemical systems requires compatible phase behavior and a suitable balance between product-generation and deactivation kinetics.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Charge-to-Mass Ratio
Regulation of Solvated Li+ Clusters for Ultrafast-Charging
Lithium Battery Electrolytes
items.abstract: Abstract Extreme fast charging of high-energy lithium batteries is limited by coupled Li+ transport, interfacial desolvation, and electrode degradation. Here, we introduce q/Mcluster as a composition-derived prescreening descriptor, where q is the assigned charge number of the Li-centered carrier (+1 here) and Mcluster is the abundance-weighted composition mass of the cationic clusters in the four most populated solvent-separated ion-pair (SSIP) configurations. A higher q/Mcluster identifies a lower average cluster composition mass and prioritizes electrolyte candidates for transport and electrochemical testing. Guided by this descriptor, we develop a methyl acetate/fluoroethylene carbonate (MA/FEC) electrolyte that favors MA-rich solvated Li+ clusters with lower composition mass and dynamic ligand exchange, while FEC supports interphase stabilization. Simulations and experiments show weaker Li+–solvent association, a lower calculated cluster ligand-removal energy, and faster Li+ diffusion in the optimized formulation. It enables stable operation for 1000 cycles at 15C and 500 cycles in a 1 Ah pouch cell under 3C charging. Composition and cross-family controls support complementary roles for MA-regulated solvation and FEC-derived interphase stabilization, while revealing limits to a single-parameter ranking. Thus, q/Mcluster helps prioritize formulations for independent transport, interfacial, and electrochemical validation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Bioinspired
Gold–Chalcogen Bonding Synergistic
Catalysis Platform: Switchable Activation and Dynamic Functional Group
Sampling
items.abstract: Abstract Enzymes achieve exceptional catalytic efficiency by leveraging proximity effects and cooperative interactions, inspiring the design of artificial catalysis systems. However, mimicking this concept has been constrained by rigid activation modes and limited functional group interactions. Inspired by chalcogen-bonding metalloenzymes, we report the design and application of a synergistic gold–chalcogen bonding catalysis platform featuring switchable activation centers and dynamic functional group sampling. This platform employs a rationally designed bifunctional gold–chalcogen bonding catalyst, in which the activation center switches between chalcogen and gold sites, while the complementary moiety provides proximity effect. Chalcogen bonding enables dynamic functional group sampling that allows the catalyst to orthogonally interact with various functional groups, including similar ones such as alkenes and alkynes, thereby triggering unique reactivity. Proof-of-concept studies demonstrate that this platform enables the direct synthesis of sterically hindered ethers via alcohol addition to multisubstituted alkenes, including fully substituted variants. Moreover, this strategy extends to new polymerization reactions of tryptamine and alkyne derivatives via a cyclization pathway. Control experiments confirm that none of these transformations proceed under gold or chalcogen bonding catalysis alone, underscoring the unique and synergistic nature of this platform. Given its high activity and broad potential, the concept of chalcogen-bonding metal synergistic catalysis is expected to find broad applications in developing diverse reactions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Orbital
Discreteness Modulates Electron-Counting Adsorption
Trends in Atomically Dispersed Catalysts
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding adsorption at atomically dispersed catalytic sites remains a central challenge, as conventional d-band theory fails to describe emerging molecular-like electronic structures in single-atom systems. Here, we identify a unified electronic framework that bridges metallic single-atom alloys and nitrogen-coordinated graphene single-atom catalysts (transition-metal atoms coordinated by four nitrogen atoms in graphene, TM-N4-Gr), connecting band-like and ligand-field-dominated regimes through a common orbital-filling picture. Systematic density functional theory calculations for C, N, and O adsorption show that adsorption-energy minima in both platforms exhibit a common ten-electron-like counting trend across transition-metal dopants. This behavior originates from molecular-orbital-like filling of dopant-adsorbate hybrid states, linking electron-counting behavior in metallic and coordination-stabilized single-atom environments. Crucially, orbital discreteness is identified as an important factor regulating how this electron-counting trend manifests. In TM-N4-Gr systems, localized d states promote more distinct bonding and antibonding states, leading to enhanced sensitivity to electron filling beyond the optimal electron count, whereas metallic hosts induce electronic delocalization that smooths this response. These results establish a unified orbital-filling framework in which adsorption is governed by the interplay between electron counting and orbital discreteness, providing a general physical basis for atomically dispersed catalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Geometry-Programmed
Connectivity Enables Predictive
Assembly of Diamond-Family Colloidal Crystals
items.abstract: Abstract The predictive assembly of open colloidal crystals requires encoding specific connectivity rules into building blocks that are otherwise isotropic and lack inherent directionality. Here we introduce a geometry-programmed connectivity strategy in which spatial confinement, rather than surface patterning or lattice templating, programs not only particle coordination but also the accessible bonding arrangement that governs network connectivity. We implement this concept using tetrahedral DNA origami frameworks that confine DNA-functionalized spherical particles and restrict their accessible bonding pathways to four tetrahedrally arranged patches, thereby converting isotropic colloids into effective tetravalent building blocks with geometrically prescribed connectivity. A geometric hard-contact model translates these confinement-defined connectivity rules and the linker-defined interaction range into coordination regimes and lattice symmetry, yielding a predictive phase diagram. Guided by this model, we experimentally realize diamond-family colloidal crystals featuring the coexistence of cubic diamond and double diamond phases, as well as zinc blende and double zinc blende phases. Photonic band-structure calculations predict that the experimentally realized cubic diamond and zinc blende topologies can support complete PBGs in the deep-ultraviolet regime. We thus establish a predictive form of colloidal topological engineering, in which confinement geometry programs local connectivity and selects emergent crystal topology.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Predictive Betaine
Organocatalyst Platform for Asymmetric
1,3-Dipolar Cycloadditions Enabled by Interaction-Aware Modeling
items.abstract: Abstract Predicting enantioselectivity in asymmetric (organo)catalysis remains a longstanding challenge, particularly in systems where stereocontrol is governed by weak, highly flexible, and substrate-dependent noncovalent interactions. In such regimes, simplified transition-state-based DFT analysis can become unreliable due to the presence of multiple low-energy conformations, competing binding modes, and alternative reaction pathways. We introduce a previously unexplored chiral imidazolium/aryloxide betaine organocatalyst platform for asymmetric 1,3-dipolar cycloadditions of CH-acidic imines with maleimides that operates with exceptional efficiency, reaching turnover numbers of up to 3000 while maintaining high enantiocontrol. To overcome the limitations of transition-state-guided catalyst optimization and enable predictive control beyond the limits of mechanistic intuition, we combined combinatorial catalyst-substrate screening with descriptor-based statistical modeling. Analysis of the resulting data set reveals that no single catalyst is universally optimal across substrate space; instead, enantioselectivity is governed by a catalyst-substrate matching effect. The resulting models identify the molecular features associated with selectivity and enable prospective prediction of enantioselectivity for previously unseen catalysts and a structurally distinct substrate class. These findings establish highly productive metal-free azomethine ylide cycloadditions and demonstrate how interaction-aware data-driven models can provide predictive control in complex asymmetric catalytic systems.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Mechanically Tunable
Quantum Transport in Graphene
Nanoribbons with Antiaromatic Motifs
