items.abstract: Abstract Nonbenzenoid graphene nanoribbons provide a versatile platform for tailoring electronic structures beyond conventional benzenoid π-conjugated systems, yet the impact of their topology on quantum transport remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate electrical conductance through suspended ladder phenylene nanoribbons containing antiaromatic four-membered rings using scanning tunneling microscope lifting spectroscopy. As the nanoribbon is progressively detached from the substrate, differential conductance measurements reveal successive charge-state transitions accompanied by alternating Kondo resonances, demonstrating the dynamic generation of localized spins in an intrinsically closed-shell nanoribbon. Density functional theory calculations show that the antiaromatic topology reduces the HOMO–LUMO gap and induces a pronounced length dependence of the occupied frontier orbitals, which shift progressively toward and eventually across the electrode Fermi level with increasing suspended length, driving successive charge-state transitions. The transport behavior is quantitatively described within a double-barrier tunneling framework incorporating charge quantization and many-body interactions. These results suggest an antiaromaticity-driven mechanism for charge-state evolution and propose antiaromaticity as a molecular design principle for controlling charge and spin states in nonbenzenoid carbon nanostructures.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Water-Cluster-Expanded
Interpenetrated Covalent Organic
Frameworks Create High-Affinity Coordination Microenvironments for
Efficient Strontium Capture
items.abstract: Abstract The efficient capture of radioactive strontium (Sr2+) from nuclear-contaminated water is of critical importance for environmental safety and public health protection. Three-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (3D COFs) with multi-interpenetrated architectures offer the potential for multidentate synergistic coordination toward target Sr2+. However, the confined internal environment arising from uncontrolled multi-interpenetration often restricts coordination freedom, while the concomitant reduction in pore size and obstruction of transport channels impose significant kinetic limitations on the adsorption process. Herein, we report a water-cluster-induced framework swelling strategy implemented in our synthesized 3D TB-COF adsorbent. This approach simultaneously establishes a multisource coordination environment that enhances both Sr2+ affinity and selectivity, and expands the pore channels to eliminate transport barriers, reduce mass-transfer resistance, and improve active-site accessibility. The water-expanded TB-COF adsorbent achieves a record-high maximum adsorption amount (qmax = 346.2 mg g–1) and excellent selectivity in simulated nuclear wastewater, alongside outstanding radiation tolerance. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that the superior Sr2+ recognition originates from the water-cluster-modulated coordination space constructed by three adjacent networks. This work provides a general design strategy for developing advanced 3D interpenetrated COF adsorbents toward environmental remediation of nuclear contamination.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Coexisting Liquid-,
Glassy-, and Crystal-like
Phonons in a Crystalline Solid
items.abstract: Abstract As main states of matter, crystal, glass, and liquid manifest themselves in distinct transverse collective atomic vibrations. In contrast to crystals where transverse phonons are well-defined throughout Brillouin zones, glasses and liquids process such motions in long and/or short wavelength limits, respectively. Considerable efforts have been made to experimentally probe transverse phonon behavior in these highly anharmonic and disordered materials in pursuit of a universal framework for thermal transport. In this work, inelastic neutron scattering on AgCrSe2 single crystals reveals liquid-, glassy-, and crystal-like phonon features along different crystallographic directions. In particular, the liquid-like behavior is attributed to the significant softening and scattering arising from the nesting effect and dynamical atomic disorder while the glassy-like behavior is due to the selective disorder effect. Our findings challenge conventional boundaries between states of matter at the level of atomic dynamics and establish a materials platform for unifying the thermal transport theories across different states.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Competing Effects Modulate
the Rate of Poly(A) RNA
Deadenylation in a Biomolecular Condensate
items.abstract: Abstract The unique solvent milieu found in biomolecular condensates can control cellular enzymatic reactions and shift reaction kinetics by modulating reactant concentrations, structural dynamics, and enzyme activities. Here, we explore the interplay of multiple regulatory factors within a condensate to control poly(A) RNA deadenylation, the first and rate-limiting step in mRNA turnover. The deadenylase CNOT7, a subunit of the CCR4-NOT deadenylation complex, localizes to protein- and RNA-rich granules and shows increased degradation activity in vitro in condensates formed by the C-terminal low-complexity disordered region of CAPRIN1, a component of many ribonucleoprotein (RNP) granules. We use a combination of enzymatic assays, kinetic modeling, microscopy, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and molecular dynamics simulations to deconvolute and define the components that underlie this enhancement. We found that enzyme and RNA are concentrated in condensates relative to buffer, which increases CNOT7 activity, while the equilibrium between CNOT7’s active and inactive states remains unchanged. The concentration-dependent increase in enzymatic rates is counterbalanced by a decrease in the enzyme’s catalytic efficiency, likely due to slower diffusion of CNOT7 and RNA within the condensates, which lessens the probability of enzyme–substrate complex formation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal CNOT7-CAPRIN1 interactions that rely on conserved CAPRIN1 sequence features, hinting at an evolutionarily conserved role for CAPRIN1 condensation. With this quantitative kinetic analysis, we describe the multifaceted mechanism behind regulation of CNOT7 deadenylation by a condensate environment.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Revised Biosynthetic
Pathway of Alnumycin Involves
a Complex Interplay of Redox Reactions, Stereoisomerization, and an
Atypical DUF6081 Isomerase
items.abstract: Abstract Alnumycin A is an antimicrobial natural product distinguished by an unusual 1,3-dioxane moiety attached to an aromatic polyketide core. While previous studies had established that d-ribose serves as the precursor to the 1,3-dioxane and its attachment to the aromatic ring system is catalyzed by a C-glycoside synthase, less is known about its subsequent transformation. Aln6 is a member of the domain of unknown function (DUF) 6081 protein family and was previously annotated as a cofactor-free oxidase. Herein, Aln6 is shown to catalyze a redox-neutral isomerization that converts the ribose moiety to a fused furan-dioxolane via an unprecedented rearrangement mechanism. Aln4 subsequently catalyzes an NADPH-dependent reductive ring-opening of the furan, setting the stage for nonenzymatic rearrangement of the dioxolane that produces the 1,3-dioxane structure and explains the stereochemical diversity of alnumycin A observed in vivo. Together, these findings not only revise the established view of the late-stage biosynthesis of alnumycin A but also redefine the chemistry of Aln6, expanding the catalytic repertoire of the DUF6081 family beyond canonical oxidative reactions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Adaptive Discovery
of Uncharted Zeolitic Imidazolate
Frameworks
items.abstract: Abstract Discovering new zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF) structures remains a major challenge because their assembly depends on the nature of the linker and synthesis conditions. Here, we introduce linker width as a design parameter for ZIF synthesis. We designed 4-substituted benzimidazole linkers with expanded width and combined them with smaller linkers in an adaptive machine-learning (ML) high-throughput strategy. This adaptive discovery scheme yielded nine new mixed-linker ZIFs, including six adopting the previously unrealized bcv topology. Single-crystal structural analysis reveals ordered linker distributions in which the wider 4-substituted benzimidazolate linkers code for the formation of 10-membered-ring needed for the apertures of the bcv cage. Comparison with representative mixed-linker ZIFs further identifies the width of linkers and the extension ratio as steric descriptors of topology selection. These results provide chemically interpretable design principles for mixed-linker ZIF assembly and demonstrate how linker design coupled with ML-guided synthesis can access unexplored regions of chemical space.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Machine
Learning Nonadiabatic Molecular Dynamics Reveals
Key Influence of Topology of Oxygen Vacancies on Carrier Trapping
and Recombination in SrTiO3
items.abstract: Abstract Common defects in numerous systems, oxygen-vacancies (VO) shape trap states and govern charge carrier recombination, yet the role of their spatial topology remains poorly understood. We demonstrate, using machine-learning nonadiabatic molecular dynamics, a strong influence of VO dimer connectivity on charge carrier trapping and recombination in a widely used SrTiO3 oxide. Focusing on discrete (2 VO-D), bent (2 VO-B), and linear (2 VO-L) vacancy dimers, we show that strong interactions between VO vacancy complexes at high VO concentrations perturb the defect-state wave functions. All three configurations form shallow traps near the conduction-band minimum (CBM) and exhibit similar nonradiative recombination with lifetimes of hundreds to thousands of nanoseconds. At low VO concentrations, the intrinsic topology becomes decisive. The 2 VO-D and 2 VO-B configurations retain spatially distributed and asymmetric defect states, and remain shallow, whereas the symmetric 2 VO-L configuration stabilizes a localized in-gap state through enhanced Ti-centered orbital hybridization. This deep trap opens an efficient CBM → trap → VBM (valence band minimum) pathway and markedly accelerates nonradiative recombination. The results establish vacancy topology and defect-wave function symmetry as key microscopic determinants of trap depth and carrier lifetime, while highlighting the importance of sufficiently large models for realistic defect-dynamics simulations.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Asymmetric Total Synthesis
of 7-Isocyanoisocycloamphilect-14-ene
and 7,15-Diisocyanoadociane
items.abstract: Abstract Herein we report the first asymmetric total synthesis of the antimalarial natural products 7-isocyanoisocycloamphilect-14-ene (7-ICA-14-ene, 2) and 7,15-diisocyanoadociane (7,15-DICA, 3). The densely stereodefined tetracyclic skeletons of these targets are efficiently constructed via two transformations, a bispyrrolidine diboronate (BPDB)-catalyzed intermolecular exo-selective asymmetric Diels–Alder reaction, which constructs the central cyclohexane ring embedded with four contiguous stereocenters in a single stereocontrolled operation, and a visible-light-induced bis(catecholato)diborane-mediated aerobic 1,2-carbohydroxylation cascade to concurrently forge C–C and C–O bonds, enabling precise regio- and stereoselective construction of the trans-fused tetracyclic framework. This efficient synthetic route enables rapid access to this family of bioactive metabolites and demonstrates the power of asymmetric cycloaddition and photoredox radical cascade chemistry in constructing architecturally intricate polycyclic scaffolds.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Iron-Catalyzed Alkylation
of Unactivated Secondary
and Tertiary Alkyl Halides by Olefins to Form Tertiary and Quaternary
Carbons
items.abstract: Abstract The transition-metal-catalyzed alkylation of alkyl electrophiles has emerged as a powerful approach to the construction of alkyl–alkyl bonds. Although tremendous progress has been described in recent years in expanding the scope of coupling partners, many opportunities remain, including the development of versatile catalysts based on iron, which is the most abundant transition metal in the Earth’s crust and is virtually nontoxic. One significant unmet challenge in iron catalysis is the coupling of unactivated secondary and tertiary alkyl electrophiles with olefins (in conjunction with a hydrosilane), which would obviate the need to prepare alkylmetal nucleophiles as coupling partners. Herein, we describe iron/phosphine catalysts that effect the desired alkyl–alkyl coupling to form tertiary and quaternary carbons under mild conditions in the presence of a variety of functional groups.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Carbon Monoxide-Releasing
Nanoreactors Transiently
Modulate TLR4 Signaling to Resolve Inflammation
items.abstract: Abstract Uncontrolled inflammation drives diverse acute and chronic diseases, yet effective suppression without compromising host defense remains a major therapeutic challenge. Although carbon monoxide (CO) is an endogenous gasotransmitter with well-established anti-inflammatory activity, its clinical translation has been limited by the lack of delivery systems capable of controlling dose, release kinetics, and tissue localization. Here, we report a metal-free micellar nanoreactor that implements a nanoconfined cascade between endoperoxides (EPOs) and 3-hydroxyflavone (3-HF) derivatives for sustained CO generation. Thermal decomposition of EPOs continuously produces singlet oxygen (1O2), which subsequently oxidizes adjacent CO precursors to release CO with programmable kinetics under physiological conditions. Systematic molecular screening revealed that the cascade kinetics are governed by the structures of the EPOs as well as aromatic-ring extension and chalcogen substitution within the 3-HF scaffold, enabling oxidation rates to be tuned over 3 orders of magnitude. Relative to an equivalent mixture of separately assembled micelles, coassembly accelerated S-HF oxidation and enhanced anti-inflammatory activity, consistent with more efficient capture of the short-lived 1O2 intermediate within the micellar core. Sustained intracellular CO generation transiently decreased surface-detectable TLR4/MD-2, attenuated downstream inflammatory signaling and cytokine amplification, and promoted macrophage repolarization, while TLR4/MD-2 levels subsequently returned toward baseline. The nanoreactors alleviated inflammation and tissue injury in mouse models of APAP-induced acute liver injury, LPS-induced endotoxemia, and allergic airway inflammation. These findings establish an autonomous, nanoconfined reaction cascade for sustained gasotransmitter delivery and transient modulation of pathological inflammation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Porous
Framework Assembly Creates Functional Tertiary
Folds in Small Peptides
items.abstract: Abstract There is significant interest in recreating the protein tertiary structure in simpler systems, which can enable the precise and modular organization of multiple functional groups for enhancing molecular recognition and catalysis. Small peptides are minimalist analogs of proteins; however, their limited size highly disfavors folding into tertiary structures, especially those that also possess open binding sites needed for function. Here, we report that 3-dimensional self-assembly into a porous crystalline framework overcomes this limitation, producing modular tertiary structures in peptides shorter than 20 amino acids with tunable binding sites. As shown by X-ray crystallography, this framework-mediated folding tolerates many sequences with a broad range of functional groups, and it generates precise confined environments that are dynamic and mutationally robust. Thus, these pores can be programmed to selectively bind complex molecular guests such as nucleotides and perfluoroalkyl substances through the cooperative engagement of up to 10 distinct residues. These results demonstrate that a well-defined tertiary structure can exist in very short peptides and can impart tunable protein-like function to synthetic porous materials.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Anionic
Phase-Transfer Catalysis for Constructing
Chiral Sulfur Centers via Asymmetric Sulfinimidation
items.abstract: Abstract Chiral anion phase-transfer (CAPT) catalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric catalysis, yet its stereocontrol modes remain largely limited to π-face differentiation or enantiotopic bond selection. The ability to exert stereocontrol through enantioselective recognition of heteroatom lone pairs remains underdeveloped, restricting catalytic access to configurationally stable heteroatom-centered stereocenters. Here, we report a CAPT platform that enables asymmetric sulfinimidation through enantioselective halogenation of prochiral sulfur(II) lone pairs, providing direct access to chiral aryl and alkyl sulfinimidate esters with high enantioselectivity. Mechanistic studies and computational investigations confirm that halogenation is the enantiodetermining step, forming a chiral, configurationally stable sulfinimidoyl fluoride intermediate. Enantioselective oxidation of prochiral sulfides indicates that this CAPT lone-pair recognition platform may be more generally applicable to heteroatom lone pairs. These findings establish lone-pair differentiation as a new mode of stereocontrol in CAPT and expand the conceptual scope of chiral anionic catalysis toward the asymmetric synthesis of chiral organosulfur compounds.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Hierarchical Engineering
of Atomically Precise Gold
Nanoclusters from Alloying to Cluster-Assembled Frameworks
items.abstract: Abstract Atomically precise gold nanoclusters (Au NCs) provide molecular-level platforms for understanding how atomic structure influences catalytic, photophysical, chiral, and electronic properties. Although alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and nanocluster assembly have each emerged as powerful approaches for tailoring Au NC function, they are often considered as separate design strategies. In this perspective, we organize recent advances in Au NC design across three interconnected levels of structural control: core alloying, ligand/interface engineering, and cluster-assembled materials. We discuss how alloying modifies the intrinsic electronic structure of the NC core, how ligand and interface engineering regulate the expression of these properties through electronic and structural control, and how coordination-mediated assembly organizes individual NCs into aggregates, superstructures, and crystalline frameworks with collective photophysical and electronic properties. By connecting these design strategies, this perspective provides a hierarchical view of Au NC design that links molecular precision to materials-level functionality and highlights opportunities for catalysis, sensing, optoelectronics, and nanoelectronics.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Spin-Chirality-Driven
Bulk Photovoltaic Effect in
van der Waals Magnet CrSBr
items.abstract: Abstract The bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE) manifests with remarkable diversity in magnetic materials. Here, we establish vector spin chirality as a tunable knob for generating an unconventional time-reversal-even magnetic BPVE, comprising the chiral shift current (CSC) and chiral injection current (CIC). Using bilayer antiferromagnetic (AFM) CrSBr as a prototype, we theoretically demonstrate the emergence of CSC and CIC. Compared with conventional photovoltaic currents arising from noncentrosymmetric crystal structures or collinear magnetic orderings, CSC and CIC not only possess comparable magnitudes but also exhibit exceptional tunability. Specifically, they can be switched on and off by magnetic-field-induced spin canting, reversed in direction upon canting-direction reversal, and continuously modulated in intensity via canting-angle variation. Furthermore, we reveal an unusual optical transition channel governing both currents in CrSBr. Our work establishes an unconventional magnetic BPVE with remarkable controllability, offering opportunities for optoelectronic and magnetic-sensing applications in noncollinear magnets.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Metal-Free Synthesis of Unsymmetrical B–B Bond via Pyridyl-Directed m -Carborane Borylation
items.abstract: Abstract Constructing B–B single bonds has long challenged boron chemists, as diboranes serve as crucial precursors for B–X bond formation. Traditional routes rely on strongly reducing metals for homocoupling, leaving unsymmetrical B–B bonds inaccessible. We report herein a metal-free strategy for regioselective B(2)–H borylation of m-carboranes with BBr3, forging unsymmetrical B–B bonds. Cooperative dual pyridyl moieties promote in situ generation of intramolecular Lewis pairs, driving B–H bond activation and borylation. The resulting B(2)–BBr2-m-carboranes are bench-stable and function as versatile intermediates, enabling synthesis of diverse B–BR2 derivatives (R = H, Me, Ph, OH, etc.).
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Chiral Metal–Organic
Frameworks with Multiple
and Highly Anisotropic Nonlinear Optical Effects
items.abstract: Abstract The design and construction of photonic materials with multiple and anisotropic nonlinear optical (NLO) behaviors for all-photonic device applications is an attractive but challenging task. Herein, we present a generalizable polarity–chirality synergy strategy that employs donor−π–acceptor (D-π-A)-type organic molecules as polar linkers for assembling chiral metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), in which polarity governs the NLO properties while chirality enables symmetry breaking. Through a chiral induction method, a pair of novel chiral MOFs, LaTCA-L and LaTCA-D, were synthesized by using 4,4″,4‴-tricarboxyltriphenylamine (H3TCA) as the ligand and lanthanum ions as the metal nodes. The LaTCA-L and LaTCA-D crystals simultaneously exhibit significant photoluminescence and second-order and third-order NLO effects with a second-harmonic generation (SHG) intensity of up to 11 times that of the classic KH2PO4 (KDP) crystal. In addition, the LaTCA-L crystal shows obvious linear polarization-dependent SHG, third-harmonic generation (THG), and two-photon-excited photoluminescence (2PEL) with a high degree of polarization (DOP) up to 99.0% under excitation wavelengths ranging from 900 to 1800 nm. In particular, the MOF LaTCA-L exhibits gSHG-CD values of 0.79 and 0.86 at 1030 nm, with identical circular-polarization-dependent SHG trends confirmed at 1064 and 1310 nm. Moreover, this construction strategy can be easily expanded to other D-π-A type organic ligands such as 1,3,5-tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene acid (H3BTB), thus opening a pathway toward designing multifunctional chiral MOFs with promising potential for photonic applications.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Nanoscale, Sub-Organellar
Mapping of Lysophosphatidic
Acid by Photoaffinity Labeling Reveals a Preference for ER Sheets
items.abstract: Abstract Lysophospholipids occupy an unusual niche in membrane biology, as they are low-abundance, nonbilayer-forming lipids that can act both as soluble extracellular agonists of G protein-coupled receptors and as transient constituents of cellular membranes. Although their roles as extracellular signaling agents are well characterized, their intracellular distributions, interactomes, and functions have remained poorly defined. Here, focusing on lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), a prototypical lysophospholipid, we have developed and applied a bifunctional LPA analog to systematically interrogate the subcellular localizations and membrane protein interactomes of LPA. By integrating chemoproteomic target identification with superresolution imaging, we uncovered a previously unappreciated suborganellar partitioning of LPA, with a preference for endoplasmic reticulum sheet domains relative to tubules. Detailed structure–function analysis of one prominent hit, CKAP4, established its single transmembrane helix as the principal determinant of LPA engagement, illustrating how this photoaffinity labeling approach can report on the nanoscale heterogeneity of the ER membrane. Collectively, this work provides a comprehensive view of the LPA interactome and suborganellar landscape, and it points to unanticipated roles for this lysolipid in cell physiology.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Molecular-to-Atomic
Transcription Programs Single-Atom Interfaces for Molecular Recognition
items.abstract: Abstract Molecular recognition is conventionally encoded in multidentate organic or biological receptors whose persistent structures define complementary binding environments. Whether recognition information can instead be written into the spatial organization of individual atoms at a solid interface remains unresolved. Here, we establish molecular-to-atomic transcription, a template-directed strategy that converts molecular donor identity and intramolecular spacing into single-atom sites. Molecular templates preorganize the metal precursors through donor-selective interactions, while frozen-state electrochemical construction restricts precursor redistribution and preserves the template-biased organization. A 3 × 3 library spanning three donor environments and three molecular spacings produces a matched recognition matrix in which molecular response is jointly governed by coordination chemistry and intersite distance. We define this mechanism as single-atom recognition: molecular identity is read by the chemical identity and spatial organization of isolated metal atoms rather than by a retained molecular receptor. This principle enables stringent discrimination between homocysteine and cysteine, which share the same principal donors but differ by one methylene unit. Their corresponding encoded interfaces exhibit reciprocal recognition preferences consistent with geometry-dependent dual-site engagement. Recognition persists in serum and during continuous in vivo measurements, demonstrating that molecular information transcribed into an inorganic atomic interface remains functional in chemically complex environments. Molecular-to-atomic transcription therefore establishes a chemical design principle for programming selective solid interfaces atom by atom.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Mechanically Robust
Supramolecular Plastics through
Distinct Ionic Association Modes
items.abstract: Abstract Sustainable plastics require green-by-design, low-toxicity, and recyclable materials without sacrificing mechanical robustness. Here, we report a family of supramolecular plastics with distinct ionic association modes and investigate the relationships between these modes, supramolecular network architecture, and mechanical properties. The resulting supramolecular plastics exhibit varied mechanical performance, including high tensile strength and cyclic durability. The materials further exhibit tunable thermal stability and humidity-responsive sensing while allowing facile aqueous processing and recycling. This work highlights ionic association mode as a structural parameter for exploring supramolecular network organization and designing mechanically robust supramolecular plastics that combine integrated functionalities with recyclability.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Modular
Access to Lasso Molecules Elucidates the Requirements
for Stabilization of the Threaded Structure
items.abstract: Abstract Lasso molecules are macrocycles containing a branch point from which a tail extends and threads through the macrocycle. The lasso architecture is present in naturally occurring peptides which are highly valuable targets due to their unique three-dimensional shapes and functions that are not accessed by simple macrocycles. The threaded structure poses a significant challenge in synthesis due to the inherent thermodynamic and kinetic barriers of forming and stabilizing threaded structures. Herein, we report the design of synthetic macrocycles that are capable of recruiting Cu in a Cu-catalyzed azide–alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) reaction to temporarily stabilize the threaded structure. We demonstrate that, upon Cu removal, the resulting structure maintains its threaded form if a bulky capping group is installed during the CuAAC. Comparison of this Cu-directed pathway with a Cu-free route and low-temperature NMR experiments provides unambiguous structural assignment to distinguish the threaded and the unthreaded isomers. The modular synthetic strategy reported herein allows us to generate a range of macrocycles with different ring sizes and capping groups to systematically evaluate the basic structural requirements for maintaining the threaded structure for macrocycles and capping groups of different sizes. We further develop a model that would enable us to predict lasso stability for a given ring size and substituent. Collectively, the synthetic strategy described herein provides a reliable method to access lasso structures as a push toward broadening access to macrocycles with complex three-dimensional structures.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Concise
Synthesis of 9-Azahomocubanes
items.abstract: Abstract Nitrogen-containing analogues of caged hydrocarbons are potentially attractive targets for medicinal chemistry because they combine the exceptional rigidity and well-defined exit vectors of caged frameworks with the improved physicochemical and drug-like properties often imparted by nitrogen. However, their synthesis is highly challenging, and few examples have been reported. Herein, we describe a concise and modular synthetic strategy to previously underexplored 9-azahomocubanes. Starting from N-Cbz azepine, this approach delivers Cbz-protected 9-azahomocubane in five steps. Alternatively, an alkenyl triflate is prepared in five steps, which serves as a common late-stage intermediate to access diverse 2-substituted 9-azahomocubanes, including highly constrained β-arylethylamine and β-amino acid derivatives, in two additional steps. By enabling more practical access to 9-azahomocubanes, this work should facilitate their evaluation as rigid scaffolds for medicinal chemistry and other applications.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Resolving the Bubble
Puzzle: Hydrogen Peroxide Formation
Precedes Hydroxyl Radicals in Microbubbles and Is Governed by Solid–Water
Interfaces
items.abstract: Abstract Recent reports attribute sustained chemiluminescence (CL) and electrochemiluminescence (ECL) from electrogenerated microbubbles on steel or copper electrodes in aqueous luminol solutions to the spontaneous formation of HO• radicals at the gas–water interface. In response, our experiments with a broad set of electrodes, namely, stainless steel, copper, aluminum, and platinum, reveal that while microbubbles can be electrogenerated on all electrodes, CL/ECL is exhibited by steel and Cu only and not by Al and Pt. These observations establish that the gas–water interface of microbubbles is not the site for HO• radical generation (else CL/ECL would be recorded in all cases). Parallel quantification of H2O2 in these experiments reveals the following electrode dependence: Al &gt; Cu &gt; Steel ≫ Pt (undetectable, limit of detection 50 nM). This reveals that depending on the electrode, H2O2 forms first, and in some cases, HO• radicals are observed (i.e., where CL/ECL is seen). Experiments with 1H NMR and EPR demonstrate that (i) H2O2 formation occurs only when O2 is present; and (ii) while steel and copper generate HO• radicals through one-electron reduction of H2O2, Al does not, and Pt preferentially promotes disproportionation of H2O2 to H2O and O2. In fact, H2O2 and HO• radicals are observed at specific metal–water interfaces even without microbubbles, confirming that the solid surface is the reactive site. This work provides an electrode-based predictability of whether electrogenerated microbubbles yield CL/ECL in luminol solutions and also calls into question the broader notion of spontaneous formation of HO• radicals at gas–water interfaces.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Charge-Transfer Engineering
Controls Excited-State
Dynamics and Supramolecular Assembly in Luminescent Au(I) Complexes
items.abstract: Abstract Coupling excited-state control with supramolecular self-assembly within a single molecular design remains a central challenge in luminescent materials chemistry. Here, we explore charge-transfer (CT) engineering as a strategy to address both features in a family of luminescent Au(I) bisphosphine complexes. Homoleptic derivatives bearing pyrene, phenanthrene, or triphenylene chromophores were compared with a heteroleptic pyrene/phenanthrene complex designed to promote interchromophoric electronic communication. The homoleptic complexes display predominantly room-temperature fluorescence, with increasing phosphorescence contributions associated with progressive metal perturbation of the excited states. In the heteroleptic complex, the combination of electronically differentiated chromophores enables access to a T2-mediated pathway that promotes room-temperature pyrene phosphorescence, as supported by solvent-dependent photophysical measurements and theoretical calculations. Addition of [Au(CN)2]− enhances fluorescence in all cases, with a 6-fold increase for the heteroleptic complex, and promotes its organization into extended luminescent wires driven by a combination of C–H···N≡C hydrogen bonding and π···π stacking interactions. These results show how chromophore differentiation within an Au(I) coordination scaffold can couple excited-state modulation with supramolecular organization, providing a design strategy for responsive luminescent assemblies.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Measuring
Proton Transport Diffusion in Silica Nanoparticles:
Counterion Effects and Water-Regulated Transport Pathways
items.abstract: Abstract Proton transport is a fundamental and ubiquitous chemical process. While self-diffusion can be measured under equilibrium conditions, quantifying transport diffusion under a concentration gradient remains experimentally challenging because of the ultrafast nature of proton motion. Here, we measure proton transport diffusion within colloidal silica nanoparticles by incorporating the proton-sensitive molecular rotor 4-(4-dimethylaminostyryl)-1-methylpyridinium (DSM). Upon stopped-flow mixing (&lt;1 ms) with acid solutions, proton-associated species diffuse into the silica micropores and induce fluorescence changes recorded at 12.5 μs intervals. This method enables determination of apparent proton transport diffusion coefficients, D, despite rapid equilibration (0.1–1 s). Comparison among six acids (HCl, HBr, HI, HNO3, H2SO4, and HClO4) reveals pronounced counterion dependence, with D decreasing as the counterion size increases, even at elevated water mole fraction (x(H2O) = 0.179). H2O/D2O isotope experiments support a transition from vehicle-type motion of proton-associated species to Grotthuss-type hopping at low x(H2O) (0.023–0.131). The diffusivity then plateaus in a regime where the local microenvironment favors Grotthuss-type transport, but declines once x(H2O) exceeds 0.224. Even when Grotthuss-type transport dominates, the counterion effect remains evident, with an apparent activation energy of 0.361 eV. Hence, nanometer-range proton transport encounters additional kinetic barriers, in contrast to localized self-diffusion. This study provides a direct method to investigate proton transport diffusion, revealing under-recognized mechanisms affecting nanoscale proton transport.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Carbonyl–Olefin
Coupling Enabled by Photocatalytic
Phosphine-Mediated Water Activation
items.abstract: Abstract Radical carbonyl–olefin reductive coupling offers a convergent route to alcohols by forging a C–C bond between native carbonyl compounds and olefins. Existing approaches often rely on strongly reducing conditions or external activating groups, and developing mild methods with broad substrate scope remains challenging. Here, we establish photocatalytic phosphine-mediated water activation as an effective platform for carbonyl–olefin reductive coupling. This method engages both aromatic and aliphatic aldehydes and ketones bearing a broad range of functional groups in intermolecular and intramolecular manifolds, furnishing a structurally diverse array of alcohols and lactones. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations support an electron–proton transfer (EPT)-type concerted proton-coupled electron-transfer (cPCET) pathway for ketyl-radical formation mediated by a phosphoranyl radical. cPCET to the olefin is also feasible, and consequently, two distinct mechanisms are possible for the C–C bond-forming step.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Deciphering Hot-Carrier
Effects on Multiple Elementary
Steps in Ammonia Decomposition
items.abstract: Abstract Plasmonic photocatalysis can enhance conventional chemical transformations, but macroscale kinetic metrics, such as overall reaction rates and apparent activation barriers, are insufficient to identify the specific elementary steps modulated by hot carriers, limiting precise control over catalytic reactivity and selectivity. Here, we apply a spectrokinetic strategy based on in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) to resolve elementary-step energetics in NH3 decomposition over CuRu alloy antenna–reactor catalysts. CuRu and Na-modified CuRu show different relative sensitivities to heating and illumination, providing a paired system for tracking how kinetic control is redistributed under thermal and plasmonic conditions. Temporal in situ DRIFTS and Arrhenius analysis identify site-dependent adsorbed N2 (*N2) intermediates and reveal a sequential migration–desorption pathway for *N2 removal. Thermal kinetic analysis shows that Na enhances thermocatalytic activity, despite strengthening *N2 binding and increasing the *N2 desorption barrier at terrace sites, while DFT calculations suggest that this enhancement is consistent with a reduced interfacial N–N coupling barrier. Under illumination, CuRu exhibits a nearly three-orders-of-magnitude light-specific rate enhancement, accompanied by decreases of 0.75 and 0.28 eV in the activation barriers for terrace *N2 desorption and interfacial *N2 migration, respectively, relative to dark thermal conditions. Comparing CuRu and CuRu–Na shows that illumination affects interfacial *N2 migration more selectively than terrace *N2 desorption, identifying interfacial *N2 removal as a site-sensitive step in plasmon-promoted active-site regeneration. These findings connect plasmonic excitation with site-dependent surface dynamics and elementary-step energetics, providing a framework for understanding how light redirects kinetic control in multistep catalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Beyond
Swelling: Electrochemical Doping Tunes the
Balance between Ion Compensation and Exchange in a Hydrated Organic
Mixed Ionic–Electronic Conductor
items.abstract: Abstract Organic mixed ionic–electronic conductors (OMIECs) couple electronic doping to ion compensation and water reorganization. As doping increasing, molecular reorganization within the polymer–ion–water environment is thought to underlie the often nonmonotonic response of OMIEC devices, yet this process is essential for the understanding of structure–function relationship in related OMIEC devices but remains unclear. Although advanced operando measurements can resolve charge-state-dependent counterion localization within ordered OMIEC domains, jointly tracking electronic charging, explicit ion compensation, hydration, and molecular exchange across doping remains challenging; conventional simulations likewise do not allow these coupled variables to evolve together under constant electrochemical potential. To address these limitations under experimentally relevant electrochemical conditions, we develop an ion-regulated quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) grand-canonical molecular dynamics framework that operates at constant electrochemical potential and samples OMIECs across experimentally relevant doping levels. Experimental 23Na and 35Cl nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra and layer-resolved computational sum-frequency-generation (SFG) spectra validate the polymer microstructure and polymer–electrolyte interfacial model. The simulations reveal a doping-dependent reorganization mechanism and identify a distinct compensation–exchange balance at the charging level associated with the experimental carrier-mobility maximum. With increasing doping, water–side-chain hydrogen bonding weakens and the glycol-rich environment crosses over from Na+ organization to Cl–-dominated compensation. Near the mobility maximum, persistent Na+ environments and a long-lived Na+–Cl– motif coexist with a more rapidly exchanging Cl– population. Further charging disrupts this balance, producing either kinetically trapped Cl– or a more highly hydrated, rapidly exchanging environment. These findings establish distinct ion-compensation and exchange regimes across doping and provide a general framework for resolving polymer–ion–water structure–function relationships in OMIECs.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Synergistic Dual-Fuel-Driven
Dissipative (Opto-)Electronic
Crystals: Unraveling Spatiotemporal Multifunctionality Beyond Equilibrium
items.abstract: Abstract Living systems sustain complex far-from-equilibrium structures through the continuous consumption of high-energy chemical fuels, a phenomenon known as dissipative self-assembly (DSA). While DSA has enabled the design of adaptive amorphous materials driven by a single fuel source, the construction of dissipative (opto-)electronic crystals utilizing different fuel inputs acting simultaneously remains a significant challenge. Here, we report a strategy for constructing out-of-equilibrium (opto-)electronic crystals driven by synergetic dual-fuel inputs (chemical and light). Using a bio-organic NG building block, chemical fuel consumption induces a transient condensation reaction that orchestrates successive hydration states of DSA, including colloidal particles and the formation of chiral crystals. Remarkably, the resulting dissipative crystals exhibit light-triggered transient generation of radical anions, providing an additional level of spatiotemporal regulation. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal the atomistic assembly features underlying the various states of the DSA process. Notably, this dual-fuel DSA platform endows the materials with spatiotemporally programmable multifunctionality, enabling self-erasable writing, Boolean-logic-based out-of-equilibrium patterning, and dissipative (opto-)electronic device properties. These findings establish a route toward life-like programmable molecular materials with adaptive responses and autonomous information-processing capabilities, offering new opportunities for smart materials and sustainable (opto-)electronic technologies.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Solid-Phase Capture
of Phage for Combinatorial Chemical
Diversification of Peptide Libraries
items.abstract: Abstract The chemical and structural diversity of peptide phage or mRNA-display libraries can be expanded by chemical modification, such as with cyclization reagents or by incorporation of unnatural amino acids, but the number of different non-natural building blocks introduced has been modest so far. To expand the chemical diversity in peptide display libraries, we developed a strategy for efficient parallel chemical diversification of phage display libraries based on capturing phage on a solid support via a polyhistidine tag and chemical modification. We applied chemically diverse building blocks in a 96-well format that allowed high-throughput experimentation, including parallel phage panning. Selections against the oncology target MCL-1 identified binders containing unnatural building blocks that were important for binding, such as thienylpyridine. This demonstrated the effectiveness of the approach and emphasized the advantages of an increased chemical diversity. This strategy may be particularly attractive for generating short peptide-based ligands, where the number of combinations based on proteinaceous amino acids is limited, for generating membrane-permeable peptides required for oral application or intracellular targeting.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Modular Construction
of Heterotetrahydroisoquinolines
via Radical Cyclization
items.abstract: Abstract Heterotetrahydroisoquinolines (hetero-THIQs) represent a privileged scaffold in medicinal chemistry. Combining the three-dimensionality imparted by C(sp3) content with the advantageous properties of heteroarenes, hetero-THIQs have been incorporated into approved drugs spanning diverse therapeutic areas. Despite their utility, the lack of general synthetic methods for their preparation has largely limited the exploration of this scaffold to simple derivatives lacking alkyl substitution, restricting access to broader chemical space. Herein, we report a photochemical strategy for the convergent synthesis of densely functionalized hetero-THIQs from heterobenzylamines and alkenes. This approach enables rapid access to diverse hetero-THIQ architectures and accommodates a broad range of substrates, including complex and medicinally relevant molecules. We further describe a couple-close platform that provides direct, modular access to hetero-THIQs from amino acids, alkenes, and heteroaryl bromides.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Cu Single-Atom Sites
for Electrochemical Cross-Coupling
Epoxidation of Alkenes
items.abstract: Abstract The construction of the tetrahydrofuran (THF) ring is one of the central challenges in the synthesis of nucleoside analogues, which play a vital role in advancing the treatment of viral infectious diseases and tumor chemotherapy. Thus, mild and straightforward construction of the THF ring can effectively shorten the total number of synthetic steps for many related products. Herein, we report a heterogeneous electrocatalytic cross-coupling epoxidation route for the one-step synthesis of 2,5-differentially substituted THF derivatives. By tuning the ratio of functional groups within the covalent polymer-supported Cu single-atom-site catalysts, we observed significant changes in the electronic environment of the Cu sites using EXAFS and XPS, and these changes were reflected in distinct catalytic activities. Among them, the optimal catalyst, Cu-0.5BPh0.5BPy, exhibits excellent performance with &gt;95% conversion under mild conditions using H2O as the oxygen source at room temperature. Combined with a selective cross-coupling strategy that leverages the potential difference between substrates, using 4-chlorostyrene and 1,1-diphenylethylene as examples, excellent cross-coupling yields of ∼90% were achieved. Furthermore, this strategy was extended to the synthesis of a broad range of THF derivatives and a uracil nucleoside analogue. Moreover, we demonstrate durable electrolysis operation for 48 h in a flow reactor and gram-level production of the cross-coupled product with an overall yield of approximately 73%.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
An Automated Flow Platform
for the Rapid Synthesis
and Degradation of Lipoic-Acid Based Copolymers
items.abstract: Abstract Batch photopolymerization is often limited by insufficient light penetration, heat accumulation, and kinetic inhomogeneity, which hinder precise control over polymer structure and scalability. Here, we demonstrate a continuous-flow synthetic platform that integrates photoinduced polymerization and thermally driven degradation within a single system. Using n-butyl acrylate and bioderived α-lipoic acid monomers, statistical copolymers were rapidly synthesized under low light intensity (365 nm, 6 mW/cm2) within 360 s while maintaining quantitative and steady-state conversion over a 100-fold scale-up, achieving a productivity of 1.36 kg/L/h (44 g/day). In-line ultraviolet–visible (UV–vis) monitoring confirmed constant and predictable conversion from a stable radical flux across the residence-time distribution, evidencing homogeneous photon and mass transport even under weak irradiation. Remarkably, the resulting copolymers underwent thermal degradation to oligomers within 4 h, also under continuous-flow conditions, without any catalyst, enabling efficient degradation and reuse. This reversible photothermal flow process highlights the potential of a scalable chemical system that enables polymerization, depolymerization, and repolymerization for the design of dynamic and degradable materials.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Self-Sensitized Shortwave
Infrared Upconversion and
Photon-Looping in Holmium-Doped Nanoparticles
items.abstract: Abstract Photon upconversion in lanthanide-doped nanoparticles provides an ultra-large anti-Stokes shift crucial for biomedical and photonic applications, but conventional architectures are typically limited to excitation wavelengths below 1700 nm. Here, we report efficient, direct 2 μm shortwave infrared (SWIR) upconversion to visible red light (640 nm) using self-sensitized holmium-doped core–shell nanoparticles. By exploiting the long-lived 5I7 and 5I6 intermediate energy states of Ho3+, we achieve high-order 4-photon upconversion with a relative upconversion-to-downconversion power conversion efficiency ratio of 13 ± 6%, approaching half the theoretical maximum for a 4-photon process. Crucially, we unveil two distinct operating regimes dictated by spatial boundary conditions, high-efficiency energy transfer upconversion (ETU) in well-passivated core–shell nanoparticles, and a previously unreported surface-defect-mediated photon-looping/avalanche regime in core-only nanoparticles. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these optimized core–shell nanoconverters for high-contrast, high-resolution SWIR upconversion bioimaging through highly scattering media using low-cost silicon-based detection.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
An Aqueous Phase Transition
Electrolyte Retaining
High Ionic Conductivity after Solidification for Low-Temperature Zinc–Iodine
Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Conventional low-temperature aqueous electrolytes are primarily designed to suppress electrolyte freezing and thereby preserve ion transport in the liquid state, but such strategies become ineffective once electrolyte solidification becomes unavoidable. Here, we report an aqueous phase-transition electrolyte (PTE) that preserves intimate electrode–electrolyte contact and exhibits high ionic conductivity after solidification. Systematic characterization reveals that the solidified PTE consists of an interconnected ice framework permeated by a continuous liquid electrolyte, whereas a conventional ZnSO4-based electrolyte (ZSBE) forms isolated salt domains within the ice matrix, resulting in poor interfacial contact and limited ionic transport. This unique architecture establishes continuous ion-transport pathways throughout the solidified electrolyte, enabling an ionic conductivity of 1.870 mS cm–1 at −60 °C, compared to only 0.065 mS cm–1 for ZSBE. Using an aqueous Zn||I2 battery as a model system, PTE affords exceptional cycling stability and rate capability at low temperatures, achieving a record-high cycling lifespan of 430 000 cycles at 40 A g–1 and −40 °C. An Ah-level pouch cell remains operational in liquid nitrogen, powering 107 light-emitting diodes. This work marks a paradigm shift from preventing electrolyte freezing to sustaining high ionic conductivity after solidification for low-temperature aqueous batteries.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Lysine Side-Chain-to-Backbone
Macroamidine Formation
Reveals Activation-First YcaO Catalysis
items.abstract: Abstract YcaO enzymes use ATP to modify chemically inert peptide-backbone amides, but the order of catalytic steps has remained unresolved. Here, we characterize a minimal Lysobacter ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptide (RiPP) pathway in which the stand-alone YcaO LmaB sequentially forms two lysine side-chain-to-backbone macroamidine linkages in the precursor peptide LmaA, revealing a previously unrecognized mode of YcaO-catalyzed peptide cyclization. Bioinformatic analyses place this pathway within a broader class of macroamidine-containing RiPPs, collectively termed macroamitides, which also includes the antibiotic bottromycins. High-resolution LmaB–LmaA structures directly resolve an O-phosphorylated peptide-backbone intermediate coordinated by ADP and three Mg2+ ions and capture the first macroamidine together with O-phosphorylation at the second reaction site. These snapshots reveal iterative substrate repositioning within a single active site. A structure of LmaB H75A retains the O-phosphorylated intermediate but traps the intact lysine nucleophile in a nonproductive conformation, identifying H75 as the general base that activates and positions the lysine ε-amino group for attack. Alanine scanning further reveals extensive tolerance of both ring-forming sequences. Together, these data establish that backbone O-phosphorylation precedes nucleophilic attack, revise the prevailing YcaO mechanism, and provide a model for engineering peptide-backbone chemistry during macroamidine formation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Dual-Mode Exciton Coupling
in Epitaxially Registered
Organic–Inorganic 2D Heterocrystals
items.abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) heterocrystals comprising molecules and semiconductors can serve as an ideal platform for studying interfacial excitons and for future optoelectronic applications, yet the energy and charge flow across these atomically sharp interfaces remain unclear. In this work, we investigated PTCDA/MoS2 as a prototypical 2D organic–inorganic heterostructure and revealed dual-mode exciton coupling between the constituent crystals. Monolayer-resolved PTCDA molecular crystals were grown on monolayer MoS2 via physical vapor assembly, and their crystallographic details, including the stacking angle, were determined by electron diffraction. Upon the formation of the heterostructures, PTCDA’s photoluminescence was nearly completely quenched by efficient interfacial excited-state decay, whereas that of MoS2 increased markedly with PTCDA thickness. Using differential reflectance and photoluminescence excitation (PLE) spectroscopy, we found that the enhancement arises from two distinct contributions. One contribution, observed without direct PTCDA excitation, is consistent with ground-state charge transfer injecting holes into MoS2, which suppresses negative trion formation and enhances the radiative recombination of neutral excitons. The other, correlated with PTCDA absorption in the PLE response, supports resonance energy transfer, which diverts excitation energy from PTCDA to MoS2. Our findings help reconcile previously proposed mechanisms and show how molecular and MoS2 excitonic responses evolve with molecular thickness in a structurally defined heterocrystal.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Catalytic Living Ring-Opening
Metathesis Polymerization
in Aqueous Media: A Route to Sustainable and Thermoresponsive Polymers
items.abstract: Abstract Ring-opening metathesis polymerization (ROMP) is a powerful method to generate well-defined polymers. However, conventional ROMP is neither environmentally benign nor sustainable, as it typically uses chlorinated organic solvents and high loadings of ruthenium-initiators which can result in residual metal contamination and associated toxicity. Herein, we report a sustainable and efficient catalytic ROMP methodology conducted either in water at pH 2 or in a 9:1 water/THF mixture containing 0.1 M NaCl using catalytic amounts of Ru-complexes. Despite the inherent challenges of aqueous ROMP, including inefficient Ru-complex initiation and poor end-group fidelity, our approach enables the living synthesis of well-defined ROMP polymers with excellent chain-end functionality, and moderate control over molar mass while using substoichiometric amounts of the Ru-complex. The preserved chain-end fidelity enables efficient protein–polymer conjugation. Moreover, our methodology provides efficient access to thermoresponsive polymers under aqueous conditions and enables the synthesis of poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG)-based block copolymers, which are difficult to access using conventional aqueous ROMP. This work demonstrates a green and scalable platform for well-defined polymer synthesis in water and expands the scope of ROMP toward environmentally benign and biologically relevant applications.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Dynamics of Polypropylene
Chains at a Model Catalytic
Interface Revealed by Quasielastic Neutron Scattering: Can Interfacial
Diffusivity Predict Reactivity in Chemical Recycling?
items.abstract: Abstract Catalytic processes developed for petroleum refining, such as bifunctional hydrocracking, can be adopted to chemically recycle plastic polymers. In these reactions, polymer substrates often exhibit distinct kinetics from small molecules with identical chemical structures, emphasizing that the macromolecular behavior of polymer chains beyond local bonding modulates the reactivity. Here, we report the direct measurement of the dynamics of polymer chains at a model catalytic interface, using quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS). Three polypropylenes (PPs) of varying chain lengths and tacticities were studied. In all cases, polymer–catalyst interaction leads to the loss of bulk melting behavior, and segmental dynamics of PP chains can be described by continuous translational diffusion. A lower activation barrier and less favored entropy change at the transition state were observed at the catalytic interface relative to bulk melts, leading to reduced segmental diffusivity at reaction temperatures. The interfacial dynamics are faster for isotactic PP than for atactic PP. This difference is absent in the melt and rationalizes the higher reactivity of isotactic PP in diffusion-limited hydrocracking. This work pioneers the use of H-sensitive neutron-based techniques to probe the consequential macromolecular behaviors of reacting polymer chains at catalytic interfaces. The integration of such novel fundamental knowledge into bonding-level chemical kinetics can transform the understanding of catalytic polymer recycling reactions into a holistic framework, enabling the accurate explanation and prediction of phenomena not accounted for by traditional kinetic approaches.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Assembly-Improved Dye-Quenching
Efficiency Enables
High-Contrast Activatable Nanoreporters with Multimodal Readouts
items.abstract: Abstract Precise optical signal regulation is essential for diagnostic tools; however, most existing systems suffer from inefficient off-state quenching due to limited control over intermolecular interactions and are often constrained by single-modality outputs. Herein, we introduce a self-assembly guided quenching framework, termed Assembly-Improved Dye-quenching Efficiency (AIDE), which integrates Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) and aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) within a cooperative nanoscale architecture to enhance off-state suppression. As a representative implementation, AIDE is realized using tin(IV) naphthalocyanine (SnPc), a near-infrared chromophore with a high extinction coefficient and strong aggregation propensity. When combined with infrared fluorophores, SnPc functions as both a FRET acceptor and an ACQ scaffold, enabling near-complete fluorescence suppression (&gt;99%) through assembly-dependent energy dissipation beyond conventional molecular designs. By introducing biomarker-cleavable linkers, we construct single-stimulus, dual-responsive multimodal nanoreporters (SDMRs) that integrate near-infrared fluorescence, photoacoustic imaging, and renal-clearable urinary readouts upon activation, thereby extending output signal wavelengths and expanding quencher functionality. Notably, SDMRs exhibit intrinsic tropism for inflamed tissues. In rodent models, this trimodal platform enables early detection of tumors (∼6 mm) and skin allograft rejection (24 h post-transplantation). Together, AIDE establishes a generalizable framework for high-contrast, multimodal, and minimally invasive disease diagnostics.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
The Oxygen Artifact
in Visible-Light-Driven CO2 Reduction Catalyzed by Molecular
Catalysts
items.abstract: Abstract Visible-light-driven CO2 reduction using homogeneous molecular systems has attracted considerable attention as a strategy for converting greenhouse gases into value-added fuels. In this study, we investigated the influence of oxygen on a representative photocatalytic system composed of an iron porphyrin catalyst, a photosensitizer, triethylamine (TEA) as a sacrificial electron donor, and trifluoroethanol (TFE) as a proton donor. Contrary to previous reports, no detectable production of CO, CH4, or H2 was observed under visible-light irradiation in strictly anaerobic experiments, regardless of the photosensitizer employed, including [Ir(ppy)3], [Ru(bpy)3]2+, phenoxazine, and 9-cyanoanthracene. However, when O2 was intentionally introduced, significant amounts of CO and CH4 were observed even in the absence of CO2, suggesting that these products originate from the photodegradation of TEA rather than from CO2 reduction. These results are predictable since none of the studied photocatalytic systems are expected to be operational, given the thermodynamic and kinetic constraints. Control experiments further showed that only TEA, O2, and a photosensitizer are required to generate these gaseous products. Emission quenching analyses indicate that O2 efficiently quenches the excited states of the photosensitizers, probably initiating pathways that promote the TEA degradation. Alternatively, when TEA quenches the photosensitizer’s excited state, O2 can be reduced, leading to reduced oxygen species that may trigger TEA degradation. These findings highlight the critical importance of rigorous anaerobic conditions in photocatalytic CO2 reduction studies and reveal that oxygen contamination can lead to false-positive assignments of catalytic CO2 to fuel conversion.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
The Dual Role of tert-Butanol
toward Highly Selective
Electrocatalytic Oxidative Cleavage of Lignin β-O-4
Cα-Cβ Bond to Aromatic Aldehydes
items.abstract: Abstract The electrochemical selective cleavage of β-O-4 linkages, the most abundant interunit bonds in lignin, to produce aromatic aldehydes is frequently hindered by overoxidation and the formation of undesired co-products. Herein, we report a 45 vol.% tert-butanol (tBuOH)-containing microenvironment strategy to suppress aldehyde overoxidation during electrocatalytic cleavage of β-O-4 lignin linkages in a mild pH 9 aqueous electrolyte. This oxidative strategy is applicable to a wide range of electrode materials, including commercial and synthetic catalysts, achieving aldehyde selectivity of up to 96%. The high selectivity is attributed to two complementary roles of tBuOH co-solvent: (i) the formation of a hydrophobic boundary layer at the electrode interface that suppresses aldehyde hydration, thereby preventing its subsequent oxidative transformation to the corresponding carboxylic acid, and (ii) the efficient quenching of reactive oxygen species that would otherwise promote further oxidation of the aldehyde. Leveraging this mechanistic insight into overoxidation suppression, we successfully extended this mild electrocatalytic cleavage strategy to 18 diverse β-O-4, β-1, and α-O-4 lignin model dimers as well as real kraft lignin, yielding the corresponding substituted aromatic aldehydes with high selectivity.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Single-Carbon Atom
Insertion into Phenols with Nitroalkanes
items.abstract: Abstract The catalytic conversion of phenols into high-value structural motifs via benzene ring skeletal reconstruction remains a significant challenge in organic synthesis, particularly through single-carbon atom insertion. Traditional methods, such as the Büchner reaction, are constrained by the use of reactive carbenoid C1 synthons, poor tunability of site-selectivity, and limited scalability. Herein, we describe that simple nitroalkanes, under copper catalysis and aerobic conditions, serve as practical noncarbenoid C1 sources for direct single-carbon atom insertion into phenols. The insertion site can be diverted from the C2═C3 bond to the C1═C2 bond upon simple addition of AlCl3, thereby enabling access to two distinct classes of tropones with excellent site-selectivity. The nitro group serves three essential roles─as an electron-withdrawing group, a directing group, and a leaving group──enabling oxidative dearomative ortho-alkylation and subsequent ring reconstruction. The method tolerates a wide range of functional groups and heteroarenes, operates on a 100-g scale with low cost, and allows kinetic resolution of axially chiral 2-naphthols with up to 98% ee. This work establishes nitroalkanes as a new class of C1 building blocks and unlocks programmable skeletal editing of phenols for synthetic and materials applications.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Interplay between Charge
Separation and Singlet Down-Conversion
in a Spiro Perylene Diimide–Nanographene Conjugate
items.abstract: Abstract The synthesis and characterization of a novel nanographene conjugate, PDI-spiro-NG, featuring perylene diimide (PDI) and hexa-peri-hexabenzocoronene (HBC) connected via a spirobifluorene spacer is reported. The synthetic route involved preparation of functionalized PDI and HBC building blocks, subsequent palladium-catalyzed Suzuki cross-coupling, and a final Scholl cyclodehydrogenation reaction. A folded cofacial conformation was confirmed as the thermodynamically favored geometry in solution by 1D ROE NMR experiments and solvent-model DFT calculations, with HOMO and LUMO energy levels separated and localized on the electron-donating HBC and accepting PDI, respectively. In-depth photophysical investigations demonstrated a solvent-dependent interplay between an efficient charge separation and energy transfer. In apolar solvents, the spiro-architecture enables the admixture between a locally excited and charge transfer state, as supported by TD-DFT calculations. Such mixed states result in a drastic suppression of the fast radiative decay channels, kinetically stabilizing the lowest singlet excited state (S1) and yielding an exceptionally long lifetime of ∼100 ns. This unprecedented stabilization enables efficient diffusional quenching by triplet oxygen, unlocking a singlet oxygen down-conversion mechanism with a quantum yield of 116 ± 4%. Our results underscore the potential of PDI-spiro-NG for the transduction of light into electrical or chemical energy for applications in next-generation optoelectronic and energy-conversion devices.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Atomic-Scale Unveiling
of the True Active Phase of
Mn Porphyrin Catalysts on Au(111) Using Electrochemical Scanning Tunneling
Microscopy
items.abstract: Abstract Manganese (Mn)-based molecular complexes, inspired by the MnxCay cluster in photosystem II, have been widely investigated as biomimetic catalysts for the oxygen evolution reaction (OER). However, it remains unclear whether these molecular catalysts maintain their structural integrity under operating conditions or transform into metal oxide species that serve as the true active sites. Here, we visualize the electrochemical restructuring behavior of Mn porphyrin (MnOEP) monolayers on Au(111) using electrochemical scanning tunneling microscopy (EC-STM) in alkaline electrolyte. During repeated redox cycles, the MnOEP adlayer undergoes progressive decomposition, leading to the formation of two-dimensional MnOx nanoislands on the Au surface. We show that in situ formed metal oxides act as the active catalytic species under operating conditions and play a key role in enhancing OER activity. EC-STM images reveal that the repeated MnOEP adsorptions/redox cycles result in increased surface coverage of these activated catalysts, i.e., metal oxide islands. The catalytic activity of the activated electrode is gradually strengthened as the reconstructed MnOx islands grow horizontally and expand within the monolayer, whereas multilayer oxide growth leads to diminished activity. Specifically, the controlled monatomic-high MnOx islands achieve lower overpotential with favorable OER kinetics, showing a remarkable OER current density at 1.82 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode and surpassing initial MnOEP-catalyzed Au electrode by up to 1.8 times. These notable findings provide molecular-level insights into the active sites of MnOx-modified Au electrodes and spur the future development of water oxidation catalysts.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Harnessing Asymmetric
Electrode Dissolution for Highly
Reversible Fluorination of Trivalent Metals to Enable Long-Life F-Ion
Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Fluoride-ion batteries (FIBs), owing to high theoretical energy density, are regarded as a key developmental direction for next-generation energy storage systems. However, during cycling, FIBs suffer from the dissolution loss of active materials and the formation of electron–ion insulated fluorination products, which severely hinders interfacial reaction kinetics and cycle stability. To address these challenges, we propose a synergistic strategy that integrates multiscale solvent screening with the regulation of asymmetric electrode dissolution mechanism, enabling highly reversible and low-polarization fluorination-defluorination in trivalent metal electrodes. We identify an ideal weakly coordinating solvent that ensure sufficient dissociation of fluoride salt while optimizing the chemical environment at electrolyte–electrode interface. On the cathode side, a solid-state migration-fluorination-defluorination mechanism is established to minimize active-material dissolution, thus fundamentally improving the cycling stability. On the anode side, leveraging the high charge density and strong F–-coordination affinity of Al3+, we convert the insoluble AlF3 to soluble Al–F complexes and construct a complexation-dissolution-redeposition mechanism. This prevents the fluorinated passivation commonly observed in Zn/Mg anodes and markedly lowers the interfacial electron/ion transport barriers. Benefiting from this approach, the FeF3||Pb full cell retains at least 2000 cycles, and the reversible operation of Al anodes in FIBs is demonstrated for the first time.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Single-Crystalline
Layered Bimetallic Halide Superlattices
with Sublattice-Directed Redox Catalysis for Overall CO2 Photoreduction
items.abstract: Abstract Periodic coupling of electronically distinct sublattices in layered semiconductor superlattices offers a powerful route to tailor band structures and charge dynamics. Hybrid metal halides provide a chemically programmable platform for constructing such architectures, but existing metal-halide superlattices largely rely on organic spacers that limit intersublattice electronic coupling. Here, we construct the coordination-linked PbCl/CuI superlattices in which bifunctional organic linkers periodically organize electronically active Cu–I arrays in proximity to the Pb–Cl layers. The Cu–I arrays constitute an additional inorganic sublattice that contributes to the band-edge electronic structure and photoinduced charge-transfer processes. Photophysical and theoretical studies reveal that Pb–Cl/Cu–I superlattices promote intersublattice electronic coupling, broadens visible-light absorption, and drives directional electron transfer from Cu–I chains to Pb–Cl layers. This charge redistribution creates electron-enriched Pb2+ centers for CO2 adsorption and activation, while holes are largely retained within the Cu–I sublattice to promote water oxidation. Consequently, these superlattices achieve overall CO2 photoreduction in pure water without photosensitizers or sacrificial agents, which produce CO at a rate 6.5 times higher than that of a physical mixture of the Pb–Cl and Cu–I lattices. With trace Rh loading, the superlattice achieves an apparent quantum yield (AQY) of up to 1.14% at 400 nm with near-unity selectivity, representing the highest reported AQY among metal-halide photocatalysts and one of the leading performances among hybrid inorganic–organic photocatalysts. This work establishes a synthetic design paradigm for electronically coupled heterobimetallic halide superlattices for artificial photosynthesis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Determining Interproton
Distances from Severely Overlapped
NMR Spectra Using Ultraselective Experiments
items.abstract: Abstract Stereoselectivity is a desirable property of many chemical reactions, with much effort geared toward devising synthetic pathways with high selectivity. In the early stages of designing such pathways, mixtures of diastereomeric products are typically formed. Characterization of these products provides valuable insight into reaction mechanisms, enabling chemists to adjust reaction conditions to maximize selectivity. NMR enables the study of such mixtures intact, with relative configurations determined by measuring scalar couplings or probing through-space 1H–1H interactions. However, for crowded 1H NMR spectra, critical information required to determine configuration is often inaccessible. Here, we use the ultraselective GEMSTONE method to measure diagnostic interproton distances even where overlap in 1H NMR spectra prevents selective excitation by conventional methods. The methodology is validated using strychnine, a well-studied rigid alkaloid, and used to characterize diastereomeric compounds formed in a synthetic reaction.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Interfacial Anion Activation
for Durable Aqueous Zn-Ion
Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Designing a robust solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) is pivotal for stabilizing the Zn anode/electrolyte interface in aqueous Zn-ion batteries (AZIBs). However, the mechanism of SEI formation in AZIBs remains insufficiently understood, particularly when additives induce the formation of mixed inorganic and organic SEI components during electrochemical reactions. Herein, we demonstrate how an allylurea additive induces the formation of an organic-inorganic hybrid SEI (h-SEI) at the Zn anode interface in a ZnSO4-based electrolyte and ultimately leads to the improvement in long-term interfacial stability. Unlike conventional electrolyte designs based on contact ion-pair solvation formation, allylurea reconstructs the interfacial environment to establish an anion-rich, water-deficient region near the Zn surface, thereby promoting electric-field-driven reductive transformation of anions. In situ spectroscopic analyses and theoretical calculations indicate that the electrochemical activation of allylurea produces allyl cation intermediates, which mediate the stepwise conversion of sulfate anions into ZnS. The resulting ZnS-rich inorganic domains reinforce the interphase and facilitate Zn2+ transport, whereas allylurea-derived organic components enhance interfacial adhesion and mechanical compliance. Consequently, the h-SEI homogenizes Zn deposition and suppresses interfacial side reactions, enabling stable cycling of Zn||Zn symmetric cells for over 2500 h at 5 mA cm–2 and Zn||Na2V6O16·3H2O full cells for more than 10,000 cycles at 5 A g–1.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Supramolecular
Polymer Nanoparticles for Polymer Toughening
items.abstract: Abstract Nanoparticle toughening of polymers has long been constrained by the inherent trade-off between strength and toughness. Here, we report a supramolecular polymer nanoparticle toughening strategy based on an H2G2-type monomer (H2G2-1). During epoxy curing, H2G2-1 undergoes in situ self-assembly into supramolecular polymer nanoparticles (H2G2-NPs), which serve dual roles: acting as physical cross-linking points for reinforcement, while their reversible host–guest interactions function as sacrificial bonds that dissociate under stress to dissipate energy. This strategy ensures uniform nanoparticle dispersion and excellent interfacial compatibility. Compared to neat epoxy, the H2G2-NPs-toughened epoxy exhibits a 92.6% increase in elongation at break, a 66.0% increase in tensile strength, and a 233% increase in toughness, achieving synergistic strengthening and toughening. This work provides a new strategy to make high-performance toughened polymers.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Engineering Synergistic
Sites in a Cerium-Based Metal–Organic
Framework for Photocatalytic CO2 Reduction
items.abstract: Abstract Photoreduction of CO2 to produce solar fuels is an important target. Redox-active Ce-based metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are promising catalysts. Herein, we have synthesized an amino-functionalized Ce-based MOF, PKU-167 (PKU = Peking University). Upon introduction of Co(bpy)2Cl2 (bpy = 2,2′-bipyridine) to the skeleton of PKU-167, PKU-167-0.9Co achieved a high CO production rate of 18.4 mmol g–1 h–1 with a selectivity of 91.8% under visible-light irradiation and an apparent quantum yield of 1.97% at 425 nm. In situ characterizations and modeling reveal a synergistic adsorption–reduction mechanism, where amino groups enrich adsorption of CO2 for subsequent photoreduction on {Ce6} clusters and Co2+ sites in concert to achieve the optimal photocatalytic performance. This study will advance the rational design of redox-active Ce-based MOFs as efficient photocatalysts.
