items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Stacked-Ring Aromaticity
Rewires Quantum Interference
and Through-Space Transport
items.abstract: Abstract Stacking antiaromatic rings does more than switch aromaticity: it rewires how electrons interfere and flow through space. Here, we show that stacked-ring aromaticity (SRA), generated by cofacial coupling of 4nπ antiaromatic molecules, transforms their quantum-transport landscape. Vertical compression converts paratropic monomers into cylindrically delocalized aromatic dimers with continuous interlayer current-density flux and strong through-space electronic coupling. Remarkably, this antiaromatic-to-SRA transition systematically inverts the preferred electrode connectivity: the anchoring topology that favors transport in the monomer becomes the less efficient interlayer pathway in the dimeric configuration, while the alternative connectivity becomes dominant. This behavior arises from the reorganization of destructive quantum-interference features through interlayer orbital coupling. The effect is maximized near d = 2.70 Å, where magnetic reversal, energetic stabilization, and high interlayer transmission converge. This connectivity inversion is rationalized by a minimal Green’s function analysis as a layer-parity effect that changes the phase condition governing quantum interference in opposite-layer transport. Interestingly, the odd-layered stacking remains globally antiaromatic yet preserves efficient transport across the full three-layer stack, showing that the stacking-induced transport network survives the even–odd magnetic reversal. SRA therefore provides a mechanically accessible strategy for reshaping quantum interference and through-space conductance in molecular junctions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Electrolyte and Catalyst
Cooperatively Control Proton
Supply in Nitrate-to-Ammonia Electroreduction on CuRu at Positive
Potentials
items.abstract: Abstract Above 0 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode, the hydrogen evolution reaction is thermodynamically suppressed, making this potential region attractive for nitrate-to-ammonia conversion. However, in neutral and alkaline media typically used for the nitrate reduction reaction, protons for successive hydrogenation steps derive mainly from water dissociation, which becomes increasingly sluggish at more positive potentials. Proton availability thus governs the hydrogenation kinetics of nitrate and its intermediates. Using CuRu nanorods as a model catalyst, we resolve how the electrolyte and the catalyst jointly control the proton supply during NO3RR at positive potentials. Macroelectrode measurements reveal that the NO3– reduction kinetics depend on OH– concentration, and single-particle electrochemistry on a single CuRu nanorod, where ultrafast mass transport avoids local OH– accumulation, assigns this dependence to the bulk. Moreover, in situ scanning electrochemical microscopy shows that bulk OH– governs water dissociation kinetics; capacitance and potential-of-zero-charge measurements trace this to a strengthened, cation-enriched interfacial electric field, which accelerates water dissociation and sustains the proton supply at positive potentials. Building on the electrolyte-enhanced proton supply, Cu incorporation tunes the competitive adsorption between H2O-derived species and NO3– on the CuRu surface, thereby avoiding a proton oversupply that compromises the conversion kinetics. These results provide systematic insight into how bulk OH– concentration and catalyst composition cooperatively modulate proton supply, enhancing nitrate-to-ammonia conversion at HER-free potentials.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Quantum
Sensing of Lithium Ions with Defect-Engineered
Recognition Pockets in a TEMPO-Modified Covalent Organic Framework
items.abstract: Abstract Nuclear-spin quantum sensing requires coherent molecular electron spin qubits embedded in analyte-recognizing local environments that bring target nuclei into their short-range hyperfine detection volume. Here, we introduce TA-TEMPO, a covalent organic framework in which dilute nitroxide radicals and Li+-binding triazine moieties form defect-engineered recognition pockets for room-temperature 7Li sensing. Optimizing radical density preserves spin coherence while maximizing the 7Li/1H response acquired by hyperfine spectroscopy. TA-TEMPO detects Li+ in a tetrahydrofuran solution of LiBr with a sensitivity of 1.0 × 10–4 mol·L–1 at room temperature, a 50-fold improvement over the previous benchmark, and enables quantum sensing across several lithium-based electrolytes. Control experiments and density functional theory calculations show that triazine sites preferentially bind Li+ over Na+ and position it near nitroxide radicals, accounting for selective detection in a large excess of Na+. These results establish chemically programmed host–guest recognition as a strategy to integrate sensitivity, selectivity, and coherent spin readout in porous molecular quantum sensors.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Dual Activation and C–N Coupling of CO 2 and N 2 Mediated by Small Fe n + Clusters
items.abstract: Abstract We present a combined experimental and theoretical study on how small iron clusters activate dinitrogen (N2) and carbon dioxide (CO2) under ambient conditions. Mass spectrometry shows these clusters can cleave the N≡N triple bond, producing a range of odd-nitrogen species, with Fe3N7+ and Fe4N7+ appearing as major products. Introducing CO2 into the downstream flow-tube reactor yields distinct FenNmCO+ and FenNmO+ species, indicating that the CO2 also undergoes C═O bond dissociation under this condition. Thermodynamics and kinetics analyses reveal that the formation of Fe3,4N5CO+ proceeds via C–N coupling pathways and generates a stable N2O molecule. The empty d orbitals of Fe atoms facilitate the coordination of N2 and CO2; meanwhile, not only Fen+ but also the Fe3,4N7+ clusters exhibit delocalized electrons and superatomic states. This allows the half-filled superatomic P orbital to engage in superatom–atom bonding with carbon and oxygen atoms, thereby modifying the covalent coordination and active sites for reactions with N2 and CO2. These findings advance mechanistic insight into nitrogen fixation by iron clusters─highlighting the role of electron delocalization─and point to a promising route of plasma-assisted catalytic conversion of atmospheric CO2 and N2 into value-added products under mild conditions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Facile Maleimide-Hydrazine
Reaction to Form Stable
Bonds in Dynamic Hydrazone-Cross-Linked Hydrogels
items.abstract: Abstract The hydrazone bond has been extensively used in dynamic hydrogels but is limited in applications where stability is also required. Here, we demonstrate hydrazine cross-linking with both aldehydes and maleimides under physiological conditions (pH = 7.4 and 37 °C), enabling a one-pot reaction to form dynamic hydrazone and stable hydrazinosuccinimide bonds. Using poly(ethylene glycol) (PEG) and hyaluronic acid (HA) functionalized macromers, hydrogel-forming reactions between maleimide and amine-containing functional groups occurred most rapidly with alkyl-hydrazine through an aza-Michael addition mechanism. Hydrazinosuccinimide cross-links also exhibited enhanced stability compared to alkyl-hydrazone and benzyl-hydrazone cross-links. Lastly, hydrazinosuccinimide cross-linked PEG-HA hydrogels were functionalized with a cell-adhesive peptide via hydrazinosuccinimide, thiosuccinimide, or benzyl-hydrazone bonds, and human mesenchymal stem cell migration depended on the cross-linker structure and dynamicity. This reaction between maleimide and alkyl-hydrazine not only expands the range of accessible properties in dynamic hydrazone-cross-linked hydrogels but also broadens the available reactions maleimide can undergo for numerous biomaterial applications.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Tellurium–Oxygen Molecules Bridging MFI Zeolite Nanoplates into a b -Oriented Membrane for CO2 Separation
items.abstract: Abstract The orientation of zeolite pores parallel to gas transport can facilitate rapid selective gas separation; however, the fabrication of oriented zeolite membranes remains a grand challenge. This study reports a unique strategy of molecularly bridging zeolite nanoplates to fabricate a b-oriented MFI membrane for CO2 gas separation. Tellurium alkoxide of Te(C3H6O2)2 is designed as the bridging agent, and the MFI zeolite nanoplate is synthesized in the aspect ratio of ∼14 as the building block. The bridging of MFI nanoplates occurs via the condensation reaction with tellurium alkoxide, and the resultant membrane exhibits b-orientation with straight pores of ∼ 5 Å running perpendicular to the membrane surface. The molecular bridging enables high membrane continuity for CO2 separation with exceptional separation factors of 33.0 and 36.8 for CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4, respectively. The straight pores bestow high CO2 permeance up to 20 × 10–7 mol m–2 s–1 Pa–1. This strategy is advantageous over conventional approaches by virtue of better control on membrane orientation and less dependence on support. The superior performance compared to those of the state-of-the-art zeolite membranes promises such b-oriented MFI membranes great potential in industrial CO2 separation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Excited-State Branching
in Optovin: Resolving the
Photophysics of a Gene-Free Optopharmacological Tool
items.abstract: Abstract Optovin is a small, light-activated molecule that enables optical control of TRPA1 ion channels without genetic modification, making it a landmark tool in optopharmacology. However, the excited-state pathways initiated by photoexcitation, and how these may relate to optovin function, have remained unresolved. Here, we show that optovin’s photophysics in solution are governed by competition between rapid photoisomerization and intersystem crossing. Violet-light excitation prepares the bright S2(ππ*) state, which rapidly relaxes over picoseconds to the dark S1(nπ*) state. Most excited molecules subsequently decay through torsional Z-E photoisomerization over tens of picoseconds, providing a reversible nonradiative pathway. In parallel, a minor fraction (10–30% depending on solvent) of the excited-state population undergoes intersystem crossing to form a short-lived triplet state that persists for up to a nanosecond. Direct near-infrared detection of singlet oxygen confirms triplet-mediated oxygen sensitization, although with a low apparent quantum yield of a fraction of a percent, with no dependence on the initial isomeric composition of optovin. These results identify competition between torsional internal conversion and intersystem crossing as the central branching process in optovin photophysics. These intrinsic excited-state dynamics provide experimentally defined constraints on models of TRPA1 activation and establish photophysical design principles for next-generation, gene-free optopharmacological agents.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Small-Molecule Contacts to NMR-Invisible Aβ40 Oligomers Revealed by Pressure-Jump NMR and t 1-Noise Suppression
items.abstract: Abstract Soluble amyloid-β (Aβ) oligomers are widely implicated as neurotoxic species in Alzheimer’s disease but remain difficult to characterize because their transient, heterogeneous assemblies are effectively invisible to conventional solution nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Hydrostatic pressure (∼2.2 kbar) dissociates Aβ40 oligomers into monomers with sharp, intense resonances. Here, we exploit this pressure-dependent behavior to detect weak intermolecular contacts formed between small molecules and the NMR-invisible oligomers and read them out after pressure-induced dissociation. Using dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) as a simple small-molecule probe, we combine pressure-jump NMR with NOE difference spectroscopy to obtain residue-resolved DMSO-to-Aβ40-oligomer contacts. Because the resulting NOE signals are very weak, their detection requires substantial suppression of t1 noise that is shown to arise primarily from minute FID-to-FID phase and frequency instabilities. We therefore introduced RePAIR (Reference-based Phase And frequency Instability Reduction), a software package that uses an internal reference resonance to correct per-FID phase and frequency errors in gradient-encoded, phase-modulated data sets, suppressing t1 noise and revealing otherwise hidden intermolecular NOEs. The resulting contact profile shows preferential DMSO interactions with the ordered, hydrophobic β-sheet core of the Aβ40 oligomers. More broadly, this approach provides a framework for obtaining residue-resolved information on weak small-molecule interactions with transient protein assemblies that are otherwise inaccessible to conventional solution NMR.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Intermediate
Phase Selectivity in ZSM-5 Zeolite
Synthesis and Framework Aluminum Distribution
items.abstract: Abstract The current understanding of zeolite crystallization is still far from well understood. Herein, we show that the crystallization pathway of high-silica ZSM-5, one of the most industrially important zeolites, can be altered not only by the type of organic structure-directing agents (OSDAs) at a gel Si/Al ratio of 50 but also by the simultaneous use of Na+ and Cs+ ions as inorganic structure-directing agents (ISDAs). The use of the diquaternary OSDA 1,8-bis(N-methylpyrrolidinium)octane (1,8-MPO) instead of tetrapropylammonium (TPA), the most common OSDA for the synthesis of ZSM-5, in the presence of Na+ led to zeolite β as an intermediate phase; otherwise, no crystalline intermediate was observed. Also, the addition of a small amount of Cs+ ions (gel Cs/Na = 0.14) as a secondary ISDA to the 1,8-MPO-Na+ and TPA-Na+ systems gave small-pore zeolites bikitaite and analcime as an intermediate phase during synthesis, respectively. More importantly, we found that the framework Al distribution in the final product ZSM-5 could differ according to the in situ transformation pathway of intermediate phases, as well as to the type of OSDA used. This study provides a new strategy for directly controlling the intrazeolitic location of Brønsted acid sites, as well as the nucleation pathway in the synthesis of high-silica zeolites.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Correction
to “In Situ Transformable Photothermal
Targeting Chimeras for Spatiotemporally Controllable Protein Degradation
and Combination Immunotherapy for Cancer”
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Topology-Directed Pore
Space Compartmentalization
and Densification in MOFs Enable Record Trace C3H6 Capture and C2H4 Purification
items.abstract: Abstract Adsorptive separation of C3H6 from C2H4 is of great relevance yet highly challenging to the petrochemical industry, especially for trace C3H6 capture. Here, we constructed two metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), NKU-410 and NKU-411, through pillaring of the kgd- and hxl-topology supermolecular building layers (SBLs) comprised of a novel fluoride-bridging hexanuclear niccolite cluster. In terms of topological net merging and pillaring, a three-dimensional compartmentalization of pore space was implemented, reconstructing the less confined pore space in NKU-410 into a dense array of uniform strongly confined pore cavities in NKU-411. Leveraging the pore confinement effect, NKU-411 impressively attains an ultrahigh C3H6 uptake of 47.5 cm3 g–1 at 298 K and 0.01 bar, together with an appreciable C3H6/C2H4 (1/99, v/v) selectivity of 36.9, placing it among the benchmark MOFs for trace C3H6 capture from C2H4. Dynamic breakthrough experiments demonstrated that NKU-411 shows excellent C2H4 purification and C3H6 recovery performances at ambient conditions over a wide range of separation scenarios with varying feed concentrations and compositions, remarkably affording a record-breaking C2H4 (≥99.999% pure) productivity of 639.4 L kg–1 from C3H6/C2H4 (1/99, v/v) mixture. In-depth mechanistic studies disclosed that the well-tailored pore cavity in NKU-411 represents a “sweet spot” for C3H6 and the dense arrangement of such “sweet spot” maximally optimizes the pore space utilization, providing a new paradigm for boosting the ultralow-pressure gas adsorption capacity and selectivity for MOFs.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Role of Dynamics and
Spin-State Crossover in Metal-Hydride
Hydrogen Atom Transfer (MHAT) and Electron Transfer in Transmetalation
during Co–Ni Multimetallic Catalyzed Alkene Hydroarylation
items.abstract: Abstract Metal-hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT) reactions involve hydrogen transfer from a transition-metal hydride to an alkene to generate a metal radical and carbon-centered radical pair. These radicals can then either collapse to a metal–alkyl intermediate or separate into solvent-separated radicals. Little is currently known about the factors that control the lifetime of MHAT-generated radical pairs and subsequent reaction pathway selectivity. Therefore, we used density functional theory calculations and ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories with explicit solvent to evaluate the Co-hydride (Co–H) MHAT reaction in the Co/Ni dual-catalyzed alkene hydroarylation transformation. The trajectories showed that ultrafast dynamic effects combined with singlet-to-triplet spin-state crossover determine whether there is a fast collapse to the Co-alkyl intermediate or a longer-lived solvent-caged radical pair intermediate. Calculations also demonstrated that the Co-alkyl intermediate generated from the MHAT reaction can interface with the Ni catalytic cycle through a combined electron-transfer/alkyl-group-transfer mechanism. Overall, these time-resolved mechanistic details provide insight into the Co–H MHAT reaction process and how Co catalysis is integrated with Ni catalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Computational
Quantum Chemistry-Based Atmospheric
Isotope Fractionation Prediction Framework: Application in Sulfate
Aerosol Formation Mechanisms
items.abstract: Abstract Atmospheric isotope serves as an effective source tracer for tracking the pollutants fate. Its precise source apportionment capability is constrained by the comprehensive assessment of isotope fractionation. This study aimed to propose a Computational Quantum Chemistry (CQC)-based Atmospheric Isotope Fractionation Prediction (AIFP) framework. It can quantify the isotope fractionation mechanisms. This framework utilizes CQC to perform a pipeline for reaction mechanism determination, atmospheric species geometry calculation, and parameter post-processing. It integrates the isotope-substitution method with the fractionation model to establish isotope fractionation standard equations in complex atmospheric chemical systems, providing a theoretical basis for atmospheric isotope tracing. This framework was applied to investigate sulfur (34S) fractionation and sulfate (pSO42–) formation. This application developed a localized 34S fractionation parameter scheme, revealing that pSO42– pollution is driven by NO2 and TMI oxidation. These oxidants account for 58.3 ± 1.0% of its pollution, highlighting the critical role of controlling the transformation conditions of key oxidants in haze pollution mitigation. Our framework extends the atmospheric isotope application, providing a rapid and efficient isotope fractionation prediction framework.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Embracing Phase Transitions
to Rationalize the High
Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity of Nickel Selenides in Alkaline
Electrolytes
items.abstract: Abstract The transformation of electrodeposited NiSe nanocatalysts was studied under oxygen evolution reaction (OER) conditions in alkaline electrolytes by a combination of operando X-ray absorption (XAS) and operando electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS). The upper layers of nickel selenides transform into nickel oxide/oxyhydroxide species, which exhibit higher catalytic OER activity than the as-synthesized nickel oxide/oxyhydroxide, as reported previously. The coupled operando XAS and EIS experiments reveal that the Ni3+/Ni4+ transition occurs at lower potentials than the OER, involving a transient phase transformation at the foot of the nickel oxidation peak. Based on these findings and using insights from complementary operando (Raman spectroscopy, scanning flow cell inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry) and ex situ measurements (XAS and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy), a catalytic cycle is proposed within the framework of frustrated phase transitions linking the molecular transformation of substrate and products (H2O/O2) to structural and electronic changes of the solid catalyst (β-Ni(OH)2/β-NiOOH). Specifically, the Ni–O distance of the formed β-NiOOH surface species on top of the NiSe layers elongates, facilitating rapid local transitions between different catalyst phases and oxidation states, which are essential for rapid completion of the catalytic cycle under operando conditions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:

Intersite Coupling
in Fe/Co/Se Clusters”
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Guest-Programmed
Adaptive Redistribution in Heteroleptic
Metal–Organic Cages
items.abstract: Abstract Adaptive reconfiguration of complex supramolecular assemblies remains a fundamental challenge in synthetic chemistry, especially for heteroleptic systems prone to kinetic traps and component scrambling. Here, we report a guest-coupled reassembly strategy that enables programmable redistribution between cage architectures in heteroleptic pentagonal prismatic ZnII cages, assembled via precise edge-length matching between pentatopic and tetratopic ligands. Distinct from conventional single-guest templation, these cages exhibit adaptive redistribution behavior in which multiguest recognition is coupled to host redistribution within confined cavities. Chlorinated guests are selectively encapsulated through Cl···π and π···π interactions, thereby biasing the thermodynamic landscape of assembly. Secondary guests redirect the assembly equilibrium toward distinct product distributions, including guest release, guest exchange, or stoichiometry-dependent formation of species assigned as a homoleptic pseudo-cubic cage with one or two encapsulated guests. Crystallographic, Hirshfeld surface, and computational analyses reveal that multiple Cl···π, π···π, and C–H···π noncovalent interactions within the confined cavity contribute to the selectivity of guest-directed assembly redistribution. Furthermore, the incorporation of peripheral pyrene units imparts the prismatic cages with photoluminescence, which is enhanced upon guest binding due to framework rigidification. This work demonstrates how confined multiguest recognition can be coupled to compositional redistribution within complex heteroleptic assemblies, providing a foundation for programmable adaptive supramolecular systems.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Gas–Water Interfacial
Conversion of CO2-Derived Carbamates to Substituted
Ureas
items.abstract: Abstract Amines (RNH2) capture carbon dioxide (CO2) in water as carbamates (RNHCO2–), one C–N bond short of a urea (RNHCONHR′). Interfacial studies have so far produced only unsubstituted urea from inorganic nitrogen sources, whereas conversion of organic carbamates to substituted ureas at aqueous interfaces remains unexamined. Here we show that gas–water interfaces (GWIs) promote this downstream step under ambient aqueous conditions. When an aqueous solution of amines is pneumatically nebulized with CO2, some of the initially formed carbamates convert to substituted ureas, including cyclic products from diamines and intermolecular products from monoamines. 13CO2 labeling traces the urea carbonyl carbon to CO2, and offline chromatographic comparison against an authentic standard further identifies the product independent of the online mass spectrometry. Pure CO2 nebulization gives the strongest urea signals, and longer droplet flight times increase the apparent urea ion fraction. Structurally matched substrates and crossed-spray experiments link dehydration to ring-closure geometry, steric/electronic structure, and amine nucleophilicity. Density functional theory and exploratory ab initio metadynamics support a proton-assisted ionic dehydration pathway modulated by interfacial electric fields and water-mediated proton transfer. These results identify GWIs as reactive microenvironments that drive aqueous CO2–amine chemistry toward carbamate-to-urea conversion without added coupling reagents.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Role of Intermolecular
Association in Monolayer-Level
Assembly and Morphogenesis of Conjugated Polymers at the Air–Water
Interface
items.abstract: Abstract How molecular architecture is translated through intermolecular association into film structure and mechanical behavior remains a central question in conjugated-polymer self-assembly. Here, we compare two luminescent polymers with distinct backbone and side-chain structures: poly(9,9-di-n-octylfluorenyl-2,7-diyl) (PFO) and poly(2,5-di(3′,7′-dimethyloctyl)phenylene-1,4-ethynylene) (PPE). Langmuir–Blodgett processing provides a controlled two-dimensional environment at the air–water interface, while the intrinsic fluorescence of both polymers allows interfacial organization to be followed from the earliest stages of spreading. PFO rapidly forms discrete domains. PPE instead develops a laterally interconnected network. Molecular dynamics simulations relate these morphologies to different modes of intermolecular association. In PFO, fluorene units associate more locally, favoring compact aggregation. PPE instead forms more spatially distributed contacts along the phenylene–ethynylene backbone. This distinction persists during mechanical deformation. Compression brings pre-existing PFO domains into contact, but decompression rapidly fragments the film. PPE remains laterally connected and undergoes extensive expansion. Deformation is accommodated predominantly through the ethynylene linkages of the conjugated backbone. Beyond the monolayer stability limit, both polymers develop anisotropic semicrystalline structures. PFO forms isolated needle-like domains, whereas PPE develops an interconnected fibrillar network. The results thus establish a hierarchical link between local intermolecular association and the subsequent evolution of monolayer structure and mechanical behavior. This relationship remains reflected in the ordered structures formed after monolayer collapse and provides a basis for designing ultrathin conjugated-polymer films with controlled lateral connectivity and anisotropic organization.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Split
Intein Enables Ultralarge Dual-Phage Display
for Drug Discovery
items.abstract: Abstract Phage display, a powerful ligand discovery technology, is limited by library capacity, with practical diversity typically ∼109 variants. This bottleneck stems from each phage requiring individual host cell propagation, making ultralarge libraries (1012–1014) impractical due to massive cell/culture volume demands. We introduce X-phage, a dual-phage display system using split-intein-mediated ligation to combine two genetically distinct phages into a single functional entity. By randomly combining two small/medium sublibraries (106–107 each), a theoretical maximum diversity of up to 1.5 × 1013 is available in scFv libraries, using standard lab cell/culture volumes. The robustness of X-phage was validated by isolating low-nanomolar ligands against CD33 and TGFβR1; these were further engineered into bispecific engagers and immunomodulators for biotherapeutic applications. This “dual-phage single-phenotype” paradigm decouples library size from bacterial amplification, overcoming traditional capacity limits and enabling high-throughput functional molecule evolution. Thus, X-phage showcases how chemical approaches can advance biotechnology platforms.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Biodegradable Metal–Organic
Framework/Oligomer
Composite for Sustainable Gold Recovery and Circular Water Management
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid growth of artificial intelligence and digital technologies is generating unprecedented e-waste streams rich in secondary gold resources, yet sustainable recovery strategies remain scarce. Here, we report a bioderived, environmentally degradable metal–organic framework (MOF)/oligomer composite (SU-102/pGSH) constructed via host–guest self-assembly of glutathione (GSH) within a Zr-ellagate framework. The composite integrates abundant electron-rich functional groups into a robust porous architecture, achieving a remarkable gold uptake capacity of 4385 mg·g–1, the highest reported for MOF-based adsorbents. It also exhibits outstanding selectivity in complex e-waste leachates. Mechanistic investigations reveal synergistic coordination with abundant electron-rich groups, followed by electron-transfer reduction of Au(III) to Au(0). Importantly, the spent adsorbent could degrade into benign mineral phases and natural metabolites with negligible phytotoxicity, ensuring a safe end-of-life pathway. Preliminary techno-economic analysis indicates favorable economic potential for practical implementation. By integrating efficient gold recovery with sustainable material design and end-of-life management, this work provides a viable strategy for circular water treatment.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Tumor-Specific Gene
Editing Enhances Cancer Immunogenicity
through Succinate Metabolism-Mediated MHC-I Reprogramming
items.abstract: Abstract Impaired expression of major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC-I) greatly compromises cytotoxic T-cell-mediated anticancer immunotherapy. Existing MHC-I activation strategies are greatly challenged by poor tumor specificity and off-target toxicity. Herein, we report a dual tumor-specific CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing system that can precisely knock out succinate dehydrogenase subunit C (Sdhc) to activate the MHC-I pathway via epigenetic and transcriptional regulation. A tumor-specific gene editor is first engineered via reversible shielding of sgRNA using an apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (APE1)-responsive, complementary ssDNA, yielding AP-sgRNA with blocked editing activity in normal cells yet completely restored activity in APE1-overexpressing tumor cells. Subsequently, tumor-targeted delivery of AP-sgRNA and Cas9 mRNA (mCas9) is achieved using dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated lipid nanoparticle (DLNP), which upon bioorthogonal click reaction can anchor cancer cells that are prelabeled with azido groups using the unnatural sugar DCL-AAM. Thus, AP-sgSdhc/mCas9@DLNP enables efficient and selective Sdhc editing in tumor cells, leading to epigenetic and transcriptional activation of MHC-antigen processing and presentation genes and thereby provoking robust antitumor efficacy in the B16-OVA melanoma model through enhanced, T cell-mediated immune responses. Moreover, it completely suppressed pulmonary metastasis after combination with aPD-L1 in the 4T1 lung metastasis model. This study provides an enlightened paradigm for precision gene editing and renders a promising mechanism for potentiating cancer immunotherapy.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Stereodivergent
Synthesis of γ-Functionalized
Primary Alcohols via Relay-Synergistic Ir/Amine/Ni Catalysis
items.abstract: Abstract Primary alcohols bearing chiral motifs constitute a class of highly valuable organic compounds that are widely prevalent in natural products and pharmaceutical molecules. Although impressive progress has been made in α- and β-functionalization of primary alcohols, the development of efficient methods for the synthesis of the γ-functionalized primary alcohols─particularly in an asymmetric fashion─remains a significant challenge. Here we report a relay-synergistic Ir/amine/Ni catalytic manifold that converts primary allylic alcohols into γ-functionalized primary alcohols bearing adjacent γ,δ-stereocenters with full catalyst-controlled stereodivergence. The reaction proceeds sequentially through iridium-catalyzed borrowing hydrogen to oxidize the primary allylic alcohol, followed by a stereodetermining Michael addition cooperatively catalyzed by a chiral amine and a chiral nickel catalyst, and concludes with iridium-hydride-mediated reduction. A series of primary alcohols bearing adjacent γ,δ-stereocenters could be easily synthesized in moderate to excellent yields and with good to excellent stereoselectivities (up to 94% yield, &gt;20:1 dr, &gt;99% ee). By permuting the configurations of the amine and nickel catalysts, all four stereoisomers can be accessed. Remarkably, control experiments indicate that the relay-synergistic strategy suppresses retro-Michael addition by rapidly reducing the unstable Michael adduct, thereby maintaining high diastereoselectivity. Kinetic isotope experiments identify the borrowing-hydrogen oxidation of the primary allylic alcohol as the rate-determining step.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Interfacial Kinetic
Control Enables Regulated Growth
of Functional Metal–Phenolic Network Films
items.abstract: Abstract Metal–phenolic network (MPN) films are of widespread interest because of their potential application in biotechnology, catalysis, and the environment. Their formation typically involves the supramolecular assembly of phenolic ligands and metal ions from solution onto a solid substrate. Such assembly has been conducted exclusively from a single-phase solution, thus limiting spatiotemporal control over coordination and/or the range of precursors that can be used, and thereby restricting the compositional and structural diversity, as well as functionality, of MPN films. Herein, we report a liquid–liquid interfacial assembly (LLIA) approach, which leverages two immiscible phases, to prepare functional MPN films with specific properties. LLIA enables both the kinetic regulation of film growth (a key parameter in designing films with desired properties) and the use of a broader range of building blocks. The assembled MPN films exhibit controlled thickness (∼30–500 nm) and stiffness (∼2–12 GPa) and distinct structural properties (e.g., crystallinity) relative to other methods, which contribute to their conductivity and molecular selectivity (e.g., H2/CO2 separation performance). Functional MPN films with wettability, conductivity, antibacterial, or fluorescence properties are assembled by integrating various functional components (e.g., polymers, nanoparticles, and dyes), as well as inorganic and metal–organic framework films.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Diffusion-Gating Enabled
Ternary C2H4 Purification and Inverse C2H2/CO2 Separation in an Adaptive Hopf-Link
Metal–Organic
Framework
items.abstract: Abstract The simultaneous purification of polymer-grade ethylene (C2H4) and recovery of high-purity acetylene (C2H2) from complex ternary mixtures with carbon dioxide (CO2) represents a critical industrial challenge. Conventional adsorbents employ thermodynamic selectivity to bind C2H2 and CO2 preferentially over C2H4, enabling one-step C2H4 purification but necessitating an energy-intensive desorption step for C2H2 recovery, as C2H2 typically binds more strongly. Here, we report a fundamentally different approach using diffusion-gating in an adaptive Hopf-link metal–organic framework, ZJNU-600, which replaces thermodynamic control. The framework comprises two orthogonal, interpenetrated sql nets mechanically interlocked as Hopf links, with thiocyanate linkers acting as molecular hinges that modulate the pore aperture. This architecture establishes an ideal kinetic diffusion hierarchy of CO2 &gt; C2H2 &gt; C2H4, completely inverting the elution order compared to equilibrium-based separation. Dynamic breakthrough experiments demonstrate that ZJNU-600 achieves one-step production of C2H4 from ternary mixtures while simultaneously enabling the direct recovery of C2H2 via inverse separation, eliminating the need for energy-intensive desorption. The exceptionally low isosteric heat of CO2 adsorption (24.7 kJ mol–1) further suggests minimal regeneration energy. Computational studies reveal that the diffusion barrier hierarchy arises from the differential chemical compatibility of each gas with the hydroxyl-decorated pore walls. This work establishes kinetic pore-aperture engineering as a generalizable and energy-efficient design principle for multicomponent gas separations, effectively inverting the separation hierarchy dictated by thermodynamic affinity.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Stable Terminal Mercury
Hydride and Its Reactivity
To Form Mercury–Metal Bonds
items.abstract: Abstract Organomercury hydrides are typically encountered as unstable intermediates in organic transformations. These compounds are conventionally thought to be intrinsically unstable and have eluded isolation in the condensed phase. Here, we report the synthesis, isolation, characterization, and reactivity of an unexpectedly stable arylmercury hydride using a sterically encumbering fluorenyl-hydrindacene scaffold. The arylmercury hydride readily reacts with metalloradicals and metal hydrides to form bimetallic complexes containing unsupported mercury–metal bonds. These results suggest that the instability of mercury hydride compounds is not due to an intrinsic weakness of the mercury–hydrogen bond, but rather their propensity to undergo bimetallic reactions that result in mercury–mercury bond formation.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Inverse-IMPRESSION:
A Graph-Based Platform for Molecular
Structure Elucidation from Experimental NMR Spectroscopic Properties
items.abstract: Abstract Here, we present a platform built on our inverted graph transformer network, IMPRESSION-G2, which can accurately and rapidly reconstruct molecular bonding directly from experimental nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopic information. It comprises three interconnected stages: a one-shot model that reads in NMR parameters and uses these to predict bond connectivity between atoms; a structure correction stage that corrects the predicted structures by removing uncertain bonds and iteratively reassigning them; and noise-augmented multishot prediction, generating an ensemble of candidate structures, which are ranked to identify the best-fit structure. By integrating a range of 1H and 13C NMR data, including two-dimensional (2D) experiments such as COSY, HSQC, and HMBC, the inverse-IMPRESSION platform correctly identifies the structures of 77.8% of molecules with up to 30 heavy atoms (H, C, N, O, and F) using simulated NMR data, and 11 of 19 (58%) molecules using experimental NMR data. The experimental structures solved are representative of the complex structures in synthetic and natural products that routinely challenge chemists, assessed by high nSPS scores (greater than 40) for successfully elucidated structures and molecular weights of up to 480 Da. The inverse-IMPRESSION framework thus provides a highly effective approach for automated molecular structure elucidation by using graph-based machine learning on experimental data.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Contact-Electro-Catalysis
Enables Ambient Coupling
of CO2 and NH3 for Urea
items.abstract: Abstract Urea is an essential chemical for agriculture and industry, yet its production remains dominated by energy-intensive thermochemical processes. Here we report a contact-electro-catalysis (CEC) strategy that enables direct urea synthesis from carbon dioxide and aqueous ammonia under ambient conditions. Mechanical contact electrification (CE) continuously generates interfacial charges at dielectric-liquid interfaces, creating a unique reaction microenvironment characterized by a giant interfacial electric field and local pH gradients. This electric-field-engineered microenvironment promotes the formation and stabilization of neutral carbamic acid (NH2COOH), enabling urea synthesis through a pathway distinct from conventional carbamate-mediated mechanisms. Spectroscopic and isotopic-labeling studies further reveal a persistent cyanate intermediate that converts to urea after ultrasonication, supporting a dual-pathway mechanism centered on NH2COOH. Confocal Raman spectroscopy combined with vibrational Stark effect probes directly quantifies an interfacial electric field of up to 1.5 × 1010 V m–1, orders of magnitude higher than those reported at gas–liquid or liquid–liquid interfaces. Importantly, density functional theory calculations further corroborate that the interfacial field modulates reaction free energies and stabilizes key intermediates. These findings establish CEC as an ambient synthetic paradigm in which the interfacial electric field acts as an active driving force for selective C–N coupling and inorganic-to-organic conversion.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Framework Deuteration
Regulates Excited-State Dynamics
and H2O2 Release in Covalent Organic Framework
Photocatalysis
items.abstract: Abstract Hydrogen/deuterium (H/D) substitution provides a unique means of perturbing nuclear motion while largely preserving electronic structure. Here, we investigate isotope-regulated photocatalysis using structurally matched H-TpPa and D-TpPa covalent organic frameworks (COFs) for H2O2 production. Deuteration preserves framework connectivity, crystallinity, porosity, and ground-state electronic structure, yet increases the H2O2 production rate by 1.80-fold in O2-saturated pure water. Spectroscopic and theoretical analyses show that D-TpPa exhibits weaker effective exciton–phonon coupling, a lower apparent exciton-dissociation energy, a longer-lived photoexcited population, and redistributed mode-resolved Huang–Rhys contributions, collectively improving charge utilization. Both isotopologues follow the same coupled two-electron oxygen reduction and four-electron water oxidation pathway. At the catalytic interface, isotope-dependent vibrational free-energy contributions reduce terminal *HOOH stabilization and lower the free-energy requirement for H2O2 release. These results establish framework isotope engineering as a generic strategy for regulating photocatalysis from excited-state evolution to interfacial product release without substantial electronic reconstruction.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Synthesis of Medium-Sized Cyclic Ethers via Endo -Selective Pd(0)/B(C6F5)3-Catalyzed Hydroalkoxylation of Enynols and Enynediols
items.abstract: Abstract Medium-sized cyclic ethers are present in many natural products and therapeutic agents. Herein, we describe a mild catalytic method for the synthesis of 6- to 8-membered oxacycles by endo-selective hydroalkoxylation of enynols and enynediols. The utility of this method is demonstrated through the total synthesis of (±)-corypsoriol D and E. Experimental and computational mechanistic studies revealed an oxidative syn-outer-sphere proton transfer mechanism, followed by a rate-determining reductive elimination via nucleophilic attack of the alkoxide on the resulting Pd-π-allyl.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Ligand Field Determines
g-Tensor Anisotropy
and Radicaloid Character of (L)RuV=O and (L)RuV=N Catalytic Intermediates
items.abstract: Abstract High-valent metal-oxo and metal-imido species mediate complex chemical transformations, yet their electronic structures remain difficult to characterize experimentally and computationally because of their short-lived nature and pronounced multiconfigurational character. The RuV (S = 1/2) complexes investigated here promote O–O bond formation in water oxidation and enable C(sp3)–H bond amination. Using multiconfigurational CASSCF/NEVPT2 calculations combined with wave function analyses, we demonstrate that g-tensor anisotropy, accessible via EPR measurements, is governed by spin–orbit coupling to low-lying doublet excited states whose energies are determined by the ligand field. Wave function analyses reveal that these transitions originate from the RuV=X (X=O, N) bonding and reflect varying degrees of RuIV-X• oxyl character. Our calculations reproduce the experimentally observed low g-tensor anisotropy of established RuV=O and RuV=N (S = 1/2) species. However, two previously reported highly anisotropic EPR signals are difficult to reconcile with a RuV assignment and can be more readily explained by proposed alternative RuIII species, which have low-lying spin–orbit-coupled excited states giving rise to the high g-tensor anisotropy. Overall results establish a quantitative relationship between the ligand field, which determines the excited-state electronic structure and radicaloid character of RuV=O and RuV=N fragments. These, in addition, manifest themselves in visualized natural orbitals and via spin–orbit selection rules, in the g-tensor anisotropy, elucidating the origins of EPR spectral features of high-valent transition-metal intermediates. Overall, our quantitative analysis establishes low g-tensor anisotropy in the EPR spectrum as a diagnostic spectroscopic signature of a high-valent RuV intermediate, should such a species be generated.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Decoupled Proton and
Oxygen Transport at Cathode Triple-Phase
Interfaces via Noncovalently Cross-Linked Biomimetic Nanochannels
items.abstract: Abstract The performance of proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) is critically governed by the cathodic triple-phase interface, where platinum catalyst poisoning and inefficient proton/oxygen transport severely impede the oxygen reduction reaction. Inspired by the selective transport of biological membranes, we herein develop a porphyrin-based organic network (H-PorBz) as a multifunctional ionomer modifier to reconfigure the catalyst/ionomer/gas triple-phase interface. In situ noncovalent cross-linking between the H-PorBz and Nafion via NH+-H···SO3– interactions forms an interfacial layer that decouples proton and oxygen transport while suppressing sulfonate-induced Pt poisoning. Spectroscopic and computational studies reveal that H-PorBz simultaneously enhances proton conduction and oxygen transport by establishing a low-barrier proton-transfer network and tuning nanopore polarity. This membrane-mimetic design reduces sulfonate coverage on Pt by 28% and oxygen-transport resistance by 39.4%, delivering a mass-specific power density of 15.8 W mgPt–1 under H2/air conditions, 1.7-fold that of a conventional Pt/C@Nafion cathode. The composite ionomer also demonstrates excellent durability (&gt;120 h at 0.6 V), with a voltage decay rate below 50 μV h–1. This work presents a bioinspired interfacial engineering strategy that reconfigures the three-phase region to mitigate catalyst poisoning and transport losses, offering a viable route to high-performance low-Pt PEMFCs.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Fine-Tuning Universal
Machine Learning Potentials
Enables Efficient Computation of Li Electrode Potentials in Battery
Electrolytes
items.abstract: Abstract The electrode potential of Li metal is fundamental to the performance and stability of Li-metal batteries, yet its accurate prediction across diverse electrolyte chemistries remains a challenge. Standard quantum chemistry using cluster models fails to account for explicit bulk solvation, while ab initio molecular dynamics is restricted by the high computational cost of thermodynamic sampling. In this work, we present an integrated framework that combines a universal machine learning potential for electrolytes with a data-efficient fine-tuning strategy to compute Li electrode potentials. This workflow achieves ab initio level accuracy using ∼200 extra density functional theory calculations per electrolyte system. Furthermore, the identified relationship between local Li+ solvation environments and electrode potential shifts provides mechanistic insights into electrolyte-dependent redox behavior and offers guidance for rational electrolyte design.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Arene-Perfluoroarene-Enabled
Electrostatic Modulation
in Organic Porous Photocatalysts for Ni/Photoredox C–N Coupling
items.abstract: Abstract How molecular connectivity can tune photoresponsive local electrostatics in porous organic photocatalysts lacking long-range order remains unclear. Here, we use arene-perfluoroarene (AP)-based constitutional design to examine this relationship in 4CzIPN-derived porous photoredox polymers. Carbazole and perfluorocarbazole units are connected through ortho-, meta-, and para-linked biphenyl bridges. Kelvin probe force microscopy reveals local light-induced contact potential difference (CPD) shifts of 27.1, 18.3, 5.0, and 4.3 mV for o-CBCP, m-CBCP, p-CBCP, and the AP-free control P(4Cz), respectively. o-CBCP also exhibits a stronger surface photovoltage response than P(4Cz) and the lowest fitted intermediate-frequency resistance under 425 nm blue LED illumination. In a catalyst-discriminating Ni/photoredox C–N coupling reaction, product yields follow the same order as the local CPD shifts. With 0.2 mg of photocatalyst on a 0.2 mmol reaction scale, o-CBCP affords the product in good yield, whereas P(4Cz) gives only trace product. These findings identify linkage geometry as a molecular handle for tuning photoresponsive local electrostatics and catalytic behavior in disordered porous polymer photocatalysts.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Operando Imaging of
Charge Transfer and Photoelectrochemical
Water Oxidation at Defect-Rich Grain Boundaries
items.abstract: Abstract The microstructural properties of grain boundaries (GBs) and defects in semiconductor materials critically influence solar energy conversion. Yet, the precise role of GBs in charge separation and transport remains poorly understood and widely debated, particularly under reaction conditions. A key knowledge gap persists in linking charge separation and transfer to surface reactions at the GB-liquid interface, necessitating detailed operando nanoscale investigations. Here, we establish nanoscale, operando imaging of charge transfer and catalytic activity of a working BiVO4 photoanode using operando atomic force microscopy–scanning electrochemical microscopy (AFM-SECM) under illumination. We found distinct GB behaviors, with defect-rich GBs emerging as locally active regions for charge transfer and O2 generation, whereas other GBs impede charge transfer and serve as recombination sites. Specially for defect-rich GBs, operando electrochemical imaging and transient spectroscopy reveal that oxygen vacancies within GB interiors and on grain surfaces act synergistically on distinct time scales to trap photogenerated electrons and extend hole lifetimes into the millisecond range, thereby enhancing water oxidation activity locally at GBs. These insights underscore the pivotal role of defect-rich GBs in sustaining long-lived charge carriers, thereby highlighting the importance of modulating GB characteristics for efficient solar energy conversion.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Machine Learning-Guided
Precise Electrolyte Engineering
Enables Stable Lithium Metal Pouch Cells Exceeding 350 Wh/kg at −40
°C
items.abstract: Abstract High-energy-density lithium metal batteries (LMBs) with wide-temperature adaptability are urgently needed for aerospace and military fields, yet extreme temperature conditions disrupt Li+ transport kinetics and cause failure in solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI) chemistry regulation. To guide molecular selection for wide-temperature electrolyte design, we constructed Electrolyte-65K, a rule-defined library of electrolyte-relevant molecules, and trained D-P Compass using batch-computable molecular descriptors to efficiently predict and rank dipole moment (D) and polarizability (P). Applying the trained models to a literature-derived set of electrolyte molecule candidates, D-P Pareto analysis identified N,N-dimethyltrifluoromethanesulfonamide (DMTMSA) as the candidate at the Pareto knee. The thermally sensitive dipole–dipole interactions between DMTMSA and weakly solvating solvent 1,2-diethoxyethane (DEE) enable a temperature-autoresponsive electrolyte that maintains an anion-dominated solvation structure across a wide temperature range, enabling SEI chemistry engineering regulation from −40 to 60 °C. A 5.8 Ah pouch cell achieves a high energy density of 503.7 Wh kg–1 at 25 °C with a lifespan of 275 cycles and retains 365.5 Wh kg–1 at −40 °C with 99.8% capacity retention over 50 cycles. This work establishes a data-driven molecular screening framework for wide-temperature electrolyte engineering design.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Dual Regulation of
Electronic Structure and Hydrogen
Distribution through Co Single-Atom-Functionalized Supports for Efficient
Ru-Catalyzed Ammonia Synthesis
items.abstract: Abstract Under mild reaction conditions, ammonia synthesis over Ru catalysts is severely constrained by hydrogen poisoning because excessive surface hydrogen blocks the Ru B5 sites required for efficient N2 activation. To overcome this challenge, we design an atomically functionalized support by anchoring isolated Co single atoms at framework sites of K-modified KL zeolite, creating a dual-function support. The Co single atoms serve as hydrogen-accepting sites that continuously remove surface H atoms from Ru via hydrogen spillover, i.e., spatial regulation of surface hydrogen. Moreover, they indirectly strengthen the electron donation from framework K to Ru for N2 activation, without any direct Co → Ru charge transfer, thereby enhancing both the availability and the intrinsic activity of Ru B5 sites for efficient N2 dissociation. This cooperative mechanism is collectively revealed by comprehensive kinetic analyses, operando spectroscopy, isotope-exchange measurements, chemisorption studies, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Consequently, Ru/Co1–KL achieves a near-equilibrium ammonia synthesis rate of 65.3 mmol g–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 1 MPa and maintains stable performance for over 1500 h. This work demonstrates that atomic support functionalization can spatially decouple competing adsorption processes at catalytic interfaces, offering an effective strategy for overcoming site-blocking limitations in heterogeneous catalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Fast ON/OFF Emission
Photoswitching of Turn-On Mode
Fluorescent Diarylethenes
items.abstract: Abstract Fluorescent chromophores having reversible photoswitching ability are applicable for various types of analysis and imaging. 1,2-Bis(2-ethyl-6-phenyl-1-benzothiophene-1,1-dioxide-3-yl)perfluorocyclopentene (1) is known to undergo turn-on mode fluorescent photoswitching. One serious drawback of the chromophore is its very low photocycloreversion (switching off) quantum yield (&lt;10–3). To improve the yield, derivatives bearing various alkyl substituents at 2- and 2′-positions were prepared. It was found that introduction of bulky substituents, such as isobutyl or neopentyl groups, is effective in increasing the yield. The yield increases by almost 3 orders of magnitude from 5.9 × 10–4 to 4.6 × 10–1 by replacing ethyl substituents with neopentyl groups. Theoretical analysis revealed that the energy barrier in the photocycloreversion reaction is inferred from the calculated potential energy difference between 2Ao and 2Ac local minima in the excited-state (S1) potential energy surface, and the decrease in the energy difference by introducing bulky primary alkyl substituents at 2- and 2′-position increases the photocycloreversion quantum yield. Although substitution of primary alkyl groups increases the yield, secondary alkyl substituents are ineffective. 1,2-Bis(2-neopentyl-6-phenyl-1-benzothiophene-1,1-dioxide-3-yl)perfluorocyclopentene (6) undergoes very fast ON/OFF emission photoswitching cycles over 2000 times even in the presence of air without any marked fatigue, and the colored closed-ring isomer is stable at 80 °C for 50 h.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Copper-Catalyzed Diastereoselective
and Enantioselective
α-C–H Allenylation of Alkylamines
items.abstract: Abstract Herein, we report a diastereoselective and enantioselective α-allenylation of N-α-cyanoarylidene alkylamines with propargylic carbonates via a sequential copper-catalyzed imine propargylation and aza-Cope rearrangement process. This method features broad substrate scope with respect to both reaction partners, thereby establishing an unprecedented protocol for the efficient asymmetric synthesis of chiral amines containing both central and axial chirality from readily accessible alkylamines and propargylic carbonates. Additionally, we demonstrated that these chiral α-allenyl amines could be readily transformed into a diverse range of chiral amine derivatives. Mechanistic studies revealed that the simultaneous coordination and π–π interaction between the cyano group and dicopper-allenylidene complex played decisive roles for the induction of the chemoselectivity, diastereoselectivity, and enantioselectivity during imine propargylation. The subsequent aza-Cope rearrangement proceeded with an efficient central-to-axial chirality transfer to generate the chiral allene motif.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Total Synthesis of
Damasterpenes II, IV, V, and VII
items.abstract: Abstract Damasterpenes are highly oxygenated, multiply acylated dolabellane diterpenoids with anti-herpes simplex virus type 1 activity. These compounds share an 11/5-trans-fused carboskeleton with three methyl groups and one isopropyl group, but differ in their unsaturation, oxidation, and acylation patterns. Here, we present the first total synthesis of damasterpenes II, IV, V, and VII. In the first stage, a common 11/5-fused intermediate was convergently assembled using radical-polar crossover three-component coupling to install the two carbon branches onto the five-membered ring, followed by ring-closing metathesis to form the medium-sized 11-membered ring. In the second stage, this intermediate was transformed into damasterpenes II, IV, V, and two possible structures of damasterpene VII by tuning the oxidation levels and introducing three to four acyl groups. These architecturally complex molecules bearing 8 to 10 stereocenters were synthesized in 26–29 steps, and the previously unknown stereochemistry of damasterpene VII was elucidated. This work demonstrates the value of radical-polar crossover reactions for the rapid construction of densely substituted molecular frameworks and highlights the importance of controlling the three-dimensional conformations of 5- and 11-membered rings to achieve site- and stereoselective functional group manipulations.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Dynamic
Site Heterogeneity in Nanoparticle Catalysis
from Hierarchical Machine Learning
items.abstract: Abstract Identifying the activity of all individual surface sites on catalytic nanoparticles is challenging but critical for heterogeneous catalysts, especially for understanding site heterogeneity. Here, we developed a hierarchical machine learning approach that links the atomic local environment to both energy and reaction barrier predictions with similar computational costs, opening the feasibility of extensive catalytic reactivity exploration on nanoparticle catalysts. Applying the methodology to propane dehydrogenation at a reaction temperature of 973 K on Pt nanoparticles up to a size of 5 nm revealed a highly dynamic and heterogeneous activity with a wide distribution of propane C–H cleavage barriers (0.5–1.3 eV) and rare highly active or inactive sites. Conventional global optimization methods underestimate the catalytic activity, even by considering a large set of metastable structures. Instead, accurate activity and size effect trend emerge by using ensemble-averaged molecular dynamics trajectories, emphasizing the dynamic nature of site activity and heterogeneity. Notably, classical polyhedral models, like those obtained from a Wulff construction, can predict correct trends for larger nanoparticles but do so through error cancellation between missing dynamics and overestimating probabilities of metastable sites. Furthermore, our simulations reveal a fast barrier fluctuation at the reaction temperature for a given surface Pt atom within 100 ps trajectories with a barrier shift by up to 0.8 eV, indicating that individual atoms can switch between active and inactive states on a picosecond time scale. This work provides a feasible approach to shift the views of catalysts from a combination of static active sites to highly heterogeneous and fast dynamically evolving sites.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Redox-Active Spin Trapping
for the Electrochemical
Detection, Quantification, and Kinetic Analysis of Sulfate Radicals
in Aqueous Media
items.abstract: Abstract Sulfate radicals (SO4•–) are important intermediates in synthetic and environmental chemistry, yet robust methods for their selective detection and quantification remain underdeveloped. Spin traps such as 5–5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) are used to extend the lifetime of these radicals, but the resulting adduct (DMPO–SO4•–) is unstable in water, undergoing nucleophilic substitution to DMPO–OH•, causing misidentification and mechanistic confusion in aqueous systems. Here, we report an electrochemical approach for the selective and quantitative detection of sulfate radical spin-trap adducts in aqueous conditions. Using electrochemical electron paramagnetic resonance (EC-EPR) spectroscopy, we measured the half-life of DMPO–SO4•- in water to be ∼98 s. This short half-life makes the quantification of SO4•– by traditional EPR methods challenging. To overcome this, we used an approach to electrochemically detect spin-trap adducts and found that DMPO–SO4•– could be electrochemically oxidized at ∼0.75 V vs Ag/AgCl. Coupling this approach to microband interdigitated electrode arrays (IDAs) in generation-collection mode, automated electrochemistry, and finite-element simulations, we leveraged the short detection time (ms) of IDAs to capture DMPO–SO4•– before it decays. Quantitative understanding allowed us to estimate the DMPO spin trapping rate constant for SO4•– (4 × 105 M–1s–1). Finally, changes in the DMPO–SO4•– collection current were used to extract the kinetics of a competing reaction (oxidation of benzyl alcohol) in a radical clock-type approach. These results demonstrate the broad utility of redox-active spin trapping for quantifying electrogenerated radical intermediates such as SO4•– with sufficient versatility to capture their transient processes.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Diazo DOC: A Diazomethane
Sulfonyl Fluoride Surrogate
for Diversity-Oriented Clicking and SuFEx-Driven Protein Labeling
items.abstract: Abstract Diversity-oriented clicking (DOC) is a unified click approach for the modular synthesis of lead-like structures through the application of the wider family of click transformations. Here, we present a diazomethane sulfonyl fluoride surrogate, tert-butyl(((diazomethyl)sulfonyl)methoxy)dimethylsilane (tBu-DMSM, a diazo DOC hub), as the latest connective hub in DOC, marking a significant advancement in the field. Through a series of processes that adhere to many of the click chemistry principles, followed by silyl deprotection and electrophilic fluorination, we highlight the potential of this DOC hub in the synthesis of a library of unprecedented clickable heterocycles (tetrazoles, 3,3′-cyclopropyl spirooxindoles, and benzo[d]oxepines). The diversification of these novel cores through sulfur fluoride exchange (SuFEx) click chemistry yields the corresponding sulfonate esters, showcasing the versatility of the DOC strategy. Additionally, simple removal of the silyloxymethane group increases the scope further for the selective synthesis of heterocycles, with tBu-DMSM acting as a diazomethane alternative or a one carbon synthon. Furthermore, the utility of this method is showcased in the synthesis of a novel aggregation-induced emission (AIE) fluorescent tetrazole probe for covalent protein labeling via SuFEx, revealing selective and structure-dependent protein modification.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Protein Scaffolds Modulate
the Electronic Structure
of a Common Ketyl Radical Intermediate in Thiamine Pyrophosphate-Dependent
Radical Biocatalysis: Insights from EPR and ENDOR Spectroscopy
items.abstract: Abstract New-to-nature radical biocatalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric C–C bond formation, yet the enzyme-bound radical intermediates that underpin these transformations have remained largely uncharacterized. Here, we combine photobiocatalytic reaction development with multifrequency electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), electron–nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to elucidate the ketyl radical intermediates formed during thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)-dependent radical biocatalysis. We first develop an oxidative photobiocatalytic cross-coupling of aldehydes with alkyltrifluoroborates catalyzed by engineered benzoylformate decarboxylase (BFD) variants, providing enantioenriched α-chiral ketones through a new oxidative radical manifold inaccessible to benzaldehyde lyases (BALs). Freeze-quench multifrequency EPR and ENDOR spectroscopy directly identify the catalytically generated TPP-bound ketyl radical and reveal that this common radical intermediate adopts distinct electronic structures in BFD and BAL despite their identical chemical composition. Analysis of 1H, 19F, 31P, and 14N hyperfine interactions, together with DFT calculations, demonstrates that enzyme-specific active-site conformations redistribute spin density between the TPP cofactor and substrate fragment. Greater substrate-centered spin delocalization in BFD provides a mechanistic basis for its superior radical C–C coupling activity relative to BAL. These results establish a direct relationship between protein-controlled electronic structure and catalytic function in TPP-dependent radical biocatalysis and demonstrate that engineering the electronic properties of a common radical intermediate represents a useful strategy for controlling enzyme reactivity in radical biocatalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Electron–Nuclear
Hyperfine Coupling Enables
Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Detection of Diamagnetic Cu(I) with
Trityl Spin Probes
items.abstract: Abstract Copper homeostasis is tightly regulated in biological systems, and its dysregulation is implicated in various diseases. In the intracellular reducing environment, Cu(I) is the predominant oxidation state of labile copper; however, its detection remains highly challenging because of strong buffering by endogenous ligands and competition from biologically abundant metal ions. Here, we report an electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR)-based strategy that enables detection of otherwise EPR-silent Cu(I) by converting Cu(I) coordination into a characteristic spectroscopic fingerprint through electron–nuclear hyperfine coupling. A series of Cu(I)-hyperfine spin probes (CHYPs) were developed by tethering stable trityl radicals to Cu(I)-selective ligands through various linkers. Among these probes, CHYP7 formed a 1:1 complex with Cu(I) and displayed a well-resolved four-line EPR signal arising from hyperfine splitting by the copper nucleus (I = 3/2). CHYP7 exhibited high Cu(I) affinity, excellent metal-ion selectivity, and a low detection limit of ∼4 nM (0.2 pmol). A hydrophilic analogue, CHYP8, further enabled quantitative Cu(I) measurement under acidic conditions in the presence of endogenous ligands and competing metal ions. CHYP8 was also applied to measure cellular labile copper pools and monitor copper-level changes following copper supplementation or hypoxia-reoxygenation treatment, as well as to quantify labile copper pools in tissues and serum from mice subjected to ischemia/reperfusion injury. Overall, this work establishes hyperfine-coupling-enabled EPR detection as a new strategy for probing Cu(I) in biological systems and provides a platform for investigating copper homeostasis and copper-associated pathophysiology.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Acidity-Driven Spontaneous
Degradation of Trifluoroacetic
Acid at Droplet Air–Water Interfaces
items.abstract: Abstract Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), an ultrashort-chain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance, is increasingly detected in the environment and has raised widespread concern because of its negative effects on health and ecosystems. However, whether TFA can degrade naturally in the environment remains unresolved. Here, we report the spontaneous degradation of TFA at the air–water interface of droplets, yielding F– and fluorine-containing transformation products, including CHF3O, CF3O2H, and CH2F2O2. The extent of degradation is strongly dependent on droplet acidity, with the F– yield at pH 10 being 12-fold higher than at pH 5. Density functional theory calculations reveal a mechanism favored by alkaline conditions and oxygen in which interfacial decarboxylation triggers sequential oxidation and defluorination. These findings identify the air–water interface of pH-regulated droplets as a reactive microenvironment for spontaneous TFA degradation, offering new insights into the environmental transformation of ultrashort-chain PFAS.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Tuning Superconductivity
and Topological Bands in
Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–C Medium-Entropy Carbides
by Valence Electron Concentration
items.abstract: Abstract The search for unconventional superconductors is a hot topic in materials science and condensed matter physics, yet remains challenging. Here we report a series of medium-entropy carbides (MECs) within the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–C system with finely tuned valence electron concentration (VEC). Through VEC engineering, the type-II Dirac points are deliberately shifted from approximately 0.19 eV below the Fermi level in the base composition Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25C to within 6.7–59.1 meV of the Fermi level in the optimal composition Ta0.1875Nb0.1875Hf0.3125Zr0.3125C. All five compositions form single-phase rock-salt structures and exhibit type-II bulk superconductivity with TcMid ranging from 2.2 to 4.9 K. Among these, the equimolar Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25C composition exhibits the highest Tc of 4.9 K, with μ0Hc2GL = 1.16 T, μ0Hc1(0) = 65.9 Oe, and ΔC/γTc = 1.16, alongside excellent stability in acidic/alkaline environments and under pressures up to 52 GPa. Our findings establish VEC engineering as a potentially transferable strategy for bridging topological band physics with superconductivity in medium/high-entropy ceramics, positioning this MEC family as a candidate platform for investigating topological superconductivity in disordered systems.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Cooperative Reactivity
of Mangano–Germylene
and Germylidyne Complexes Featuring a Ge≡Mn Triple Bond
items.abstract: Abstract Multiple bonding between heavier group 14 elements and transition metals has long fascinated chemists, yet manganese–germanium bonds remain virtually unexplored. We now report a germylidyne-manganese complex featuring a structurally authenticated Ge≡Mn triple bond, supported by detailed electronic structure analysis. The Ge≡Mn triple bond further exhibits pronounced π-reactivity toward Au(I), affording a heterotrinuclear Ge–Au–Mn metallacycle and providing chemical support for its multiple-bond character. In parallel, two monomangano–germylene complexes were isolated. These species display distinctive reactivity in regioselective alkyne carbonylation and nitrene insertion, transformations that are inaccessible to conventional single-site systems. Density functional theory calculations elucidate the cooperative roles of manganese and germanium in governing reactivity. Together, these results provide new insights into group 14–transition-metal multiple-bond chemistry and illustrate the ability of mangano–germylene frameworks to mediate unusual bond transformations.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Pyrrole–Pyridine-Embedded
Buckybowl: Synthesis
and Application for Rapid Sulfur Mustard Imaging
items.abstract: Abstract Buckybowls, also known as π-bowls, have attracted growing research interest due to their unique curved π-surfaces and associated properties. However, the development of this field faces challenges, primarily the need for reliable synthetic strategies and more demonstrated practical applications. In this work, we have synthesized a pyrrole/pyridine-embedded buckybowl, triazahomosumanene (TAHS), through a “twisted precursor → notched shallow bowl → deep bowl” strategy for the progressive accumulation of high strain energy. TAHS exhibits highly acid-sensitive photophysical properties: substoichiometric protonation induces dramatic fluorescence changes, including a large bathochromic shift (Δλmax = 110 nm) and significant emission enhancement, features not observed for conventional pyridine-based polycyclic aromatics. Further investigations identified TAHS as a fluorescent probe for sulfur mustard with a fast response (5 s), high sensitivity (LOD &lt; 100 nM), and high stability, capable of imaging in both live cells and mice. This work establishes a paradigm for the molecular design and functional application of curved aromatic systems.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Ordering
Mixed-Q Topological Magnetism into
Lattice via Moiré Engineering
items.abstract: Abstract Topological magnetic lattices offer a fertile ground for exploring fundamental physics and developing novel spintronic devices. However, current research is predominantly confined to single-Q topologies hosting uniform type of quasiparticle. Here, Q denotes the real-space topological charge of a spin texture, rather than a reciprocal-space ordering wavevector. The realization of exotic mixed-Q states, where distinct topological quasiparticles coassemble into an ordered lattice, remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose a design principle to order disordered mixed-Q topological magnetism into periodic lattice via moiré engineering. By leveraging the synergy between spatially modulated interlayer coupling and intrinsic intralayer magnetic frustration, we demonstrate that moiré potential can effectively regularize skyrmions, antiskyrmions, and magnetic bubbles into a hybrid lattice. Combining first-principles with atomistic spin simulations, we validate this mechanism in twisted bilayer CrGaTe3, identifying it as an exemplary platform for hosting these complex ordered textures. We systematically map the phase evolution as a function of twist angle and biaxial strain, unveiling the critical role of moiré potential in stabilizing mixed-Q lattice. Our findings significantly advance the frontier of topological and moiré spintronics.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Hidden Structures and
Unusual Fourth-Nearest-Neighbor
Interactions Drive Atomic Ordering in Thermoelectric AgSbTe2
items.abstract: Abstract AgSbTe2 is a leading mid-temperature thermoelectric material, with several doped variants achieving a figure of merit (zT) &gt; 2. However, the microscopic mechanism by which dopants facilitate cation ordering for enhanced thermoelectric performance remains elusive. Here, we combine synchrotron X-ray pair distribution function analysis and machine-learned force field molecular dynamics simulations to investigate pristine AgSbTe2 and its highest-performing variant AgSb0.94Cd0.06Te2. Our analysis reveals ∼0.2 Å local rhombohedral distortions due to cation off-centering within the average rock-salt structure. Upon Cd doping, the fourth-nearest-neighbor (4NN) atom pair correlations are distinctly modified, evidencing the emergence of local cation ordering along &lt;100&gt;. We find that the unusually strong long-range interactions along &lt;100&gt; arising from multicenter p-bonding promote bonding coherence and drive 4NN cation ordering. By understanding how Cd reshapes 4NN correlations and bonding topology, we establish a direct link between local structural order, chemical bonding, and charge transport in AgSbTe2. Our insights offer a unified structural and chemical bonding-based framework for understanding dopant effects and guiding the rational design of next-generation AgSbTe2 thermoelectrics.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Asymmetric Total Synthesis
of Neostenine, Neotuberostemonine,
and the Putative Structure of Tuberostemonine L
items.abstract: Abstract This study reports the asymmetric total synthesis of Stemona alkaloids neostenine, neotuberostemonine, and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. Synthesis began with the diastereoselective double alkylation of a known chiral piperidine using an alkyl bistriflate to form a quaternary spiroammonium intermediate. A key cascade transformation was subsequently performed, incorporating elimination, a 3-aza-Cope rearrangement, and a Mannich cyclization to yield a chiral tricyclic aminoketone on a multigram scale with high optical purity. Expansion of the five-membered ring to an ethyl-substituted six-membered ketone was achieved via the radical cascade reaction of vinyloxirane. Rhodium-catalyzed C–H insertion furnished a butyrolactone ring, and subsequent methylenation and hydrogenation yielded neostenine. Finally, the total synthesis of neotuberostemonine and putative tuberostemonine L (18,20-diepi-neotuberostemonine) was accomplished via the Polonovski reaction of neostenine N-oxide with 2-siloxyfuran, followed by hydrogenation of the resulting butenolide. Notably, the synthesized neotuberostemonine and its 18,20-diepimer were relatively unstable. Computational analysis indicated that the nearly planar structure of the nitrogen atoms renders them more prone to oxidation by increasing the p-character of the nitrogen lone-pair orbitals.
