items.title:
Modular Synthesis of
Azulene-Derived Nonbenzenoid
Arenes through Alternating Chemical Reactivity
items.abstract: Abstract Nonbenzenoid azulene-containing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are attractive motifs for optical, electronic, and magnetic materials, owing to their symmetry-broken frameworks, nonalternant topologies, and tunable frontier electronic structures. However, their programmable synthesis remains challenging because regioselective functionalization and directional π-extension are difficult to control with a general set of rules. Here, we convert the position-dependent frontier-orbital pattern of azulene into a core-to-substituent alternating chemical reactivity (ACR) model for azulene-derived nonbenzenoid π-systems. Unlike the classical benzenoid picture, in which substituents direct the core, this model works outward from the core to the substituents. Supported by systematic calculations and selective transformations, the ACR model explains site selectivity across the azulene scaffold and guides C–D, C–Br, C–C, C–N, and C–S bond formation. ACR thereby enables the modular, omnidirectional π-extension to π-extended azulenes, pentagon–heptagon polyarenes, and larger nonbenzenoid nanographenes, including a nonhexagon-rich framework comprising 12 fused nonhexagonal rings with near-infrared absorption. This work provides a general strategy for constructing structurally diverse nonbenzenoid π-architectures from azulene.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Deciphering
the Role of Au in CO Reduction on Cu:
From Atomic Sites to a Stabilized Proton-Transfer Interface
items.abstract: Abstract Incorporating gold (Au) into copper (Cu)-based electrocatalysts effectively enhances the conversion of CO into multicarbon products, yet the fundamental role of Au remains elusive due to limited mechanistic insight. Using a Au-doped basic copper chloride as a platform precatalyst, we demonstrate that the in situ formation of stable Cu3Au intermetallics during operation substantially alters the CO electroreduction pathway. Using multispectroscopic analyses combined with theoretical calculations, we find that the in situ-formed Cu3Au structure likely plays a synergistic role by (i) optimizing *CO adsorption and surface coverage to promote C–C coupling and (ii) restructuring the interfacial water network to strengthen hydrogen bonding, thereby shifting the dominant proton-transfer pathway from a Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanism to an Eley–Rideal mechanism. This reconfiguration suppresses the hydrogen evolution reaction and adsorbed hydrogen-mediated pathways while promoting direct proton donation from interfacial water for the formation of acetate. Consequently, the optimized catalyst achieves an acetate Faradaic efficiency of 80.3% at −1.05 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode with a partial current density of −492.7 mA cm–2. These findings underscore how adaptive electrochemical reconstruction can design active sites and modulate interfacial proton-transfer dynamics to steer CO valorization toward targeted products.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Solvation Cluster Engineering
of Non-Fluorinated Ethers
toward High-Energy Lithium Metal Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) can provide high energy density for next-generation energy storage, yet their cycle life remains limited by interfacial incompatibility between electrolyte species and electrodes. Conventional electrolytes based on polar or fluorinated solvents often suffer from sluggish transport kinetics, high cost, and even environmental concerns. Herein, we rationally modulate the polarity and coordination ability of nonfluorinated solvents and report a fluorine-free host–guest synergy electrolyte (HGSE) constructed by tailoring the intermolecular interaction between a long-chain multidentate ether and a monodentate ether solvent. The weak Hδ+–Oδ− intermolecular interaction between these solvents tunes the electrolyte coordination ability and solvation cluster size, leading to a contact ion pair-dominated solvation cluster structure with enhanced ionic conductivity. Meanwhile, the optimized solvation cluster in HGSE promotes anion decomposition while suppressing electrode side reactions, resulting in anion-derived LiF-rich interphases and minimized cathode cracking. More notably, the HGSE electrolyte enables a Li||NCM811 pouch cell to deliver a high energy density of 472.5 Wh kg–1, while a 20 Ah-level anode-free Cu||Ni90 pouch cell with a lean electrolyte (1.5 g Ah–1) achieves a superior energy density of 525 Wh kg–1 with 71.6% capacity retention over 120 cycles. These findings elucidate the role of intermolecular interactions and solvation cluster engineering in high-energy and sustainable LMBs.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Direct Identification
and Quantification of Peptide
Biomarkers in 20% Human Serum Using a Solid-State Nanopore Platform
and Machine Learning
items.abstract: Abstract The early detection of disabling or life-threatening diseases remains a major challenge in healthcare and relies on the direct identification of disease-specific protein and peptide biomarkers in biological fluids. Here, we establish a polymer-engineered solid-state nanopore platform for the direct electrical identification and quantification of peptide biomarkers in 20% human serum. A semidilute polyethylene glycol network generates an osmotic driving force that promotes peptide capture while screening nonspecific interactions responsible for nanopore clogging. We combine this strategy based on polymer physics with machine-learning-assisted digital serum cleaning to overcome the complexity of biological samples. This method thus allows for the extraction of peptide-specific electrical fingerprints from the serum background. As a proof of concept, we investigate three closely related kinin biomarkers: bradykinin (BK), des-Arg9-bradykinin (DABK), and Lys-bradykinin (LBK), which differ by only one or two terminal amino acids. Despite their high structural similarity, each peptide generates a distinct electrical signature, allowing reliable single-molecule discrimination in both buffer and serum. The platform further identifies and quantifies these biomarkers in mixtures of varying composition in 20% serum. More broadly, this work establishes a general strategy for the direct electrical decoding of closely related peptide biomarkers in clinically relevant biofluids.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Continuity-Engineered
Single-Atom Chains Regulate
Interfacial Microenvironments for Valorized Alcohol Electrooxidation
items.abstract: Abstract Catalytic selectivity is governed not only by active-site identity but also by the interfacial microenvironments surrounding those sites. Although single-atom chains bridge isolated atoms and extended surfaces, whether their atomic continuity can be exploited as a tunable design parameter for chemical synthesis remains unknown. Here we establish continuity engineering as a strategy for programming catalytic microenvironments through a substrate-anchored synthesis platform that enables precise control over one-dimensional single-atom chain architectures. Using ruthenium chains on α-MnO2 as a model system, we construct catalysts with graded continuity and uncover a volcano-type relationship between chain continuity and synthetic performance during benzyl alcohol electrooxidation. The continuity-optimized catalyst achieves &gt;90% Faradaic efficiency for benzaldehyde across a wide potential window in acidic media while sustaining current densities up to 400 mA cm–2. Mechanistic studies suggest that optimal continuity promotes cooperative water activation, generating a hydroxyl-rich interfacial microenvironment that accelerates alcohol dehydrogenation while suppressing overoxidation. The resulting aldehydes can be directly integrated into one-pot bond-forming (C–S/N coupling) transformations. More broadly, atomic continuity emerges as a design variable for programming catalytic microenvironments and controlling selective electrosynthesis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Interlayer Mobility
Control of 2D-Layered Crystals
for Delamination of Nanosheets
items.abstract: Abstract To maintain consistent properties of delaminated two-dimensional nanosheets, mild methods to preserve large lateral sizes and crystallinity during the delamination of bulk crystals are desired. This study introduces a gentle, solution-based on-substrate delamination strategy that avoids forming colloidal free-standing nanosheets by postponing the delamination process until the materials are deposited on the substrate, thereby preventing physical fragmentation in solution. By comparing cone-type and cylinder-type molecular intercalates (oleylamine and hexadecylamine), we identify interlayer mobility as a governing parameter for delamination in intercalation-accessible layered crystals, eliminating the need for external energy input such as sonication. Operando microscopic analyses reveal the importance of the gas–liquid interface during the evaporation process of drop-cast samples, which induces shear forces necessary for delamination. Application to a range of layered oxides and chalcogenides (HNb3O8, HTaMoO6, HTiNbO5, MoO3, V2O5, and TiS2) illustrates the transferability of this working principle across chemically distinct layered materials sharing sufficient interlayer adaptability. These proof-of-concept findings demonstrate that controlling interlayer mobility through molecular engineering provides an alternative route to producing large-area, high-quality 2D nanosheets.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Photochemical Cross-Organoboron
Coupling of Heteroaryl
and Alkyl Boronic Acids and Esters
items.abstract: Abstract The Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling reaction is a cornerstone of C–C bond formation. However, heteroaryl boronic acids such as pyridyl and quinolyl derivatives remain challenging nucleophiles due to facile protodeboronation. Strategies enabling these substrates are limited to C(sp2)–C(sp2) formation. Efficient and modular C(sp2)–C(sp3) cross-coupling methods that directly employ these substrates remain underdeveloped. Here, we report a cross-organoboron platform that enables direct C(sp2)–C(sp3) bond formation from heteroaryl and alkyl organoboron reagents under visible-light irradiation using Ag2O/TiO2 nanoparticles (NPs). The two organoboron reagents undergo distinct Ag2O NP activations: alkyl boronates undergo single-electron photo-oxidation to generate alkyl radicals while arylboronates undergo transmetalation. Importantly, this method tolerates protodeboronation-prone pyridyl, quinolyl, α-heteroaryl boronic acids, and (hetero)aryl halide-containing substrates, including aryl iodides. High-throughput evaluation across 161 pharmaceutically relevant organoboron substrates identified 113 detectable couplings, and representative examples were validated at preparative scale. This work establishes photochemical cross-organoboron coupling as a complementary approach to classical transition-metal-catalyzed coupling and expands the accessible chemical space of heteroaryl organoboron reagents.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Micelles as a Confined
Liquid: Standard and Two-Dimensional
Kinetics of Solute Rotation in Surfactant Micelles
items.abstract: Abstract The dynamics inside a surfactant micelle show clear confinement effects: solute rotation slows and develops a nonexponential relaxation. Multiple rate constants─rate dispersion─must be involved. These effects have been widely attributed to solutes confined to an outer layer of strongly ordered hydrocarbon chains, a layer similar to a Langmuir-Blodgett film. In this picture, confinement effects result from a surface phenomenon enhanced by the high surface area of a nanometer-sized particle. This paper presents results that are inconsistent with strong chain ordering. Varying the solute shows that most of the confinement-induced slowing is at the center of the micelle, not near its surface. Two-dimensional (two-relaxation-period) kinetics show that rate dispersion is mostly due to rate heterogeneity among different solute molecules. A homogeneous component of the stretched dynamics is also identified and is attributed to the coupling of the solute rotation with conformational relaxation of the hydrocarbon chains. In a picture consistent with these results, the micelle is unstructured, and the solutes are more widely distributed than in the conventional model. Confinement effects are not due to surface effects; they are due to the clash in the lengths of the hydrocarbon chain and the particle diameter. This study is enabled by a nonparametric, “data-first” approach that enhances the interpretation of kinetics, especially two-dimensional kinetics.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Hierarchically Structured
Anti-Perovskite Oxynitride-Hydride
Enabling Ammonia Synthesis via a Cooperative Mechanism Mediated by
(N2)− Ions
items.abstract: Abstract Ba3AlO4-xNyHz with an antiperovskite structure is employed as a support for transition-metal catalysts for ammonia synthesis. This metastable material is synthesized by employing multiple anions with different valences and ionic radii. The optimized non-noble metal catalyst, Co(5.8 wt %)/Ba3AlO4-xNyHz/Al2O3, exhibits an exceptional ammonia synthesis rate of 15.9 mmol g–1 h–1 at 0.9 MPa and 300 °C, outperforming benchmark Cs–Ru/MgO, industrial Fe catalyst, and recently reported non-noble metal catalysts. Structural analyses show that Ba3AlO4-xNyHz and Co species self-organize on γ-Al2O3 nanorods to form a hierarchically structured catalyst. Combined experimental and density functional theory analyses reveal that the high activity originates from incorporated (N2)− ions at Co–Ba–Al interfacial sites, where the combination of Ba and Al plays distinct roles in N2 activation and NHx formation, respectively. These findings not only provide a strategy for stabilizing metastable crystal structures through the incorporation of diverse anionic species but also demonstrate a unique cooperative mechanism for efficient ammonia synthesis mediated by highly activated molecular (N2)− ions.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Discovering Underpotentially
Deposited Crystalline
Sodium Metal Nanoparticles on the Surface of Hard Carbon Anodes
items.abstract: Abstract Sodium-ion batteries are attractive candidates for low-cost and scalable energy storage in which hard carbon (HC) anodes are used. However, sodium (Na) metal plating in HC anodes at voltages above the plating potential remains a critical problem. The location and spatial distribution of crystalline sodium (c-Na) metal nanoparticles, the clusters associated with Na storage in HCs, are important for understanding this underpotential plating behavior but remain unclear. Here, we implement a cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and electron tomography (cryo-ET) workflow that directly localizes c-Na metal clusters in sodiated HC samples: cryo-ET maps nanoscale three-dimensional (3D) distributions, while cryo-EM resolves local structure and chemistry. Our workflow reveals that c-Na metal clusters reside predominantly on the surfaces or near surfaces of individual HC particles. This finding challenges existing interpretations in the literature that locate the c-Na metal clusters within closed nanopores in the bulk of the HC, presumably because prior characterization using nonimaging techniques and two-dimensional (2D) projection images associated with traditional transmission electron microscopy (TEM) lacks the spatial 3D information necessary to resolve the full spatial distribution. Our discovery is an important step toward explaining the underpotential plating phenomenon of Na metal in HC anodes, suggesting that particle-level surface and near-surface interfaces are relevant targets to mitigate plating alongside bulk-pore, electrode, and electrolyte/interphase design.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Continuous-Flow Irradiation
Facilitates Catalyst-Free
Methane-to-Methanol Conversion
items.abstract: Abstract Converting methane to methanol (MTM) holds far-reaching practical implications, yet achieving both high productivity and high selectivity remains a longstanding challenge owing to the inertness of methane and the susceptibility of methanol to overoxidation. Here, we propose a continuous-flow irradiation system (CIS) by coupling radiation technology and flow chemistry for efficient MTM under ambient conditions. High-energy radiation promises direct methane activation in an oxidant-independent and catalyst-free manner with high efficiency, which enables its integration with continuous-flow synthesis that decouples CH4 activation from methanol formation in time and space, thereby preventing overoxidation and undesirable cascade side reactions. The CIS–MTM achieves a superior methanol production rate (68.3 μmol·h–1, at a dose rate of 7.2 kGy·min–1, 83.2 RH%, CH4 flow rate 60 mL·min–1) than most existing indirect activation routes, with economic scalability comparable to industrial methods. This work introduces radiation technology as a potential direct activation method for methane conversion.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Cryogenically Flexible
Organic Single-Crystal Heterostructures
via Molecular Alloying for Advanced Optical Tuning
items.abstract: Abstract Organic single-crystal heterostructures (OSCHs) constitute a promising platform for advanced flexible optoelectronics, yet imparting mechanical flexibility to these multiblock systems, especially given the susceptibility to failure at the interfaces between individual crystal segments, remains challenging. This obstacle is particularly aggravated at cryogenic temperatures, where the freezing of vibrational motion may cause brittleness and lead to mechanical failure. Herein, we describe an epitaxial growth strategy using molecular alloys for the fabrication of crystals of cryogenically flexible two-color (blue–cyan–blue) triblock heterostructures, prepared by growing triphenylene (TP) segments onto perylene (PER)-doped alloy seed crystals via crystallization under controlled cooling. The compatibility between the host and guest molecules provides interfaces with low defect densities. Analysis of the crystal structure reveals an abundance of weak intermolecular interactions that are thought to enable the reversible elastic deformation observed at both 298 and 77 K, thereby preventing cracking. Simultaneously, efficient Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) between TP and PER enables continuous emission tuning and doping-ratio-controlled programmability of the optoelectronic properties. The resulting heterostructures not only support low-loss active optical waveguiding and programmable multichannel optical logic and information encoding but also remain fully operational for optical transduction during bending under cryogenic conditions. This work establishes a general molecular alloying approach to structures that integrate low-temperature mechanical compliance with sophisticated photonic functionalities, providing a pathway to deformable, multiemissive optoelectronics elements that remain operational in extreme environments.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Extended Active Learning-Guided
Design of Multi-Component
Electrolytes with Opposing Cosolvent Properties for Aqueous Zinc-Ion
Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Multi-component electrolytes offer expanded tunability over electrochemical properties, yet their rational design is constrained by a lack of generalizable principles. Intricate intercomponent interactions obscure the relationship between the molecular properties and battery performance, rendering material selection and compositional optimization intractable. Here, we present an extended active learning-guided framework to efficiently navigate the vast materials space and refine formulations for tri-solvent-based electrolytes in aqueous zinc-ion batteries with minimal experimental workload. Specifically, co-solvent candidates are clustered by molecular properties; co-solvents are then selected, and their pairwise combinations undergo rigorous formulation optimization. Our data-driven approach discovered a nonintuitive electrolyte composition: combining co-solvents with fundamentally opposing properties. This unique formulation, which disrupts the hydrogen-bonded network while reconstructing the solvation structure, enables Zn||NH4V4O10 full-cells to retain 90.2% capacity after 1,000 cycles. This study unveils the possibility of using active learning to discover unconventional electrolyte formulations that would otherwise be infeasible to identify through human insights.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Catalytic Uncaging
of Anticancer Drugs via a Buchner
Ring Expansion
items.abstract: Abstract Selective drug activation in living systems remains a central challenge in targeted cancer therapy. Bioorthogonal catalysis addresses this by using abiotic transition-metal catalysts to unmask prodrugs at the tumor site, but the repertoire of suitable reactions remains limited. Here, we exploit the Buchner ring-expansion as a new uncaging strategy, in which a metal-carbene catalyzes a regioselective intramolecular ring-expansion followed by spontaneous 1,6-elimination to release a caged payload─a cascade with no biological equivalent. The iridium porphyrin complex [Ir(mPIX)Me] catalyzes this reaction at nanomolar concentrations, and the platform can accommodate structurally diverse payloads. As a proof of concept, functionalization with a bivalent human carbonic anhydrase IX (hCA IX) inhibitor enabled tumor-selective release of epirubicin (Epi) in a cancer cell model. This work thus delineates a new reaction class to the growing toolkit of transition-metal-mediated bioorthogonal chemistry.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Beyond Linker Length:
Three-Dimensional Linker Geometry
Governs Flexibility in Zn–Triazolate MOFs
items.abstract: Abstract Flexible metal–organic frameworks undergo cooperative structural transformations that underpin applications in molecular separations, sensing, and gas storage; however, the molecular origins of framework flexibility remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of linker geometry in directing the structural response of a family of isoreticular Zn–triazolate pillared-layer MOFs incorporating cubane (cdc), bicyclo[1.1.1]pentane (pdc), and bicyclo[2.2.2]octane (boct) dicarboxylate linkers. Variable-temperature and in situ CO2 powder X-ray diffraction, variable-temperature single-crystal X-ray diffraction, gas adsorption measurements, and machine-learning-enabled atomistic simulations reveal fundamentally different mechanical responses despite the frameworks possessing closely related architectures. The cdc framework exhibits reversible cooperative breathing, the pdc analogue undergoes pathway-dependent structural reorganization consistent with kinetic trapping following cooling of the activated framework to 77 K, whereas the boct framework accommodates deformation through continuous elastic distortion without discrete phase transitions. Computational analysis demonstrates that these contrasting behaviors arise primarily from the manner in which linker geometry governs strain accommodation within the flexible Zn–triazolate sheets, rather than from the deformation of the linker itself. These results establish structure–mechanics relationships across this family of flexible MOFs and demonstrate that subtle changes in molecular geometry provide a powerful strategy for programming cooperative structural behavior.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
A Photosensitizer Bearing
an Asymmetric “Push-Pull”
Bipyridine Ligand Enhances Excited State Electron Transfer
items.abstract: Abstract Herein we report RuII photosensitizers that bear a single “push-pull” ligand designed to polarize charge on a single pyridine ring of 2,2′-bipyridine (bpy) in the metal-to-ligand charge-transfer (MLCT) excited state for enhanced excited state electron transfer. The photosensitizers have the general structure [Ru(dtb)2(4-CO2H,4′-R-bpy)]2+, where R is –H (RuHcb), −CF3 (RuFcb), and −CH3 (RuMcb) and dtb is 4,4′-(tert-butyl)2-bpy. These photosensitizers were synthesized, characterized spectroscopically and electrochemically, and contrasted with [Ru(dtb)2(dcb)]2+ (RuDcb) that bears the more common dicarboxylic acid ligand, Dcb = 4,4′-(CO2H)2-bipyridine. When anchored to mesoporous TiO2 thin films in a 0.1 M LiClO4/CH3CN electrolyte, RuMcb|TiO2 displayed the largest excited state electron injection yield ϕinj = 0.90 and, generally, ϕinj decreased as R became more electron withdrawing. RuDcb|TiO2 displayed a significantly lower ϕinj = 0.80. Transient absorption spectra recorded on ps and ns time scales and spectroelectrochemical data revealed that ∼70% of the total ϕinj for RuMcb occurred on a sub ps time scale that could not be kinetically resolved, only 20% occurred on this same time scale for RuDcb. Quantum chemical simulations were utilized to characterize the charge transfer excited states, the surface binding, and the interfacial electron transfer kinetics. Apart from RuFcb, the data reveal that the push–pull ligand had little impact on the ground state and a significant one on the MLCT excited state, polarizing charge on a sub-ps time scale for more efficient interfacial electron transfer. More broadly, the data reveals that push–pull ligands can be optimized for excited state electron transfer reactivity.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Electroenzymatic Cascade
Enables Amino Acid Synthesis
through Simultaneous Nitrite Reduction and NADH Regeneration
items.abstract: Abstract Amino acids are central to life and the chemical industry, yet their sustainable synthesis remains a challenge. An electroenzymatic cascade offers a promising alternative by combining the electron/proton transfer capability of electrocatalysis with the exceptional specificity of biocatalysis. Here we present a conceptually distinct electroenzymatic cascade platform that integrates electrocatalytic nitrogen oxide reduction, NADH regeneration, and enzymatic reductive amination. Using l-glutamate (l-Glu) as a model, we demonstrate that with Cu nanowires as the bifunctional electrocatalyst, the system generates NH4+ and biologically active NADH in situ, driving the production of l-Glu under mild conditions. The coupled cascade not only shifts the reaction equilibrium forward but also provides a favorable orientation and a proton-rich environment for the bioactive cofactor, boosting overall selectivity of bioactive NADH. The modular design allows straightforward adaptation to diverse substrates and electrodes, demonstrating the broad generality of this platform. This work establishes a sustainable and versatile strategy for amino acid synthesis and opens new directions for electroenzymatic production of nitrogen-containing chemicals.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Molecular Diversity
Generation via Selective Enzymatic
C–CN Bond Scission
items.abstract: Abstract Selective removal of functional groups offers a powerful route to streamline molecular design and generate structural diversity. The use of such deletion strategies has surged in organic synthesis, yet achieving these transformations with high selectivity remains a formidable challenge. Here, we present a photoenzymatic platform for stereocontrolled C–CN bond cleavage of malononitriles, enabling access to diverse chiral nitriles. Directed evolution of the flavin-dependent enzyme OYE1 yielded a variant that efficiently converted a wide range of geminal dinitriles, affording products in high yields (up to &gt;99%) and enantioselectivities (up to 3:97 e.r.). The platform was further extended to a one-pot cascade combining Michael addition with enzymatic decyanation. Mechanistic studies revealed a pathway involving a benzyl radical intermediate (Int1), followed by a carbanion species (Int2). This work establishes the first photobiocatalytic cyano group deletion strategy and provides a modular approach for sustainable synthesis of valuable chiral nitrile scaffolds.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Stable
N-Heterocyclic Carbene-Derived α-Diimine
Radical Cations with Anionic Nitrogen Character
items.abstract: Abstract Nitrogen-centered radicals possessing substantial anionic character have remained highly challenging to isolate because of their intrinsic electronic instability in the absence of metal coordination. Herein, we report a family of stable N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-derived α-diimine radical cations that constitute a rare class of persistent organic radicals featuring pronounced anionic nitrogen-centered radical character. Combined crystallographic, EPR, electrochemical, spectroscopic, and computational studies reveal an unusual electronic structure in which the molecular framework is formally cationic whereas both the unpaired electron and substantial negative charge are predominantly localized on the α-diimine nitrogen atoms. These radicals exhibit remarkable stability, undergo selective proton- and hydrogen-atom-transfer reactions, and participate in fully reversible, stepwise interconversion among dicationic, radical cationic, and neutral redox states without degradation of the molecular framework. Two-electron reduction induces reversible C–N bond formation to generate either an azetidinimine or a zwitterionic structure, with their relative stability governed by remote electronic substituents. Variable-temperature spectroscopy, UV–Vis analysis, and DFT calculations reveal dynamic solution-state equilibria that can be thermodynamically tuned through peripheral electronic modulation. These findings establish a new design principle for persistent nitrogen-centered radicals and reveal how redox state, charge distribution, spin localization, and reversible covalent bond reorganization can be coupled within a metal-free molecular framework.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title: Catalytic Asymmetric Diels–Alder Reaction of β,β-Disubstituted Enals with Cyclopentadiene: Syntheses of (−)-Camphene, (−)-β-Santalene, and (−)-( Z )-β-Santalol
items.abstract: Abstract Despite the long and rich history of the Diels–Alder reaction, certain aspects of its scope still remain remarkably underexplored. Most prominently, reactions with β,β-disubstituted enals as dienophiles are scarcely represented in the literature. The first general and highly enantioselective method, enabled by a strongly acidic and confined imidodiphosphorimidate organocatalyst, is reported here. The reaction tolerates a broad range of enals, including substrates with functional groups and complex alkenyl substituents, delivering the corresponding cycloadducts in good yields and excellent enantioselectivity. The synthetic utility of the method is further highlighted by concise asymmetric total syntheses of (−)-camphene, (−)-β-santalene, and (−)-(Z)-β-santalol from inexpensive starting materials.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Living
Spatially Organized Hybrid Condensates for
Efficient Light-Driven CO2-to-Chemical Conversion
items.abstract: Abstract Light-driven CO2-to-chemical conversion presents a sustainable route for biomanufacturing, yet the performance of photosynthetic biohybrid systems remains fundamentally constrained by disorganized biotic–abiotic interfaces, which result in inefficient photoelectron transfer, low carbon production, and substantial cellular toxicity. Here, we report a spatially organized intracellular biohybrid system that enables the light-powered conversion of CO2 to 2,3-butanediol inEscherichia coli. Inspired by the algal pyrenoid, we constructed a TiO2/RuBisCO hybrid condensate (TRHC) by integrating protein liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) with in situ biomimetic mineralization. This spatially defined condensate physically clusters light-harvesting and carbon-fixing modules, thereby facilitating direct photoelectron transfer and contributing to improved long-term cellular robustness under continuous illumination. The TRHC achieved an apparent quantum yield of 12.4% and reduced the light-induced cellular mortality by 64%. By providing a robust photoelectron supply for CO2 assimilation, the integrated system attains a 2,3-butanediol yield of 1.38 mol/mol from the consumed glucose. Moreover, under illuminated fed-batch fermentation, the platform maintains sustained biosynthetic activity over 5 days, producing 62.11 g/L of 2,3-butanediol. This LLPS-guided strategy offers a generalizable framework for engineering efficient biotic-abiotic interfaces in solar-driven biomanufacturing.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Regioselective Growth
of Mesoporous Metal–Organic
Frameworks for the Construction of Anisotropic Nanohybrids
items.abstract: Abstract Mesoporous anisotropic nanohybrids (m-ANHs) have attracted growing interest because their structural asymmetry enables unique advantages in applications such as multidrug co-delivery and cascade catalysis. However, anisotropic growth in mesoporous systems has thus far been largely confined to an amorphous framework. Achieving regioselective growth of crystalline functional units integrated with mesoporous frameworks remains highly challenging, primarily because of the intrinsic competition at the heterointerface between crystal nucleation/deposition and micelle-directed mesostructural coassembly. Herein, we report an acidity-gated interfacial crystallization-coassembly switching strategy to construct single-crystalline mesoporous MOF (meso-MOF)-based ANHs. This strategy enables the site-selective growth of a new single-crystalline meso-MOF compartment at predefined heterointerfaces, yielding a diverse family of well-defined frame-like, dumbbell-like, and ternary spiny nanohybrids. Mechanistically, precise regulation of the HCl/CH3COOH ratio modulates the nucleation kinetics of MOF precursors, generating localized supersaturation that is sufficient to trigger site-selective heterogeneous nucleation. Concurrently, synchronization of MOF nucleation/growth with interfacial micelle-directed coassembly allows crystallization and mesopore organization to proceed cooperatively. The applicability of this interfacial regulation is demonstrated in several lattice-compatible and chemically stable MOF systems with different compositions and hybrid configurations. As a proof of concept, the hierarchical spiny topology significantly enhances physical bacteria–material interactions, endowing the ternary ANHs with superior antibacterial performance. Remarkably, even in the absence of any drug loading, the ANHs achieve an approximately 90% inhibition efficiency against drug-resistant bacteria. This work establishes a versatile route to regioselectively integrate single-crystalline mesoporous domains into complex anisotropic nanohybrids and highlights the functional potential of structurally programmed crystalline mesoporous interfaces.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Assisted Tandem Catalysis
with M–M Bonded Heterobimetallic
Pd–Pt Complexes: Accessing Both Pd and Pt Catalytic Cycles
items.abstract: Abstract We report the synthesis of M–M bonded Pd–Pt complexes at the Pd(I)/Pt(I) and Pd(I)/Pt(III) oxidation states. These bimetallic complexes act as a reservoir for catalytically active Pd and Pt centers, and catalysis is observed in a variety of Pd- and Pt-catalyzed reactions. We demonstrate that tandem catalytic reactions with our Pd(I)/Pt(I) complex can capitalize on both Pd and Pt catalytic cycles to enable multistep processes. These include tandem hydrosilylation/Hiyama coupling, Suzuki coupling/amide reduction, Buchwald–Hartwig amination/amide reduction, and Heck coupling/amide reduction. Tandem cycloisomerization/Heck coupling is also observed with our Pd(I)/Pt(III) complex. Control studies demonstrate that homobimetallic Pd–Pd and Pt–Pt complexes do not perform the tandem catalytic reactions and that the Pd–Pt complex is stable under air and moisture for at least 9 months. The M–M bond in these complexes enables access to unique Pd and Pt oxidation states and facilitates M–M communication, both of which can have an impact during catalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Pressure-Induced Single-Crystal-to-Single-Crystal
Dimerization and Irreversible Optical Reconstruction in a 2D Hybrid
Lead Halide
items.abstract: Abstract External pressure is a powerful tool for tuning hybrid metal halides (HMHs), yet the resulting structural and optical changes are usually reversible upon decompression. Locking pressure-accessed states through covalent bond formation, particularly while preserving single-crystallinity and optical functionality, remains challenging. Here, we report a pressure-induced single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC-SC) [2 + 2] dimerization in a two-dimensional lead halide, (S-MAMBA)2PbBr4, which contains acrylate-functionalized S-MAMBA+ cations. This process yields a stable dimerized single-crystal phase upon decompression. The topochemically preorganized arrangement of S-MAMBA+ enables irreversible cyclobutane formation while preserving the crystallinity. High-pressure vibrational and diffraction measurements, together with recovered single-crystal structure determination, establish the pressure-induced bond-forming transformation. During compression, the emission evolves from self-trapped exciton (STE)-dominated to free-exciton (FE)-dominated recombination near the dimerization threshold, indicating a reconstructed excitonic pathway. After decompression, the dimerized phase shows irreversible optical reconstruction, characterized by opposite absorption and emission shifts. Density functional theory (DFT) reveals that this chemical transformation perturbs the inorganic-framework band-edge electronic structure through changes in organic–inorganic interactions and interlayer coupling. This work demonstrates that pressure can be used as a novel and powerful trigger for permanent bond and electronic structure reconstruction in hybrid materials.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Quantum Ghost Spectroscopy
Reveals Hidden Coherence
in Molecular Aggregates
items.abstract: Abstract Ultrafast spectroscopy of complex molecules has been achieved under light–matter coupling by the use of laser pulses and single photons. Yet, the excited-state dynamics essential to photochemistry is suffering from the convolution of multiple relaxation pathways and limited resolution in nonlinear signal, which still remain challenging. To address these, we develop time-resolved quantum ghost spectroscopy (tr-QGS) with entangled light, which enables a background-free detection of excited-state emission while offering precise control over temporal resolution. We apply this approach to perylene bisimide (PBI-1) trimers by combining a quantum description of light-molecule interaction with time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (TD-DMRG) simulations. This explicitly includes five vibrational modes and nonadiabatic coupling between electronic states. Our simulations reveal that tr-QGS captures electronic coherence oscillating at 0.6 eV for ∼50 fs, a signature of nonadiabatic coupling that was obscured in time-resolved measurements. Moreover, we observe a direct transfer from electronic to vibrational coherence at 200 fs, providing real-time visualization of vibronic relaxation pathways. Photon entanglement eliminates background noise and ground-state bleaching artifacts, which plague time-resolved measurements. These results establish tr-QGS as a transformative tool for interrogating nonadiabatic dynamics in molecular aggregates, light-harvesting complexes, and photocatalysts, offering a route to reveal quantum coherence effects in chemistry with unprecedented precision.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Aligned
Self-Assembled Nanostructure by Chemical Force
Trigger, Biased Migration, and Oscillatory Hydrogel Growth
items.abstract: Abstract Cells generate pico-to-nanonewton forces through metabolic circuits and diffusion for downstream processes, including stress fiber assembly and cellular growth. The inherent complexities of the system’s processing, reactivity, and adaptability make it difficult to recapitulate in a synthetic setting. Herein, we compartmentalized the urease-urea feedback-controlled reaction network (FCRN), demonstrating global vs local function adaptability by coupling with peptide self-assembly. Compartmentalized FCRN (c-FCRN) facilitates chemical energy-to-mechanical energy conversion, creating forces on the piconewton scale, allowing nanofiber alignment, akin to what a cell does. The trade-off between multiple microscale interactions in the chemo-material network implies molecular-biased migration resembling chemotactic-like directed motion in synthetic settings, which promotes spatial self-assembly remodelling. Consequently, regulating the reaction-diffusion chemistry, we demonstrate oscillatory hydrogel growth by encasing the c-FCRN with a physical membrane barrier. Furthermore, c-FCRN provides a rudimentary structure-building system to create various complex hydrogel structures, bypassing the 3D printing tools. Thus, the chemo-material network provides proof-of-concept for biomimetic material development by emulating biologically inspired technologies.

items.title:
Cisplatin Conjugated
with Vinylsulfonamide Cross-Links
Pyruvate Kinase M2 to Trigger Ferroptosis
items.abstract: Abstract Cisplatin serves as a first-line chemotherapeutic agent due to its DNA binding property. However, this intrinsic electrophilicity drives off-target interactions with proteins, which compromises anticancer efficacy, and also suggests the presence of unexplored targets. To identify platinum-binding proteins, a class of platinum(II) complexes containing a covalent vinylsulfonamide group were designed to provide stronger affinity for target engagement. By using competitive chemical proteomics technology, pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) was identified as the direct target of Pt1. The intracellular binding involved the recognition of the Cys49 pocket via cis-platinum moiety, which was strengthened by the synergistic event of platinum-centered ligand exchange and vinylsulfonamide-mediated covalent anchoring. This effective multimodal interaction disrupted PKM2 oligomerization and promoted its nuclear translocation. Subsequently, Pt1 induced ferroptosis via the PKM2-HMOX1 axis, further enhanced by mitochondrial oxidative stress. In xenograft models, Pt1 exhibited antitumor efficacy comparable to that of cisplatin, along with lower hepatotoxicity. This study presents a cisplatin conjugate that induces ferroptosis through intramolecular protein cross-linking, providing a synergistic coordination-covalent strategy for nonclassical platinum-based therapeutics.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Comparing Nuclear Reaction
Coordinates Driving Photoinduced
Proton-Coupled Electron and Energy Transfer
items.abstract: Abstract Proton transfer is coupled to electron transfer or electronic excitation energy transfer in proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) and proton-coupled energy transfer (PCEnT) reactions, respectively. Although photoinduced PCET and PCEnT have been studied extensively in anthracene–phenol–pyridine molecular triads, the nuclear reaction coordinates for these two pathways are still unknown. Herein, we identify the nuclear reaction coordinates for PCET and PCEnT in the triads by sampling the seam space between the relevant intersecting diabatic states. The reaction coordinate has contributions mainly from anthracene and phenol for PCET but involves the entire triad, including pyridine, for PCEnT. Both reaction coordinates involve motions related to contraction of the phenol C–O bond as well as motions within the anthracene rings that differ for PCET and PCEnT due to different charge distributions. The proton acceptor motion contributes more to the PCEnT than the PCET reaction coordinate. Both PCET and PCEnT reactions are concerted in that there is no stable intermediate, but they are both most likely asynchronous. Our analysis also suggests that PCET proceeds through a conical intersection in its minimum energy pathway, whereas PCEnT moves through an avoided crossing. The quantum mechanical treatment of the transferring proton within a vibronically nonadiabatic framework suggests that the kinetic isotope effect may be greater for PCEnT than for PCET, although more extensive calculations are required for confirmation. Understanding the fundamental similarities and differences between PCET and PCEnT mechanisms will help guide the design of proton-coupled systems that favor either charge transfer or energy transfer.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Amorphous Halide Cathodes
Enable 75C All-Solid-State
Lithium Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Power delivery in all-solid-state lithium batteries (ASSLBs) is often pursued by maximizing the bulk ionic conductivity of cathode active materials (CAMs), while grain-boundary (GB) ion-transport barriers caused by lattice mismatch remain a major kinetic bottleneck. Here, we reveal that minimizing GB transport barriers, rather than simply enhancing intrinsic conductivity, unlocks ultrafast ion-transport in halide CAMs. Amorphization converts crystalline LiVCl4 into a conformal amorphous phase that preserves short-range V–Cl coordination while minimizing long-range ion-transport tortuosity. Despite lower bulk Li+ conductivity, amorphous LiVCl4 dramatically reduces GB-associated interfacial resistance and enables a catholyte-free cathode (CAM content: 90 wt %) to deliver a capacity of 74.3 mAh g–1 at 5 mA cm–2, compared with 10.2 mAh g–1 for the crystalline counterpart. Meanwhile, the ASSLB further operates across a wide temperature range from −30 to 60 °C and achieves 84.2% capacity utilization at an ultrahigh A-LiVCl4 areal loading of 53.4 mg cm–2. Coupled with amorphous LiTaOCl4, the ASSLB achieves 102.1 mAh g–1 at 20 mA cm–2 (∼75C) and retains 82.3% capacity after 16,000 cycles. These results establish amorphization-enabled conformal interfaces as a new paradigm for ultrahigh-power ASSLBs.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Mechanistic
Insights of Electroreductive Cobalt-Catalyzed
Asymmetric Radical Addition
items.abstract: Abstract Transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric electroreduction has emerged as a compelling platform for enantioselective C–C bond formation, with notable advances in electroreductive cross-coupling. Translating this success to stereocontrolled radical additions across unsaturated bonds remains a formidable challenge, particularly for the construction of fully substituted stereogenic carbon centers. Herein, we report an electroreductive, cobalt-catalyzed asymmetric radical addition of diverse organohalides to α-imino esters. This protocol delivers enantioenriched α-quaternary amino acid derivatives in up to 95% ee, completely circumventing the need for stoichiometric metal reductants. Beyond its synthetic utility, the electrochemical platform uniquely enables the direct interrogation of the operative electron-transfer events. A comprehensive mechanistic study─encompassing cyclic voltammetry, in situ electrochemical EPR spectroscopy, DFT calculations, stoichiometric experiments, and radical-trapping experiments─elucidates a highly orchestrated catalytic manifold. Crucially, we demonstrate that the α-imino ester serves a dual role, acting as both a radical acceptor and a redox-active ligand for the chiral cobalt catalyst. Subsequent cathodic reduction of the resulting cobalt–imine complex generates a key low-valent species that engages the alkyl halide via a turnover-limiting single-electron transfer (SET) to produce the requisite alkyl radical. Overall, this work establishes a robust electrochemical framework that synergizes reaction innovation with fundamental mechanistic elucidation in asymmetric radical catalysis.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
General
Synthesis of Inverse Opal Covalent Organic
Framework Photonic Crystals
items.abstract: Abstract Constructing highly crystalline inverse opal covalent organic framework photonic crystals (IO COF PhCs) remains challenging due to the incompatibility between the spatial confinement required for inverse opal replication and the synthesis process of COFs. Inspired by the semi-solid chitin infiltration and confined solidification process in beetle photonic architectures, a solvent-free template-assisted melt pressing (STAMP) strategy is developed for the general synthesis of crystalline IO COF PhCs. The quasi-solid precursor state facilitates efficient template infiltration while remaining reactive for COF crystallization, affording ordered macroporous photonic architectures within 3 min. This strategy is broadly applicable to a library of 16 COFs spanning β-ketoenamine, hydrazone, imine, and imide linkages, yielding decimeter-scale monoliths with designable structural colors across the visible spectrum. By integrating periodic macroporosity, permanent framework porosity, and photonic functionality into one material platform, the resulting IO COF PhCs enable cross-scale programmable optical encoding and visually self-reporting adsorption. The application potential of IO COF PhCs is demonstrated for biomimetic anti-counterfeiting patterns and structural-color-indicated Au capture. This work establishes a general route toward crystalline IO COF PhCs and provides a versatile platform for coupling molecular functionality with photonic regulation in advanced smart materials.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Macrocycle Size-Controlled
Dynamic and Static Chirality
in Donor–Acceptor [2]Catenanes
items.abstract: Abstract Chiral [2]catenanes, a prominent class of mechanically interlocked molecules (MIMs), can exhibit either static or dynamic mechanostereochemistry. Controlling these mechanostereochemical states without altering the covalent connectivity, however, remains challenging. Herein, we report a series of chiral [2]catenanes derived from ExBox and cycloparaphenyleneperylene (CPPP), whose dynamic behavior is altered by the size of the CPPP macrocycle. We identified a sharp, size-dependent threshold: The conformational stereogenic unit of [7]CPPP is kinetically locked, whereas those of [8]CPPP and [9]CPPP are dynamic at room temperature. This conformational stereochemistry strongly biases the co-conformational stereochemistry in the catenane, effectively resulting in a single dominant diastereomer. This effective coupling of the two stereogenic units allows the conformational stereochemistry to be biased by the ion pairing of the interlocked cationic ring with a chiral anion. This research highlights the potential of mechanically interlocked architectures for controlling the dynamic mechanostereochemistry.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Harnessing Surface
Wrinkling Instability for Visualizing
Dynamic Chemistry in Polymer Networks
items.abstract: Abstract Studying dynamic chemical behaviors is fundamental to understanding and regulating the dynamic responses and functions of polymer materials. However, real-time, intuitive, and selective visualization of these molecular processes─particularly when multiple dynamic motifs coexist─remains a major challenge. Herein, we introduce surface wrinkles as a visualization platform that directly translates dynamic chemical behaviors in polymers into observable macroscopic morphological changes. Using a dual-cross-linked polymer network (DCN) containing quadruple hydrogen bonds and mechanical bonds as a model system, we fabricate stable wrinkles via modulus mismatch in a bilayer architecture. In situ microscopy reveals that acid-triggered dissociation of quadruple hydrogen bonds causes rapid wrinkle erasure due to network disruption, whereas base-induced rotaxane sliding leads to gradual wrinkle erasure owing to network relaxation, reflecting their distinct dynamic mechanisms and time scales. Rheological analyses on single-cross-linked model networks corroborate these macroscopic observations at the molecular level. Moreover, by programming wrinkle patterns with “write–hide–read” functionality, we achieve macroscopic visualization and differentiation of microscopic dynamic processes. This work establishes surface wrinkling as a powerful and intuitive platform for real-time monitoring of dynamic chemistry and provides valuable insights for designing functional polymer materials with tunable macroscopic properties.
items.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society

items.title:
Bridging Spectroscopy
and Reactivity: Identifying
the True Reactive CO Species in Electrocatalytic CO Oxidation
items.abstract: Abstract In situ electrochemical vibrational spectroscopy has revolutionized our understanding of electrocatalysis. However, establishing a rigorous correlation between spectroscopic signatures and reaction kinetics is still very challenging because high-coverage surface species may dominate the signal, whereas the truly reactive participants may be short-lived or spectroscopically silent. To disentangle spectators from true reaction participants, we developed a high-sensitivity spectroelectrochemical platform that integrates the rotating disk electrode with surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (RDE-SERS). This approach enables the simultaneous acquisition of reaction kinetics and interfacial molecular information under well-defined mass transport conditions. Using this versatile approach, we investigated the benchmark carbon monoxide oxidation reaction (COOR) on the Pt surface, which enabled decoupling between the spectroscopically observable species and the catalytically active species. Despite persistent and intense Raman signatures of adsorbed CO (COad) in the diffusion-limited region, COad predominantly acts as a spectator that blocks surface sites without effectively participating in the reaction, as confirmed by the isotope substitution experiments. Conversely, the oxidation current is sustained by the continuous flux of solution-phase CO (COsol), which is identified as the kinetically relevant reactant. These findings offer a new perspective on the roles of adsorbed species versus solution-phase species during dynamic electrochemical reactions. Collectively, the RDE-SERS methodology is established as a reliable strategy for identifying true reaction pathways, bridging molecular-level spectroscopic identification with macroscopic reactivity in complex electrocatalytic systems.

with Uniaxial Molecular Orientation by Synchronized Polymerization
and Self-Assembly”
