This protocol is broadly applicable to the one-carbon ring-expansion and concomitant functionalization of diverse 5-, 6-, 7-, 8-, 12-, 13-, 14-, and 16-membered ketones using various redox-active esters that bear a wide range of functional groups. Remarkably, the strategy can also be extended to three-carbon ring-expansion, enabling remote functionalization of ketone frameworks. Furthermore, the methodology is applicable to acyclic ketones, enabling a chain-extension/cross-coupling cascade. The synthetic utility of the methodology is demonstrated through late-stage scaffold remodeling of drugs and natural products, as well as the synthesis of 3-methylmuscone. Mechanistic investigations, supported by DFT calculations, shed light on selectivity in the coupling step and provide compelling evidence for a homolytic bimolecular substitution (SH2) pathway.

items.title: Light-Reconfigured Adsorption over Zeolite-Confined Amorphous Multicomponent Alloy Nanoparticles Enables Photothermal Dry Reforming of Methane
items.abstract: Abstract High-temperature dry reforming of methane (DRM) over Ni-based catalysts is limited by sintering and coking, while competitive adsorption can further restrict efficient utilization of CH4 and CO2. Here, we report a one-step hydrothermal strategy to encapsulate amorphous NiCoCuZnMn multicomponent alloy nanoparticles with partially oxidized Zn/Mn-containing surface domains within a TS-1 zeolite matrix, affording a structurally confined photothermal catalyst (denoted MA@TS-1). Under illumination, MA@TS-1 reaches a CO production rate of 21.85 mmol g–1 h–1 at 450 °C and sustains continuous operation for 500 h. Kinetic analysis, pulse-response experiments, in situ DRIFTS, and illumination-dependent XPS collectively show that irradiation changes both the adsorption response and the surface electronic state of the catalyst. CO2 pre-adsorption strongly suppresses subsequent CH4 net retention in the dark, whereas the corresponding CO2-induced pulse-response loss is markedly attenuated under illumination. Concurrently, opposite XPS shifts of Ni and the Zn/Mn-associated species are consistent with illumination-induced interfacial electronic redistribution accompanied by relative electron enrichment of Ni-rich sites. Control catalysts and qualitative DFT calculations further support a model in which CH4 activation preferentially involves Zn/Mn oxide-associated interfacial regions, whereas CO2 activation is favored at Ni-rich sites. These results show that light-responsive electronic and adsorption modulation can accompany photothermal heating and provide a route to regulating competitive adsorption in multicomponent DRM catalysts.

items.title: Electrolyte Cation Engineering Selectively Regulates Competing Urea Oxidation Pathways
items.abstract: Abstract The electrochemical urea oxidation reaction (UOR) has emerged as an attractive anodic reaction for various energy conversion systems. Recently, increasing attention has been directed toward controlling UOR selectivity on Ni-based electrocatalysts following the recognition that the UOR can produce over-oxidized products. However, existing studies have focused predominantly on catalyst design to regulate surface-bound intermediates, whereas whether electrolyte-mediated noncovalent interactions can selectively control competing UOR pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we show that rational electrolyte engineering using alkali-metal cations selectively regulates the UOR pathway by modulating the interfacial hydrogen-bonding network. Electrochemical rate deconvolution and product analysis reveal that weakly hydrated cations selectively accelerate the direct oxidation pathway, promoting the formation of the over-oxidized NO2– and NCO– products, while leaving the indirect pathway essentially unaffected. In situ attenuated total reflectance surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS) measurements, together with molecular dynamics simulations of cation hydration dynamics, indicate that weakly hydrated cations create a more dynamic interfacial water environment with faster water exchange, thereby facilitating interfacial OH–-mediated successive dehydrogenation during direct urea oxidation. Leveraging this mechanistic understanding, the electrolyte-engineering strategy was applied to a cascade urea-to-ammonia conversion system, achieving a urea-to-ammonia conversion efficiency of 77.5% and approximately threefold higher ammonia productivity in CsOH than in LiOH. These findings establish electrolyte engineering as a complementary strategy to catalyst design and highlight noncovalent electrolyte–electrode interactions as an effective handle for controlling reaction pathways and product selectivity in an integrated UOR-based nitrogen conversion system.

items.title: Hydrogen-Ion-Mediated Ni/Ni(OH)2 Dual Sites to Synergistically Accelerate *OH/Organics Adsorption for Highly Efficient Electrochemical 5-Amino-1 H -tetrazole Electrooxidation within a Wide Potential Range
items.abstract: Abstract Nitrogen-rich azo-tetrazole compounds are essential structural scaffolds for energetic materials, dyes, and agrochemicals, owing to their favorable energetic and physicochemical properties. Potassium 5,5′-azotetrazolate (PZT), as a representative and efficient nitrogen-rich azo-tetrazole material, is conventionally synthesized via thermochemical oxidative coupling, which suffers from safety hazards and environmental pollution. Electrochemical synthesis offers a compelling alternative, but the severe competitive oxygen evolution reaction (OER) impedes achieving highly-efficient N–N coupling activity and Faradaic efficiency (FE). Herein, a core–shell CF@CuO@Ni/Ni(OH)2 electrode is fabricated through controlled H+-mediated electrodeposition. The CF@CuO core provides a three-dimensional (3D) conductive scaffold and suppresses the competing OER, while the Ni0/Ni(OH)2 shell undergoes electrochemical reconstruction into coexisting NiO/NiOOH working phases. The catalyst reaches 10 mA·cm–2 at 1.16 V vs RHE and maintains a Faradaic efficiency above 94% over a broad potential range of 1.2–1.6 V. Combined electrochemical, spectroscopic, kinetic, and computational analyses prove that surface-adsorbed *OH initiates 5-AT dehydrogenative coupling via a PCET pathway on the reconstructed NiO/NiOOH surface. NiO triggers synergistic *OH/5-AT adsorption, while NiOOH facilitates dehydrogenation. In a continuous-flow AEM electrolyzer, the system operates at 500 mA cm–2 over 300 h while sustaining PZT production (purity ≥99%) and H2 evolution. Extension to DAT and DAF further demonstrates the transferability of the catalyst toward related amino-functionalized N-heterocycles undergoing oxidative N–N coupling. This work establishes that reconstructed NiO/NiOOH dual sites, supported on an OER-suppressing CuO scaffold, enable selective and energy-efficient N–N oxidative coupling of amino heterocycles.

items.title: Competitive Interactions between Propylene Combustion Products Regulate Catalyst Durability over Facet-Tuned Pt/TiO2
items.abstract: Abstract While product-induced inhibition is widely recognized in heterogeneous catalysis, the joint influence of co-generated products on time-dependent catalytic deactivation remains underexplored. Herein, uniform colloidal Pt nanoparticles were deposited on anatase TiO2 supports selectively exposing (101) or (001) facets to fabricate two facet-controlled model Pt/TiO2 catalysts. We uncovered the intrinsic deactivation mechanism for low-temperature lean propylene combustion via stability tests, alternating feed kinetics, in situ DRIFTS, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Time-on-stream reaction tests recorded persistent activity decay for both catalysts, with far more serious decay observed on Pt/TiO2(101). Multiple characterization results excluded Pt sintering/encapsulation, C3H6/O2 poisoning, and partial Pt oxidation as dominant degradation factors. Instead, CO2 adsorption and subsequent carbonate accumulation on TiO2 surfaces were identified as the primary deactivation sources, which cut off supplementary oxygen delivery at metal–support interfaces. DFT adsorption energy data proved that H2O possessed a stronger surface affinity than CO2 on both facet types, and in situ generated H2O competed for adsorption sites to curb carbonate accumulation. Apart from this competitive effect, reaction-derived H2O alleviated excessive coverage of Pt sites by C3H6 and facilitated the adsorption and activation of gas-phase O2. Thanks to the relatively high water-binding capacity of TiO2(001), the corresponding Pt/TiO2(001) catalyst maintained abundant interfacial water during operation and exhibited much milder carbonate-triggered decay. These findings clarified the competitive co-adsorption interplay between CO2 and H2O across Pt–TiO2 interfaces and offered general kinetic guidance for developing durable catalysts toward industrial hydrocarbon lean combustion.

items.title: Simultaneous Stabilization of Copper Species and Regulation of the Cu+/Cu0 Balance on SiO2 for Selective Ethanol Dehydrogenation
items.abstract: Abstract Selective ethanol dehydrogenation is a promising route for acetaldehyde production; however, achieving stable copper catalysts on inert supports with a well-balanced Cu+/Cu0 ratio remains challenging. Herein, we report a urea-assisted strategy to simultaneously stabilize copper species and regulate the Cu+/Cu0 balance on a silica support. The gradual release of ammonia promotes the formation of interfacial Cu–O–Si linkages and basic copper nitrate species, which serve as precursors for Cu+ and Cu0, respectively. The resulting catalyst exhibits highly dispersed copper species with a balanced Cu+/Cu0 distribution, delivering high activity, &gt;95% acetaldehyde selectivity, and stable performance in ethanol dehydrogenation. Mechanistic studies reveal that Cu+ sites facilitate ethanol activation, while Cu0 sites promote C–H bond cleavage. However, excessive Cu+ species lead to the formation of strongly adsorbed enolic intermediates, which trigger C–C coupling and byproduct formation. This work highlights the importance of Cu+/Cu0 synergy and provides a general strategy for designing stable and selective copper-based catalysts on inert supports.

items.title: A Two-Water-Assisted Deacylation Pathway in Class C β-Lactamase ACC-1 Revealed by High-Resolution Crystallography and QM/MM Calculations
items.abstract: Abstract β-Lactam antibiotics are among the most widely prescribed antibacterial agents, yet their clinical efficacy is increasingly compromised by β-lactamase-mediated resistance. Class C β-lactamase ACC-1 hydrolyzes third-generation cephalosporins such as cefotaxime through a covalent acyl-enzyme intermediate, but the molecular basis of deacylation remains unresolved. Here, we report high-resolution synchrotron and room-temperature X-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) crystal structures of the cefotaxime-acylated ACC-1. These structures reveal a previously unrecognized two-water configuration near the acyl center, comprising the previously proposed deacylating water, Wat1, and an additional ordered water molecule, Wat2, positioned at a Bürgi–Dunitz angle suitable for nucleophilic attack. Quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) calculations identify a previously unrecognized two-water-assisted deacylation pathway in which the substrate C4-carboxylate and Wat1 cooperatively activate Wat2 as the nucleophilic deacylating water. This pathway exhibits a substantially lower activation free-energy barrier than the alternative substrate-assisted and Tyr150–Lys67 general-base pathways examined. Together, these findings revise the deacylation mechanism of class C ACC-1 β-lactamase by revealing how an ordered water network and the substrate C4 carboxylate can cooperate to promote acyl-enzyme hydrolysis. This atomic-level mechanism provides a foundation for rational design strategies aimed at developing β-lactam antibiotics and β-lactamase inhibitors that resist or disrupt enzymatic hydrolysis.

items.title: Effects of Zeolite Framework on Direct Reduction of Esters to Ethers Using H2 on Pt-Zeolite Catalysts
items.abstract: Abstract The direct reduction of esters to ethers using H2 represents a fundamental selectivity challenge for heterogeneous catalysis and offers a method to increase the hydrothermal stability of chemicals and fuels derived from renewable resources. Prior studies revealed that ethers derive from a series of reactions that involve in situ formation of hemiacetals by hydrogen transfer on metal nanoparticles, followed by diffusive transport to Brønsted acid sites that cleave the carbonyl C–O bond. The competing hydrogenolysis pathway proceeds by a similar bifunctional mechanism; however, hydrolysis and transesterification occur by direct reactions of esters solely at Brønsted acid sites. Here, we find that rates and selectivities reflect the intrinsic reactivity at individual Brønsted acid sites, which depends upon the topology of the aluminosilicate support. Pt-Faujasite (FAU) provides ether formation rates at least an order of magnitude greater than smaller pore zeolites that possess similar Pt loadings and Si/Al ratios (e.g., mordenite framework inverted (MFI), beta (BEA), and ferrierite (FER)). Correlations between formation rates and activation energies for ether formation with heats of adsorption of propyl acetate across Pt-zeolites and Pt-AlMCM41 suggest that dispersive interactions among the zeolite pore wall, surrounding molecules (e.g., propyl acetate), and transition states contribute to differences in performance among these catalysts. These effects appear responsible for Pt-FER providing the highest ether selectivities observed (∼50%), although the specific structural features responsible for this behavior remain uncertain and may reflect framework-specific confinement and transport effects. However, ether selectivities also appear sensitive to other zeolite properties, including channel dimensionality, which may influence diffusive transport between Pt and Brønsted acid sites. These findings illustrate that the topology of the aluminosilicate support impacts rates and selectivities for ester reduction by orders of magnitude: these differences reflect contributions of inter-function transport reminiscent of other bifunctional catalysts for hydrotreating reactions but also evidence from comparisons to titration calorimetry that the local solvation of reactive intermediates at Brønsted acid sites influences catalysis.

items.title: Carboxylation of Bio-Based 2-Furoic Acid with CO2 to 2,5-Furandicarboxylic Acid over CuAlO x Catalysts
items.abstract: Abstract Direct C–H carboxylation with CO2 as a renewable C1 source stands out as an atom-economical strategy for CO2 utilization. However, the low reactivity of C–H bond and intrinsic inertness of CO2 limit carboxylation efficiency. This work presents a cooperative CuAlOx-Cs2CO3 catalytic system for the C–H carboxylation of 2-furoic acid (FA) with CO2 to produce 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid (2,5-FDCA), a key bio-based monomer for polyethylene furanoate (PEF). By integrating a hydrotalcite-derived Cu2AlOx catalyst into a Cs2CO3-promoted system, the 2,5-FDCA yield increases from 13% to 91% at 190 °C under 2 MPa CO2 with 1.33 equiv Cs2CO3, with a reduction of 61 kJ·mol–1 in apparent activation energy. The high Cu-normalized apparent activity (33.2 mmolFA gCu–1 h–1) with 96.8% selectivity to 2,5-FDCA is achieved. Mechanistic and theoretical analyses reveal that Cu2AlOx promotes the activation of both FA and CO2. The interaction of Cu2AlOx with the carboxylate group of FA elongates the C5-H bond and facilitates Cs2CO3-promoted deprotonation, while Cu2AlOx activates CO2 mainly via bidentate carbonate species that enhance the electrophilicity of the carbon center, thereby lowering the C–C coupling barrier. The resulting 2,5-FDCA is a viable monomer for producing PEF with rigid furan-based backbones, underscoring its potential for engineering plastic applications. This synergistic strategy offers an atom-economical route to bio-based 2,5-FDCA and provides mechanistic insights into substrate and CO2 activation in direct C–H carboxylation.

items.title: Facet-Dependent Regulation of Reactive Oxygen Species Generation and Utilization Governs Biomass Oxidation
items.abstract: Abstract Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are key intermediates in radical-mediated heterogeneous oxidation, yet the relationship between ROS generation and their effective utilization remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that crystal facets can differently influence ROS generation and utilization during biomass-derived alcohol/aldehyde oxidation. Using CuO catalysts, predominantly exposing either the (001) or (111) facet as model systems, we show that the CuO(001) facet preferentially promotes hydroxyl radical (·OH) generation through efficient tert-butyl hydroperoxide activation, whereas the CuO(111) facet promotes efficient interfacial utilization of surface-associated ·OH during the hydrogen-abstraction step. Despite producing fewer EPR-detectable radicals, CuO(111) exhibits higher catalytic performance for the base-free oxidation of 5-hydroxymethylfurfural to 2,5-furandicarboxylic acid, achieving quantitative HMF conversion and an FDCA yield of 85.7% under mild conditions (80 °C, 4 h). Time-resolved kinetic analysis, radical trapping experiments, electron paramagnetic resonance spectroscopy, and density functional theory calculations reveal that facet-dependent adsorption configurations regulate oxidant activation and subsequent hydrogen abstraction, thereby determining whether generated ROS undergo productive interfacial reactions or non-productive accumulation. This work provides mechanistic insights into the relationship between ROS generation, ROS utilization, and catalytic performance, highlighting the importance of considering the productive participation of generated ROS in catalyst evaluation.

items.title: Toward the High-Yield Generation of Vanillic Acid from Lignin by Selective C–C Cleavage over CuO Nanoparticles
items.abstract: Abstract The selective cleavage of C–C bonds in lignin for scalable production of phenolic biochemicals constitutes a major obstacle, owing to lignin’s inherent structural complexity, the poor selectivity of existing catalysts, and the complicated separation process. Herein, we report a strategy to overcome this by improving the lignin side-chain C–C selective cleavage using a CuO nanoparticles (CuO NPs) catalyst through a one-pot oxidation process under mild conditions. The CuO NPs (&lt;10 nm) were prepared by super-slow in situ precipitation of Cu2+ on GO. Morphology analysis revealed the presence of both CuO NPs and single Cu atoms, which exhibited an average size of 8 nm. Under mild conditions (140 °C, 1 atm), the CuO NPs/GO catalyst facilitated the selective cleavage of lignin Cα–Cβ side chains, resulting in over 95% lignin conversion and 10.8 wt % pure vanillic acid (VA), a record efficiency for isolated VA production. The high selectivity could be attributed to the presence of CuO NPs on the GO support. DFT simulations suggest that the CuO NPs decrease the formation energy barrier of active [O] species significantly, resulting in selective oxidation of the double bond in the lignin-derived intermediate, enol ether. By elucidating the key factors governing bond selectivity, our findings provide a foundation for the rational design of C–C bond oxidation catalysts in biomass valorization. The economic analysis based on a daily lignin feedstock of 500 tons demonstrates an estimated gross margin of ∼20%.

items.title: Electronic Control of Mechanistic Divergence in Iron-Catalyzed Olefin Carboamidation to β- and γ-Lactams
items.abstract: Abstract Regiodivergent synthetic strategies employing common precursors provide a powerful means of accessing structurally distinct molecular scaffolds. Herein, we report an electronically controlled, regiodivergent iron-catalyzed intramolecular olefin carboamidation of styrenyl dioxazolones that selectively affords either β- or γ-lactams using a range of carbon nucleophiles, including electron-rich arenes, allylsilanes, and propargylsilanes, thereby providing access to arylated, allylated, and allenylated products, respectively. Combined Hammett analysis, experimental mechanistic studies, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations support the involvement of a common azabicyclo[2.1.0]pentanone intermediate and reveal two electronically differentiated pathways: 1) strain-releasing SN2-type aziridine ring-opening promoted by electron-withdrawing substituents to deliver five-membered γ-lactams and 2) solvent-assisted aziridine ring-opening promoted by electron-donating substituents to generate a benzylic carbocation intermediate, followed by SN1-type trapping with a carbon nucleophile to furnish four-membered β-lactams.

items.title: Synergistic-Tandem Active Sites Engineered in Pd-Doped Mo5N6 Nanosheets for Efficient CO2 Photoreduction to Acetic Acid
items.abstract: Abstract CO2 photoreduction into multicarbon products such as acetic acid represents a promising strategy for addressing the greenhouse effect and energy shortages. However, the process is limited by kinetically sluggish C–C coupling and inefficient proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET). Herein, we construct Nv-Pdδ+ tandem active sites in Mo5N6 nanosheets via low-valent Pdδ+ (2 &lt; δ &lt; 4) doping, which simultaneously introduces abundant stable nitrogen vacancies (Nv) and adjacent Pdδ+ centers. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that the Nv sites promote CO2 activation and reduce the energy barrier for *CO dimerization, while the neighboring Pdδ+ sites efficiently drive water splitting to supply H*, thereby facilitating the hydrogenation of key *OCCO intermediates. Accordingly, the optimized Pd0.5-Mo5N6 achieves a high acetic acid selectivity of 90.1% with an evolution rate of 33.24 μmol·g–1·h–1 under solar irradiation. This work establishes a tandem active-site design strategy for efficient and durable photocatalytic synthesis of multicarbon products from CO2.

items.title: Regulated Density of Atomic Cu Sites Dictates Switching from C1 to C2+ Products in CO Electroreduction
items.abstract: Abstract Single-atom catalysts (SACs) are generally considered C1-selective in CO2/CO electroreduction, as spatially isolated sites cannot efficiently sustain adjacent CO-derived intermediates required for C─C coupling. Here we show that this selectivity bias is not intrinsic to atomically dispersed Cu, but depends on single-atom site density. Across a series of Cu–N3O catalysts with different Cu site densities, increasing site density drives a clear selectivity crossover from H2 and CH4 formation to C2+ products. The total C2+ Faradaic efficiency (FE) rises from 9.6% on the low-density to 78.1% on the high-density at 1 bar CO, and further reaches 87.7% at 7 bar CO, whereas the low-density remains C1-selective. In situ attenuated-total-reflection surface enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy (ATR-SEIRAS) reveals that dense Cu single atoms sustain a larger *COatop population and simultaneously shift interfacial water from strongly hydrogen-bonded species towards free-water-rich configurations. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations show that higher site density stabilizes CO-containing surface states and lowers the barrier of the acetate-forming pathway. These findings identify a CO-rich and proton-accessible interfacial state that favors C─C coupling over C1 hydrogenation, establishing site density as a structural descriptor for multicarbon electrosynthesis on single-atom catalysts.

items.title: Synergistic Facet Engineering and Axial Asymmetric Coordination of Single-Atom Cu Polarize Nitric Oxide Intermediates to Boost Photocatalytic Nitrate Reduction to Ammonia
items.abstract: Abstract Sluggish charge dynamics and poor *NO polarization at active sites hinder the efficiency of photocatalytic nitrate reduction to ammonia (PcNRA). To address these issues, an atomic-level regulation strategy synergizing facet engineering with axial coordination was developed. Specifically, isolated Cu sites were anchored onto an electron-rich, ultrathin BiVO4 substrate exposing (040) facets. Functionalized ligands featuring distinct donor heteroatoms (S, N, O) were then systematically introduced, yielding a series of single-atom catalysts (S/N/O-Cu/BVO) with tailored axial microenvironments. A comprehensive methodology combining multidimensional spectroscopy and computational chemistry was established to verify this single-atom axial coordination. Detailed analyses of characteristic binding energies and absorption edge shifts via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and synchrotron X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS) identified localized coordination field effects. Crucially, these effects are distinct from conventional electronic metal-support interactions (EMSI), providing spectroscopic confirmation of successful axial ligand incorporation and guiding the prediction of their configurations. Building upon these spectral findings, density functional theory (DFT) models were constructed and optimized, conclusively validating the asymmetric axial coordination configurations within the system, specifically Cu-S2O1, Cu-N2O1, and Cu-O4. Catalytic evaluations demonstrated that S-Cu/BVO achieves the highest ammonia yield at 435 μmol·h–1·g–1. In-situ spectroscopy and DFT calculations elucidated the multidimensional synergistic mechanism driving this enhanced activity: (1) The prominently exposed (040) facets act as an interfacial electron sink, efficiently directing photogenerated electrons toward the Cu sites; (2) The axial S ligands reconstruct the electronic structure of the Cu centers via strong orbital coupling, thereby improving effective orbital overlap with nitrate; (3) The resulting asymmetric Cu-NO-S bridging configuration polarizes the critical *NO intermediate, substantially lowering the kinetic barrier for the rate-determining step.

items.title: Nickel-Catalyzed Electroreductive Cross-Electrophile Coupling of Aryl/Alkenyl Triflates with Alkyl Bromides Assisted by an Organo-Mediator
items.abstract: Abstract Given the thermodynamic stability of the C(sp2)–O bond, the development of simple and efficient strategies for its functionalization holds significant practical value. In this study, we report an electroreductive, one-pot nickel-catalyzed cross-electrophile coupling (XEC) of aryl/alkenyl triflates with diverse (1°, 2°, and 3°) alkyl bromides. Rapid in situ generation of Ni0 species enables efficient activation of the C(sp2)–O bond, yielding a broad range of C(sp2)–C(sp3) coupling products. Notably, the ligand functions as an organo-mediator to assist alkyl halide activation and prevent the over-reduction of substrates. This protocol is distinguished by its broad substrate scope, scalability, and mild reaction conditions.

items.title: Favorable Carrier Dynamics in a Narrow-Gap Layered Oxynitride Enable Efficient Molecular Hybrid CO2 Photoreduction
items.abstract: Abstract Efficient interfacial electron transfer from light-harvesting semiconductors to molecular catalysts remains a major challenge in molecular–semiconductor hybrid photocatalytic CO2 reduction, particularly for narrow-bandgap semiconductors, whose reduced thermodynamic driving force often requires assistance from metallic electron-transfer mediators such as Ag. Here, we show that, despite its narrow bandgap of 2.1 eV, the layered perovskite oxynitride K2LaTa2O6N (KLTON) functions as an effective semiconductor support for a supramolecular RuRu′ CO2-reduction catalyst without relying on Ag nanoparticles. The RuRu′/KLTON hybrid selectively converted CO2 to formate under visible-light irradiation with &gt;99% selectivity, a turnover number of 691, and an apparent quantum yield of 6.1 ± 0.6% at 420 nm. Loading a small amount of Ag further increased the turnover number to 1077, but this 1.5-fold enhancement was modest compared with the larger Ag-induced activity enhancements reported for several conventional oxynitride-based hybrids, highlighting the weak Ag dependence of the KLTON-based system. Spatial photodeposition of Ag and MnOx revealed spatially differentiated surface redox reactivity on the terraced layered structure of KLTON, while time-resolved microwave conductivity and transient infrared absorption measurements showed favorable photogenerated-carrier dynamics and demonstrated that Ag loading modifies the electron dynamics of KLTON. Time-resolved emission measurements further revealed an additional nonradiative decay pathway at the Ru(II) photosensitizer/KLTON interface, consistent with interfacial electronic interaction without uniquely assigning its microscopic origin. These results identify favorable carrier dynamics and weak Ag dependence as key features of the KLTON-based molecular hybrid and highlight layered narrow-bandgap mixed-anion semiconductors as promising support materials for visible-light-driven molecular photocatalysis.

items.title: The Emerging Potential of Janus-Type Di-N-heterocyclic Carbene Transition Metal Complexes in Homogeneous Catalysis
items.abstract: Abstract The article explores the catalytic potential of the emerging class of Janus-type di-N-heterocyclic carbenes that have attracted attention in recent times. The article details different aspects of these Janus-type di-N-heterocyclic carbenes particularly from their classifications, expansion in synthesis approaches, to finally their utility in different homogeneous transformations.

items.title: Mechanism-Driven Size Optimization of Fully Exposed Rh Cluster Catalysts for Butane Dehydrogenation
items.abstract: Abstract Nonoxidative butane dehydrogenation offers a direct route to C4 olefins, yet it remains challenged by the need to promote C–H activation while ensuring olefin desorption and suppressing C–C cracking. Here, we report a mechanism-guided study that combines density functional theory calculations with experimental validation to rationally design Rh-based catalysts for butane dehydrogenation. A series of Rh models with distinct geometric configurations on a graphene surface, including isolated Rh atom, fully exposed Rh2 and Rh3 clusters, and extended Rh surfaces, were constructed to elucidate the structure–activity relationship. The calculations reveal a volcano-type dependence of dehydrogenation activity on the Rh geometric configuration. Fully exposed Rh3 clusters exhibit optimal energetics for sequential C–H activation, whereas isolated Rh atoms and Rh nanoparticles show inferior activity. Experimental studies on Rh/nanodiamond@graphene catalysts confirm the prediction, demonstrating that fully exposed Rh clusters with an average Rh–Rh coordination number of approximately 1.9 achieve the best balance between C–H activation, olefin desorption, and C–C bond cleavage suppression. This study highlights highly efficient Rh active sites by regulating the geometric configuration and electronic property and provides a general strategy for designing dehydrogenation catalysts.

items.title: Kinetic Limitations of Single-Atom Catalysts in Hydrazine Oxidation
items.abstract: Abstract Single-atom catalysts (SACs) have attracted considerable interest, displaying impressive performance for a wide plethora of electrocatalytic reactions. However, the important question whether isolated sites are always beneficial remains unresolved. Here, by using the hydrazine oxidation reaction (HzOR) as a model reaction, we examine how isolated single-atom metal sites restrict the adsorption mode of intermediates to the monodentate configuration, which leads to weak intermediate stabilization and poor reaction kinetics. This contrasts with bulk metal sites where availability of the bidentate adsorption configuration offers better intermediate stabilization and dehydrogenation kinetics. As a result, Ir, Pt, and Pd SACs were found to require high HzOR overpotentials of 0.90, 1.21, and 1.19 V at 3 mA cm–2, respectively. Comparatively, their Ir, Pt, Pd nanoparticle counterparts with similar metal loading exhibit considerably lower overpotentials of only 0.35, 0.83, and 0.64 V at 3 mA cm–2, respectively. Taken together, our work contributes towards a more complete understanding of SACs, emphasizing the importance of considering site structure and the mechanistic demands of the reaction.

items.title: Multiplexed Ultrahigh-Throughput Evolution for Esterase Selectivity across a Broad Substrate Scope
items.abstract: Abstract Directed evolution of enzymes is generally performed toward a specific substrate, which predictably improves enzyme activity toward the probe substrate. However, it is difficult to predict whether evolved enzymes will be selective or promiscuous toward other substrates. Multiplexed directed evolution can identify enzyme variants with selectivity/promiscuity across multiple substrates, but is typically performed using plate-based screening assays that are limited to testing a few hundred mutants. Combining substrate multiplexing with ultrahigh-throughput evolution technologies is a promising avenue for deeper exploration of the mutational landscape, but it has not been investigated whether enzymes evolved using multiplexed ultrahigh-throughput methods exhibit selectivity/promiscuity toward a broader scope of small-molecule substrates beyond the probes used during evolution. Here, we performed multiplexed ultrahigh-throughput evolution of Bacillus subtilis (BS2) esterase, merging yeast surface display with masked acid chloride probes, to identify a panel of mutants with improved selectivity toward the phenylcyclopropyl (pCP) ester protecting group relative to not only the probe substrate, but also a broad panel of 90 additional esters. Additionally, we applied the platform to identify a promiscuous mutant with improved activity across a broad substrate scope. Finally, we applied the highly pCP-selective BS2 variant, together with a selective variant for the methylcyclopropyl (mCP) ester protecting group, to demonstrate proximity labeling in mammalian cells with two orthogonal enzyme/probe systems, opening new opportunities in multiplexed proximity labeling. Overall, this study presents an efficacious method to identify enzyme variants with desired selectivity profiles that may be extended to multiple applications in chemical biology and synthesis.

items.title: Data-Driven Investigation of Asymmetric Photo-Organocatalyzed Alkylation of Indoles
items.abstract: Abstract Enantioselective dual catalysis represents a powerful strategy for the preparation of functionally dense optically active compounds. Photocatalysis, paired with organocatalysis, undeniably represents a popular choice that takes advantage of radical and polar reactivity for crafting challenging bonds. Despite the interest in this methodology, the detailed analysis of the effects governing selectivity between the two catalytic cycles has not been extensively studied. Herein, we report a data-driven mechanistic study campaign to disclose the factors that influence the enantioselectivity of a photo-organocatalytic alkylation of indoles. Data science tools were used to generate a virtual library of potential substrates, thus ensuring the selection of a statistically diverse training set. Subsequent multivariate linear regression (MLR) analysis led to the identification of substrate electronic features as the key factor affecting the stereochemical outcome. Moreover, comprehensive mechanistic experiments unveiled the key role of the in situ generated oxindole intermediate that connects the two catalytic cycles in determining the observed selectivity. These findings lay the foundation for developing asymmetric dual catalytic transformations of synthetic relevance and provide a general platform for interrogating other complex catalytic systems.

items.title: Quantum Chemical Insight into Species Competition in Electrochemical Upgrading of Bio-Oil
items.abstract: Abstract Bio-oil derived from lignocellulosic biomass represents an alternative to fossil fuels as an energy source and chemical feedstock. Fast pyrolysis of lignocellulosic biomass yields a rich mixture of oxygenated organic species with low energy density and low stability, which can be electrochemically upgraded to increase energy density and stability and produce value-added chemicals. Here, we focus on electrocatalytic hydrotreatment of furfural (FF) and 4-propylphenol (4-PP), two constituents of raw bio-oil. In a binary mixture, the presence of FF has been shown to inhibit the reduction of 4-PP. The underlying mechanisms of these competing reactions are probed using density functional theory (DFT) and experimental electrochemical deposition techniques. The binding energies of FF and 4-PP, as well as their respective reduction products and associated reaction thermodynamics, are examined comparatively on multiple facets of single-crystal platinum and ruthenium catalysts. FF is shown to bind competitively compared to 4-PP, particularly on Pt(111) and Ru(0001), and hydrogenation products such as tetrahydrofurfuryl alcohol (THFA) and 4-propylcyclohexanol (4-PCOL) were found to bind less strongly to the surfaces than the reactants. FF reduction side products, including dimers furoin (FUI) and hydrofuroin (HF), were also found to bind competitively with 4-PP. No thermodynamic barriers were observed for FF hydrogenation to THFA, whereas 4-PCOL formation is favored on Pt facets, and propylcyclohexane (PC) formation is favored on Ru. The presence of barriers to 4-PP hydrogenation indicates that FF hydrogenation is thermodynamically favored on Pt and Ru. Further, limiting potential calculations suggest that the FF reduction pathways are generally favorable around 0 V vs. RHE. In contrast, the 4-PP reduction pathways require a more cathodic bias, achieved at potentials less than -0.1 V vs. RHE. The adsorption behavior of FF-derived reduction products on polycrystalline Pt is experimentally validated using a Quartz Crystal Microbalance (QCM). Such experiments yield estimates of aqueous-phase free energies of adsorption, which are compared with computational results that are correlated to the aqueous phase. Overall, the DFT model results suggest that the observed inhibition of 4-PP by FF is due to competitive adsorption and favorable FF reaction thermodynamics.

items.title: Photoredox-Mediated Three-Component Carboamination of Reverse Exo -Glycals: Modular Access to C 4-Quaternary Furanosides and Spironucleosides
items.abstract: Abstract Quaternary stereocenters on densely functionalized furanoside frameworks are challenging to construct with high chemo-, regio-, and stereocontrol, especially in the presence of nitrogen-containing motifs and multiple downstream diversification handles. Here, we disclose a sequence-programmed three-component radical carboamination of reverse exo-glycals that provides modular access to C4-quaternary furanosides through a distinct radical retrosynthetic logic. In this photoredox process, an N-centered radical adds to an electron-rich reverse exo-glycal to form a pseudo-anomeric radical, which is then intercepted by a Giese acceptor, enabling concomitant C–N and C–C bond formation in a single step. The protocol accommodates diverse N-radical precursors and electron-deficient alkenes, is further extendable to distinct pyranose- and furanose-derived reverse exo-glycals, supports late-stage glyco-functionalization of structurally complex molecules, and furnishes a spiro-glycosyl donor on preparative scale. Subsequent Vorbrüggen glycosylation enables divergent entry to structurally distinct spironucleosides. Preliminary biological profiling of these compounds reveals a modest antiviral signal against influenza A (PR8) at 50 μM, supporting the utility of this platform for probing underexplored spironucleoside chemical space. Mechanistic experiments support the proposed photoredox-mediated radical relay, while DFT studies provide a plausible basis for the contrasting reactivity of representative N-radical precursors. Collectively, this work offers a concise and programmable strategy for the synthesis of quaternary-center furanosides and their downstream spirocyclic derivatives from readily available carbohydrate feedstocks.

items.title: Disrupting Interfacial Hydrogen-Bonding Networks via Dynamic Reconstruction Strategy for Enhanced CO2-to-C2+ Electrocatalysis
items.abstract: Abstract The morphology and microenvironment of ion-conducting polymers (ionomers) on the catalyst electrode surface critically govern the CO2 electrocatalytic performance. Herein, we report a dual-reconstruction strategy that synergistically tailors the surface structure of the Nafion ionomer using positively charged molecules and solvent effect. By combining a low-dielectric-constant solvent (isopropanol) with arginine cations, the optimized electrode achieves an 83.6% Faradaic efficiency for multicarbon (C2+) products at a high current density of –500 mA cm–2 in 1 M KOH. Based on experimental characterization and MD simulations, we propose a structural model in which the Nafion side chains are oriented away from both the catalyst surface and the electrolyte phase. In situ spectroscopic analyses, theoretical calculation, and experimental evidence suggest that this structural reorganization disrupts the interfacial hydrogen-bonding network, suppresses the competing hydrogen evolution reaction, improves effective gaseous CO2 accessibility, and facilitates C–C coupling along an energetically favorable *OC–COH pathway. This work provides valuable insights into microenvironment engineering of ionomer–catalyst interfaces for efficient CO2 electrolysis.

items.title: Gallium-Containing ZSM-5 Zeolites Improve Hydrocracking Selectivity to Propane
items.abstract: Abstract Polyolefin hydrocracking over Brønsted acidic ZSM-5 produces light hydrocarbons with narrow product distributions, but further increases in propane and butane selectivity are required to improve process economics and sustainability. Here, we examined the effect of various metal and metal oxide dopants, namely Pt, Pt-Sn, SnOx, ZnOx, and GaOx, on ZSM-5-mediated polyolefin hydrocracking and identified GaOx as a selective promoter for light gas formation. Incorporation of gallium oxide (3 wt % Ga) was shown to increase propane selectivity from 40 c-wt %, achieved over ZSM-5, to near 60 c-wt %, reaching a combined propane and butane selectivity of 85 c-wt %, while maintaining solids conversion. To elucidate the role of gallium oxide, we used ex situ and operando characterization techniques to probe acidity, local coordination environment, and the spatial distribution of GaOx species. Extra-framework gallium oxide introduced via incipient wetness impregnation reduced the measured acid site density from 1275 to 911 μmol g–1, decreased the Brønsted/Lewis acid site ratio, and formed a high-coverage GaOx layer on the external surface of the zeolite. Operando experiments show that Ga is present in both Ga3+ and Ga1+ under reaction conditions. Attempts to disperse gallium oxide through reductive pretreatments led to an increase in the Lewis acid site concentration and a 10 c-wt % decrease in propane selectivity, highlighting the importance of the specific location, structural, and acidic configurations. Systematic variation of impregnation methods to control location and dispersion revealed a synergistic interaction between gallium oxide and zeolite acid sites, with propane selectivity strongly influenced by spatial proximity of GaOx to acid sites. Furthermore, vapor-phase flow reactions with a model compound demonstrated a decrease in intermediate product formation compared to the zeolite alone. The optimized catalyst was validated across diverse polyolefin substrates and resulted in similar increases to propane selectivity, yielding &gt;80 c-wt % combined C3–C4 selectivity across the range of polyolefin substrates.

items.title: Stabilizing Cobalt Sites with d10-Configured p-Block Cations for Iridium-Free Proton Exchange Membrane Water Electrolysis
items.abstract: Abstract Proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE) requires anode catalysts that sustain acidic oxygen evolution in practical stacks with minimal noble-metal content. Cobalt spinel oxides are cost-attractive but dissolve rapidly in acid as cobalt sites over-oxidize under anodic bias. Here we show that incorporation of d10-configured p-block cations (Sb, Ge, In, and Ga) into Co3O4 stabilizes cobalt sites by promoting robust heterometallic Co–O–M interactions. Density functional theory predicts dopant-driven charge redistribution that suppresses over-oxidation of octahedral Co while maintaining favorable binding of oxygen intermediates. Operando Co K-edge X-ray absorption and time-resolved dissolution measurements confirm reduced oxidation-state dynamics and cobalt loss, whereas a d-block d10 control (Zn) shows no such stabilization. In a PEMWE single cell at 80 °C, Sb/Co3O4 reaches &gt;3500 mA cm–2 at 2.0 V and operates for &gt;1000 h at 250 mA cm–2. This work establishes p-block d10 incorporation as a general route to iridium-free PEMWE anodes.

items.title: In Situ X-ray Spectroscopic Identification and Kinetic Control of Highly Hybridized Co(IV) States in Cobalt Oxide Amorphous Catalysts
items.abstract: Abstract Valence dynamics of transition metals are central to oxygen evolution reaction (OER) mechanisms, yet in situ spectroscopic studies capturing these dynamics within amorphous catalysts remain limited. Here, we present in situ X-ray spectroscopy of amorphous catalysts, where CoBi exhibits higher OER performance compared to CoPi. While our data shows successive valence changes toward high-valent states in both catalysts, distinct initial electro-structural states dictate the intermediate evolution. Co(III) dominates in both catalysts at open-circuit potential, yet the Co(III)–O–Co(III) bridge structure observed in CoBi is absent in CoPi. Under active OER, Co(IV) species are identified as distinguishable spectral intensities; these are assigned to highly hybridized low-spin (LS) Co(IV) with reduced electron–electron repulsion, as validated by resonant inelastic X-ray spectroscopy (RIXS) analysis of Li0.75CoO2. Density functional theory supports the conversion from tetrahedral (Td) Co(II) to octahedral (Oh) Co(III) and suggests that factors other than thermodynamic pathways are likely responsible for the performance gap. The lower formal oxidation, larger Co–O length, smaller Co–O–Co angle, prominent pre-edge dipole character and absent oxo-bridging in CoPi suggest a kinetically inefficient Co(IV) state. These findings demonstrate that the initial electro-structure strongly influences the formation of productive high-valent active species and the resulting OER activity.

items.title: A Descriptor-Based Approach to Predict the Catalytic Activity of Zinc CO2 Hydration Catalysts
items.abstract: Abstract Carbonic anhydrase (CA) catalyzes CO2 hydration with turnover frequencies approaching 106 s–1, but native enzymes lack stability under conditions typical of industrial carbon capture. Small-molecule zinc mimics can be more stable under harsh conditions, but product inhibition by bicarbonate limits efficiency. A general framework for predicting turnover across ligand scaffolds has remained elusive. We report the analysis, by experiment and computation, of speciation and catalytic activity of zinc complexes as CA mimics. A literature data set of twelve Zn-ligand complexes was constructed, and the binding free energy (ΔGbind) of bicarbonate to zinc was calculated by DFT with DLPNO-CCSD(T) refinement. ΔGbind strongly correlates with the intrinsic rate constants of these Zn-ligand complexes for CO2 hydration with R2 = 0.90 at pH 9, 25 °C, and saturated CO2 (1 atm). By comparison, combining the commonly used descriptors ΣE(2), qZn, and %Vburied resulted in R2 = 0.74. Examining additional Zn catalysts (for example, the coordination species [ZnL4(OH)]+, where L is 1-methylimidazole) revealed that chemical speciation must be accounted for to describe the observed dependence of catalytic activity on ligand stoichiometry. Furthermore, accurate ranking of catalytic activity for several of the modified cyclens considered requires accounting for steric congestion (%Vburied), as ΔGbind alone does not capture active-site occlusion. These results define a transferable framework that integrates ΔGbind, speciation, and steric properties to enable the design of Zn-based CO2 hydration catalysts.

items.title: Oxyfunctionalization of Primary Benzylic C(sp3)–H Bonds with Water by a Molybdenum-Dependent Dehydrogenase
items.abstract: Abstract The selective oxyfunctionalization of C(sp3)–H bonds remains a central challenge in chemical synthesis. Although oxygenases and peroxygenases provide biocatalytic alternatives to metal-based chemical methods, their practical use is constrained by costly cofactor regeneration, toxic co-substrates, or limited selectivity. Molybdenum (Mo)-dependent alkyl dehydrogenases circumvent these limitations by employing water, rather than O2 or H2O2, as the oxygen source for hydroxylation in conjunction with an electron acceptor. Here, we combine enzymatic, structural, and computational analyses to characterize a Mo-dependent p-cymene dehydrogenase (pCDH) from an anaerobic hydrocarbon-degrading bacterium. Isolated pCDH selectively hydroxylates a variety of benzylic and allylic C(sp3)–H bonds. A 2.0 Å cryo-EM structure of the heterotrimeric enzyme in complex with p-cymene captures key states of the catalytic cycle. Structure-guided QM/MM modelling and docking rationalize the substrate scope and radical mechanism. These results identify water-dependent Mo-dehydrogenases as promising catalysts for selective C(sp3)–H oxyfunctionalization.

items.title: Oriented Charge Flow in a Dual-Active-Site CdS Framework Enables Coupled CO2 Reduction and Biomass Alcohol Oxidation
items.abstract: Abstract Solar-driven conversion of CO2 into value-added chemicals provides an effective pathway for carbon resource utilization. However, the sluggish kinetics of CO2 reduction and the reliance on sacrificial electron donors limit its practical viability. Herein, we present a bifunctional photocatalyst consisting of spatially separated Ag2S and Au cocatalysts anchored on hollow CdS (Ag2S-Au/CdSH), which enables efficient concurrent CO2 photoreduction to CO and selective oxidation of aryl alcohols to benzaldehyde in a sacrificial-agent-free system. The rational integration of dual-active sites induces oriented charge flow, significantly enhancing photogenerated carrier separation and utilization, as evidenced by ultrafast spectroscopy showing extended electron lifetimes. This synergistic architecture delivers markedly higher production rates of 1.2 mmol g–1 h–1 for CO and 2.5 mmol g–1 h–1 for benzaldehyde, representing approximately 8-fold and 5-fold enhancements over pristine CdS, respectively. Comprehensive in situ spectroscopic studies combined with density functional theory calculations elucidate the distinct roles: Au sites strengthen CO2 adsorption and stabilize intermediates for reduction, while Ag2S promotes alcohol dehydrogenation. This synergistic dual-site architecture maximizes redox efficiency by matching reaction potentials and minimizing carrier recombination. This work provides mechanistic insights into catalyst design for integrated CO2 valorization and biomass upgrading, providing a basis for efficient chemical production.

items.title: Electric-Field-Assisted Oxygen-Vacancy Engineering Promotes Low-Temperature Ammonia Decomposition over Ru/CeO2 through Interfacial H Migration
items.abstract: Abstract Ammonia decomposition provides a promising route for on-demand hydrogen production, but conventional thermocatalytic systems are constrained by severe kinetic limitations at low temperatures, limiting their compatibility with low-grade heat utilization. Herein, we develop an electric-field-assisted oxygen-vacancy engineering strategy to promote low-temperature NH3 decomposition over Ru/CeO2 catalysts. Ru/CeO2 catalysts with tunable oxygen-vacancy concentrations were prepared via a pre-impregnation and solid-state grinding method. Structural and spectroscopic characterizations reveal that oxygen vacancies intrinsically strengthen Ru–CeO2–x interfacial electronic interactions, promote charge redistribution, and generate relatively electron-enriched Ru sites. More importantly, the applied electric field further amplifies this vacancy-mediated interfacial regulation and facilitates H-species transfer/removal. The optimized Ru/CeO2-OV3 EF catalyst achieves 35.3% NH3 conversion at 150 °C under a high GHSV of 30,000 mL gcat–1 h–1 and exhibits an electric-field-assisted apparent activation energy of only 12.28 kJ mol–1. In situ DRIFTS, TPD measurements, impedance analysis, and DFT calculations collectively suggest that defect-associated O sites near oxygen vacancies provide favorable accommodation sites for migrated H species, while the electric field promotes interfacial polarization and accelerates H transfer from Ru sites to the CeO2–x surface. This synergistic effect reduces H coverage on Ru active centers, regenerates available Ru sites for sustained NH3 activation, and enables stable low-temperature operation. This work clarifies how an external electric field amplifies oxygen-vacancy-mediated interfacial electron/H transfer and provides a rational strategy for efficient low-temperature hydrogen production from ammonia.

items.title: Engineered Asymmetric Ceδ+-O-P Structures via CeO2-CePO4 Heterojunctions for Continuous Dimethyl Carbonate Synthesis from CO2 and Methanol
items.abstract: Abstract Chemical fixation of CO2 with CH3OH into value-added chemicals, such as dimethyl carbonate (DMC), plays a crucial role in carbon neutrality and resource recycling. However, its efficiency is limited by the ineffective synergistic activation of CO2 and CH3OH. Here, we employ a strategy to construct CeO2-CePO4 heterojunctions by phosphate-functionalized CeO2, introducing an asymmetric Ceδ+-O-P structure for CO2 and CH3OH activation. The prepared Ce0.8P0.2Oσ catalyst achieves a CH3OH conversion of 28.6% with nearly 100% DMC selectivity and retains its performance for 300 h during continuous DMC synthesis at 140 °C. Experimental characterization supports the formation of local Ceδ+-O-P sites in the catalyst. DFT calculations based on one selected idealized strained model containing a specific local Ceδ+-O-P site show a distinct Bader charge for Ce–O–P and Ce–O–Ce coordinated oxygen atoms within this model. Within the same model, the local Ceδ+-O-P site is associated with elongation of the C–O bond in CH3O* and a lower energy barrier for its dissociation into *CH3 and *O, providing a model-specific interpretation of the enhanced DMC yield. This work develops a design strategy for asymmetric catalytic site via composite oxide heterojunctions engineered for CO2 and CH3OH activation, exhibiting great potential for large-scale continuous CO2 chemical fixation to high-value-added chemicals.

items.title: Advances in Photothermal CO2 Hydrogenation to Methane: Mechanistic Insights into Catalytic System Design across Different Scales
items.abstract: Abstract The ever-escalating accumulation of atmospheric CO2 and the growing demand for renewable energy conversion and storage have intensified research into solar-driven CO2 utilization technologies. Photothermal catalytic CO2 hydrogenation to methane has emerged as a promising approach for simultaneous carbon resource recycling and solar energy conversion, synergistically integrating the merits of photocatalysis and thermocatalysis. However, achieving high activity, selectivity, and long-term durability concurrently remains a central challenge, demanding precise control over photothermal conversion efficiency, charge transfer, and mass transport. Rational structural regulation spanning multiple length scales, from individual atoms to clusters, nanoparticles, and macroscopic reactors, is pivotal to overcoming such limitations. This review systematically summarizes research progress from a multiscale catalytic system design perspective, covering single atoms, nanoclusters, nanoparticles, supports, and macroscopic reactors. At each scale, the corresponding structure–activity relationships are analyzed, and the modulation mechanisms of active sites, photothermal effects, charge migration, and mass transport are elaborated. On this basis, we critically evaluate the advantages and bottlenecks of current research and put forward design guidelines and future development directions for next-generation high-performance catalytic systems. This review aims to provide both theoretical insights and practical references for the rational design of advanced photothermal CO2 methanation catalysts.

items.title: Promoting Efficient H2 Dissociation in Photothermal CO2 Hydrogenation through Functional Separation and Synergistic Coupling of Active Sites
items.abstract: Abstract Efficient H2 dissociation and subsequent spillover of active hydrogen species are critical factors for achieving high activity in CO2 hydrogenation reactions. Herein, we constructed a well-designed and highly dispersed Cu–In bimetallic catalyst supported on CeO2. This catalyst enables the spatial separation of plasmonic enhancement, H2 activation, and CO2 conversion sites, thereby significantly improving H2 dissociation capability and H-spillover efficiency. Comprehensive investigations using multiple transient characterizations, together with in situ/operando spectroscopy, reveal that the three components are tightly coupled through H-spillover, electron transfer, and interfacial interactions. Specifically, the Ce sites on the CeO2 surface serve as the active centers for CO2 conversion via a redox mechanism, while the available indirect but consistent evidence suggests that In species likely act as the primary H2 dissociation sites, promoting the reduction of Cu species and the regeneration of oxygen vacancies on the CeO2 surface through H-spillover. Meanwhile, the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) effect of Cu significantly enhances the light absorption and photothermal conversion efficiency of the catalyst. The photoexcited LSPR electrons generated by Cu are further transferred to the In species and CeO2 surface, thereby facilitating H2 dissociation and the redox cycling of Ce sites. Such a “functional separation–synergistic enhancement” strategy effectively improves the catalytic activity, and the optimal catalyst achieves a CO yield of 230.1 mmol gcat–1 h–1 W–1 cm2 under 1.5 W cm–2 light irradiation at the surface temperature of 300 °C, significantly outperforming both the corresponding dark reaction and the monometallic Cu/CeO2 and In/CeO2 counterparts. This work provides important design principles and mechanistic insights for constructing highly active CO2 hydrogenation catalytic systems by enhancing H2 dissociation and H-spillover processes.

items.title: Dynamic Change in Oxygen Storage and Release Mechanisms of Pd/CeO2–ZrO2 Catalyst by Isotope Imaging
items.abstract: Abstract Oxygen storage and release on oxygen storage materials such as CeO2–ZrO2 solid solution (CZ) are key phenomena for high-performance automotive three-way catalyst (TWC). In order to clarify the microscopic oxygen dynamics on TWC, oxygen storage distribution in a model catalyst comprising dense CZ substrate with Pd is visualized by combining oxygen isotope labeling and reaction quenching. The effects of temperature, oxygen storage duration, and hydrogen reduction (oxygen release) duration on 18O concentration distribution in the bulk and surface of the model catalysts are systematically investigated. In the temperature range of ≤400 °C, oxygen release and storage originated primarily from the Pd-CZ-gas triple phase boundary (TPB) and Pd surface, while the contribution from the bare CZ surface is limited. Oxygen incorporated from around the TPB diffuses in three directions: toward the CZ depth, CZ surface, and Pd surface. Furthermore, during the oxygen release process, the disappearance of the oxide layer (PdO) on the Pd and the subsequent exposure of metallic Pd accelerate oxygen release from the TPB, expanding the oxygen vacancy region deeper into the CZ directly beneath the Pd. Conversely, in the temperature range of ≥500 °C, in addition to the TPB-mediated process, the oxygen exchange on the entire CZ surface and bulk diffusion are activated, significantly expanding the storage and release regions. This study demonstrates that the OSC (oxygen storage capacity) mechanism in Pd/CZ catalyst is not static; rather, the dominant oxygen release/storage sites and transport pathways dynamically change depending on the temperature and the presence of a PdO layer.

items.title: Local Electric Fields at Organic-Inorganic Hybrid Interfaces Drive Electrocatalysis
items.abstract: Abstract The local electric field generated at organic-inorganic hybrid interfaces can profoundly influence electrocatalytic reactions, yet how molecular interfaces regulate local field distributions and reaction pathways remains poorly understood. Here, we combine grand-canonical density functional theory with in situ surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy to investigate CO2 reduction at cobalt phthalocyanine-copper (CoPc-Cu) interfaces. Density functional theory calculations show that CoPc creates a confined interfacial microenvironment and modifies the charge distribution at the Cu surface, producing non-uniform local electric fields that are experimentally probed using the vibrational Stark effect of adsorbed CO. Theory and experiment reveal that this field heterogeneity modifies CO adsorption across neighboring Cu sites and increases the adsorption-energy difference between adjacent CO intermediates, thereby lowering the barrier for C–C coupling. Consistent with this mechanism, CoPc-Cu exhibits an enhanced C2+/C1 product ratio, particularly at modest cathodic potentials where the confined hybrid interface is preserved. This work provides direct in situ evidence that organic-inorganic hybrid interfaces can regulate electrocatalytic selectivity through local electric-field engineering, offering design principles for field-enhanced CO2 electroreduction.

items.title: Gold-Catalyzed Chemoselective Dearomative Ring-Opening Modes of Indoles
items.abstract: Abstract A gold-catalyzed dearomative cyclization of indoles with ynone-nitriles assisted by a Lewis or a Brønsted acid has been developed, which provides an efficient route to 4-azafluorenones via an unexpected indole ring-opening process. The key strategy involves the attack of an iminyl intermediate to the indoleninium species at its highly electrophilic C2 position, with both intermediates being generated spontaneously during the dearomatization process. By varying the gold catalyst and acid additives, the 1+1 and 2+1 component reactions can be achieved selectively.

items.title: Redox Control of S -Sulfocysteine Formation in Adenosine Phosphosulfate Reductase
items.abstract: Abstract Sulfur assimilation fuels bacterial growth by supplying the reduced sulfur required for the biosynthesis of sulfur-containing biomolecules. Adenosine 5′-phosphosulfate reductase (APSR) catalyzes the reductive step of this pathway, converting adenosine 5′-phosphosulfate (APS) to adenosine monophosphate. This reaction proceeds through nucleophilic attack by catalytic C256, located in the flexible C-terminal tail, on the sulfur atom of APS, forming a thiosulfonate enzyme intermediate. Here, we investigate this reaction in APSR from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, an opportunistic pathogen associated with severe infections, particularly in patients with cystic fibrosis. APSR contains an iron–sulfur [4Fe–4S] cluster, which participates in redox steps of the reaction. Here, we show that the redox state of the iron–sulfur cluster also controls the catalytic step. Multiscale molecular simulations investigate how oxidized and reduced cluster states affect APS binding, active site organization, and the nucleophilic attack step. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations show that the oxidized [4Fe–4S]2+ cluster stabilizes substrate interactions and the conformation of the C-terminus, facilitating a catalytically productive orientation of C256. The activation barrier of 17.7 ± 1.7 kcal mol–1 from quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) umbrella sampling MD simulations at the B3LYP-D3(BJ)/6-31G(d) level is consistent with kinetics experiments performed on an ortholog enzyme. The redox state of the iron–sulfur cluster shows its role in modulating the conformation of conserved K144, which is important for transition state stabilization in the nucleophilic attack. These findings illuminate the mechanism of this P. aeruginosa target and provide broader insight into the roles of iron–sulfur clusters in controlling enzyme reactivity.

items.title: Dual Reaction Pathways on Ga2O3-ZnO/Cu for Efficient CO2-to-Methanol Conversion
items.abstract: Abstract The design of metal–support interfaces is critical for overcoming the persistent trade-off between CO2 conversion and methanol selectivity in CO2 hydrogenation. Though an inverse catalyst with an oxide-on-metal configuration provides a platform for tuning interfacial properties, the distinct roles of multi-interfaces with different electronic properties and how they collectively govern reaction pathways remain largely unexplored. Herein, we constructed an inverse Ga2O3-ZnO/Cu catalyst to engineer dual pathways for efficient CO2-to-methanol conversion. Comprehensive characterization reveals that Ga2O3 induces charge redistribution in the catalyst for more oxygen vacancies, which enhance CO2 adsorption. The Cu-ZnO interface facilitates the formation of key intermediates along the formate pathway. Meanwhile, Ga also introduces a RWGS + CO* hydrogenation pathway to preferentially convert CO2 to methanol. In addition, Ga2O3 loading-enabled smaller Cu nanoparticles further enhanced H2 dissociation and spillover on the surface. Consequently, the optimized Ga2O3-ZnO/Cu catalyst achieves a high space time yield of methanol (728.73 gCH3OH kgcat–1 h–1) with a high methanol selectivity of 82.37% at 220 °C and 3 MPa. This work provides insights into engineering reaction pathways for methanol synthesis via the rational design of synergistic active sites.

items.title:
Metal-Free Oxidized Carbon Nitride/
                    <scp>l</scp>
                    -Proline Synergistic Catalysis: Highly Enantioselective Direct Synthesis of C2-Quaternary Indolinones via Dearomative Oxyalkylation Cascades
items.abstract: Abstract Herein, we report a metal-free, cooperative oxidized graphitic carbon nitride/l-proline catalysis for enantioselective dearomative oxyalkylation of 2-arylindoles. The developed method leverages the band structure of g-C3N4 to efficiently generate singlet oxygen (1O2) under visible light and aerobic conditions, driving an oxidative dearomatization cascade. The resulting intermediates are intercepted via an l-proline-mediated Mannich addition, providing direct access to C2-quaternary indolin-3-ones in high yields (up to 88%) and with enantioselectivities (up to 99% ee). By integrating heterogeneous carbon nitride photocatalysis with asymmetric organocatalysis, this protocol offers a robust, recyclable alternative to traditional noble-metal catalysis for enantioselective synthesis of C2-quaternary indolin-3-ones.

items.title: Copper-Mediated Valence Tautomerism Enables α -C(sp3)–H Alkylation of 1,3-Dicarbonyl Compounds and Tryptophans via Photocatalysis
items.abstract: Abstract Carbonyl α-C(sp3)–H functionalization is a key approach to access functionalized pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and bioactive peptides. Conventional two-electron enol tautomerization strategies for this transformation often suffer from harsh reaction conditions and limited substrate tolerance. While valence tautomerism (VT) enables radical-type C–H activation, such reactivity has been exclusively realized with nickel catalysis, and copper-mediated VT remains unexplored for α-C(sp3)–H activation of carbonyls. Here, we present a dual photoredox/copper catalytic strategy that exploits copper-mediated VT to generate α-carbonyl alkyl radicals. These radicals undergo radical–radical cross-coupling with nucleophilic radicals generated by photocatalytic decarboxylation, delivering α-carbonyl alkylation products. The protocol features mild conditions and broad functional group tolerance, supporting peptide late-stage modification and gram-scale synthesis. Mechanistic studies and density functional theory (DFT) calculations validate a Cu(III)-mediated VT pathway for radical generation. This work establishes copper as a viable VT catalytic platform, expands the scope of dual photoredox/metal catalysis, and offers a versatile tool for biomolecular derivatization.

items.title: Nickel-Catalyzed Regiodivergent and Enantioselective Hydrosilylation of Internal Alkenes
items.abstract: Abstract Enantioselective hydrosilylation of alkenes represents a direct and economical route to chiral organosilanes. However, achieving good regio- and enantioselectivity from the same alkene for the divergent synthesis of chiral silanes remains a formidable challenge, particularly for internal alkenes. In this work, we present a ligand-controlled nickel-catalyzed regiodivergent and enantioselective hydrosilylation of 1,2-disubstituted alkenes. This approach provides a direct access to both α- and β-trifluoromethylsilanes with high regio- and enantioselectivity. The resulting enantioenriched silane products are amenable to various stereospecific transformations. Moreover, density functional theory (DFT) calculations elucidate the origin of the observed regio- and enantioselectivity.

items.title: Photoinduced Enantioselective α-Alkylation of Active Methines with Nonactivated Alkenes Using a Chiral Ytterbium Lewis Acid
items.abstract: Abstract Catalytic enantioselective alkylation is a fundamental strategy for constructing molecular frameworks bearing chiral carbon centers. Herein, we report a photoinduced highly enantioselective catalytic α-alkylation of active methine compounds with nonactivated alkenes to construct chiral quaternary stereocenters. Cooperative catalysis using an organophotocatalyst and a chiral ytterbium Lewis acid bearing an Indapybox ligand efficiently promotes the alkylation of open-chain 2-substituted β-ketoesters, affording the desired products in high yields with high enantioselectivities (up to 96% yield and 96% ee). The reaction exhibits a broad substrate scope with respect to both the alkene and β-ketoesters components. Furthermore, the resulting products can be readily transformed into optically active 5-pyrazolone and 5-isoxazolone derivatives while maintaining high optical purity.

items.title: Poly(Ionic Liquid)-Engineered Interfacial Water Reorganization for Selective Acidic CO2-to-Formic Acid Electroreduction
items.abstract: Abstract Acidic CO2 electroreduction offers a promising route to improve carbon utilization compared with alkaline or neutral systems. However, maintaining high product selectivity at industrially relevant current densities remains challenging because local CO2 depletion and excessive proton availability intensify the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). Herein, we develop a bismuth sulfide (Bi2S3) catalyst modified with a long-chain imidazolium poly(ionic liquid) layer (PIL@BS) for electrocatalytic CO2-to-formic acid conversion at pH 2. In a flow cell containing 3 M KCl, PIL@BS catalyst delivers a high Faradaic efficiency for formic acid (FEFA = 98.4%) at a current density exceeding 300 mA cm–2 and maintains over 80% FEFA after 120 h of continuous operation. Even at low 15 vol % CO2 concentration typical of industrial flue gas, PIL@BS retains higher FA selectivity than unmodified BS, underscoring the effectiveness of PIL in suppressing HER under CO2-limited conditions. Structural characterizations and electrochemical analyses reveal that the PIL backbone creates a hydrophobic interface while preserving CO2 affinity and high ionic conductivity, effectively mitigating the flooding issues and enhancing the local availability of CO2. Operando spectroscopies further show that PIL-regulated interface facilitates access to weakly hydrogen-bonded water. Such interfacial water reorganization disrupts the extended hydrogen-bond network, attenuating the continuous proton-relay pathways that promote the competing HER while maintaining localized proton transfer for CO2 reduction. Combined with theoretical calculations, these findings indicate that the PIL-modified microenvironment enables a direct and energetically favorable hydrogenation pathway toward FA formation. This work highlights the PIL-engineered interfacial microenvironment as a key factor for overriding the intrinsic selectivity of a catalyst and enabling practical CO2 valorization.

items.title: Spatially Decoupled Reaction-Diffusion Microenvironments in Mordenite Enable Highly Selective Methane-to-Methanol Conversion
items.abstract: Abstract The selective oxidation of methane to value-added oxygenates represents a formidable challenge in heterogeneous catalysis, fundamentally limited by the thermodynamic trade-off between activating the reactant and preventing the subsequent overoxidation of fragile products. This vulnerability is deeply tied to the spatial accessibility within the catalytic microenvironment; highly open channels, while facilitating mass transfer, indiscriminately expose the generated products to secondary oxidation. Herein, we develop a site-selective construction strategy to establish spatially decoupled reaction-diffusion microenvironments within mordenite (MOR). By utilizing pyridine as a pore-blocking agent to occupy 12-membered ring (12-MR) channels, we preferentially localize the active Cu species, identified as bent mono-μ-oxo dicopper cores, within the well-defined 8-membered ring (8-MR) side pockets. This architecture induces a profound dual spatial effect. At the reaction level, the 8-MR acts as a nanoscopic kinetic shield by providing a customized local topology that suppresses the reactivity of oxygenated intermediates while retaining sufficient methane activation capability. Crucially, at the mass-transfer level, Cu incorporation into the 12-MR main channels is largely suppressed, allowing these channels to serve as unobstructed diffusion pathways and reducing the probability that desorbed methanol recontacts oxidative Cu sites during outward transport. Furthermore, by eliminating the structural heterogeneity inherent to non-selective synthesis, this spatially defined microenvironment and homogeneous Cu coordination structure enable the elucidation of the intrinsic structure-performance relationship. Under continuous operating conditions, this spatially engineered catalyst exhibits high methanol selectivity and productivity, ranking among the leading Cu-MOR systems for methane-to-methanol conversion. These findings demonstrate that designing a decoupled reaction-diffusion microenvironment can regulate catalytic selectivity beyond electronic-structure modulation, while also offering a generalizable method for the site-selective placement of metal ions within zeolite.

items.title: SIFT-MS Enables Product-Specific Insight into Electrochemical Pulsed CO2 Reduction in Membrane Electrode Assemblies
items.abstract: Abstract Pulsed electrolysis is a promising operating strategy for electrochemical CO2 reduction, but understanding how products form, accumulate, and are released during dynamic operation remains challenging, particularly in membrane electrode assemblies (MEAs). Conventional product analysis methods provide limited time resolution, making them poorly suited for resolving product-specific changes during pulses that are on the timescale of seconds. Here, selected-ion-flow-tube mass spectrometry (SIFT-MS) was used as a quasi-real-time analytical technique to measure the product concentrations during pulsed CO2 electrolysis in a MEA using a copper oxide nanoparticle-derived cathode catalyst. Methodology development for the SIFT-MS technique established the sampling and pulsing criteria required for reliable semi-quantitative analysis of the concentration of reaction products. Applying these methodology developments to pulsed electrolysis experiments unveiled how molecular structure influences product retention within the electrode and subsequent transport into the MEA outlet stream under pulsed CO2R conditions. A comparison of the measured concentrations of ethanol, ethylene, and acetaldehyde provided evidence that the formation of ethanol occurs through multiple contributing reaction pathways. The analysis of the measured concentrations of acetaldehyde, propionaldehyde, and 1-propanol provided evidence for the sequential formation of products through which the formation of aldehydes precedes the formation of 1-propanol. Overall, this work establishes SIFT-MS as a product-specific, quasi-real-time analytical technique for probing pulsed CO2R in membrane electrode assemblies that can unveil crucial information to aid in the development of future MEA electrolyzers and operational strategies.

items.title: Liquid Gallium Nanoislands on Zeolite: A Dynamic Confinement Strategy to Break the Catalytic Trade-Off in Hydrodeoxygenation
items.abstract: Abstract Breaking the pervasive activity–selectivity–stability trade-off in catalytic hydrodeoxygenation (HDO) remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we report a bifunctional nanoisland catalyst (GaNPs-Pt/Beta) that overcomes this limitation by utilizing liquid gallium nanodroplets anchored on Beta zeolite as mobile nanoislands. These islands effectively restrict platinum single-atom migration and agglomeration. Concurrently, Brønsted acid sites provided by the zeolite sea facilitate the dehydration-etherification process. This synergy enables highly efficient transfer hydrogenation at the gallium–platinum interface, achieving selective C–O bond cleavage while preserving C═C bonds under mild conditions. Benefiting from this island-sea architecture, the GaNPs-Pt/Beta catalyst delivers high catalytic activity, achieving &gt;99% cinnamyl alcohol conversion and 93.8% β-methylstyrene selectivity within 6 h at 160 °C, with recyclability demonstrated over nine cycles involving intercycle regeneration. This strategy is scalable to diverse α,β-unsaturated aldehyde/alcohol chemicals, demonstrating that zeolite-based liquid metal nanoislands provide a versatile platform for the sustainable synthesis of high-value chemicals.

items.title: Adsorbate Site Hopping—More Facts and Fiction: Driving Forces and Relevance for Heterogeneous Catalysis
items.abstract: Abstract Adsorbate site hopping, defined here as surface-confined migration of adsorbed species or adsorbate equivalents between distinct sites, is a widespread phenomenon in heterogeneous catalysis and includes spillover between different surface phases. Because it enables communication between spatially separated functionalities, site hopping has often been viewed as a route to bifunctional catalytic synergy and, in some cases, to performance beyond constraints imposed by Brønsted–Evans–Polanyi relationships. However, its catalytic value is conditional rather than universal.
