This topology-programmed assembly converts dynamic peptide fibers into a structurally stabilized supramolecular interface, leading to prolonged tumor retention and sustained local immune checkpoint blockade. Meanwhile, ultrasound-activated SeAD induces immunogenic cell death and systemic antitumor immunity. By coupling confinement-stabilized peptide recognition with sonodynamic immune activation, EHSeAD@MS achieves durable local tumor intervention, immune microenvironment remodeling, and suppression of distant and metastatic lesions. It establishes a molecular design principle for balancing structural integrity and adaptive recognition in peptide supramolecules, providing a strategy for long-lasting peptide-based cancer immunotherapy.

items.title:
Direct Imaging of
Energy Dissipation in Surface Acoustic
Waves
items.abstract: Abstract Unraveling the spatial distribution and energy dissipation of high-frequency surface acoustic waves (SAWs) is essential for advancing nanoacoustic architectures and probing low-dimensional wave–matter interactions. However, visualizing these dynamics at the subwavelength scale remains challenging due to the optical diffraction limit and severe topographic artifacts, such as surface defects and roughness, in scanning probe measurements. Here, we establish scanning thermal microscopy (SThM) as a robust metrological paradigm to map nanoscale energy dissipation and resolve complex acoustic wavefields through their localized thermal signatures. Leveraging this platform, we demonstrate how microgeometries sculpt the acoustic energy landscape and enable quantitative extraction of wave scattering parameters. Furthermore, by interrogating the h-BN/LiNbO3 van der Waals (vdW) interface, we capture localized temperature signatures of interfacial energy exchange. We observe anomalous nonlinear thermal scaling at the 2D heterointerface, consistent with the intrinsic nonlinear damping of the 2D heterostructure. This work highlights the capability of SThM to probe acoustic energy dissipation, establishing a diagnostic framework for subwavelength acoustic wavefields and heterogeneously integrated devices.

items.title:
Temporal Dosing
Tunes Glutathione Gradient across
Liver-Blood-Tumor Axes to Boost the Chemotherapeutic Potency of Prodrug
Nanoassemblies
items.abstract: Abstract Redox-responsive prodrug nanodelivery systems hold immense promise in cancer therapy, offering advantages of improved pharmacokinetics, enhanced tumor selectivity, and increased safety. However, compared with standard therapeutic formulations, prodrug nanodelivery systems fail to yield superior antitumor efficacy at equivalent doses, attributable to inadequate drug activation and intratumoral accumulation. Herein, the three-in-one drug-release module, comprising an α-disulfide bond, an ethylene glycol moiety, and a short carbon chain, was covalently linked to paclitaxel (PTX) to construct three prodrug nanoassemblies (PSBA10 NPs, PSBA12 NPs, PSBA14 NPs). Notably, PSBA10 NPs, which possessed the shortest carbon chain, exhibited hypersensitive redox-responsive drug release and potentiated antitumor efficacy. Although PSBA10 NPs exhibited better safety than paclitaxel solution (Taxol) at equivalent doses, superior efficacy remained unattainable. Interestingly, a temporal-dose-regulated glutathione (GSH) gradient across the liver-blood-tumor axis increased the intratumoral accumulation of PSBA10 NPs by approximately 3-fold, resulting in pronounced antitumor efficacy superior to Taxol. This transient depletion of GSH in the liver and blood reduced the cleavage of disulfide bonds in the systemic circulation, enhancing tumor accumulation and selective activation of PSBA10 NPs. Our study highlighted a tumor treatment model based on the synergistic strategy of structural optimization and GSH gradient regulation across the liver-blood-tumor axis to boost the efficacy of chemotherapy.

items.title: Sulfur-Induced Local Structure Reconstruction and Weak Na–Anion Interactions Enable Fast Na+ Transport in x Na2S-TaCl5 Electrolytes
items.abstract: Abstract Amorphous solid electrolytes offer opportunities for fast ion transport, yet the structural origins governing their performance remain difficult to resolve due to the absence of long-range order. While mixed-anion strategies have recently emerged to improve ion transport in sodium halide electrolytes, how sulfur incorporation modifies the local structure and Na+ transport remains poorly understood. Here, we develop a series of xNa2S-TaCl5 mixed anion solid electrolytes to elucidate the impact of sulfur on the structure and Na+ transport. Structural analyses reveal that sulfur incorporation reconstructs the connectivity of Ta-centered polyhedra while progressively disrupting the long-range crystalline ordering to form an amorphous framework. More importantly, neutron pair distribution function analysis reveals the sulfur-induced reconstruction of the local Ta-centered structure, with the emergence of coexisting edge-sharing- and corner-sharing-like motifs from the isolated polyhedra in crystalline NaTaCl6. Simulations further show that sulfur shifts the local polyhedral connectivity toward a larger proportion of edge-sharing configurations relative to the O-containing analogue. Matched-composition machine-learning molecular dynamics (MLMD) comparing O- and S-containing amorphous models suggest that sulfur weakens Na-anion binding, shortens Na–anion residence times, and lowers the barrier for Na+ migration relative to the O analogue. As a result, the optimized composition achieves a high room-temperature ionic conductivity of 3.25 mS cm–1 with a low activation energy of 0.28 eV. When evaluated in all-solid-state sodium batteries with an uncoated NaNi1/3Mn1/3Fe1/3O2 cathode, the cell delivers a discharge capacity of 112 mAh g–1 after 100 cycles (82.6% retention) with a high average Coulombic efficiency of 99.8%, demonstrating stable interfacial compatibility with uncoated layered oxide cathodes.

items.title: Issue Publication Information
Issue Editorial Masthead

Automated Perovskite
Film Fabrication with High-Resolution
Data Acquisition and Machine Learning Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Lead halide perovskite solar cells have emerged as promising candidates for next-generation photovoltaics; nevertheless, fabrication of the perovskite photoactive layer remains highly intricate with film formation strongly modulated by various processing and environmental factors. Here, we report an environment-controlled, robot-assisted platform for automated thin-film fabrication designed to quantify and visualize perovskite crystallization in situ. Beyond precise control of each processing step, the system captures dynamic phenomena spanning subsecond color evolution and millisecond antisolvent droplet behavior while simultaneously recording slower environmental parameters (temperature, humidity/moisture, and concentrations of oxygen and volatile organic compounds). For optoelectronic assessment, we implemented time-resolved microwave conductivity (TRMC) measurements together with photoluminescence intensity quantification by using a complementary automated evaluation system. By combining machine-learning regression with SHAP (Shapley additive explanations) analysis, we identify the environmental parameters that most impact film properties and propose a feedback strategy to refine data and extract precise effects of process factors. A comparative study of a two-cation perovskite, (FAPbI3)0.87(MAPbBr3)0.13, and a three-cation perovskite, FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3, further reveals markedly different sensitivities to environmental factors (FA, formamidinium; MA, methylammonium), in particular, temperature and resultant phase transition kinetics during thermal annealing. Based on the ML analysis and feedback, we tuned the antisolvent droplet velocity and obtained the maximized power conversion efficiency of 24.4%. Notably, this manual device fabrication was consistent with the results obtained by the automated system. This work establishes a practical route to stable, quantitative, and mechanistically informed investigation of solution-processed photovoltaic films.

items.title:
Facile
Polyiodides Conversion Enabled by Facet Engineering
for Durable Zinc–Iodine Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Aqueous zinc–iodine (Zn–I2) batteries are highly promising for grid-scale energy storage, yet their practical viability is severely plagued by the polyiodides shuttle effect and sluggish liquid–solid conversion kinetics, which fundamentally arise from the contradictory energetic demands between soluble intermediate confinement and solid-product desorption. Herein, we rationally construct a dual-facet spinel cobalt oxide to precisely decouple these competing interfacial behaviors. By regulating the proportional exposure of strongly coordinating (100) and weakly coordinating (111) facets, a tailored surface microenvironment is constructed that effectively circumvents the inherent thermodynamic trade-off, breaking the single adsorption limitation intrinsic to uniform catalysts. In situ iodine L3-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy and three-dimensional synchrotron-based nanocomputed tomography reveal that this specific facet modulation substantially reduces the activation barrier for rate-determining polyiodides oxidation, facilitating spatially uniform solid-iodine deposition. Driven by these structural advantages, the assembled Zn–I2 batteries with c/o-Co3O4 deliver a high specific capacity of 161.1 mAh g–1 at 16 A g–1 and an ultralow capacity decay rate of 0.00055% per cycle after 50,000 cycles at 10 A g–1. Furthermore, the batteries also exhibit a broad operational temperature ranging from −30 to 60 °C, highlighting the strong potential for practical applications. This work provides a perspective on facet engineering for achieving wide-temperature-tolerant aqueous iodine storage.

items.title:
Band-like
Transport with Hall Mobility &gt;70 cm2 V–1 s–1 in Stoichiometric
Perovskite Crystals via Ion Confinement and Strain Relaxation
items.abstract: Abstract Despite substantial progress in optoelectronic applications, lead–halide perovskites remain underperforming in field-effect transistors (FETs) due to multiphase instability, ion migration, and grain boundary scattering. Here, a dual-ion co-incorporation strategy was applied to CsxFA1–xPbI3–yBry single crystals. By systematically mapping a phase stability diagram, we pinpoint an optimal stoichiometry of Cs0.1FA0.9PbI2.7Br0.3 that integrates phase stability engineering with atomic-level ion confinement. Structural analysis reveals that 10% Cs+/Br– co-incorporation induces strain-relaxed lattice contraction (−1.23% along the a-axis relative to FAPbI3) and reinforces Pb–I bonds via octahedral distortion. This yields superior crystallinity (FWHM = 0.04°) and reduced I– migration, thereby enabling the investigation of FET and gated Hall effect carrier mobilities as functions of temperature. Consequently, champion two-terminal FET devices exhibit an electron mobility of 25.1 cm2 V–1 s–1 at room temperature, which increases to 126 cm2 V–1 s–1 at 120 K. Furthermore, high-resolution four-terminal measurements on a single crystal quantify and correct for contact-resistance effects, validating the relationship: Hall mobility (μHall) &gt; linear regime mobility (μlin) &gt; saturation regime mobility (μsat) with values of 89, 79.2, and 71.6 cm2 V–1 s–1, respectively. These findings collectively elucidate intrinsic band-like electron transport behavior in lead–halide perovskite single crystals, distinguishing it from hopping transport in organic semiconductors. By achieving a defect-minimized lattice, this compositional engineering paradigm overcomes the mobility bottleneck in perovskite FETs, facilitating the transition from photoelectronic applications to FET integration.

items.title:
Copper-Catalyzed
Covalent Nanostructure Synthesis
on Atomically Flat Highly Oriented Pyrolytic Graphite (HOPG)
items.abstract: Abstract On-surface Ullmann-type coupling has been widely employed for constructing atomically precise carbon-based nanostructures, yet its implementation remains largely restricted to metal substrates, where strong molecule–substrate interactions perturb intrinsic electronic properties and hinder further device integration. Extending on-surface reaction to chemically inert surfaces such as highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) is fundamentally challenged by the competition between reaction activation and molecule desorption under ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) conditions. Here, we demonstrate classical Ullmann coupling on HOPG catalyzed by exogenous copper (Cu) atoms. Two brominated precursors, 2,4,6-tris(4-bromophenyl)-1,3,5-triazine (pTBPT) and 5,10,15,20-tetra(4-bromophenyl) porphine (TBrPP), are employed to investigate how exogenous Cu regulates the critical competition between molecular desorption and reaction activation. For pTBPT, scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) reveals the formation of uniform and well-ordered oligomeric structures at 350 °C, whereas in the absence of Cu, molecules desorb without reaction. Synchrotron radiation X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (SR-XPS) and density functional theory (DFT) calculations further indicate that Cu atoms simultaneously promote molecular anchoring and reduce the activation barrier for dehalogenative coupling. As a complementary system, STM and XPS analysis of TBrPP reveals a critical competition between molecular desorption and dehalogenative coupling. While HR-XPS reveals in situ metalation at room temperature, STM imaging confirms that complete molecular desorption occurs at 200 °C, preventing subsequent dehalogenative coupling. These findings provide mechanistic insights into how transition metal mediates the interplay between surface reaction and desorption, while offering a strategy for the fabrication of structurally defined covalent nanostructures on electronically decoupled platforms.

items.title:
A Hyaluronic Acid-Stabilized
Zinc-Loaded Probiotic
Mitigates Nanoplastic Toxicity across the Microbiota–Gut–Brain
Axis
items.abstract: Abstract Nanoplastics are emerging stressors that perturb host physiology across the gut–immune–brain continuum, yet scalable interventions remain limited. Here, we engineer ZG@EcN@HA, a biohybrid living system created by vacuum-assisted intracellular loading of zinc gluconate into Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN) followed by an outer hyaluronic acid (HA) shell. This architecture preserves probiotic culturability under gastric challenge and supports sustained zinc availability in intestinal conditions. In zebrafish chronically exposed to polystyrene nanoplastics, we observe reproducible neurobehavioral impairment coupled with inflammatory activation, redox imbalance, barrier stress, neurotransmitter dysregulation, and multiorgan histopathology. ZG@EcN@HA yields the most coherent rescue compared with single-component controls, restoring behavioral outputs and realigning immune–redox–neurochemical readouts. ASV-based profiling shows recovery of microbial diversity and a shift toward a control-like community structure, including reduced dominance of inflammation-linked taxa. Intestinal transcriptomics and integrative correlation analyses further support normalization of barrier/metabolic programs and attenuation of innate inflammatory signaling. Together, the data identify a materials-enabled strategy for microbiota–gut–brain protection against chronic nanoplastic stress.

items.title:
Dopant Engineered
Y-Doped Hafnia-Zirconia Nanolaminates
with 0.26 nm Equivalent Oxide Thickness for Dynamic Random Access
Memory Capacitors
items.abstract: Abstract Y-doped Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 demonstrated feasible field-induced ferroelectric properties for capacitor dielectrics in dynamic random access memory (DRAM) by stepwise cycling, which enabled low-voltage charge boosting. However, practical implementation remains limited by high cycling stress and leakage current density (J) degradation. This study reported a Y-doped ZrO2/HfO2/ZrO2 nanolaminate with middle-inserted and top-inserted Y2O3 layers, enabling low-voltage charge boosting with substantially decreased stepwise cycling stress. This effect arose from a more uniform distribution of oxygen-vacancy-dopant complexes, thereby decreasing the energy barrier for the tetragonal-to-polar orthorhombic phase transition. The middle-inserted Y2O3 layer underwent substitutional diffusion, stabilized the tetragonal phase and suppressed J by acceptor doping. In contrast, the top-inserted Y2O3 layer displayed limited bulk diffusion, resulting in minimal lattice strain and phase change, but further suppressed J. Consequently, a 5.2 nm-thick film achieved an ultralow equivalent oxide thickness of ∼0.26 nm while satisfying the DRAM J criterion (J &lt; 10–7 A cm–2 at ±0.8 V), outperforming all previously reported DRAM dielectrics.

items.title:
Oxygen-Promoted
Dehydrogenation on Size-Selected Cu–Pd
Pentamer Clusters for Low-Temperature Hydrogen Release from Cyclic
Hydrocarbons
items.abstract: Abstract Despite extensive studies on cycloalkane and cycloalkene dehydrogenation for liquid organic hydrogen carrier applications, the mechanisms governing selective H2 release under mild conditions remain poorly understood. Here, subnanometer CuxPdy pentamer clusters supported on ZrO2 represent a highly active and selective class of low-temperature dehydrogenation catalysts. Pd5 exhibits the highest benzene and molecular H2 formation rates from dehydrogenation of cyclohexene, followed by Cu2Pd3 and Cu3Pd2, whereas Cu5 is inactive. All active catalysts favored H2 over H2O as the hydrogen-containing product and completely suppressed combustion pathways, with no detectable CO2 formation. Oxygen-lean conditions further favored H2 formation across all active catalysts, with H2 selectivity exceeding 99% for Pd5. Kinetic analysis of Cu3Pd2 reveals positive fractional apparent orders in both C6H10 and O2 and an effective apparent activation energy of approximately 66 kJ·mol–1, while reactant composition and temperature systematically control H2/H2O branching. In situ XPS and in situ GIWAXS reveal that catalytic activity and cluster stability arise from the interplay of atomic composition, electronic structure, metal–oxygen interactions, and the chemical environment, with Cu exhibiting a composition-sensitive redox response and Pd-containing clusters accommodating oxygen while retaining electronically active Pd-derived states near the Fermi level. DFT/MLIP free-energy calculations identify kinetically accessible O-assisted first C–H activation pathways involving H transfer to cluster-bound O, with barriers strongly dependent on cluster composition and O configuration. These findings establish an ensemble-based structure–activity framework for controlling dehydrogenation pathways and provide design principles for catalysts that efficiently promote selective hydrogen release suitable for hydrogen carrier applications.

items.title:
When Transition
Metal Dichalcogenides Twist: Opportunities
for Spintronics and Quantum Technologies
items.abstract: Abstract Moiré superlattices form quantum-active interfaces in which geometric reconstruction of stacked two-dimensional (2D) materials generates emergent quantum phases that are not present in the parent materials. These engineered interfaces give rise to a wide range of quantum phenomena, including strongly correlated electronic states, flat-band formation, topological phases of matter, and spin–valley locking, all of which can be tuned in situ through the twist angle. Twisted hetero/homostructures of 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) exhibit an unprecedented degree of control over electronic and spin degrees of freedom, driving rapid advances in the emerging field of twistronics and opening pathways toward next-generation spintronic device applications. In this Review, we examine the fundamental concepts, applications, and prospects of twisted 2D TMDs. We outline the evolution from three-dimensional (3D) to 2D materials and the concept of twistronics, then highlight the emergent structural and magnetic properties of twisted 2D TMDs and their heterostructures. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and future directions toward applications in spintronic and quantum technologies.

items.title:
Centrosymmetry Breaking
of Cobalt–Vanadium-Layered
Double Hydroxide Nanosheets via Nitrogen Doping for Enhanced Piezocatalytic
Tumor Therapy
items.abstract: Abstract Piezocatalysis has emerged as a promising tumor therapeutic strategy because it enables oxygen-independent generation of multiple reactive oxygen species (ROS) with deep tissue penetration. However, the piezocatalytic efficiency of piezoelectric nanomaterials remains constrained by limited lattice distortion, low carrier separation efficiency, and insufficient catalytic active sites. Herein, we report the centrosymmetry breaking of cobalt–vanadium-layered double hydroxide (CoV-LDH) nanosheets via nitrogen doping for efficient ultrasound (US)-mediated piezocatalytic tumor therapy. Owing to the nitrogen doping-induced disruption of the centrosymmetric structure and lattice distortion in CoV-LDH, nitrogen-doped CoV-LDH (N-CoV-LDH) achieves an ultrahigh piezoelectric coefficient of 89.4 pm·V–1, which is superior to that of previously reported piezocatalytic nanomaterials. Moreover, nitrogen doping introduces an unsaturated coordination environment, significantly promoting the adsorption and activation of O2 (Eads = −2.63 eV) and H2O (Eads = −2.37 eV), thereby enhancing piezocatalytic redox reaction kinetics (k &gt; 1.1 × 103 min–1·g–1). Consequently, under low-power US stimulation (0.15 W·cm–2), N-CoV-LDH nanosheets exhibit markedly enhanced ROS generation efficiency, including that of hydroxyl radicals (·OH), superoxide anions (·O2–), and singlet oxygen (1O2). This robust piezocatalytic ROS generation induces tumor cell apoptosis and immunogenic cell death, thereby activating an antitumor immune response characterized by dendritic cell maturation, M1 macrophage polarization, and T cell activation. Ultimately, N-CoV-LDH-mediated piezocatalytic therapy achieves suppression rates of 97.78% for primary tumors and 87.67% for metastatic tumors, establishing an efficient therapeutic paradigm for suppressing tumor metastasis and recurrence.

items.title:
Ion
Transport Enhancement
in Charge-Regulating Hydrogels
items.abstract: Abstract Weak polyelectrolyte hydrogels are emerging as a versatile platform for ion transport and separation, desalination, and energy applications. However, a predictive understanding of how dynamic charge regulation at the nanoscopic scale influences ionic mobility in these polymer networks remains elusive. Here, using large-scale molecular simulations, we dissect the coupled mechanisms governing small-ion transport in weak polyelectrolyte hydrogels, and reveal how charge density, competitive binding, and dynamic charge regulation jointly control ion mobility. By systematically isolating these effects, we uncover a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence of ion self-diffusion on hydrogel pKa and salt concentration for multivalent ions. Strikingly, allowing the hydrogel backbone to dynamically regulate its charge eliminates this nonmonotonicity and leads to dramatic enhancements in ion mobility, with diffusion coefficients increasing by more than a factor of 2 for trivalent ions. We attribute this effect to a protonation-assisted hopping mechanism that continuously remodels the local electrostatic landscape, providing an additional molecular-scale pathway for ion unbinding beyond translational escape and accelerating ion-pair kinetics without affecting the fraction of free ions. Our results demonstrate that dynamic nanoscale charge regulation can decouple ion mobility from equilibrium binding strength, offering a powerful design lever unavailable in fixed-charge materials. Building upon these insights, we propose simple molecular design principles for next-generation ion-conducting hydrogels and suggest alternative strategies for nanostructured membranes, energy materials, and biologically inspired charge-adaptive soft matter.

items.title:
Chirality-Functionalized
Covalent Organic Frameworks
for Enantioselective Neuroprotection with Restored Neuroactive Signaling
in Alzheimer’s Disease
items.abstract: Abstract Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is driven by amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation and a cascade of interconnected neurotoxic events, including oxidative stress, glutamate excitotoxicity, calcium dysregulation, and impaired neuroactive ligand–receptor signaling. To address the multifactorial nature of AD pathology, chiral d- or l-cysteine-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF) nanoparticles are developed as a multitarget nanotherapeutic platform. Both enantiomers effectively inhibit Aβ aggregation, scavenge reactive oxygen species, reduce extracellular glutamate levels, and attenuate calcium dysregulation. In parallel, d/l-Cys-COFs rescue compromised neuroactive ligand–receptor signaling, as evidenced by normalized expression of neuropeptide Y and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. In transgenic AD mice, d/l-Cys-COF treatment significantly improves memory and cognitive performance. Notably, the d-enantiomer affords superior neuroprotection through enhanced suppression of pathological intracellular calcium overload, whereas restoration of neuroactive ligand–receptor signaling remains chirality-independent. These findings identify chirality as a key design element for multitarget nanotherapeutics against AD, with enantioselective efficacy arising primarily from differential regulation of calcium dysregulation and shared restoration of neuroactive signaling contributing to the overall therapeutic benefit.

items.title:
Ultrasensitive
Enantioselective Chiroptical Sensing
with Large-Area Twisted Aligned Carbon Nanotube Films
items.abstract: Abstract Enantioselective chiroptical sensing is gaining traction across various applications. However, intrinsic molecular chiroptical responses are weak, and existing amplification approaches add synthesis, manufacturing, or operational complexity that limits sensitivity and scalability. Here, we present an enantioselective sensing paradigm merging adsorption-driven chirality induction with large-scale optical transduction in twisted stacks of aligned carbon nanotube (CNT) films. Chiral molecules adsorb onto CNTs to form chiroptically active composites that are macroscopically assembled by alignment and rotational stacking, yielding large ultraviolet circular dichroism (CD). We resolve enantiomer handedness and quantify concentration in single-enantiomer aqueous solutions using a single sensor without lithography, hotspot delivery, or a paired opposite-handed reference. We achieve high sensitivity with estimated sub-μM minimum detectable concentrations for glucose and provide a proof-of-concept demonstration with alanine. Neither analyte-only solution shows detectable CD under the present measurement conditions. We demonstrate Langmuir-type adsorption behavior using molecular dynamics simulations and reproduce experimental results using optical simulations. This platform provides a foundation for future development toward cost-effective in situ enantiomer monitoring in aqueous environments.

items.title:
Strain-Engineered
Deterministic Quantum Dots for Telecom
O-Band Emission Using Buried Stressors
items.abstract: Abstract The deterministic realization of quantum light sources operating at telecom wavelengths is essential for long-distance fiber-based quantum communication and distributed quantum computing. In this work, we demonstrate that telecom O-band emission can be achieved from site-controlled InGaAs/GaAs quantum dots (QDs). Our concept utilizes a buried AlAs/AlOx stressor layer with the unique feature of inducing a well-defined and controllable tensile strain field at the growth surface, enabling both site-selective nucleation at the mesa’s centers and a redshift of QD emission to the ∼1.3 μm wavelength range. This concept not only eliminates the need for strain-reducing layers (SRLs), which are known to degrade optical coherence, but also provides spatial control and spectral tunability. The grown telecom QDs show single-photon emission with g(2)(0) = (5.0 ± 1.0) × 10–2 at 4 K and (2.8 ± 0.3) × 10–1 at 77 K, demonstrating the quantum nature and thermal stability of the emitters. The emission characteristics of complex excitonic states are analyzed using 8-band k·p and configuration-interaction modeling, which quantitatively reproduces the experimental observations. Finally, we present a theory-supported strategy to further redshift the emission toward the center of the O-band and beyond by employing a multiburied stressor approach. This combined framework of experiment and theory establishes the buried stressor concept as a scalable route toward highly coherent, position-controlled O-band quantum emitters compatible with scalable photonic integration.

items.title: Au Nanoparticle-Functionalized Antheraea pernyi Silk Nanofibrils: A Spatially Adaptive Anti-Inflammatory and Pro-Regenerative Paradigm for Disparate Chronic Epithelial Diseases
items.abstract: Abstract Management of disparate chronic epithelial diseases relies on fragmented site-specific protocols yet remains hindered by common pathological barriers and sustained inflammation. Herein, we developed a top-down strategy to exfoliate short nanofibrils from Antheraea pernyi silk fibers featuring inherent Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) motifs, followed by in situ growth of Au nanoparticles. The resulting platform (Au@ASFs) achieved superior spatial adaptability via catalytic oxygen propulsion, navigating across barriers to reach deep-seated lesions. Once localized, Au@ASFs provided phase-spanning multifunctional therapy through near-infrared (NIR)-triggered photothermal sterilization. Through RGD–integrin interactions, they also promoted hemostasis and M2 macrophage polarization to resolve persistent inflammation while enhancing fibroblast migration, angiogenesis, and neuronal differentiation. In vivo, Au@ASFs (+NIR) significantly improved closure of infected diabetic oral ulcers from 43.1 to 95.5% by day 7 and restored colon length in ulcerative colitis from 66.3 to 97.7% of healthy controls. In infected diabetic wounds, Au@ASFs (+NIR) increased closure from 63.8 to 89.1% by day 14. Transcriptomic analysis of wound tissues revealed reprogramming through suppressed NF-κB inflammatory signaling, activated Wnt5a/GSK-3β signaling for neuronal differentiation, and modulated PI3K-Akt signaling for tissue regeneration. Collectively, Au@ASF (+NIR) consistently resolves chronic epithelial diseases across disparate anatomical sites, establishing a unified drug-free paradigm that transcends site-specific constraints.

items.title:
Emergent
Higher-Order Optical Nonlinearity in Self-Assembled
Polar Supertextures
items.abstract: Abstract Giant optical nonlinearities enable advanced materials control and bridge exotic light-matter phenomena to next-generation photonics. However, materials exhibiting strong higher-order optical nonlinearity beyond the second order are typically rare. Here, we report the discovery of a giant and ultrafast second-harmonic generation (SHG) in self-assembled polar skyrmions under mid-infrared excitations. The transient SHG intensity exhibits a distinctive power dependence originating from higher-order nonlinearity. More generally, we show that large higher-order nonlinearity emerges across diverse domain structures in polar superlattices. Phase-field simulations demonstrate a strong and periodic local permittivity variation within each polar texture at equilibrium, and further confirm the fast polarization oscillation in polar skyrmions with mid-infrared excitations. This intense local permittivity modulation can satisfy epsilon-near-zero conditions, unlocking dramatically enhanced nonlinear optical responses without photonic engineering. Consequently, the self-assembled polar topologies with strong inherent optical nonlinearity could establish a platform for quantum information processing and high-speed optical communications.

items.title:
Synergistic Tuning
of Diffusion Enables Surface-Passivation-Directed
Electrodeposition of Shaped Bimetallic Nanoparticles
items.abstract: Abstract Many applications for shape-controlled metal nanoparticles require their immobilization on a surface, creating a need for development of direct substrate-based synthesis routes for increasingly complex materials. Colloidal chemical syntheses for shape-controlled nanoparticles are common, but transferring insight from synthesis in solution to growth on a substrate requires accounting for significant differences in reagent diffusion between these two growth environments─a nontrivial challenge. In the present work, we establish fundamental principles for rationally adapting reaction parameters from colloidal syntheses to electrodeposition such that the growth of nanoparticles on the electrode proceeds under comparable reagent diffusion conditions to those that drive shape direction during colloidal growth. To demonstrate these principles, we successfully translate reaction conditions from colloidal synthesis to electrodeposition for a series of dilute bimetallic (silver) gold nanoparticles whose shapes are controlled by surface deposition of silver: concave cubes, octahedra, rhombic dodecahedra, truncated ditetragonal prisms, and tetrahexahedra. By comparing open-circuit potential measurements of the colloidal syntheses with chronopotentiometry measurements from galvanostatic electrodeposition, we determine the adjustments required to establish ideal growth kinetics for each electrodeposition. We identify specific synthetic handles─mode of mass transport, surfactant concentration, applied current density, and secondary metal concentration─required to modulate reagent transport to the electrode surface, as well as the direction they must be modified so that the relative rates of silver and gold ion reduction mimic colloidal growth. These generalizable synthetic parameters for controlling reagent diffusion and concentrations near the electrode surface open possibilities for the electrodeposition of complex multimetallic and shaped nanomaterials.

items.title:
Phase Homogenization
via Decoupled Nucleation and
Growth for High-Efficiency Quasi-Two-Dimensional Perovskite Light-Emitting
Diodes
items.abstract: Abstract Quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) perovskites with multiquantum-well structures hold great potential for light-emitting diodes (LEDs) due to their cascaded energy funnels, yet their performance is hampered by defect-rich low-n phases and disordered crystallization. Here, we present a phase-homogenization strategy that combines a self-adaptive solvent by doping ethyl acetate (EA) with dimethyl phosphonate (DPP), which simultaneously modulates the polarity and evaporation kinetics of EA, guiding the crystal growth and phase distribution of quasi-2D perovskites. The strong coordination of DPP with Pb2+ also passivates deep-level traps, thereby drastically reducing nonradiative low-n-phase recombination. We further use the bridging molecules to enhance perovskite/transport layer interfaces by incorporating sodium 4-amino-1-naphthalenesulfonate tetrahydrate (SANT) into the PEDOT/PSS hole transport layer, which weakens PEDOT–PSS electrostatic attraction, enhancing conductivity while reducing acid-induced corrosion of the ITO electrode and perovskite film. SANT also templates perovskite nucleation via its functional groups, promoting ordered crystallite growth. Overall, the resulting green-emitting quasi-2D perovskite LEDs achieve a peak external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 32.81% (average 30.74%) and a luminance of 44338 cd m–2, with a lower surface temperature during operation. Moreover, the devices exhibit a 10-fold enhancement in operational stability compared to the control counterparts. Our findings provide a strategy for combining crystallization control and interface passivation in quasi-2D PeLEDs.

items.title:
Mechanics-Guided
Conformal Probes Enable Crystallographically
Resolved Anisotropic Interlayer Friction Measurements in Low-Symmetry
2D Materials
items.abstract: Abstract Interlayer sliding in two-dimensional (2D) materials is generally assumed to be weakly anisotropic, even as low-symmetry layered crystals with strongly direction-dependent properties continue to emerge. Here we adopt a mechanics-guided conformal probe design that enables quantitative measurement of crystallographically resolved interlayer friction between anisotropic 2D materials. Using Ta2NiSe5 as a model system, we demonstrate pronounced interlayer friction anisotropy approaching 2 orders of magnitude, substantially larger than its moderate in-plane friction anisotropy and the values reported for high-symmetry layered materials. Atomic-resolution lateral force mapping reveals a hierarchical friction landscape composed of atomic lattice corrugation and twist-induced moiré modulation, with the moiré wavelength evolving systematically with relative misorientation. These results show that interlayer friction in low-symmetry 2D materials is governed by a multiscale, orientation-dependent potential energy landscape and constitutes an independent mechanical degree of freedom. The conformal probe platform provides a general route to probe and engineer direction-selective interlayer mechanics in van der Waals systems.

items.title:
Subshell-Confined
Symmetry Lowering and Prolonged
Excited-State Dynamics in Large Silver Nanoclusters
items.abstract: Abstract Symmetry breaking has the potential to counteract the shortening of excited-state lifetimes with increasing nuclearity and metallicity but is difficult to accomplish in large nanoclusters, whose multishell frameworks are strongly coupled. Here, we report a four-shell silver nanocluster, Ag104, in which the principal reconstruction is concentrated in an Ag52S22 subsurface shell, and whose inner core and outer ligand-protected motifs retain closely similar topologies relative to its highly symmetric Ag100 analogue – a structurally related pair that enables the correlations accompanying localized symmetry distortion to be examined. The two clusters also differ in composition and thiolate substitution pattern, so the comparison probes coupled structural and electronic changes. Electronic-structure calculations and real-space charge analyses showed that subshell-confined symmetry breaking lifts electronic degeneracies, redistributes oscillator strength, and induces pronounced spatial charge separation, thereby reducing electron–hole overlap. Ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy further revealed an unexpected order-of-magnitude increase in carrier lifetime from ∼500 ps in Ag100 to ∼5 ns in Ag104 and distinctly activated phonon-assisted relaxation in Ag100 compared to Ag104. This establishes a strategy for engineering large atomically precise nanoclusters with long-lived excited states.

items.title:
Watching Electrochemical
Interfaces in Motion with
High-Speed Atomic Force Microscopy
items.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical processes involve transient phenomena, including nucleation and growth, phase transformations, dissolution, ion transport, and interfacial restructuring, which are difficult to capture simultaneously at nanoscale and in real time under electrochemical controls. High-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM), originally developed for dynamic biological imaging, combines nanometer-scale spatial resolution with frame times of approximately 0.1–5 s/frame, extending into the subsecond regime, enabling direct visualization of electrochemical interfaces under operando conditions. This perspective highlights emerging applications of HS-AFM in electrochemistry, including electrodeposition, nanoparticle dissolution, corrosion, lithiation-induced morphological evolution, protein adsorption, and nanobubble dynamics. HS-AFM reveals that mechanistic insight often resides in transient, nonequilibrium pathways rather than equilibrium structures alone. Advances will enable real-time nanoscale correlation of interfacial structure, kinetics, and electrochemical function.

items.title:
Disulfidptosis-Driven
Immune-Activated Multimodal
Therapy for Glioblastoma with Systemic Safety Control
items.abstract: Abstract Effective glioblastoma therapy requires simultaneous solutions to poor blood–brain barrier (BBB) penetration, insufficient tumor-selective killing, and treatment-related systemic toxicity. We hypothesized that a BBB-penetrating nanoplatform capable of generating distinct H2S exposures in tumor and normal tissues could enhance antitumor efficacy while mitigating doxorubicin (DOX)-induced cardiotoxicity. Here, DOX-loaded metastable molybdenum disulfide nanoflowers functionalized with an I6P8 peptide (DOX@MSI) were developed. After BBB transport and tumor accumulation, the acidic, H2O2-rich, and GSH-rich microenvironment accelerates nanoplatform degradation, promoting GSH depletion and enhanced H2S/DOX release. High local H2S upregulates xCT, while H2S/DOX-mediated mitochondrial inhibition suppresses NADPH regeneration, synergistically triggering disulfidptosis. Meanwhile, H2S suppresses the JAK2/STAT3/IDO axis, alleviating DOX-induced immunosuppression and enhancing immunogenic cell death and T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity. In contrast, slower degradation under physiological conditions enables sustained low-level H2S release, reducing the level of oxidative stress and ERK-associated apoptosis in cardiomyocytes. Together with NIR-enhanced photothermal therapy, DOX@MSI suppresses orthotopic glioblastoma while reducing cardiac injury, thereby integrating tumor-selective multimodal therapy with active organ protection.

items.title:
All-in-One
Mitochondria-Targeted Iron-Based MOF “Nanomissiles”
for Synergistically Potentiated Tumor Ferroptosis, Dual Phototherapy,
and Chemotherapy
items.abstract: Abstract Pronounced heterogeneity and adaptability of tumors inherently curtail monotherapeutic efficacy, necessitating rationally integrated multimodal regimens that enable precise intervention, overcome resistance, and eradicate heterogeneous cell populations within the complex tumor microenvironment (TME). All-in-one mitochondria-targeted “nanomissiles” were created by emodin (Em)-Fe3+-gated, doxorubicin (DOX)-loaded PCN-600(FeIII) (denoted as DOX@ME) nanoparticles for synergistic multimodal tumor therapy integrating ferroptosis, photodynamic therapy (PDT), mild photothermal therapy (MPTT), and chemotherapy. DOX@ME achieved on-demand release of DOX in response to the TME [such as low pH, glutathione (GSH), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and adenosine-5′-triphosphate (ATP)] and near-infrared laser, via the disassembly of the Em-Fe3+ gating films and/or the degradation of the PCN-600(FeIII) nanocarriers. Under both 660 and 808 nm laser irradiation, DOX@ME effectively triggered apoptosis via chemotherapy, PDT, and MPTT while robustly accelerating reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, GSH depletion, glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) downregulation, and lipid peroxide (LPO) accumulation to enhance ferroptosis. Moreover, DOX@ME could alleviate thermotolerance by depleting intracellular ATP and downregulating protective heat shock protein 70 to boost the curative efficacy of MPTT. DOX@ME exhibited excellent antitumor efficacy and good biocompatibility and biosafety in A549 tumor-bearing nude mice. Collectively, DOX@ME demonstrates robust clinical translational potential for precision cancer therapy.

items.title:
Nanoscale Immune
Activator for Enhancing CD8+ T Cell Infiltration in Hepatocellular
Carcinoma
items.abstract: Abstract The infiltration of CD8+ T cells into the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) microenvironment is a well-established determinant of immunotherapy efficacy and patient prognosis. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing this process and the therapeutic strategies capable of modulating it remain largely unexplored. Here, we identify HCC-IN-247 as a candidate compound that enhances IFNβ-driven CD8+ T cell infiltration both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the long noncoding RNA LINC02084 directly interacts with the transcription factor GLIS1 and facilitates its recruitment to the IFNβ promoter. HCC-IN-247 was identified through screening to target the LINC02084-GLIS1 binding interface, thereby stabilizing this RNA–protein complex. Stabilization of the complex significantly enhances IFNβ transcription, which in turn upregulates CXCL10 and CXCL11 expression and promotes CD8+ T cell infiltration. Furthermore, this study engineered a nanoparticle-based delivery system, designated Lip@RA@BSA-PD-L1/IN-247, for the codelivery of HCC-IN-247 and the anti-PD-L1 antibody atezolizumab in HCC treatment. These nanoparticles exhibited robust tumor-specific accumulation and elicited potent synergistic antitumor activity against HCC in mice. Collectively, our findings establish HCC-IN-247 as an activator of the tumor immune microenvironment and provide a preclinical basis for a combined immunotherapeutic approach to HCC.

items.title:
Selective
Electronic Pre-Activation of OH Bonds in
Extremely Confined Water
items.abstract: Abstract Water under molecular-scale confinement is not simply a geometrically restricted form of bulk water, but can acquire distinct electronic, structural, and collective properties. However, how such an extremely confined state reshapes water’s intrinsic chemistry remains poorly understood. Here, using ab initio calculations and enhanced-sampling machine-learning potential molecular dynamics, we show that extreme two-dimensional confinement activates water for proton generation. Monolayer-confined water exhibits a substantially lower free-energy barrier for forming separated H3O+ and OH– ions than bulk water, and this tendency is further enhanced by lateral compression and nuclear quantum fluctuations. This enhanced reactivity does not arise from a uniform weakening of all water molecules. Instead, confinement makes OH bonds breaking selectively. The water molecule contains electronically distinct OH bonds, with weak in-plane bonds preferentially activated for proton release, while stronger dangling bonds remain relatively inactive. The surrounding hydrogen-bond network then provides disordered pathways for proton relocation, and the enhanced in-plane polarization stabilizes the charged products. Our results suggest that two-dimensional confined water can act as an active and superdielectric medium as indicated by recent experiments. Our findings reveal extreme confinement as a route to tune water-mediated chemistry, with implications for nanofluidics, geochemical pores, biological environments, and catalytic interfaces.

items.title:
Kinetic Access to
Focal Conic Domains in Photonic
Cellulose Nanocrystal Films
items.abstract: Abstract Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) self-assemble into cholesteric structures that enable sustainable photonic films, but controlling their pitch, domain morphology, and angular color response remains challenging. Here, we investigate how salt concentration and sonication dose jointly regulate the evaporation-induced self-assembly of CNC suspensions. Across 24 dish-cast films, polarized optical microscopy, time-lapse imaging, rheology, electron microscopy, and angle-resolved spectroscopy reveal that these processing parameters affect not only the cholesteric pitch but also tactoid nucleation, transport, coalescence, and the onset of kinetic arrest. Increasing NaCl concentration generally blue-shifts the photonic response, whereas sonication red-shifts it by fragmenting CNC bundles, with the magnitude of this effect decreasing as ionic content increases. At intermediate ionic content, low sonication doses produce extended cholesteric domains with comparatively narrow spectral responses, while the abundance of focal conic domains (FCDs) increases with sonication dose, culminating in FCD-rich films at moderate sonication. Refined parameter scans show that FCDs form within a finite processing window. Time-lapse imaging shows that FCDs appear abruptly after tactoid growth and coalescence, as macroscopic motion becomes strongly restricted during late-stage evaporation. Concentration- and residence-time-dependent rheology further demonstrates that the material response evolves throughout the assembly pathway. The FCD-rich film retains a narrow local reflection band while exhibiting the smallest angular displacement of the reflection maximum among the films examined. These findings show that salt and sonication regulate the kinetic accessibility of elastically driven focal conic structures, providing a route to tune domain morphology, spectral bandwidth, and iridescence in CNC photonic films.

items.title:
Near-Infrared Neuromodulation:
Principles, Nanotechnology-Enabled
Platforms, and Emerging Biomedical Frontiers
items.abstract: Abstract Optogenetics enables highly specific regulation of neuronal activity with exceptional spatiotemporal precision, providing powerful tools for neural circuit interrogation and the treatment of neurological disorders. However, the limited tissue penetration of visible light restricts its application to deep neural tissues. Near-infrared (NIR) neuromodulation has emerged as a promising alternative by leveraging the superior tissue penetration and minimal invasiveness of NIR light. Recent advances in NIR-responsive nanomaterials, optical engineering, and neurotechnology have rapidly transformed the field from nonspecific photobiomodulation to cell-specific nanotransducer-mediated neuromodulation and integrated neuromodulation systems. In this review, we summarize the optical principles governing NIR propagation in biological tissues and the mechanisms underlying NIR-mediated neural stimulation. We then discuss recent advances in representative NIR nanotransducers, including photothermal, optoelectric, photoacoustic, and NIR-to-visible upconversion platforms together with integrated neuromodulation systems that combine NIR stimulation with multimodal neural recording and closed-loop feedback. We further highlight emerging applications in the central nervous system, optic nerve, and peripheral nerve disorders. Finally, we discuss the key challenges toward clinical translation, including improving tissue penetration, cell specificity, biosafety, and translation, developing intelligent multidisciplinary neuromodulation platforms, and integrating artificial intelligence with closed-loop neural interfaces to achieve adaptive, precise, and personalized neuromodulation.

items.title:
Controllable Refraction
of Highly Confined Hyperbolic
Phonon Polaritons Using van der Waals Dielectric Superstrates
items.abstract: Abstract In stark contrast with traditional refraction phenomenon in isotropic media, refraction of hyperbolic polaritons enables extreme confinement and nanofocusing of mid-infrared light. However, the tuning of hyperbolic refraction typically relies on plasmonic systems (e.g., gating graphene and phase-change materials), and therefore, the electron–electron scattering introduces inevitable propagation losses of polaritons. Herein, we demonstrate that refraction of highly confined hyperbolic polaritons in α-phase molybdenum trioxide (α-MoO3) crystal strongly depends on the dielectric superstrate. We theoretically and experimentally indicate that both the wavevector (its direction and magnitude) and the propagation direction of refracted hyperbolic polaritons can be controlled by varying the twist angle between the vdW dielectric layers of tungsten diselenide (WSe2) and α-MoO3 crystals. Moreover, we observe the total internal reflection and zero-phase propagation of nanoscale-confined polaritons in hyperbolic media. Our study of the propagation of hyperbolic polaritons not only deepens the understanding of polariton refraction at the nanoscale and in strongly anisotropic media but also promises the development of functional nanophotonic elements and devices.

items.title:
Highly Confined
Magnetophononic Polaritons and Electron–Phonon
Interactions in Atomically Thin MnBi2Te4
items.abstract: Abstract Atomically thin materials can strongly confine light into quanta of lattice vibrations, leading to strong light–matter interactions. Some of these materials can exhibit topology, which protects the edge states embedded inside the bulk from backscattering, while some host magnetism, providing another degree of freedom to control topological properties. The simultaneous observation of all of these phenomena in a single material can lead to various applications by enabling light-controlled topological electronic and nanophotonic devices. Here we demonstrate via first-principles density functional perturbation theory calculations that atomically thin MnBi2Te4 is a promising platform for hosting three highly confined, tunable, and long-propagating magnetophononic polaritons. These polaritons strongly modulate exchange interactions, especially the second polariton in 2 SL MnBi2Te4, inducing strong light–matter coupling in the presence of light. Intriguingly, this coupling not only induces an antiferromagnetic-to-ferromagnetic phase transition but also drives an electronic phase transition from trivial to topologically nontrivial states in 2 SL MnBi2Te4. We also show that these polaritonic modes have relatively weak electron–phonon scattering rates and that these scattering rates change with layer thickness and magnetic ordering due to spin–phonon coupling. Overall, our results suggest that MnBi2Te4 is a promising material for topological electronics, nanophotonics, and nanophonics capable of providing greater control of data signals via light.

items.title:
Coupled
Design of Silicon Anodes and Solid-State Electrolytes
for High-Performance All-Solid-State Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Silicon-based solid-state batteries (Si-SSBs) offer enhanced safety and higher energy density over conventional liquid-electrolyte systems, yet their practical realization is critically hindered by severe volume expansion of silicon anodes and poor interfacial compatibility with solid-state electrolytes. This review provides a comprehensive evaluation of recent advances from a coupled design perspective, integrating silicon anode engineering, electrolyte compatibility optimization, and interfacial stabilization. We systematically examine emerging strategies for silicon anodes alongside compatibility approaches tailored to each electrolyte type, with a particular focus on the coupled chemo-mechanical degradation at the silicon/electrolyte interface. A systematic compatibility mapping linking different Si architectures with specific electrolyte families reveals the most promising material combinations and their underlying design principles. Beyond materials design, we address critical manufacturing challenges including stack pressure management, scalable processing, and prelithiation techniques essential for industrial translation. Finally, we propose a forward-looking roadmap integrating multiscale characterization, AI-assisted design, and scalable fabrication, providing both theoretical guidance and practical strategies for developing high-performance, commercially viable Si-SSBs.

items.title:
Spectroscopic Identification
of Dimensionality-Driven
Anticorrelation between Charge-Density-Wave Order and Superconductivity
in Ultrathin NbSe2
items.abstract: Abstract Intertwined electronic orders in low-dimensional quantum materials often evolve in a strongly thickness-dependent manner, yet direct spectroscopic access to their mutual evolution remains a key challenge. NbSe2 is a prototypical layered superconductor in which charge-density-wave order coexists with superconductivity, but spectroscopic signatures of the charge-density-wave state are frequently obscured, limiting direct comparison with superconducting order. Here, we demonstrate all-van der Waals planar tunnel junctions as a spectroscopic platform for simultaneously probing charge-density-wave and superconducting states in NbSe2 from the bulk to the bilayer limit. Temperature-dependent tunneling spectra reveal distinct anomalies associated with charge-density-wave formation and superconducting gap opening, allowing both quantum phase transitions to be tracked within the same device architecture. We find that the charge-density-wave transition temperature increases from ∼34 to ∼56 K as the NbSe2 thickness is reduced from 11L to the bilayer, while the superconducting transition temperature decreases from ∼7.2 to ∼5.4 K. These results reveal a clear anticorrelation between the two ordered states as dimensionality is reduced. Moreover, our spectroscopic studies reveal that the emergence of charge-density-wave order modifies the electronic states of NbSe2 over a broad energy window extending up to ±300 meV, a widely anticipated but previously experimentally inaccessible characteristic. Our results provide comprehensive spectroscopic evidence for the thickness-dependent competition between charge-density-wave order and superconductivity in ultrathin NbSe2 and position planar van der Waals tunnel junctions as a powerful platform for investigating emergent quantum phases in layered materials.

items.title:
Fast-Gelling, Adhesive,
and Conductive Epidermal Electrode
for Accurate Physiological Signal Monitoring and Real-Time Brain-Controlled
Drone Flight
items.abstract: Abstract Conductive hydrogel electrodes are vital components for achieving human-machine interfaces. However, the inherent trade-off between high conductivity and favorable mechanical/adhesive properties remains a significant challenge for hydrogel-based epidermal electrodes. Here, we developed a multifunctional MXene/WPU/PAA (MWA) hydrogel electrode that combines robust mechanical properties, strong adhesion, and excellent conductivity. The introduced MXene nanosheets can induce free-radical polymerization, resulting in fast gelation (&lt;5 min) at room temperature. Theoretical analyses reveal that MXene nanosheets form abundant hydrogen bonds with polymer chains, thus enhancing the cross-linking density and mechanical strength of the hydrogel electrode. The MWA hydrogel can form a stable skin-electrode interface, enabling high-fidelity multimodal physiological signal monitoring. Specifically, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for sEMG reached 36.0 dB, while the SNR for ECG was 30.1 dB, outperforming the Ag/AgCl electrodes. The MWA hydrogel exhibits outstanding adhesion under repeated cycles and simulated sweat conditions, reaching 94.2 and 55.5 kPa, respectively. Furthermore, the MWA hydrogel electrode demonstrates precise scalp EEG monitoring, enabling wireless drone flight control via real-time brainwave decoding. This work provides insight into MXene-polymer interactions and demonstrates the applicability of the developed electrode to brain-computer interface applications.

items.title:
The Temperature
Dependence of the Pathogenic Bacterial
Adhesin Complex SdrG:Fgβ under Sustained Loads: A High-Force
Slip Bond
items.abstract: Abstract Staphylococcus epidermidis is the leading cause of medical-implant-related infections. This pathogen attaches to medical implants coated in host fibrinogen via adhesin proteins. To resist high shear forces, adhesin-ligand rupture forces can exceed 2000 pN, a force that is much higher than streptavidin–biotin (150–300 pN). Yet, these adhesin-ligand complexes have a quite moderate KD (∼380 nM). This nanomechanics is explained, in part, by catch-bond behavior where adhesin-ligand lifetimes increase with force. Notably, prior reports of adhesin catch-bond mechanics at both low (3–30 pN) and high (1100–1400 pN) forces have lifetimes that are difficult to reconcile. Here, we combined constant-velocity and constant-force assays and thereby showed slip-bond behavior over six decades of lifetimes first for SdrG:Fgβ (1000–2400 pN) and then for SdrE:CFH (800–2200 pN) from Staphylococcus aureus. Individual lifetimes for SdrE:CFH exceeded 15 min at 800 pN. To investigate the thermodynamics of SdrG:Fgβ stability, we measured its lifetime using the constant-force assay as a function of both force (1000–1800 pN) and temperature (10–37 °C). Analysis yielded the enthalpic-dissociation barrier (ΔH‡ = 40 ± 4 kBT) and, assuming an enthalpy-dominated barrier, the dissociation attempt frequency (∼6 × 1010 s–1). Our results unambiguously demonstrate high-force slip-bond behavior for two different adhesin-ligand pairs and provide biophysical parameters governing the stability of key virulence factors.

items.title:
Inhalable Multifunctional
Liposomes Disrupt the Inflammation-Oxidative
Stress Cycle for Acute Lung Injury Therapy
items.abstract: Abstract Acute lung injury (ALI) is characterized by an uncontrolled cycle of inflammation and oxidative stress. However, conventional therapeutics are limited by physiological pulmonary barriers and poor targeted bioavailability. In this study, an inhalable multifunctional liposomal system (designated as R&I/Lip@PEG-M) was elaborately engineered to codeliver Resveratrol and IMD-0354 to disrupt the inflammation-oxidative stress cycle for ALI therapy. Upon nebulized inhalation, the negatively charged R&I/Lip@PEG-M liposomes would efficiently penetrate the mucus barrier, extensively accumulate in the pulmonary alveoli, and be specifically taken up by alveolar macrophages via mannose-mediated targeting recognition. Particularly, the internalized liposomes could exert combined therapeutic effects by scavenging intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and blocking the NF-κB signaling pathway to inhibit inflammation. In the LPS-induced ALI mouse model, the designed R&I/Lip@PEG-M significantly reduced the population of inflammatory macrophages, reprogrammed the redox microenvironment, and successfully mitigated lung damage and pulmonary edema.

items.title: Three-in-One Injectable Hydrogel Orchestrating Host-Bacteria Targeting, Retention, and Autophagy for Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus -Infected Mastitis Therapy
items.abstract: Abstract MRSA mastitis is clinically refractory and characterized by progressive inflammation driven by intracellular bacteria that form persistent niches in mammary epithelial cells and macrophages to evade antimicrobial clearance. Conventional antibiotics, particularly β-lactams, are widely used but suffer from poor intracellular accumulation, failing to reach these reservoirs. Even nanocarrier-based strategies struggle to achieve efficient endosomal escape and precise intracellular targeting. Herein, we report a fibronectin-functionalized, fluorinated PLGA nanoparticle encapsulating amoxicillin and sulbactam (Fn-F-PLGA@A/S) engineered with a 2.5% (w/w) fluorinated core for efficient endosomal escape. The fibronectin decoration enables sequential targeting of both host integrins and bacterial fibronectin-binding proteins (FnBPs). Fn-F-PLGA@A/S achieved efficient intracellular delivery, clearing 90% of intracellular MRSA in macrophages and epithelial cells within 4 h in vitro. To prolong mammary retention, Fn-F-PLGA@A/S was loaded into a thermosensitive hydrogel. In a murine MRSA mastitis model, a single intramammary dose of the gel formulation achieved &gt;90% bacterial reduction, attenuated TNF-α and IL-6, and preserved alveolar architecture and tight junctions. Proteomic analysis revealed upregulation of AMPK-mediated autophagy, suggesting that beyond direct antibiotic action, the potent intracellular clearance achieved by Fn-F-PLGA may involve the engagement of host autophagic machinery, potentially facilitating the sequestration of MRSA within degradative compartments. Collectively, by integrating sequential targeting, sustained local retention, and autophagic engagement, this platform provides a robust strategy to address the key limitations of conventional antibiotics against intracellular pathogens in refractory infections.

items.title:
Size-Dependent Surface
Evolution Controls Luminescence
in Ln3+-Doped Nanocrystals
items.abstract: Abstract Lanthanide-doped luminescent nanocrystals (NCs) hold significant promise for bioimaging, theranostics, catalysis, sensing, lighting, and displays, motivating an in-depth understanding of their optical properties. This work reveals the profound, yet widely disregarded, impact of surface structure changes on the luminescence of growing NCs through a model study of Eu3+ surface-exchanged Sr2YF7 NCs. Contrary to expectation, a stark drop in luminescence intensity exceeding several orders of magnitude was observed as the particle size increased. Atomic-resolution electron microscopy imaging shows that the NCs evolve from spheroidal to cuboidal morphologies during growth, with a shift in preferentially exposed crystal facets from {111} to {200} that renders lattice distortion less favorable. High-resolution optical spectroscopy probing surface Eu3+, together with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and reaction kinetics study, reveals a high extent of Eu3+ exchange in the small spheroidal NCs with lattice distortion extending far from the surface into the interior. This starkly contrasts the situation in the large cuboidal NCs, where the extent of Eu3+ residing in the surface region is severely limited, thereby causing the dramatic drop in luminescence. These findings demonstrate surface structure control as a powerful strategy for tailoring the luminescence properties of Ln3+-doped NCs and other nanomaterials for advanced applications.

Abstract Dynamic DNA nanomachines are programmable devices capable of executing certain controlled movements, structural reconfigurations, and functional tasks. Over the past few decades, extensive advancements have been made in designing DNA-based molecular systems driven by strand displacement, catalytic reactions, enzymatic processes, chemical or physical stimuli. The development of DNA nanotechnology has further enabled the construction of highly precise and complex DNA nanomachines. Herein, we review dynamic DNA nanomachines from a motion-to-function perspective, emphasizing how programmable movement, structural reconfiguration, or autonomous operation can be converted into biomedical output. Structural platforms, driving mechanisms, biomedical functions, and translational barriers are discussed. Particularly, we focus on the systems in which DNA dynamics directly contribute to biosensing, bioimaging, therapeutic activation, cell regulation, and molecular decision-making. This framework distinguishes dynamic DNA nanomachines from static DNA nanostructures, which also highlights the design requirements needed to move these systems toward practical biomedical applications.

items.title:
In-Situ Visualization
of Thermal Transformation Pathways
in Leaf-Shaped Zeolitic Imidazolate Framework Derived Nanocarbon
items.abstract: Abstract Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are versatile precursors for nanostructured, heteroatom-doped carbons. However, understanding the spatiotemporally resolved mechanisms that govern crystalline-to-amorphous framework collapse, diffusion-mediated reorganization of transient intermediates, and the subsequent formation of graphitic carbon remains challenging. Here, we elucidate the transformation of the 2D leaf-shaped zeolitic imidazolate framework ZIF-L into Zn-dispersed N-doped carbon using a combination of in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). These measurements directly capture the sequential collapse of the layered MOF framework and the associated morphological evolution under controlled heating, decoupled from beam-induced effects during electron microscopy. Complementary ex-situ pyrolysis (700–1100 °C), together with high-resolution TEM, synchrotron X-ray pair distribution function (X-PDF) analysis, and electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS), reveals the diffusion of Zn-containing species, ligand decomposition, and progressive graphitization within the amorphous matrix. We identify temperature-dependent stages involving ligand breakdown, migration of Zn–Nx species, followed by Zn loss, and ultimately forming porous N-doped carbon at 1000 °C that exhibits the strongest electrochemical response within this series. These findings establish temperature-dependent structure–property relationships that enable the thermal engineering of MOF-derived ORR catalysts.

items.title:
Acoustic
Cavitation-Enhanced Remodeling of Lymph Node
Microenvironment Enables Deep Infiltration for Potent Cancer Vaccination
items.abstract: Abstract The efficacy of peptide-based tumor vaccines is often constrained by the size-exclusion barrier of the subcapsular sinus (SCS), which restricts infiltration of macromolecules into the lymph node (LN) parenchyma essential for T-cell priming. Here, inspired by the clinical contrast agent Sonazoid, we developed an ultrasound-assisted vaccine platform with tunable phase-transition behavior for the active modulation of the LN microenvironment. The system integrates phosphoserine-decorated lipid chemistry to promote cell-mediated LN trafficking, a covalently conjugated adjuvant–antigen construct for synchronized immunostimulation, and liquid-state perfluorocarbon nanodomains programmed for ultrasound-triggered liquid–gas transition. Upon localized ultrasound irradiation, the chemically programmed phase transition triggers cargo release, while the resultant acoustic cavitation generates transient openings in the SCS endothelium. This process enables deep parenchymal infiltration of vaccine components that would otherwise be excluded. Beyond the physical barrier disruption, RNA sequencing reveals that acoustic stimulation drives both structural and immunological reprogramming of LN into an immune-permissive niche. By synergizing mechanical stimulation with biological modulation, this strategy induces benign and persistent LN expansion, amplifies antitumor T-cell responses, and establishes durable immunological memory, resulting in both prophylactic and therapeutic outcomes. This approach is versatile across both model antigens and neoantigens, offering a bioinspired, two-stage LN-targeted delivery strategy that serves as a framework for designing more effective therapeutic vaccines.

items.title:
Mechanistic Insights
into Sodium Storage in N-Doped
Graphene/MoS2 Heterostructures Revealed by Operando Raman
Spectroscopy
items.abstract: Abstract Two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures offer tunable interlayer spacing and accessible surfaces that can overcome key limitations of conventional sodium-ion battery (SIBs) anodes. Here, we investigate Na+ storage mechanisms in three-layer 2D heterostructures composed of horizontally stacked graphene (G), nitrogen-doped graphene (NG), and MoS2 (M) by combining cyclic voltammetry with operando spectroelectrochemical Raman spectroscopy. Restricting the active thickness to three atomic layers enables direct spectroscopic access to interfacial charge transfer and strain during cycling. Electrochemical analysis reveals that Na+ storage is governed by two coupled factors: the permeability of the electrolyte-facing outer layer, and the electronic–mechanical interactions within the interlayer space. NG outer layers facilitate ion access and deliver up to 40-fold higher capacities than pristine graphene stacks, whereas MoS2 top layers suppress ion infiltration. Operando Raman correlates faradaic features with reversible structural changes, allowing separation of charge-doping and strain effects during cycling. The results demonstrate that Na+ storage proceeds predominantly via reversible accumulation in confined interlayer and blister-like reservoirs formed during solvent cointercalation. Incorporating MoS2 as a middle layer redistributes charge and buffers mechanical strain, enhancing cycling stability. These findings provide insights into charge storage mechanisms in 2D materials.

items.title:
A
Chronologically Programmed Core–Shell Microneedle
Patch for Staged Therapy of Spinal Cord Injury
items.abstract: Abstract Secondary injury following spinal cord injury (SCI) is not a unidimensional pathological process; rather, it involves a spatiotemporally organized cascade that rapidly evolves from an acute inflammatory storm and tissue breakdown to stalled repair and impaired regeneration in the subacute phase. However, most current therapeutic strategies depend on single-dose administration or isolated targets and thus fail to keep pace with the dynamic progression of SCI. Here, we developed a core–shell microneedle platform that aligns drug delivery with SCI progression by temporally decoupling the release kinetics of distinct therapeutics. The shell enabled rapid methylprednisolone (MP) release to suppress inflammatory cascades and restrict the expansion of secondary injury during the acute phase, while the core achieved sustained release of miR124-enriched M2 macrophage-derived exosomes (M2-miR124-Exo), promoting neuroprotection and microenvironmental remodeling during the subacute phase. This “suppression-then-repair” strategy synchronized treatment timing with stage-specific pathological demands, overcoming the limitations of conventional single-window delivery systems. Mechanistically, the platform promoted neuronal survival and axonal regeneration partly through modulation of key signaling pathways, including MAPK. In vivo, the platform markedly improved locomotor recovery in SCI rats, reduced lesion size, and exhibited no detectable systemic toxicity. These findings establish a programmable, pathology-guided delivery paradigm that addresses the spatiotemporal mismatch in SCI therapy and offers a promising strategy for precision intervention in complex CNS injuries.

items.title:
Visible Light Modulates
Macrophage Phenotype and Photoresponsive
Carbon Monoxide Delivery
items.abstract: Abstract Photoresponsive drug delivery systems are often described as bioorthogonal. However, certain wavelengths and intensities of visible light are known to modulate cellular phenotypes. This apparent discrepancy highlights a gap in knowledge with direct implications for the design of photoresponsive drug delivery systems. In this report, we investigated the response of primary macrophages to visible light (405–630 nm) due to their broad tissue distribution, phenotypic plasticity, and central role in orchestrating immune responses across diverse pathologies. We found distinct wavelength-dependent changes in cytochrome c oxidase activity, metabolic function, cytokine secretion, and biomarker expression at clinically relevant intensities of light. Further investigation of red light (630 nm) demonstrated complex dose-dependent metabolic and phenotypic responses. To illustrate the clinical implications of these findings, we employed 470 nm-triggerable carbon monoxide-releasing micelles to deconvolute the individual and combined effects of light exposure and therapeutic payloads. Our findings suggest that macrophages respond in a wavelength and intensity-dependent manner, and incorporating photoresponsive carbon monoxide-releasing systems elicits distinct immunomodulatory responses compared to irradiation alone. This work establishes a basic design framework for leveraging light parameters such as wavelength and intensity to achieve desirable immunomodulatory responses with photoresponsive drug delivery systems for specific disease applications.

items.title:
Displacement-Field-Induced
Ionization of Defect States
in High-Quality hBN
items.abstract: Abstract Encapsulation of two-dimensional (2D) materials with hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is widely used to fabricate ultraclean van der Waals (vdW) heterostructures for optoelectronic and quantum transport studies. These devices are often operated under strong out-of-plane displacement fields that tune the electronic properties of the active 2D material, while the surrounding hBN is typically assumed to remain electronically inert. This assumption, however, neglects defect states that are present even in high-quality hBN crystals. Here, we probe their response to the applied displacement field using monolayer graphene encapsulated between hBN crystals as a sensitive charge sensor. Increasing the displacement field induces notable charge transfer between graphene and hBN, producing additional electron doping of ≈10–20 × 109 cm–2 even at the moderate displacement field (∼0.5 V nm–1), while simultaneously increasing carrier-density inhomogeneity of the graphene layer. Both effects are consistent with ionization of defect states within the hBN bandgap, with the bulk density ∼1–7 × 10–5 nm–3 varying across different hBN crystals. Our results show that displacement-field-induced defect ionization in hBN can modify the electronic response of vdW heterostructures, with direct implications for device design and interpretation of experiments.

items.title:
Riveting Rubidium
in Alkali-Metal Layers: High-Performance
P2-Type Layered Oxide Cathodes for Potassium-Ion Batteries
items.abstract: Abstract Layered manganese-based oxides for potassium-ion batteries (PIBs) suffer from severe structural degradation, primarily due to irreversible phase transitions, Jahn–Teller distortion, and sluggish K+ diffusion kinetics. Here, we propose an alkali-metal site riveting strategy by selectively incorporating oversized Rb+ ions into the prismatic sites of P2-type K0.55Mn0.8Ni0.1T0.1O2. The introduced Rb+ acts as a rigid pillar, expanding the interlayer spacing and reinforcing adjacent transition-metal–oxygen (TM–O) bonds. This synergistic modulation not only widens the two-dimensional diffusion channels for rapid K+ transport but also effectively suppresses the detrimental P2–P′2 phase transition and mitigates Jahn–Teller distortion of Mn3+. Consequently, the optimized K0.55Rb0.025Mn0.8Ni0.1Ti0.1O2 cathode delivers a high reversible capacity of 105.3 mAh g–1 at a current density of 20 mA g–1, outstanding rate capability (56.1 mAh g–1 at 500 mA g–1), and long-term cycling stability with 82.1% capacity retention after 500 cycles. Furthermore, a pouch cell paired with a soft carbon anode achieves 81.3% capacity retention over 300 cycles. This work demonstrates that anchoring oversized cations in alkali-metal layers provides a universal and effective strategy toward near-zero-strain layered oxide cathodes for advanced PIBs.

items.title:
Visualizing Single-Cell
Secretion with Electrochemiluminescence
Imaging
items.abstract: Abstract Secretory proteins encode cellular states not only through their abundance but also through their intracellular transport before being released. However, visualizing protein secretion behavior with molecular specificity and a low background remains challenging. Here, we report VEGF-responsive electrochemiluminescence (ECL) nanoemitters that enable spatiotemporal mapping of intracellular protein distribution at different stages of the secretion process by integrating a metal–organic framework (MOF) confining Ru(bpy)32+ with DNA tetrahedral gates (DTGs) programmed with aptamers. The MOF core provides bright, stable, and electrically addressable ECL emission, whereas the discrete DTGs regulate coreactant accessibility and prevent premature emission until VEGF recognition triggers gate displacement and restores ECL activity, converting intracellular molecular recognition events to quantitative optical signals.
