This architecture enables rapid, concentration-dependent, and selective activation, allowing high contrast discrimination of VEGF-rich tumor cells from epithelial cells. Under DFO stimulation, single-cell ECL imaging revealed heterogeneous VEGF upregulation and mapped its progressive redistribution from the perinuclear region to the cell periphery during secretion. This gated ECL platform enables quantitative spatiotemporal visualization of protein secretion behavior beyond the static molecular localization.

items.title:
Flexible Nanofibrous
Membrane with Valley-Cell Array
of Rapid Thermal Response and Stability for Efficient Water Harvesting
Performance
items.abstract: Abstract We demonstrate a flexible nanofibrous membrane featuring a valley-cell array (NMVA). Inspired by honeycombs and spider silk, the NMVA is rationally designed using poly(vinyl alcohol), carbon black, and MOF-303 as its main components. The synergistic effect of the flexible honeycomb network, abundant hydrophilic sites of MOF-decorated nanofibers, rapid photothermal response, and multidimensional structural stability favors highly efficient adsorption and desorption dynamics during water harvesting. The valleys of the honeycomb cell arrays enhance light capture for photothermal conversion and water release, while the abundant hydrophilic sites facilitate water molecule capture and uptake. As a result, NMVA achieves a high water uptake capacity of ∼0.41 g g–1 at 25 °C and 30% RH, and can release 92% of the absorbed water within 30 min under 1 sun irradiation. For an integrated NMVA in outdoor conditions under sunlight of ∼0.76 kW m–2 on average, water harvesting capacities reach 3.85–5.0 L kg–1 day–1 at 42–68% RH through continuous all-day water uptake–release over seven cycles. This study provides insights into the design of novel materials that can be extended into the realms of water engineering for energy systems and portable devices.

items.title:
Nanoedge-Regulated
Impedance Sensing for Sensitive
Cardiomyocyte Mechanophysiological Investigation and Functional Drug
Assessment
items.abstract: Abstract Cardiomyocyte contraction drives the pumping action of the heart and is fundamental to cardiac mechanophysiology research. Conventional optical and force-based approaches for cardiomyocyte contraction detection are limited by phototoxicity or potential alterations in cell morphology and physiology. Electrical impedance sensing is a label-free approach for noninvasive contraction recording, but current sensor optimization still mainly relies on substantial adjustments to electrode size or pattern. Herein, we present a nanoedge-regulated impedance sensing (NERIS) approach. Electrode structures with different pit depths are designed to regulate the cell-electrode interface to precisely optimize impedance properties. Increasing pit depth shifts the peak impedance response to lower frequencies, potentially reducing detection system bandwidth demands. At the optimized frequencies, long-term recordings support quantitative analysis of cardiomyocyte mechanophysiology. Furthermore, functional cardiac drug assessment is performed by characterizing contractile responses to norepinephrine and isradipine. This NERIS approach is expected to be widely applied in cardiomyocyte mechanophysiology and cardiac drug assessment.

items.title:
Poly(acrylamido)
PEG-Alternative Lipids Rescue mRNA
Efficacy during Repeated Dosing and Enhance Immune Cell Delivery
items.abstract: Abstract Following the successes of the messenger RNA (mRNA) lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines against COVID-19, mRNA-LNPs are being explored for varied multidose applications including cancer immunotherapies and protein replacement therapies. LNPs rely on poly(ethylene glycol)-lipid (PEG-lipid) coatings for stability, but increasing anti-PEG antibody prevalence threatens repeat-dose efficacy and increases pseudoallergic risk, creating an urgent need for alternatives. Here, we introduce poly(acrylamido) lipids (PAM-lipids), a family of polymer lipids that effectively replace PEG-lipids in mRNA-LNP formulations. Systematic variation of monomer chemistry, molar mass, and end group reveals critical structure–activity relationships determining LNP size, polydispersity, and transfection efficiency. Varying PAM monomer chemistry allows minimization of antipolymer antibody cross-reactivity, with multiple PAM-lipids demonstrating no anti-PEG antibody binding. Several PAM-LNPs exhibit superior mRNA transfection efficacy to PEGylated clinical benchmarks in vitro and in vivo across multiple cell types, organs, routes of administration, and mRNA cargos. In particular, lead PAM-LNPs enhance mRNA delivery to dendritic cells (up to 120-fold in vitro and 3-fold in vivo) and macrophages (4-fold in vivo), with 2.5-fold superior lymph node expression, driven in part by increased cellular association and lymphoid targeting. Crucially, PAM-LNPs evade circulating anti-PEG antibodies to rescue lost mRNA efficacy after repeated dosing, resulting in 300% mRNA expression relative to that of PEG-LNPs. These findings demonstrate PAM-lipids as a chemically varied, immunologically compatible family of PEG alternatives for mRNA-LNP therapeutics.

items.title:
Divide and Conquer
Strategy Using Piezoelectric Nanofiber
Scaffolds for Stage-Specific Delivery of Bone-Targeted Exosome Mimetics
with Ago/AntagomiR-126
items.abstract: Abstract Bone regeneration is a temporally regulated process requiring stage-specific biochemical cues and biomechanical stimulation; however, current scaffold-based delivery systems largely rely on passive release and fail to adapt to the dynamic healing phases. While previous PVDF-based scaffolds have focused on enhancing piezoelectric output or osteoconductive properties, they primarily function as passive materials without the dynamic regulation of therapeutic activity. Here, we present a multifunctional piezoelectric scaffold that enables mechanically triggered, temporally controlled delivery of bone-targeted exosome mimetics (EMs) loaded with AgomiR or AntagomiR-126. The scaffold features a three-dimensional piezoelectric architecture that generates electromechanical activation under physiological loading, allowing for coupling between mechanical stimulation and therapeutic release. In addition, these components are functionally integrated to coordinate phase-specific miRNA activity during the repair. Alendronate-functionalized EMs enable bone-selective localization, while AgomiR-126 promotes early angiogenesis and progenitor recruitment and AntagomiR-126 enhances late-stage osteogenic differentiation. In vivo studies demonstrated that this system significantly improved bone repair. Rather than introducing a new component, this work establishes a mechanically gated, temporally programmed miRNA delivery strategy for phase-specific bone regeneration.

items.title:
Effect of Chiral-Induced
Spin Selectivity in Half-Metallic
La0.67Sr0.33MnO3 Thin Films
items.abstract: Abstract Magnetism induced by the proximity effects of chiral molecules is a physical phenomenon that can be demonstrated with molecular layers as thin as 1 nm deposited on thin films of conventional ferromagnets. Although the chiral-induced spin selectivity effect has been widely explored in the context of spintronic applications involving charge transport through chiral molecules, due to its capacity to generate high spin polarizations at room temperature, the accompanying process of induced magnetization without applied current likewise presents opportunities for exploitation. In this work, we demonstrate that, unlike conventional ferromagnets, where the induced magnetization aligns with the chiral axis of the polymer, the CISS effect in half-metallic ferromagnets (La0.67Sr0.33MnO3) favors a quasi-perpendicular magnetization configuration. This preference for quasi-perpendicular magnetization is caused by the formation of a thermally driven steady state, which, due to different transport probabilities into the molecule, results in a modification of the domain-wall energy landscape. These results provide insight into the chiral-induced spin selectivity effect without net currents and also clarify mechanism for controlling magnetization within half-metallic thin films for spintronic devices.

items.title: High-Throughput In-Operando Terahertz Time-Domain Spectroscopy of Chemical Vapor Deposited Graphene for pH Sensing
items.abstract: Abstract Reliable pH sensing in liquid environments underpins applications in energy storage, biosensing, and process monitoring, yet conventional graphene-based electrical devices introduce ohmic contacts, encapsulation layers, and electrochemical artifacts that can obscure intrinsic behavior. These approaches also fail to capture the strong spatial variability of commercial CVD graphene. Here, we present a fully contactless methodology for quantifying pH-dependent conductivity of large-area CVD graphene using through-substrate reflection terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS). A customized liquid cell with a THz transparent window preserves unrestricted access to the graphene–electrolyte interface while enabling centimeter-scale conductivity mapping and in-operando single-point monitoring during sequential pH modulation. By integrating spatially registered Raman mapping with automated quality-metric filtering, we extract statistically robust trends across thousands of pixels rather than isolated device regions. We show that pristine monolayer graphene exhibits the highest baseline conductivity and strongest pH sensitivity, whereas O2-plasma-introduced defects systematically suppress both. This scalable, remote, and inert probing approach establishes THz-TDS as a powerful platform for high-throughput characterization and robust liquid-phase sensing in thin films and 2D systems.

items.title:
Electric-Field
Tunable Spin Texture in Dual-Gated
HfS2/Graphene van der Waals Heterostructures
items.abstract: Abstract Spin–charge interconversion provides the essential link between spin information and electrical signals in spintronic devices. In spin–orbit coupled systems, spin–charge interconversion can contain multiple components associated with different spin-polarization directions, reflecting the underlying spin texture. Tuning this spin texture, therefore, provides a way to control not only the magnitude of spin–charge interconversion but also the balance among its different components. Graphene-based van der Waals heterostructures provide an attractive platform for this purpose because interfacial spin–orbit coupling can host multiple spin–charge interconversion channels that couple to different spin-polarization directions. Here, we demonstrate electric-field control of spin texture in a dual-gated HfS2/graphene van der Waals heterostructure, where independent control of carrier density and vertical electric field allows us to disentangle electrostatic doping from electric field-induced spin–orbit effects. Nonlocal spin precession measurements show that, near zero vertical electric field, spin–charge interconversion is dominated by a spin Hall component with out-of-plane spins. Increasing the vertical electric field enhances additional in-plane spin components with Rashba–Edelstein-like character, including contributions both parallel and perpendicular to the charge current. These results provide experimental evidence that a vertical electric field can reconfigure the effective spin texture and control the corresponding spin–charge interconversion components, demonstrating electrical tunability of spin–orbit functionalities.

items.title:
Enhanced Magneto-Optical
Kerr Effect in Nano-Magnetic
Metamaterials with Near-Perfect Coherent Absorption
items.abstract: Abstract The ability to control magnetic systems without external magnetic fields has attracted attention recently, with all-optical magnetic switching showing increasing promise. Gaining fine control over light-matter interactions in magnetic nanostructures is essential for advancing opto-magnetic technologies but remains challenging because strong optical coupling must be achieved within ultrathin magnetic structures at the target wavelength. Here, we show that coherent optical interference can increase this interaction in patterned magnetic metasurfaces. Arrays of permalloy nanomagnets are placed on a thin dielectric spacer above a reflective back-plane, forming a magnetic metasurface whose reflected wavefront is defined by the nanomagnet geometry, fill factor, and spacer thickness. Destructive interference between the metasurface and back-plane reflections yields near-perfect absorption, exceeding 95% for circular nanomagnet arrays in both simulation and experiment. The absorbed power is dissipated almost entirely within the nanomagnets, with only a few percent lost in the metallic back-plane. Enhanced absorption is also accompanied by a stronger magneto-optical Kerr effect, driven by both increased light–nanomagnet interaction and reduced reflected background. These results provide a general approach for achieving high optical absorption and strong magneto-optical response in nanoscale magnetic systems, supporting advances in optically addressable spintronics, magnetic sensing, and all-optical magnetic control.

items.title:
Noise-Suppressed
High-Performance WSe2 Phototransistors
Enabled by Optically Programmed Remote Contact Doping
items.abstract: Abstract Improving the sensitivity of two-dimensional semiconductor phototransistors requires increasing photocurrent while minimizing noise. However, conventional doping approaches often place charged dopants in or near atomically thin channels, introducing charge scattering, trap states, and noise that limit the signal-to-noise ratio. Here, we address this signal-noise trade-off in WSe2 phototransistors by using photoinduced charge trapping in patterned hBN to implement contact-selective remote doping. Under illumination with a negative gate voltage, trapped holes in hBN electrostatically n-dope WSe2 while remaining spatially separated from the transport channel. Patterned hBN confines the doping to selected regions, allowing the WSe2 near the metal electrodes to be remotely doped while leaving the channel undoped. This remote contact doping simultaneously suppressed the device noise by approximately 100–fold, reduced the effective density of electrically active traps by approximately 100–fold, and lowered the activation energy by 30–80 meV, indicating improved contact quality and more efficient carrier injection. As a result, the contact-doped phototransistors simultaneously exhibit enhanced responsivity of 99.7 A/W and a specific detectivity of 2.26 × 1011 Jones. These results establish optically programmed remote contact doping as a phototransistor-compatible contact-engineering approach to overcome the signal–noise trade-off in 2D phototransistors.

items.title:
Gas Separation through
Graphene Nanopores Enabled
by Thermally Robust Porous Organic Polymer Reinforcement
items.abstract: Abstract Porous single-layer graphene (PG) offers an ideal platform for molecular-sieving membranes due to its atomically thin inorganic lattice and its ability to incorporate molecularly selective pores. However, the use of PG for high-temperature gas separation remains limited by the lack of a mechanically reinforcing film (MRF) that enables crack-free transfer onto porous supports and stable operation under pressurization. Here, we introduce a fluorinated porous organic polymer (FPOP) that provides the mechanical and thermal robustness needed to operate PG membranes at high temperature. The FPOP layer is deposited directly on PG from a molecular precursor solution. Upon drying and thermal annealing, it develops into a continuous cross-linked film that conforms to PG, maintains strong adhesion, and helps to avoid crack formation during the transfer of PG to a macroporous support. The FPOP film exhibits a quasi-ordered structure, forms an interface with graphene, and remains stable under pressurized conditions up to 350 °C. FPOP-supported PG membranes exhibit selective gas transport at elevated temperature (350 °C) and maintain their performance during extended mixed-gas operation. The membranes retain selective transport after humid/oxidative exposure and ambient storage. Importantly, the porous FPOP can regulate transport through enlarged nonselective graphene defects, thereby improving the selectivity of PG membranes. Overall, we demonstrate FPOP as a thermally stable MRF platform that enables crack-free PG transfer, high-temperature operation, and regulation of nonselective transport pathways.

items.title:
Nano-Bioadhesives
for Gastrointestinal Hemostasis
and Healing: Integrating Artificial Intelligence for Precision Design
and Application
items.abstract: Abstract Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding and mucosal injury remain clinically challenging because most bioadhesives lose performance under acidic, enzymatic, and peristaltic conditions. Nanotechnology has advanced adhesive design by enhancing mechanical integrity, degradation control, and antimicrobial activity; however, translating these gains into consistently favorable clinical outcomes is still difficult. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a route to accelerate and derisk development. Here, we identify predictive, multiobjective materials design as the AI domain most critical for GI nanobioadhesives because adhesion, hemostasis, degradation, biosafety, and healing must be optimized simultaneously. Predictive modeling, molecular simulations, and high-throughput experimentation enable rational control of adhesion strength, degradation kinetics, and biocompatibility, while machine-learning models expedite the discovery of optimal polymeric nanoparticle formulations. Emerging strategies such as digital twins and closed-loop optimization further support patient-specific and adaptive adhesive systems. By integrating AI-guided design with nanotechnology platforms, next-generation GI bioadhesives could unify rapid hemostasis, antimicrobial protection, and regenerative functions, thereby improving reliability and clinical translation. This review outlines the synergy between AI and nanotechnology and highlights priorities for advancing GI adhesive therapies from bench to bedside.

items.title:
Zooming into the
Cytoskeleton: Nanodefect-Initiated
Microtubule Catastrophe Filmed by High-Speed Atomic Force Microscopy
items.abstract: Abstract Microtubule catastrophe is widely attributed to an end-driven loss of the GTP cap, implying that structural failure is confined to filament termini. Here, we show that this view is incomplete. Using high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM), we directly visualize nanoscale structural failure in paclitaxel-treated microtubules in real time. We identify spontaneous lattice nanodefects that emerge within the filament shaft and act as internal initiation sites for disassembly. These defects arise from localized protofilament decoupling and lattice strain accumulation, which disrupt the cooperative interactions within the microtubule wall. Once a critical threshold is reached, these sites nucleate disassembly that propagates as distinct collapse trajectories, including bidirectional spreading from intralattice defects and inward convergence from opposing ends, in addition to classical end-initiated depolymerization. Rather than uniformly stabilizing the lattice, paclitaxel maintains microtubules in a metastable state in which internal stress heterogeneity persists and enables defect-driven failure. Our results establish lattice decoupling as a primary structural trigger of microtubule catastrophe and redefine it as a defect-mediated, spatially encoded transition. These findings provide a nanoscale mechanistic framework for understanding heterogeneous responses to microtubule-targeting chemotherapeutics, suggesting that drug resistance may arise from modulation of lattice integrity and defect propagation rather than drug binding alone.

items.title:
Sliding
Ferroelectric Tunnel Junctions with Ultrahigh
Tunneling Electroresistance
items.abstract: Abstract Sliding ferroelectricity in van der Waals materials offers an appealing route to compact, nonvolatile, atomically thin ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs) with low switching energy, but achieving a large resistance contrast in such devices remains challenging because the weak out-of-plane polarization provides limited electrostatic modulation of the tunneling barrier. Here, using bilayer rhombohedral MoS2 as a sliding ferroelectric barrier, we demonstrate room-temperature sliding FTJs with tunneling electroresistance (TER) values exceeding 3.2 × 105. We show that this giant contrast arises from a height–width hybrid tunneling mechanism, in which polarization reversal simultaneously modulates the tunnel barrier height and switches a nanoscale interfacial depletion width, yielding exponential amplification of the tunneling contrast. Spatially resolved tunneling, piezoresponse, and Raman measurements reveal that local strain, rather than ferroelectric domain walls, dominates spatial variations in the TER by modulating the sliding ferroelectric dipole strength, the OFF-state depletion width, and the resulting TER amplification. Finally, planar 3R-MoS2 FTJs further validate this mechanism by exhibiting a TER above 105, a switching energy density of several fJ μm–2, and projected endurance beyond 106. These results provide fundamental insight into the nanoscale electrostatics in sliding ferroelectric-based tunnel junctions while pointing toward low-energy, high-contrast nonvolatile memory applications.

items.title:
Peptide
Coacervates with Cathepsin B-Triggered
Intracellular Cargo Release
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding the molecular grammar of liquid–liquid phase separation has enabled rational design of peptide coacervates as intracellular therapeutic carriers with tunable viscoelasticity, controlled cargo partitioning, and enhanced cellular uptake. However, sequence-level determinants governing coacervate disassembly remain poorly characterized. Encoding protease-recognition motifs within phase-separating peptides offers controlled, localized catalytic disassembly without requiring global perturbation via macroscopic triggers such as pH, ionic strength, temperature, or redox potential. Yet, enzymatic cleavage of coacervates is spatially biased and constrained by limited enzyme partitioning, restricted substrate accessibility, and altered kinetics relative to the dilute phase. Here, we test whether the lysosomal protease cathepsin B (CatB)─often upregulated in cancer cells─acts on coacervates assembled from phase-separating peptides encoding CatB-recognition motifs to enable intracellular cargo release in cancer cells. Common CatB-recognition motifs (GFLG and EVCit), developed for linker-based delivery systems under dilute conditions, preserved phase separation but exhibited poor CatB-triggered cleavage and cargo release. In contrast, a de novo motif, FRFV, designed from CatB subsite preferences, retained catalytic activity as confirmed by mass spectrometry and enabled protease-triggered cargo release in vitro and in cancer cells. Thus, protease-recognition motifs require reevaluation within dense-phase architectures to enable efficient intracellular cargo release through coacervate disassembly.

items.title:
Stress-Resilient
Skin Wound Protection via Bioinspired
Dual-Tier Architecture
items.abstract: Abstract Mechanical tension destabilizes wound repair and drives fibrotic progression, yet current protection materials rarely reconcile the contrasting requirements of load-bearing and interfacial adaptability. To address this persistent mechanical conflict, a dual-tier hydrogel architecture was developed by integrating a stiff protective tier with a compliant adaptive tier to redistribute deformation and maintain secure adhesion under load. The stiff tier intercepted external stress, the compliant tier accommodated deformation, and dual interfaces regulated force transmission to avoid stress concentration on wound sites. The construct preserved bioadhesion energy exceeded that of various commercial products, and ex vivo distraction tests showed controlled wound opening with deformation control ratios of 70–90% compared with 30–40% for the commercial Mepiform patch. In a tension-driven murine model, the dual-tier patch demonstrated a reduction in scar area of approximately 97%, restored collagen angular dispersion and fiber diameter toward unwounded patterns, and lowered proliferative, inflammatory, immune, and mechanotransduction signals with significant improvement over Mepiform. These findings underscore the value of architecture-driven material design for achieving stable wound protection under fluctuating mechanical conditions.

items.title: Issue Publication Information
Issue Editorial Masthead

Low Energy Excitations
in a [4]Triangulene Honeycomb
Antiferromagnet
items.abstract: Abstract Carbon-based synthetic lattices offer a versatile platform for the realization and control of correlated quantum effects at the nanoscale. Advances in on-surface synthesis have enabled the fabrication of increasingly complex molecular frameworks, providing opportunities for the exploration and engineering of custom tailored electronic and magnetic phases. Here, we report the design, on-surface synthesis, and characterization of a two-dimensional (2D) covalent organic framework (COF) assembled from D3h symmetric S = 3/2 [4]triangulene building blocks arranged in a honeycomb structure. Combined scanning probe microscopy and spectroscopy, corroborated by first-principles density functional theory (DFT) and GW calculations, establish an antiferromagnetic (AFM) insulating ground state. Low energy spectroscopy resolves spin excitations in both one-dimensional (1D) chains and extended 2D networks, providing direct insight into the emergent spin dynamics and establishing a modular platform to explore quantum magnetism in a π-conjugated organic system.

items.title:
Crown Ether-Functionalized
Covalent Organic Framework
Membranes for Precise Monovalent Cation Separation
items.abstract: Abstract Membrane-based separation offers a highly promising paradigm for the precise extraction of monovalent cations, which is critical for bioinspired engineering and advanced ion-separation applications. However, efficient discrimination among these cations remains profoundly challenging owing to their nearly identical valence states and comparable subnanometer hydrated diameters. Herein, we report the rational design and fabrication of crown ether (CE)-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF) membranes that achieve efficient mono/monovalent cation separation while maintaining rapid ion transport. The integration of CE moieties into the framework architectures plays a dual role: narrowing the channels to the angstrom scale while simultaneously serving as specific recognition sites for target cations through host–guest interactions. Consequently, the optimal CE-functionalized TFP-TDA-2 COF membrane exhibits an exceptional K+/Na+ selectivity of 64 with a K+ permeation rate of 41.2 mmol m–2 h–1, surpassing previously reported COF membranes. Theoretical simulations reveal that, while the COF channels provide rapid transport pathway, synergistic CE recognition substantially lowers the thermodynamic dehydration and translocation barrier for K+ relative to Na+. Furthermore, the modular nature of this strategy enables the specific recognition of other targeted cations through precise side-chain engineering by covalently anchoring different crown ether derivatives. This study demonstrates an effective structural engineering strategy for efficient monovalent cation separation, offering an approach for the development of next-generation, single-ion-selective membranes for broad real-world applications.

items.title:
Monolithic
3D Stacked Carbon Nanotube/Indium–Tin–Oxide
Complementary Transistors for High-Frequency Logic and Sense Amplifier
Integration with Memory
items.abstract: Abstract Complementary field-effect transistors (CFETs) maximize 3D integration density but face two fundamental bottlenecks: the stringent thermal budget of silicon-based sequential stacking and the inherent electrical mismatches in homogeneous material systems. To overcome these challenges, we demonstrate a monolithic 3D-stacked heterogeneous CFET architecture integrating back-end-of-line (BEOL)-compatible p-type carbon nanotube (CNT) and n-type indium–tin–oxide (ITO) channels. Both materials exhibit high carrier mobility and low-temperature process, which simultaneously resolve the bipolar transport disparity and mitigate thermal degradation. Consequently, the resulting CFET inverters exhibit favorable statistical uniformity and symmetric transfer characteristics, enabling the fabrication of versatile logic gates. Besides, a 5-stage ring oscillator (RO) achieves a high frequency of 334 MHz, with a 0.3 ns stage delay, demonstrating potential applications of CFET in high-speed digital circuits. Furthermore, bridging logic and memory, a CFET-based sense amplifier (SA) is integrated with an ITO-based planar capacitorless (2T0C) dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) cell. This hybrid system achieves data write/read operations and signal amplification, providing an architectural platform for next-generation ultradense 3D logic and memory systems.

items.title:
Multi-Terminal Reconfigurable
Silver Nanowire Network
for Associative-Learning-Like Response and Path Optimization
items.abstract: Abstract Emulating associative-learning-like responses and hardware-state-guided path optimization using reconfigurable physical networks offers a promising route toward adaptive neuromorphic hardware. Herein, a multiterminal reconfigurable Ag nanowire network is presented. This network exhibits a honeybee-inspired associative learning response and provides experimentally measured conductance states for ant colony pathfinding simulations. By employing a multielectrode array to deliver synchronized odor-like and nectar-like electrical stimuli, the network dynamically reconfigures its conductance pathways in a training-dependent manner. Following training, the postsynaptic current increases by 2 orders of magnitude after the first learning cycle and reaches a sustained suprathreshold level after three cycles, demonstrating that the device can simulate long-term memory consolidation. Software simulations further show that the experimentally measured Ag NW learning states can modulate a handwritten digit recognition model through a hardware-derived memory gate, enabling conditioned-stimulus-only recognition to improve progressively during associative learning. Furthermore, specific stimulation protocols reconfigure the conductance pathways of the Ag NW network, and the resulting hardware conductance states are used as weighting factors in ant-colony-inspired software simulations. With these hardware-derived weights, the simulated optimal path length is reduced from 1643.54 units to 1415.18 units, corresponding to an improvement of approximately 14% in path-search efficiency. This study highlights the potential of integrating reconfigurable physical networks with bioinspired algorithms, offering a hardware-software codesign platform for future adaptive neuromorphic systems.

items.title: Nanomesh Bioelectronics Inspired by Basement Membrane for In Situ Monitoring of Oxidative Stress at the Alveolar-Capillary Barrier
items.abstract: Abstract Inhalable pollutants can cross the alveolar-capillary barrier into the bloodstream, and pollutant-elicited oxidative stress at this barrier is a well-recognized pathogenic driver of systemic diseases. However, direct quantification of oxidative stress at the dynamic alveolar-capillary barrier has remained unattainable due to the lack of sensing tools, substantially limiting our understanding of pollutant toxicology and associated pathogenesis. Herein, we develop nanomesh bioelectronics that simultaneously function as a basement membrane analogue and an electrochemical sensor. The bioelectronic interface recapitulates the native basement membrane’s nanofibrous architecture, ultrathin geometry, high permeability, and mechanical properties, while exhibiting stable electrochemical responses to H2O2 under cyclic stretching. When incorporated into lung-on-a-chip, the bioelectronics enable simultaneous reconstruction of the alveolar-capillary barrier and in situ quantification of oxidative stress during respiratory stretching. Using benzo[a]pyrene as a model carcinogenic pollutant, we uncover a biphasic regulatory role of vascular endothelium: an intact endothelium reinforces epithelial resistance to pollutant stimuli, whereas endothelial dysfunction converts protective crosstalk into pathological oxidative amplification. Rat models further confirm that systemic vascular health shapes pulmonary responses to environmental insults. The proposed bioelectronics provide a versatile tool for engineering biological barriers and dissecting intercompartmental crosstalk.

items.title:
Optical
Fourier Surfaces for Free-Space Computer-Generated
Holography
items.abstract: Abstract Computer-generated holography can shape electromagnetic fields by encoding wavefront information in nanostructured surfaces. However, despite significant progress, hologram designs for visible and near-infrared wavelengths remain largely limited by fabrication constraints. Most implementations rely on lithographic methods that produce discretized surfaces that do not match the wave nature of light. Further advances would benefit from accurate, continuous (grayscale) control of interfacial profiles, which would allow straightforward design principles from Fourier optics to be applied. In this work, we introduce optical Fourier surfaces as a versatile, intuitive platform for free-space computer-generated holograms. Exploiting these arbitrarily wavy surfaces, we demonstrate three different design strategies for computer-generated holography. First, we use an analytical linear design approach based on sinusoidal lenses and gratings as fundamental holographic building blocks. Second, we enhance diffraction efficiencies through an iterative Fourier-transform algorithm. Finally, we extend our framework with differentiable inverse design, creating wavelength-multiplexed holograms that reconstruct distinct diffraction responses in a predefined image plane. Our results combine advanced thermal scanning-probe lithography with flexible design strategies to create useful structures for photonic applications, particularly in settings where rapid prototyping is crucial.

items.title:
Achieving
Robust Ferroelectric Properties of Hf0.6Zr0.4O2 Thin Films through the Pseudofield-Inducing
Effect of Al0.85Sc0.15N Bottom Electrode
items.abstract: Abstract Although ferroelectric (FE) Zr-doped HfO2 (HZO) is a promising material for ferroelectric random-access memory (FeRAM), achieving high remnant polarization (Pr) with a low coercive field (EC) at film thicknesses ≲10 nm remains challenging. This work demonstrates a multifunctional bottom electrode (BE) strategy by inserting a pristine, down-poled ferroelectric Al1–xScxN (ASN) layer into the BE, thereby inducing high mechanical stress and an internal field during HZO crystallization. The pristine down-polarization of ASN increased the c-axis preference of the overlying HZO film, as indicated by the contrast in the electrical characteristics and surface potential responses depending on the ASN poling direction. The ASN-containing BE imposes additional in-plane tensile stress on HZO due to ASN’s low thermal expansion coefficient, facilitating orthorhombic phase formation. Consequently, 9 nm-thick HZO on the ASN-containing BE exhibits a large 2Pr of 81 μC/cm2 by conventional polarization-electric field (P-E) measurement and 68 μC/cm2 by positive-up-negative-down (PUND) compared with that of the TiN BE (43 μC/cm2, and 41 μC/cm2) with a pristine negative-bias imprint. These effects enable a high 2Pr/EC ratio without a significant increase in EC after wake-up, resulting in faster switching characteristics. Furthermore, it also enables the 5 nm-thick HZO film to overcome the pristine pinched hysteresis associated with tetragonal-phase stabilization, thereby achieving robust ferroelectric performance while suppressing wake-up behavior.

items.title:
Carbene-Mediated
Stabilization of Reactive Copper–Chalcogenide
Clusters: Defining the Operational Limits of Strong-Field Ligands
in Multinuclear Nanoassemblies
items.abstract: Abstract Atomic precision in metal–sulfur assemblies offers a transformative pathway to programmable nanomaterials, with applications spanning energy-efficient optoelectronics to highly selective CO2 reduction catalysis. However, the inherent lability of the metal–sulfur bond remains a formidable barrier to the rational design of robust frameworks. While strong-field ligands such as cyclic (alkyl)(amino)carbenes (CAACs) are gold-standard scaffolds for stabilizing reactive monometallic centers, their impact on the structural fidelity of multinuclear clusters remains elusive. Herein, we report a combined experimental and theoretical investigation of a CAAC-supported Cu8(μ3-S)4 cluster─a high-impact prototype for metal-chalcogenide systems with relatively weak metal–sulfur bonds. Through electrochemical and protonation studies, we demonstrate that while the potent σ-donor ability of the CAAC ligand successfully enforces solution integrity and thermal resilience, the structural boundaries of the multinuclear scaffold under chemical stress are ultimately governed by the core topology and metal–sulfur bond lability rather than local metal–ligand bonding. In-depth density functional theory (DFT) analysis demonstrates that while the CAAC ligands actively strengthen the peripheral Cu–S bonds via a pronounced inverse trans influence, the trigonal pyramidal (μ3-S) motifs remain vulnerable to proton-induced bond labilization and oxidative S–S coupling. Our findings establish that the design rules for multinuclear assemblies diverge fundamentally from monometallic species: whereas CAACs successfully passivate peripheral coordination sites to thermal decomposition, they do not preclude internal, core-mediated degradation pathways. These clear boundaries reveal that achieving structural durability in functional base metal–sulfur assemblies requires pairing strong local donors with supramolecular and/or multidentate ligand strategies designed explicitly to buttress the metal–sulfur core.

items.title:
Correction to “Cellular
Transmigration Increases
Nanoparticle Penetration Into Solid Tumors”

Unfolding
of Field-Free Spin–Orbit Torque Magnetization
Switching in a van der Waals Heterostructure
items.abstract: Abstract Heterostructures of 2D materials offer high tunability of magnetic properties, including current-induced magnetization switching by unconventional spin–orbit torques. The microscopic mechanisms governing spin-torque switching in van der Waals systems, however, remain insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate current-induced magnetization reversal in an Fe3GeTe2 (FGT) and WTe2 heterostructure using scanning harmonic magneto-optical Kerr effect microscopy. Spatially resolved magnetization maps show that field-free switching unfolds from asymmetric domain nucleation at the edges of the FGT flake, followed by domain wall propagation. This switching behavior is deterministic and bipolar, consistent with spin–orbit torques arising from the injection of both in-plane and out-of-plane spins from WTe2 into FGT. The critical currents for up-to-down and down-to-up switching differ because of asymmetric domain nucleation and directional domain wall pinning effects. Micromagnetic simulations reproduce the switching behavior observed experimentally, showing how the initial domain nucleation sites are determined by the sample geometry and combined influence of in-plane and out-of-plane spins and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Finally, by systematically varying the field-like and damping-like torque components and sweeping the spin polarization between in-plane and out-of-plane, we identify the torque configurations that yield the most efficient switching in van der Waals magnets with different shapes.

items.title:
Enhancing Capacitance
by Increasing Electric Double
Layer Disorder in Ionic Liquid Mixtures
items.abstract: Abstract Supercapacitors, possessing rapid charge–discharge time scales and cycle lifetimes, provide opportunities to mitigate fluctuations from intermittent energy sources. However, while supercapacitors exhibit lower energy densities to lithium-ion batteries, advancing supercapacitor energy density is necessary to improve their utility in applications requiring rapid operating time scales. Supercapacitor energy densities critically hinge on interfacial capacitances and electrolyte voltage windows. Ionic liquids have been heavily investigated as supercapacitor electrolytes due to promising properties like high electrochemical stability, nonflammability, and nonvolatility. Yet, energy densities of ionic liquid-derived supercapacitors are often limited by low interfacial capacitances due to pronounced ion–ion correlations. Here, we show capacitance can be significantly enhanced in ionic liquids over wide voltages by mixing ionic liquids to improve electric double layer entropy. Importantly, capacitance increases exhibited by mixtures persist over the entire electrochemical stability window, showing like-charged co-ions often play similar roles to oppositely charged counterions when determining double layer capacitance. By leveraging electrochemical impedance spectroscopy and surface forces measurements, we conclude that capacitive enhancements originate from changes in short-range nanostructures in ionic liquids, where atomic force microscopy measurements reveal that mixing ionic liquids results in more compact bound ion layers with increased disorder and compressibility. Notably, we find that long-range decay lengths are statistically similar between neat ionic liquids and an equimolar mixture at potentials where we report up to 150% capacitance enhancement, indicating decoupling between the bulk electrostatic decay length and interfacial capacitance. Overall, our results reveal that modulating compositional entropy of ionic liquid double layers provides avenues to increase supercapacitor energy densities and advance next-generation energy storage.

items.title:
Ferroelectric Switching
of Skyrmion Topology in 2D
Multiferroics
items.abstract: Abstract Deterministic switching of skyrmion topology is a central frontier in topological spintronics, yet current paradigms rely almost exclusively on dissipative-current-driven spin torques. Here, we propose a fundamentally distinct mechanism for the nonvolatile switching of the skyrmion topology in two-dimensional multiferroics. We reveal that the intrinsic magnetoelectric coupling intimately links the out-of-plane ferroelectric polarization to interlayer magnetic exchange. Consequently, an electric-field-driven polarization reversal deterministically converts the interlayer coupling between the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic states. This macroscopic exchange reversal directly flips the microscopic skyrmion core polarity and reverses its topological charge, thereby stabilizing the two electrically addressable topological phases. Guided by our established design principles, we rigorously validate this mechanism in a Co2CF2/MoN2 multiferroic heterostructure by using combined first-principles calculations and atomistic spin simulations. Our findings bypass the limitations of continuous current injection, establishing a robust physical framework for energy-efficient multiferroic topological spintronics.

items.title:
Frustrated Lewis
Pair Engineered Metal–Organic
Frameworks for Enhancing Peroxidase Mimicking
items.abstract: Abstract Natural enzymes achieve catalytic efficiency through the synergistic coupling of substrate activation and the efficient utilization of reactive intermediates. However, current nanozyme design paradigms focus predominantly on modulating substrate activation while overlooking the efficient utilization of highly reactive intermediates─a limitation that severely constrains substantial gains in catalytic activity. Inspired by the frustrated Lewis pair (FLP) composition of Fe2+ and tetrahydrobiopterin in tryptophan hydroxylase, we propose an FLP engineering approach to integrate 2,5-pyrazine-dicarboxylic acid (Pz) into the Materials of Institut Lavoisier-101 metal–organic framework (MIL-101(Fe)-H MOF) to construct MIL-101(Fe)-Pz MOF. This construct features pyrazine-nitrogen as a Lewis base and unsaturated Fe sites as Lewis acids. Compared with the Lewis acid-only MIL-101(Fe)-H MOF control, the as-fabricated FLP substantially accelerated the peroxidase-like activity of MIL-101(Fe)-Pz MOF, increasing the maximum reaction velocity by 4.83-fold when H2O2 was used as the substrate and by 17.88-fold when 3,3′,5,5′-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) was used as the substrate. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses revealed that the distinct electronic interactions within FLP facilitate electron transfer, promote H2O2 activation, improve hydroxyl radical utilization, and lower the reaction energy barrier, thereby boosting the reaction kinetics. This work highlights the indispensable role of substrate activation and active intermediate utilization in enhancing nanozyme performance and also provides guidance for the design of next-generation bioinspired nanozymes.

items.title:
Experimental
Approaches for Quantifying the Desolvation
Step in Aqueous Reaction Equilibria
items.abstract: Conspectus This Account focuses on recent studies aimed at detecting and quantifying changes in surface hydration, as needed to define the contribution of water in biothermodynamics. Solvation details are vital for the analysis of binding and conformational equilibria; knowledge of desolvation energies may improve the design of molecular structures and lead to therapeutics of higher specificity, in addition to elucidating the forces that drive all biomolecular interactions in a living cell. A central question for this field of research is the adequacy of the thermodynamic equation employed for describing reaction equilibria in water. We maintain that the classical equation represents an unbalanced reaction with regard to the solvent and, therefore, must be corrected by adding a term that accounts for changes in solvation when two surfaces make contact. The revised equation predicts that the equilibrium ratio of products to reactants (K) will not be constant with changes in concentration when the corresponding change in solvation energy (ΔGS) is significant in magnitude; if the sign of ΔGS is positive and unfavorable, the observed value of K should decrease with increasing reactant concentration, and, if the sign is negative and favorable, the observed value of K should increase. This conjecture leads to a straightforward experimental test of the equation that yields the change in solvation free energy per mole of product formed. The modified equilibrium expression has been corroborated by several model binding reactions in water using isothermal titration calorimetry to measure the equilibrium ratio as a function of concentration. This Account will discuss these results noting that, in all cases thus far, the change in solvation energy is unfavorable when one of the binding surfaces contains a polar functional group. At the other end of the polarity spectrum, the observed equilibrium ratio is found to be constant with changing concentrations when two nonpolar surfaces are involved, suggesting ΔGS ≈ 0 for hydrophobic interactions. When viewed from the perspective of hydration thermodynamics, the hydrophobic effect may be more aptly named the “aqua indifferens” effect. Importantly, the solvent-balanced framework establishes a new path for interpreting the effects of secondary solutes on binding and conformational equilibria. We demonstrate that favorable secondary solutes decrease the desolvation penalty, ΔGS, by reducing the average free energy of the bulk solvent, whereas unfavorable solutes increase the desolvation penalty. Overall, this body of work suggests a fundamental shift in the application of thermodynamics to aqueous reaction equilibria.

items.title:
Synthesis of
Axially, Planar and Helically Chiral
Molecules via Rhodium-Catalyzed Asymmetric C–H Functionalization
Reactions
items.abstract: Conspectus An important goal of organic synthesis is to explore chemical space by efficiently building up molecular diversity. Axially, planar and helically chiral skeletons are prevalent in pharmaceuticals and natural products, and their significance is underscored by their widespread applications as privileged scaffolds of chiral ligands and catalysts in asymmetric catalysis. Therefore, the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of these chiral architectures has garnered considerable attention and inspired a broad range of synthetic methodologies. Among the various synthetic strategies developed, transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric C–H functionalization has emerged as an atom- and step-economical approach. In this Account, we present a concise review of the enantioselective synthesis of different types of chiral molecules, including biaryl atropisomers, helically chiral compounds, planar chiral ferrocenes, and planar chiral macrocycles, by our group via rhodium-catalyzed asymmetric C–H functionalization reactions. Since our initial reports in 2014, we have introduced several strategies based on both Rh(I) and Rh(III) catalytic systems. For Rh(I) catalysis, TADDOL-derived chiral monophosphonite ligands were utilized to achieve enantioselective C–H arylation of 1-arylisoquinolines and planar chiral ferrocenes. For Rh(III) catalysis, chiral cyclopentadienyl (Cp) rhodium complexes, including the Cramer-type catalysts and our newly designed 1,1′-spirobiindane-derived chiral CpRh(III) complexes (SCpRh), were utilized to enable a diverse array of axially chiral 1-arylisoquinolines through atroposelective C–H arylation, alkylation, alkynylation, olefination, cyanation, indolylization, and selenylation. The same Rh(III) catalytic system enables, via C–H activation and annulation with alkynes, the synthesis of biaryl atropisomers, planar chiral metallocenes, isoquinoline-based macrocyclic atropisomers and helical azoniahelicenes. We anticipate that rhodium-catalyzed asymmetric C–H functionalization will be widely applicable in the construction of synthetically useful axially, planar, and helically chiral compounds. The development of more diverse and efficient methods for synthesizing these chiral architectures will continue to grow, opening new avenues for asymmetric catalysis, natural product synthesis, pharmaceutical science, and materials science.

items.title:
N-Heterocyclic Carbene (NHC)-Catalyzed Synthesis
of Atropisomers Beyond C–C Axial Chirality
items.abstract: Conspectus Axial chirality is a prominent stereochemical element found in various natural products, pharmaceuticals, ligands, catalysts, and functional materials. While substantial progress has been made in the atroposelective synthesis of C–C axially chiral biaryls, the construction of atropisomers featuring C–N, C–O, and N–N chiral axes remains challenging owing to their lower rotational barriers and diminished configurational stability. In recent years, N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC) catalysis has emerged as a versatile platform for addressing these challenges, enabling the efficient and enantioselective synthesis of diverse atropisomeric architectures through unique activation modes and reaction pathways. This Account highlights advances in NHC-catalyzed synthesis of atropisomers beyond the traditional C–C axial chirality. The utilization of the unique reactivity modes of NHCs in Stetter reaction, (3 + 3) annulation, acid activation strategy, N-acylation, O-acylation, and imine umpolung have unlocked the access to these distinct atropisomeric motifs beyond the C–C chiral axis. In 2021, we have reported the NHC-catalyzed desymmetrization of prochiral N-aryl maleimides via a Stetter–aldol cascade/oxidation sequence, providing axially chiral N-aryl succinimides with excellent stereocontrol. DFT studies indicated that the aldol step proceeds without direct involvement of carbenes. Complementarily, kinetic resolution (KR) of racemic N-aryl aminomaleimides through NHC-catalyzed (3 + 3) annulation furnished highly enantioenriched products bearing both axial and central chirality. Subsequent NHC-catalyzed atroposelective amidation provided access to N-aryl phthalimides and maleimides via direct N–C(O) bond formation. More recently, we demonstrated NHC-catalyzed dynamic kinetic resolution (DKR) of cyclic imides having rotationally restricted C–N bond for the synthesis of C–N axially chiral pyridinones through (3 + 3) annulation. Subsequently, we turned our attention to the synthesis of N–N atropisomers where NHC-catalyzed atroposelective amidation has allowed the synthesis of N–N axially chiral 3-aminoquinazolinones in high yields and enantioselectivities. Furthermore, NHC-catalyzed atroposelective (3 + 3) annulations of indole- and pyrrole-derived enamines have been achieved providing structurally complex heterocycles with N–N axial and central chirality with excellent stereoselectivity and configurational stability. Later, this annulation strategy has been extended to the diastereo- and enantioselective synthesis of N–N axially chiral quinolinones and quinoxalinones. Finally, we demonstrated the synthesis of a highly challenging class of C–O atropisomers, the diaryl ethers because of the flexibility of the dual C–O axis. The NHC-catalyzed atroposelective desymmetrization strategy enabled the enantioselective synthesis of axially chiral diaryl ethers possessing dual C–O axes, delivering products with excellent enantioselectivities. Furthermore, we have also demonstrated a DKR approach that affords C–O axially chiral benzonitriles through NHC-catalyzed atroposelective umpolung of aldimines. It is reasonable to believe that the recent advances highlight the power of NHC catalysis in expanding axial chirality beyond classical C–C biaryl frameworks. By integrating mechanistic insights, catalytic innovation, and synthetic applications, this Account is likely to provide a comprehensive overview of NHC-enabled atroposelective synthesis and serves as a valuable guide for developing novel atropisomers with potential applications in asymmetric catalysis, drug discovery, and materials science.

items.title:
Gas-Phase Structural
Characterization of Metabolites
by Ion Mobility-Mass Spectrometry
items.abstract: Conspectus Metabolite structural characterization and annotation remain major challenges in mass spectrometry-based metabolomics. High-resolution mass spectrometry has greatly expanded metabolome coverage and sensitivity, but mass spectrometry alone often cannot distinguish isobaric and isomeric metabolites, particularly stereoisomers. Ion mobility–mass spectrometry (IM–MS) addresses this limitation by adding an orthogonal gas-phase separation dimension, in which differences in molecular size, shape, and conformation are translated into measurable differences in ion mobility. Importantly, collision cross-section (CCS) derived from ion mobility provides a quantitative molecular descriptor that complements mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio, retention time, and MS/MS information for metabolite characterization and annotation. In this Account, we describe the evolution of IM–MS from an additional separation dimension toward a unique technology for gas-phase structural characterization of complex metabolome. We first examine conventional and emerging ion mobility technologies that enhance gas-phase resolving power and enable the separation of structurally related metabolites and isomers. We then discuss CCS measurement, experimental databases, computational prediction, and chemical derivatization strategies that extend ion mobility-based structural characterization to increasingly complex and challenging metabolite isomers. As the dimensionality of liquid chromatography (LC)–IM–MS increases, computational strategies are developed to preserve and integrate m/z, retention time, CCS, and MS/MS information rather than reducing mobility data to conventional features. Finally, we examine the extension of IM–MS to spatial metabolomics, where ion mobility-resolved structural information is integrated with metabolite localization across tissues. We further discuss its application to single-cell metabolomics, where IM–MS enables the resolution of molecular heterogeneity at the single-cell level. Looking forward, establishing CCS as a standardized and transferable structural descriptor, while balancing resolving power, acquisition speed, and metabolome coverage, will be critical for the continued advancement of IM–MS. Integrating multidimensional IM–MS data with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) approaches may further improve evidence-based structural annotation. Ultimately, IM–MS has the potential to shift metabolomics from detecting more molecular features toward defining molecular structures in their biological context.

items.title:
Nonreductive
Catalytic Cyclizations of Carbon Dioxide
into Synthons for Fine-Chemical, Pharmaceutical, and Polymer Applications
items.abstract: Conspectus Nature enables the transformation of carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen via photosynthesis representing a crucial chemical process for life on earth. This carbon fixation process also helps to balance the global carbon cycle controlling the uptake of carbon from the atmosphere. Ever since the industrial revolution, anthropogenic carbon emissions have increased at such a pace resulting in an imbalance of the carbon cycle and, as a consequence, effects known as global warming and the occurrence of more extreme weather patterns. The “excess” of carbon dioxide is commonly perceived as waste, with little to no value to humanity. Thus, ideally technologies able to transform this waste carbon into value-added compounds and materials would be economically of interest to various communities. The principal technology to complement the chemical diversification that Nature can provide for carbon dioxide conversion is catalysis. Catalysis offers an approach to activate substrates in different ways building on diverse reactivity principles and contemplating on the possibility to activate CO2 directly or the coreactant. This includes the use of Brønsted or Lewis bases, transition metals, photo- and organo-catalysis, offering us a wide variety of activation modes. In this Account, we feature our extensive efforts in the area of catalytic carbon dioxide conversion with a particular emphasis on the activation of cyclic ethers and epoxy alcohols/amines used as partnering reagents. These two substrate classes require different chemical environments and thus the selection of the catalyst, additive and the reaction conditions (solvent, temperature, pressure) are crucial to control the process outcomes in terms of chemo- and stereoselectivity, and activity. The modular character of these coreagents will be highlighted together with the specific design features of the catalytic process, as to offer not only an overall good performance but also using cheap, attractive and easy-to-construct catalysts that mediate the straightforward activation of epoxides/oxetanes, and/or epoxy alcohols/amines. The latter category of precursors embeds two distinct functional groups (an oxirane flanked by either an alcohol or amine) and thus provides more ample opportunities for catalytic activation. Besides the different substrate categories, our focus was initially on improving the catalytic activity under metal and metal-free catalysis, delineating the relationship between the structure, functionality and substitution degree of cyclic ethers and how these features affect the catalytic coupling with carbon dioxide. As soon as we realized the limiting nature of these coupling reactions, especially in terms of the steric requirements, we turned our attention to epoxy alcohols/amines as alternative precursors. These complementary precursors provided new entries to otherwise difficult or impossible to prepare heterocycles with high (stereochemical) control. Moreover, the manifold by which these transformations take place were studied in detail and revealed the unique intermediacy of a long-thought elusive hemicarbonate species, which helped to advance a whole range of additional CO2 conversions. Closely associated with these findings are the development of new synthetic procedures for larger-ring carbonates and carbamates (ring size ≥ 6) that provide synthons of value for fine chemical/pharmaceutical and polymer applications. Over the past decade, our research on nonreductive catalytic carbon dioxide valorization has resulted in access to a significantly larger area of chemical space with a main focus on the creation of CO2-derived heterocycles. This chemistry should be both inspiring and synthetically useful for various communities, including those developing sustainable carbon recycling methods, homogeneous catalysis and alternative polymer development, going thus beyond the preparation of the heterocycles themselves.

items.title:
From In-Vitro
Protein Assembly to In-Situ Functional
Analysis: Cell-Permeable Synthetic Protein Probes for Exploring Ubiquitination
and PTM Biology in Native Cellular Environments
items.abstract: Conspectus Post-translational modifications (PTMs) are mainly low-abundance, transient, and spatiotemporally regulated molecular events that govern protein function across nearly all cellular processes, including protein degradation, inflammatory signaling, DNA damage repair, and chromatin regulation. Recent advances in genetic code expansion and proximity labeling have substantially expanded the toolkit for studying PTM-mediated processes in live cells. However, these approaches typically rely on genetic manipulation, which limits their application in primary cells, hard-to-transfect cell lines, clinical specimens, and other native cell systems (genetically unmodified live cells) where minimal perturbation is essential. The continued development of chemical protein synthesis has made it possible to access structurally defined PTM-modified protein tools with extraordinary precision. Yet, the central challenge for their in-vivo application is no longer simply the preparation of defined proteoforms, but rather how to deliver these in-vitro-assembled protein tools into native cells in an active form and translate them into functionally interpretable biological signals. In this Account, we summarize a series of studies carried out in our laboratory since 2020, organized around the theme of “chemical synthesis in vitro ─ delivery into live cells ─ functional analysis in situ”. By combining solid-phase peptide synthesis, protein segment ligation, and enzymatic modification, we have introduced precisely defined PTMs, photo-cross-linking groups, and affinity handles into ubiquitin (Ub) and histone PTM probes. For relatively small and structurally stable tools (e.g., mono-Ub, di-Ub, and histone-tail probes), covalent conjugation with cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) enables efficient delivery into native cells, allowing in-situ interrogation of Ub writers, erasers, and modification-dependent protein interaction networks. When the probe architecture expands to more-complex and conformationally sensitive species, such as E2–Ub conjugates, we developed a noncovalent CPP cluster assembly strategy to increase the local positive charge density of proteins and to minimize the interference of CPP conjugation with protein conformation and target recognition. This approach enabled the delivery of E2–Ub structure-mimetic probes into live cells and the mapping of stimulus-dependent E2–E3 interaction networks in situ. Through these case studies, we emphasize that the design of cell-permeable synthetic PTM probes should not only consider how to obtain structurally defined proteoforms, but also take into account compatible delivery strategies and intracellular function maintenance at the probe construction stage, so as to advance synthetic protein tools beyond “structurally precise assembly” toward “functional interrogation in native cells”.

items.title:
Dancing with
Nitro Groups: Synthesis and Structures
of Fully Nitrated Compounds
items.abstract: Conspectus Full nitration increases oxygen content but also intensifies electron withdrawal, steric congestion, and electrostatic repulsion, making further substitution difficult and often reducing chemical or thermal stability. Fully nitrated compounds are therefore more than candidate oxidizers or explosives. They provide demanding molecular models for understanding how multiple strongly electron-withdrawing groups reshape reactivity, bond polarization, molecular geometry, and crystal packing. Their stability is also multidimensional. A compound may resist thermal decomposition yet remain susceptible to water, moist air, or light, making chemical robustness as important as decomposition temperature and mechanical sensitivity. For the purposes of this Account, fully nitrated compounds are molecular scaffolds in which all substitutable positions of the parent framework are occupied by nitro or nitro-bearing functionalities. Locally edited derivatives and ionic assemblies are discussed as related polynitro systems. At the molecular level, alternating nitro and nitroamino groups introduce hydrogen-bond donors and modify electron delocalization. TNTNB thereby achieves markedly improved resistance to water, acids, and bases relative to hexanitrobenzene, whereas DNTP illustrates how the same substitution concept can increase packing efficiency and crystal density, albeit with a thermal-stability penalty. Studies of octanitropyrazoles and decanitrobipyrazoles further show that the attainable degree of nitration cannot be described by a universal numerical ceiling. Substitution sequence, relative positions, and backbone geometry determine whether densely nitrated groups can be accommodated. These principles culminated in BITE-202, a bitriazole carrying 12 nitro groups that shows no detectable changes after 180 days in water and decomposes at 164 °C. Its behavior is consistent with greater separation of neighboring substituents, a planar conjugated backbone, and a more uniform electrostatic-potential distribution. Full nitration can also provide a platform for functions beyond maximizing oxygen content. Using fused BITE-203 as a stable reference scaffold, replacement of one ring-bound nitro group by an azide produced the azide-edited fused derivative FTT and introduced a locally distinct electrostatic region. Initiation experiments, rather than calculated energetic parameters alone, established the resulting functional change: β-FTT initiated cyclotrimethylenetrinitramine (RDX) with a reported minimum primary charge of 30 mg, whereas BITE-203 did not under the same conditions. Stabilization can then be extended beyond covalent structure into the lattice. Hydrogen-bonded frameworks encapsulate nitroformate, cationic metal–organic frameworks immobilize dinitramide or polynitroazolate counterions, and polynitro frameworks invert the conventional host–guest relationship. In the latter systems, an octanitro anionic framework adapts to incorporate hydrazinium and neutral hydrazine, retaining the neutral guest until framework decomposition and creating a self-redox energetic lattice. Together, these results establish a hierarchical design principle: the properties of fully nitrated compounds depend not only on how many nitro groups are present but also on where they are placed, how their electronic effects are distributed, and what role they assume in the crystal lattice. Remaining challenges include the apparent density plateau of many neutral fully nitrated crystals, limited formulation-compatibility and aging data, and the need for scalable synthesis. Future progress will increasingly rely on crystal engineering and multicomponent assembly to coordinate energetic, stabilizing, and functional roles that a single molecule cannot readily satisfy.

items.title:
The Blessings
and Curses of Carbonaceous Deposits
in Ferrierite-Catalyzed Skeletal 1-Butene Isomerization
items.abstract: Conspectus Carbonaceous deposits have long been cast as the villain in zeolite catalysis: clogging pores, poisoning active sites, and gradually strangling catalyst performance during hydrocarbon conversion. Yet in a fascinating paradox, these same “poisons” can enhance catalyst performance in several industrially important reactions through synergistic interactions with zeolite acidity. Two prominent examples stand out: methanol-to-hydrocarbon/olefin reactions (MTH/MTO) and skeletal isomerization of linear butenes to iso-butene. Understanding this counterintuitive behavior has been a challenge in zeolite catalysis for decades. Skeletal butene isomerization requires a Brønsted acidic catalyst of intermediate acid strength. Zeolites with 10-ring (10-R) windows deliver high selectivity to iso-butene while suppressing oligomerization reactions. Ferrierite (framework type FER, with perpendicularly intersecting 8-R and 10-R channels) emerged as the superior catalyst, exhibiting the highest iso-butene selectivity and remarkable resistance to deactivation. The catalytic behavior of FER presents a remarkable contradiction. Within 24 h, around 6 wt % carbonaceous deposits accumulate and reduce the accessible micropore volume by up to 98%. One would expect immediate deactivation. Instead, catalyst performance continues to improve for up to 100 h, reaching peak activity only after the pores are effectively inaccessible. Deactivation finally occurs after 100–200 h on stream. This led Guisnet and colleagues in 1995 (Guisnet, M.; et al.J. Chem. Soc., Chem. Commun.1995, 31, 1685−1686, 10.1039/c39950001685.) to propose that carbocationic deposits themselves are the active species. However, the formation mechanism, precise location, and nature of these deposits and their interaction with zeolite acidity have remained points of debate. In this Account, we describe our systematic investigation of the reaction location, reactive species, and mechanisms governing catalyst activation and deactivation. Through probe molecule adsorption, operando spectroscopy, and operando titration experiments, we demonstrate that catalysis occurs at the pore mouths, where monoaromatic carbonaceous deposits interact with internal Brønsted acid sites. Rather than functioning as classic carbocations, these deposits are presumed to act as weakly acidic “proton-on-demand” reservoirs that mediate proton transfer to reactants outside the pores. This mechanism explains why conventional Brønsted acid sites become undetectable by ex situ methods after just 2 h, yet catalytic activity not only persists but improves far beyond this point. We further reveal that catalyst deactivation stems from external carbonaceous deposits that compress the zeolite structure and block the access to pore mouths, while internal deposits cause unit cell expansion. Oxidative regeneration successfully restores activity across multiple cycles without zeolite framework degradation, and strategic incomplete regeneration retaining around 1 wt % residual coke accelerates catalyst startup. These findings establish that effective skeletal butene isomerization requires a synergy between three elements: Brønsted acidity from the zeolite framework, structural confinement at the pore mouths, and carbonaceous deposits that mediate acid-catalyzed reactions from the inside of the zeolite outward. This understanding provides a framework for rational catalyst design and regeneration strategies, with implications extending to other zeolite-catalyzed hydrocarbon transformations where “beneficial coke” plays an activating role.

items.title:
From Membranes to Catalyst Layers: Molecular and Interfacial
Design of Anion-Exchange Polyelectrolytes
items.abstract: Conspectus Sustainable electrochemical energy conversion relies on functional materials that enable efficient transport while withstanding demanding operating environments. Anion-exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs) and anion-exchange membrane water electrolyzers (AEMWEs) are attractive platforms because their alkaline environments enable the use of nonprecious-metal catalysts and hydrocarbon-based polymer electrolytes. Anion-exchange polyelectrolytes (APEs) are central to these devices, serving as both free-standing anion-exchange membranes (AEMs) and catalyst-layer anion-exchange ionomers (AEIs). Although AEMs and AEIs share related polymer chemistries, their distinct operating environments and functional roles impose different requirements on molecular design. Our work on AEMs has focused on the coupled requirements of hydroxide transport, chemical stability, dimensional control, and mechanical durability. We first examined how polymer architecture and chain packing affect the formation of ion-conducting domains and confined transport environments. As conductivity improved, chemical degradation and mechanically induced failure became increasingly relevant, leading us to investigate cation stability, local electronic environments, dimensional constraints, and molecular-level stress dissipation. These studies showed that AEMs cannot be optimized on the basis of a single performance metric but instead require the coordinated regulation of ion transport, molecular stability, and mechanical response. We also extended this work to kilogram-scale polymer synthesis and continuous roll-to-roll membrane fabrication, where synthetic reproducibility and processing compatibility become additional constraints on molecular design. The requirements change when APEs are used as catalyst-layer ionomers. AEIs form nanometer-scale films around catalyst particles and must provide local hydroxide conduction while allowing water and gas transport, maintaining catalyst accessibility, and contributing to interfacial integrity. Our studies on AEIs have therefore examined multiphase transport, catalyst-ionomer interactions, interfacial adhesion, ionomer distribution, and catalyst-layer structure. Fluorinated and porous ionomers were used to regulate oxygen transport and gas-bubble removal, while conformational and interfacial design was used to reduce unfavorable catalyst-ionomer interactions. Further control of adhesion, ionomer-film organization, and catalyst immobilization showed that catalyst-layer performance also depends strongly on how the ionomer is distributed and organized during electrode formation. The studies discussed in this Account suggest that APE molecular design should be matched to the specific operating environment and functional role of the polymer within the membrane-electrode assembly. For AEMs, this includes balancing transport, durability, and manufacturability; for AEIs, it additionally requires control of local transport, catalyst interactions, and catalyst-layer organization.

items.title:
Cobalt-Catalyzed
Asymmetric Reductive Addition to
Carbonyls and Related Polarized Unsaturated Bonds
items.abstract: Conspectus The catalytic asymmetric construction of carbon–carbon bonds through the addition of carbon-based fragments to carbonyl compounds represents a fundamental transformation in organic synthesis, providing direct access to enantioenriched alcohols and amines that are ubiquitous structural motifs in pharmaceuticals, natural products, and functional molecules. Classical approaches typically rely on stoichiometric organometallic reagents, such as Grignard and organolithium reagents, which suffer from intrinsic limitations including air and moisture sensitivity, restricted functional group compatibility, and the requirement for preformed nucleophilic reagents. These drawbacks often increase synthetic complexity and reduce overall efficiency. Therefore, the development of catalytic asymmetric addition strategies that directly utilize stable and readily available precursors, while avoiding the preparation of sensitive organometallic intermediates, represents a longstanding and highly desirable goal. In this context, reductive coupling of organic halides as latent carbon nucleophiles offers an attractive alternative strategy. The seminal Nozaki–Hiyama–Kishi (NHK) reaction established the feasibility of directly employing organic halides in carbonyl additions; however, its reliance on chromium catalysis and stoichiometric metal reductants limits its practicality and broader application. Despite substantial advances, the development of general catalytic asymmetric methods capable of controlling radical-mediated carbon–carbon bond formation, particularly for constructing sterically congested tetrasubstituted stereocenters and contiguous stereogenic centers, remains a formidable challenge. The pursuit of sustainable and efficient catalytic processes has stimulated growing interest in earth-abundant first-row transition metals, among which cobalt has emerged as a particularly promising catalyst because of its rich single-electron redox chemistry, versatile coordination behavior, and intrinsic ability to mediate radical transformations. In this Account, we summarize our recent efforts in exploiting cobalt catalysis for the asymmetric reductive addition reactions of carbonyl-derived electrophiles and related polarized unsaturated systems with organic halides. This strategy, herein termed cobalt-catalyzed asymmetric reductive addition (CARA), utilizes readily available metal reductants under mild conditions and enables stereocontrolled radical addition processes directed by chiral cobalt complexes. Through this platform, we have developed modular approaches for the synthesis of diverse enantioenriched molecules, including amino acids, alcohols, amides, and sulfinamides, directly from readily available precursors. The development of this catalytic platform is discussed from three perspectives according to the reaction partners: (1) asymmetric reductive addition of simple organohalides for the construction of sterically demanding tetrasubstituted stereocenters; (2) enantioconvergent radical additions of racemic alkyl halides for the formation of contiguous stereogenic centers; and (3) reductive additions to other polarized unsaturated bonds, including isocyanates and sulfinylamines. Through extensive mechanistic investigations and DFT calculations, we have established that these transformations share a common radical addition pathway that is mechanistically distinct from the classical NHK reaction. We anticipate that this Account will stimulate further exploration of catalytic asymmetric reductive additions beyond those of conventional organometallic reagents. Continued development of cobalt-based radical platforms, together with advances in catalyst design and mechanistic understanding, may provide new solutions to longstanding challenges in stereoselective synthesis.

items.title:
Watching Chemistry Across Ages via Synchrotron Radiation
X-ray Microimaging Techniques
items.abstract: Conspectus While this special issue highlights various developments and applications of ultrafast imaging techniques, our focus here is on significantly longer time scales.
