Instead of examining dynamic systems at submillisecond resolutions, we explore how imaging methods can be utilized to analyze materials that are static at the time scale of data collection to trace reactions that occurred years, decades, or even centuries ago. Some ongoing reactions were quenched at the time of object creation and provide insights into the manufacturing processes used by past civilizations. Others have developed beyond the initial creation of the object, either through deliberate techniques, such as prolonged drying processes in paintings, or via incidental factors that may ultimately cause degradation. It is generally assumed that a rapid chemical reaction indicates artists’ intentions, while reactions occurring over months or years are typically viewed as alterations rather than intentional processes. Therefore, the rate of chemical reactions and their chronology is a crucial factor for scholars for distinguishing between original and nonoriginal materials. When analyzing fragments from cultural heritage objects, it is essential to assess not only the chemical nature of constituents but also their spatial distribution. This information can provide valuable insights into the physical and chemical processes involved in their formation (dissolution, diffusion, precipitation, reduction/oxidation...), as well as their potential origin. Synchrotron radiation (SR)-based micro-X-ray techniques offer both the chemical sensitivity and lateral resolution necessary for these applications. Below, we present three representative examples of study of chemical processes in heritage science. The first case demonstrates how a fragment from an artwork or a craft object can offer insights into the technical and artistic practices developed centuries ago. This is illustrated through studies that elucidate the physicochemical phenomena involved in the production of ancient ceramic glazes from various archeological contexts, such as brown glazes from Song China (10−12th-century) and luster glazes from the Abbasid Caliphate (8−13th-century). The second case examines the reactions involved in degradation phenomena, highlighting that certain heritage materials can be dynamic over periods of months or years. This example also emphasizes the importance of preparing and analyzing mock-up samples to study their evolution under natural and artificial aging conditions. This case is demonstrated with several examples of pigment degradation in paintings, with a focus on the emerald green used by James Ensor (1860–1949) and Robert Delaunay (1885–1941). Finally, the last case shows that, in some cases, attributing the origin of a chemical compound to a material intentionally used by the artist or to degradation phenomena is not straightforward. This is illustrated by the analysis of the origin of different unusual lead compounds detected in Leonardo da Vinci’s (1452−1519) and Rembrandt van Rijn’s (1606−1669) oil paintings.

items.title:
Chemical Ordering
of High-Entropy Nanomaterials for
Pathway-Directed Electrocatalysis
items.abstract: Conspectus High-entropy nanomaterials (HEMs) have emerged as versatile electrocatalytic platforms, because their multielement compositions provide diverse electronic configurations and coordination environments. However, high configurational complexity alone does not define the catalytic sites. Differences in elemental interactions and reduction kinetics can lead to segregation, phase separation, and structural heterogeneity, while random site occupation complicates the identification of catalytic sites and structure–activity correlations. High-entropy chemical ordering (HECO) addresses this challenge by organizing selected elements over defined spatial scales while retaining the multielement diversity. Drawing on our studies and related works, this Account describes three connected strategies. Electrospinning-enabled coordination confinement uses metal–polymer coordination and a polymer-derived carbon matrix to establish homogeneous multielement phases and regulate atomic transport. Directional atomic migration organizes selected elements at surfaces and interfaces through segregation, exsolution, and migration trapping. Diffusion-mediated bulk ordering produces preferential occupation of crystallographic sublattices and long-range ordered high-entropy intermetallics (HEIs). Local electronic polarization and intermediate adsorption help determine the elementary steps favored at different sites, while structural evolution under operating conditions can modify these relationships. Spatial organization can influence the intermediate transfer, reaction selectivity, and competing pathways. These considerations can guide the design of new surface-, interfacial-, and bulk-ordered HEMs with catalytic functions tailored to pathway-directed electrocatalysis.

items.title:
Planar-Chiral Cyclophanes: From Synthetic Strategies
to Configurational Stability Control
items.abstract: Conspectus Planar-chiral cyclophanes, which feature rigid aromatic ring conformations locked by flexible ansa chains, are structurally distinctive scaffolds found in bioactive natural products and pharmaceutical agents. They are also widely employed as privileged frameworks in asymmetric catalysis and as functional materials. The intrinsic conformational strain of these macrocycles confers enhanced configurational stability and improved cell permeability, which are properties that are particularly appealing for drug development and chiral material design. Despite their structural significance, precise control over the rotational barrier of the aromatic ring and reliable prediction of the conformational behavior of the ansa chain remain challenging, thereby impeding both methodological advancement and practical applications of planar-chiral cyclophanes. Consequently, the development of efficient asymmetric synthetic routes and systematic investigations of their configurational stability are of paramount importance. This Account reviews the asymmetric catalytic strategies reported by our group, which have enabled the synthesis of over 500 optically active cyclophanes. Type I and Type II cyclophanes, accessed by installing bulky substituents on the aromatic ring and shortening the ansa chain, have been efficiently assembled via Pd-catalyzed C–H activation, N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-catalyzed oxidative esterification, and chiral phosphoric acid (CPA)-catalyzed transfer hydrogenation. These methodologies exhibit broad substrate scope and are compatible with the late-stage structural diversification of drug molecules. Importantly, these studies elucidated the intrinsic relationship between the occurrence of planar chirality and two key determinants, namely, the steric hindrance of the aromatic substituents and the length of the ansa bridge. Our previous studies have also revealed that replacing the benzene ring with an indole ring further influences macrocyclic stability. Consequently, indole-based planar-chiral cyclophanes have been constructed via a Rh-catalyzed C–H activation/intramolecular oxidative annulation with high enantioselectivities. This approach enables macrocyclization, indole ring formation, and planar chirality control in a single step and is further applicable to the synthesis of challenging derivatives bearing all-carbon ansa chains. Subsequently, this Account examines the more structurally intricate Type III cyclophanes, revealing that a cooperative NHC/CPA-catalyzed macrolactonization and a CPA-catalyzed asymmetric macrocyclization enabled the formation of Type III cyclophanes bearing either a distal quaternary carbon stereocenter or a benzylic stereocenter on the ansa chain. Relative to their unsubstituted counterparts, these Type III cyclophanes exhibit higher rotational barriers. Notably, the introduction of a naphthyl group at the benzylic position permits a two-atom extension of the ansa chain without compromising the planar chirality. These findings reveal a dual dependence on the macrocyclic ring size and the position of the ansa chain substituents in these strained macrocyclic systems. In summary, this Account describes the precise construction of planar-chiral cyclophane scaffolds, which have been employed for the late-stage functionalization of bioactive molecules and successfully converted into novel chiral ligands and organocatalysts, thereby expanding the molecular repertoire of planar-chiral cyclophanes. More significantly, systematic investigations into configurational stability have revealed the cooperative influence of ring size, substituent steric hindrance, and the position of bulky substituents along the ansa chain on the rotational barrier. Collectively, the findings presented herein provide both a theoretical and practical foundation for the design of configurationally stable functional molecules with potential for future applications in asymmetric catalysis and beyond.

items.title:
The Long and
Lucky Road to Continuous Molecular Monitoring:
A Personal History of Electrochemical Aptamer-Based Sensors
items.abstract: Conspectus “Continuous molecular monitoring”, the ability to measure specific molecules in vivo, in real time, and at high frequency, could transform biomedical science and clinical practice. It could, for example, expose physiological dynamics that current “sample-then-analyze” paradigms obscure and improve the personalization of medical treatment, such as via feedback-controlled dosing that responds automatically to a patient’s changing physiology. Unlocking the full potential of continuous molecular monitoring requires a reagentless, reversible sensing mechanism both selective enough to deploy in the body and general enough to detect almost any analyte, a combination that had long proven elusive. Enzymatic sensors, for example, including the continuous glucose monitor, often work well in vivo but are limited to the small number of analytes for which suitably transforming enzymes exist. “Affinity biosensors”, in contrast, do not require the chemical transformation of their target, rendering them far more general. However, these have historically relied on adsorption to generate a signal (e.g., binding-induced changes in mass), a mechanism that performs poorly in unprocessed biofluids in vitro, much less in vivo. In this Account, I describe the near-30-year effort required to create and bring to clinical trials the first affinity biosensor architecture that performs well in vivo: electrochemical aptamer-based (EAB) sensors. To achieve this, EAB sensors use the binding-induced folding of an electrode-attached aptamer to alter the electron transfer kinetics of an attached redox reporter, a biomimetic signaling mechanism that is reagentless, spontaneously reversible, highly selective, and thus supports the real-time, in vivo measurement of almost any analyte for which a suitable aptamer is available. The road to EAB sensors began in the late 1990s with coincidentally convergent evidence suggesting that binding-induced folding is a near-universal property of destabilized proteins. Through the years-long contributions of many creative collaborators, this ultimately evolved into a nucleic acid-based, electrochemical biosensor architecture of broad utility. However, while even the first examples worked well in blood serum in vitro, EAB sensors drift when placed in the body, a problem ultimately solved by an engineering insight: the strongly frequency-dependent signaling of EAB sensors makes it possible to use them as their own drift-correcting reference. Leveraging this, in 2017, we demonstrated the first real-time, multihour in vivo monitoring of circulating drugs, an advance since extended to a wide range of analytes, to week-long in vivo operation and to feedback-controlled drug delivery. Given these unique measurement and control capabilities, EAB sensors can answer scientific questions and solve clinical problems that other technologies cannot. Seconds-resolved EAB sensor measurements are beginning to reveal, for example, previously unrecognized regulatory and clearance mechanisms and to reshape our understanding of drug and metabolite transport within the body, and the recent successful clinical trial of wearable EAB sensor “patches” supporting real-time measurements of the antibiotic vancomycin suggests the technology could similarly advance the measurement of drugs and biomarkers in healthcare. In short, I believe the continuous molecular monitoring that EAB sensors enable is poised to revolutionize our understanding of physiology and our ability to detect, monitor, and treat disease.

items.title:
Electrochemically
Generated Platform Oxidizers: An
Enabler for the Hydrogen Economy
items.abstract: Conspectus A highly attractive alternative anode reaction for electrochemical hydrogen production is the formation of platform oxidizers instead of molecular oxygen. These platform oxidants are high-value products and can therefore help cofinance hydrogen production. For most electro-organic reactions, the electrochemical conditions for hydrogen production would be incompatible, due to the high current density required, whereas the anodic production of platform oxidizers demonstrates technical complementarity. The broad range of applications for such platform oxidants and versatility allow for broad applications and large-scale use, including the synthesis of complex, high-value target products. For platform oxidizing agents that utilize elements that are in limited supply or pose environmental concerns, a closed-loop system must be established between their production and recycling. The recovery and regeneration of reaction waste into platform oxidizing agents must ensure that no cross-contamination occurs during the production of the target products and that these platform oxidizing agents can be transported and stored safely. Among many other platform oxidants, periodates and peroxodicarbonates are the most promising. This is because either a wide range of applications is already known, or the resulting byproducts serve as critical reactants for processes involving biogenic feedstock. Periodates have also been demonstrated to work in a closed-loop system: if these platform oxidants are used on-site, much simpler and easier-to-store starting compounds can be used, which then yield harmless coproducts that do not need to be recovered, e.g., alkali carbonates. In most cases, these platform oxidizers can be produced in an undivided electrolytic cell. This improves the energetics of the electrolytic reaction. The anodic reaction typically occurs at electrodes with a high overpotential for the oxygen-evolution reaction. Due to the temporary storage of the platform oxidants, this approach can contribute efficiently to the transformation of the chemical industry, as it allows safe hydrogen generation on demand and is tailored to the electricity supply.

items.title: Issue Publication Information
Issue Editorial Masthead

Toward Sustainable
Production of Reduced Phosphorus
Compounds
items.abstract: Conspectus Although phosphate is the thermodynamically stable and overwhelmingly abundant form of phosphorus in Nature, the modern phosphorus chemicals industry still relies heavily on white phosphorus (P4) as its central feedstock. In the thermal process, phosphate rock is reduced with coke and silica at temperatures around 1500 °C to produce P4, which is then converted to intermediates such as PCl3 before further conversion to value-added phosphorus compounds. This reaction sequence is effective, but involves the reduction of phosphate under high temperature, followed by additional redox and functionalization steps before many target phosphorus compounds are obtained. We therefore asked whether phosphate-derived feedstocks could be converted more directly into reduced phosphorus compounds, making the production of P4 as an intermediate unnecessary while retaining the synthetic flexibility needed for producing a large variety of phosphorus compounds. That question led to three areas of investigation. The first exploits the strong thermodynamic driving force of Si–O bond formation to achieve oxygen-abstraction reduction of phosphate-derived substrates. This led to the discovery of the bis(trichlorosilyl)phosphide anion,[P(SiCl3)2]−, a previously unknown P(−3) synthon that can now be accessed from trimetaphosphate, orthophosphate salts, and phosphoric acid. It can be further converted to value-added phosphorus compounds, such as phosphines, hexafluorophosphate, or phosphonium salts. Protonation of [P(SiCl3)2]− gives bis(trichlorosilyl)phosphine,HP(SiCl3)2, which undergoes selective radical hydrophosphination and gives synthetic access to primary phosphines, chlorophosphines, phosphinic acids, phosphonic acids, and phosphonium salts. The second strategy uses mechanochemistry to convert condensed phosphates directly to phosphite through hydride phosphorylation. Ball milling with alkali-metal hydrides provides a solvent-free route to a P(III) product while retaining the PO3 framework of the starting material. This route also works with biologically recovered polyphosphate feedstocks, which is important for the recycling of sewage sludge. The same mechanochemical platform further proved useful for the analogous redox-neutral phosphorylation of acetylides, giving alkynyl phosphonates directly from condensed phosphates. Finally, strongly reducing mechanochemical conditions based on supported alkali-metal dispersions gave access to ortho-phosphite,PO33−, a previously “missing” phosphorus oxoanion. This new anion can be converted further to phosphite salts, tris(trimethylsilyl) phosphite, and alkyl phosphonates. Taken together, these studies show that condensed phosphates and phosphoric acid can be directly used as feedstocks for synthetic phosphorus chemistry, without relying on P4 as an intermediate. This approach enables the identification of reactions that preserve P–O bonds where desirable and creates new opportunities to link phosphorus recovery from waste streams with the synthesis of value-added phosphorus compounds. Determining whether such routes are also more sustainable relative to established manufacturing processes will require a comparative assessment of energy demand, reagent production, waste generation, and process hazards.

items.title:
Covalent Organic
Pillars: Programmable Nanotubular
Cavitands
items.abstract: Conspectus For more than half a century, the construction of molecular host compounds has emerged as a central theme in supramolecular chemistry, driven by the promise of controlling molecular recognition, transport, and reactivity. While a wide variety of macrocyclic hosts have been developed, achieving deep-cavity cavitands with confined inner spaces extending over several nanometers has remained challenging. This limitation has hindered systematic investigations of how confinement governs molecular behavior within the so-called “inner phase”, as originally articulated by Cram. Motivated by these challenges, our laboratory has pursued the design and synthesis of a family of covalent organic pillars (COPs)─single-molecule nanotubular architectures assembled through dynamic covalent imine condensation of aldehyde-functionalized paracyclophane building blocks with diamine linkers. In this Account, we summarize our efforts to establish COPs as a versatile class of open-ended nanotubular cavitands, offering highly preorganized one-dimensional cavities with lengths exceeding 2 nm that encapsulate guests with complementary size and surface properties. By adopting an isoreticular design strategy, we demonstrate that systematic variation of linker structure and length enables the construction of a series of COPs with precisely tunable cavity length, sidewall composition, and effective channel width. This modularity provides a rare opportunity to correlate host geometry with recognition behavior in a quantitative and predictive manner. Beyond host–guest chemistry, we show that COPs also provide a powerful platform for exploring dynamic stereochemical phenomena during self-assembly from inherently chiral yet stereolabile macrocyclic building blocks. Whereas COPs constructed from rigid diamine spacers undergo exclusive narcissistic chiral self-sorting, yielding pairs of enantiomeric nanotubular structures, incorporation of flexible aliphatic diamine spacers leads to pronounced odd–even effects in chiral self-sorting, giving either racemic mixtures of chiral COPs or achiral meso-COPs, depending on linker parity. This conformational flexibility further endows COPs with adaptive host–guest recognition behavior, enabling cooperative accommodation of guests through a balance of host deformation and guest distortion. A distinctive feature of our work is that the molecular structures of essentially all COPs and their key host–guest complexes are elucidated by single-crystal X-ray crystallography, providing a rigorous structural foundation that remains rare for deep-cavity molecular hosts. Overall, our studies establish COPs as a precision design paradigm for nanotubular cavitands that bridge the gap between discrete macrocycles and extended porous frameworks, thereby opening a new regime of molecular control in supramolecular chemistry.

items.title:
Cross-Electrophile
Coupling through Direct Electrolysis
items.abstract: Conspectus Electrochemical reduction is a powerful means of generating reactive radical and anionic species with a degree of modularity and versatility that rivals other traditional chemical and photochemical reduction approaches. Our group has been motivated by the goal of using electrolysis as an enabling tool to develop reactivity and selectivity that are inaccessible using traditional reductants. In particular, we have leveraged the characteristics of direct electrolysis to promote sequential electron-transfer events that enable net-reductive radical-polar crossover, generating nucleophilic anionic intermediates from electrophilic reactants that undergo umpolung reactions with additional electrophiles. Guided further by physical organic principles, we identified systems that selectively activate a variety of common electrophiles to engage in a diverse array of formal cross-electrophile coupling (XEC) reactions. In this Account, we first describe the development of electroreductive cross-coupling of alkyl halides and its extension to silicon–silicon bond formation. This mechanistic framework was then applied to three-component dialkylation of alkenes using two distinct alkyl halides with high site- and chemoselectivity. Beyond alkyl halides, we further expanded the scope of electroreductive XEC to the deoxygenative functionalization of alcohols with a collection of heteroatom-based electrophiles. These transformations were enabled by in situ activation strategies that convert alcohols into reductively active intermediates, allowing them to behave analogously to alkyl halides and undergo borylation, silylation, and related coupling reactions. Finally, we recognized that an analogous activation logic could also enable the reductive functionalization of carbonyl compounds including ketones, aldehydes, and esters, which remains a major synthetic challenge that cannot be readily resolved by direct cathodic reduction. The continued evolution of activation methods ultimately enabled the formal geminal difunctionalization of electronically unbiased aldehydes and ketones that would otherwise require strongly reducing potentials to activate. These methods provided efficient access to densely functionalized sp3-carbon centers while demonstrating that product selectivity can be regulated through Faradaic control, a unique feature of electrochemistry.

items.title:
Quantitative
Determination of the Hydration Shell,
Counterion Association and Intermolecular Distances in Nanoscale Macroionic
Solutions and Their Correlations to the Self-Assembly Behaviors and
Phase Transitions of Macroions
items.abstract: Conspectus Hydrophilic macroions with characteristic sizes of 1–6 nm represent a unique transition stage between simple ions and large colloidal particles. Typical macroions include well-defined molecular clusters, metal–organic cages (MOCs), small nanoparticles, and biomacromolecules such as globular proteins. In this regime, classic Debye–Hückel limiting theory is inapplicable due to the large sizes of macroions, while DLVO theory is also inadequate because macroionic solutions remain thermodynamically stable, with negligible van der Waals attractions compared to colloids. In the past two decades, our group has been devoted to understanding the behavior of macroionic solutions. We discovered the assembly behavior (formation of hollow, spherical, single-layered blackberry-type structures) and new phases (gelation and coacervation) in dilute macroionic solutions. However, it was not until recently that we were able to quantitatively determine the molecular-level interactions in macroionic solutions, clarifying the origin of these phenomena and leading us to discover more phase transitions and outline a whole picture of macroionic solutions. This fundamental progress will help scientists deal with more complex macroionic solutions, such as the poorly understood polyelectrolyte and biomolecular solutions. In this Account, we highlight how modern techniques enable the quantitative determination of intermolecular interactions in macroionic solutions and how these interactions dictate the self-assembly and macrophase transitions, summarized as follows: (1) Determination of the hydration shell thicknesses of metal-oxide molecular clusters in solution, achieved for the first time by using the analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC) technique and correlating this value with the macroionic charge density. (2) Determination of the number of associated counterions and their average distances to the central macroion for different metal counterions by using the anomalous synchrotron small-angle X-ray scattering (ASAXS) technique. (3) Determination of the intermolecular distances between macroions in their dimeric state with different counterions. The gradual decrease in the intermolecular distance reveals the increasing strength of counterion-mediated attraction. (4) Successful correlation of the change of intermolecular distance in the dimers with the self-assembly (into blackberry structures of different sizes) and macrophase transitions (gelation, coacervation, and crystallization) in macroionic solution. (5) Correlation of the delicate difference in intermolecular interactions/distance to the intriguing self-recognition and chiral recognition features of macroions, which we reported earlier.

items.title:
Beyond Long-Term
Protection by Intelligent Poly(lactic
acid) Nanofibers: Structuring Multiscale Hierarchies for Passive Sensing
items.abstract: Conspectus Recent advances in electrospun biodegradable polymer nanofibrous membranes (NFMs) are reshaping the design of functional materials from passive morphological optimization toward programmed charge regulation and function-oriented structural engineering. Extending this concept to biobased poly(lactic acid) (PLA), however, remains challenging because PLA exhibits weak cooperative alignment of ester dipoles, a low dielectric response, and a limited number of highly polar or ionizable groups. These molecular characteristics give rise to shallow charge traps, insufficient interfacial polarization, and rapid charge dissipation across crystalline–amorphous regions. Therefore, the key scientific issue is not only how to fabricate porous PLA membranes but also how to organize their molecular conformations, crystalline domains, filler interfaces, and fibrous networks into a multiscale charge-regulation system. Electrospinning provides an effective route for addressing this issue because electric-field stretching, jet elongation, solvent evaporation, and phase separation can simultaneously regulate PLA chain orientation, crystalline morphology, fiber assembly, and pore architecture without altering the chemical structure of PLA chains. On this basis, research has progressed from single-parameter optimization toward multidimensional structural regulation. First, tuning electrospinning parameters, including voltage, collection distance, solution viscosity, and collector motion, promotes axial chain orientation and cooperative ester-dipole alignment. This oriented conformation enhances crystalline ordering, enriches crystalline–amorphous interfaces, and creates favorable charge-trapping domains, while more ordered fiber assembly narrows pore-size distributions and improves airflow continuity. Second, stereocomplexation between poly(l-lactide) and poly(d-lactide) introduces tightly packed stereocomplex crystallites through stereospecific interchain interactions. These ordered crystallites intensify dipolar polarization, deepen trap energy levels, and improve charge-storage stability, thereby mitigating the poor electret durability of pristine PLA. Third, nanoscale filler interfacial engineering with electroactive porous or dielectric fillers, such as metal–organic frameworks and titanium dioxide, introduces dielectric heterogeneity, defect-rich interfaces, unsaturated coordination sites, and high-surface-area contact domains. These features enrich multilevel charge-trapping sites, promote interfacial polarization, facilitate localized charge regeneration, and impart additional functions, including adsorption, antibacterial activity, humidity tolerance, and photothermal or optical regulation. An increasingly systematic understanding of the processing–structure–electroactivity–function relationship is accelerating the transition of PLA NFMs from mechanistic studies to engineering applications. The coordinated regulation of fiber orientation, stereocomplex crystallization, and nanofiller-mediated heterointerfaces enables coupled charge generation, capture, trap-mediated storage, interfacial migration, and dynamic regeneration. These charge-regulation pathways allow PLA membranes to harvest and retain charges generated during particle filtration, electromechanical deformation, airflow-induced friction, and physiological motion, while suppressing charge decay under humid or dynamically changing conditions. In particulate matter filtration, they couple electrostatic adsorption with optimized porous architectures to achieve efficient particle capture and low airflow resistance. In electromechanical conversion, they enhance triboelectric and piezoelectric responses for biodegradable self-powered systems. In health monitoring, stable charge transduction improves physiological signal acquisition and sensing reliability. In this Account, we critically summarize how electrospinning process regulation, stereocomplexation, and nanofiller interface engineering govern multiscale structures and electroactivity in PLA NFMs. We establish a processing–structure–electroactivity–function framework that involves fiber morphology, crystalline organization, interfacial polarization, charge trapping, and application performance across molecular, interfacial, and membrane scales. It essentially highlights hierarchical structuring as the key to designing intelligent biodegradable nanofibers for efficient filtration, self-powered sensing, wearable health monitoring, and adaptive protective systems.

items.title:
Beyond Partial
Readouts: Toward Integrative Mechanism
Inference in Catalytic Oxidation
items.abstract: Conspectus Oxidative reactive species (ORSs) provide a shared mechanism language for catalytic oxidation in both natural systems and industrial applications. Mechanism investigation seeks to explain how these processes proceed and how they can be regulated, conventionally focusing on identifying the dominant ORS and quantifying its contribution to substrate transformation. Yet ORSs are short-lived, present at low concentrations, and are rapidly interconverting, making their mechanism roles inseparable from the complex environment in which they form, transform, and decay. Disagreements among established identification methods have consequently become a recurring source of controversy across well-studied oxidation systems. Typically, ORS participations are examined through chemical probing, quenching, or direct spectroscopic detection. The widely used chemical approaches assume that each reagent reacts selectively with a single target species, allowing an experimental response to be read as a mechanism assignment. Such selectivity is scarcely attainable where multiple reactive species coexist and interconvert, so refining reagents or instruments alone cannot reconstruct the underlying chemistry once each response is assigned to one species. Our previous work on spin-trapping electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) exposed this vulnerability, revealing that even this widely trusted probe can enter the reaction chemistry. Reconstructing these signals into kinetic profiles successfully resolved when each reporting product forms, evolves, and decays, although temporal resolution alone cannot trace the reactions linking these stages. To organize this chemistry, we cast catalytic oxidation as a directed reactive species network, mapping each reactive species onto a node and every route of generation, interconversion, transformation, and dissipation onto an edge. External substrates or reporters couple to these nodes through distinct reactions weighted by their rate constants. Therefore, ORS dominance is not an intrinsic property of any node but a condition-dependent property of the network, set by how reaction conditions distribute reactive flux and by the substrate or reporter through which the network is read. Whether through probing, quenching, or direct detection, each measurement returns a low-dimensional projection of this high-dimensional network, so conflicting assignments may reflect one dynamic mechanism rather than incompatible chemistries. Recovering the hidden organization behind these partial projections thus becomes an inverse problem. In this Account, we revisit current ORS identification strategies, examine how chemical, kinetic, and spectroscopic evidence constrains mechanism interpretation, and present a network basis for reconstructing the hidden chemistry behind the resulting observations. Realizing this route appeals to AI-assisted inference under chemist-centered judgment and to structured databases built under this network view through automated experiments, literature mining, and modeling orchestrated by agentic workflows. Thus, it offers not only a reinterpretation of the mechanism puzzles accumulated over decades but a new point of departure for the work ahead.

items.title:
Selenium-Containing
Polymers: In Vivo Modulation and
Radioprotection
items.abstract: Conspectus Selenium is an essential element widely utilized across biological systems, where it imparts unique chemical functionality to biomacromolecules. While selenoproteins are well appreciated in humans, other selenium-containing biomacromolecules remain largely absent, and the development of selenium-based therapeutics has lagged. Here, from the perspective of molecular design, we introduce a series of selenium-containing polymers with diverse molecular structures and elucidate their in vivo effect, aiming to advance selenium chemistry toward defined biological functions. In this account, we establish a unified framework linking molecular structure, chemical reactivity, and in vivo functionality of selenium-containing polymers, thereby redefining their role beyond conventional drug carriers. We first delineate the distinct redox-responsive behaviors of monoselenide and diselenide motifs and their divergent biological consequences in vivo. We then introduce selenium-doped carbonized polymer dots for the treatment of liver and kidney diseases. Finally, we discuss selenium-containing melanins as a previously unrecognized class of selenium-enriched biomacromolecules with exceptional radioprotective capability, arising from their conjugated structures and selenium-specific electronic properties. By integrating these structurally related yet functionally diverse systems, this account highlights general design principles for in vivo modulation using selenium polymer chemistry. Bridging the gap between biological selenium utilization and synthetic molecular design unlocks new opportunities for selenium-based therapeutics and establishes selenium-containing polymers as a distinctive platform in biomedical science.

items.title:
Programming
Photodynamic Therapy with Glycopolymeric
Photosensitizers: From Carbohydrate Recognition to Light-Activated
Nanomedicine
items.abstract: Conspectus Glycopolymers are synthetic macromolecules that display multiple carbohydrate motifs and mimic the multivalent presentation of glycans in biological systems. Advances in controlled polymerization now allow chain length, sugar density, sequence, composition, and topology to be tuned with increasing precision. As a result, glycopolymers have progressed from models of carbohydrate-lectin recognition to materials for receptor- and transporter-mediated targeting, drug delivery, and precision therapy. Studies of fructose-containing micelles showed that cellular interactions depend not only on sugar identity or total sugar content but also on chain length, local density, spatial arrangement, and carbohydrate accessibility. These principles were then applied to drug delivery, where polymer composition and self-assembly improved the aqueous encapsulation of poorly soluble drugs, regulated nanoparticle size, and promoted intracellular distribution. Glycopolymers therefore became functional materials that control both biological recognition and the organization of therapeutic molecules. Glycopolymeric photosensitizers extend this concept to photodynamic therapy (PDT), in which photosensitizers convert light into localized photochemical effects. Porphyrins are attractive because of their optical properties and ability to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS), but their use is limited by poor aqueous dispersibility, aggregation, nonspecific uptake, altered photochemical activity, and inadequate intracellular localization. Photosensitizer delivery is therefore not simply a solubilization problem; it requires coordinated control over molecular organization, biological targeting, and intracellular transport. Glycopolymers can address these challenges through physical loading or covalent incorporation. Physical loading is simple and adaptable but may provide limited control over loading and retention, whereas covalent attachment allows more precise regulation of photosensitizer content and placement. To combine photosensitizer organization with carbohydrate-mediated targeting, we developed several covalent glycopolymeric photosensitizers. Porphyrin-containing random and block glycopolymers revealed how polymer sequence influences aggregation, intracellular ROS generation, and photocytotoxicity. Porphyrin-core star glycopolymers further showed that arm length, carbohydrate identity, and corona composition affect recognition, uptake, and PDT response, while related systems enabled combined therapeutic functions. Their synthesis also evolved from conventional ATRP, which requires added catalytic systems and does not directly link photosensitizer function with polymer formation, toward light-mediated polymerization. In photoATRP, we developed a triple-function zinc porphyrin that serves as initiator, photocatalytic component, and photosensitizer. A complementary self-photocatalyzed PET-RAFT strategy used a polymerizable porphyrin that participates in polymerization and becomes covalently embedded in the glycopolymer. This Account traces the evolution of glycopolymers from multivalent recognition to targeted drug delivery and glycopolymeric photosensitizers. Here, “programming” refers to the deliberate design of molecular architecture, the control of nanoscale assembly, and the integration of polymer synthesis with photosensitizer function. It emphasizes how carbohydrate presentation, polymer architecture, self-assembly, and photochemistry jointly govern recognition, intracellular transport, and therapeutic performance and how integrating polymer synthesis, targeting, and photosensitization may guide next-generation precision phototherapeutics.

items.title:
High-Efficiency
Excimer Luminescence from Discrete
π–π Stacked Dimers
items.abstract: Conspectus Molecular aggregates serve as an important platform for the practical applications of organic luminescent materials. Within these aggregates, both molecular arrangements and intermolecular interactions provide crucial avenues for modulating the luminescence properties. Given that organic chromophores are typically characterized by planar and rigid π-conjugated units, π–π stacking and π–π interactions are determinative for the formation of aggregates and the regulation of photophysical properties. However, strong π–π stacking usually leads to luminescence quenching in organic aggregates, due to the forbidden radiative transition and the activated nonradiative transition. Specifically, the strong π–π stacking facilitates the formation of excited dimers, i.e., excimers, and these excimers have long been regarded as “dark” states that are detrimental to luminescence. This inherent quenching effect is in conflict with the requirement for high luminescence efficiency of organic materials in optoelectronic applications. In this Account, we highlight our recent findings: strong π–π stacked dimers can achieve high-efficiency excimer luminescence when they are spatially discrete in aggregates. The findings stem from the crystal packing structure observation of a thianthrene-modified anthracene compound, which exhibits a unique discrete π–π dimer stacking of anthracene with an unexpectedly high photoluminescence quantum yield (Φ) of 80%. Theoretical and experimental investigations reveal that this discrete π–π dimer stacking promotes the formation of a pure and single excimer state. Building on this, high-efficiency excimer luminescence can be ascribed to the special nature of this excimer state: a hybridized local and charge-transfer state, which consists of two locally excited components of the monomers and two charge-transfer components between the two monomers. Compared to the monomer, although the radiative transition rate of the excimer is reduced by 2 orders of magnitude, the suppression of nonradiative transition rate is even more significant. The combined effect of these factors enables high-efficiency excimer luminescence to be achieved in discrete π–π stacked dimers. Based on these findings, a molecular design principle was proposed to construct the discrete π–π stacked dimers. The molecular structure consists of two moieties: a planar aromatic core (π moiety) and a unilateral substituent (side moiety). On the one hand, the unilateral substituent is attached to the π moiety to guarantee the dimer formation in antiparallel π–π stacking with the aid of steric hindrance. On the other hand, two substituents can act as the spacers to isolate the formed π–π dimers from each other by means of their appropriate size and orientation. To verify the universality of this design strategy, various π and side moieties were combined together to prepare a series of crystalline materials with discrete π–π stacked dimers and tunable emission colors. Furthermore, the efficient excimer luminescence was also achieved in films and nanoparticles, indicating that they have unique application potential in stimuli-responsive systems, organic light-emitting diodes, and biological imaging. As a perspective, these discrete π–π stacked dimers, which act as “mini-excitons”, provide an ideal transitional model for understanding of the photophysical properties from single molecule to aggregates, and facilitate further exploration of supramolecular luminescence properties.

items.title:
Evolution of
Aggregation-Induced Emission Materials
in Cancer Diagnosis and Therapy: Toward Clinical Translation
items.abstract: Conspectus As one of the most formidable threats to human health, cancer demands technologies that can sensitively detect malignancies, precisely guide intervention, adapt to dynamic disease states, and support clinical decision-making. Phototheranostics based on organic fluorophores have shown great promise in cancer management owing to their tunable structural design, tumor-targeting capability, real-time imaging output, and biocompatibility with diverse therapeutic modalities. However, conventional fluorophores often suffer from aggregation-caused quenching in concentrated or biological aggregate states, leading to weakened signals, insufficient sensitivity, and limited therapeutic efficacy. The discovery of aggregation-induced emission (AIE) provides a conceptually distinct solution to this problem. AIE materials are weakly emissive in the molecularly dispersed state but become highly luminescent upon aggregation, thereby turning aggregation from a detrimental process into a useful photophysical mechanism. By precisely controlling molecular motion, AIE materials can exhibit advantages including high signal-to-noise ratio, large Stokes shifts, and excellent photostability, making them a versatile molecular toolbox for tumor-oriented phototheranostic systems. Over the past two decades, they have evolved beyond simple fluorescent probes into integrated platforms for cancer theranostics. In this Account, we propose a concept-driven framework, termed AIMS (Analyze-Intervene-Modulate-Select), to organize the evolution of AIE materials in cancer diagnosis and therapy according to their distinctive roles within cancer management. The first generation, “Analyze”, refers to AIE materials used mainly as diagnostic tools. These systems enable sensitive detection of tumor-associated biomarkers, in vivo lesion visualization, and multimodal intraoperative identification. The second generation, “Intervene”, generates all-in-one theranostic platforms that couple imaging with phototherapy, facilitating radiotherapy sensitization, immune activation, or postoperative control. The third generation, “Modulate”, describes intelligent and adaptive AIE platforms that respond to therapy-induced stress, microenvironmental shifts, or dynamic biological feedback during treatment, transforming static theranostics into systems capable of modulating therapeutic trajectories. The emerging fourth generation, “Select”, represents a data-driven paradigm linking the design of AIE materials with artificial intelligence, multiomics, patient stratification, model selection, and indication prioritization. Through AIMS, we organize the accumulated capabilities of AIE materials around four functional roles. By clarifying which role is most relevant to a given application, AIMS guides future research in prioritizing design objectives, integrating the functions needed for the intended task, and matching material innovation to specific needs in cancer management.

items.title:
Negative Photochromism
of Biaryl-Bridged Imidazole
Dimers: Designing Biradical-Mediated Reaction Networks
items.abstract: Conspectus Negative photochromism reverses the usual behavior of T-type photochromic molecules: a thermally stable colored state is converted by light into a less absorbing metastable state and subsequently recovers thermally. Because the photoproduct attenuates excitation light less strongly, negative photochromism is attractive for optically dense materials and systems requiring an intrinsic thermal reset. The challenge is to combine long-wavelength excitation, efficient photoconversion, controllable state populations and thermal lifetimes, and adaptation to different operating environments. Our studies of biaryl-bridged imidazole dimers originated from efforts to accelerate radical recombination in hexaarylbiimidazole (HABI) photochromes by covalently bridging the two imidazole units and suppressing diffusional separation of the photogenerated radicals. Introduction of a 1,1′-binaphthyl bridge unexpectedly produced negative photochromism. In the resulting 1,1′-binaphthyl-bridged imidazole dimer (BN-ImD), the thermodynamically stable colored state (5MR) contains a diazafulvene chromophore absent from conventional HABI photochromes. Visible-light excitation cleaves a C–N bond to generate a short-lived biradical intermediate (BR), which recombines either to regenerate 5MR or to form the metastable colorless state (6MR). Thermal cleavage of the interimidazole C–C bond of 6MR regenerates BR, completing a thermally resettable 5MR–BR–6MR network. This behavior revealed that molecular bridging can control not only radical proximity but also the covalent states and reaction pathways accessible through BR. This reaction-network perspective provides several design coordinates. Extension of the π-conjugated bridge and donor substitution enable long-wavelength excitation, whereas differential tuning of 5MR and 6MR absorptions can produce large spectral separation and wavelength-selective bidirectional switching. Molecular asymmetry can bias BR recombination among competing covalent products, and excitation intensity can open nonlinear pathways to alternative states. Conformational restriction alters activation barriers and thermal recovery, while transient spectroscopy and global kinetic analysis separate BR formation, product branching, and thermal regeneration as distinct contributions. Structural modification can also open access to 7MR and 8MR states and generate kinetic hierarchies spanning rapid radical recombination, seconds-scale switching, and hours-to-days thermal equilibration. The 5MR/6MR contrast can also be translated into function, including turn-on fluorescence, four-photon-like fluorescence responses under two-photon excitation, operation in polar and aqueous media, and light-driven reorganization of lyotropic and chiral nematic liquid crystals. This Account organizes these developments around four interdependent design principles─spectral control, kinetic control, branching selectivity, and environmental integration. The central message is that negative photochromism in this family is best designed by controlling the reaction profile as a whole: which states are accessible, how BR is partitioned among them, how rapidly the connecting pathways operate, and how the network responds to excitation wavelength, photon flux, and environment.

items.title:
Metal–Ligand
Coordination Nanomaterials Tailored
to the Cancer-Immunity Cycle
items.abstract: Conspectus The successful implementation of antitumor immunity hinges largely on a chain of stepwise events known as the cancer-immunity cycle (CIC). In this cycle, tumor cell death caused by T lymphocytes triggers inflammatory rounds of antigen-presenting cell (APC)-mediated antigen presentation and T-cell stimulation, sustaining active tumoricidal immunity, whereas tumor immunosuppressive networks impose multifaceted detrimental effects on essential elements involved in the CIC, which are considered therapeutic targets for improved tumor immunotherapy. Tremendous evidence has thrown light on the pivotal roles of metal ions in oncology, especially in antitumor immunity. Metal ions participate in modulating the step-by-step events occurring in the CIC, principally via their structural, catalytic, or modulatory interactions with immunosensors, ion transporters, and downstream effectors, as exemplified by Mn2+ that sensitizes cyclic GMP–AMP synthase and the stimulator of interferon genes pathway to trigger antitumor T-cell immunity. Owing to their lack of targeting ability, metal ions used alone cannot serve as immunotherapeutics. Inspired by the excellent targeting properties of nanomedicines and the unique ability of metal ions to self-assemble with diverse functional ligands, recent decades have witnessed rapid advances in metal–ligand coordination nanomaterials for enhanced tumor immunotherapy. Unlike other nanomedicines, metal coordination complexes can serve as multifunctional immunotherapeutic platforms, due to their chemical tunability and design versatility. Their unique composition and structure allow them to exhibit substantial outstanding properties, blazing the promising trail of tumor immunotherapy. In this Account, we summarize our recent breakthroughs in the development of metal–ligand coordination nanomedicines, especially in the therapeutic mechanisms tailored for CIC, with the ultimate purpose of ameliorative cancer immunotherapy. These promising nanomedicines are designed on the basis of stepwise events within the CIC, in which the targets can be subdivided into (1) tumor cells, (2) APCs, and (3) T cells. Once targeted to tumor cells, these nanomaterials generally induce immunogenic tumor cell death, leading to the release of numerous danger-associated molecular patterns that exert immune-stimulating effects on the APCs. Metal coordination complexes also directly activate APCs by the intrinsic immunostimulatory properties of metal ions or by delivering other adjuvants. Both pathways promote APC activation and antigen presentation for the subsequent priming of antitumor T-cell responses. Apart from indirect APC-to-T immunostimulatory pathways, these nanomedicines directly act on T cells and reinforce their antitumor functions, including activation, trafficking, infiltration, and tumor-killing capabilities. In addition, both future challenges and the anticipated development blueprint of these medicines as clinical therapeutics are emphasized.

items.title:
From Anti-Sintering to Anti-Dispersion: Preserving
Reactive Metallic Pt Ensembles in Light-Alkane Oxidation
items.abstract: Conspectus A long-standing principle in supported noble-metal catalysis is to maximize metal dispersion and prevent nanoparticle sintering. This dispersion-centered, anti-sintering paradigm is rational because highly dispersed species increase apparent metal utilization and often expose low-coordinated sites with distinct electronic structures. For low-temperature oxidation of C2+ light alkanes, however, dispersion alone does not define the working catalyst. Propane is considered here as a representative model because its complete oxidation couples initial alkane adsorption and C–H activation with subsequent dehydrogenation, C–C bond cleavage, and deep oxidation of Cx intermediates. These functions require a balance between alkane-accessible metallic Pt ensembles and oxygen or interfacial functions that sustain complete oxidation. Excessive dispersion can disrupt this balance by promoting Pt oxidation, strong oxygen binding, or stabilization of isolated species, whereas less-dispersed Pt can preserve the contiguous metallic sites needed for alkane activation under suitable reaction conditions. In this Account, we propose anti-dispersion as a design concept for constructing and preserving the appropriate working Pt ensemble. Pt dispersion is treated not as a monotonic activity descriptor but as a reaction-dependent variable coupled to metallic character, ensemble availability, oxygen coverage, accessible-site density, and support anchoring. Anti-dispersion therefore encompasses both controlled restructuring of over-dispersed Pt into reactive metallic ensembles and prevention of their subsequent fragmentation under working conditions. Our studies reveal these two complementary dimensions. Size-controlled Pt/CeO2 model catalysts show that increasing Pt size can enhance metallic character and intrinsic activity for propane oxidation, while the overall rate reflects a trade-off between ensemble reactivity and exposed-site density. Controlled sintering of Pt on MgAl2O4 further demonstrates that lower dispersion can be beneficial when it generates metallic surfaces that remain alkane-accessible within the relevant oxygen-coverage window. Conversely, active metallic Pt ensembles on CeO2 can fragment during propane oxidation and become stabilized as isolated Pt spectators. Selective blocking of the corresponding atom-trapping sites suppresses this reaction-induced redispersion and preserves metallic Pt ensembles. Extending this concept across oxide supports shows that anti-dispersion must be adapted to the dominant anchoring environment. Depending on the support, the relevant strategy may involve blocking support-templated Pt oxide formation, moderating acid-site-mediated anchoring, or competitively occupying hydroxyl sites that otherwise over-disperse Pt. The unifying objective is to regulate the anchoring landscape selectively while retaining useful interfacial functions for oxygen management, Cx-intermediate conversion, water tolerance, and durability. Together, these results shift catalyst design from maximizing Pt dispersion to controlling the working ensemble. The optimum state is defined not by particle size alone but by whether the Pt ensemble remains metallic, contiguous, and alkane-accessible under the relevant feed and support environment. This perspective complements conventional anti-sintering and may guide other catalytic reactions in which isolated atoms are insufficient and contiguous metallic ensembles are required for bond activation.

items.title: Issue Publication Information
Issue Editorial Masthead

Transition-Metal-Catalyzed
Multicomponent Cycloadditions
items.abstract: Abstract Transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions provide a powerful strategy for constructing complex cyclic frameworks from simple unsaturated building blocks with high atom and step efficiencies. This Review highlights the progress made in transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions based on the size of the cyclic products formed. First, reactions that construct five-membered rings, including [2 + 2 + 1], [3 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 1 + 1] cycloadditions, are discussed with an emphasis on key reactive intermediates, such as carbon monoxide, vinylidenes, carbenoids, and nitrenes. Next, six-membered-ring-forming processes, particularly [2 + 2 + 2], [3 + 2 + 1], [4 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions, are described, highlighting combinations of alkynes, alkenes, and heteroatom-containing components. The Review then covers strategies for constructing seven-membered rings via [3 + 2 + 2] and [4 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions. Finally, emerging methods that enable the formation of eight- and nine-membered rings through higher-order multicomponent cycloadditions are described. This Review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the conceptual framework, mechanistic principles, and synthetic possibilities of transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions by organizing them according to ring size and cycloaddition components.

items.title:
Named Reactions
under Mechanochemical Conditions:
A Critical Survey
items.abstract: Abstract Mechanochemistry has progressed from a niche interest to a core method for solvent-free synthesis, providing sustainable and mechanistically unique alternatives to traditional solution-based chemistry. When controlled impact, shear, or vibrational energy is applied under solvent-free or solvent-lean conditions, reactions are promoted within dynamically renewed interfacial regions, revealing new patterns of selectivity, energy efficiency, and process design. This review surveys the historical development, fundamental principles, and analytical frameworks of mechanochemistry, together with an extensive compilation of named organic reactions conducted under mechanochemical conditions. By comparing mechanochemical reactions with their solution-phase counterparts, this review clarifies how stress-induced activation, microsolvation (η control), and auxiliary-mediated interfaces influence reaction kinetics, selectivity, and scalability. Emerging platforms, such as twin-screw extrusion (TSE), resonant acoustic mixing (RAM), and bead mills, extend these advantages toward scale-up and, in the case of TSE, continuous manufacturing, bridging laboratory-scale discoveries and industrial applications. Mechanochemistry functions both as a practical enabling platform and as a conceptual framework for Green Chemistry, embracing atom economy, solvent reduction, and operational safety within a unified solid-state synthetic framework.

items.title:
Lithium–Oxygen
Batteries: Fundamental and Practical
Considerations
items.abstract: Abstract Lithium–oxygen batteries (LOBs) have emerged as a compelling next-generation energy storage technology for aviation due to their high theoretical energy densities and the use of abundant oxygen as a cathode reactant. Unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), which are limited by the mass of intercalation materials and one-electron redox processes, LOBs leverage multielectron oxygen redox chemistry to achieve gravimetric energy density exceeding 3,500 Wh kgLi2O2–1 based on lithium peroxide and up to 5,200 Wh kgLi2O–1 for lithium oxide. However, practical implementation of LOBs remains constrained by significant challenges including low round-trip efficiency and low system-level energy density, the latter arising from the need for oxygen management in both open and closed architectures. The electrolyte viscosity, oxygen solubility, volatility, and chemical stability toward reactive oxygen species can profoundly influence discharge capacity, rate capability, reversibility, and long-term stability. This review provides a comprehensive assessment of recent progress in LOBs, focusing on electrolyte designs, electrode engineering, and strategies for mitigating parasitic reactions as well as the interplay between material-level properties and system-level constraints, offering a critical perspective on the path toward realizing high-energy, practical LOB systems.

items.title:
Harnessing Contact Electrification and Static Charge
for Chemical Reactions: Fundamentals and Applications of Contact Electrocatalysis
items.abstract: Abstract The chemical industry is the largest industrial energy consumer and the third-largest emitter of CO2 globally. Despite efforts to enhance energy efficiency, many chemical reactions still require significant external energy due to fundamental thermodynamic barriers. Thus, transitioning to a sustainable chemical industry requires new renewable energy or catalytic technologies that reduce energy demand. In catalytic systems, flowing liquids, moving parts, and gas separation mean local static charge is often generated on the nanoscale. This review explores the static charge formation at solid–solid, solid–liquid, and solid–gas interfaces, such as those that occur in catalytic reactions, and then extends this discussion to a deeper focus on how these generated static charges can be used for catalysis, including electrostatic catalysis, static charge electrochemistry, and contact electrocatalysis (CEC). CEC, where motion-induced charge separation leads to local static charge formation, is then specifically examined, exploring why and how it has emerged as an exciting tool to enable these green chemical transformations. The focus is to highlight the most recent developments in CEC, with mechanistic interpretation, factors that affect CEC performance, and emerging applications, and to provide outlook and guidance for the field─specifically highlighting the need to build structure–property relationships for CEC performance and static charge formation for target chemical reactions.

items.title: Issue Publication Information
Issue Editorial Masthead
Diffusion Models for Small-Molecule Design
items.abstract: Abstract Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a class of generative models for controllable small-molecule design in drug discovery capable of progressively transforming noisy or partially specified molecular states into candidate structures under structural, geometric, and property constraints. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological foundations and representative applications of diffusion-based molecular generation, emphasizing the alignment among molecular representations, generative dynamics, controllable design, and evaluation and validation. Particular attention is given to recent advances in property- and structure-guided generation, target-aware and fragment-based design, multiobjective optimization, and synthesis-aware generation. We also discuss the roles of data sets, computational evaluation, and prospective experiments in assessing the chemical and biological relevance of generated molecules. By organizing these developments within a unified conceptual framework, we provide computational chemists and drug discovery researchers with a structured roadmap that balances the mathematical rigor with chemical intuition. Throughout, we highlight current methodological limitations and unresolved challenges and conclude with future directions toward chemically credible and experimentally grounded molecular design. To facilitate navigation of this rapidly evolving field, we introduce an interactive companion platform (https://diffsmd.scbdd.com) that provides a curated, continuously updated repository of model architectures and visualizations.

items.title:
Two-Dimensional
IR Spectroscopy: Mapping Structure
and Dynamics in Complex Molecular Environments
items.abstract: Abstract Complex, dynamically heterogeneous environments such as lipid membranes, electrocatalytic interfaces, soft polymer matrices, crowded biological media, and phase-separated assemblies are characterized by spatially distinct microenvironments, multiscale structural dynamics, and short-range interactions. Microscopic interactions are poorly captured by bulk descriptors. In this article, we review how ultrafast two-dimensional infrared (2D IR) spectroscopy and related vibrational methods provide direct access to these complex molecular landscapes by resolving inhomogeneous ensembles, picosecond environmental fluctuations, and exchange between local states. When combined with vibrational probes and modern molecular simulation, these spectroscopic observables reveal how local interactions, such as electrostatics, hydrogen bonding (H-bonding), and ion pairing and aggregation generate microscopic heterogeneity and govern multiscale dynamics. We organize discussions around representative classes of complex environments, including hydration and electrostatics in lipid membranes, molecular environments and dynamics in biomolecular condensates, confinement and crowding in self-assembled and interfacial systems, including electrochemical interfaces, polymers/gels and soft matter, electrolytes and ion-specific effects, and aqueous cosolvent mixtures relevant to solvation and cryopreservation. Looking ahead, ongoing advancements in vibrational probe design, multidimensional spectroscopy, and molecular simulation are expected to enable more quantitative and predictive analyses of heterogeneous molecular environments across chemistry, materials science, and biology.

items.title:
Rearrangement
Reactions in Polymers
items.abstract: Abstract Rearrangement reactions are critical transformations in organic synthesis, and a comprehensive look at how they have been utilized so far in polymeric contexts is missing. Historically, these transformations have been implemented within the polymer periphery (e.g., side chains), and recently, there has been an expanding effort to implement them into polymer backbones. Considering these efforts, we compile the history of rearrangement reactions as applied in polymer contexts, detailing mechanisms, reaction conditions, goals for implementation of rearrangement, and location of implementation (i.e., propagating species, side chains, polymer backbones). In organizing this work, we hope to guide the further development of rearrangements as general tools for polymer modification and design.

items.title:
How to Engineer Biological Nanopores for Single-Molecule
Capture and Discrimination
items.abstract: Abstract Protein-based biological nanopores have emerged as versatile tools for sequencing biopolymers, identifying molecules, and probing reactions at the single-molecule level. Many biological nanopores have been characterized, revealing the significance of nanopore size, shape, and chemical composition in molecular detection and discrimination. Advancements in understanding the nanofluidic properties of nanopores have complemented engineering approaches expanding the possible applications of nanopore technology. Through a combination of structural insights, rational design, systematic screening, and molecular dynamics simulations, researchers have developed nanopores capable of distinguishing between ions, nucleic acids, peptides, and folded proteins with remarkable specificity and sensitivity. Building upon three decades of progress, this Review highlights recent engineering innovations, discusses ongoing challenges, and explores the prospects in the field.

items.title:
Engineering
Reversible Wet Adhesion: Physicochemical
Principles from Molecular Interactions to Functional Biointerfaces
items.abstract: Abstract Interfacial hydration fundamentally constrains adhesion in aqueous and physiological environments by preventing intimate contact, competing for binding sites, and weakening the load-bearing interfaces. Although wet adhesives have been extensively designed for durable fixation, emerging technologies in soft robotics, wearable bioelectronics, and minimally invasive medicine require interfaces that can form adhesion, recover after reuse, or detach on-demand under hydrated conditions. This Review discusses reversible wet adhesion through two operational modes: Mode I, cyclic reusability through repeated restoration of adhesion over attachment-detachment cycles, and Mode II, on-demand detachability through trigger-induced conversion of a stable adhesive state into a weakly adherent state through a controlled, low-damage release pathway. We examine supramolecular interactions, dynamic covalent chemistry, mesoscale architectures, biomimetic designs, and hybrid strategies as complementary routes for regulating hydration, interfacial binding, mechanical dissipation, and adhesive state transitions at wet interfaces. We analyze how contact formation, hydration history, fracture pathways, loading history, test geometry, and biofluid exposure shape the measured performance. We further assess current methods for quantifying reusability, switching, durability, and biofluid tolerance, emphasizing failure mode-informed evaluation and standardized reporting criteria. Integrating hydration thermodynamics, binding kinetics, mechanical dissipation, and stimulus-gated interfacial transitions, this Review develops design and evaluation principles for reversible wet adhesive systems in complex aqueous and biointerfacial environments.

items.title:
High-Entropy
Materials for Electrochemical Gas Conversion
items.abstract: Abstract High-entropy materials (HEMs) are composed of multiple principal elements stabilized by the configurational entropy. They establish a new design paradigm in electrocatalysis by leveraging local disorder and multielement synergy to create diverse and tunable active site environments. While HEMs have been broadly reviewed, a focused and reaction-specific assessment of their role in gas-involved electrocatalysis is absent. This review fills that gap by examining entropy-driven design principles, entropy-guided synthesis, nanoscale structural control, and advanced characterization of HEMs and by linking these aspects to their reaction-specific catalytic behavior in gas-involved electrocatalysis. We build a unified framework linking high-entropy chemistry to catalytic function across five key reactions: the CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR), hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR), oxygen reduction reaction (ORR), nitrogen reduction reaction (NRR), and nitrogen oxidation reaction (NOR). We provide comprehensive coverage across all major HEM families, including high-entropy alloys, oxides, chalcogenides, hydroxides, fluorides, MXenes, and single-atom configurations, highlighting features unique to each system. Key challenges and future directions are outlined, including scalable synthesis, active-site identification, machine-learning-guided discovery, and interfacial engineering. This review provides a reaction-focused framework for advancing HEM-based electrocatalysis and offers guidance for designing next-generation materials for clean energy technologies.

items.title: Introduction: Fabrication at All Scales
Issue Publication Information
Issue Editorial Masthead

Photoinduced
Charge Separation via Symmetry-Breaking
items.abstract: Abstract Photoinduced symmetry-breaking charge separation (SB-CS) is a fundamental process in molecular photophysics that underpins energy and charge transport in reaction centers and organic, supramolecular, and hybrid materials. Despite extensive investigations across diverse systems, SB-CS is often described in system-specific terms, obscuring the underlying unifying principles. In this Review, we establish a coherent framework demonstrating that SB-CS can be understood within a multidimensional parameter space defined by electronic coupling, energetic driving force, and nuclear reorganization. We critically analyze how the interplay between locally excited and charge-transfer states governs charge separation and recombination dynamics, highlighting the existence of an optimal intermediate coupling regime that enables efficient symmetry-breaking while suppressing nonproductive decay pathways. By integrating insights from solution, solid-state, and single-molecule measurements, we show that environmental fluctuations and structural heterogeneity play a central role in driving charge localization rather than merely acting as spectators or perturbations. Importantly, we distinguish universal physical principles from system-specific manifestations, allowing the formulation of transferable design rules for achieving efficient and long-lived charge-separated states. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward predictive, data-driven models that link molecular structure to SB-CS dynamics, providing a foundation for the rational design of next-generation optoelectronic and energy-conversion materials.

items.title:
Ultrafast Nonlinear Vibrational Spectroscopy of Aqueous
Solutions at Surfaces and in Heterogeneous Environments
items.abstract: Abstract Water and aqueous electrolytes at surfaces, interfaces, and in confinement behave differently from the bulk, yet linear spectroscopy rarely combines the chemical specificity, surface selectivity, and temporal resolution needed to resolve electric double-layer formation, specific-ion adsorption, and hydration at interfaces and under nanoconfinement. This review assesses how ultrafast nonlinear vibrational spectroscopy, comprising two-dimensional infrared spectroscopy, vibrational sum-frequency generation (SFG), and time-resolved SFG, probes the hydrogen-bond network and the dynamics of interfacial water and electrolytes on femtosecond-to-picosecond timescales. We first establish vibrational benchmarks for bulk water and simple electrolytes, then treat soft aqueous boundaries, including air–water, hydrophobic and hydrophilic, lipid, surfactant, and nucleic acid interfaces. We next examine solid–liquid and electrochemical systems, spanning metal oxides, minerals, and field-induced effects, before turning to water and proton dynamics in nanoconfined geometries and complex architectures. Throughout, experimental results are set against theoretical and computational frameworks, from polarizable force fields to machine-learning potentials. Our aim is to identify which molecular-level features of interfacial water are now firmly established, where the prevailing mean-field description of the electric double layer breaks down, and which experiments would resolve the outstanding discrepancies.

items.title:
Strain-Release
Cycloadditions: Bicyclobutanes and
Beyond
items.abstract: Abstract Strain-release cycloadditions have emerged as powerful reactions for converting distorted ring systems into complex and otherwise hardly attainable organic molecular architectures. This Review encompasses the fundamentals of strain, its role in governing cycloaddition pathways, and offers a systematic examination of strained carbocycles and heterocycles, from bicyclo[1.1.1]butanes and 1-azabicyclo[1.1.1]butanes, housanes and aza-housanes, 2H-azirines and aziridines, azetidines, cyclopropanes, cyclobutanes, oxiranes, oxetanes, and strained alkynes and alkenes. Across these motifs, the general principles that dictate reactivity, the breadth of known cycloadditions and activation strategies, from Brønsted and Lewis acid catalysis to transition-metal activation, photocatalysis, and double strain-release mechanisms, are highlighted. Key opportunities, current limitations, and future directions are outlined.

items.title:
Interface Engineering
in Perovskite Light-Emitting
Diodes: Fundamentals, Characterization, Strategies, and Applications
items.abstract: Abstract Interface engineering has emerged as a critical strategy for advancing perovskite light-emitting diodes (PeLEDs), enabling remarkable improvements in the device efficiency, stability, and spectral purity. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of interface engineering in PeLEDs, beginning with the fundamental principles that govern carrier injection, transport, and recombination at heterojunctions between perovskite emitters and charge-transport layers. We then survey advanced characterization techniques, including photoelectron spectroscopy, scanning probe microscopy, and time-resolved optical methods, that elucidate interfacial energy-level alignment, defect states, charge dynamics, and degradation pathways. On the basis of these insights, we systematically discuss versatile engineering strategies, such as self-assembled monolayers, dipole interlayers, dimensional regulation, and passivation schemes, to mitigate non-radiative recombination, balance charge fluxes, and enhance operational stability. Finally, we highlight emerging applications spanning high-resolution displays, flexible lighting, and lasing while outlining key challenges and future directions toward commercial realization. This Review aims to offer a holistic framework linking interfacial design to device performance, guiding next-generation PeLED development.

items.title:
Tuning Interfacial Electron Transfer for Boosting
Electrochemiluminescence: Methods, Mechanisms, and Bioanalytical Applications
items.abstract: Abstract The interfacial electron-transfer process acts as a pivotal kinetic determinant of electrochemiluminescence (ECL) efficiency, governing the generation of excited-state emitters and thus dictating the intensity and stability of ECL signals. Currently, harnessing diverse nanomaterials has driven significant advances in the development of novel ECL luminophores and the activation of coreactants. However, most of these luminophores exhibit low ECL efficiency in aqueous media, and the intrinsic reaction and activation mechanisms remain ambiguous because of their complex structures and compositions. Notably, tuning electron-transfer pathways at the molecular/atomic level can not only enable efficient signal amplification but also facilitate the tracking of reaction pathways, thereby providing deeper insights into the fundamental mechanisms underlying ECL processes. This Review comprehensively summarizes advances during the past five years in tuning interfacial electron transfer to enhance ECL.
