Though mucin backbone amino acid sequences are encoded in the genome, the ultimate properties of mucins depend heavily on glycosylation, which is shaped dynamically by the sets of glycosyltransferases expressed in individual mucus-producing cells. The substantial energy and intracellular organization required to produce mucin glycoproteins pays off in their crucial and versatile biological functions, ranging from cleaning tissue surfaces to lubrication to microbiome management. Mucins are of particular interest in human health due to their roles in protecting the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts and their dysfunction in various diseases. Studying the elaborate maturation process during mucin biosynthesis and polymerization, decoration with glycans, and formation of interpolymer interactions may help identify vulnerabilities that can be overcome nutritionally or medically. Understanding the principles of mucin construction will provide the framework for strengthening mucus hydrogels both physically and functionally.

items.title:
Recovery of
a Minor Cryo-EM Particle Population Reveals
Conformational Equilibria Linking Cofactor Loading, Turnover, and
Reactivation in Methionine Synthase
items.abstract: Abstract Cobalamin-dependent methionine synthase (MetH) is a highly dynamic enzyme that requires large-scale domain rearrangements to facilitate turnover and reactivation. Despite significant biochemical and structural efforts, a full picture of the conformational changes underlying the transition between MetH turnover and reactivation has remained elusive. Here, we leverage state-of-the-art cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) methods to reanalyze an old dataset and gain new insights into these changes. By utilizing a neural-network particle picker, performing careful classification of particles, and incorporating high-resolution information to determine initial particle orientations, we uncovered and reconstructed a minor population of reactivation-state MetH (∼4.5–5 Å resolution) from a dataset that is dominated by resting-state MetH. This structure represents the first fully intact structure of the enzyme with a physiological cobalamin cofactor bound. These findings highlight the potential for improved cryo-EM methodology to uncover previously hidden details about enzyme function and deepen our understanding of structural ensembles.

items.title:
Redox Cofactor
Diversity in Biological Hydride Transfer
Reactions
items.abstract: Abstract Hydride-transfer reactions play central roles in biological redox chemistry across all domains of life. These transformations rely on specialized cofactors that enable the efficient transfer of reducing equivalents in oxidoreductive reactions. Nature has evolved several cofactors for this purpose, including nicotinamides, flavins, F420, pyrroloquinolone quinone (PQQ), and mycofactocin (MFT). Although these cofactors perform related functions, they differ in their structure, redox properties, reaction mechanisms, and biological distribution. This Review outlines these cofactors, highlighting common themes in hydride transfer mechanisms and how cofactor chemistry is linked to their biological function. In particular, F420, PQQ, and MFT are niche cofactors that expand our understanding of the diversity of cofactors and redox metabolism. Ultimately, understanding the chemistry and biology of redox cofactors offers broader applications in biotechnology and biocatalysis.

items.title:
Broadening the
Substrate Specificity of a Sugar Kinase
to Span
                    <scp>l</scp>
                    - and
                    <scp>d</scp>
                    -Sugars for Coupled Activation
Reactions
items.abstract: Abstract Sugar-1-phosphates are key intermediates in the synthesis of nucleotide sugars, which serve as essential building blocks for glycans from prokaryotes to eukaryotes. Compared to mammalian glycomes, those of microbes are enriched in deoxy l-sugars, many of which are activated as nucleotide β-l-sugars in the cell. The in vitro and cellular construction of many biologically relevant microbial polysaccharides, natural product glycoconjugates, surface glycoproteins, and antigens relies on nucleotide β-l-sugars. Yet, there remain few efficient chemical or biochemical routes toward the activated forms of these sugars or their sugar-1-phosphate starting materials. Here, we perform rational and unbiased engineering of the sugar kinase domain of the microbial l-fucose salvage enzyme FKP (Fucokinase/GDP-fucose pyrophosphorylase) and expand its substrate scope to span noncanonical l- and d-monosaccharides. We show that point mutations outside of the active site enable efficient phosphorylation of the prokaryote-specific sugar 6-deoxy-l-talose, and an active site mutation facilitates the phosphorylation of d-glucose. Coupling of FKP and its mutants with nucleotidyltransferases facilitates the production of diverse nucleotide sugars in one pot, highlighting facile in vitro methods to produce necessary starting materials that can be used in the enzymatic production of microbial and eukaryotic glycans.

items.title:
Slower Motions
and Dramatic Conformational Populations
Present in A:G Mismatched DNA Phosphates
items.abstract: Abstract Mismatches such as A:G base pairs arise in DNA primarily due to improper nucleotide incorporation during replication as well as formation of a heteroduplex. Repair of these mismatches and prevention of deleterious mutations is vital to an organism’s survival. Mismatch Repair (MMR) is the primary repair pathway for general DNA mismatches and follows replication to maintain genomic integrity; however, some details of mismatch recognition are unknown. Repair invariably requires precise and localized DNA–protein interactions and binding processes that depend on the specific properties, such as conformational structure and dynamics, of the repair protein and the damaged dsDNA substrate. Therefore, it is likely that the conformational properties of damaged, mismatched or modified DNAs will be different than canonical duplexed DNA. The work herein demonstrates a dramatic shift in time scale of motions and conformational populations for the phosphate flanking an A:G mismatched base pair. 31P NMR results show the motions are in the intermediate time scale (10–3 s), which is orders of magnitude slower than prior results (10–5–10–9 s), and the population of the BII substate shifts to ∼ 99%. These perturbations could be utilized in a phosphate tracking mechanism during indirect readout by repair enzymes such as MutS.

items.title:
Distributed
Structural Elements of DWORF Coordinate
Activation of the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum Calcium Pump SERCA
items.abstract: Abstract Many physiological processes are controlled by changes in cytosolic calcium, including muscle contraction, neuronal transmission, and cell proliferation. In muscle, the sarco-endoplasmic reticulum calcium ATPase (SERCA) restores resting cytosolic calcium by transporting calcium into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, thereby promoting relaxation. In cardiac muscle, SERCA is regulated by phospholamban (PLN) and dwarf open reading frame (DWORF), which inhibit and activate SERCA, respectively. To investigate the mechanism of DWORF-mediated activation, we focused on Trp22, an unusual tryptophan residue positioned near the center of the DWORF transmembrane domain. This position resembles the recently identified transmembrane binding site for small-molecule SERCA activators, suggesting that Trp22 may play a direct role in activation. Consistent with this hypothesis, calcium-dependent ATPase measurements in reconstituted membranes showed that a Trp22-Ala substitution completely abolished SERCA activation. We next tested whether residues outside the central transmembrane region contribute to activation by modulating SERCA-DWORF interactions. Phosphomimetic substitutions at the N-terminal residues Ser7, Thr8, and Ser10 eliminated SERCA activation, suggesting that the N-terminus modulates DWORF positioning. More strikingly, substitutions within the C-terminal motif Tyr31, Val32, Phe34, and Ser35 profoundly altered function. Tyr31-Ala, Val32-Ala, and Phe34-Ala converted DWORF from an activator to an inhibitor, whereas Ser35-Ala and Ser35-Pro caused loss of activation. Together, these results support a coordinated mechanism in which Trp22 acts as a critical determinant of SERCA activation, the N-terminus provides the potential for reversible regulation, and the C-terminus constrains the DWORF transmembrane helix in an activation-competent state.

items.title:
A Comparative
Biophysical Study of Conserved Ubiquitin-like
Protein Folds
items.abstract: Abstract Ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like proteins (Ubls) constitute a conserved protein family that shares a common β-grasp structural fold despite substantial sequence and functional divergence. How this highly conserved fold is maintained while accommodating diverse biological functions remains an open question in protein structural biology. In this study, we provide atomistic insights into the structural features that determine the stability of these conserved ubiquitin-like folds. Using an integrated biophysical approach combining solution NMR spectroscopy, molecular dynamics simulations, and chemical denaturation experiments, we systematically compare the protein dynamics and thermodynamic stability of ubiquitin and representative Ubls, including SUMO1, SUMO2, NEDD8, and Hub1. Our results reveal that ubiquitin exhibits exceptional thermodynamic stability relative to other Ubls, whereas Ubls display a broad range of stability profiles without a uniform trend toward destabilization. Biophysical and molecular dynamics analyses show that the reduced stability of Ubls is not associated with the loss of the conserved fold but is accompanied by differences in local structural flexibility. Together, these findings indicate that the conserved ubiquitin fold has been maintained despite sequence divergence and variation in stability and dynamics, supporting functional diversity while preserving structural integrity.

items.title:
Histidine-51 Facilitates the Conformational Change
and Deprotonation of Horse Liver Alcohol Dehydrogenase–NAD+ Complexes
items.abstract: Abstract Structural studies suggest that His-51 in wild-type horse liver alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH1E) facilitates proton transfer between the hydroxyl group of a ligand bound to the catalytic zinc and bulk solvent. Previous work showed that the Gln-51 substitution increases the pK values for pH dependencies for various enzymatic reactions by about 1.5 units, and stopped-flow studies on the binding of NAD+ and pyrazole suggested that the equilibrium position for the global conformational change of the enzyme–NAD+ complex became disfavored by 1000-fold. That conclusion needed confirmation. Here, X–ray crystallography of six ternary complexes of H51Q ADH with NAD+ and pyrazole, caprate, 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol, or 2,3,4,5,6-pentafluorobenzyl alcohol, and NADH and water or N-cyclohexylformamide shows that all complexes have the same closed conformation as wild-type ADH. Gln-51 fits in the region occupied by His-51 and does not affect the positions of bound coenzymes or inhibitors that coordinate to the catalytic zinc. Stopped-flow studies show that the rate-limiting formation of ternary complexes with H51Q ADH and NAD+ depends upon deprotonation of the ligands that bind to the catalytic zinc (pyrazole or 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol). Furthermore, the binding of NAD+ and trifluoroethanol monitored by fluorescence and proton release show that the H51Q substitution disfavors the conformational change by about 3-fold as compared to wild-type ADH. The pK values of the enzyme–NAD+ complexes with water and other zinc ligands increase because His-51 no longer facilitates the deprotonation. The roles of the zinc-water and His-51 in the mechanism are exposed.

items.title: Structure and Dynamics of Burkholderia pseudomallei OXA-57, a Distinctive Low-Efficiency Class D β-Lactamase with Carbapenem-Hydrolyzing Activity
items.abstract: Abstract The Gram-negative bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei causes the severe disease melioidosis. β-Lactams, including carbapenems, are the primary treatment for B. pseudomallei infections, but are susceptible to chromosomal serine β-lactamases (SBLs), including the class D enzyme OXA-57. Here we show that recombinant OXA-57 is active toward penicillins and first-generation cephalosporins, slowly hydrolyzes carbapenems, including imipenem and meropenem, but is inactive toward oxyimino-cephalosporins (e.g., ceftazidime). Unlike many OXA enzymes, OXA-57 is sensitive to the mechanism-based SBL inhibitor clavulanic acid, but less so to the diazabicyclooctane avibactam and not to the cyclic boronate vaborbactam. Crystal structures of covalent OXA-57:avibactam and OXA-57:meropenem complexes reveal limited hydrogen-bonding interactions with bound ligands. In molecular dynamics simulations, the bound meropenem acyl-enzyme is mobile, with the 6α-hydroxyethyl group able to sample different orientations, while the water molecule necessary for deacylation is bound only transiently. These observations are consistent with the low level of meropenem turnover, supporting proposals that limited carbapenemase activity is a general property of OXA β-lactamases, and highlight the potential importance of OXA-57 in B. pseudomallei β-lactam resistance.

items.title:
Covalent Labeling
of Human Neuroglobin with a 19F-Probe to Study its
Conformational Changes Using 19F NMR
items.abstract: Abstract It is of interest to develop new approaches to probing protein conformational changes and protein–protein interactions. In this study, we covalently labeled human neuroglobin (Ngb) with a 19F-probe containing a Ph-OCF3 group at Cys120 and by introducing cysteine residues at specific positions in the C120S Ngb mutant. 19F NMR provides valuable insights into its conformational changes upon cleavage of the intramolecular disulfide bond of Cys46-Cys55, as well as its interactions with protein partners such as cytochrome c (Cyt c) through the formation of the Ngb-Cyt c complex. This study presents a convenient approach to investigating the dynamic properties of heme globins regulated by disulfide bonds and protein–protein interactions.

items.title:
Fuzzy Interactions Open Perspectives toward Drugging
Conformational Heterogeneity
items.abstract: Abstract Fuzzy interactions enable specific biomolecular recognition while maintaining conformational freedom of the interacting partners. Here, we propose that fuzziness can be exploited for allosteric regulation to provide context-specific functional outputs. Using receptor signaling as an illustrative example, we demonstrate how heterogeneous binding modes with ligands can be fine-tuned through transient interactions. Fuzzy interactions interfere with alternative positions or modulate the mobility to mimic the landscapes of specific functional states that are linked with certain environmental conditions. Furthermore, using allosteric drugs targeting the ABL1 tyrosine kinase, KRAS oncogene, and IDH2 enzyme as examples, we demonstrate how fuzzy interaction mechanisms can affect allosteric couplings in a functionally meaningful manner through rewiring heterogeneous contact patterns. These notions could be helpful for drug development, targeting dynamic conformational ensembles and biasing them toward context-specific functional states.

items.title: Indirect Readout Drives Cre- loxP Recognition Thermodynamics
items.abstract: Abstract Cre, a site-specific tyrosine DNA recombinase, enables targeted manipulation of genetic material without the production of cytotoxic double-strand DNA breaks. Though widely deployed in biotechnology, an incomplete understanding of how Cre recognizes its cognate loxP target limits its broader application in human health. Cre is highly specific for its cognate loxP sites, comprising an inverted pair of recombinase binding elements (RBEs) and an asymmetric spacer. Structural studies have shown that Cre protomers make few direct base-specific contacts to each RBE, suggesting that specificity arises through indirect readout, wherein noncognate sites are unable to adopt favorable binding-coupled conformations. We designed a set of loxP half-site variants predicted to alter local DNA shape characteristics, including minor-groove geometry and base-step parameters, and measured the thermodynamics of Cre binding by isothermal titration calorimetry. Variable-temperature thermograms and nuclear magnetic resonance spectra reveal that unfavorable mutations at noncontacted positions in the RBE reduce signatures of binding-coupled conformational changes. Moreover, mass photometry of Cre binding to oligonucleotides containing two properly spaced RBEs revealed that noncontacted positions in the intervening 8-base pair spacer influence cooperative dimerization of two Cre protomers at loxP sites and their synapsis to form catalytically active Cre4-loxP2 complexes. These results demonstrate that noncontacted positions contribute to specificity by encoding favorable DNA mechanics, offering new design principles for engineering Cre variants that target alternative DNA sequences.

items.title:
What Computational
Simulations Tell Us about Cryptochromes
in Magnetoreception
items.abstract: Abstract The ability of migratory birds to orient using the Earth’s magnetic field has been proposed to rely on a radical-pair mechanism operating within Cryptochrome 4, a blue-light flavoprotein. In this perspective, we review how computational approaches have shaped our molecular understanding of cryptochrome-based magnetoreception. We organize the discussion around the three steps that connect light absorption to a cellular signal: the photochemical step, in which light absorption by FAD drives a hole-hopping electron-transfer cascade along a conserved tryptophan tetrad; the spin-dependent step, in which the resulting radical pair interconverts between singlet and triplet states under the influence of the magnetic field; and the structural step, in which this transient information is converted into a long-lived signaling state. The early electron-transfer events are now described with growing confidence and appear conserved across avian orthologs, although the relative stability of the final radical-pair states remains debated. The spin-dependent step remains more problematic: once the fluctuations of the hyperfine couplings and a realistic number of nuclear spins are included, the predicted magnetic sensitivity at geomagnetic field intensities becomes very small, and explaining the magnitude of the effect is still a central open problem. The postactivation conformational dynamics, involving intrinsically disordered regions, remains the principal challenge. We suggest that atomistic multiscale modeling, integrated with artificial intelligence-based approaches, has become indispensable for connecting the conserved photochemistry to this downstream process.

items.title: Issue Publication Information
Issue Editorial Masthead

Beyond the Active
Site: Allosteric Tail of HIV-1
Protease Is a Potential Target for Inhibiting Dimerization
items.abstract: Abstract HIV protease (HIVPR) is one of the key targets in AIDS therapy. All ten FDA-approved drugs targeting this enzyme compete with the substrates in binding to its active site. However, the emergence of drug-resistant mutants in active and nonactive sites of HIVPR has compromised the efficacy of these drugs. Nonetheless, darunavir (DRV) and tipranavir (TPV) have exhibited greater success than the other eight drugs, presumably due to their dual mode of action: (i) inhibiting protease activity and (ii) blocking protease dimerization. Although crystal structures have explained the inhibitory mechanism of protease activity, the mechanism of inhibiting the dimerization process is poorly understood. In this study, we employ advanced molecular dynamics simulation methods to identify the precise binding motifs of DRV and TPV with monomeric HIVPR. Our results suggest that both inhibitors bind stably to an allosteric pocket located in the tail region of the enzyme. Results also elucidate reversible association–dissociation of the drugs between the conventional active site and the newly identified tail cavity through surface diffusion. Structural analysis revealed that drug binding to the tail pocket induces a conformational extension of the C-terminal α-helix, a change that sequesters the terminal residues required for stable dimer formation. Our finding aligns very well with the reported ESI-MS spectra showing the tail interface as a crucial domain in forming a stable HIV protease dimer. Our result paves the way for designing a new class of HIVPR drugs that could target the C-terminal to effectively lock it in the monomeric form, potentially bypassing the cross-resistance due to active-site mutations.

items.title:
Thermophilic
Adaptation of a Minimal Hammerhead Ribozyme
Comes with a Functional Penalty
items.abstract: Abstract Life has adapted to extreme environments, such as elevated pH, extreme temperatures, and environments with a lack of oxygen. The biomolecules made by organisms that live in extreme environments must adapt to remain folded and functional. Recent computational studies have shown that rRNA, tRNA, and certain mRNAs adapt in thermophilic organisms through an increased GC content. However, few previous studies have assessed the efficiency of adapted thermophilic RNAs. The work presented herein uses minimal hammerhead ribozymes as a model system to determine the effects of high-temperature adaptation, through increased GC base pairing in the ribozyme secondary structure. Two hammerhead ribozymes were designed based upon the minimal hammerhead 16 (HH16) ribozyme, a well-characterized model system. The mesophilic ribozyme has a moderate GC content (44%) in stems I, II, and III, while the thermophilic ribozyme has nearly double the GC content (76%) in those same stems. Both ribozymes share a conserved catalytic core and loop. Thermal denaturation experiments show that the model thermophilic ribozyme is more thermostable with a higher single (cooperative) melting temperature than the model mesophilic ribozyme. However, thermostability is accompanied by a functional penalty. While at certain temperatures, the thermophilic ribozyme reaches the lower observed rates of the mesophilic ribozyme, the thermophilic ribozyme never reaches the same maximal rate of catalysis as the mesophilic ribozyme.

items.title:
Correlation Length-Scale Control in High-Precision
Born–Oppenheimer Calculations of He2+
items.abstract: Abstract We present a variational framework for high-precision Born–Oppenheimer calculations and apply it to the electronic ground state of the helium molecular ion, He2+. To obtain uniform accuracy from the short-range well to the dissociation limit, the variational expansion combines fully correlated molecular ECG basis functions with a frozen asymptotic monomer–pair sector optimized in the noninteracting limit. This sector stabilizes the variational optimization at large internuclear separations, where the interaction energy becomes much smaller than the monomer contributions. The resulting BO potential converges to subppb relative numerical accuracy across the entire range and provides a reliable foundation for high-precision rovibrational calculations. In particular, nonrelativistic dissociation energies are obtained with estimated uncertainties of the order of 10–4 cm–1. Although developed here for He2+ within an ECG framework, the approach should also be applicable to larger molecular systems with weak interfragment interactions.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Theory of Localized
Surface Plasmon Resonance at Electrochemical
Interfaces
items.abstract: Abstract Electrochemical plasmonics enables in situ optical probing and modulation of electrochemical interfaces. Experiments have shown that the localized surface plasmon resonance (LSPR) at the interface between a metal nanoparticle and an electrolyte solution is sensitive to electrode potential, nanoparticle morphology, electrolyte composition, and chemisorption. Theoretical modeling is instrumental to mechanistic understanding of these experimental observations. It has, however, remained challenging to model the LSPR under experimentally relevant conditions, namely, to treat the solid–liquid interfaces at nanoparticles with diameters of approximately 10 nm at controlled electrode potentials. Here, we tackle this challenge by employing an approach based on nonequilibrium density-potential functional theory. The approach captures the effects of surrounding medium and nanoparticle size on the LSPR, showing semiquantitative agreement with experimental data. Beyond electroneutral conditions, the approach is used to analyze the electrode potential effects on the LSPR. A blueshift at more positive electrode potentials is obtained and is attributed to a less extended electron density profile at the interface. In contrast to conventional models that neglect electron spill-out, this blueshift indicates that changes in the spatial electron distribution can outweigh the contribution of electron number to the potential-dependent resonance shift. This framework connects electrical double-layer structure with plasmonic response and provides a basis for interpreting optical measurements at electrochemical interfaces.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Force Calculation
at the Complete Active Space Configuration
Interaction Level Based on the Neural Network Quantum State Approach
items.abstract: Abstract The neural network quantum state (NNQS) approach provides an artificial intelligence-based representation of many-electron wave functions for quantum chemistry. Although a full configuration-space NNQS can achieve high accuracy, its direct use for force evaluation and geometry optimization remains computationally demanding, motivating a reduced-space treatment. Here, we implement analytic interatomic force calculations at the complete active space configuration interaction (CASCI) level based on the highly expressive QiankunNet architecture. By constructing an effective second-quantized Hamiltonian within a prescribed active orbital space and solving the coupled-perturbed Hartree–Fock equations, we obtain analytic forces including orbital response contributions. Benchmark calculations demonstrate the compact representational capability of QiankunNet and its close agreement with conventional CASCI references for both energies and forces, even in strongly correlated systems. We further apply the resulting forces to construct reaction potential energy surfaces for both ethylene torsion and cyclobutadiene isomerization, and to optimize the anthracene geometry for vertical singlet–triplet energy gap calculation. This work offers a practical route toward efficient force-based simulations of multireference chemical systems.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Potential Energy Surfaces in Multilayered Form: Deep
Learning Based Regression of Analytical Hierarchical Tree Structures
Using Unstructured Clouds of Data-Points
items.abstract: Abstract In this work, we introduce analytical hierarchical tree structures, aka multilayered parametric functions, in the context of regression of multidimensional surfaces, such as molecular or interparticle potential energy surfaces. From a technical perspective, our binary trees stem from the ideas underlying the so-called hierarchical Tucker decomposition by replacing columnwise the factors by piecewise polynomials interpolated from randomized multivariate distributions. We refer to our approach as hierarchical Tucker finite basis representation (HT-FBR). Furthermore, our trees can be transformed into a computational graph a recursive representation in terms of operators. Our optimized HT-FBR function is smooth, continuous and differentiable. Using a single-entry rule and our direct index-flow theorem, it can be efficiently evaluated at any system configuration within the definition domain. As a consequence, we show that it is possible to optimize the HT-FBR parameters using clouds of scattered data-points in combination with a deep-learning based approach. Specifically, we show that such optimization process is very efficient when employing a backpropagation-like scheme. To assess the power of our approach, we illustrate these features in the context of multidimensional fitting of potential energy surfaces for two systems: (i) a common benchmark, a (6D) PES for the description of the cis–trans isomerization of HONO and (ii) the 12D coupled diabatic potential energy surfaces of ethene. As reference set for this last case-study, we have employed the database generated through a series of direct dynamics variational multiconfigurational Gaussian trajectories (DD-vMCG) trajectories. As a final remark, our HT-FBR representation is fully compatible with both trajectory- and wavepacket-based methods such as such (ML-)MCTDH. As a consequence, it enables a direct comparison of different nonadiabatical dynamical methods.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title: Ab Initio Conical Intersection Dynamics from Coarse-Grained Electronic Quantum Geometry
items.abstract: Abstract Conical intersections are important for many ultrafast photochemical processes, yet fully quantum simulation of ab initio conical intersection dynamics is one of the main challenges in theoretical chemistry. Quantum geometric molecular dynamics unifies all non-Born–Oppenheimer effects in the bounded electronic overlap matrices between adiabatic states, but a direct implementation requires electronic structure information on an exponentially large nuclear grid; here, we introduce a coarse-grained local diabatic ansatz in which electronic quantum geometry is resolved only along a small set of reactive coordinates, while the remaining nuclear degrees of freedom are retained in the wave function and represented with tensor networks. Benchmark calculations for a 4-mode pyrazine model reproduce multilayer multiconfiguration time-dependent Hartree dynamics, and the same framework captures internal conversion, spectra, and geometric-phase-induced nodal structure in the full 24-mode pyrazine model. We further demonstrate direct coupling to ab initio electronic structure calculations for a pseudohydrogen chain H6, without constructing a global diabatic Hamiltonian. These results provide a route toward fully quantum simulations of excited-state relaxation and photochemical dynamics in high-dimensional molecular systems from first principles.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title: Thermodynamics of Metal–Hydroxide Interactions
items.abstract: Abstract Metal-bound hydroxide species play central roles in biological catalysis, ligand exchange, and metal-ion selectivity, but their accurate representation in classical molecular dynamics simulations remains challenging because of the strong electrostatic and ion-induced dipole interactions associated with hydroxide coordination. In this work, we develop 12–6–4 Lennard-Jones nonbonded parameters for metal–hydroxide interactions involving Mg(II), Ca(II), Mn(II), Fe(II), Co(II), Ni(II), Cu(II), Zn(II), and Cd(II) in both TIP3P and OPC water models. The hydroxide–water C4 parameter was first optimized to reproduce the experimental hydration free energy of hydroxide, followed by systematic optimization of metal–hydroxide C4 terms against experimental metal–hydroxide binding free energies derived from stability constants. Potential of mean force calculations were used for parameter refinement, while thermodynamic integration calculations provided an independent validation through closed thermodynamic cycles. The optimized parameters reproduce experimental binding affinities within chemical accuracy for both water models and correct the severe overbinding observed with conventional 12–6 and default 12–6–4 models. Structural validation against density functional theory calculations further shows that the modified parameters provide reasonable metal–oxygen distances, with the OPC water model generally giving closer agreement with quantum mechanical geometries. Analysis of the potential of mean force (PMF) profiles reveals ligand-exchange barriers and solvent-mediated second-shell intermediates during hydroxide dissociation. Overall, the resulting parameter set provides a classical framework for modeling metal–hydroxide interactions in aqueous and biological environments where both thermodynamic accuracy and structural realism are required.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Beyond the Exchange
Picture of Singlet–Triplet
Gaps
items.abstract: Abstract Molecules with inverted singlet–triplet gaps are promising candidates for next-generation organic light-emitting diode emitters, but identifying general principles that explain and guide singlet–triplet inversion remains challenging. Here, we investigate substituted heptazines, vibrational ensembles of azupyrene and isopyrene, and a chemically diverse molecular set using CIS, EOM-CCSD, and wave function-based state matching. The CIS analysis reveals an intermediate level of electronic response between direct exchange and correlation: state-specific configuration relaxation redistributes the gap among exchange, orbital-energy, and electron–hole Coulomb contributions. Correlation beyond CIS generally lowers the gap, with a larger reduction associated with greater relative double-excitation character in the singlet. However, the final gap also depends on the positive CIS baseline, so similar doubles content can occur in systems with either positive or negative gaps. Within related molecular data sets, a larger CIS baseline is accompanied by a stronger correlation-driven reduction, but this relationship does not hold across chemically diverse molecules. These findings establish the importance of balancing the full state-specific singles baseline against correlation-driven gap reduction when interpreting and designing singlet–triplet energetics.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
MemBack: An Equivariant
Graph Neural Network for Backmapping
Lipid Membranes
items.abstract: Abstract Backmapping coarse-grained (CG) simulations to atomistic resolution is central to multiscale molecular simulation but remains challenging for chemically complex lipid membranes. We introduce MemBack, an SE(3)-equivariant graph neural network (GNN) that reconstructs CHARMM36 lipid structures from Martini 3 configurations by single-pass heavy-atom prediction followed by automated postprocessing. Across chemically diverse systems, MemBack achieved a mean superposition-free per-lipid heavy-atom RMSD of 0.65 Å while retaining comparable accuracy for membrane systems and lipid species excluded from training. At the membrane scale, MemBack preserved structural organization across resolutions: in a 16-component red-blood-cell (RBC) membrane model excluded from training, bilayer thickness, area per lipid (APL), and acyl-chain order closely matched the atomistic reference after only restrained minimization; in a native phase-separated Martini 3 membrane, the lateral organization of ordered and disordered domains was likewise retained directly after backmapping, without atomistic equilibration. Native Martini 3 systems containing up to 1.4 million reconstructed atoms remained consistent with their parent coarse-grained configurations and could be propagated in atomistic simulations, providing an efficient interface between Martini 3 and CHARMM36 membrane simulations.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Functional and Density-Driven Errors in Density Functional
Theory: Quantum Monte Carlo Benchmarks for Solids
items.abstract: Abstract We introduce a systematic analysis of density functional approximation errors in solids by separating functional-driven from density-driven contributions using quantum Monte Carlo densities of silicon, sodium chloride, and copper as reference. Typically, functional errors dominate, but we identify important exceptions where the xc component of the density-driven error exceeds the functional error, notably for SOGGA11 in the semiconductor and the insulator. Material dependence is striking: 61% of functionals show error cancellation in silicon versus 16% in copper, and only five functionals surpass LDA accuracy for metallic copper even with exact densities. For silicon and sodium chloride, GILL or BECKE exchange combined with PBE, PW91, or P86 correlation achieves near-exact xc energies on QMC densities, while copper requires specialized functionals like PBEsol or PBELYP. High-quality densities consistently reduce density-driven errors across all systems. Historical analysis reveals that 1990s GGA functionals outperform many modern meta-GGAs, contradicting expectations of systematic improvement along Jacob’s ladder. These results provide practical guidance for functional selection and highlight implications for machine learning potential development, where material-dependent error cancellation may compromise transferability.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Accurate Flexible-Monomer
Force Fields from First
Principles. I. Automatic Development of Three-Body Nonadditive Contribution
items.abstract: Abstract A method for automatic generation of flexible-monomer three-body (3B) nonadditive contribution to intermolecular force fields (FFs) has been developed. It is an extension of the method developed earlier for two-body contributions. Together with one-body contributions and a polarization model accounting for four- and higher-body contributions, these components form a complete FF that can be used to simulate molecular clusters and condensed phases. The method was used to develop 3B potential energy surfaces for (H2O)3, (HF)3, and HF–(H2O)2, enabling simulations of water, hydrogen fluoride, and some mixtures of the two. The fitting errors of these 3B surfaces are generally smaller than those of the published analytic expansion fits and on par with the best neural network model for the water trimer. The properties of small clusters predicted by the FFs developed here are more accurate than those given by the published benchmarks from single-point ab initio calculations for such clusters, and we had to compute more accurate benchmarks of this type to evaluate the quality of our FFs.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
FMO-xTB:
Fragment Molecular Orbital Method
with GFN1-xTB for Large-Scale Quantum-Mechanical Simulations
items.abstract: Abstract We present the fragment molecular orbital method (FMO) combined with the GFN1-xTB extended tight-binding approach (FMO-xTB) for efficient quantum-mechanical calculations of large molecular systems. Both the two-body (FMO2) and three-body (FMO3) expansions are formulated, and fully analytic energy gradients including the response contribution from the self-consistent embedding potential are derived and implemented. The FMO-xTB method inherits the broad element coverage of GFN1-xTB, which employs element-specific rather than atom-pair-specific parameters and is parametrized for all spd-block elements up to radon (Z = 86), representing a significant practical advantage over FMO-DFTB approaches. The accuracy of FMO-xTB is systematically benchmarked against nonfragmented xTB calculations for water clusters, anthracene aggregates, and pentacene supercells. FMO3-xTB reproduces the reference energies with deviations on the order of 10–4 hartree for organic semiconductor systems. The covalent bond fragmentation capability using the hybrid orbital projection (HOP) boundary treatment is also implemented with fully analytic gradients and validated for polyalanine α-helices and B-DNA double helices, yielding FMO3-xTB energy deviations on the order of 10–6 hartree for polyalanine and in the millihartree range for B-DNA. Near-linear scaling is achieved with effective scaling exponents between b = 1.06 and b = 1.28, compared to cubic scaling for nonfragmented xTB. Parallelization over multiple CPU cores yields significant speed ups, and a complete energy and gradient evaluation of a pentacene supercell containing 23 760 atoms is feasible within minutes on a single computing node, enabling routine molecular dynamics simulations of systems with tens of thousands of atoms. The method is implemented in the DIALECT software package.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Assessing the Bethe–Salpeter Equation within
the GW Approximation (GW/BSE) for Excitation Energies of BODIPY and
Aza-BODIPY Derivatives
items.abstract: Abstract Boron-dipyrromethenes (BODIPYs) are a class of fluorescent molecules known for their highly tunable optical properties and diverse array of applications, ranging from medical imaging to photovoltaics. BODIPY excited states are characteristically difficult to model computationally, and time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) is known to consistently overestimate BODIPY excitation energies, producing mean absolute error (MAE) values often exceeding 0.3 eV. To assess an alternative approach, we turn to the Bethe–Salpeter equation within the GW approximation (GW/BSE), which has recently been gaining traction for its ability to eliminate many common issues of TD-DFT (such as the self-interaction error, unequal treatment of local and charge-transfer excitations, and strong functional dependence) at an equivalent computational cost. Using experimental and CASPT2 excitation energies for a set of 17 substituted BODIPYs and aza-BODIPYs, we present a comprehensive benchmark of the GW/BSE method. The assessment includes analysis of basis set convergence with the (aug)-cc-pVnZ (n = D, T, Q) basis set series, comparison of evGW and G0W0 schemes to evaluate the effect of self-consistency in the GW calculation, and evaluation of the impact of different DFT starting points (PBE, LC-ωPBE, and PBE0 with varying levels of exact exchange). Results demonstrate that GW/BSE with an appropriately selected Kohn–Sham starting point can produce MAE values under 0.1 eV while maintaining strong linear correlations, significantly outperforming TD-DFT and cementing GW/BSE as a valuable tool for the prediction of BODIPY excitation energies and design of future BODIPY derivatives.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
TDDFT Gradients
and Nonadiabatic Couplings with Minimal
Auxiliary Basis Set Approximation for Fewest-Switches Surface Hopping
Dynamics
items.abstract: Abstract The electronic structure calculations remain a major bottleneck in ab initio nonadiabatic molecular dynamics. We develop an efficient TDDFT-based FSSH implementation in the GPU4PySCF package for medium-sized molecular systems. Our approach combines density fitting, TDDFT with minimal auxiliary basis sets (TDDFT-ris), and an approximate Z-vector solver to reduce the computational cost of TDDFT excited states and derivative coupling calculations. These approximations introduce modest changes in the relaxation time scales while maintaining high computational efficiency. Benchmark results show that, for 73-atom systems with a triple-ζ basis set, individual electronic structure calculations are completed within 1 min on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Correction to “Protein-Based
Determination
of Model Redox Potentials for the High-Potential and Low-Potential
Redox Transition of [4Fe-4S]-Cys4 Clusters Using Continuum Electrostatics”
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Benchmarking Nonpolarizable
Mg2+ Parameters
Reveals Trade-Offs in RNA Conformational Sampling
items.abstract: Abstract In molecular dynamics simulations of RNA, Mg2+ ion force field parameters remain highly sensitive to the choice of water model and nucleic acid force field. The choice of Mg2+ force field parameters requires intentional thought, and although recent trends in nucleic acid force field development increasingly use the OPC water model, the compatibility of Mg2+ parameters with the OL3/OPC combination is insufficiently characterized. Here, we benchmark a panel of Mg2+ force fields: first in water boxes containing OPC with a single Mg2+ ion, and then in simulations with the Varkud satellite ribozyme stem loop V (SLV) as a model RNA, using the OL3 force field with LJbb corrections (OL3-LJbb). While most Mg2+ models are designed to reproduce the experimental ordering of hydration shells, they still differ substantially in diffusion coefficients and hydration free energies, reflecting the known trade-off between reproducing hydration thermodynamics and ion-oxygen distances in divalent-cation parametrization. These differences translate directly to RNA simulations, where Mg2+ models with slower diffusion and overly favorable hydration free energies promote long time-scale RNA binding events (“chelation”) and disrupt Mg2+-driven conformational changes. Together, these results highlight the need to validate divalent ion parameters specifically within the water model and RNA force field environment used for production-phase RNA molecular simulations, as well as demonstrate the Varkud satellite ribozyme as a sensitive benchmark for Mg2+/RNA/solvent force field compatibility.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
GPU-Accelerated
Large-Scale Nonadiabatic Excited State
Molecular Dynamics
items.abstract: Abstract Nonadiabatic molecular dynamics is essential for simulating photoinduced processes, but its application to large molecular systems is often limited by the cost of repeatedly evaluating excited-state energies, forces, and nonadiabatic couplings. Here, we present a GPU-accelerated implementation of trajectory surface hopping within PYSEQM (https://github.com/lanl/PYSEQM/), a PyTorch-based semiempirical quantum chemistry framework. The module combines semiempirical model Hamiltonians with configuration-interaction singles excited states and introduces the nonadiabatic coupling vectors and time-derivative couplings required for surface-hopping dynamics. The implementation further includes treatments of trivial crossings and electronic decoherence, providing a complete framework for propagating coupled electronic and nuclear dynamics. To improve GPU utilization, independent trajectories are propagated concurrently in batches. Benchmark calculations show that this strategy substantially increases aggregate simulation throughput as the batch size is increased for small molecules. We demonstrate the applicability of the method to large molecular systems by simulating the excited-state population dynamics of methyl- and tert-butyl-substituted molecular nanostar dendrimers, which contain dense manifolds of electronically excited states. These calculations show that semiempirical surface-hopping dynamics can be extended to molecular systems that remain challenging for conventional ab initio approaches. In addition, the differentiable PyTorch formulation provides a data-science route for optimizing semiempirical Hamiltonian parameters against reference excited-state properties and, ultimately, dynamical observables. PYSEQM therefore provides a platform for high-throughput nonadiabatic molecular dynamics and for the development of data-driven semiempirical models for photophysics and photochemistry.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Algebraic Diagrammatic
Construction of the Multichannel
Dyson Equation
items.abstract: Abstract The multichannel Dyson equation (MCDE) was recently introduced as a new approximation scheme to compute the one-body Green’s function [Riva et al. Phys. Rev. Lett.2023, 131, 216401.] in many-body systems. The physical content of this novel approximation scheme is further clarified by recovering it from (an extended version of) the algebraic diagrammatic construction (ADC) truncation scheme. It is thus demonstrated that the MCDE approximation lies in between the so-called ADC(2) and ADC(3) truncations of the dynamical self-energy. Building on this clarification, the MCDE approximation is benchmarked against ADC(2) and ADC(3) on the periodic one-dimensional Hubbard model with 4-, 6- and 8-site lattices. It delivers an improved treatment over ADC(2) of both the quasiparticle peaks and the so-called satellites in the spectral strength distribution, and performs comparably to or better than ADC(3) in the strong-coupling regime.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Multilayer Multistate
Reaction Coordinate Model for
Nonadiabatic Dynamics in Open Quantum Systems
items.abstract: Abstract Simulating nonadiabatic quantum dynamics in complex condensed-phase systems is computationally challenging due to the high dimensionality of the nuclear environment. To address this, we introduce the multilayer multistate reaction coordinate (ML-MRC) model, a general hierarchical transformation of the multistate harmonic (MSH) Hamiltonian that maps the complex bath into a structured chain of collective modes. We demonstrate that the ML-MRC framework allows the MSH model to be reformulated into hierarchies of arbitrary depth, from single-layer reaction coordinates to full-chain representations, while maintaining rigorous mathematical equivalence. This flexibility is validated across diverse physical systems, including the spin-boson model, the Frenkel exciton model for the photosynthetic light-harvesting Fenna–Matthews–Olson complex, and a realistic photoinduced charge transfer model for a carotenoid-porphyrin-fullerene triad in tetrahydrofuran. Furthermore, this hierarchical structure enables a robust dimensionality reduction strategy, where truncating the chain yields low-dimensional effective Hamiltonians that accurately reproduce the nonadiabatic dynamics of the untruncated model at a reduced computational cost. Finally, the ML-MRC model reveals valuable mechanistic insights through reaction coordinate trajectories, which are shown to synchronize remarkably with electronic population dynamics across multiple systems.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Periodic Trends
in Radical-Mediated Exchange Coupling
and Magnetic Anisotropy in Ln2N2 Complexes
items.abstract: Abstract Large crystal-field anisotropy and strong exchange interactions are key ingredients in the design of next-generation molecule-based magnetic materials. Radical-bridged lanthanide complexes are particularly promising in this regard owing to their highly anisotropic ground states and strong exchange interactions mediated by the radical bridge. Here, we present a comprehensive ab initio investigation of the magnetic and exchange anisotropy in the {[((Me3Si)2N)2(THF)Ln]2(N2)}− complexes, where Ln = Gd3+, Tb3+, Dy3+, Ho3+, and Er3+. For the isotropic gadolinium (Ln = Gd3+) analogue, the microscopic origins of the exchange interaction are disentangled using density functional theory calculations, revealing significant contributions from both direct and kinetic exchange mechanisms, with the latter dominating due to efficient virtual Gd-to-radical electron transfer involving out-of-plane Gd 4f orbitals and the radical π* orbital. For the anisotropic complexes (Ln = Tb3+, Dy3+, Ho3+ and Er3+), crystal-field and exchange interactions are described using irreducible tensor-operator model Hamiltonians parametrized from multiconfigurational ab initio calculations. The resulting framework employs a reduced set of physically transparent parameters, facilitating systematic comparison across the lanthanide series. While the crystal field potential is largely constant across the series, the exchange interactions vary significantly.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Grand-Canonical Path Reweighting for Constant-Potential
Langevin Dynamics
items.abstract: Abstract Constant-potential molecular dynamics provides an important framework for studying the structural, thermodynamic, and kinetic properties of electrochemical systems at a prescribed electrochemical potential, but independent simulations under different electrochemical conditions can be computationally demanding, particularly for rare-event kinetics. Here, we develop a trajectory reweighting framework based on extended-phase-space Langevin dynamics, in which the electron number Ne is treated as an additional dynamical degree of freedom and the nuclear and electronic degrees of freedom evolve within a unified Langevin framework. The proposed approach enables thermodynamic and kinetic properties at different electrochemical potentials to be obtained from a single ensemble of reference trajectories. We validate the method for the Volmer reaction at a Pt/water interface, where the reweighted trajectories reproduce both the thermodynamic properties and reaction rates obtained from direct dynamical simulations at the target electrochemical potential. The reweighting is performed entirely in postprocessing and introduces negligible additional computational cost. Furthermore, this dynamical reweighting approach can use well-sampled reference trajectories generated under conditions where the reaction proceeds more rapidly to estimate reaction rates under conditions where the reaction is slower.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Multireference QM/MM Nonadiabatic Dynamics with Quantum
Nuclei in Explicit Environment: Implementation in COBRAMM and Application
to the Sub-100 fs Energy Transfer in NADH
items.abstract: Abstract We present a mixed quantum-classical framework for simulating nonadiabatic excited-state dynamics in explicit environments. The method combines a fully quantum-mechanical treatment of both electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom in the high-level (HL) region with classical propagation of the surrounding low-level (LL) environment. The HL dynamics is described using a linear vibronic coupling Hamiltonian parametrized at the multireference (XMS-CASPT2) level of theory, while bidirectional systembath coupling is incorporated through a dynamically updated electrostatic embedding scheme. The implementation, integrated into the COBRAMM suite, interfaces Quantics, OpenMolcas, and AMBER. Benchmark tests assess the stability, energy conservation, and approximations underlying the protocol. Among those, we highlight the crude adiabatic approximation, which allows to avoid explicit QM calculations for the update of the Hamiltonian during the dynamics, making the simulation time dependent only on the size of the active space required for the initial parametrization. As a proof of concept, we investigate the sub-100 fs excitation energy transfer (EET) in solvated NADH. Compared to simulations with a frozen environment, the explicit dynamical response of the solvent enhances the charge transfer (CT)-mediated EET pathway. The results highlight the critical role of fast librational solvent modes in ultrafast nonadiabatic phenomena and establish the presented protocol as a robust approach for treating environment-driven internal conversion in rigid photoresponsive molecular systems.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
AnhDis: A Scheme
for Anharmonic Nuclear Ensembles
and Absorption Spectra
items.abstract: Abstract The Nuclear Ensemble Approach (NEA), typically implemented using the harmonic Wigner approximation in Cartesian normal coordinates, has shown significant limitations when applied to molecules with large-amplitude bending and torsional motions. On the one hand, rectilinear displacements fail to follow the curvature of these motions at finite amplitudes, introducing artificial bond stretching. On the other hand, harmonic potentials can inadequately describe confinement along these motions. Both limitations can lead to artificial spectral broadening and spurious transitions. In this work, the Anharmonic-Distribution (AnhDis) scheme is presented. The method is based on constructing mode-resolved potential energy surfaces through explicit scans along curvilinear paths in internal coordinates, represented in the present implementation by polynomial fits or piecewise cubic Hermite interpolation (PCHIP). By solving the resulting one-dimensional vibrational Hamiltonians, nuclear probability densities that account for anharmonic confinement and wave function asymmetry are obtained. Temperature effects are incorporated through Boltzmann weighting of the vibrational eigenstates. AnhDis thus combines curvilinear nuclear ensembles with an independent-mode treatment of anharmonicity. Comparisons with reference simulations and experimental data across atmospherically relevant molecules demonstrate that the proposed method captures absorption spectral profiles while reducing Cartesian sampling artifacts and revealing system-dependent anharmonic effects.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Regularized Frozen
Natural Orbital Approach to CASPT2:
Extension to Restricted Active Space Wave Functions, Different Multiplicities
and Assessment of Correlation Effects
items.abstract: Abstract The frozen natural orbital (FNO) method is a well-known approximation that significantly reduces the cost of many-body perturbation theory treatments for obtaining correlation energies in a systematic and controlled manner, enabling the simulation of larger and more realistic molecular systems. Here, we implement FNO on top of restricted active-space self-consistent field (RASSCF) wave functions within second-order perturbation theory, leading to the FNO-RASPT2 method. To account for the additional approximations incurred when using RASSCF wave functions, as well as to apply it to states of different molecular charge and spin multiplicity, we introduce a regularization approach via a level-shift in the orbital deletion procedure, which helps avoid singularities resulting from vanishing denominators due to the reduced occupation of restricted (active) virtual orbitals and that we show does not significantly influence the final energies obtained. Numerical results on vertical excitation energies showcase the FNO to be up to ∼4.0 times faster than the parent computation while retaining ∼95% of the dynamic correlation energy and being within 0.1 eV of the reference calculation, with the CASPT2 equations – the main bottleneck in large molecular systems – registering over an order of magnitude speed-up. An in-depth analysis shows the regularized FNO approach to retain electron correlation appropriately for internal and semi-internal contributions, while displaying larger deviations for the external term, which originates from the initial FNO truncation based on an approximated one-electron reduced density matrix. Ongoing efforts are directed toward improving and extending our current implementation to the calculation of analytic gradients and nonadiabatic couplings to enable faster nonadiabatic molecular dynamics simulations in larger and more realistic molecular systems.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Local, Non-Redundant
Molecular Coordinates from Disjoint
Primitive Families: Symmetry-Adapted Construction and Applications
items.abstract: Abstract Internal coordinates express molecular motion in chemical terms, but primitive functions are redundant, and global delocalization mixes coordinate families. We introduce extended symmetry-adapted local coordinates (ESALCs), which organize diverse chemical primitives into disjoint families and complete, nonredundant bases. The internal-coordinate form, ESALC-I, assigns general primitives to perceived chemical domains, forms local symmetry-adapted combinations, selects exact rank through the Wilson B matrix, and retains complete molecular-symmetry subspaces within a basin of fixed topology and symmetry. When bond assignments become ambiguous, the Cartesian form, ESALC-C, supplies a full-system basis with overall translations and rotations removed. Tests on covalent, fragment, and metal-contact systems establish rank, analytic derivatives, and symmetry. Stationary-Hessian comparisons for cyclobutane and norbornane show low coupling with chemically interpretable ESALC-I families. Full geometry optimizations demonstrate use with established programs.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
A Charge-Consistent
Long-Range Machine-Learned Interatomic
Potential Compatible with Quantum Linear System Algorithms
items.abstract: Abstract Charge equilibration in machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) requires repeatedly solving linear systems, providing a promising target for quantum linear-system algorithms (QLSAs). However, conventional electronegativity equalization schemes suffer from spurious fractional charges between neutral fragments at large separations. To address this limitation, we incorporate atom-condensed Kohn–Sham density functional theory approximated to second order (ACKS2) into a long-range equivariant neural-network MLIP. Across benchmark systems, the ACKS2-based model improves energy, force, and charge predictions. At a molecule–metal interface, ACKS2 restores molecular fragments to near-neutral charge states upon separation while preserving local charge redistribution near adsorption. Because ACKS2 charge equilibration reduces to solving a linear system, the classical solver can be directly replaced with the Harrow–Hassidim–Lloyd algorithm during inference, demonstrating compatibility with quantum linear-system solvers. These results indicate that ACKS2 provides a promising framework for charge-aware MLIPs and highlight a potential pathway toward atomistic simulations based on QLSAs.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Transferable Machine
Learning of Electronic Hamiltonians
with Superposition-of-Atomic-Potentials Features
items.abstract: Abstract Machine learning of electronic Hamiltonians offers a unified route to electronic wave functions and physical observables. We introduce a Hamiltonian learning framework built on electronic features derived from the superposition-of-atomic-potentials (SAP) approximation, an efficient self-consistent-field initial guess that captures essential electron–electron screening. SAP quantities define a symmetry-adapted intrinsic atomic orbital learning basis and provide physics-informed inputs to an orbital-based graph neural network that predicts converged Kohn–Sham Fock matrices. To extend the approach to larger basis sets, we further develop a downfolding scheme that predicts large-basis electronic structure from minimal-basis features. On the QM9 data set, the model accurately reproduces frontier and core orbital energies, dipole moments, and the full density of states. For organic charge-transport materials, it yields accurate intermolecular transfer integrals for benzene, tetracyanoquinodimethane (TCNQ), and tetrathiafulvalene (TTF) dimers. The model also generalizes to unseen substituted-benzene heterodimers, with a mean absolute error of 4.8 meV. These results establish SAP-based Hamiltonian learning as a transferable and scalable tool for high-throughput electronic-structure prediction.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
A Systematic Benchmark
of Multifidelity Training Strategies
for Reactive Machine Learning Potentials
items.abstract: Abstract Training reactive machine learning potentials (MLPs) requires extensive quantum chemical labeling of nonequilibrium configurations along reaction pathways, motivating the use of data from lower levels of theory through pretraining and Δ-learning. However, whether combining these strategies consistently improves accuracy and downstream performance remains unclear. Here, we benchmark direct and residual training, each with and without pretraining, across DPA-2, DPA-3, MACE, and DPA4-Neo, using 17.6 million configurations labeled with GFN2-xTB and 198,622 configurations labeled at the ωB97X-D/def2-TZVP level. With the full DFT training set, pretrained Δ-learning achieves the lowest energy or force MAE averaged over three training seeds in 31 of 32 combinations of architecture, data set, and property. Learning curves for DPA4-Neo nevertheless show that direct finetuning reaches the MAE of a model trained from scratch on the full data set using no more DFT training configurations than pretrained Δ-learning in all eight combinations of data set and property, while avoiding repeated GFN2-xTB evaluations during inference. Pretrained Δ-learning also improves reaction energies and forward barriers across all four architectures on GDB-10-rxn and reduces median Hessian eigenvalue errors for the evaluated DPA4-Neo checkpoint. However, local force errors can remain incompletely corrected, and these improvements do not consistently increase the success rates of reaction search workflows initialized from specified reactant and product geometries, indicating that the preferred protocol depends on the data budget, target property, and downstream workflow.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Reduction of Finite-Size
Effects for Second-Order
Møller–Plesset Perturbation Theory with Singularity Subtraction
items.abstract: Abstract Second-order Møller–Plesset perturbation theory (MP2) for periodic systems suffers from finite-size errors (FSEs) that have inverse volume scaling due to the Coulomb kernel singularity in reciprocal space. This error scaling limits the routine applicability of MP2 and other methods that rely on it to real materials, requiring prohibitively dense k-point meshes for convergence toward the thermodynamic limit (TDL). We introduce MP2 singularity subtraction (MP2SS), a systematic approach that applies the singularity subtraction strategy to reduce MP2 FSEs. The method employs auxiliary functions and fitting procedures that consider both the singularities present at the origin in reciprocal space and also the discontinuities in the MP2 structure factor that arise from finite k-point sampling. We present three possible MP2SS configurations (Gaussian, exponential, and tuned) which use different combinations of decay functions and demonstrate their performance for gapped systems. Across a range of extended solids and molecular crystals at large basis sets, MP2SS reduces the prefactor in MP2 FSEs and subsequently the computational resources required to converge to the TDL. MP2SS with the Gaussian auxiliary function provides the most robust corrections. Our results establish singularity subtraction as a powerful and flexible approach for mitigating finite-size errors in periodic correlation methods and provide a foundation for extending the technique to higher-order perturbation theories and other post-Hartree–Fock (HF) methods.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Relativistic Dirac–Coulomb–Breit
Four-Component
Multireference Perturbation Theory within the Small Tensor Product
Distributed Active Space Framework
items.abstract: Abstract We present a four-component multireference second-order perturbation theory (4C-MRPT2) within the small tensor product distributed active space (STP-DAS) framework. The formulation is compatible with the Dirac–Coulomb (DC), Dirac–Coulomb–Gaunt (DCG), and Dirac–Coulomb–Breit (DCB) Hamiltonians and inherits the memory-efficient and massively parallel STP-DAS algorithm, enabling perturbative treatments over very large external spaces. Benchmark calculations on noble-gas and group-13 atoms demonstrate that 4C-MRPT2 efficiently recovers all-electron dynamic correlation while providing new insight into relativistic correlation effects. The calculations show that the Breit contribution to the correlation energy increases rapidly with atomic number and reaches approximately 4% of the total correlation energy for Xe. The method also shows that second-order correlation energies are only weakly dependent on the choice of multiconfigurational reference orbitals and that frozen-core and frozen-virtual approximations substantially reduce computational cost with minimal loss of accuracy.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Surface Evaporation Protocol for Solution-Processed
Bulk-Heterojunction Films via Coarse-Grained Simulations
items.abstract: Abstract We present a coarse-grained molecular dynamics protocol for simulating solvent evaporation applied to P3HT:PCBM bulk-heterojunction (BHJ) films. Prior reported protocols lacked an explicit air–film interface or resorted to monatomic solvents with heavily coarse-grained solute models to work. Our approach maintains an explicit air–film interface, handles polyatomic solvents, and is better suited for complex molecular models. The resulting films reproduce experimentally reported vertical segregation (a P3HT-enriched skin over a PCBM-enriched subsurface) and an in-plane preferential orientation of P3HT backbones and π-stacking that originates at the interface and propagates downward with the drying front. A Marcus-type charge extraction model applied to the dried films revealed faster in-plane hole transport in the P3HT domains than through the film thickness, while electron transport in PCBM domains suggested the opposite trend. The results suggest an active upper surface with a large capacity for generating free charges emerges during the film’s formation that might benefit OPVs with an inverted architecture. Both the evaporation protocol and the charge transport model are formulated in general terms with the purpose of enabling the transfer of the algorithms to other systems.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
SPINKS (Spin Inversion
Kinetics Suite): A Fully Automated
Python–ORCA Framework for End-to-End Computation of Spin-Crossing
Probabilities, Microcanonical, and Canonical Reaction Rate Constants
items.abstract: Abstract We present SPINKS (Spin Inversion Kinetics Suite), a freely available, fully automated Python–ORCA computational framework for an end-to-end evaluation of spin-forbidden reaction kinetics directly from an initial molecular geometry. SPINKS automatically generates, executes, monitors, and processes the ORCA electronic-structure calculations required to determine the minimum-energy crossing point (MECP) between two potential-energy surfaces. It then extracts the spin–orbit coupling (SOC), energy gradients, and Hessians required to construct the reaction coordinate and subsequently evaluates the reduced mass, crossing velocity, and vibrational and rovibrational densities of states. These quantities are used to calculate Landau–Zener and weak coupling spin-crossing probabilities and the corresponding microcanonical and canonical reaction rate constants within the framework of nonadiabatic statistical theory. The workflow automatically generates graphical visualizations and comprehensive text-based outputs while permitting user customization of ORCA input files throughout the calculation. SPINKS shows excellent agreement during validation tests against the independently developed Nonadiabatic Statistical Theory (NAST) package. The NAST program requires manual preparation and transfer of electronic-structure quantities, whereas SPINKS integrates ORCA-based electronic-structure calculations with nonadiabatic dynamics and kinetic calculations within a single end-to-end automated workflow. SPINKS is freely distributed and operates within an accessible software ecosystem based on the free and open-source Python language and the ORCA quantum-chemistry package, which is freely available for academic use. The SPINKS framework provides a practical, reproducible, and extensible platform for routine investigation of spin-forbidden chemical reactions.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Approaching Coupled
Cluster Accuracy with Positive
Semidefinite Vertex Corrected Self-Energies
items.abstract: Abstract Hedin’s formalism of functional derivatives is a successful method for systematically constructing correlated electronic theories, largely due to the success of its lowest-order self-energy expansion, the GW approximation. Beyond GW, diagrammatic resummation schemes attempt to mix correlations simultaneously across all particle-particle and particle-hole channels. Because such a comprehensive treatment is computationally prohibitive for realistic molecular systems, a highly effective alternative is to fully account for electronic correlations in one specific channel, typically the particle-hole channel. This idea was recently implemented for molecular systems, yielding a self-energy expressed in terms of excited-state energies and transition amplitudes from the solution of the Bethe–Salpeter equation, rather than the random-phase approximation used in GW. While this approach is predictive and numerically efficient, it violates the fundamental positive-definiteness constraint on the electron spectral function in certain energy ranges. In this study, we resolve this physical flaw by deriving a positive-semidefinite (PSD) extension of the theory using a rigorous framework based on the nonequilibrium Green’s function formalism. The PSD constraint introduces new scattering channels and triplet intermediate states and restores the correct physical behavior. We demonstrate that it consistently improves quasiparticle energies across standard molecular benchmarks, with an accuracy comparable to coupled-cluster reference calculations.

items.title:
Equivariant Interatomic
Potentials without Tensor
Products
items.abstract: Abstract Foundational machine-learned interatomic potentials have emerged as powerful tools for atomistic simulations, promising near first-principles accuracy across diverse chemical spaces at a fraction of the cost of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the most accurate equivariant architectures rely on Clebsch–Gordan tensor products whose computational cost scales steeply with angular resolution, creating a trade-off between model expressiveness and inference speed that ultimately limits practical applications. Here we introduce Geodite, an equivariant message-passing architecture that replaces tensor products while incorporating physical priors to ensure smooth, well-behaved potential energy surfaces. Trained on the Materials Project trajectories dataset of inorganic crystals, Geodite-MP achieves accuracy competitive with leading methods on benchmarks for materials stability prediction, thermal conductivity, phonon-derived properties, and nanosecond-scale molecular dynamics, while running 3–5× faster than models performing similarly. By combining predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and physicality, Geodite enables faster large-scale atomistic simulations and high-throughput screening that would otherwise be computationally prohibitive.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Low-Scaling Equation-of-Motion Coupled Cluster Method
for Open-Shell Systems: I. IP-EOM-DLPNO-CCSD
items.abstract: Abstract We present the formulation and implementation of an unrestricted/open-shell domain-based local pair natural orbital equation-of-motion coupled-cluster method with single and double excitations for vertical ionization potentials (UHF IP-EOM-DLPNO-CCSD). The method extends the open-shell DLPNO–CCSD reference calculation to the (N – 1)-electron sector by reusing the localized occupied orbitals, pair domains, pair lists, and pair natural orbital spaces generated for the correlated ground state. Removal of an α or β electron is treated in separate spin sectors. The one-hole sector is retained in the fully localized occupied space, whereas the two-hole–one-particle sector is represented in compact, spin-resolved PNO spaces. The accuracy is controlled by the standard LoosePNO, NormalPNO, and TightPNO hierarchy. For ionized states dominated by one-hole character, canonical and local calculations performed with the same quasi-restricted-orbital (QRO) reference give typical RMSD differences of a few hundredths of an eV for the main-group radical and transition-metal benchmark sets. A representative TightPNO comparison for naphthalene further indicates that the additional local IP-EOM approximation contributes less than 0.10 eV for the ten matched states examined. Larger delocalized systems show less regular threshold dependence, and even predominantly one-hole states can exhibit changes greater than 0.1 eV between NormalPNO and TightPNO. Timing calculations for anionic acenes up to heptacene, with 1038 basis functions, show low-order effective scaling for the IP-EOM step. Applications to C70– and to the Pheophytin radical anion, the latter containing 3020 basis functions, demonstrate that the method can treat large open-shell molecular systems beyond the size range routinely accessible to canonical IP-EOM-CCSD. Finally, comparisons with available experimental data for the N-carbazolyl radical and the ovalene radical cation provide additional context for the calculated vertical ionization energies.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Can Phaseless Auxiliary-Field
Quantum Monte Carlo
with Broken Symmetry Trials Describe Iron–Sulfur Clusters?
items.abstract: Abstract Phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) has in several cases been found to perform well on strongly correlated systems, including compounds containing transition-metal elements. Here, we benchmark the method for three iron–sulfur clusters ([2Fe-2S], [4Fe-4S], and the FeMo cofactor) using a hierarchy of systematically improved trial states derived from coupled cluster (CC) theory, including up to quadruple excitations relative to the Hartree–Fock (HF) reference, as well as multi-Slater trial states derived from unrestricted density matrix renormalization group wave functions. Our results reveal for these systems that, as the symmetry-broken trial is improved beyond the mean-field level, the phaseless AFQMC energy can become less accurate, and in some cases even less accurate than the underlying trial projected energy itself, displaying an inverted energy pattern that is only corrected once the trial fidelity is sufficiently high. For [2Fe-2S], we show that a decreased accuracy in the AFQMC energy can coincide with a simultaneous improvement in the trial state and the walker ensemble, as measured by their fidelity relative to the exact ground state, a behavior which is allowed by the nonvariational nature of the phaseless AFQMC energy estimator. We further find that this is not solely due to the use of spin-unrestricted trial states, as the inversion persists in [2Fe-2S] when we explicitly break the symmetry of the Hamiltonian by applying a fictitious local spin-Zeeman field. Instead, we find that the energy inversion is related to the choice of measurement trial in the estimator, where using a high-order CC trial state for measurements may introduce errors that are suppressed when the measurement wave function is restricted to lower excitation subspaces.
