In particular, measuring the energy with the mean-field reference while guiding the walkers with a CC trial removes the inverted pattern and improves the overall accuracy across the iron–sulfur clusters, with a possible exception for [4Fe-4S] where energies with a CCSDT guide may be less accurate than those guided by CCSD for some broken-symmetry families. Taken together, our findings suggest that the relatively accurate energies obtained with an HF trial state in these systems arise from favorable error cancellation, warranting significant caution about the reliability of phaseless AFQMC with such trials for strongly correlated transition-metal systems of this kind.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Sequence Model-Based Prediction and QM/MM Assessment
of CYP2C19 Variant Effects on Mephenytoin Oxidation
items.abstract: Abstract Cytochrome P450 2C19 (CYP2C19) genetic variation contributes to interindividual differences in drug metabolism, yet relating sequence-level variation to substrate-specific catalytic mechanisms remains challenging. Here, we combine a generative sequence model based on the maximum entropy (MaxEnt) framework for mutation scoring, published biochemical activity data, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, and quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics adaptive steered molecular dynamics (QM/MM ASMD) calculations to examine CYP2C19 variant effects on S-mephenytoin oxidation. In the primary correlation analysis, MaxEnt scores showed nonsignificant negative rank trends with Vmax and CLint, whereas Km showed no corresponding rank association. CYP2C19*1A (WT) was used as the reference system, and CYP2C19*23 and CYP2C19*26 were selected as contrasting variants for atomistic analysis. MD simulations revealed variant-dependent changes in conformational sampling, correlated motions, and substrate positioning, but the population of geometries satisfying a predefined reactive distance-angle criterion did not reproduce the experimental activity trend. At the production pulling rate, the Seed 1 QM/MM-ASMD profiles showed a lower C12 oxygen-addition barrier for CYP2C19*23 and a higher barrier for CYP2C19*26 relative to CYP2C19*1A. Additional CYP2C19*1A and CYP2C19*23 starting configurations yielded a lower three-seed mean barrier for CYP2C19*23 at that pulling rate, although the barrier ranges overlapped and starting-configuration dependence was appreciable, and a slower-pulling control showed substantial rate sensitivity. The sampled NIH-shift profiles exhibited apparent low barriers in all three systems; however, substantial discrepancies between partition-level nonequilibrium-work estimators precluded establishing quantitatively converged CV2 barrier magnitudes. Thus, the calculations support qualitative differences among the sampled reaction profiles but do not quantitatively reproduce the magnitude of the experimental kinetic differences. The combined sequence, MD, and QM/MM workflow provides a framework for prioritizing variants and developing substrate-specific mechanistic hypotheses while making the sampling limitations explicit.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Reweighting Free
Energy Profiles with Universal Machine
Learning Interatomic Potentials for Fast Consensus Building
items.abstract: Abstract Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have made density functional theory (DFT)-level molecular dynamics highly affordable. However, their rapid proliferation makes it prohibitively expensive to benchmark every new model against the potential of mean force (PMF), the bridge between microscopic atomic fluctuations and macroscopic thermodynamic and kinetic observables. Reweighting the trajectory of a single “source” MLIP onto a suite of target potentials offers a cheaper route, but it is hindered by the statistical collapse of exponential free energy perturbation when the phase-space overlap between potentials is low. We show that for system sizes of practical interest, this collapse is essentially unavoidable, and we quantify it with an information-theoretic diagnostic, the reweighting entropy, that indicates when reweighting can be trusted. To sidestep the collapse, we introduce a systematic, scalable reweighting framework spanning exponential reweighting, the Gaussian approximation, and the energy-only estimator. When applied to the intramolecular radical cyclization of hexenyl (17 atoms), all three estimators perform well and reproduce the target ωB97M-V/def2-TZVP PMF. However, when extended to Li+ transport through a water-solvated zeolite (601 atoms), only the energy-only estimator recovers the PMFs of a diverse suite of MLIPs from a single source simulation by discarding the noisy entropic contribution to the free energy correction. An independent, brute-force umbrella sampling of one of the most divergent targets (MACE-MATPES-r2SCAN) for this system confirms it: beyond the shape of the PMF, both the reaction and activation free energies are recovered within chemical accuracy. The same analysis reveals that the studied MLIPs partition into two clusters, one of plain generalized gradient approximation (GGA) models (PBE, PBE-sol) and one of meta-GGA and/or dispersion-corrected models (PBE-D3, r2SCAN, r2SCAN-D4), reflecting differences in their training data and DFT reference. The resulting protocol thus offers an affordable and reliable route to cross-model consensus on materials properties, even when exact reweighting is statistically intractable.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Consistency, Cancellation,
and Experiment in Quasi-Harmonic
Thermochemistry
items.abstract: Abstract For weakly bound molecular complexes, the Gibbs energy is often limited less by the electronic interaction energy, now computed to near chemical accuracy, than by the statistical-mechanical treatment of their low-frequency intermolecular vibrations. The standard remedy, Grimme’s quasi-harmonic correction, rescales the entropy of these modes toward a free-rotor limit while leaving their energy harmonic; because both derive from the same partition function, this is thermodynamically inconsistent. Applied consistently to energy and entropy, the correction largely cancels over the dominant intermolecular modes, whereas the entropy-only form leaves a one-sided shift that grows with system size. We test this against experiments: carboxylic acid dimerization, methanol vapor association, and sulfuric acid–ammonia nucleation in the CLOUD chamber. The entropy-only correction departs from experiment in all three cases, while the plain harmonic treatment matches the dimerization data and, supplemented by a physically grounded anharmonic term, the measured alcohol vapor properties and nucleation barriers. For such complexes, thermodynamic consistency is a prerequisite that no empirical entropy correction can replace.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
FermiLink: An Agent Harness for Multidomain Scientific
Simulations
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) agent harnesses have been developed for autonomous scientific simulations, but most current agent harnesses are tested on a single or a small set of software packages. Herein, FermiLink, an extensible open-source agent harness, is introduced for multidomain scientific simulations. Its key design principle is the separation of package knowledge bases from simulation workflows, so that simulation workflows in FermiLink, from figure-level simulations to full-paper-level research on high-performance computing clusters, operate uniformly among supported packages via a four-layer progressive disclosure mechanism. This agent harness is specifically optimized for high-performance computing (HPC) clusters, enabling multiday, multistep scientific simulations in the absence of human intervention. Using OpenAI Codex as the agent provider, the capabilities of FermiLink are demonstrated across approximately 50 scientific software packages spanning nine research domains from chemistry to engineering. Systematic benchmarks on 132 real-world figure-level reproduction tasks with 44 packages show that FermiLink reproduces 74 (56.1%) of published figures with simulations, among which 30 (22.7%) achieve high-fidelity agreement and 35 reach qualitative agreement with the target figures. A smaller set of human expert-guided reproduction benchmarks with 10 packages in physics and chemistry further highlights the importance of expert insights for improving the simulation fidelity. Beyond reproduction, a single-blinded study demonstrates that FermiLink can produce research-grade results on unpublished polariton physics problems when provided with sufficiently detailed research objectives. Overall, FermiLink provides a scalable research infrastructure that may accelerate the path from scientific questions to computational results across diverse domains.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Alchemical Transfer
Free Energy Perturbation Simulations
Reveal Entropic Mechanism Governing the Binding of a Charged Peptide
to a Protein Target
items.abstract: Abstract We combined alchemical transfer free energy perturbation (FEP) and replica exchange with solute tempering (REST) molecular dynamics to probe the energetics of the binding of a charged peptide to a protein target. For this purpose, we have selected the coreNLS peptide KKPKKE, the conserved fragment from the nuclear localization signal (NLS) sequence in viral capsid protein binding to nuclear transporter importin-α (impα). This peptide binds to impα, natively forming a specific pose similar to that resolved experimentally. The two main outcomes of our work are as follows. First, we further develop the FEP methodology. Alchemical transfer is a rarely used version of FEP, in which an unbound peptide is gradually decoupled, while the bound peptide is coupled. Because the net charge of the system remains unchanged, no charge-related corrections within FEP are necessary. Additionally, our FEP protocol utilizes a “laissez faire” soft-walled flat-bottom spherical restraint, which does not affect a ligand as long as it occupies the major NLS binding site in impα. We showed that combining FEP with REST molecular dynamics affords exhaustive sampling of the binding process and reduces the free energy error down to 0.4 kcal/mol. Second, we found that the coreNLS binds impα with moderate affinity of ΔGb0 = −4.6 kcal/mol. We analyzed the factors contributing to binding energetics. Direct interactions between the peptide and impα favor binding and are likely to be responsible for largely native binding pose of the coreNLS. These direct binding interactions are supplemented by the gains in water–water, ion–ion, and water–ion interactions. Both, direct and indirect, enthalpic gains are about equally important, but cannot compete with severe enthalpic losses stemming from the expulsion of water and ions from the binding interface. As a result, the net binding enthalpy is unfavorable. The factor, which ultimately “saves” coreNLS binding to impα, is a strong entropic gain occurring upon water and ion release from the binding interface. Based on our investigation, we classify the mechanism governing coreNLS binding to impα as entropic. Our isothermal titration calorimetry measurements confirm the estimates of ΔGb0 provided by FEP. By connecting with our prior studies and other reports, we propose that such binding mechanism may be applicable to other charged peptides reflecting complex interplay between binding enthalpy and entropy. Interestingly, our data suggest that the ligands binding diffusively or by adopting specific poses may utilize an entropic binding mechanism.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Exploring Chemical Concepts and Reactivity from Conceptual
Density Functional Theory in Excited States via the ΔSCF Approach
items.abstract: Abstract Along with the recent development of the ΔSCF approach for excited state electronic structure description using density functional theory (DFT), we extend and develop conceptual density functional theory (CDFT) for evaluating chemical concepts and reactivity descriptors for both ground and excited states. Thereby, the fundamental energy functionalEJ[{npσ},v(r)] based on the generalized adiabatic connection Kohn–Sham (GAC-KS) theorem is introduced. Offering a straightforward interpretation of the reactivity of excited states analogous to that of the ground state. In this framework, ground state CDFT naturally emerges as a special case when the derivative with respect to the number of electrons is taken at the frontier orbital occupation, i.e., dN = dnf. Starting from the ground state system, the spin-polarized analytical linear response function (LRF) is tested to examine the atomic shell structure for alkali atoms as well as the reactive region upon electron addition and removal processes using the Fukui kernel. The behavior of the LRF is then illustrated for ground, singly excited, and doubly excited states of a set of molecular systems, revealing the expected trends and nature of bond polarizability and bonding character. The analytical Fukui function is also presented here for its ability to describe local electrophilicity and nucleophilicity for ground and excited states. An inverse relationship for the condensed electrophilic and nucleophilic Fukui functions is observed between the ground and excited states for a set of small molecules, including substituted benzenes. The dual descriptor obtained from the analytical Fukui function via a finite difference approximation is applied to interpret the Woodward–Hoffmann (WH) rules for pericyclic reactions. For both thermally driven and photoinduced ring cyclization processes at the ground and excited states, respectively, the dual descriptor successfully translates the WH rules from molecular orbital context into a purely density-based language.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
A Computational
Framework for the Determination of
the Binding Affinity of Peripheral Proteins to Homogeneous Membranes
items.abstract: Abstract Peripheral membrane-binding proteins (PMPs) are essential to immunological and neurological processes, and disruptions in their membrane interactions are implicated in cancer, neurodegeneration, and autoimmune diseases. Their functional diversity arises from the wide range of mechanisms by which they associate with lipid surfaces, motivating atomistic computational frameworks capable of quantifying binding energetics. We present such a methodology and demonstrate it using Bacillus thuringiensis phosphatidylinositol-specific phospholipase C (BtPI–PLC), a 296-residue virulence factor that preferentially associates with phosphatidylcholine (PC) membranes. Experimental studies report dissociation constants near 24 μM for wild-type BtPI–PLC binding to PC vesicles, corresponding to a standard free energy of −6.6 kcal/mol. BtPI–PLC associates with membranes through cation−π interactions involving Y88 and Y246, hydrophobic contacts from helix B, and other noncovalent interactions, making comprehensive sampling challenging. Here, we present a statistical mechanical geometrical route formulation based on the potential of mean force for the quantitative characterization of dilute PMP binding to homogeneous membranes. Using enhanced sampling via well-tempered metadynamics and extended adaptive biasing force, we obtain a computational estimate of the standard binding free energy, −6.2 ± 0.3 kcal/mol, consistent with experimental estimates for BtPI–PLC membrane association.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Nucleophilicity
from a Conceptual DFT Viewpoint: A
Four-State Ensemble-Inspired Model
items.abstract: Abstract By taking advantage of the fundamental convexity of the exact energy as a function of the number of electrons, we extrapolate the straight-line segments connecting the N and N + 1 states and N – 2 and N – 1 states in a four-state ensemble-inspired model. These segments intersect at a unique point that determines a fractional charge transfer condition,ΔNint−=−λ, which naturally contemplates the reactivity of the cation and neutral forms in terms of their hardness. The energy evaluated at the intersection point, Ni, and the energy evaluated at −λ in the ensemble segment,Nl, give rise to our proposed descriptors that contribute to the electronic panorama of the donation process and describe the reactivity of a set of molecules in specific conditions. The performance of the indicators as nucleophilic indices was evaluated in five chemical reactions: the oxidation of metals, the proton affinity of amines, the stability of coordinated metals that follow the Irving–Williams series, and the kinetic substitution of indoles and alkenes. The nucleophilicity indices proposed are an important complement to the electrophilicity index because they are based on a different response that, although they may lead to similar results with respect to the correlation with a given property, they may be used to recognize dominant aspects of the electronic structure in a chemical interaction. The results obtained support their use as complementary descriptors of the intrinsic electronic contribution to nucleophilic reactivity within specified reaction families.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Intra- and Intermolecular
Interactions in Cellobiose:
Benchmarking Accelerated Computational Methods for Cellulose
items.abstract: Abstract Access to accelerated computational methods at the electronic and atomistic scales is important in materials modeling, as it will allow more realistic system descriptions. Against this background, a systematic study of a range of electronic/atomistic methods applied to cellobiose monomers and dimers is presented, with the aim of identifying methods that achieve a significant acceleration of cellulose computations compared to hybrid DFT methods while retaining adequate accuracy. We benchmark such methods, namely the semiempirical quantum-mechanical tight-binding GFNn-xTB (n = 1,2) and G-xTB methods, the MACE-OMol-0 machine-learning potential, and the CHARMM36 force field, against three DFT references (ωB97M-V, B3LYP-D3, PBE-D3) for gas-phase cellobiose monomers and dimers, focusing on structures, energies, and vibrational properties. Cellobiose monomers and dimers, as presented in this work, do not represent the structural complexity of cellulose, but they provide tractable structural models for assessing the qualities of the selected computational models regarding cellobiose–cellobiose intermolecular interactions that are also present in cellulose. We find that (i) the chain–chain and sheet–sheet dimer interactions are of comparable magnitude, suggesting that both intermolecular dispersion and hydrogen bonding make important contributions to dimer stability, so accurate treatment of noncovalent interactions the calculations is essential; (ii) GFN2-xTB and G-xTB reproduce most conformations well, with a speed-up of two to three orders-of magnitude compared to the DFT calculations, but fail for puckered, strained conformations, artificially improving apparent dimer-energy agreement with DFT; (iii) MACE reaches near-DFT accuracy with a further order of magnitude speed-up, although in a few cases fails to reproduce the hybrid DFT conformations. This is especially true for the chain–chain dimer structure, which is also reflected in a significant deviation of the chain–chain energy-distance potential curve, which highlights the importance of system-dependent model validation (as was done here) and suggests a need for model fine-tuning for cellulose systems; (iv) CHARMM36 has some conformational and energetic limitations,but being 30,000× faster than G-xTB (itself orders of magnitude faster than DFT), remains practical for qualitative studies.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Rigid Molecule
Packing Similarity Index Based on Dual
Quaternions
items.abstract: Abstract Mapping comparisons between periodic 3D rigid-molecule (or fixed molecular conformer) arrangements to a scalar value, typically referred to as a similarity index, is essential in fields such as crystal structure prediction (CSP) and molecular engineering. Evaluating crystal lattice similarity is crucial for filtering random structure pools and differentiating polymorphs. Here, we introduce a configurational similarity index based on dual quaternions to simultaneously capture relative rigid-molecule (fixed molecular-conformer) positions and orientations in crystal lattices. Within this framework, pairs of molecular configurations with known atomic correspondence are compared using a metric derived from the product of their dual quaternions. After validating the metric on water dimer configurations, we employ it to contrast clusters of molecules representing different molecular packing motifs. This pairwise comparison is condensed into a single index, Drt, which measures total crystal packing similarity. Using Drt to screen pools of randomly generated structures for oxalic acid, maleic hydrazide, and formamide, we successfully retrieve packing motifs similar to the experimental references. Upon geometry optimization, these identified structures converge to the corresponding optimized experimental configurations, highlighting the reliability of this metric for integration into CSP methodologies.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Real-Time Multidimensional
Spectroscopy for Organic
Molecules in Cavities: Dark-State Dynamics and Optical Signatures
items.abstract: Abstract Ultrafast multidimensional spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful tool for probing organic exciton–polaritons in optical microcavities, revealing rich dynamical properties at the femtosecond timescale. However, the dark states and their crosstalk with polaritons still remain challenging, due to the ultrafast dynamics and optical responses that lead to large ambiguities in the interpretation of time-domain spectroscopic experiments, which signify the properties of highly excited states. Here, we develop a fully quantum-mechanical approach to simulate ultrafast two-dimensional polaritonic spectroscopy (2DPS) of organic systems with strong vibronic coupling. By incorporating the time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (TD-DMRG) method into spectroscopic simulations, our approach enables direct visualization of dark-state dynamics and their excited-state absorption (ESA) signals in organic molecules confined in Fabry–Pérot cavities with realistic vibrational environments. Our results reveal two distinct classes of dark states, namely, lower-polariton (LP) polarons and dark polaritons, which are clearly distinguishable from bright polaritons in 2DPS signals. Time-resolved spectra further exhibit their relaxation dynamics, showing by separated timescales and pathways for energy migration, e.g., ∼200 fs for polaron decoupling. Furthermore, these findings provide new theoretical insights into light-induced phases in organic materials and offer guidance for the design of polaritonic devices.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Systematic Improvement
of Trial States in Phaseless
Auxiliary-Field Quantum Monte Carlo
items.abstract: Abstract We extend the use of coupled cluster (CC) trial states in the phaseless auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) method beyond single and double excitations to include both triple and quadruple excitations. With this AFQMC/CC hierarchy, we are able to systematically benchmark the method’s performance on molecular systems as the quality of the trial is improved. Our results show that the phaseless AFQMC energy improves systematically and is typically significantly more accurate than the energy of the underlying trial state. However, the relative improvement compared to the trial CC energy decreases as we ascend the CC hierarchy. As the CC wave function is usually further approximated when used as an AFQMC trial, we also explore the relationship between the components of the CC wave function and the resulting AFQMC/CC error. Our results suggest that improving the representation of the CC wave function in the AFQMC trial does not always lower the bias even when it increases the fidelity of the trial with the exact ground state.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
DEGAUSS-3p: A Three-Site
Water Model from Soft Gaussian-Charge
Electrostatics and a Rare-Gas-Informed Double-Exponential Potential
items.abstract: Abstract Classical fixed-charge water models combine point-charge Coulomb interactions, which diverge at short distances and neglect charge penetration, with a Lennard–Jones 12–6 repulsion whose r–12 dependence does not reflect the near-exponential decay of quantum-mechanical exchange repulsion. The DEGAUSS force field replaces both with finite, Gaussian-smeared charge densities and a double-exponential van der Waals potential, with adjustable short-range softness and rare-gas-informed starting values for the double-exponential exponents. DEGAUSS-3p is parametrized directly for liquid water using these interaction forms. The resulting rigid three-site model captures the density anomaly and tetrahedral organization of liquid water, with a balanced description of structural, thermodynamic, and dynamic properties. Gaussian electrostatics and double-exponential repulsion thus provide an effective basis for modeling liquid water with finite interactions at short distances.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Free Energy Landscape
Perturbation for Estimating
Mutation-Induced Population Shifts from Reference Molecular Dynamics
Ensembles
items.abstract: Abstract Mutations can alter protein function by redistributing probability among conformational states, even when structural changes are modest. Directly estimating a perturbed conformational free energy landscape with molecular dynamics is expensive because each mutation requires a new converged simulation. Here, we introduce Free Energy Landscape Perturbation (FELP), a state-local reweighting framework that estimates mutation-induced population shifts from a reference ensemble. FELP partitions a reference trajectory into discrete microstates, evaluates restrained reference-to-perturbed energy differences for configurations sampled within each state, and combines spatially regularized state-local Zwanzig factors with the reference state probabilities to estimate the perturbed state distribution. FELP estimates how a perturbation changes the relative probabilities of conformational basins and reports effective-sample and overlap diagnostics that identify when the predicted shift lacks support in the sampled reference ensemble. We describe the FELP estimator, its implementation, and its performance on capped dipeptides, chignolin, T4 lysozyme, and the EGFR kinase domain. FELP is intended for perturbations that reshape populations within a sufficiently sampled reference landscape, providing a practical bridge between local alchemical energy evaluation and ensemble-level mechanistic interpretation.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Systematic Correction
of Kohn–Sham-Derived
Excitation Energies via a Quantum Monte Carlo Approach
items.abstract: Abstract Developing and applying accurate methods for the calculation of excitation spectra remains an outstanding problem in electronic structure. Here, we present the first application of auxiliary boson-corrected diffusion Monte Carlo (ABCDMC) to ab initio systems of atoms and ions in the second row of the periodic table and molecules. In ABCDMC, the many-body electron–electron correction to the density functional theory (DFT) exchange-correlation energy is captured statistically via an auxiliary boson ground state obtained with diffusion Monte Carlo. Moreover, the kinetic-energy contribution to correlation is included up to the limit of a finite active-space expansion. The excitations are described as a product of a linear combination of Fermionic functions derived from DFT and the auxiliary boson state. The corrections to the DFT-derived excitation spectra are obtained by statistically sampling an observable on the auxiliary boson state. We benchmark ABCDMC on the experimental excitation spectra of second-row neutral atoms (Li–F), cations (Be+–Ne+), dications (B2+–Na2+), and the carbon dimer against full configuration interaction (FCI). For the atomic set (96 excitations), ABCDMC improves local density approximation excitation energies for low-lying single excitations up to the n = 3 shell, reducing the mean signed error from −0.059 to less than 0.001 Ha and the root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) from 0.102 to 0.037 Ha using at most 25 determinants per species. An O+ convergence study shows systematic improvement as the determinant space is enlarged and double excitations are included. For the carbon dimer, ABCDMC matches FCI within 9 mHa RMSD for 11 low-lying excitations using 16 determinants. Overall, these results indicate that ABCDMC is particularly promising for the calculation of low-energy excitations with very small active spaces. However, the method is not designed to correct basis-set errors associated with diffuse wave functions and the cusp condition errors at the core in atomic systems using Gaussian bases which are also present in the underlying DFT. The compact determinant expansions used here suggest that ABCDMC may be useful for larger systems and, in future work, for correcting DFT band structures of solids, provided a sparse multireference basis can be constructed.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
A Machine Learning
Approach for Computationally Efficient
Prediction of State-to-State Transition Cross Sections for Molecular
Collision Processes
items.abstract: Abstract A neural network model is adopted to develop a machine learning approach for the prediction of rotational state-to-state transition cross sections for inelastic molecule + molecule collisions. This method is applied to H2O + H2 system that includes 200 rotational states of the water molecule as a target and all states of H2 projectile up to j = 8. It is shown that with a relatively small subset of transitions used for training and validation of the neural network, one can have a fast and reliable prediction of cross sections and rate coefficients with a mean relative error of ∼7%, which is comparable to the accuracy of the method used to generate the original dataset. This demonstrates that the calculation of rate coefficients based on cross sections predicted by the machine learning approach may dramatically reduce the CPU effort associated with numerical solution of the molecular scattering problem, which opens ample opportunities for accelerating the generation of collisional databases for astrochemical and other applications.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
AdaptivePy: A Unified
Python Framework for Adaptive
Sampling in Molecular Dynamics
items.abstract: Abstract Adaptive sampling accelerates the exploration of conformational space in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations by repeatedly analyzing the accumulated trajectories and seeding a new round of simulations from informative configurations. A growing collection of adaptive sampling policies has been proposed, each built around a particular notion of what makes a configuration informative, yet these methods are scattered across separate and often incompatible implementations, which complicates their systematic comparison and their combined use in meta-adaptive sampling schemes. Here, we present AdaptivePy, a compact and extensible Python framework that implements nine seed-selection policies behind a single configuration-driven interface, spanning simple population-based baselines, several established machine-learning and geometry-based methods, and two ensemble or meta-sampling policies introduced in this work. We show that the shared implementation reproduces the characteristic selection behavior of each policy on a series of analytic benchmark landscapes. We also introduce a new adaptive sampling scheme that employs TS-DAR, a deep learning framework originally designed to identify transition states, as an acquisition criterion that drives the discovery of an entire multibasin landscape starting from a single basin. We further demonstrate that the common interface enables meta-adaptive sampling policies, which aggregate the rankings of several policies into a single set of seeds. We apply all nine policies to explicit-solvent simulations of alanine dipeptide and the miniprotein chignolin. The policy that performs best depends on the system, on the performance metric, and on the amount of accumulated sampling, justifying the use of meta-policies that combine different algorithms. AdaptivePy thereby provides a unified testbed for the adoption, benchmarking, and continued development of adaptive sampling methods for biomolecular MD simulations.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
The Stress Localization
Function─A Stress-Derived
Real-Space Descriptor for Chemical Bonding Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Existing quantum-chemical topology descriptors, including the Laplacian of the electron density, the Electron Localization Function (ELF), and the Localized Orbital Locator (LOL), characterize bonding through the density and its low-order derivatives, but they trace the localization of electrons rather than the local balance between the kinetic and potential energy densities and sometimes fail in cases such as heavy atoms, hypervalent centers, and bonds of intermediate character. To address these deficiencies, we introduce the Stress Localization Function (SLF), a real-space bonding descriptor constructed from the quantum-mechanical stress tensor. The trace of the stress tensor is the local virial field, which connects the kinetic and potential energy at each point in space. The SLF is obtained by taking its magnitude, comparing it to the value for a uniform electron gas of the same local density, and mapping the result onto a bounded scale, in analogy to the ELF or LOL. Applied to atoms across the periodic table, the SLF resolves the complete electronic shell structure, including the outermost shells of heavy atoms that the Laplacian fails to recover and that stress-based indicators have not resolved with any single choice of parameter. For the 4d elements, the SLF recovers the full complement of shells with no adjustable parameter. It registers the number of occupied shells rather than the nominal period, as shown by palladium’s anomalous 4d105s0 configuration. The core value is essentially universal (≈0.578), transferable from free atoms to bonded environments. Across a benchmark set of single, double, and triple bonds, the SLF decreases monotonically with bond order while simultaneously tracking bond polarity through the electronegativity of the bonding partner, separating two distinct chemical effects within a single scalar field. The descriptor further characterizes nonprototypical bonding, including three-center bonds, as in the textbook example of H3+ and boranes, the hypervalent center in BrF3, and the σ-donation and π-back-donation of metal carbonyls. The SLF thus provides a stress-derived, energetic view of electron organization that complements existing density-based descriptors.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
A Two-Bead-Per-Amino
Acid Coarse-Grained MD Model
with Hydrogen Bonding (2BPA-HB) to Probe DNAJB6b-Mediated Suppression
of Polyglutamine Aggregation in Huntington’s Disease
items.abstract: Abstract Polyglutamine (polyQ) aggregation plays a central role in several neurodegenerative diseases, including Huntington’s disease. DNAJB6b, a molecular chaperone involved in protein quality control, is known to efficiently suppress polyQ aggregation, but its antiaggregation mechanism remains unclear. In this work, we investigate the interaction between DNAJB6b and the polyQ region (Q48) of mutant Huntingtin Exon 1 (mHttEx1) using a custom-built coarse-grained molecular dynamics model. The model incorporates a two-bead-per-amino-acid representation with hydrogen bonding (termed 2BPA-HB) and is calibrated against all-atom molecular dynamics data in terms of geometry, hydrophobicity, and hydrogen bonding. The model reproduces the tertiary structure of DNAJB6b and its interactions with Q48 and reveals an inverse correlation between DNAJB6b concentration and Q48 aggregation propensity. Our simulations show that DNAJB6b undergoes cocondensation with polyQ molecules, thereby shielding the polyQ from forming the intermolecular hydrogen bonds necessary for amyloid formation. The 2BPA-HB CGMD model enables efficient exploration of DNAJB6b conformations, supporting future studies of chaperone-mediated aggregation suppression and therapeutic development.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Smoothed Truncated
Coulomb Potential for Periodic
Gaussian-Basis Hartree–Fock Exchange
items.abstract: Abstract Truncated Coulomb (TC) potentials reduce finite-size errors and accelerate thermodynamic-limit convergence in periodic Hartree–Fock (HF) calculations, but their use with Gaussian basis sets is complicated by the evaluation of electron repulsion integrals (ERIs), particularly for nonspherical truncation domains and all-electron calculations. We introduce the smoothed truncated Coulomb (sTC) potential as a systematically improvable approximation to a parent TC potential. A real-space Gaussian convolution smooths the sharp truncation boundary, and a single dimensionless parameter, η, controls the width of the smoothing window, which can be tightened to systematically approach the TC reference. The smoothing by sTC enables a dual-space algorithm for evaluating periodic Gaussian-basis ERIs that requires neither a large plane-wave basis nor new molecular integral kernels and is applicable to both pseudopotential and all-electron calculations, including the important Wigner–Seitz-cell truncation boundaries. Benchmarks spanning insulating, semiconducting, layered, metallic, and molecular-crystal systems show that sTC-based HF closely reproduces TC results in pseudopotential calculations and extends TC-quality calculations to all-electron settings. Across these systems, sTC substantially improves thermodynamic-limit convergence relative to the probe-charge Ewald method while remaining practical for all-electron calculations in which direct TC-based calculations are computationally challenging.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Capturing Transient Polaron Formation Dynamics: A
Time-Dependent Polaron Transformation Approach
items.abstract: Abstract Static polaron transformations impose an equilibrium environmental displacement at the initial time and can therefore misrepresent transient polaron formation. We introduce a time-dependent (TD) polaron transformation that describes the dynamical formation of polarons. We first present the TD polaron transformation for the spin–boson model via an infinite sequence of interaction-picture transformations. Each transformation in the sequence cancels the residual term generated by its predecessor; the ordered transformation sequence combines exactly into a displacement operator whose amplitude is zero at the initial time. We then generalize this recursive elimination to any suitably partitioned Hamiltonian. When the generated operator algebra closes, the ordered sequence of transformations reduces to an exact closed form; otherwise, a truncated sequence provides a systematic short-time approximation. For the transformed spin–boson Hamiltonian, we derive a second-order Nakajima–Zwanzig quantum master equation with two-time bath correlation functions. We benchmark this quantum master equation against numerically exact matrix-product-state dynamics and hierarchical equations of motion using Landau–Zener sweeps coupled to a thermal bath, whose tunable crossing time acts as a clock for polaron formation. We find that the TD-polaron quantum master equation outperforms the static formulation in regimes where transient polaron formation competes with the system evolution. The TD-polaron transformation is therefore applicable to nonequilibrium processes such as sudden charge injection, while the underlying sequential elimination scheme extends to other suitably partitioned Hamiltonians.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Adaptive Substructure
Sampling for Molecules with
Flexible Alkyl Substituents
items.abstract: Abstract The exponential growth of conformational space in molecules with flexible side chains presents a fundamental bottleneck for atomistic sampling methods. A large fraction of this complexity arises from weakly coupled, quasi-degenerate torsional degrees of freedom that contribute little to chemically meaningful structural diversity while dramatically increasing computational cost. We present a substructure-based conformational sampling framework that separates flexible side chains from the molecular core at the graph level. Detached substituents are replaced by capped surrogate groups, enabling independent sampling of subsystems and systematic reconstruction of approximate full-molecule ensembles. A limiting variant neglects explicit sampling of the side chains and assumes extended reference conformations. This approximation is rationalized using high-level electronic-structure data for linear alkyl chains, which show that folded conformations become thermodynamically competitive only beyond well-defined lengths, particularly in solution. The approach is implemented within CREST and reduces the effective dimensionality of conformational sampling for molecules with extended flexible substituents.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Approximating Hartree–Fock Theory via an Efficiently
Local Reformulation
items.abstract: Abstract We explore a reorganized framework for the Hartree–Fock equations that allows varying patterns of locality to be imposed on the molecular orbitals while maintaining a highly efficient self-consistent field optimization algorithm. Rather than limiting orbitals’ spread and then variationally minimizing the energy within those limits, our reorganization neatly pairs each local degree of freedom with a specific solution condition that itself has a naturally local interpretation. These pairs can each be turned on or off, and, regardless of the sparsity pattern used to make such choices, the overall method maintains a fast self-consistent field optimization. We use this structure to test reaction-matched schemes for imposing orbital locality and, through Fock builds that exploit this locality, achieve competitive timings even in modestly sized molecules. Our initial tests also suggest that this approach to imposed orbital locality can be arranged so as to do minimal damage to both Hartree–Fock and MP2 reaction energy predictions.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Quantum Control of Molecular Photodissociation Reactions
with Intense Laser Fields
items.abstract: Abstract Quantum control of molecular reaction dynamics has been a challenging subject of research for many years. Here, a new control scheme is proposed to modify the fragment distributions of molecular photodissociation reactions. The scheme is applied to the A-band photolysis of CH3I, which is simulated using a realistic wave packet model. The control scheme applies a single moderately intense (1010–1013 W cm–2) pump pulse to excite CH3I. This pulse produces light-induced conical intersections (LICIs) between the ground and excited electronic states, that reshape the natural diabatic potentials, generating new adiabatic light-induced potentials (LIPs). The new LIPs lead to different photodissociation dynamics, producing different fragment distributions compared to the weak-field regime. Complete inversion of the branching ratio I*(2P1/2)/I(2P3/2) between the two dissociation channels is achieved, with the previously dominant I*(2P1/2) channel practically suppressed, and the minor I(2P3/2) channel becoming the dominant one. Experimental implementation of the scheme appears straightforward and of universal application to photodissociation processes.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
A Quantum-HPC Hybrid
Workflow for Reaction-Center
Electronic Dynamics: Application to a Cytochrome P450-Inspired Iron-Complex
Model
items.abstract: Abstract We introduce population-transfer dynamics as a practical validation observable for active-state-derived reduced Hamiltonians in multistate reaction-center chemistry. In transition-metal systems, missing couplings or configurations can compromise the reliability of reduced active space models along a reaction coordinate, even when the overall spectrum is reproduced reasonably well. Using a cytochrome P450-inspired Fe-complex model, we construct a reaction-coordinate-dependent effective Hamiltonian from state-averaged complete active-space self-consistent field (SA-CASSCF) calculations, map it to a quantum circuit representation suitable for current hardware, and propagate the dynamics from the reactant-side ground state. At the spectrum level, the reduced Hamiltonian reproduces the SA-CASSCF reference with an RMS deviation of 0.030 eV and a maximum absolute deviation of 0.143 eV. As a dynamics-based diagnostic, the product-manifold population pP(t) identifies a pronounced near-degeneracy window around x ≈ 0.3, where state mixing is strongest; specifically, computed from classical exact time evolution reaches 0.488 at x = 0.3 after 10 fs, compared with 7.26 × 10–2 at x = 0.2 and 5.90 × 10–3 at x = 0.0. To render the workflow executable on current trapped-ion hardware, we quantify the NISQ-relevant trade-off between dynamical fidelity and circuit resources through coupling pruning and first-order Trotterization. A coupling cutoff of ε = 0.02 eV reduces the nonzero coupling set from 32 to 7 while preserving the dominant transfer pathways, and a Trotter step number of M = 30 provides the best practical operating point among the tested values. Finally, we demonstrate the end-to-end workflow on Quantinuum’s trapped-ion quantum computer Reimei. The hardware reproduces the key reaction-coordinate trend identified by the classical reduced model, including the pronounced maximum at x = 0.3, where the measured product population is 0.42 on hardware and 0.43 on the matched emulator. Overall, this work establishes a dynamics-based diagnostic route for assessing the adequacy of active-space-derived reduced Hamiltonians and shows that chemically interpretable multistate electronic dynamics can already be executed on current trapped-ion hardware under realistic device constraints.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Algorithm for Locating
SCF Solutions Reveals Conceptual
Limitations of the Broken-Symmetry Approach Applied to the Oxygen-Evolving
Complex
items.abstract: Abstract Broken-symmetry (BS) calculations of polynuclear open-shell transition-metal complexes are widely used but rely on critical assumptions including the existence and stability of the self-consistent-field (SCF) solutions and the Heisenberg structure of magnetic interactions. We develop a new algorithm for systematic generation and analyses of SCF solutions and apply it to the oxygen-evolving complex (OEC). Several of these solutions are either electronically unstable or exhibit non-Heisenberg character, challenging the conventional interpretation of BS calculations. With homotopy continuation, the DFT solutions continuously transform into the Hartree–Fock solutions through an electron transfer in metal–oxo fragments, explaining a strong functional dependence of BS calculations. The Brueckner coupled-cluster method with double excitations establishes which SCF solutions provide the best reference determinant for correlated wave function treatments. Expansion of the developed methodology further strengthen the understanding of electronic structure in the Kok cycle of the OEC.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Correction to “Thermodynamic
Perturbation Theory
for Charged Branched Polymers”
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title: A Machine-Learned Symbolic Committor for a Chemical Reaction: Isomerization in Retinal and p -Coumaric Acid
items.abstract: Abstract The thermal cis-trans isomerization of C═C double bonds in chromophores is a prototypical high-barrier reaction whose mechanism hinges on subtle out-of-plane bending motions. Combining machine-learning-guided path sampling (AIMMD) with symbolic regression, we learn an interpretable committor for two chemically distinct chromophores, N-retinylidene-lysine and p-coumaric acid anion, in vacuo from unbiased molecular dynamics trajectories generated by two-way shooting. Parametrizing the committor with a neural network and sampling it uniformly across the full range allows the model to resolve the reaction coordinate across the full transition region, not only at the isocommittor surface pB(x) = 0.5. A feature-attribution analysis identifies four proper dihedrals around the reactive bond as the informative coordinates, while the improper dihedrals at the sp2-hybridized carbon atoms prove unsuitable because reactant, transition, and product states share the same values. Symbolic regression then distills the committor into compact analytical expressions─to our knowledge the first committor both learned and distilled into closed form for a chemical reaction─and shows that a coupling of all four dihedrals is required to reproduce the S-shaped, stepwise pathway seen in the transition-path ensemble. This S-shape is absent from the minimum free-energy path: it arises from the dynamics of the short transition events combined with the mass asymmetry between heavy-atom and hydrogen-bearing dihedrals, and the larger asymmetry of p-coumaric acid yields the more pronounced S-shape this picture predicts. An interpretable, machine-learned committor, though a function of configuration alone, thus exposes dynamical features of the mechanism to which the free-energy surface is blind. The workflow requires no prior assumptions about the reaction coordinate and extends naturally to other high-barrier isomerizations and, combined with a reactive potential, opens a path toward bond-breaking chemical reactions.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
An Efficient Neural
Network Architecture for Molecular
Vibrational States: From Rigid Molecules to Molecular Complexes
items.abstract: Abstract Accurately solving the nuclear Schrödinger equation for molecular complexes exhibiting noncovalent interactions remains a challenge due to the exponential scaling of basis sets and the presence of strongly anharmonic, large-amplitude motions. Recently, we proposed a neural network (NN) method to tackle high-dimensional vibrational problems and successfully applied it to C3H8 in full dimensionality; however, applying the method to molecular complexes has been hindered by difficulties in representing delocalized wave functions across multiple minima. In this work, we present a substantially improved NN-based methodology that overcomes these limitations through two key developments: (i) a novel NN architecture specifically designed to capture the asymptotic behavior and delocalization characteristics of weakly bound complexes, and (ii) an efficient training protocol that optimizes the variance of local energies. We demonstrate that this approach achieves subcm–1 accuracy for the vibrational ground and excited states of CH4 with substantially fewer parameters than the previous method requires. Crucially, for the prototypical water dimer (H2O)2, the new method successfully computes both ground state and intramolecular excited states with ∼1 cm–1 accuracy using ∼6000 NN parameters. This work establishes a robust and scalable framework for performing full-dimensional, fully coupled vibrational calculations on molecular complexes, providing an efficient approach for accurate spectroscopic predictions of such systems.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Global Potential Energy Surface Exploration Using
Generative Stochastic Surface Walking (Gen-SSW)
items.abstract: Abstract Global potential energy surface (PES) exploration offers a unique way to predict the structure of material from first principles. Here, we develop Gen-SSW method to enable autonomous and fast global PES exploration, which combines a general-purpose SE(3)-equivariant 3D diffusion model, LASP-Gen, with stochastic surface walking (SSW) global optimization. Contrary to the conventional SSW global PES exploration that requires a long serial trajectory to overcome high barriers between large structural basins, Gen-SSW establishes an autonomous, massively parallel global optimization framework, which realizes global PES exploration via divide-and-conquer: many short SSW trajectories are performed based on the seed structures batch-generated from LASP-Gen. By applying Gen-SSW across complex materials, we show that (i) LASP-Gen can efficiently yield a structural pool with huge structure diversity and reasonable local chemical bonding patterns, and (ii) By docking LASP-Gen with SSW, Gen-SSW can identify efficiently low-energy polymorphs of materials, as exampled by ionic materials (TiO2, LiFePO4), amorphous alloys (Ge2Sb2Te5), strong covalent materials (boron) and molecular crystals (phenol crystal). In particular, we find a new boron allotropy, namely α̃-B, that is only 6 meV/atom above α-boron but 17 meV/atom more stable than γ-boron, and suggest a synthetical route for making this new phase via solid–solid phase transition.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Paired-Isotopologue
Hessian Benchmarking for Second-Order
Validation of Machine-Learned Water Potentials
items.abstract: Abstract Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are commonly validated against energies and forces, yet vibrational predictions depend on the curvature and mode information encoded in the Hessian of the potential-energy surface. Here, we introduce a paired-isotopologue Hessian benchmark for MLIPs using hydrogen-bonded water as a test system. For each MD-sampled water-cluster geometry, a common electronic Hessian is combined with matched HH, DH, and DD mass patterns, enabling the controlled evaluation of vibrational frequencies, normal modes, and isotope responses across nine universal, molecular, and water-specific potentials. Model rankings differ across force-, Hessian-, and vibration-based evaluations, while the paired isotopologue response follows the broad vibrational ordering and remains consistent across structural sources. Beyond global error measures, local coordinate analysis distinguishes Hessian errors with markedly different relevance to specific vibrational observables. Along isotope paths, near-degenerate modes can lose individual mode overlap without a corresponding loss of the vibrational subspace. Together, these results establish Hessian and mode-space validation as necessary complements to energy- and force-based evaluations of MLIPs intended for vibrational calculations.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Unraveling the
Ultrafast Photodynamics of Molecular
Photoswitches in β-Adrenergic Receptors by First-Principles
Nonadiabatic Dynamics Simulations
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding how protein environments regulate the photodynamics of chromophores is a central task in quantum biology and remains a major challenge. This challenge is particularly significant for G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), which are natively nonphotochromic but can be optically controlled via synthetic photoswitchable ligands. Such artificial photoreceptors are new and important because they not only enable the photocontrol of signaling processes beyond those regulated by rhodopsins but also deepen our fundamental understanding of quantum effects in light-protein interactions. However, the ultrafast nonadiabatic dynamics of these ligands in GPCRs remain difficult to resolve experimentally, while traditional computational approaches fail to describe these processes accurately and efficiently. Here, we employed a multiscale framework to comprehensively characterize how receptor binding, mutations, receptor subtype, chemical substitution, and binding pocket electrostatics regulate the photodynamics of photoswitchable antagonists (OPs) of β-adrenergic receptors (β-ARs). This framework integrates extensive first-principles ground-state conformational sampling, absorption-spectra calculations, and nonadiabatic dynamics simulations. Chemical substitutions influence how excitation energy, excited-state lifetimes, and quantum yields (QY) respond to receptor binding, subtype changes, and binding-pocket mutations. The F289A and Y199A mutants generally accelerate excited-state dynamics by reducing local contacts, whereas the D113E mutation slows the dynamics of OP2 in β2-ΑR by reducing the excited-state driving force. Neutralizing the charge of the counterion D113 residue via protonation increases the QY of OP2 in β2-ΑR by altering the local electrostatic and hydrogen-bonding environment. The ultrafast photoisomerization of the ligands does not require large binding-pocket expansion. Overall, this work provides new insights into how binding-pocket environments regulate the photochemical properties of photoswitchable ligands targeting GPCRs.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Data-Driven Approach
for Predicting Long-Time Anomalous
Transport from Short Trajectories
items.abstract: Abstract Molecular simulations provide detailed microscopic trajectories but often do not reach the long-time transport regime. Predicting long-time transport from ensembles of short trajectories is particularly challenging in heterogeneous materials, where static spatial disorder and viscoelastic memory can produce similar transient dynamics while leading to different behaviors at longer times. We introduce the spatial-disorder generalized Langevin equation (SD-GLE), a likelihood-based generative framework that represents local effective potential landscapes as realizations of a Gaussian random field and temporal correlations through a memory kernel; variational Bayesian inference jointly learns both components from short trajectory ensembles and uses them to generate long trajectories in statistically equivalent environments. In controlled benchmarks, SD-GLE recovers the prescribed disorder covariance and memory kernel, while application to randomly cross-linked polymer networks demonstrates an accurate prediction of size-dependent long-time and non-Gaussian tracer transport, including the crossover to hopping-dominated motion. By linking short-time microscopic motion that departs from simple diffusion to long-time transport behavior, SD-GLE provides a bottom-up modeling strategy that is applicable to a broad range of molecular systems with complex transport dynamics.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Multistate-Averaged
Kohn–Sham ΔSCF Method
for Excitation Energies, Transition Properties, and Absorption Spectra
and Its Relation to Ensemble Density Functional Theory
items.abstract: Abstract The ΔSCF (Δ-Self-Consistent-Field) approach is an attractive alternative to time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) for excited-state calculations, particularly for Rydberg, charge-transfer, and doubly excited states, for which conventional linear-response TDDFT performs poorly. However, conventional ΔSCF methods based on the unrestricted Kohn–Sham formalism suffer from spin- and spatial-symmetry breaking, optimize the ground- and excited-state determinants independently, leading to nonorthogonal Kohn–Sham determinants that complicate the calculation of transition properties, and require a separate SCF procedure for each excited state of interest. In order to address these limitations, we present a potential-averaged multistate-averaged Kohn–Sham (pa-MSTA-KS) method, which averages the Hartree-exchange-correlation potential of the ground state with state-averaged Hartree-exchange-correlation potentials of one or several excited states during a single SCF procedure. Unlike restricted open-shell Kohn–Sham (ROKS) approaches, pa-MSTA-KS yields canonical SCF equations and can be implemented in any standard KS code with minimal effort. The pa-MSTA-KS method avoids spin-symmetry breaking by construction, yields orbitals that describe ground and excited states simultaneously, and enables the direct evaluation of transition dipole moments and the simulation of full UV/vis absorption spectra based on a single SCF calculation. For excitation energies of the QUEST1 data set and for absorption spectra of water, ethylene, and ammonia, pa-MSTA-KS outperforms TDDFT in accuracy. By combining the generalized-adiabatic-connection Kohn–Sham formalism with ensemble density-functional theory, we provide a formal basis for the pa-MSTA-KS method and derive a new decomposition of the ensemble correlation energy into state- and density-driven contributions.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title: Multipolar Polarizabilities in Materials: Ab Initio Calculations with Wannier Functions
items.abstract: Abstract We develop a first-principles approach based on maximally localized Wannier functions for the calculation of higher order multipolar response properties in crystals including dipole–quadrupole, quadrupole–quadrupole, and dipole-octupole polarizabilities. The method is based on an interpolation procedure of the electronic structure of materials, and it is formulated by extending molecular perturbation theory to periodic crystals. General symmetry considerations are used to determine relations between different components and to prove that the dipole–quadrupole polarizability vanishes in centrosymmetric systems. The approach is applied to compute and analyze the multipole–multipole polarizabilities of several representative materials, including centrosymmetric systems (bulk graphite, h-BN, MoS2, and 2H-phase WTe2) and noncentrosymmetric ones (bulk Td–WTe2 and bulk Te). The multipole–multipole polarizabilities are further related to optical gyration with specific application to Te and Td–WTe2. The proposed algorithm possesses several advantages, including conceptual simplicity, computational efficiency, and relatively low computational cost for the computation of multipolar response in materials.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Limitations of Fixed-Point-Charge Force Fields for
Metal Coordination Modes in Proteins: A Multilevel Study of Ca2+ in Integrin αVβ3
items.abstract: Abstract Standard biomolecular force fields often present limitations in modeling metal coordination modes. We combined classical and QM/MM molecular dynamics to investigate Ca2+-mediated binding of cRGD to integrin αVβ3. We show that different metal coordination modes imply variations in the partial charges of the metal-coordinating atoms, which, if incorporated in the force field, substantially alter the free energy landscape. These results highlight the value of QM-based multilevel approaches to accurately capture metal coordination modes in biomolecular systems.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Many-Body Second-Order
Green’s Function Theory
for Ab Initio Molecular Quantum Electrodynamics
items.abstract: Abstract In this work, we develop two many-body quantum electrodynamic methods to calculate the ground-state energies of strongly coupled light-matter molecular systems. Specifically, we extend the second-order many-body Green’s function theory (GF2) for electronic systems to incorporate electron–boson couplings. We employ two ansätze to treat the bosonic part of the system, namely, the coherent-state (CS) and Lang–Firsov (LF) transformed vacuum state. These are combined with the GF2 method to construct two new approaches, which we refer to as CS-GF2 and LF-GF2. We benchmark CS- and LF-GF2 by studying various molecular systems inside an optical cavity. We investigate H2 and LiH potential energy surfaces, keto–enol tautomerization energy barrier, van der Waals interactions between two H2 molecules, and the torsional potential energy surface of the ethylene molecule, C2H4. Both methods provide similar energy profiles, with relatively small differences between CS-GF2 and LF-GF2. Comparisons with the reference calculations also reveal remaining limitations at stretched bond lengths and near the twisted ethylene configuration. We additionally benchmark CS-GF2 against exact diagonalization for a two-site Hubbard–Holstein model and observe that it closely reproduces the coupling-induced energy change in the weakly interacting regime while improving upon CS-MP2 in the strongly interacting regime. Overall, the results demonstrate that CS-GF2 and LF-GF2 provide self-consistent descriptions of correlated molecular electron–boson systems, offering a many-body Green’s function alternative for studying ground-state cavity-modified systems.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
LipidMem-BigSMILES
(LiMBS): A Standardized Representation
Language for Lipid Membrane Systems
items.abstract: Abstract Molecular dynamics simulations of lipid membranes lack a standardized, machine-readable representation, creating significant barriers to reproducibility, data sharing, and AI-driven analyses. Current membrane descriptions are fragmented across software-specific input files, making it difficult to reconstruct published systems or compare results among studies. Here, we introduce LipidMem-BigSMILES (LiMBS), a line notation not a simulation tool or membrane-building program, for lipid membrane simulations that extend SMILES, BigSMILES, and CG-BigSMILES to membrane systems. LiMBS version 1.0 uses a dual-block architecture that separates a system-level descriptor block from a chemical structure block, enabling the independent specification of membrane geometry, composition, environmental conditions, and molecular identity. The framework supports planar bilayers, vesicles, and bacterial outer membranes in atomistic, coarse-grained, and supercoarse-grained resolutions within a unified syntax. We provide a reference tool that reads, checks, and standardizes LiMBS strings, and we show that its output can be handed off to existing membrane-building software for system construction. LiMBS1.0 is human-readable, machine-readable, tool-independent, and compatible with FAIR data principles, providing a standardized description layer for membrane simulations that supports reproducible reporting, interoperable databases, and AI-enabled membrane biophysics.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Periodic Electron
Density Overlap Descriptors for
Crystal Band Gap Prediction
items.abstract: Abstract A valence electron density encodes spatial electronic structure that complements an atomic position representation. We examine whether a periodic adaptation of the smooth overlap of electron densities (SOED) improves the modeling of density functional theory band gaps in inorganic crystals. Atom-centered neighborhoods are sampled directly from periodic valence density grids, expanded in radial functions and spherical harmonics, and summarized by rotationally invariant power spectra. A scaffold density constructed from atomic positions supplies a SOAP-inspired control with the same overlap machinery. We evaluate 40490 structures from MP-20-Charge after filtering undefined Pauling electronegativities and repartitioning by reduced formula. A validation-selected electronic SOED ensemble attains a held-out RMSE of 0.6179 eV, compared with 0.6595 eV for a local chemistry-matched SOAP control. The reduction of 0.0415 eV has a 95% formula-cluster bootstrap interval of 0.0255 to 0.0578 eV. Five formula-group splits, including the primary split, give mean errors of 0.6315 and 0.6581 eV, respectively. These results support periodic density overlap descriptors for modeling computed band gaps when valence charge densities are available.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
FIREX: Fast-Ion
Replica EXchange Enables Rapid Sampling
of Mg2+ Pairing with Nucleic Acids
items.abstract: Abstract We introduce Fast-Ion Replica EXchange (FIREX), a Hamiltonian Replica Exchange-based sampling strategy specifically designed to enhance the sampling of metastable divalent cation binding with phosphate groups, e.g., in nucleic acids. We parametrize the scheme and demonstrate its convergence and efficiency on a model DNA dodecamer with Mg2+ ions, using two force fields with very different ion-pairing properties to test its robustness. The highest replica is driven by a “fast-ion” Hamiltonian combining a reduced ion charge with a tuned pair-specific Lennard-Jones interaction between the ion and phosphate oxygen atoms, yielding rapid exchange as well as moderate binding affinity, amenable to efficient sampling. By enabling the robust quantification of divalent ion interactions in simulations, FIREX could be instrumental in refining force fields to better capture ion–molecule interactions. The provided guidelines for the design of fast-ion models suitable for FIREX are general and could be extended to other force fields or types of biomolecular moieties, such as carboxylated protein side chains, phosphorylated proteins, or other interaction sites on nucleic acids. We further demonstrate how FIREX can be efficiently combined with the REST2 method to achieve simultaneous sampling of ion binding and biomolecular conformations with the Amber-OL15-ECC force field, while convergence remains challenging with the original Amber-OL15. This shows that different HREX schemes, including REST2, can be merged into a combined, highly cost-effective HREX scheme and is a step toward robust, computationally efficient sampling of charged biomolecules in interaction with divalent ions.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
Quantitative Pathway-Resolved
Kinetics from Neural
Network-Guided Weighted Ensemble Simulations
items.abstract: Abstract Many crucial biomolecular processes, such as ligand dissociation and conformational switching, occur via multiple competing transition pathways. While standard rare-event sampling methodologies provide rigorous estimates of the global transition rate, they typically collapse the underlying mechanistic heterogeneity into a single global constant, obscuring the relative kinetic contributions of distinct channels. Here, we introduce a path-resolved weighted ensemble (WE) framework that quantitatively assigns steady-state flux to competing transition channels without modifying the underlying unbiased dynamics. In our approach, initial reactive trajectories generated via direction-guided adaptive sampling are clustered by dynamic time warping (DTW) and smoothed into neural-network-refined representative paths. These refined routes are formulated as path collective variables (PathCVs) to preseed and guide channel-specific WE simulations. We demonstrate the robustness of this framework across systems of increasing complexity. On a model three-hole potential, the method accurately captures a temperature-dependent pathway crossover. In the benzamidine–trypsin complex, it isolates the dominant unbinding route while quantifying the fluxes of subdominant channels. Finally, for imatinib dissociation from Abl kinase, the method reveals that the clinically relevant N368S resistance mutation drastically redistributes reactive flux from the P-loop/hinge channel toward the αC-helix channel, accelerating escape. This framework successfully translates qualitative pathway classification into rigorous, pathway-specific kinetic observables, offering a powerful tool for understanding mutation-induced mechanistic shifts in biomolecular function.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title: Chemical Similarity Enables a Unified Free-Energy Framework for f -Block Solvation Thermodynamics
items.abstract: Abstract f-Block elements underpin many essential technologies, yet their efficient mutual separation remains a foundational challenge in chemistry. The lanthanide series provide a stringent test case: the trivalent lanthanide ions (Ln3+) exhibit near-identical solvation chemistry across the series, distinguished only by the lanthanide contraction. Here, we turn this chemical similarity into a computational advantage. Treating each solvated Ln3+ as a distinct alchemical state, we exploit configurational overlap between neighboring ions by applying the multistate Bennett acceptance ratio (MBAR) to estimate relative hydration free energies from pooled ensembles. We extend this framework to biased simulations by coupling coordination-number-based well-tempered metadynamics with MBAR, enabling enhanced sampling of rare coordination fluctuations within a unified free-energy estimator. Benchmarked in water as a controlled, well-characterized solvent, the workflow yields convergence, overlap, and effective sample size (ESS) diagnostics alongside free-energy trends in good agreement with experiment. MBAR-enabled energy–entropy decomposition reveals discrepancies in the underlying energetic and entropic contributions despite good agreement in total free energy, motivating a multifidelity test with a machine-learned polarizable interatomic potential. MBAR-based reweighting reveals insufficient Hamiltonian overlap, exposing a transferability bottleneck; the pooled classical ensemble does not support reliable post hoc reweighting to the target Hamiltonians. Domain-specific fine-tuning, renewed sampling, and explicit overlap reassessment are therefore required before MACE-polar can be incorporated as a higher-fidelity layer. This framework establishes “UfS”─a unified free-energy framework for f-block solvation─as a scalable, uncertainty-aware approach to lanthanide solvation thermodynamics and a foundation for future applications to related actinides, speciation-rich environments, and data-driven design of new separations chemistries.

items.title:
Enabling Structure-Only
Initialization and Out-of-Distribution
Generalization in GNN-Based Molecular Dynamics Simulators
items.abstract: Abstract Machine-learning-based simulators offer the potential to model the dynamics of complex systems more efficiently than classical approaches while retaining differentiability, a key property for materials design. Graph neural network (GNN)-based simulators have shown strong performance across a range of physical domains, including molecular dynamics. However, their reliance on temporal context for accurate prediction limits their use in inverse design settings, where simulations must be initialized from a single static configuration. Moreover, inverse design requires robust out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, as candidate structures typically lie outside the training domain. Here, we address both challenges by introducing two complementary strategies that enable the stable and accurate structure-only initialization of GNN-based simulations. To directly target OOD generalization, we propose an inference-time physics-based optimization framework that constrains model predictions to remain physically consistent during the rollout. In addition, we introduce a differentiable, GNN-based barostat that enables accurate tracking of system dimensions and pressure, which is critical for capturing macroscopic responses and supporting OOD generalization. We evaluated these approaches in the context of uniaxial compression of disordered elastic networks spanning a broad range of geometries, Poisson’s ratios, and microscopic behaviors. We find that, together, these methods substantially improve rollout stability and enable reliable OOD generalization, including regimes with distinct, more complex dynamics than those the in training data. These results show that when properly initialized and constrained, GNN-based simulators can serve as efficient and generalizable tools for materials discovery and structural optimization, advancing their use in materials, molecular, and dynamical system design.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.abstract: Abstract Molecular electric dipole and quadrupole moments are fundamental descriptors of charge distribution and intermolecular electrostatics, with applications spanning spectroscopy, force-field parametrization, and the design of proton-conducting materials. Despite their importance, extracting multipole moments from DFT typically requires specialized postprocessing, and validated benchmark datasets remain scarce for chemistries of interest. Here, we present an open-source, basis-set-agnostic Python framework that automates the calculation of molecular dipole and quadrupole moments from plane-wave and Gaussian-type-orbital DFT, supporting both total-electron-density and charge-density-difference formulations, and benchmark it against experimental references for 99 dipole and 54 quadrupole moments across five density functional approximations. We further apply the framework to generate a data set of 242 substituted azoles relevant to nonaqueous proton conduction and show that computed dipole and quadrupole moments provide complementary information about molecular charge distribution. As a preliminary exploration of these data as machine-learning targets, an unoptimized random forest baseline trained on identity-based structural descriptors predicts dipole moments to within 0.5 D for weakly perturbing substituents but yields larger errors for strongly electron-withdrawing groups; these errors correlate with the Hammett σp constant, motivating the use of electronically resolved descriptors in future modeling efforts. The framework, benchmark results, and azole data set are released openly to support high-throughput electronic structure data generation, force-field parametrization, and machine-learning studies of multipole-aware materials design.
items.journal: Journal of Chemical Theory and Computation

items.title:
P3MaZe: a Mass-Zero
Constrained-Dynamics Formulation
of Particle–Mesh Electrostatics
items.abstract: Abstract We introduce P3MaZe, a real-space particle–mesh electrostatic method that combines the standard short-range/long-range decomposition of Particle–Particle Particle–Mesh (P3M) electrostatics with the Mass-Zero constrained dynamics (MaZe) framework. In this formulation, the smooth long-range electrostatic potential is represented on a mesh as a zero-inertia auxiliary field, while the discretized Poisson equation is enforced as a holonomic constraint during molecular dynamics.
