Closely related proteins use nearly the same cluster of residues, whereas more divergent proteins substitute alternative proton-handling residues and modify electrostatically important fixed-charge groups to preserve cluster proton affinity. Thus, E-channel reversible proton-loading is preserved during sequence evolution by maintaining a local “electrostatic architecture,” often involving quite different evolutionary solutions. Thus, conservation of E-channel proton loading depends more strongly on the local electrostatic environment than on conservation of the individual residues that create it.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Short-term flexibility and long-term stability in models of mind perception
items.abstract: Understanding how people decide whether someone or something possesses a mind is central to a myriad of psychological, biological, and philosophical questions. It shapes fundamental processes at the individual (e.g., social interaction) and societal level (e.g., morality and ethics). While mind perception has been studied, it remains unclear which internal model people use when ascribing mental capacities to entities. Across four experiments (total N = 256), we explored what model people hold and its flexibility when ascribing agency and experience to entities encountered in everyday life and which differ in animacy and socialness (e.g., humans, pets, robots, voice assistants, tools). Using representational similarity analysis combined with lab-based experiments, a 6-wk long social interaction intervention, and longitudinal real-life exposure, we tested which model people use to ascribe agency and experience by comparing observed rating data to theoretical models. We demonstrated that an animacy distinction underlies the representational structure of experience attributions, while internal models for agency attributions are more idiosyncratic and flexible. When receiving explicit information on one entity, the internal model of agency changes. People update their model by incorporating this information, generalizing across the entire category of entities. We found no evidence that extended exposure to or ownership of inanimate technology, such as robots or voice assistants, or pets leads to restructuring of the models for experience or agency. Overall, these results provide insight into the internal models people hold when perceiving minds, the flexibility thereof, and offer ways to understand the roots and consequences of mind perception.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Peak water: Trends in decoupling regional and global water use
items.abstract: Water use for human activities, including food and fiber production, energy generation, and residential, commercial, and industrial supply, has grown significantly over the past century, driven by rising populations, expanding economic activity, and changes in technologies and consumer demands. Traditional water planning has long assumed that the demand for water, like other resource demands, will grow in perpetuity, shaping infrastructure development, land-use decisions, and water-system investments. However, recent data and analysis challenge this assumption, suggesting that total water use in certain regions and sectors has peaked or even begun to decline, despite continued population and economic growth. This paper’s primary contribution is to reevaluate the status of “peak water” and decoupling based on observational and statistical data, as well as multimodel simulations. Data on global, national, and regional water withdrawals indicate that certain peak water-use levels are being reached and the paper discusses past, current, and projected demand estimates; potential drivers of observed water use reductions; and different strategies for managing and modeling water use in the future. These findings indicate that the long-presumed correlation between water-resource use, economic development, and human well-being can be decoupled and that models of water use should reflect this. Decoupling solutions must focus on efficiency technologies, regulatory water-use caps, environmental flow protections, and enhanced monitoring networks.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title:
Direct CO
                    <sub>2</sub>
                    splitting using light-based catalysis and an oxygen reservoir
items.abstract: As the dominant anthropogenic greenhouse gas, the conversion of CO 2 into value-added products is vital for achieving a circular economy. CO 2 activation typically requires coreactants, high temperatures, or significant electrical input, any of which increases cost or limits scalability. Here we demonstrate a straightforward way to split CO 2 directly into carbon monoxide and oxygen using light. By combining a light-driven antenna-reactor photocatalyst with a material that acts as an oxygen reservoir, CO 2 can be decomposed directly into CO and oxygen with light only. Under illumination, photoexcited carriers induce CO 2 bond dissociation, while cerium oxide adsorbs the released oxygen into vacancy sites, preventing recombination. The oxygen can then be released from the ceria by flowing nitrogen under white light illumination, a process that can be repeated multiple times, restoring full photocatalytic activity. This demonstrates a practical and scalable strategy for efficient CO 2 conversion, shifting the chemical equilibrium of CO 2 dissociation in a controllable manner.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title:
Leptin Receptor
                    <sup>+</sup>
                    cells create a perisinusoidal niche for thrombopoiesis in the bone marrow by synthesizing CXCL14
items.abstract: Leptin Receptor-expressing (LepR + ) stromal cells in the bone marrow are a critical source of growth factors for the maintenance of hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) and most restricted hematopoietic progenitors. An important unresolved question is whether they also regulate terminal differentiation in some hematopoietic cells. We found that bone marrow LepR + cells promote thrombopoiesis by synthesizing the chemokine CXCL14. Cxcl14 -expressing LepR + cells extend fine processes that wrap around perisinusoidal megakaryocytes. Deletion of Cxcl14 from LepR + cells did not significantly alter HSC function or most aspects of bone marrow hematopoiesis, including megakaryocyte generation; however, it significantly reduced the numbers of proplatelet-forming megakaryocytes in the bone marrow and platelets in the blood, as well as platelet quality. Megakaryocytes from Lepr-cre; Cxcl14 fl/fl mice expressed lower levels of genes that encode granule proteins as compared to control mice, leading to the release of platelets with fewer α-granules and defective thrombus formation/growth. CXCL14 promoted platelet formation by remodeling lipid metabolism in megakaryocytes, increasing fatty acid transporter expression and enabling megakaryocytes to take up more polyunsaturated fatty acids from circulation. A high fat diet rescued the formation of proplatelet-forming megakaryocytes and platelets, as well as platelet function, in Lepr-cre; Cxcl14 fl/fl mice. CXCL14 protein was sufficient to promote platelet formation by megakaryocytes in vitro and in vivo. LepR + cells thus create a perisinusoidal niche for thrombopoiesis by producing CXCL14, which regulates lipid metabolism and terminal differentiation in megakaryocytes.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: The evolution and function of eukaryote-to-cyanobacteria horizontal gene transfer
items.abstract: Prokaryote-to-eukaryote horizontal gene transfer (HGT) has emerged as a driver of eukaryotic evolution. In contrast, eukaryote-to-prokaryote HGT remains poorly characterized, limiting insight into how eukaryote-derived genes influence prokaryotic evolution and function. Here, we reconstructed a comprehensive and well-resolved phylogeny of 469 high-quality Cyanobacteria genomes spanning all orders. Leveraging this framework, we identified 204 candidate functionally diverse genes of eukaryotic origin in cyanobacteria, likely representing 59 putative transfer events, including 197 genes not previously documented. All 204 candidates were intronless, consistent with intron loss during their evolutionary history. Transcriptomics reveal that HGT-acquired genes are expressed at significantly higher levels than both genome-wide and functionally matched non-HGT-acquired genes, suggesting functional importance. Notably, 138 genes exhibited functional annotations absent from the host cyanobacteria. We further characterized a granule-bound starch synthase (GBSS) putatively acquired by Crocosphaera from an ancestral archaeplastid lineage, enabling starch synthesis that may facilitate energy storage for nocturnal nitrogen fixation. These findings reveal that eukaryote-to-prokaryote gene transfer is an underappreciated driver of cyanobacterial evolution and function, with broad implications for microbial ecology, functional adaptation, and cross-domain genetic exchange.

items.title: Two-phase NEUROD1 pioneer activity synchronizes sensory neuronal differentiation and subtype specification
items.abstract: Temporal control of neuronal differentiation is essential for establishing stable neuronal identities, yet the transcriptional and epigenetic mechanisms underlying this process remain poorly understood. Using auditory neurons as an in vivo model, we investigate the role of the proneural factor NEUROD1 in regulating neuronal differentiation timing and subtype specification. To bypass early neuronal loss in germline Neurod1 deletion mutants, we generated a delayed, self-terminating conditional knockout mouse ( Neurod1ST ) that permits analysis of later differentiation stages. Integration of NEUROD1 chromatin binding and histone profiling at embryonic day (E) 11.5 with transcriptomic analyses across E11.5, E14.5, and E18.5 reveals a two-phase regulatory program during auditory neuron development that parallels dynamic Neurod1 expression. In the first phase, coinciding with Neurod1 upregulation during early neuronal differentiation, NEUROD1 preferentially binds putative enhancers of neuronal differentiation genes and promotes their transition to active chromatin states, consistent with pioneer factor activity. Loss of Neurod1 disrupts these epigenomic transitions, resulting in persistence of progenitor-like states with premature activation of differentiation and axonogenesis programs. This dysregulation is accompanied by activation of alternative regulatory networks, leading to defective neuronal migration and innervation, progressive identity instability, and apoptosis. In the second phase, marked by reexpression of Neurod1 in developing Type Ib/Ic precursors, Neurod1 deletion selectively impairs Type Ic specification while promoting a Type Ib-like identity. These findings identify NEUROD1 as a temporal regulator that coordinates developmental progression and stabilizes auditory neuron identity through phased regulatory activity, providing a mechanistic framework for how pioneer transcription factors couple chromatin remodeling to developmental timing.

items.title: ChREBP drives diabetic kidney disease, and its inhibition confers renal protection
items.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) represents a major medical burden. Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a leading cause of CKD, but intracellular pathways that can be pharmacologically targeted are poorly defined. Using transcriptome screening of DKD model mice we found that a carbohydrate-responsive element–binding protein (ChREBP)-dependent transcriptional cascade is markedly up-regulated in diabetic kidneys. Genetic ablation of ChREBP in diabetic mice ameliorated DKD, establishing ChREBP as a potential causal driver. A chemical screen based on ChREBP transcriptional activity identified D-532 as a small-molecule inhibitor that is effective in human and rodent cells. Oral administration of D-532 protected multiple diabetic mouse models from DKD progression and suppressed ChREBP and its downstream targets, including genes associated with excessive reactive oxygen species production. These findings position ChREBP as a pharmacologically targetable transcriptional driver of DKD and provide proof of concept that ChREBP inhibition can confer renal protection.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Emergent long-tailed dynamics in spin ice
items.abstract: In this study, we reveal long-tail dynamics spontaneously arising from a magnetic system. Specifically, we consider a classical spin system and demonstrate the emergence of a spin-ice physics when drive-induced heating is well suppressed. We show that at high driving frequencies, magnetic monopole excitations exhibit nonergodic stochastic dynamics characterized by power-law-distributed trapping times with long tails—a behavior that persists even in the absence of driving. At intermediate driving frequencies, the system eventually heats up to an infinite-temperature state. However, contrary to conventional wisdom of Floquet heating, the heating time in our model is extremely sensitive to different initial-state realizations and also follows a long-tailed power-law distribution, which arise specifically due to periodic driving. We show that an effective short-range attractive interaction between monopoles is responsible for the long-tailed distributions observed in both monopole and heating dynamics.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: People know who to ask for favors despite underestimating compliance
items.abstract: Whether and how people approach social interactions hinges on how they expect others to respond. Extensive social psychology research suggests that people are inaccurate interpersonal perceivers, overestimating negative responses (e.g., discomfort) and underestimating positive responses (e.g., appreciation) across a variety of social situations. However, this conclusion is based almost exclusively on mean-level bias analyses that obscure the dyadic nature of interpersonal judgment and rely on a narrow conceptualization of interpersonal accuracy. Leveraging research on favor-asking and anticipated compliance as an exemplar, we demonstrate that interpersonal accuracy takes multiple theoretically distinct forms, and that the prevailing conclusion that people misunderstand their influence over others—because they tend to underestimate compliance—is likely overgeneralized. Across four studies (13,196 directed dyadic ratings), we show that people accurately differentiate between who will comply with their favor requests (dyadic meta-accuracy) despite the average tendency to underestimate compliance (mean-level bias). This pattern emerged for specific and general favor requests, among well- and newly-acquainted individuals, and beyond what could be expected due to self-projection. Through this dyadic lens, people are highly adept judges of their influence over others, as they are able to target their requests toward individuals who are uniquely likely to acquiesce to them—and can avoid wasting time on those who are not. Thus, our research refines existing implications for how people approach asking for favors. More broadly, by aligning theory, measurement, and level of analysis, our studies elucidate the need for greater theoretical precision and empirical breadth in interpersonal accuracy research.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Dynamical geometric modes in non-Euclidean plates
items.abstract: Continuum elastic shells with residual stresses can exhibit complex motions that require vanishing elastic energy to excite, also called geometric zero modes, enabling them to be driven by weak and generic energy inputs. Despite recent interest in these modes, we understand very little about their dynamical properties. Plates with a curved, rather than flat, in-plane geometry, also called non-Euclidean plates, are one example in which residual stresses and geometry combine to produce a continuum of ground states. The plate can explore these states through a geometric zero mode when it has the shape of a minimal surface—a surface with zero mean curvature. We demonstrate that a non-Euclidean plate with the shape of a saddle minimal surface exhibits the predicted continuous stability, but this degeneracy is ultimately lifted by aging. Despite developing a preferred configuration, the zero mode remains the softest mode. Using a combination of analytical theory and experiments, we show that the elastodynamics of this soft mode is captured by the dynamics of a damped pendulum. A periodic driving uncovers resonance phenomena in this pendulum mode, such as small oscillations and steady rotations, but mixes with an additional flapping mode at high frequencies.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Selectively disrupting lysine acetyltransferase p300 and ZEB1 interaction prevents tumor progression while enhancing antitumor immunity
items.abstract: Both p300 acetyltransferase inhibitors and bromodomain inhibitors show therapeutic promise in cancer, but they mostly exhibit limited efficacy and may elicit severe adverse effects due to their lack of targeting selectivity. Thus, selectively disrupting p300 interactions with specific pro-oncogenic targets that are specifically expressed in neoplastic cells could serve as a safe and effective strategy for cancer treatment. Here, we demonstrate that p300 interacts with the pro-oncogenic transcription factor, ZEB1, and catalyzes its acetylation at an evolutionarily conserved K80 residue, stabilizing its expression in aggressive cancer cells. Ectopic expression of wild-type ZEB1 (mostly in acetylated status) but not the acetylation-deficient ZEB1 mutant modulates cytokinome of cancer cells, creating an immune-suppressive tumor microenvironment to support cancer progression. Underlining the importance of ZEB1 posttranslational processing, the K80-acetylated transcription factor is highly expressed in human cancers where its high-level expression is associated with poor prognosis. Importantly, we identify a small molecule compound, WY6, that undergoes high-affinity binding to p300 TAZ2 domain (a domain critical for ZEB1 binding) and consequently disrupts ZEB1 binding to p300, thereby suppressing K80 acetylation. WY6 treatment of tumor cells effectively represses p300-mediated ZEB1 acetylation, promoting its ubiquitination and subsequent degradation. Moreover, in vivo, WY6 potently suppresses orthotopic tumor growth without eliciting obvious toxic side effects and exhibits a synergetic effect when combined with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade immunotherapy. Collectively, our data demonstrate that selective disrupting of p300 and ZEB1 interaction effectively prevents tumor progression and may offer a promising therapeutic strategy for p300–ZEB1 axis-driven malignancies.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Elastic interactions of mechanically polarizable cells
items.abstract: Cells mechanically interact through the deformations they generate in their surrounding extracellular matrix. We present an analytical theory of the elastic interactions between cells that actively adapt their forces in response to local deformations of their environment. Cells are represented as localized contractile force generators, modeled as polarizable point force dipoles, whose adaptive forces are determined self-consistently with those of surrounding cells. Analysis of the associated elastic interaction energy identifies a generic short-ranged interaction arising from the mutual adaptation of cellular forces. This induced-dipole interaction is analogous to the van der Waals interaction between molecules and likewise is shown to be generally attractive for cells that enhance contractility in response to stretch. Furthermore, unlike the long-ranged elastic interaction between nonpolarizable force-dipoles, that peaks at intermediate matrix stiffness and then weakens as the matrix softens, the induced-dipole interaction strengthens monotonically as the matrix softens and can reverse the interaction from being repulsive at long cell distances to being attractive at short separations. Analytical calculations are presented to illustrate the mutual polarization of forces in pairs of interacting cells on a substrate. The identification of a generic, short-range cohesive elastic interaction between cells is important for understanding cell behavior at short separations and provides a physical mechanism driving cell accumulation on soft substrates.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Physical distancing to prevent influenza-like illness on a college campus: The eX-FLU trial
items.abstract: Public health recommendations often advise people to isolate when infected with influenza-like illness (ILI) with the goal of promoting physical distancing and limiting face-to-face interactions when risk of transmission is highest. Because isolation may have negative consequences, it is important to carefully assess whether encouragement to physically distance actually prevents cases of ILI. College campuses can be especially vulnerable to outbreaks of ILI and are ideal environments for assessing the impact of encouragement-to-physically-distance interventions. The eX-FLU cluster-randomized trial followed 579 students on a college campus over a ten-week period during flu season to evaluate such an intervention. Students in the trial were randomized to receive the intervention—encouragement to isolate in their dorm room when symptomatic for ILI—or control. Evaluating the effect of this intervention is challenging because of dependence between students in the trial and an anticipated spillover effect of the intervention. Moreover, while the intervention was designed to affect both face-to-face interactions and ILI infections, the effect on ILI infections is of primary public health interest. In this paper, a randomization-based testing procedure is proposed to assess the intervention effect specifically on ILI infections in the presence of dependent data and spillover effects. The testing procedure is shown theoretically and empirically to control the type I error rate and have good statistical power to detect an intervention effect in trials similar to eX-FLU. When applied to the eX-FLU data, this testing procedure gives moderate evidence that the intervention reduced ILI infections.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Quantifying the hierarchical topological decay of fluid knots
items.abstract: In this paper we analyze the hierarchical topological cascade of knotted and linked filaments associated with the natural decay of superfluid vortex tangles. This is done by using an algebraic reformulation of knot polynomial invariants to quantify the topological states of the cascade process. By interpreting the evolutionary paths associated with vortex knot dynamics as geodesic flows in an appropriate knot polynomial space defined by adapted Jones polynomials [X. Liu, R. L. Ricca, J. Phys. A Math. Theor. 45 , 205501 (2012).], we introduce an entanglement index to quantify the probability density of occurrence of each topological state. By this method we analyze all prime knots, links, and composites up to 8 crossings, and show that this measure detects accurately the decreasing topological complexity observed in simulations and laboratory experiments. By a comparative analysis carried out with data based on an alternative measure (complexity degree), we show that this entanglement index proves to be a more robust and reliable quantifier. The theoretical framework proposed here can be applied to other types of physical systems, where networks of filamentary structures are subject to continuous topological change and reorganization.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: The quantum agreement theorem
items.abstract: Intersubjective consistency asks when different observers of a physical system, reasoning from a shared theory, will agree on their probability assessments. Classical probability theory provides a benchmark in the form of the Agreement Theorem [R. J. Aumann, Ann. Stat. 4 , 1236–1239 (1976)]. We study the quantum mechanics (QM) analog to the classical Agreement Theorem in a finite-dimensional tripartite setting in which two observers obtain information via local projective measurements. We represent their mutual awareness by common certainty, which is formally an infinite hierarchy of certainty operators concerning the probability of an event of interest. We first prove that if the observers’ measurements commute with one another and with the property of interest, common certainty forces their probability assessments to coincide, thereby recovering a QM analog to the classical Agreement Theorem. We then construct a one-parameter family of qutrit–qubit–qubit models in which one observer’s measurement does not commute with the property and common certainty of disagreement occurs—a distinctively QM phenomenon. The mechanism is coherence between branches distinguished by one but not the other observer’s measurement. When measurement outcomes are stored in a classical register, the resulting dephasing removes this coherence and restores agreement. Finally, we prove that QM does not permit the extreme 0 - 1 configuration in which Alice is certain of a property and is also certain that Bob is certain of its negation. These results aim to turn debate in QM about observer-dependent facts into precise mathematical conditions for when intersubjective agreement or disagreement in QM can be sustained.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: The p38α MAPK–MK2 axis drives chemotherapy-mediated nuclear actin remodeling to promote ovarian cancer progression
items.abstract: Nuclear F-actin facilitates DNA damage repair and contributes to cancer chemoresistance. However, the regulatory mechanisms controlling its dynamic polymerization in response to genotoxic stress remain poorly defined. A major barrier in nuclear actin research is the lack of tools for precise, high-throughput analysis. To systematically investigate nuclear F-actin assembly in DNA damage response, we developed a deep learning pipeline, named nFANet, for high-throughput detection and analysis of nuclear F-actin. Here, using ovarian cancer—a malignancy where chemoresistance is a major clinical obstacle—as a model, we showed that platinum-based chemotherapy robustly induces nuclear F-actin assembly. A subsequent kinome screening, in combination with the application of nFANet, identified the kinase p38α MAPK as a critical upstream regulator of platinum-induced nuclear F-actin assembly. Mechanistically, the p38α MAPK–MK2 signaling pathway promotes formin-mediated nuclear F-actin assembly in response to chemotherapy. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition or genetic knockout of the p38α MAPK–MK2 pathway sensitized ovarian cancer cells to platinum-based therapy. Our work uncovers a key mechanism governing nuclear actin remodeling under genotoxic stress and lays the foundation for identifying a patient subgroup likely to benefit from therapeutic targeting of this pathway.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Diffusional depth profiling using electrochemiluminescence microscopy
items.abstract: Electrochemiluminescence (ECL) microscopy has emerged as a powerful 2D imaging technique with exceptional spatial resolution, enabling visualization of biological entities, nanomaterials, and multiphase systems. Conventional ECL experiments rely on coreactant concentrations in large excess of the luminophore to generate a bright signal in the vicinity of the electrode. While effective for surface interrogation, this confinement limits resolution in the z-dimension, making 3D imaging challenging. Here, we show that introducing an excess of luminophore enables access to 3D information through diffusion of the emission layer away from the electrode. By tuning the concentration ratio of tris(2,2’-bipyridine)ruthenium(II) ([Ru(bpy) 3 ] 2+ ) to tri-n-propylamine (TPrA), we control emission layer diffusivity. Initially, ECL arises from heterogeneous oxidation of both species at the electrode. As TPrA is depleted, the mechanism shifts to chemiluminescence, where [Ru(bpy) 3 ] 3+ oxidizes TPrA, generating a diffusing emissive layer that extends in the z-direction over time. Simulations and scanning electrochemical microscopy capture these diffusion profiles and highlight the role of concentration ratios. We apply this “diffusional depth profiling” to spirulina algae and spheroid cell models, insulating bodies that block light coming from the evolving emissive layer, revealing 3D morphology. This work uncovers the important influence of time and concentration on ECL emission layer expansion for depth profiling micro-to-mesoscale entities across biology and materials science.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Synergy between Gq and Gi proteins for the antipsychotic-like effects of mGlu2 receptors
items.abstract: The capacity of one G protein–coupled receptor (GPCR) to modulate signaling outputs of another is a phenomenon with potential implications for neuron function and therapeutic action. Notably, Gi/o-coupled receptors have been shown to generate calcium signals after costimulation of Gq-coupled receptors, an effect resulting from a crosstalk between signaling cascades. But the relevance for brain function and for therapeutic applications remains largely unclear. Here we show that Gi/o-coupled metabotropic glutamate 2 (mGlu2) receptors can generate calcium signals in neurons. It results from either agonist activation or constitutive activity of a Gq-coupled receptor endogenously coexpressed with mGlu2, independently of dimerization. Specifically, the constitutively active platelet-activating factor receptor (PAFR) plays an essential role in mGlu2-calcium signaling in hippocampal neurons, an effect largely inhibited by PAFR inverse agonists and genetic variants. This mGlu2-PAFR crosstalk is required for the cognitive and behavioral rescue produced by mGlu2 agonists in a mouse model of NMDA receptor hypofunction. These data highlight the complexity of GPCR signaling and provide key insights on therapeutic strategies for psychiatric disorders.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Linear scaling reveals low-dimensional structure in observable microbial dynamics
items.abstract: Microbial communities often exhibit apparently complex dynamics driven by myriad interactions among community members and with their environments. Yet, practical modeling and control are often based on a limited number of observables, raising fundamental questions: are these observed dynamics low-dimensional? If so, how does the low dimensionality enable predictions with limited information? Here, we report an emergent simplicity that the temporal dynamics of observable microbial populations can be captured by low-dimensional representations. Using variational autoencoders, we define a critical latent dimension ( E c ) that operationally quantifies the smallest latent dimension required for high-fidelity reconstruction of observable microbial dynamics under a specified criterion. Despite the complexity of unobserved background dynamics, we find E c to be drastically lower than the community’s apparent degrees of freedom. E c scales linearly with the number of observables, providing an empirical principle for determining representation complexity. This principle holds across simulations of pairwise interacting communities, consumer–resource dynamics, spatially distributed microbial patches, and plasmid transfer, experiments with engineered and environment-derived communities, and human microbiomes. Our findings establish a scaling law for microbial community dynamics and demonstrate that low-dimensional representations of observable dynamics retain information useful for selected prediction tasks without direct measurement of the complete community.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Dynamic supercoiling sponsors transcription amplification by MYC
items.abstract: Dysregulated MYC provokes profound changes in cancer gene expression. Although usually considered an E-box-dependent transcription activator, an alternate model is that MYC is a universal amplifier of transcription. Although MYC participates in pause release, its full role in the transcription cycle remains poorly illuminated. MYC also stimulates topoisomerases to resolve DNA topological issues complicating its transactions; how this stimulation is coordinated with its transcriptional role has not been examined. We have developed a system that discriminates between MYC-driven activation versus amplification in any cell. This system enables the interrogation of genes, cofactors, and compounds that execute or modulate MYC activity. Using a combination of biochemical and cellular assays, we reveal dynamic interplay between MYC-driven transcription amplification and DNA supercoiling. Because the early stages of transcription are sensitive to DNA supercoiling, Reducing TOP1 activity 1 either through genetic knockdown or low-dose inhibition, potentiates transcription amplification by MYC. By increasing promoter melting and RNA polymerase loading, negative supercoiling provides the early transcription complexes upon which MYC acts to increase output.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Principles of use of tensile J-curve materials in antagonistic arrangements
items.abstract: Natural ligaments are soft connective tissues that provide high stretchability for dexterous flexibility but switch to high stiffness to protect the musculoskeletal system from excessive deformation. These two functions cannot be independently tuned in conventional engineering materials with linear or hyperelasticity. Biological materials achieve this tailored behavior through a highly nonlinear tensile response characterized by a J-shaped curve, featuring an extended “toe region” of low force up to intermediate strains followed by an inflection, called the “heel region” which marks the onset of nonlinear stiffening. Here, we aim to study the characteristics of J-curves to establish principles for their use in robotic mechanisms. We define and measure the J-curve features responsible for protectiveness and mobility, describe the effective stiffness and the level of nonlinearity as a function of pre-stretch, and elucidate how the J-curve decouples flexibility from damage protection. Experimental measurements reveal the performance advantages of twisted and coiled elastomeric J-curve materials in engineered antagonistic arrangements and highlight their unique design space compared with linear elastic systems. Furthermore, we present a conceptual analysis of exploiting J-curve materials in energy-efficient running as an outlook toward their use in bioinspired robots.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Chromatin dynamics secondary to dexamethasone exposure identifies 67 genes linked to elevated IOP and primary open-angle glaucoma
items.abstract: Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) is a chronic neurodegenerative disorder, and elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) represents its only modifiable risk factor. We modeled increased IOP by treating three primary human trabecular meshwork cell strains with dexamethasone and generated a high-resolution map of promoter-centered chromatin contacts and regulatory modules. We identify dynamic changes in chromatin compartments and looping, cis-regulatory elements, and transcription factor hubs corresponding to altered expression profile. By integrating Genomewide association studies associated variants with dexamethasone induced chromatin landscape, we ascertain 29 target genes linked to 23 lead IOP variants and 57 genes for 46 POAG variants, with 19 shared between the two. Pathway analysis of 67 IOP- and POAG-associated genes reveals enrichment in vesicle transport, TLR, MAPK, and hippo-YAP signaling pathways. We also uncover transcriptional regulatory role of 103 noncoding lead variants. Our studies provide a mechanistic framework of genetic complexity accompanying steroid-induced IOP and related POAG pathology.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: PPP1R1B differentially modulates alcohol intake and emotional comorbidity through distinct prefrontal circuits
items.abstract: Excessive alcohol consumption frequently co-occurs with anxiety and depression in alcohol use disorder (AUD), yet the specific neural circuits and molecular mechanisms coordinating these comorbid conditions remain poorly defined. The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), particularly its prelimbic (PL) and infralimbic (IL) subregions, projects to key reward and emotion centers like the nucleus accumbens (Nac) and basolateral amygdala (BLA), but the functional heterogeneity of these projections is unclear. Using chemogenetics, retrograde tracing, electrophysiology, spatial proteomics, and cell-type-specific gene editing in mice subjected to a 4-wk intermittent access to alcohol (IAA) paradigm, we selectively manipulated glutamatergic projections from the PL and IL to the Nac core, Nac shell, and BLA and assessed alcohol intake, anxiety-like, and depression-like behaviors. Chemogenetic activation of PL-Nac core projections reduced short-term alcohol intake, anxiety-, and depression-like behaviors, while IL-BLA activation decreased alcohol consumption and anxiety-like behaviors only. Retrograde tracing revealed mirror-image anatomical segregation of projection-defined neuronal subpopulations within PL/IL linking spatial organization to functional divergence. IAA induced pathway-specific synaptic adaptations. Spatial proteomics nominated protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunit 1B (PPP1R1B) as a candidate molecule in PL-Nac core neurons. Independent immunostaining confirmed PPP1R1B downregulation, and circuit-specific knockout recapitulated alcohol-related and affective phenotypes, whereas overexpression reversed them. In IL-BLA neurons, PPP1R1B manipulation modulated alcohol intake and anxiety, but not depression. These findings define a subregion- and projection-specific organizational logic in the mPFC for differentially regulating alcohol consumption and emotional comorbidity, with PPP1R1B as a key molecular determinant. This provides a neural pathway–molecule framework for targeted intervention in AUD.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Multi-omics characterization of white matter free water reveals genetic and vascular determinants of neurological disorders
items.abstract: White matter free water (FW-WM), quantified using diffusion MRI, reflects extracellular water content and microstructural alterations within water matter, but its genetic architecture and clinical relevance remain largely uncharted. We conducted a multi-omics study integrating 42,039 individuals from the UK Biobank and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohorts to characterize tract-specific FW-WM across genetic, phenotypic, and proteomic dimensions. Genome-wide association analyses identified 27 independent loci and prioritized 88 genes, which were enriched in the genomic functional elements of vascular endothelial cells, pericytes, and astrocytes. Notably, 20 loci (74%) were novel compared to conventional white matter metrics. Both genetic predisposition to higher FW-WM and imaging-derived FW-WM were associated with a spectrum of neurological disorders. Specifically, imaging-derived FW-WM showed strong associations with stroke (OR = 3.14) and dementia (OR = 4.15), while higher baseline FW-WM predicted progression from MCI to AD (HR = 2.58). Bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses further supported genetically predicted associations between hypertension and FW-WM, which were together associated with increased risks of stroke and cognitive impairment. Integrative proteomic analyses further nominated PEAR1 and ANGL3 as candidate proteins potentially linking hypertension-related vascular processes to FW-WM variation. Together, these findings provide a multi-omics characterization of FW-WM that connects genetic susceptibility, vascular factors, and neurological outcomes, supporting FW-WM as a tract-specific imaging phenotype with potential utility for neurological risk stratification.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Recurrent hybridization between highly divergent paramecium species
items.abstract: The process of speciation, through which two reproductively isolated species emerge from an ancestral population, is often gradual, including a period during which gene flow still occurs, and hence speciation remains reversible. However, if isolation persists, the progressive accumulation of genetic incompatibilities ultimately locks the speciation process, reaching the point where hybrid offspring are inviable or sterile. In plants and animals, the establishment of species barriers is quite rapid: Beyond a net genetic divergence of 0.02 substitutions per synonymous site, interspecific introgressions become extremely rare. Here we report that in ciliates, species barriers can be broken despite huge genetic divergence. We show that the genome of Paramecium sonneborni contains hundreds of DNA segments that were acquired by recurrent horizontal transfers from multiple very distant lineages (synonymous divergence ~1 substitution/site). These segments approach the size of full-length chromosomes, which indicates that they were introgressed by interspecific mating. These data show that in the ancestry of P. sonneborni , hybridization events with highly divergent species occurred repeatedly and led to viable and fertile offspring. We propose that this unexpected promiscuous sexual behavior is made possible by the fact that paramecia separate somatic and germline functions in two types of nuclei: The elimination of non-self-DNA fragments during the development of the somatic genome allows individuals of a species to remain phenotypically the same, despite recurrent genetic flow from distant species into their germline.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 moderates the activity of phytochrome A in persistent canopy shade conditions
items.abstract: In nature, plants perceive and respond to complex vegetative environments through the phytochrome (phy) photoreceptor-signaling system. The Canopy Adaptation Strategy, elicited by phyA, together with the Shade Avoidance Syndrome, regulated by phyB, enables plants to adapt to diverse forms of vegetation shade. The phyA High Irradiance Response mode, which involves photocycle-coupled nuclear shuttling, is essential for sensing sustained far-red-rich conditions typical of canopy or occlusive shade. Our research identifies PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTOR 7 (PIF7) as a key regulator of phyA function. We show that PIF7 overexpression (PIF7ox) effectively suppresses phyA action. Under persistent shade, PIF7 and phyA both accumulate and associate within nuclear photobodies, with this interaction mediated by the C-terminal domain of PIF7 and the PAS-PAS domain of phyA. PIF7 also interacts with FAR-RED ELONGATED HYPOCOTYL 1 (FHY1) and FHY1-LIKE transport facilitators, thereby interfering with phyA cytosolic-nuclear shuttling. This coordinated molecular targeting by PIF7 constitutes an effective strategy for modulating phyA function under persistent shade conditions.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Phosphatases regulating ERK activation and ERK-dependent cell migration
items.abstract: Extracellular signal-regulated kinases (ERKs) have essential roles in development and are implicated in numerous diseases. ERKs are activated by phosphorylation and are regulated by dephosphorylation. To study the ERK phosphatases, we adapted a method to monitor ERK activity in live, unfixed preparations that accommodates the highly dynamic temporal and spatial features of ERK activation. We evaluated 140 human phosphatases using an in vivo reporter (ERK-SPARK) for high-throughput screening in human cells, and we used an in vivo Drosophila model for functional validation of their phosphatase homologs. We found that EYA family phosphatases are critical regulators of ERK signaling both in Drosophila and in mammalian cells and found that inhibition of human EYA4, a homolog of Drosophila Eyes Absent phosphatase, enhances migration of ERK-responsive tumor cells. These findings have important implications for the development of therapeutics.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Lipid droplets buffer hydrogen sulfide–induced redox imbalance
items.abstract: The electron transport chain is a signaling hub for hydrogen sulfide (H 2 S) that serves both as a respiratory substrate and an inhibitor. While acute sulfide toxicity is well characterized, cellular adaptations to chronic H 2 S, particularly microbially-derived sulfide exposure in colon, is poorly understood. We report that chronic, low-level H 2 S exposure (4 to 20 µM) drives robust carbon sequestration in lipid droplets (LD) across several human cell lines, driven by a coordinated remodeling of redox and nucleotide metabolism. Specifically, H 2 S-induced reductive shifts in nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and coenzyme Q (CoQ) pools are accompanied by glycerol-3-phosphate accumulation and cytidine triphosphate (CTP) depletion. Lipidomic analysis reveals increased neutral lipid synthesis and triacylglyceride accumulation concomitant with decreased CTP-dependent synthesis of membrane phospholipids. Mitochondrial expression of a water-generating NADH oxidase attenuates LD accumulation and spatially confines the origin of H 2 S-induced reductive stress signaling to this compartment. Interestingly, LD abundance increases even after H 2 S withdrawal, continuing over 48 h, during which time the reductively-shifted NAD and CoQ pools slowly reoxidize. Inhibition of fatty acid synthesis during sulfide exposure impairs cellular recovery of respiration. These findings establish an active role for LDs in stress response and reveal that lipid biogenesis is a strategy for countering H 2 S-induced redox imbalance. The sulfide–LD–redox axis uncovered in this study has implications for understanding how gut-derived H 2 S, shaped by diet and microbiome, can influence metabolic health.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Intermittent Cauchy walks enable optimal 3D search across target shapes and sizes
items.abstract: Efficiently locating rare targets requires balancing the exploration of novel space with the exploitation of local vicinities. While this tradeoff is well documented in simplified environments, its behavior in realistic three-dimensional environments remains unclear. Here, we analyze intermittent Lévy walks in three dimensions and show that search efficiency becomes strongly dependent on target geometry, with volume, surface area, and elongation governing performance across the Lévy spectrum. Against this geometric complexity, the Cauchy walk ( μ = 2 ) emerges as a robust, near-optimal solution across a wide range of target geometries. Specifically, we prove that for convex targets of surface area Δ in a domain of volume n , the optimal expected detection time scales as n / Δ , and that the Cauchy walk achieves this scaling up to polylogarithmic factors, while other Lévy strategies are suboptimal in different geometric regimes. Our findings provide a theoretical framework for biological movement patterns, including marine predator foraging and immune surveillance, and inform the design of efficient search algorithms for engineered systems such as autonomous nanoscale explorers.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs
items.abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub–grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert–vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub–grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity science with ecology, offering a pathway toward bottom-up ecosystem understanding.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: RE1 silencing transcription factor is reduced in endometriosis, and uterine deletion in mice alters progesterone responsiveness
items.abstract: Endometriosis is a steroid-dependent gynecologic disease characterized by progesterone (P4) resistance, subfertility/infertility, and pelvic pain; however, the molecular mechanisms underlying impaired P4 responsiveness in endometriosis tissue are not fully understood. RE1 silencing transcription factor (REST), a transcriptional regulator implicated in steroid hormone signaling, has emerged as a potential mediator of P4 responsiveness. Here, we investigated the role of REST in endometriosis using human tissues and a uterine-specific Rest conditional knockout mouse model. Immunohistochemical analysis of eutopic endometrium and ectopic lesions from patients with endometriosis revealed significantly reduced nuclear REST expression compared with control endometrium, suggesting loss of functional REST in disease. To assess the physiological consequences of REST deficiency, uterine-specific Rest knockout (Rest d/d ) mice were generated. Rest d/d females exhibited progressive subfertility and hyperestrogenic uterine tissue characteristics that displayed a blunted responsiveness to P4 treatment. Loss of Rest selectively altered expression of P4-responsive genes associated with endometriosis pathology, despite preserved P4 receptor expression. Following induction of experimental endometriosis, female mice that developed endometriotic-like lesions using Rest-deficient donor tissue developed significantly larger lesions that were less responsive to P4 treatment compared to lesions induced using control tissue. Mechanical sensitivity was modestly increased in mice receiving Rest-deficient tissue, whereas vaginal hyperalgesia was unaffected. These findings identify loss of nuclear REST as a feature of endometriosis and support a role of REST in subfertility, lesion progression, and blunted response to P4. REST may represent a molecular contributor to altered P4 responsiveness and a potential therapeutic target in endometriosis.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Phylogenetic profiling reveals evolutionary coupling between methyltransferases and the cytoskeleton
items.abstract: Methylation is a fundamental post-translational modification best understood as regulating chromatin structure and gene expression, yet there is emerging evidence that methylation also shapes cytoskeletal organization, regulating key processes such as mitosis and cell migration. Proteomic studies have revealed cytoskeletal protein methylation is widespread, however little is known about the enzymes responsible for these modifications, or their evolutionary relationship to other, better known substrates for methylation, such as chromatin. To address this question, we applied phylogenetic profiling across the complete repertoire of human methyltransferases to identify conserved functional relationships extending beyond chromatin. Unbiased clustering revealed extensive coevolution between methyltransferases and many components of the cytoskeleton, uncovering a previously unrecognized evolutionary network linking canonical chromatin regulatory enzymes to cellular structural systems. Evolutionary Trace analysis of the H3K36 methyltransferase family recovered known catalytic and regulatory domains while identifying additional evolutionarily constrained residues, suggesting previously unappreciated functional interfaces. Comparative analyses further distinguished deeply conserved methyltransferase–cytoskeletal relationships from those that emerged later during eukaryotic evolution, indicating that cytoskeletal methylation comprises both ancient and lineage-expanded regulatory programs. Leveraging these evolutionary signatures, we identified and experimentally validated a previously unrecognized association between the methyltransferase NSD3 and α-tubulin. Together, these findings reveal that methyltransferases traditionally viewed as chromatin regulators participate in an evolutionarily conserved network that coordinates nuclear and cytoskeletal functions. More broadly, they establish phylogenetic profiling as a powerful approach for discovering noncanonical activities of chromatin-associated enzymes and suggest that regulation of chromatin organization and cellular architecture evolved as interconnected processes.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Wearable interstitial fluid sensing of time-resolved uric acid for early prediction of flare-associated pain in an induced mouse model
items.abstract: Gout flare is driven by hyperuricemia (HUA) and inflammatory responses to monosodium urate (MSU) crystals, yet single time-point serum uric acid (UA) measurements cannot capture the biochemical dynamics preceding flare onset or explain the timing of severe pain manifestation. Here, we present a skin-attachable interstitial fluid (ISF)-based electrochemical sensing platform for time-resolved, minimally invasive UA monitoring in a controlled, induced mouse model of gout flare-associated inflammation and pain. The platform integrates an enzyme-based UA sensor, a thin insertion electrode, and battery-free near-field communication (NFC), enabling time-resolved in vivo tracking of ISF UA dynamics. By establishing disease-stage-specific models comprising HUA, MSU-only inflammation, and gouty arthritis flare (GA flare) conditions, we separately examined metabolic and inflammatory contributions to flare-associated UA dynamics. Time-resolved ISF monitoring revealed that the GA flare group exhibited pronounced UA fluctuation patterns that were not reproduced by either condition alone. The peak timing of UA dynamics was temporally decoupled from pain-related behavioral responses, indicating that flare-associated pain onset cannot be explained by a single UA concentration. A machine learning framework using ISF UA time-series features identified predictive information preceding peak pain, whereas analyses using earlier events defined by sustained decreases in paw withdrawal threshold showed lower and event-definition-dependent performance. These findings establish time-resolved ISF UA monitoring as a framework for resolving flare-associated biochemical dynamics and evaluating subsequent pain progression in an induced mouse model.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Modest loss of sleep increases susceptibility to cybersecurity threats
items.abstract: Sleep restriction leads to impaired cognitive processing across domains. I examined whether the transition to daylight saving time (DST), typically accompanied by compromised sleep, would lead to an increase in the probability of falling prey to a simulated phishing attack using a fully naturalistic experiment with random assignment and blinding. A predatory email was sent to employees at the University of California, Irvine (N = 11,218) either on the morning of Monday following the transition to DST or one week earlier. The transition led to a ~13% increase in the probability of clicking a suspicious link, without affecting the probability of opening the email or reporting it as spam. These results demonstrate that even modest, mundane, and acute loss of sleep has real-life, potentially hazardous, implications for cognitive function.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Structural insights into the evolution of mitochondrial protein import from the trypanosome ATOM complex
items.abstract: The translocase of the outer membrane (TOM) mediates the import of most mitochondrial preproteins. In the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei , this machinery is replaced by the atypical translocase of the outer membrane (ATOM), whose composition differs substantially from the canonical TOM complexes of fungi and metazoans. Here, we report the cryoelectron microscopy structure of the T. brucei ATOM complex at 2.8 Å resolution. The structure resolves all previously identified components together with an additional, previously uncharacterized subunit. Despite its divergent composition, ATOM retains a conserved dimeric channel architecture and a protein-conducting pathway closely resembling those of opisthokont TOM complexes, indicating that the core mechanism of mitochondrial protein translocation was established early in eukaryotic evolution. In contrast, the receptor and intermembrane-space regions exhibit distinct architectures, revealing extensive evolutionary diversification and multiple examples of convergent evolution. Together, these findings provide a near-atomic view of the ATOM translocase and offer insights into the origin, conservation, and diversification of the mitochondrial protein import machinery across eukaryotes.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Physiologic and pharmacologic role of the glucocorticoid receptor in germinal center B cells and plasmacytic differentiation
items.abstract: In diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL), a malignancy derived from germinal center (GC) B cells, somatic hypermutation aberrantly targets glucocorticoid receptor (GR) binding sequences in the super-enhancer (SE) of multiple oncogenes. These events abrogate GR binding and deregulate the expression of the SE-linked gene, suggesting an important role of GR in normal and transformed GC B cells. Using a GC-specific Nr3c1 knockout mouse model and multi-omics analyses in murine and human GC B cells, here we show that, under physiological conditions, GR constitutively localizes to the nucleus, where it transcriptionally modulates signaling pathways implicated in GC homeostasis and plasmablast differentiation in part by antagonizing the repressive function of BCL6 on the plasma cell master regulators IRF4 and PRDM1. While loss of baseline GR activity led to mild GC hyperplasia and impaired plasmacytic differentiation, pharmacologic doses of glucocorticoids, a key component of DLBCL chemo-immunotherapy, were preferentially toxic to GC in a GC B cell–autonomous manner. These findings uncover a physiological role for GR in the GC reaction as well as in promoting plasmablast/plasma cell formation and provide insights into the specific activity of glucocorticoids in the treatment of DLBCL.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Dormancy stabilizes structured food webs
items.abstract: Theory predicts that strong species interactions drive instability in large ecosystems, but strong interactions are common in nature while strong instability appears rare. This discrepancy motivates enduring interest in ecological mechanisms that limit or counteract instability. Dormancy—reversible metabolic suppression—may be one. Dormancy is a ubiquitous life history trait found in organisms ranging from bacteria to trees. Dormant individuals form “seed banks” that are temporarily disengaged from demographic processes and species interactions, creating a memory of past ecological dynamics. Seed banks can stabilize predator–prey interactions, but whether, when, and how they affect the stability of larger ecological networks is uncertain. We show that dormancy stabilizes oscillatory dynamics in a minimal mathematical model and illustrate how dormancy converts high oscillation frequency into strong restoring force. We find that dormancy can have qualitative stabilizing effects in structured food webs that undergo Hopf bifurcations and exhibit oscillatory instability, but rarely in unstructured networks or networks with symmetric (competitive or mutualistic) interactions. This classification remains accurate when only some species go dormant and drive stabilization. Our results clarify when dormancy can promote stability, indicating that it may be an important but overlooked stabilizing factor in food webs.
