Such a Majorana edge reconstruction can “screen” a Pfaffian or AntiPfaffian bulk, so that transport signatures become indistinguishable from those of the PH-Pfaffian. We argue that this physically natural scenario is consistent with experiment.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Dysregulation of mechanosensing signaling in monocytes of patients with systemic sclerosis is associated with skin inflammation
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a severe autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation and progressive fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, resulting in substantial organ dysfunction and increased mortality. Fibrosis is driven in part by infiltration of immune cells, including monocytes that become activated within fibrotic tissue. However, how the mechanical properties of fibrotic skin regulate their function remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that increased stiffness activates human monocytes through mechanosensing. Reanalysis of single cell RNA sequencing datasets revealed that skin infiltrating monocytes exhibit heightened inflammatory signatures as compared to circulating counterparts, with further amplification in SSc. Using collagen-coated hydrogels modeling physiological and fibrotic stiffness, we show that increased stiffness enhances CD86 expression, and broadly upregulates inflammatory transcriptional programs in human monocytes. Mechanistically, stiffness-driven activation was associated with chromatin remodeling and epigenetic reprogramming, identifying the transcription factor Specificity Protein 1 (SP1) as a central regulator. CRISPR–Cas9-mediated disruption or pharmacologic inhibition of SP1 significantly attenuated stiffness- induced inflammatory gene expression, whereas we found no evidence for involvement of the canonical YAP/TAZ–TEAD axis, and pharmacological modulation of PIEZO1 neither reproduced nor blocked the response. Further, monocytes from patients with SSc displayed altered transcriptional trajectories and an exaggerated inflammatory response to high stiffness, accompanied by reduced expression of wound healing and antifibrotic programs. Together, these findings identify SP1-dependent mechanosensing as a previously unrecognized pathway controlling human monocyte activation in the skin and provide mechanistic insight into how tissue stiffness sustains inflammation in SSc.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Polarized twin walls in a halide perovskite
items.abstract: Halide perovskites have emerged as promising materials for next-generation photovoltaics, laser sources, and X-ray detectors. There is intense debate as to whether some photoactive halide perovskites exhibit ferroelectric behavior and whether it might be possible to utilize the bulk photovoltaic effect to enhance the performance of halide perovskite solar cells. Here, using low-dose scanning transmission electron microscopy, we identify ferroelastic twin walls in vapor-deposited CsPbI 3 thin films, parallel to {110} and {112}. Remarkably, despite CsPbI 3 being centrosymmetric and nonpolar, we observe directly that Pb atoms shift at {110} twin walls driving a local ferroelectric-like polarization. These polar twin walls form an intrinsic array of nanoscale interfaces, spaced ~30 to 50 nm apart, embedded within the nonpolar perovskite lattice. In contrast, {112} twin walls do not show a polar displacement of Pb but strongly suppress octahedral tilt and off-center Cs atom displacements, revealing a different untapped structural degree of freedom. These findings reveal previously hidden nanoscale polarization in halide perovskite semiconductors, opening opportunities for enhanced conductivity and photovoltaic behavior through domain wall engineering.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Intermittent gas–liquid rearrangement controls the mixing of gases in porous media
items.abstract: Gas mixing in porous media governs important environmental and industrial applications in which multiple gas components share the available pore space with liquid water, simultaneously undergoing gas mixing and gas–liquid redistribution. Currently, this process is represented by macroscopic models that ignore pore scale dynamics. We demonstrate that this is not generally valid, and can lead to large errors in the mixing rate. We use 4D X-ray imaging to investigate nitrogen injection into a porous sandstone saturated with krypton and water, jointly imaging the gas mixture composition evolution and multiphase flow of gas and water. In contrast to the smooth, continuous representation of the conventional advection–diffusion model, our results show that gas mixing evolves through a sequence of distinct regimes controlled by gas connectivity. Initially, immiscible gas–water displacement generates gas composition variance as the different gases occupy neighboring pores separated by water. As gas connectivity increases, intermittent gas–liquid interfacial rearrangements rapidly connect regions of contrasting gas composition, driving a fast decay in composition variance. Once connectivity stabilizes, mixing is controlled by a confined diffusion process within the quasi-static gas network. At later times, further mixing is driven slowly by multicomponent Ostwald ripening, whereby trapped gas ganglia exchange solutes through the surrounding liquid phase. These findings provide insights into gas mixing in porous media, suggesting concepts for upscaling the role of pore scale multiphase flow in gas mixing in the subsurface.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Some theoretical limitations of t-SNE
items.abstract: t-distributed Stochastic Neighborhood Embedding (t-SNE) has gained popularity as a dimension reduction technique, especially for visualizing data. It is well-known that dimension reduction may lose important data features. We provide a mathematical framework for understanding this loss for t-SNE, establishing several quantitative results across different scenarios that demonstrate how important structural information is lost.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Atypical phenylalanine ammonia-lyases that enhance phenylpropanoid production in plants
items.abstract: Plants synthesize diverse phenylpropanoids, which provide us essential medicine, nutrients, and biomaterials while also acting as a major global carbon sink. Phenylpropanoids are primarily derived from L-phenylalanine (Phe) via Phe ammonia-lyase (PAL), a highly regulated enzymatic activity that limits phenylpropanoid production. However, it remains poorly understood how different plant species regulate PAL enzymes. Phylogeny-guided biochemical screening uncovered complex and diverse feedback regulation of PAL enzymes from 14 different plant species. This screening found a previously uncharacterized PAL clade, namely PALnc (from noncanonical), with some members exhibiting feedback activation by p -coumaric acid, caffeic acid, and 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvic acid in vitro. Transient expression of two PALnc genes, from Elaeis guineensis ( EgPALnc ) and Piper methysticum ( PmPALnc2 ), in Nicotiana benthamiana leaves elevated phenylpropanoid content, supported by the high in planta stability of PALnc proteins compared to canonical PALs. Whereas overexpression of Arabidopsis thaliana PAL1 ( AtPAL1 ) in stable Arabidopsis transgenic lines resulted in very low accumulation of AtPAL1 protein and minor metabolic effects, introduction of EgPALnc rendered high content of EgPALnc protein and hyperaccumulation of hydroxycinnamates derivatives. Our findings uncover a previously overlooked diversity in the regulation of the entry step of phenylpropanoid biosynthesis across various plants and identify atypical PALs within the PALnc clade as valuable tools to debottleneck and enhance phenylpropanoid production in planta.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Trust as a hidden driver of epidemic-relevant behavior: Institution- and behavior-specific associations across 20 national survey waves
items.abstract: Compartmental models of infectious disease transmission make assumptions about human behaviors. Specifically, they parameterize interactions across population groups, assumed to have distinct epidemiologically relevant behavioral patterns, primarily through contact matrices stratified by demographic variables such as age, gender, or socioeconomic status. Although such demographic characteristics are readily measurable, they may inadequately capture the social and psychological forces that govern protective behaviors. Drawing on 20 waves of a national survey conducted throughout the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States, we show that institutional trust—particularly trust in public health agencies, physicians, and hospitals—is a dominant predictor of protective behavior adoption. For mask wearing during periods of strongest pandemic activity, institutional trust explains more behavioral difference across population groups than age, income, education, and partisan affiliation combined. In unadjusted analyses, the difference in protective behavior adoption between individuals with the highest and lowest trust in the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) was four- to six-fold larger than the corresponding differences by age, income, or education, and exceeded the difference between Democratic and Republican respondents. This association was institutionally specific (the relationship attenuates for trust in banks), and behaviorally specific (trust in the CDC is associated with protective behaviors but not visiting a doctor). The latter suggests that trust modifies voluntary compliance with public health recommendations rather than healthcare access or use. These findings identify institutional trust as a candidate stratifying variable for models of behavior-coupled transmission dynamics, and as a measurable target for public health surveillance.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity
items.abstract: In this study, we propose a perspective on neural synchronization. Beyond reflecting shared understanding between individuals, we suggest it serves as a biological marker of social homogeneity. We examined fMRI neural responses of 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives. While explicit measures of emotional response, agreement, and engagement showed no significant differences in within-group variance, religious participants—representing a tighter social structure—exhibited significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and brain networks. Remarkably, synchrony values predicted religious orientation with an accuracy of up to 92%. We conclude that a community’s homogeneous social structure drives pervasive neural alignment, positioning neural synchrony as a potential signature of group cohesion beyond explicit behavioral measures.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Normalized Raman imaging for studies of tissue physiology of the kidney
items.abstract: Conventional histology relies on fixation, embedding, sectioning, and staining methods that distort cellular architecture, extract lipids, and introduce variability, limiting reproducibility. We present a pipeline for automated histopathology in the mouse kidney using normalized stimulated Raman imaging (NoRI) that enables quantitative, label-free protein and lipid measurements at high spatial resolution. NoRI computationally corrects protein, lipid, and water Raman signals, allowing quantitative biomass measurements while preserving tissue architecture, facilitating analysis by convolutional neural networks (CNN) for quantitative, morphological feature extraction. Applied to mouse kidney, CNN analysis of NoRI images was able to accurately classify tubule types (F1=0.93; harmonic mean of precision and recall against immunofluorescence-defined labels), anatomical regions (F1 = 0.91), and biological sex (F1 = 0.97), revealing greater cytoplasmic lipid (+6.5 to 7.3 mg/mL; P ≤ 0.028) and nuclear protein (+26.3 mg/mL; P ≤ 0.001) in female tubules. Using acute kidney injury (AKI) in mice as a disease model to test our histopathology pipeline combining NoRI and CNNs, we captured dynamic lipid and protein organization and quantified brush border remodeling and lipid droplet changes over 25 d postinjury. Spatial lipid quantification was central for feature classification in AKI (F1 = 0.99). Quantitative NoRI images also significantly outperformed equivalent raw stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) images in distinguishing early time points (24 to 48 h) of ischemia–reperfusion injury [F1 = 0.99 (NoRI) vs. 0.84 (SRS); P < 0.0001], demonstrating the improvement of NoRI over conventional SRS imaging. These results establish our pipeline, which combines NoRI imaging with advanced CNN analyses, as a reproducible, quantitative method for histopathology and feature discovery.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: USP46 restrains K63-linked polyubiquitination–dependent aggregation and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in lupus nephritis
items.abstract: The activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome necessitates its aggregation within the dispersed trans-Golgi network (dTGN) and subsequent transport from the dTGN to the microtubule organizing center (MTOC), a process facilitated by HDAC6. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing the formation of NLRP3 aggregates remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we demonstrate that proteasome impairment induces polyubiquitination and aggregation of NLRP3 at the MTOC. We demonstrate ubiquitin-specific protease 46 (USP46) as a key factor that recognizes NLRP3 as a substrate and restricts nondegradative K63-linked polyubiquitination at lysine residue K930, thereby preventing excessive aggregation, transport to the MTOC, and inflammasome activation. Furthermore, myeloid-specific knockout of USP46 exacerbates renal injury and inflammation in both lipopolysaccharide-induced-induced endotoxic shock and pristane-induced lupus nephritis models. Our findings provide insights into the regulatory mechanisms underlying the aggresomal activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: An aggregation-prone region in talin controls talin self-interactions and regulates integrin adhesion complex dynamics
items.abstract: Talin is a mechanosensitive scaffold that couples integrins to the actin cytoskeleton and coordinates signaling at integrin adhesion complexes. A second integrin-binding site (IBS2) has been proposed within the R11–R12 region of the talin rod, although the molecular basis of this interaction has remained unclear. Here, we show that talin R11 contains a cryptic aggregation-prone region (APR) embedded within Helix50. Mechanical unfolding of R11 exposes this motif, enabling high-affinity talin–talin interactions and force-dependent self-association. The isolated APR forms amyloid-like fibers in vitro, and APR-disrupting gatekeeper mutations suppress fiber formation, talin self-association, and cellular recruitment. We therefore designate this motif Aggregation-Prone Region 1 (APR1). Mitochondrial-targeting experiments demonstrate that APR1-dependent recruitment occurs in cells independently of focal adhesions and integrins. APR1 overlaps the vinculin-binding site in Helix50, and vinculin disrupts preexisting talin assemblies, revealing a mechano-chaperone function for vinculin. Disruption of APR1-mediated self-association does not impair adhesion formation but instead generates larger, more talin-rich adhesions with altered assembly dynamics and signaling properties, indicating a role for APR1 in regulating adhesion remodeling. Together, these findings identify force-dependent talin self-association as a mechanism in mechanotransduction and suggest that the region previously designated IBS2 functions primarily as an aggregation-prone regulatory element.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Maize genetic diversity is largely unstructured by human ethnolinguistic diversity in its center of origin
items.abstract: Population structure and environmental features often capture major axes of genetic variation in many species. Yet the impacts of human activity often remain unquantified. For domesticated species that rely on human activity for survival and dispersal, human movements and cultural differences may play key roles patterning genetic diversity. Maize is a staple crop of enormous cultural importance to indigenous peoples of the Americas, but cannot survive or disperse without farmers. Using publicly available genotyping and passport data from approximately 2,000 traditional maize varieties, more than 500 whole genome sequences of humans from Mexico, and indigenous linguistic maps, we quantify anthropogenic effects on maize genetic diversity in the Americas. Maize shows very little overall structure, highlighting the effectiveness of indigenous farmers in moving and mixing maize populations. While principal components of maize diversity show meaningful correlations to human genetic diversity, our linear modeling suggests little additional impact of human population structure beyond shared geography. Though differences in maize diversity are often patterned by language locally, we find only weak genome-wide effects at larger spatial scales. Despite the relatively weak global signal of anthropogenic effects, linguistic Genome-wide association, outlier F ST analyses, and selection scans identified loci associated with specific languages. Leveraging landscape-level sequencing data, we highlight how anthropogenic factors have shaped patterns of maize genetic diversity across Mesoamerica.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Dynamic virulence decomposition disentangles host and pathogen contributions over the course of infection
items.abstract: Decomposing virulence into host and pathogen effects is key to understanding how virulence is generated during infection, and how host and pathogen contributions evolve over time. Conventional virulence decomposition is, however, not designed to quantify how these contributions vary throughout an infection. Building on conventional virulence decomposition, we developed a dynamic framework that integrates disease space analysis to quantify these changing contributions. We applied this framework to existing data from house finches ( Haemorhous mexicanus ) experimentally infected with the emerging bacterial pathogen, Mycoplasma gallisepticum , examining two biologically meaningful infection phases: an early phase dominated by innate immune responses and a later phase in which the adaptive immune response is fully activated. Our analyses revealed that virulence components evolved differently across infection phases, with pathogen exploitation, per-parasite-pathogenicity (PPP), and host resistance each exhibiting distinct trajectories. These findings corroborated several known evolutionary patterns, while also revealing the evolution of increased PPP in this system. In contrast, the apparent evolution of host tolerance inferred from aggregated peak measurements was not supported by phase-specific analyses, demonstrating that aggregated and phase-specific measures can provide different mechanistic insights into virulence. By linking conventional virulence decomposition with disease space analysis, our dynamic virulence decomposition framework provides a general approach for quantifying how host and pathogen processes shape virulence over the course of infection.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: A DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold is essential for perinuclear theca assembly and fertilization
items.abstract: Fertilization is a fundamental biological process that enables the fusion of a spermatozoon with an oocyte to initiate embryonic development. However, the underlying mechanisms leading to fertilization failure remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrated that the actin-related protein (Arp) family members ACTRT2 and ACTRT3 are essential for fertilization in both humans and mice, whereas ACTL10 is dispensable for fertility and the human-specific ACTL8 may play a role in early spermatogenesis. Ultrastructural and immunofluorescence analyses revealed that, during spermatogenesis, ACTRT2 or ACTRT3 deficiency disrupts the assembly of subacrosomal layer of the perinuclear theca (SAL-PT), leading to acrosome detachment and subsequent manchette abnormalities, which in turn impairs the formation of the postacrosomal sheath of the PT. These structural defects were accompanied by reduced abundance of the candidate sperm-borne oocyte-activating factors PAWP and PLCζ. Moreover, knockout of Actrt2 or Actrt3 severely impaired spermatozoa’s ability to penetrate the zona pellucida during in vitro fertilization. Mechanistically, ACTRT2, ACTRT3, ACTL7A, ACTL7B, and ACTL9 form a testis-enriched Arp complex in the SAL-PT and maintain the stability of one another. This complex interacts with the PT protein CAPZA3, which subsequently binds and stabilizes PLCζ. Additionally, the Arp complex interacts with DPY19L2/FAM209-associated proteins to mediate acrosome anchoring to the nuclear envelope. Therefore, these findings established a sequential DPY19L2/FAM209-associated protein–Arp complex–CAPZA3 scaffold extending from the nuclear envelope to the acrosome that is indispensable for fertilization. Collectively, we defined a previously unidentified structural and molecular framework for fertilization and provided insights into the diagnosis and treatment of fertilization failure.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Comprehensive classification of HCN1 variants linked to neurodevelopmental disorders with and without epilepsy
items.abstract: Hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated 1 (HCN1) channels mediate the cationic I h current, a fundamental regulator of neuronal excitability and synaptic integration, and are predominantly expressed in the cortex and hippocampus. Although HCN1 variants have been increasingly identified in patients with epilepsy, from milder forms to developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEE), genotype–phenotype correlations remain poorly defined. Here, we used patch-clamp electrophysiology and confocal imaging in HEK293 cells to functionally characterize 43 HCN1 variants identified in patients with neurodevelopmental disorders, with or without epilepsy. Based on biophysical properties, we established a classification system comprising four distinct functional classes: I) low or no current; II) hyperpolarizing shift in voltage dependence; III) depolarizing shift in voltage dependence; and IV) generation of an instantaneous current. The molecular basis for this classification was further interpreted using available cryo-EM structures of HCN1. Integration with clinical data from 50 patients revealed a striking correlation between functional class and clinical presentation. Loss-of-function variants prevailed among individuals with milder phenotypes or without epilepsy, with the latter distinctively clustering within the channel selectivity filter. In contrast, gain-of-function and mixed variants were predominantly associated with DEE. Finally, we demonstrate that allosteric modulators, including peptides NB6 and TRIP8b nano and the small molecule J&J12e, effectively normalize channel function across three of the four classes in vitro. These findings establish a biophysical framework for interpreting HCN1 variants, demonstrating that the direction of channel dysfunction is a major determinant of epilepsy risk and severity, and providing a conceptual foundation for future class-based precision medicine approaches.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Intrinsically motivated humans and agents in open-world exploration
items.abstract: What drives exploration? Understanding the intrinsic motivation to explore is a long-standing challenge in both cognitive science and AI. In this study, we directly compare adults, children aged 8 to 12 y, and AI agents exploring a complex, open-ended environment called Crafter ( 1 ). We study how three common information-theoretic intrinsic objectives—entropy, information gain, and empowerment—relate to their behavior. We find that all three are positively correlated with human exploration progress for both children and adults, although entropy and empowerment are more strongly related to exploration progress in children than information gain. Furthermore, across agents and humans we observe that entropy initially increases rapidly, then plateaus, while empowerment increases continuously, suggesting that in early exploration they look for novel states, while in advanced exploration they look for states they can control. Finally, we find preliminary evidence that private speech about goals may aid exploration in children. Our data are available at https://github.com/alyd/humans_in_crafter_data .
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Lead impairs long-term memory by disrupting mitochondrial redox homeostasis in Drosophila
items.abstract: Lead (Pb) exposure remains a major environmental risk factor for cognitive dysfunction, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying Pb-induced memory impairment are poorly understood. Here, we show that both developmental and adult-onset Pb exposure selectively disrupts protein-synthesis-dependent long-term memory (LTM) in Drosophila melanogaster while sparing other memory forms. Using a mitochondria-targeted redox biosensor (mito-roGFP2-Orp1), we found that Pb elevates mitochondrial oxidative stress and disrupts redox homeostasis in cholinergic neurons and in dorsal-anterior-lateral (DAL) neurons, a critical locus for LTM consolidation. Pb-induced redox imbalance suppresses training-induced de novo protein synthesis in DAL neurons, thereby impairing memory consolidation. Antioxidant treatment with epigallocatechin gallate restores mitochondrial redox balance and rescues LTM by reinstating activity-dependent protein synthesis in DAL neurons. These findings identify mitochondrial redox dysregulation as a key mechanism linking environmental Pb exposure to impaired memory consolidation. Our results further establish a genetically tractable platform for dissecting neurotoxic mechanisms and for evaluating antioxidant-based strategies to mitigate Pb-induced cognitive dysfunction.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: A tetravalent bispecific protein enables targeted degradation of VCAM-1 and VEGFR for treatment of choroidal neovascularization
items.abstract: Wet age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a leading cause of irreversible vision loss, is driven by pathological choroidal neovascularization (CNV). Although anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (anti-VEGF) therapies remain the clinical standard, their utility is constrained by incomplete responses in nearly 50% of patients and off-target risks—such as geographic atrophy—stemming from non-specific VEGF blockade. Here, we identify a robust correlation between vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) and VEGF/VEGF receptor (VEGFR) expression in aqueous humor from AMD patients and in murine CNV models. Thus, we engineered a tetravalent bispecific protein, RHV, by functionalizing an L-rhamnulose-1-phosphate aldolase scaffold with peptides that selectively bind VCAM-1 and the VEGFR on neovessels. The tetravalent design confers high apparent affinity, enhancing pathological endothelial targeting while sparing healthy retinal vasculature. RHV induces concurrent internalization and lysosomal degradation of both VCAM-1 and VEGFR via a head-to-tail binding mode, leading to sustained inhibition of the VEGF/VEGFR, PI3K/AKT and Apelin/APJ signaling pathways. In murine CNV models, a single intravitreal injection of RHV exhibits superior ocular retention and lesion penetration, achieving therapeutic efficacy comparable to aflibercept [a ligand-trap fusion protein for VEGF-A, VEGF-B and placental growth factor (PIGF)] at one-quarter of the molar dose. This dual-receptor degradation-based strategy represents a targeted and durable approach for treating ocular neovascularization.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Entropic tightening of knots in granular chains under vibration
items.abstract: Knots are common in long chains, from DNA and proteins to everyday strings, yet direct observation of knot dynamics is difficult. Using granular chains on vibrating platforms, we directly visualize knot dynamics and find that knot cores spontaneously tighten, a behavior observed across different knot types. We quantitatively explain spontaneous knot tightening using knot-tube theory: segments confined within the knot core experience entropic loss and tend to escape the core to gain conformational entropy. Although driven granular chains are not in thermodynamic equilibrium, their steady-state knot-size statistics are approximately captured by equilibrium statistical mechanics and Monte Carlo simulations. Analyses of state-transition probabilities and time-reversal asymmetry suggest a weak violation of detailed balance when the granular dynamics are projected onto the knot-size coordinate. Finally, we discuss the possible relevance of knot tightening to topoisomerase-mediated DNA unknotting.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Municipal sludge disposal emerges as a major, hidden, and rapidly growing atmospheric mercury source
items.abstract: Wastewater treatment greatly reduces mercury pollution in aquatic ecosystems but does not eliminate it. Here, we identify municipal sludge disposal as a major, long-overlooked atmospheric mercury source. In China, sludge disposal emitted 42 - 10 + 18 Mg in 2024, exceeding 10% of national anthropogenic emissions and ranking third after cement production and nonferrous metal smelting. These emissions have increased by nearly a thousandfold since the 1970s and are concentrated in densely populated urban areas, driven by the rapid expansion of sludge incineration, codisposal, and composting. Our findings reveal a cross-media pollution transfer embedded in sustainability transitions and call for sludge disposal to be incorporated into UNEP mercury budget and Minamata Convention assessments.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title:
The purinergic receptor P2Y
                    <sub>13</sub>
                    controls the activation and mode of division of adult ventricular–subventricular zone neural stem cells
items.abstract: The ventricular–subventricular zone (V-SVZ) is the most active germinal area in the mammalian brain and it continues to generate newborn neurons throughout life. This area harbors a population of neural stem cells (NSCs) that exist in different states of activation: quiescent NSCs, primed NSCs, and activated NSCs. There are currently few specific markers to effectively discern each state. Likewise, the molecular signals that control the transition from quiescence to activation remain largely unexplored, and the factors that controls whether dividing NSCs differentiate or self-renew are poorly understood. Here, we present evidence that the metabotropic P2Y 13 purinergic receptor plays a critical role in regulating adult neurogenesis. We found that P2Y 13 is specifically expressed in NSCs within the adult V-SVZ and that its levels can be used to distinguish quiescent from activated NSCs. P2Y 13 signaling promotes NSC activation, enhancing lineage progression as opposed to their self-renewal. Conversely, pharmacological blockade or genetic silencing of P2Y 13 receptors favors NSC quiescence. Thus, we consider the metabotropic P2Y 13 purinergic receptor a pivotal modulator of NSC dynamics.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Patterns of implicit and explicit attitudes V: Increases in bias from 2021 to 2025
items.abstract: Between 2007 and 2020, implicit and explicit intergroup attitudes declined in bias steadily and were forecasted to continue toward attitude neutrality. But, since 2020, 5 y of new data (2021–2025) from 2.8 million U.S. respondents reveal that past trends have stalled or, in some cases, even reversed. The largest reversals in bias emerged for sexuality, transgender, race, and skin-tone bias which increased by 12 to 22% on implicit measures and by 24% to more than tripling on explicit measures. Age, disability, and body weight bias also increased, but at relatively slower rates. Breakpoint analyses showed that implicit attitudes were early indicators of change, reversing trend ~1 y earlier than explicit reports. For most topics, reversals were widespread across demographic groups and even extended to an international sample of 274,884 non-U.S. respondents. However, younger respondents (<20-y-old)—who had previously shown the largest decreases in bias—now showed the largest increases in bias; these trends also interacted with politics and gender (e.g., young conservative men were the most likely to increase). Exploratory analyses ruled out various single-cause explanations. Instead, we suggest that the best explanation is that 2020–2021 marked a turning point in the sociopolitical climate, whereby co-occurring existential threats from the COVID-19 pandemic, amplified economic insecurity, political sectarianism, and online toxicity prompted increases in intergroup bias. These data underscore how large populations of individual-level attitudes are continually shaped and altered by macro, societal-level events.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via decomposition-based multiobjective optimization design
items.abstract: Metamaterials offer unprecedented control over physical fields through their microstructure, but current design methods cannot meet the demands of scenarios involving active sources, multiphysics field coupling, and multifunctional requirements. Moreover, existing approaches are generally developed for specific functions, making it difficult to integrate different functionalities and select the functional priorities within a single structure. To overcome these limitations, this study presents a systematic inverse design framework for multifunctional multiphysics metamaterials via multiobjective optimization. To uniformly explore the Pareto front, which clearly exhibits trade-offs among functionalities and facilitates the selection of functional priorities, we employ dynamic normalization into the decomposition-based multiobjective evolutionary algorithm. A robust anisotropic unit-cell database is constructed and used for generating metamaterials with optimized microstructures for multifunctionality. Three complex cases are studied that can simultaneously achieve mechanical cloaking plus stress minimization, thermal cloaking plus stress minimization, and direct current cloaking plus thermal stress minimization. Furthermore, the proposed framework is employed in potential engineering problems, for example, to realize mechanical cloaking by embedding functional components in structural materials, while minimizing the surrounding stress on functional components for mechanical protection when the assembled structures are compressed, thereby decoupling the interaction between functional and structural components. This systematic framework expands the capabilities of metamaterials in complex multiphysics coupling, offering a robust blueprint for future intelligent, structurally and functionally integrated systems.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Amphipathic helices repurpose a Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter to function at Plasmodium –erythrocyte membrane contact sites
items.abstract: The interface between the malaria parasite Plasmodium spp. and its host erythrocyte critically mediates nutrient uptake, lipid exchange, and protein export required for parasite replication and thus pathogenesis. Approximately half of this interface consists of narrow membrane contact sites, a region defined by only 3 to 4 nm of aqueous space between the parasite plasma membrane and the parasitophorous vacuole membrane. Despite its extent, the region remains largely uncharacterized and inaccessible, not least due to its narrowness. The sole identified resident is the Plasmodium falciparum Niemann-Pick Type C1-Related protein, PfNCR1, an essential Patched/NPC1-like cholesterol transporter, suggesting this conserved transporter family has evolved an unconventional adaptation for localizing to membrane contact sites that can reveal a mechanism to access the region. Here, using live-cell microscopy and assessment of cholesterol homeostasis, we identify a helix–linker–helix (HLH) domain as the necessary modification for efficient PfNCR1 localization. We find that correct localization is required for the parasite to maintain low cholesterol levels, connecting targeting to function. Using a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored fluorescent reporter as a minimal membrane-associated protein, we show that the HLH domain is sufficient to drive localization to the narrow membrane contact site region. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that targeting depends on the physicochemical character of the targeting domain rather than a specific primary sequence, identifying amphipathicity as a determining property of the HLH domain. Taken together, we propose physicochemical partitioning as a fundamental principle for protein targeting at the Plasmodium –erythrocyte interface, and for driving direct functional interactions of a Patched/NPC1-like protein with a second membrane.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Progressive shifts in soil respiration response to long-term nitrogen enrichment across global forests and grasslands
items.abstract: Soil stores the largest pool of actively cycling carbon (C) on land, and its dynamics under global changes are critical for projecting climate feedbacks. Global nitrogen (N) deposition has more than doubled since the 1860s; however, the temporal dynamics of soil C emissions under prolonged N deposition are poorly understood. Here, using a global time-series dataset compiled from 38 long-term experiments in forests and grasslands, we find that the response of soil respiration (Rs) to N addition systematically shifts from a transient increase persisting for approximately 2 y to a sustained suppression over time (mean effect = −6%; 95% CI = [−10%, −3%]). Rs in forests and grasslands followed consistent nonlinear trajectories, characterized by a rapid initial decline in the magnitude of the response, which progressively leveled off. Notably, suppression of Rs emerged when cumulative N inputs exceeded a threshold of ~100 kg N ha −1 . Consequently, the suppression was both stronger and occurred more rapidly under high-level N additions (>50 kg N ha −1 y −1 ). These temporal dynamics were associated with N-induced soil acidification and related changes in microbial properties. Overall, these findings indicate that accurate prediction of land–atmosphere C fluxes under global change requires models to capture the reported temporal dynamics.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration
items.abstract: Adaptive evolution associated with dispensable gene loss is widespread in the animal kingdom. However, loss of genes essential for embryonic survival and the mechanisms that evolved to bypass negative selection and extinction are less well known. Here, we show that all Gadiformes, an ecologically dominant order of codfishes, lost the aqp1ab -type genes that are essential for the formation of hydrated pelagic eggs and embryonic survival of marine teleosts in oceanic environments. Despite such gene loss, codfishes produce some of the most highly hydrated pelagic eggs of all marine teleosts. To resolve this apparent paradox, we initially confirmed that the mechanisms of osmotic drive are conserved with other pelagic-egg-producing marine teleosts, and then conducted comparative transcript analyses of aquaporin water channels in distantly-related freshwater and marine teleosts. This uncovered Aqp4-type channels that have been chromosomally linked to the Aqp1-type channels in jawed vertebrate genomes for >450 million years as the primary candidates. Using immunolocalization, functional assays, and inhibition experiments with zebrafish and Atlantic cod as model organisms, we show that short isoforms of Aqp4 are required for egg ovulation in more ancestral lineages of freshwater teleosts and were recruited to the oocyte hydration pathway of codfishes. By contrast, the oldest and most modern lineages of marine teleosts producing pelagic eggs still utilize the aqp1ab genes for egg hydration. Our data thus reveal that codfishes survived essential gene loss by functionally co-opting freshwater ovulatory pathways to marine egg hydration.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Modified Newtonian Dynamics and galaxy clusters
items.abstract: First proposed by Milgrom in 1983 as an alternative to the standard Cold Dark Matter (CDM) paradigm, Modified Newtonian Dynamics (MOND) has gained renewed momentum in light of persistent nondetections of exotic dark matter particles and growing tensions facing CDM on galactic scales. While MOND perfectly reproduces galactic rotation curves, it encounters notable challenges in explaining the equilibrium of galaxy clusters. Although it reduces the overall dark matter budget in these massive systems, an unidentified mass component remains required. This paper investigates the hypothesis that this missing mass is baryonic: composed of nonradiating ordinary matter such as stellar remnants, gas too diffuse to initiate star formation, or compact, ultra-dense clouds of cold molecular gas with low volume filling factors. Using a sample of 106 clusters mapped in X-rays, emitted by the hot intracluster medium composing most of the visible mass, we derive first the total mass within the Newtonian dynamics, assuming hydrostatic equilibrium and spherical symmetry. Then, with the modified Poisson equation, we reconstruct the spatial distribution of the invisible missing matter within the MOND framework. In the sample, the relaxed systems harboring cooling flows, known as cool-core clusters, have the highest peaks of dark missing mass. Its density profile reveals a pronounced central concentration bounded by a steep truncation immediately beyond a core radius of 20 to 30 kpc, confirming previous studies. MOND reduces the necessary dynamical mass by a factor of 4 to 10. The residual missing mass is proportional to the total gas mass, being roughly twice lower.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: QnAs with Alison Gopnik
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Profile of Françoise Combes
items.abstract: Françoise Combes’s childhood curiosity motivated her to pursue a career in science. Her studies in physics at the École Normale Supérieure in Paris eventually led her to focus on astrophysics. With help from mentors, such as astrophysicists Evry Schatzman and Pierre Encrenaz, Combes has had a distinguished career in astrophysics. She is renowned for her work studying the formation and evolution of galaxies and their dynamics and her research on dark matter. In her Inaugural Article, she describes her latest work exploring alternatives to dark matter.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Hepatocyte-derived exosomal miR-122 mediates liver-to-brain crosstalk and neuroinflammation in alcohol-exposed Alzheimer’s disease mice
items.abstract: Neuroinflammation and microglial activation are common features in Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and excessive alcohol consumption. Alcohol induces liver damage and inflammation, and altered serum aminotransferases have been reported in patients with AD. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) and their cargo are emerging as mediators of intercellular communication in AD and alcohol-induced liver injury. However, the effects of alcohol use on AD progression remain to be elucidated. In this study, we evaluated the effects of repeated binge drinking on the liver and brain in the APP/PS1 mouse model of AD. Alcohol-exposed APP/PS1 mice showed elevated serum alanine aminotransferase levels, indicating liver injury absent in controls, along with increased pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in both liver and brain. Alcohol increased the biogenesis and release of sEVs in AD mice and in mouse hepatocytes. These sEVs were enriched in mature miR-122-5p that is predominant in hepatocytes. In vivo, miR-122-5p was detected in the brain of alcohol-exposed AD mice suggesting EV-mediated miR-122-5p transfer to the brain. Microglial uptake of hepatocyte-derived sEVs was confirmed in vitro. sEVs from alcohol-treated hepatocytes sensitized BV-2 microglia to LPS stimulation, significantly enhancing CCL2, CXCL2, CCL3, and TNF-α production. Transfection of microglia with a miR-122-5p mimic partially recapitulated the pro-inflammatory sensitization by sEVs from alcohol-exposed hepatocytes, which was reversed by miR-122-5p inhibitor delivery. ADAM10, a miR-122-5p target, was reduced in both wild-type and AD brains after alcohol exposure, with cell-specific effects. These results suggest that alcohol-induced hepatocyte-derived sEVs may modulate liver-to-brain signaling via miR-122-5p and contribute to neuroinflammation in AD.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Coacervate droplets as a liquefier for the solid-to-liquid transition of RNA aggregates
items.abstract: Biomolecular condensates are functionally gated by their material properties. While RNA is a primary structural scaffold, its sequence-specific interactions can aberrantly drive condensates into dysfunctional solid aggregates. Yet, actively reversing this solidification to restore function remains a fundamental challenge, impeding progress in synthetic biology and therapeutics interventions. Here, we establish that complex coacervates can be engineered as liquefiers to actively remodel solid RNA–peptide aggregates into functional liquid droplets. Integrating systematic experiments with all-atom simulations, we decode a multiscale mechanism: coacervate infiltration at the micrometer scale mediates molecular buffering at the nanometer scale, which fluidizes the crosslinked network to drive macroscopic liquefaction. This capability is governed by a design rule, where coacervates formed by small-molecular anions exhibit optimal efficacy. We deploy this principle to functionally rescue silenced RNA within a model of pathologically solidified ribonucleoprotein assemblies. Our work provides a general framework for the active, compositional control of biomolecular phase behavior, with direct implications for managing pathological aggregation and engineering functional condensates in synthetic and living systems.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Epigenetic aging during the COVID-19 pandemic: A prospective longitudinal study with prepandemic baseline data in children, adolescents, and adults
items.abstract: Psychosocial stress is a risk factor for aging-related diseases. The COVID-19 pandemic placed a psychosocial burden on individuals, potentially increasing the risk for aging-related diseases for which epigenetic clocks are used as early biomarkers. Based on four epigenetic clocks (DunedinPACE, GrimAge2, Horvath, and PedBE), we investigated whether epigenetic aging changed during the pandemic and whether these changes were associated with objective and subjective pandemic-related stressors and preexisting individual risk factors for poorer physical and mental health. We used prospective longitudinal data (n = 1,028), including repeated salivary DNA collection from children (n = 359, MAGE = 9.5 y), adolescents (n = 385, MAGE = 15.5 y), and adults (n = 284, MAGE = 24.3 y). Saliva was collected before the first phase of containment measures in Germany in March 2020 and after the second phase in 2021. We observed significant increases in epigenetic age acceleration (PedBE: b = 0.17, P < 0.0001; GrimAge2: b = 0.08, P < 0.0001) and pace of aging (DunedinPACE: b = 0.13, P < 0.0001) across all age groups. Prepandemic physical health and parental socioeconomic status, but not objective pandemic stressors, were significantly associated with this change. In adolescents, higher perceived pandemic burden was associated with a larger increase in pace of aging (DunedinPACE: b = 0.04, P = 0.01). Together, these findings suggest that prepandemic individual risk factors for poorer physical and mental health are accompanied by measurable increases in epigenetic aging during the COVID-19 pandemic, with adolescence representing a sensitive phase to its psychosocial burden.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Spontaneous gas film expansion at an oil–water interface
items.abstract: Spontaneous interfacial separation of oil and water, by inserting a gas film between the two liquids, is thermodynamically unfavorable because the oil–water interface is replaced by oil–gas and water–gas interfaces with a higher combined interfacial energy. Here, we demonstrate that microstructural confinement enables this transition after bubble introduction through the coupling of wetting, capillarity, and gas transport. Spontaneous oil imbibition into a water-submerged micropillar array, together with local contact-line pinning, deforms the oil–water interface into a metastable meniscus and generates a local pressure deficit in the confined oil. This deficit, combined with the bubble’s interfacial configuration, lowers its air partial pressure and promotes dissolved-air uptake from the surrounding water. Geometric confinement, reduced oil pressure, and low oil–gas interfacial tension favor bubble lateral invasion of adjacent oil-filled cells over vertical extrusion. As the gas front advances, meniscus relaxation and oil redistribution promote further wetting, renewing the capillary conditions that support gas film propagation. We develop a coupled transport-capillarity framework that captures these morphological transitions and predicts a characteristic timescale for gas film evolution, determined by the interaction among geometry, capillarity, and gas-phase transport. Spatially varying the microstructure further controls the propagation pathway and morphology of the gas film. These findings show how favorable wetting can support an energetically costly interfacial transformation through a confinement-induced capillary pressure field, providing a general mechanism for gas-mediated separation in confined multiphase systems.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Coupled outward and inward oxide growth during metal oxidation
items.abstract: Metal oxidation is traditionally described as a dichotomy: oxide scales grow either outward via cation diffusion or inward via anion diffusion, with the dominant pathway determined by the prevailing point defects in the oxide lattice. Here, we demonstrate that these two modes are not mutually exclusive but intrinsically coupled within a single oxidation process. Using in situ environmental transmission electron microscopy to monitor the oxidation of copper—a canonical cationic system—we directly visualize simultaneous oxide propagation at both the O 2 /Cu 2 O surface interface and the buried Cu 2 O/Cu interface. Complementary simulations reveal the mechanistic origin of this behavior. Outward cation transport during surface oxide growth injects a sustained flux of vacancies into the underlying metal lattice, which facilitates inward oxygen incorporation and drives oxide growth at the buried interface. This vacancy-mediated feedback couples cationic and anionic transport process, providing a unified framework in which surface cationic growth directly enables inward anionic-driven growth. By identifying vacancy injection as a key mediator of interfacial mass transport, this work provides a mechanistic basis for predicting oxidation kinetics and defect-regulated solid-state transformation pathways in reactive environments.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Forcing dataset updates impact regional but not global Earth radiation budget trends in the GFDL AM4 climate model
items.abstract: The availability of up-to-date forcing datasets is critical for reconciling Earth system model simulations with contemporary observations. With the newly released CMIP7 forcing dataset, which extends the historical record through 2021, this study provides a systematic evaluation of how using updated forcings over the “middle-of-the-road” SSP2-4.5 scenario forcings influences the simulated radiation budget in the GFDL AM4 climate model. The updated forcing dataset used in the atmosphere model does not improve the agreement between the simulated global-mean top-of-the-atmosphere radiation trends and the satellite-observed trends. Regionally, we identify pronounced shifts in radiative energy partitioning between atmosphere and surface. Specifically, during 2001–2021, accelerated reductions in sulfate and black carbon aerosols over East Asia drive a significant decline in atmospheric solar absorption that matches observations, while a substantial increase in organic aerosols at higher latitudes induces a localized increase in atmospheric absorption that does not match observations. The substantial influence of localized forcing changes on simulated regional climate underscores the necessity for routine updates of forcing datasets.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Hypothalamic lncRNA Synage prevents age-related sperm quality decline by suppressing A-type potassium currents in GnRH neurons
items.abstract: Age-related decline in male fertility, including diminished sperm quality, poses significant risks to offspring health and is exacerbated by modern trends toward delayed parenthood. Focusing on the hypothalamus–pituitary–testis axis, which governs hormonal control of male reproduction, we identified Synage , a long noncoding RNA expressed in the hypothalamic medial preoptic area (mPOA). We found that Synage expression in gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons decreases with age, correlating with reduced sperm quality and male fertility. mPOA-targeted Synage _B (brain-specific isoform) supplementation increases serum testosterone and improves sperm count and progressive motility in 12-mo-old mice. Conversely, conditional deletion of Synage in GnRH neurons in young mice reduces GnRH neuron firing, decreases serum LH and testosterone levels, impaires sperm quality, and reduces male fertility. Mechanistically, Synage interacts with the heat shock protein HSPA8 and stabilizes the HSPA8–KCHIP4 interaction. Synage loss increases KCHIP4 abundance and its association with the Kv4.2 channel, promoting Kv4.2 membrane recruitment and enhancing A-type potassium currents ( I A ), thereby reducing GnRH neuronal excitability. Consistent with this model, GnRH neurons from 12-mo-old mice also exhibit reduced excitability. Together, these findings support a role for age-dependent Synage loss in reproductive decline, at least in part through dysregulation of the HSPA8–KCHIP4–Kv4.2 pathway and reduced GnRH neuron excitability. These findings identify Synage as a candidate regulator of reproductive aging and motivate further investigation of its translational potential.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Dissociation of gravity and limb dynamics in motor control
items.abstract: Human movements remain accurate across substantial variations in mechanical loading, yet how the nervous system anticipates and compensates for intrinsic and extrinsic forces when generating muscle commands remains unresolved. Because the forces acting on the body are complex and nonlinear, dynamical modeling provides a powerful framework for identifying the computations underlying motor control. Here, we exploited parabolic flight to dissociate gravitational loading from intrinsic limb dynamics and directly test how these mechanical components are represented in motor commands. We analyzed kinematics and shoulder muscle activity from nine participants performing visually guided pointing movements in microgravity (0g), normogravity (1g), and hypergravity (2g). Inverse dynamics revealed that the gravity-independent component of muscle torque remained invariant across gravitational conditions. In striking contrast, muscle moments estimated from muscle activation showed systematic scaling of not only static but also phasic components with gravitational load, particularly during movement deceleration. This divergence arises because activation-derived muscle moments capture cocontraction, and thus impedance-related control, that is absent from net torques obtained by inverse dynamics. Gravity-dependent regression analyses further showed that muscle activation could be reconstructed from a compact set of mechanical variables dominated by gravity-dependent torque and movement velocity, revealing a low-dimensional structure of motor control. Together, these findings support a control architecture in which motor commands integrate predictive compensation for limb dynamics with gravity-dependent regulation of muscle cocontraction. This dual strategy provides a mechanism for maintaining stable and accurate movement across changing mechanical environments and offers a unified framework for understanding motor control under variable external loads.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: How 20th-century immigrants did not have to change their last names in order to become American
items.abstract: Reports of parents’ names in Social Security Application records allow us to quantify at a population level the extent and nature of historical last name changes by immigrants. Our analysis of European, Middle Eastern, and Asian immigrants of the early to mid-20th-century finds that more than 80% kept their last names. Computational linguistic analysis shows that most of those who did change preserved their surname’s ethnic signal, leaving only about 5% of all immigrants trying to disguise their foreign origins. Of these, Jewish immigrants had the highest rate of ethnicity-concealing last name changes; Italian, Japanese, and Chinese immigrants all had the lowest. Our proposed framework helps understand the variation: name changes were rarest where ethnic community networks were densest and where passing as unmarked was least credible—as among visibly non-White immigrants. Our findings challenge the dominant assimilationist narrative that immigrants in this era had to shed their foreign identities to enter the American mainstream. “Becoming White” by adopting an English surname was not a large part of historical immigrant experience. Rather, the overwhelming majority of immigrants chose to openly preserve their ethnic origins. Our results also suggest that nominal record linkage of historical immigrant populations may be more feasible than previously assumed.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Engineered T cell–agonist chimera for logic-gated STING activation and augmented cancer immunotherapy
items.abstract: The efficacy of adoptive T cell therapy against solid tumors is markedly hindered by the immunosuppressive microenvironment. Here, we demonstrate that stimulator of interferon genes (STING) activation in tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) enhances the intratumoral infiltration and cytotoxicity of adoptive T cells. We next design a TAM-targeted nanoagonist and engineer a T cell – agonist chimera (SNTC) via covalent surface anchoring, to achieve synchronized biodistribution of STING agonist with adoptive T cells. The nanoagonist is locally released in tumor tissue in response to the elevated reduction potential on T cell surface, followed by intracellular glutathione-mediated restoration of STING agonist in TAM, thereby enabling AND logic-gated STING activation. SNTC not only reshapes tumor stroma and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment to augment adoptive T cell function but also enhances the antigen presentation ability of TAM to activate endogenous T cells. SNTC elicits robust antitumor efficacy in melanoma tumor-bearing mice, resulting in over 40% survival beyond 60 d. Moreover, combining tumor-infiltrating T lymphocyte (TIL)-based SNTC with immune checkpoint blockade therapy leads to sustained tumor regression in mouse model of orthotopic pancreatic tumor. Collectively, SNTC holds translational potential to optimize STING activation for adoptive T cell therapy of cancer.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Senescent CD8 T effector memory cells are functionally impaired, enriched in aging and disease, and a barrier to immunotherapy
items.abstract: Senescent cells play important roles in various biological processes that promote fitness and health; however, their timely elimination by immune cells is critical to maintain tissue homeostasis and prevent disease. Despite this, senescent cells accumulate systemically with age, suggesting that certain immune cells also become senescent and dysfunctional during aging. In support of this, we previously demonstrated that CD8 T cells, immune cells capable of targeting senescent cells, increasingly develop characteristics of senescence with advancing age in humans. Here, we characterized the senescence state of human SA-βGal-expressing (SA-βGal high ) CD8 T effector memory (EM) cells, their functional capabilities, and their enrichment in aging and disease. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed that SA-βGal high CD8 T cells with unique transcriptional signatures develop in all stages of T cell differentiation, including in CD8 T EM cells, which increased in abundance with human aging. SA-βGal high CD8 T EM cells expressed various classical markers of senescence and were significantly impaired in their ability to proliferate, produce cytokines, and eliminate senescent human stromal cells. Gene signatures of senescent SA-βGal high CD8 T EM cells were enriched in CD8 T cells from older human donors, patients with age-related disorders, cancer, and in smokers. Furthermore, we show that T cell senescence is distinct from and dominant over T cell exhaustion, limiting the response of CD8 T EM cells to immune checkpoint blockade. Collectively, our study demonstrates that senescence impairs CD8 T EM cell function and reveals the involvement of senescent and dysfunctional CD8 T EM cells in aging, disease, smoking, and responses to immunotherapy.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Subcellular compartment determines signal dominance: Endosomal cAMP overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation from a single receptor
items.abstract: Cells convey information not only via the identity of activated signaling pathways but also through the subcellular location where those signals originate. Whether spatially distinct signals from a single activated receptor compete to determine net cellular output has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate this principle for a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), showing that endosomal and plasma membrane signals from a single activated receptor are not merely distinct but functionally opposed, with endosomal signaling predominating to reverse the net cellular output. Using the adhesion GPCR GPR64/ADGRG2 as a model system, we show that ligand activation engages two spatially distinct G-protein pathways that are not just additive but functionally opposed: plasma membrane G 13 /RhoA activation and Gs/cAMP production that persists from endosomes following receptor internalization. The endosomal cAMP pool actively overrides concurrent plasma membrane RhoA activation, resulting in net RhoA inactivation, an outcome that is completely reversed by pharmacological blockade of endocytosis or endosomal G s inactivation. In parathyroid cells, where GPR64 is highly expressed, this endosomal signal dominance suppresses parathyroid hormone secretion independently of extracellular Ca 2+ levels. These findings support a model in which the subcellular compartment, rather than pathway identity, determines the dominant signal and the overall cellular response of a single activated receptor, with implications for understanding the complexity of GPCR signaling.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Cooling fast and slow: Characterizing the effects of vitrification in cryo-EM and the subsequent recovery of equilibrium populations
items.abstract: Single-particle cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM), a powerful class of techniques in structural biology with the potential to resolve molecular ensembles, requires that samples be vitrified to protect them from the high vacuum of the electron microscope. However, the effects of vitrification on biomolecular ensembles are unknown. To study them, we carried out extensive molecular dynamics simulations (over 50 ms) of the Trp-cage miniprotein at equilibrium and undergoing rapid cooling. We simulated seven cooling rates spanning three orders of magnitude, with the slowest coolings matching experimental rates. By inspecting molecular mobility and density-temperature trajectories for water with and without protein, we found that water vitrification is unaltered by the protein. To track protein conformation changes, and to relate them to kinetics, we made a Markov State Model (MSM) of Trp-cage from 5.4 ms of equilibrium sampling at 277 K. We observed that MSM states with a characteristic time longer than the duration of the nonequilibrium cooling tend to be more robust to artifacts induced by such cooling. Critically, although we observe that some states vanish in the equilibrium ensemble at 230 K, none do in our nonequilibrium cooled ensembles. To account for these perturbations, we developed a thermodynamic inference framework for recovering equilibrium populations from vitrified ensembles. These results indicate that cryo-EM has the capacity to be an accurate technique for the study of biomolecular ensembles.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Rapid target engagement of KRAS G12C tricomplex inhibitor RO3903 overcomes resistance and drives durable tumor regression
items.abstract: The clinical durability of first-generation KRAS G12C inhibitors is constrained by resistance mechanisms, primarily the rapid, receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK)-mediated reactivation of KRAS to its drug-insensitive, guanosine triphosphate (GTP)-bound (ON) state. Here, we perform a systematic comparative characterization of clinical and investigational KRAS G12C inhibitors, including Sotorasib, Adagrasib, Divarasib, and Elironrasib, and our structurally optimized tricomplex ON inhibitor, RO7783903 (RO3903). We demonstrate that the covalent tricomplex inhibitors RO3903 and Elironrasib effectively outpace dynamic nucleotide cycling, conferring resilience to potent RTK stimulation and overcoming the secondary KRAS mutations that drive clinical resistance to guanosine diphosphate (GDP)-bound (OFF) state inhibitors. Notably, RO3903 potently inhibits tumor growth in a dose-dependent manner across multiple preclinical models, including an orthotopic intracranial model. Furthermore, RO3903 exhibits synergistic efficacy when combined with inhibitors targeting OFF-state KRAS G12C, YAP-TEAD, EGFR/MET, or FAK, as well as with anti-PD1 antibody and anti-PD1/VEGF bispecific antibody immunotherapies. The high potency, fast target engagement, and brain tumor inhibition of RO3903 position this molecule as a valuable tool reagent and a promising partner for combination strategies to achieve durable tumor regression.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Geochemical signatures of magnetite are conserved in diverse populations of environmental magnetotactic bacteria
items.abstract: Magnetotactic bacteria (MTB) synthesize intracellular magnetite nanoparticles in a genetically controlled manner. They may represent some of the earliest biomineralizing organisms on Earth, and a unique window into ancient life and the environments that hosted it. Yet, identification of their mineralogical remains in ancient rocks is highly challenging due to the lack of reliable and lasting proxies. Previous results obtained from laboratory cultures of single strains of MTB revealed trace element and Fe isotope patterns that are not shared by any other source of magnetite, which could be used as reliable proxies for the identification of ancient MTB. However, the environmental relevance of these previous findings for environmental and mixed population of MTB is unknown. We report the trace element and Fe isotope compositions of magnetite extracted from environmental MTB collected in the water column of Lake Pavin, France, and show that the most distinctive geochemical traits (enrichment in Mo, Se, Sn, and light Fe isotopes) of magnetite produced by MTB cultivated in the laboratory are conserved in environmental populations. They represent potential biological signatures that can be searched in ancient rocks and coupled with magnetic and mineralogical tracers to support the presence of MTB and reconstruct their emergence and evolution.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Thermodynamic stabilization of substrate protein within the GroEL:ES chaperonin cage
items.abstract: The adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-regulated GroEL/ES chaperonin of Escherichia coli promotes protein folding by transiently encapsulating unfolded substrate protein in a nano-cage formed by the cylindrical GroEL and the lid-shaped GroES. How this confinement modulates the folding energy landscape, allowing accelerated protein folding unimpaired by aggregation, remains incompletely understood. Prompted by recent observations suggesting that the chaperonin cavity may favor unfolding [I. Korobko et al. , Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 119 , e2213170119 (2022)], here we reinvestigated the effect of encapsulation on protein thermodynamic stability. To allow thermal unfolding of an encapsulated substrate protein, we generated a destabilized variant of maltose-binding protein (MBP) by introducing four mutations, quadruple mutant-MBP (QM-MBP), lowering the melting temperature ( T m ) from 63.6 °C to 44.3 °C. GroEL/ES accelerated the slow spontaneous folding of QM-MBP ~20-fold. The protein reached a native-like structure while encapsulated inside GroEL:ES, as demonstrated using hydrogen/deuterium exchange and single molecule fluorescence resonance energy transfer analyses in presence and absence of the ligand maltose. Importantly, confinement in the thermally stable chaperonin shifted the cooperative unfolding transition of QM-MBP to a T m of 52.4 °C, corresponding to a stabilization by 4.6 kcal mol −1 . In-cage thermal unfolding was reversible, indicating that the environment of the chaperonin cavity is conducive to folding. These findings suggest that a thermodynamically stabilizing effect of the GroEL:ES cage contributes to promoting protein folding.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Unpacking transatlantic income inequality
items.abstract: This paper uses newly harmonized survey and register data on incomes and labor market outcomes as the basis for consistent comparisons of inequalities across 17 North American and European countries over the period 1995–2021. We examine trends in disposable income inequality in the working-age population, defined as persons aged 25 to 60, as well as its component parts of market income inequality and redistribution through government tax and transfer systems. We adjust incomes to allow for changes in education, population aging, and household structure in each country. We test for convergence across countries in demographically-adjusted disposable income inequality, along with market income inequality and redistribution. There is strong evidence of convergence over time in disposable income inequality across the 17 countries, despite a divergence in the dispersion of market income inequality driven by very heterogeneous trends for hours of work and the number of workers in households across countries. Consistent with this we find a strong convergence across countries in the dispersion of our measure of redistribution. There are reductions over time in inequality-reducing redistribution in the Nordic countries and increases in some other European and North American countries, with the net effect being more similarity across countries, a lower average level of redistribution, and a higher average level of disposable income inequality. These trends are being driven by the bottom 95% of the income distribution. Our results are robust to a variety of alternative specifications including the measure of inequality, trimming of data outliers, and sample period.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Core effectors of the Fusarium pan-effectome contribute to host specificity
items.abstract: Fusarium fungi cause economically important diseases of cereal crops, including Fusarium head blight, ear blight, and root rot. Central to these interactions are secreted effector proteins that manipulate host biology to promote infection. In turn, plants have evolved to recognize effector activity to activate immune responses and restrict disease. Despite their importance, the diversity, conservation, and evolution of Fusarium effectors remain poorly understood. Here, we present the Fusarium sambucinum Species complex Effector Compendium (FUSEC), a sequence-defined pan-effectome constructed from 188 high-quality genomes representing 27 species. FUSEC comprises 4,057 sequence-defined effector families, including a conserved soft-core repertoire of 235 families present in at least 95% of isolates. Structure-guided comparisons reorganized these conserved families into 184 structure-defined groups, revealing relationships that extend beyond sequence similarity and identifying similarities to numerous experimentally characterized fungal (a)virulence factors. Despite their broad conservation, soft-core families exhibited substantial within-family sequence diversity, and analyses of diversifying selection identified 44 candidate families undergoing adaptive evolution. Functional screening revealed that the majority of these candidates altered wheat immune responses, and CRISPR-Cas9-mediated gene deletions in Fusarium graminearum demonstrated that multiple conserved effectors contribute to cultivar-dependent Fusarium head blight severity.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Rising cell-free DNA level tracks cancer-associated methylation signal and improves multicancer detection
items.abstract: Cancer patients carry more circulating cell-free DNA (ccfDNA)—small DNA fragments shed into the blood—than healthy people. Most of this excess comes not from the tumor itself but from immune cells, suggesting that it would simply dilute the much smaller amount of tumor-derived DNA in a blood sample. Using a study of 1,480 previously untreated participants across 43 hospitals—including patients with 14 cancer types spanning all stages, patients with benign growths, and healthy volunteers—we show the opposite: as total ccfDNA rises, it becomes enriched, not diluted, in fragments carrying cancer-associated DNA methylation signatures, independent of cancer type, disease stage, and a broad panel of demographic, clinical, and technical covariates. In fact, total ccfDNA explains more variance in cancer-associated methylation signal than the disease stage itself. This basic biological finding suggests a coupling between immune cell activity and tumor methylation. It also has a practical implication: we show that rising ccfDNA concentration is associated with higher cancer detection sensitivity, even within disease stages and particularly in early-stage disease—stage I sensitivity varied from 0.55 in the lowest ccfDNA concentration tertile to 0.85 in the highest, and stage II from 0.59 to 0.86. This suggests that ccfDNA concentration should be considered as a stage-independent stratification variable for benchmarking cancer-detection tests. Interestingly, similar behavior was observed in patients with symptomatic benign lesions, suggesting a broader biological response to abnormal tissue growth and not something unique to malignancy.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Extracellular polymeric substances drive Curvibacter host adaptation and cospeciation with Hydra
items.abstract: The interactions between hosts and their microbial symbionts play a crucial role to host physiology. Bacteria can adapt to specific host environments over evolutionary timescales, leading to cospeciation and the formation of specialized host–microbe relationships. Understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying these adaptations provides key insights into the evolution of symbiosis and the stability of microbial communities. This study investigates the cospeciation and molecular adaptations of Curvibacter to its host Hydra , a well-established model for the study of host–microbe interactions. We provide strong evidence of cospeciation, as demonstrated by phylogenetic congruence between different Hydra species and their corresponding Curvibacter symbionts, along with preferential recolonization of germ-free Hydra by their native Curvibacter strains. Comparative genomic analyses reveal that host-associated Curvibacter strains exhibit distinct metabolic and biosynthetic adaptations compared to their free-living relatives. Specifically, the enrichment of proteins linked to host glycan interactions, extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), DNA metabolic processes, ABC transport, sugar metabolism, and bacterial chemotaxis highlights specialized adaptations of Curvibacter symbionts within the Hydra glycocalyx. Importantly, some of these signatures are only detectable within the Hydra vulgaris -associated Curvibacter subgroup, emphasizing the need to examine host-specific adaptations at a finer taxonomic resolution. Functional experiments identify a symbiont-specific EPS operon as a factor for host colonization, thereby establishing its role in facilitating symbiont specificity and stability.
