items.title: Mechanism of catalytic regulation by an allosteric hot spot in dihydrofolate reductase
items.abstract: Allostery is central to catalysis and regulation, yet how distal perturbations control enzyme activity remains unresolved. Here we elucidate how a distal allosteric hot spot regulates catalysis in dihydrofolate reductase, a benchmark enzyme exhibiting latent allostery. We combine enhanced conformational sampling, reactive free-energy calculations of the chemical step, and perturbation-induced nonequilibrium molecular dynamics with evolutionary analysis and experimental kinetics to obtain a comprehensive molecular description of conformational landscapes, catalytic activity, and allosteric communication. We show that a mutational perturbation at the hot spot redistributes the populations of two globally similar conformations with a subtle but critical structural difference that makes one catalytically competent and the other not. Nonequilibrium relaxation simulations further reveal that the transition between these two states in the mutant proceeds through a stepwise sequence of local structural rearrangements rather than a concerted global motion. Guided by this mechanism, we rationally engineer a compensatory second-site mutation that partially restores activity. These results provide a unified thermodynamic and kinetic view of allostery and establish a general, mechanistically guided framework for engineering allosteric regulation in enzymes.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Origami state machine with time-varying magnetic fields
items.abstract: Achieving reliable, remote control over multiple stable states in modular systems remains a challenge due to the coupling between modules and history-dependent transitions. Here, we present magnetic origami state machines that enable deterministic navigation from any unknown initial state to any target state under magnetic actuation. By assuming mutually distinct energy barriers in modular Kresling origami assemblies, we realize fully accessible transition graphs with scalable state spaces. Guided by the graph associated to the state machine, a rotating magnetic field induces a universal reset that autonomously drives the system to a known equilibrium state from arbitrary states without sensing or feedback, while pulsed magnetic inputs further enable programmable transitions to any target state via prescribed actuation sequences. A reduced-order Lagrangian mechanics model predicts snap-through dynamics across reset, stepwise programming (between graph nodes), and shortcuts (by adapting pulse magnitude and orientation) where inertia triggers simultaneous multicell transitions with a single pulse. These results establish a general framework for programmable magneto-mechanical state machines with autonomous state reset and full state-space control.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Multiscale Brownian dynamics simulations reveal effects of macromolecular crowding on protein–ligand association
items.abstract: Macromolecular crowding is known to influence the diffusive, binding, kinetic, and equilibrium properties of proteins in a range of environments such as occur inside biological cells or in highly concentrated solutions of protein therapeutics. However a quantitative understanding of the effects of macromolecular crowding on the rates of protein-small molecule binding is lacking. Here, we present an adaptive model to simulate the association of two solutes in a macromolecularly crowded environment using Brownian dynamics and to compute the corresponding bimolecular association rate constant. The adaptive model represents interactions with atomistic detail for short-range crowder–noncrowder interactions, while using a coarse-grained approach for long-range crowder–noncrowder interactions and all crowder–crowder interactions. This multiscale approach is integrated in the Simulation of Diffusional Association (SDA) software for Brownian dynamics simulation of biomolecular diffusion. We applied this model to compute the rates of association for two contrasting protein-small molecule inhibitor complexes in environments varying in macromolecular crowder type and density, and we used Markov State modeling of the encounter trajectories to analyze the binding pathways. The results reveal competing effects: While the presence of the crowders can hinder ligand binding by reducing the translational diffusion rates of the solutes and obstructing the protein binding sites, crowders can also enhance the bimolecular association rate by other mechanisms, including channeling and the caging effect.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: HAR1 receptor kinase links nodule autoregulation with repression of auxin signaling and lateral root development
items.abstract: Nitrogen-fixing root nodules develop as lateral organs on legume roots and their formation is restricted by autoregulation of nodulation (AON), a systemic mechanism with unclear evolutionary origins. We identify Lotus japonicus NUCLEAR FACTOR Y subunit A4 ( NF-YA4 ) gene as a central target of the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase HAR1, which controls both AON and root system architecture. Under nonsymbiotic conditions, HAR1 suppresses expression of NF-YA4 and its close paralog NF-YA1 , at least in part through a miR169-dependent mechanism, mirroring the Arabidopsis CLAVATA1/2-miR169- NF-YA module. Loss of HAR1 leads to NF-YA4 overexpression, broad transcriptional reprogramming, and induction of LATERAL ORGAN BOUNDARIES DOMAIN , STYLISH , and YUCCA auxin biosynthesis genes, enhancing auxin signaling and lateral root development. Grafting experiments show that HAR1 constrains NF-YA4 -mediated branching both locally in roots and systemically from shoots. Because NF-YA4 functions partly redundantly with NF-YA1 to mediate nodule emergence, our results suggest a model in which duplication and neofunctionalization of an ancestral NF-YA-dependent pathway controlling lateral root development facilitated its recruitment to the nodulation program. They also raise the possibility that AON could have evolved, at least in part, through the co-option of a LRR-RK/miR169/ NF-YA regulatory module that limited lateral root development.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: In-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling
items.abstract: Constitutive modeling is fundamental to computational solid mechanics, yet most existing approaches remain material-specific and require retraining or recalibration when materials change. Here we introduce In-Context Modeling (ICM), a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling that infers constitutive behavior from physical context rather than material-specific optimization. Using hyperelasticity as a testbed, we demonstrate that ICM can be trained once on equilibrium deformation fields spanning diverse materials, geometries, and boundary conditions, enforcing physical equilibrium without stress labels. After training, the same model can be directly deployed on previously unseen hyperelastic materials without retraining. At inference, ICM treats a small set of nonuniform strain fields as physical context to generate constitutive response in a single forward pass. Numerical benchmarks and experimental validation demonstrate accurate stress prediction across out-of-distribution materials and boundary-value problems, together with substantial reductions in deployment cost compared with per-material learning approaches. These results establish in-context learning as a retraining-free paradigm for constitutive modeling, particularly valuable for heterogeneous biological tissues such as the brain, and suggest a pathway toward foundation models for computational mechanics.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Structural basis of glycoprotein recognition by the human folding sensor UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase
items.abstract: UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGGT1) plays a central role in quality control of glycoprotein folding within the early secretory pathway, yet the molecular basis of UGGT1 substrate recognition remains poorly understood. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of human full-length multidomain UGGT1. Monomeric UGGT1 structures reveal two conformational states corresponding to “open” and “closed” architectures. Three-dimensional variability and molecular dynamics simulations suggest the existence of intermediate conformations, leading to a model in which a continuum of structural transitions underlies UGGT1 function. Notably, in the open state, the EM-maps reveal at the top of the U-shaped protein a density that bridges the sensory TRXL2 and the glucosyltransferase catalytic domains, consistent with substrate association. This observation supports a mode of binding that places the substrate near the catalytic domain. A dimeric form of UGGT1 was observed in which the glycoprotein substrate binding sites are occluded, suggesting that dimerization may regulate UGGT1 activity. To better understand the spatial relationship between the site of misfolding and that of UGGT-mediated N-glycan reglucosylation, we identified N-glycosylation sites on endogenous glycoprotein substrates by glycoproteomics. No consensus sequence was found flanking modified sites, indicating that substrate recognition relies on mechanisms beyond primary sequence. Mutations in the UGGT1 gene cause a novel congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, and the human UGGT1 structure helps explain how disease-associated missense and deletion variants disrupt function. Together, our data provide insight into the relationship between UGGT1 structure and function, integrating enzyme conformational states with client glycoprotein interaction and processing.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Deep mutational scanning of the GPCR rhodopsin reveals pleiotropic mutational effects and their roles in modulating receptor signaling
items.abstract: Biophysical pleiotropy, the phenomenon in which a mutation affects multiple protein properties, underlies many genetic diseases and shapes protein evolution, yet remains poorly understood, limiting synthetic biology and therapeutic development. Although extensively studied in soluble proteins, little is known about how pleiotropic effects shaped the evolution of receptor protein functions. Here, we developed a cell-based assay designed to assess pleiotropic effects in G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs), the largest receptor class in eukaryotes. Because our assay allows for multiple GPCR molecular phenotypes (basal activity, ligand-dependent signaling, and cellular receptor abundance) to be simultaneously assessed, we applied it to study rhodopsin, a visual GPCR that evolved for high phototransduction capabilities by maximizing light-driven responses while minimizing noise. To investigate this, we integrated our assay with deep mutational scanning to test the impacts of ~2,000 single-residue substitutions in rhodopsin across all three molecular phenotypes (~6,000 measurements). By analyzing these data in the context of rhodopsin’s protein structures, we found complex pleiotropic effects that act asymmetrically to impose joint constraints, restricting mutational tolerance in rhodopsin’s retinal binding pocket and G protein interaction interface. A dose–response analysis of rhodopsin signaling revealed that these pleiotropic constraints arise from the dual functions of its chromophore, which acts as an agonist upon light-driven isomerization but also an inverse agonist in darkness. Because these constraints reflect mechanistically driven limitations in the evolution of receptor signaling, these findings reveal a role for biophysical pleiotropy in shaping the signaling capabilities of receptor proteins.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Ddx3x deficiency in mice impairs corticofugal motor circuits and causes motor deficits that are attenuated by early-life exercise
items.abstract: The X-linked RNA helicase DDX3X is a high-risk gene for autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disability primarily in females. Individuals with pathogenic variants in DDX3X have pervasive and often severe motor manifestations. Using mouse models, we studied the circuits underlying the motor phenotypes associated with Ddx3x deficiency and examined the feasibility of an early intervention to ameliorate motor trajectories. We show that Ddx3x controls both the development and later plasticity of motor circuits connecting the motor cortex with the pontine nuclei. Ddx3x haploinsufficiency during development affects the dendritic arborization of corticopontine neurons. Juvenile-onset Ddx3x loss in corticopontine neurons is sufficient to induce adult motor impairments overlapping with those caused by chemogenetic disruption of corticopontine circuits. Further, Ddx3x mutant mice engage corticopontine circuits in skilled motor tasks in a sex-dependent manner. Last, Ddx3x haploinsufficient female mice undergoing a juvenile motor intervention show long-lasting specific benefits in their adult motor function. Together, these findings establish Ddx3x as an essential regulator of corticopontine neuron development and function and provide an early motor intervention to ameliorate motor outcomes in a mouse model of DDX3X haploinsufficiency.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Crowding limits relative bacterial surface accumulation with density-induced effective heating
items.abstract: The accumulation of microswimmers near walls has been studied for decades. While hydrodynamics and single-cell kinematics are well-explored, the role of cell-cell interactions remains understudied. However, in realistic, crowded environments such as the human gut, these interactions can be just as crucial. Here, we demonstrate that they actively weaken bacterial surface accumulation. Analysis of entrapped cell tracks reveals that crowding enhances orientational fluctuations, which increase the effective rotational diffusion and facilitate wall escape. A minimal model shows that this collective effect is equivalent to raising the system’s effective temperature with density.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Potential energy landscape networks of confined vortex matter
items.abstract: Advances in nanoscale patterning of superconducting films [Y. L. Wang et al ., Nat. Nanotechnol. 13 , 560–565 (2018)] and the availability of submicron-sized superconducting single crystals with controlled geometry allow for the investigation of superconducting vortex matter under extreme confinement [A. K. Geim et al ., Nature 390 , 259–262 (1997)]. It has been observed in these systems that the interplay between sample geometry and vortex number results in the emergence of so-called “magic number” configurations which show unusually high stability against thermal fluctuations. However, a detailed, comprehensive theoretical study of the ground state and metastable states of confined vortex matter has not yet been developed. Here we show that the intricate properties of a system of vortices under extreme confinement can be characterized in detail by mapping the potential energy landscape of the system onto a network [J. P. K. Doye, Phys. Rev. Lett. 88 , 238701 (2002)] with nodes corresponding to local potential energy minima and edges to transition states between local minima. We apply these techniques to systems featuring repelling particles/vortices confined in small containers of various geometric shapes. We demonstrate that the ground state almost always belongs to a subset of system states within the deepest network core. We find that the emergence of magic number configurations in the ground state results in a drastic decrease in the complexity of the entire network. We use large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to study the size dependence of melting in different configurations. We find that as confinement effects increase, magic number configurations transition to states with lower symmetry.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Intrinsic function of leptin receptor–regulated endothelial PD-L1
items.abstract: Programmed cell death ligand-1 (PD-L1) is an immune checkpoint protein expressed in vascular endothelial cells (ECs). In contrast to cancer, our understanding of endothelial PD-L1 in relation to metabolic syndromes and its vascular complications is less studied. For example, its regulation and intrinsic function remain unclear. Here, we showed that endothelial PD-L1 is regulated by leptin receptor signaling in male mice. In particular, endothelial PD-L1 expression is affected by leptin resistance. A lack of leptin receptors leads to PD-L1 downregulation in vascular ECs via posttranslational degradation. To understand the fundamental roles of endothelial PD-L1, RNA interference and selective knockout are employed in human endothelium and animals, respectively. Silencing or deleting endothelial PD-L1 expression delays cell cycle progression and proliferation due to rat sarcoma (RAS)/mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) inactivation. In obesity, endothelial PD-L1 deficiency impairs the EC turnover and worsens the vascular function. Overall, we provide an insight into how endothelial PD-L1 contributes to vascular homeostasis, suggesting its pathophysiological importance in maintaining cellular turnover.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: The efficiency of information gain by natural selection
items.abstract: Natural selection enriches populations for genotypes that are well adapted to their environments, accumulating information about the selective conditions in the process. Therefore, selection can be viewed as a learning process through which populations acquire information about the environment. Motoo Kimura derived a relationship between the amount of information gained by selection and a measure of the inefficiency of the selective process, known as substitution load [M. Kimura, Genet. Res. 2, 127–140 (1961)]. Due to the gradual nature of selection and the ongoing mismatch of types to the environment, a lineage that is still acquiring information has lower mean fitness than a lineage that already has it. While this has been an influential insight, we find that Kimura’s model is inconsistent with selection experiments involving Escherichia coli . To address limitations in this model and develop a more robust measure for the efficiency of selection, we turn to computational learning theory. We show that the learning-theoretic concept of regret quantifies the inefficiency of selection as a learning process in terms of relative lineage fitness. We establish bounds on the efficiency of information gain in general settings, including frequency-dependent selection and arbitrary environmental change. We experimentally validate these bounds and demonstrate that our extended theory recovers Kimura’s fundamental insight. Finally, we show that selection is an asymptotically optimal algorithm for the basic problem faced by evolving populations and that it acquires information more efficiently than comparable processes in complex environments.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Direct atomic-scale observation reveals rare earth element fractionation at mineral–water interfaces
items.abstract: Clay minerals, ubiquitous across diverse geological systems, exert fundamental controls on critical geochemical processes, particularly through their adsorptive interactions with economically vital elements such as heavy rare earth elements (HREEs). The adsorption of HREEs onto clay surfaces is not only the key process that enriches these critical resources but also a potential archive for dating significant weathering events. However, the atomic-scale mechanisms governing the preferential adsorption and fractionation of rare earth elements (REEs) at mineral–water interfaces have remained poorly constrained. Here, employing in situ atomic-scale imaging via high-resolution atomic force microscopy, we systematically investigate the adsorption behaviors of light and heavy REEs (La, Y, Yb) onto key crystallographic planes—Si-basal, Al-basal, and edge terminations—of representative clay minerals (kaolinite, illite, mica) under environmentally relevant conditions (pH 4.8 to 6.4). We directly visualize and quantitatively reveal that Si-basal planes selectively enrich HREEs with pH-enhanced adsorption capacity, whereas Al-basal planes exhibit negligible REE adsorption below pH 5.8 but preferential HREE adsorption at pH 6.4. Integrating synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, we identify the adsorption mechanism of REE on Si-basal and Al-basal/edge planes as outer-sphere complexation and inner-sphere binding, respectively. Furthermore, we quantify the contributions of distinct planes via surface complexation modeling, revealing Si-dominated to Al- and edge-controlled adsorption with elevating pH. These atomic-scale findings not only resolve long-standing debates about clay mineral-mediated REE fractionation but also redefine fundamental paradigms of surface reactivity at silicate mineral–water interfaces, offering insights into the cycling and metallogeny of other critical metals in aqueous and sedimentary environments.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Computation and sampling for Schubert specializations
items.abstract: We study a problem at the interface of enumerative algebraic geometry, algebraic combinatorics, and the statistical mechanics of vertex models with long-range interactions. We develop methods to explore the values S w ( 1 , … , 1 ) of Schubert polynomials (called principal specializations), which count reduced bumpless pipe dreams (RBPDs) with boundary permutation w ∈ S n . We exhibit counterexamples to the conjecture of Merzon and Smirnov that S w ( 1 n ) is maximized on layered permutations; the smallest such example we find is at n = 17. Despite the counterexamples, we present bounds that support a refined conjecture that the maximum of S w ( 1 n ) over all w ∈ S n grows at the same asymptotic rate as the maximum over layered permutations (found by Morales, Pak, and Panova). We implement and benchmark four recurrences for Schubert specializations: the descent formula of Macdonald, the transition formula of Lascoux–Schützenberger, the cotransition formula of Knutson, and the formula of Billey, Jockusch, and Stanley. We also explore typical random permutations drawn with probability proportional to S w ( 1 n ) , equivalently from uniformly random RBPDs. Our simulations reveal a permuton-like limit analogous to the Grothendieck setting studied by Morales, Panova, Petrov, and Yeliussizov. For sampling, we show that the standard monotone Coupling From The Past framework does not apply to RBPDs, leaving exact uniform sampling open. To bypass this, we develop an efficient Markov chain Monte Carlo sampler augmented with macroscopic “droop” updates that preserve connectivity and accelerate mixing. Our publicly available fast implementations reach n = 20 for exact computation of S w ( 1 n ) and n = 100 for Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling using a chain whose stationary distribution is uniform on RBPDs (run on a cluster).
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Elucidating molecular regulatory rules of nanoparticle biological identity via standardized deep proteomics
items.abstract: The biological identity of nanoparticles is often redefined upon exposure to physiological fluids through the formation of a protein corona (PC), However, the molecular rules linking synthetic design to biological fate remain elusive owing to the fragmented and inconsistent proteomics data. Here, leveraging a standardized deep proteomic database of 42 diverse nanomaterials, we reveal the general molecular selection rules that govern the PC formation. We demonstrate that the PC is not a product of random adsorption but is shaped by strict property-dependent recruitment. First, surface charge regulates cellular uptake, with anionic nanoparticles specifically recruiting adhesion proteins to promote Itgav-mediated endocytosis, thus forming a causal charge-corona-receptor chain. Second, PEGylation engineers immune evasion by selectively depleting specific complement and coagulation factors, rather than merely preventing protein adsorption. Third, nanoparticle geometry imposes structural constraints and selects proteins based on specific physicochemical features such as lysine content. Beyond mechanistic insights, we show that material-specific PCs can rebalance the serum proteome and enable the detection of low-abundance disease biomarkers. This work shifts the paradigm from empirical description toward rule-based prediction and provides a foundational framework for rationally engineering nanomedicines with predictable and programmable biological identities.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: A sulfotyrosine motif in the human TrkB extracellular domain is required for activation by the agonist antibody ZEB85
items.abstract: The brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)-tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB) signaling axis is a key effector of synaptic plasticity and neuroprotection. While TrkB activation is a major target to prevent neural dysfunction, stimulation with exogenous BDNF administration has not proven tractable given the unfavorable physiochemical properties of BDNF. In addition, BDNF also activates a cell death pathway by binding to the neurotrophin receptor p75. The TrkB agonist antibody ZEB85 provides an alternative route to the selective activation of TrkB. To understand the ZEB85 mechanism of action, we mapped the binding site for ZEB85 to the TrkB extracellular juxtamembrane domain and found a sulfotyrosine modification at residue 400 crucial for ZEB85 interaction and activation of TrkB signaling. We determined the structures of ZEB85 and BDNF bound to their respective binding sites on human TrkB suggesting independent sites for each ligand, despite prior evidence of direct competition. Using structure-guided BDNF- and ZEB85-binding deficient TrkB mutants, we assessed their ability to sequester ligands from full-length TrkB in cultured human neurons. We found that the BDNF binding site extends into the juxtamembrane domain of TrkB but does not require the sulfotyrosine 400 to activate TrkB. Together with biophysical analysis and AlphaFold modeling, these results explain how BDNF can displace ZEB85 from TrkB through an overlapping epitope. Our findings reveal unique features of TrkB, not present in the related neurotrophin receptors TrkA and TrkC and suggest future directions to explore the role of sulfotyrosine in TrkB signaling.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: A chemomechanical bifurcation landscape unifies sustained growth, length homeostasis, and regenerative collapse in axons
items.abstract: Axonal growth machinery is largely shared across neurons, but axons exhibit strikingly different fates depending on developmental and environmental context: sustained elongation in peripheral neurons under permissive conditions, length homeostasis in cortical neurons after target innervation, and pathological collapse into dystrophic endbulbs in injured adult central nervous system (CNS) axons. These divergent outcomes have resisted explanation by length-sensing and biomechanical models that treat long-range transport and local force generation as separate problems. We unify these phenomena through a mechanochemical model that couples bidirectional motor transport and intracellular signaling to growth-cone balance of axonal tension, actomyosin contraction, and adhesion within a single feedback loop: The lengthening axon uses its own growing transport delay to establish self-limiting mechanical feedback, as the accumulating delay reshapes signaling waveforms to progressively elevate myosin contractility against actin-driven protrusion. Two physical parameters, the transport delay and the signaling feedback strength, organize axon fate into a unified state-space landscape spanning sustained growth, length homeostasis, and pathological collapse. Reduced feedback strength weakens this self-limiting mechanical feedback by simultaneously enhancing protrusion and suppressing contractility, providing a mechanistic interpretation of axon lengthening under partial reduction of retrograde transport. Bistability in the inhibitory regime explains why mature CNS tracts persist where nascent sprouts collapse, recasting regenerative failure as a state-dependent gate rather than a capacity limit. The framework predicts that partial rather than complete inhibition of retrograde transport could shift collapsed axons across the bifurcation into a growth-permissive regime, identifying a class of interventions complementary to existing capacity-restoration strategies for nerve injury.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Global bee bioregions mirror those of other taxa despite a uniquely bimodal latitudinal diversity gradient
items.abstract: Bioregionalization, the partitioning of the globe into areas of biotic similarity, is one of nature’s most striking patterns, and highly congruent boundaries have been identified across plants, tetrapods, ants, and butterflies. However, these taxa also share a unimodal latitudinal diversity gradient (LDG), raising the question of whether bioregionalization and the LDG are mechanistically coupled or instead arise from largely independent processes acting on different timescales. Bees (Hymenoptera: Anthophila) provide a natural test, their diversity peaking at mid-latitudes rather than in the tropics. Using range estimates for 3,370 species and a phylogenetic beta-diversity framework, we recover 21 bee bioregions nested within at least six major realms (Australasia, Indomalaya-Oceania, Nearctic, Neotropics, Palearctic, and Sub-Sahara) that closely align with those of other taxa despite bees’ atypical diversity gradient. We propose that bioregionalization and species richness are decoupled because they arise from distinct processes: the former reflects historical dispersal and evolutionary history, the latter local diversification, extinction, and environmental filtering. Our analysis provides a global biogeographic framework for future bee research and highlights the processes shaping the world‘s major biogeographic boundaries.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: A symbiogenic merger enabled by oxygen initiated the evolution of eukaryotes
items.abstract: Recently, extensive genetic information about archaeal hosts at the basis of eukaryogenesis has come to light. Characterization of these first eukaryotic common ancestor (FECA) related organisms allows improved understanding of the enigmatic FECA to last eukaryotic common ancestor (LECA) transition. However, these gene-centered discoveries have the unfortunate side effect of entrenching erroneous ideas about early eukaryotic evolution. This is apparent in the two-Domain vision of life, with eukaryotes seen as specialized Asgard archaea, while underestimating the contribution of the endosymbiont to eukaryogenesis. Establishment of the alpha-proteobacterium as the future mitochondrion is treated as one of many such endosymbiotic occurrences, ignoring its unique evolutionary position. I will marshal evidence for symbiogenic mechanisms involved in the FECA to LECA transition, with a key role for the endosymbiont’s electron transport chain and its acceptor molecular oxygen, especially in the incarnation of reactive oxygen species occurring in the host cytoplasm. We should overcome overestimating gene determinism, while not sufficiently allowing for effects of biological hierarchies, emergent properties, and chance. Many eukaryotic properties are best understood by envisaging the crucial uptake of the future mitochondrion as a merger instead of an acquisition. This merger is characterized by a new kind of elaborate cellular entity emerging as a result of rapid coevolution, replacing a scenario in which already complex pre-eukaryotes acquired endosymbionts, accompanied by important, but limited, changes. Successful mergers are rare because they are intrinsically more difficult, but synergistically open up completely new areas of possibilities, as illustrated by incredible eukaryotic success.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: The ABCD hypothesis
items.abstract: If α and β are cardinals, then the cardinal exponentiation α β is the set of all functions from α into β . The ABCD hypothesis is the statement that for all infinite cardinals α ≤ β and γ ≤ δ , | α β | ≤ | γ δ | if and only if α ≤ γ and β ≤ δ . The Axiom of Determinacy, AD, states that every two-player infinite game on ω has a winning strategy for one of the two players. Let Θ be the supremum of the ordinals onto which R surjects. This paper will show that if AD holds and V = L ( R ) , then the ABCD hypothesis holds below Θ .
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Hydration at the base of the mantle transition zone by ancient subductions in Asia
items.abstract: Whether and how the subduction processes result in water enrichment at the base of the mantle transition zone (MTZ) remain elusive. The major orogenic belts of the Asian continent, including the Central Asian, Tethyan, and Alpine–Himalayan belts, which record extensive subduction processes, offer an ideal target to address the hydration of the MTZ and its relationship with subduction. Here, we map water content at the MTZ base by combining mineral physics constraints on hydrous pyrolite and global seismic observations of velocity structure and 660-km discontinuity topography. Our results indicate an average global water content of approximately 0.14 wt%, with pronounced hydration anomalies in parts of Asia. Linking these anomalies with reconstructions of past subduction events since 410 Ma reveals extensive water delivery to the MTZ, particularly beneath parts of the Mongol–Okhotsk suture zone, the Central Asian Orogenic Belt, and the Tethyan orogenic domain, where water content exceeds 0.5 wt%. These results connect ancient subduction history to present-day mantle hydration, offering insights into Earth’s deep water cycle.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Complexity functions of infinite sequences
items.abstract: We address the inverse problem for complexity functions of infinite words, which asks which functions can occur as complexity functions of infinite words. We survey our recent advances on this problem and several of its ramifications. We describe an asymptotic solution to the inverse problem, realizing every function satisfying two necessary conditions as the complexity function of an infinite word up to asymptotic equivalence. We then turn to phenomena beyond asymptotic equivalence, presenting constructions of infinite words with seemingly contradictory behavior of the discrete derivatives of their complexity functions. These lead to a solution of a 1995 problem of Cassaigne and to applications in symbolic dynamics, including the question of convergence of Rauzy graphs, as well as to the growth and asymptotic invariants of algebraic structures.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Correction for Bernabé-Rubio and Watt, Caspase-8-dependent autophagy regulates neutrophil infiltration in oral squamous cell carcinoma
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Defining and measuring proximity to criticality based on univariate time series
items.abstract: Diverse social, engineered, and biological systems are made up of multiple interacting dynamical components; to work properly, certain components must be carefully regulated so that their dynamics avoid instability. However, many desirable properties, like optimized computation and control, emerge close to the tipping point between stability and instability, i.e., near criticality. Claims that such dynamical systems operate near criticality have been controversial because it is difficult to assess proximity to criticality when control parameters are unknown, hard to manipulate experimentally, and fluctuating in response to changing environmental or internal conditions. Moreover, observations of system dynamics are often limited to time series measurements of one or a few components. Here we develop a temporal renormalization group theory for defining criticality for univariate time series models and an information theoretic definition of proximity to criticality that is independent of model parameterization. We apply this theory to order-n autoregressive models resulting in a data-analytic strategy for time-resolved estimates of proximity to criticality based on measured univariate time series. After benchmarking our approach on diverse ground-truth cases, we apply it to recordings of spiking activity in the mammalian brain. Our estimate of proximity to criticality predicts behavior and suggests that brain dynamics shift closer to criticality during wakefulness and shift away during deep sleep.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Functional redundancy between atypical CDKs reveals a vulnerability in hepatocellular carcinoma
items.abstract: The atypical cyclin-dependent kinase subfamily (CDK14–18) encompasses five related proteins with unclear function, and for which individual depletion has not demonstrated sustained therapeutic relevance. We report here that CDK16 and CDK18 compensate each other and liver cancer cells are sensitive to the concomitant inactivation of both kinases, resulting in persistent defects in DNA repair and subsequent cell death. These effects are linked to a role of CDK16/18 in regulating nucleocytoplasmatic transport through phosphorylation of nuclear pore complex components, including NUP35. Genetic ablation of Cdk16 and Cdk18 in established liver tumors driven by MYC and beta-catenin oncogenes triggers DNA damage in cancer cells without affecting adjacent normal tissue, ultimately leading to tumor regression. Collectively, these findings provide a rationale for the development of CDK16–18 inhibitors—likely targeting multiple subfamily members due to their structural similarity—as a strategy against aggressive cancers, such as hepatocellular carcinoma, where effective treatment options remain limited.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Isotopic evidence of dissolved organic nitrogen production and consumption in ocean surface waters
items.abstract: Unlike dissolved inorganic nitrogen, which is scarce in much of the tropical, subtropical, and temperate surface ocean, dissolved organic nitrogen (DON) has significant concentrations and gradients. Accordingly, the lateral transport of DON may fuel biological productivity in nutrient-depleted low-latitude surface waters. Here, we report measurements of the concentration and 15 N/ 14 N ratio (δ 15 N) of DON in surface waters over the Pacific and Atlantic basins. DON concentration is generally highest in subpolar and equatorial waters, with minima in the subtropical gyres. A δ 15 N correlation is observed between surface DON and the nitrate consumed in the surface waters, indicating in situ DON production and consumption. Samples with lower DON concentrations tend to have anomalously high DON δ 15 N, confirming net DON transport to, and consumption in, the subtropical gyres. Net local DON production or consumption appears to dominate the observed spatial variation in the DON-to-subsurface nitrate δ 15 N difference. For example, N 2 fixation tends to lower the δ 15 N of surface DON relative to subsurface nitrate mostly through encouraging DON accumulation rather than by the specific δ 15 N of the nitrogen introduced by N 2 fixation. Unique conditions appear to apply in the equatorial Atlantic, where despite high productivity, a local minimum in DON concentration and a slight elevation in DON δ 15 N suggest net DON degradation. In this phosphorus-rich, nitrogen-poor upwelling environment where low iron may restrict N 2 fixation, net decomposition of DON may supply needed recycled nitrogen to the ecosystem.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Forniceal deep brain stimulation improves memory in Rett syndrome mice by promoting the maturation of newborn hippocampal neurons
items.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is associated with an increase in hippocampal neurogenesis and memory benefits, but the causal mechanism is unclear. Here, we use a mouse model of Rett syndrome, a severe learning disability syndrome caused by MECP2 loss of function, to find that DBS promotes the maturation and integration of newborn dentate granule cells (DGCs) into the neural circuit. Suppressing hippocampal neurogenesis prevented DBS from improving learning and memory. Newborn methyl-CpG-binding protein 2 (MeCP2)-deficient DGCs in Rett syndrome mice showed attenuated development and synaptic dysfunction, but DBS rescued DGC dendritic arborization, synaptogenesis, and long-term synaptic plasticity. DBS achieves this, at least in part, by increasing the protein level and shifting the phosphorylation of potassium chloride cotransporter 2, thereby restoring the conversion of GABAergic signaling from depolarization to hyperpolarization, a process that is otherwise delayed by MeCP2 deficiency. This study pinpoints one mechanism by which chronic DBS promotes neuronal maturation and enhances memory.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Environmental RNA improves detection and surveillance of schistosomiasis transmission
items.abstract: Environmental diagnosis of schistosomiasis, a disease affecting over 250 million people globally, remains challenging, thereby limiting efficient eradication efforts. Current methods, including environmental DNA (eDNA), cannot distinguish between infectious parasite life stages present in the environment. Here, we develop and validate an environmental RNA (eRNA) approach that enables detection and quantification of Schistosoma mansoni miracidia (infective to snails) and cercariae (infective to humans) directly from water samples. We identified life stage–specific transcripts and designed ddPCR assays highly specific to S. mansoni and each life stage. Laboratory experiments demonstrate that stage-specific eRNA assays accurately detect and quantify the relative abundance of each life stage. While eRNA and eDNA assays showed similar analytical limits of detection (LOD), eRNA provided enhanced organism-level detectability due to higher target molecule availability per life stage, also resulting in longer signal persistence in water that may facilitate the detection of the highly transient free-living stages of S. mansoni in the environment, especially cercariae. Field validation at six endemic sites in Brazil confirms that eRNA outperforms eDNA and conventional snail surveys in detecting S. mansoni cercariae indicating local transmission risk to humans. By enabling living stage discrimination and improving detectability compared to eDNA, our study advances both fundamental understanding and environmental surveillance of schistosomiasis transmission, supporting elimination initiatives in affected regions.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: DCAF6 reprograms TGF-β responses through TRIM33 destruction
items.abstract: TGF-β signaling plays a pivotal role in regulating numerous cellular processes, primarily through the Smad-dependent pathway. Disruptions of the pathway are associated with developmental disorders and life-threatening diseases, such as cancer. It has been reported that TRIM33 inactivates Smad4 signaling and also drives its own signaling responses. However, the mechanism controlling TRIM33 activity has remained unclear. In this study, we identify DCAF6 as a previously unrecognized ubiquitin ligase for TRIM33. DCAF6 targets TRIM33 at Lys850 for ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation, thus abolishing TRIM33-mediated mono-ubiquitination of Smad4. As such, DCAF6 induces dual consequences: it enhances Smad4-dependent transcriptional and growth inhibitory responses, while simultaneously eliminating TRIM33-dependent developmental responses. Conversely, DCAF6 knockout suppresses Smad4-dependent responses while amplifying TRIM33-dependent responses. Therefore, DCAF6 operates as a critical regulator in the balance of TGF-β signaling between the Smad4 and TRIM33 pathways. These insights deepen our understanding of the dynamics and fate control of TGF-β signaling and may open avenues for therapeutic approaches targeting TGF-β in diseases.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: C2CD3 links tooth patterning to evolutionary tooth loss in birds and dental anomalies across vertebrates
items.abstract: Primary cilia play an essential role in molecular signaling transduction during development, coordinating cell fate decisions and morphogenesis. Defects in components of the primary cilium result in an array of developmental syndromes called ciliopathies. Here we report 24 patients with nine rare and seven novel variants in the primary cilia gene C2CD3, which has previously been implicated in the ciliopathy Orofaciodigital syndrome XIV. Patients displayed an array of dental defects impacting the number, shape, and timing of tooth development. To understand the etiology underlying these defects, murine and avian models were analyzed during embryonic development. Ap2Cre;C2cd3 ex4-5 fl/fl mouse mutants showed a range of dental defects prenatally, mimicking several of the phenotypes observed in patients. Shh was upregulated in the developing upper jaw, leading to a widening of the midline, while Shh expression in the lower jaw was reduced, highlighting the context-dependent impact of cilia on hedgehog signaling. In avian mutants carrying a C2CD3 variant, talpid 2 , tooth buds were evident with SHH expression upregulated during early development in both upper and lower jaws. Cartilage defects were additionally observed in both conditional mouse knockouts and talpid 2 embryos. These changes in Shh signaling provide a mechanism to explain the phenotypes in patients and highlight the conserved role of C2CD3 in coordinating the morphogenetic potential of the jaw and patterning of the forming dentition. Given the conserved phenotypes, alterations in C2CD3-dependent ciliogenesis may have played a role in modulating Shh signaling to alter the timing and position of tooth germs across vertebrate evolution.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Rapid green leaf volatile sensing allows intact plants to release induced volatiles earlier than wounded emitters
items.abstract: Organisms in the vicinity of attacked neighbors can respond to danger cues by activating their own defenses. However, the temporal dynamics of these interactions remain poorly resolved, despite their importance for the ensuing effects. Here, we investigated defense responses of maize plants that are exposed to induced volatiles from herbivory-induced neighbors in real time. These experiments revealed a surprising temporal paradox: Intact neighbors start emitting most induced volatiles 15 to 80 min earlier than the attacked plants themselves. This earlier responsiveness was not associated with earlier induction of defense hormones, volatile biosynthesis genes, or within-leaf volatile accumulation. Instead, receiver plants kept their stomata open, while attacked sender plants rapidly closed them, likely because of water loss. Using different volatile deficient mutants, we demonstrate that the rapid responses in receivers are triggered by green leaf volatiles, which are released from the wound sites of sender plants within minutes independently of stomatal aperture. Thus, nonattacked neighbors can act as “unhindered observers” that activate some defenses more quickly than attacked organisms themselves, as they do not have to deal with wound trauma. The resulting plant volatile concatenation patterns expand our understanding of volatile signaling and have the potential to shape population-level multitrophic interactions.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Ionic liquid–mediated cellular loading for whole tumor cell vaccines
items.abstract: Conventional whole tumor cell cancer vaccines have demonstrated limited clinical success due to insufficient immunogenicity and challenges in adjuvant codelivery, despite their rich antigen repertoire and high patient-specific activity. Here, we introduce a simple, single-step approach to load immunostimulatory CpG oligodeoxynucleotides into tumor cells undergoing immunogenic cell death using an ionic liquid–containing cocktail. Results indicate that these adjuvant-loaded tumor cells (referred to as IL-Vax) enhance the uptake of cell-based vaccines by dendritic cells and their subsequent activation, leading to potent antitumor immunity. IL-Vax offered strong protection against tumor growth in a prophylactic B16F10 melanoma mouse model. Furthermore, IL-Vax synergized with PD-1 blockade to slow tumor growth and extend survival in a therapeutic model. The modularity of IL-Vax enables the loading of different cargos or cargo combinations, which may be conducive for additional tailoring of such vaccines and potentially other cell loading applications.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Dissolved organic matter uptake balances carbon budgets of Red Sea bivalves and ascidians
items.abstract: Benthic suspension feeders have long been thought to depend solely on particulate organic matter (POM) for their nutritional needs. Our research, conducted in the Gulf of Aqaba (Red Sea), shows that the available concentration of planktonic carbon in the reef water is too low to meet the metabolic demands (measured through in situ oxygen uptake) of common bivalves ( Spondylus sp. and Chama pacifica ) and ascidians ( Polycarpa mytiligera and Halocynthia spinosa ). In situ measurements confirmed a concentration-dependent uptake of bulk dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and protein-like dissolved organic compounds (fDOM, analyzed via spectrofluorometry) by Spondylus sp. and P. mytiligera , suggesting that DOC uptake may balance their carbon budgets. Stable isotope (δ 13 C) mixing models indicate that reef-derived DOC (mean δ 13 C = −18.4 ± 0.7‰) emerges as the primary carbon source for bivalves (57% of their body composition), far surpassing contributions from particulate sources (26% from POC > 100 µm and 14% from POC < 100 µm). While ascidians still rely primarily on POM (60 to 71%), DOC plays an essential role as a supplementary food source (23 to 29%). These results challenge the prevailing assumption that POM is the exclusive food source for these organisms. Given the widespread presence of bivalves and ascidians in benthic habitats, our findings highlight their ability to bypass the microbial loop and directly utilize dissolved organic compounds, prompting a reevaluation of current benthic carbon budgets.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Antigenic landscape of a highly mutated SARS-CoV-2 spike in ongoing viral evolution
items.abstract: The ongoing emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants in an increasingly immune-experienced population is largely enabled by the plasticity of the Spike protein, which lies at the frontline of host immune pressure. Here, we investigated how extensive remodeling of the N-terminal domain (NTD) in Spike influences its antigenic properties. Using BA.2.87.1, a variant heavily mutated in this domain, we found that even large deletions do not substantially disrupt overall Spike structure or pseudovirus infectivity. However, our structural and binding analyses revealed that the NTD exhibits increased flexibility and that interaction with a heme–metabolite, known to facilitate the exposure of an immunodominant epitope, is lost. These conformational effects, coupled with 33 NTD mutations, compromised the ability of human convalescent antibodies to engage this domain, contributing to their reduced neutralizing capacity. Consequently, BA.2.87.1-like variants may escape recognition by the preexisting NTD-targeting antibodies, potentially reducing protection. Together, our results highlight the intrinsic adaptability of the Spike beyond the receptor-binding domain, with implications for immune escape during viral evolution.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Lysine crotonylation acts as an epigenetic switch for glutamate neurotransmission and spatial memory
items.abstract: Histone posttranslational modifications, particularly lysine acetylation (Kac), are critical epigenetic regulators of transcriptional programs underlying long-term memory consolidation. Beyond Kac, several other non-acetyl acylations have been identified with the ability to regulate transcription; however, their role in memory consolidation remains unknown. Here, we identify histone lysine crotonylation (Kcr) as a molecular switch for long-term memory and glutamatergic neurotransmission. We find that spatial learning induces distinct spatiotemporal patterns of Kcr across hippocampal subregions. Through genetic manipulations, we show that reducing hippocampal Kcr levels impairs memory, while increasing Kcr levels by means of crotonate administration enhances long-term memory. Single-nuclei transcriptome and chromatin accessibility analyses reveal that crotonate facilitates activation of genes regulating glutamate signaling. Cell–cell communication analysis further suggests a strengthening of glutamatergic signaling within hippocampal excitatory neurons following crotonate administration. Real-time fluorescence imaging with genetically encoded sensors functionally validates our multiomics and computational findings—demonstrating the role of Kcr in regulating presynaptic glutamate release and neuronal activity. In summary, our findings elucidate a key mechanism underlying long-term memory consolidation and excitatory neurotransmission, linking epigenetic events to synaptic function and behavior.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Auxiliary BKβ4 subunits promote nanoscale coupling between BK and voltage-gated calcium channels
items.abstract: Intracellular Ca 2+ signals are essential for many cellular processes but must be tightly regulated to ensure precise spatial and temporal control. The large conductance calcium- and voltage-activated K + channel (BK) integrates intracellular Ca 2+ signaling and membrane depolarization to generate hyperpolarizing K + currents that regulate membrane excitability. In many cell types, BK channels achieve rapid activation through functional coupling with voltage-gated calcium (Ca V ) channels that provide localized Ca 2+ signals. However, the mechanisms that regulate the nanoscale organization of BK+Ca V channel complexes remain poorly understood. Here we investigated whether the BK auxiliary subunit β 4 (BKβ 4 ), which is widely expressed throughout the brain and modulates BK gating properties, influences the spatial organization and functional coupling of BK and Ca V channels. Using proximity ligation assays, electrophysiology, and superresolution stochastic optical reconstruction microscopy, we show that BKβ 4 promotes BK+Ca V nanodomain organization by increasing channel clustering and altering their spatial proximity at the plasma membrane. These structural changes enhance functional coupling between Ca 2+ influx and BK channel activation. Notably, the effects of BKβ 4 on nanodomain organization and coupling depend on the Ca V subtype involved. Together, our findings reveal that the BKβ 4 auxiliary subunit regulates the nanoscale architecture of BK+Ca V channel complexes and thereby modulates their functional interaction.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Multiplex mapping of social roles in isolated Honduran village networks
items.abstract: Human social networks involve multiple kinds of relationships—such as friendship, health support, and economic exchange—that serve different functions and compete for limited time and resources. Here, we deploy a compositional framework to infer functional roles in directed multiplex networks. We distinguish outgoing ties that reflect social behavior of individuals’ allocation of social effort from incoming ties that capture structural dependence, or social appeal. The method accounts for heterogeneity in individual activity levels and layer density across relational domains. Applying this approach to multiplex sociocentric network data from 23,378 individuals across 176 rural Honduran villages, we uncover well-defined role structures spanning friendship, health-related support, and economic interactions. We find a pronounced asymmetry: behavioral (outgoing) roles exhibit weaker demographic association but stronger geographic organization than incoming roles. This is consistent with shared local environments at the village-wide level shaping social action. In contrast, structural (incoming) roles show more pronounced life-course transitions and socioeconomic differentiation, with little geographic association. Taken together, these patterns reveal a systematic difference in how social behavior and social appeal are organized in multiplex social systems. This approach illustrates a general framework for studying social roles, inequality, and life-course dynamics in complex social systems.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: A strain-insensitive multiplexed soft microneedle patch for robust interstitial fluid biomarker monitoring
items.abstract: Wearable microneedle sensors analyze biomarkers in situ from interstitial fluids (ISF), enabling minimally invasive, precise, and continuous monitoring of metabolic diseases. However, conventional designs either lack adequate conformability to skin or suffer from electrode fractures during skin penetration and body motion, leading to signal instability that undermines reliable multiparameter acquisition. Here, we present a fully integrated system with a soft microneedle sensor array featuring nano-hill topographies on strain-resilient electrodes to delocalize strain via geometric confinement. This design reduces signal variability by 14-fold compared to conventional designs, enabling stable, simultaneous in situ monitoring of multiple ISF biomarkers. It achieves clinical-grade accuracy for continuous glucose monitoring (mean absolute relative difference of 10.8%) and captures dynamic synchronized variations in glucose, local tissue pH, and temperature in a living subject in real time. The system integrates a reusable electronic module with a disposable microneedle array with a sensor footprint of just 1.8 cm 2 . By combining high signal stability with multiparameter synchrony in a compact form factor, this system offers a practical solution for reliable, real-time ISF analysis under dynamic in vivo conditions.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: The staphylococcal protease SspA perturbs the epidermal barrier and promotes IL-22-driven inflammation in allergen-exposed skin
items.abstract: Skin colonization by Staphylococcus aureus has emerged as a common feature of atopic dermatitis and other allergic diseases, yet it remains unclear how this bacterium contributes to inflammation and pathology. Our S. aureus secretome analysis and bioactivity-guided fractionation uncover that the serine protease SspA destroys keratinocyte junctions, increases epidermal permeability, and activates an epithelial inflammatory program linked to barrier dysfunction. SspA and house dust mite extract (HDM), when epicutaneously applied in combination, cause interleukin (IL)-22-dependent atopic dermatitis-like skin disease in mice. Spatial single-cell analysis and immunophenotyping of lesional skin of these mice reveal massive elongation and branching of epidermal nerve fibers and the formation of T cells simultaneously producing IL-13 and IL-22. Chemical denervation and the resultant dismantling of the neuroimmune signaling network reverse the pathology driven by SspA–HDM combination. These findings link S. aureus colonization to barrier perturbation, allergen sensitization, and neurogenic dermatitis.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: A glycan superbinder reveals polysialylated-CD56 as a precision biomarker for pancreatic cancer
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most lethal malignancies, largely due to the lack of reliable biomarkers for early detection. Aberrant glycosylation presents a promising source of diagnostic signatures, yet polysialic acid (polySia), a distinctive glycan, has remained underexplored, primarily owing to limitations in detection methods and recognition tools. Here, we report the development of a polySia “superbinder,” a nanoscale molecularly imprinted polymer (nanoMIP) that exhibits superior specificity and affinity for polySia over monoclonal antibodies, enabling precise recognition and quantification of this glycan. Leveraging this superbinder, we uncover a previously unrecognized association between polySia and pancreatic cancer and establish polysialylated CD56 (polySia-CD56) as a specific and robust biomarker. PolySia-CD56 outperforms multiple previously reported pancreatic cancer biomarkers, including the clinical standard carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19-9). Notably, its expression pattern is complementary to that of CA19-9, and the combined use of both biomarkers significantly enhances diagnostic accuracy to 94.1%, effectively addressing the limitation of CA19-9 in detecting CA19-9-negative patients. Together, this study not only identifies polySia-CD56 as a precise biomarker for pancreatic cancer but also highlights the potential of antiglycan nanoMIPs as transformative reagents for decoding glycosylated targets and advancing clinical translation.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Dynamics of TFIIH and Spt4/5 during the transition from transcription initiation to elongation
items.abstract: The transition of RNA polymerase II from initiation to elongation requires the timely exchange of many factors. Some initiation factors and elongation factors contact the same RNA polymerase II surfaces in an apparently mutually exclusive manner. For example, space occupied by the initiation factor TFIIH and elongation factor Spt4/5 (also known as DSIF) are predicted to overlap. To determine whether Spt4/5 actively displaces TFIIH, or binds only after TFIIH dissociates, labeled yeast nuclear extracts were combined with single-molecule fluorescence microscopy to observe their dynamics in real time. TFIIH categorically dissociates before Spt4/5 arrives, with a clear interval in between when neither factor is present. Therefore, Spt4/5 binding is not required to dissociate TFIIH from RNA polymerase II.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: TEDEdb: A multicohort analysis and resource for transposable element differential expression in cancer
items.abstract: The human genome consists of nearly 50% repetitive DNA, referred to for decades as “junk DNA.” These repetitive sequences, usually under the strict control of epigenetic silencing, can become aberrantly expressed in cancer. Some of these expressed sequences, e.g., transposable elements (TEs), can induce innate immune responses when derepressed following treatment with epigenetic therapies. As a result, epigenetic therapy has been suggested to augment cancer therapies. TEs are traditionally ignored in most RNA-seq studies and their expression is often excluded from publicly available data sources. Thus, the vast amount of publicly available RNA-seq data is an untapped resource for exploring the role of TE expression in cancer and cancer treatment. Here, we present a uniform reanalysis of over 7,000 RNA-seq samples, encompassing more than 2,000 differential expression experiments across 220 cancer cell lines and 700 drug treatments. We observed that TE expression is more prone to batch effects than gene expression alone, necessitating the use of meta-analysis techniques to probe the dataset for global trends. We confirm that DNMTi and HDACis are powerful inducers of TE expression. We also show that nonepigenetic compounds such as cyclin-dependent kinase and topoisomerase inhibitors can also induce robust up-regulation of TE-derived repetitive DNA elements and confirm that this induction is consistent with transcriptional signatures of viral mimicry response. We made all data available through a publicly available database called the Transposable Element Differential Expression Database, or TEDEdb, and created an interactive web application for its exploration located at https://dataexplorer.coriell.org/TEDEdb/
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Scaling laws link conserved gene-abundance distributions to adaptive expression in diatom communities worldwide
items.abstract: Marine microbes sustain Earth’s major biogeochemical cycles, yet how they maintain stable ecosystem functions across diverse environments remains unclear. We analyzed metagenomic and metatranscriptomic data from diatom communities sampled during the Tara Oceans global expedition. While gene abundance distributions remain statistically similar across sample, gene expression varies systematically across geographical locations, a global pattern we show reflects predictable scaling laws. Global distributions, scaling relationships, and variability among sampling stations are captured by a stochastic model linking gene abundance dynamics to gene expression. While colder waters are associated with higher transcriptional activity and warmer regions show more selective gene usage, we find that transcript abundance increases nonlinearly with transcript richness. This general scaling is captured by our model and suggests that diatom communities balance high expression of core genes with specific functional diversity. These scaling relationships hold consistently across ocean basins, with temperature, used as an effective large-scale environmental descriptor whose signature cannot be fully disentangled from spatial structure, sufficing to predict transcriptional patterns from genetic composition. Our findings reveal how the stability of gene-abundance structure in diatom ecosystems coexists with transcriptional variability, enabling flexible functional responses.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Dlx1&2 directly promote expression of Cxcl14 to control synapse development and interneuron survival
items.abstract: Dlx genes have fundamental roles in the generation, differentiation, and functions of virtually all forebrain GABAergic neurons. Here we used scRNA-Seq to identify genes that are dysregulated in Dlx1/2 conditional mutants in mouse immature CGE- and MGE-derived cortical and olfactory bulb GABAergic interneurons. Dlx1/2 -regulated genes included Cxcl14 and Nr2f2 that are important for cortical interneuron (CIN) survival. We also identified DLX2-bound putative regulatory elements (pREs) of these Dlx -regulated genes. Within the Dlx -expressing lineage, some DLX-bound pREs were specific to CINs, others appeared to be constitutively bound; the latter class having activity in mature CINs. One such pRE and its associated gene, Cxcl14 , is strongly activated by Dlx1/2 and is essential for synaptogenesis onto CINs.

items.title: Prioritize validation over discovery of novel antibiotics

items.title: Cooperative nature of residue interactions in biomolecular condensates
items.abstract: Cooperativity of residue interactions is prevalent in proteins and plays an essential role in protein folding. However, whether cooperativity exists in intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and their assembled biomolecular condensates remains elusive. Here, we reveal the presence of residue interaction cooperativity in various IDP condensates using atomistic molecular dynamics simulations. In all these condensates, cooperative residue interactions manifest as packing between finite residue motifs (3 to 5 residues) with lifetimes three orders of magnitude longer than residue contacts. Notably, these higher-order interactions (HOIs) exhibit a significant nonadditive free energy, which originates from a local low-dielectric environment. The underlying sequence patterns like “Y-X-Q”, “D-X-R”, and “S-Y-X” are identified. Furthermore, HOIs dominate the cohesive energy of IDPs and condensates can be treated as HOI-crosslinked networks. This model can successfully reproduce experimental results of condensate physical properties, including saturation concentration, viscoelasticity, and interfacial tension.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Orexin and pupillary modulation for hunger control
items.abstract: Fasting-based interventions improve metabolic health and are also explored as adjuncts in other clinical settings, but hunger remains a barrier to adherence. Fasting activates AgRP/NPY neurons (ANs), a hunger-promoting population whose inhibition reduces eating in hungry animals. Here we identify hypocretin/orexin neurons (HONs), classically associated with arousal, as rapid suppressors of AN activity. HON ablation increased AN population activity, whereas HON optostimulation rapidly suppressed it. Combined recordings of AN activity and pupil size—a direct arousal metric not previously linked to AN dynamics—revealed that HONs contributed to pupil dilation-associated AN suppression. In fasted mice, sensory stimulation rapidly recruited this pupil-HON pathway, and suppressed AN activity and eating. These findings reveal an arousal–hunger pathway through which self-initiated pupil dilations, or dilations driven by salient environmental events, interrupt fasting-induced hunger signals. They also suggest a framework for noninvasive, sensory-, and pupillometry-guided approaches to hunger control during fasting.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: The lncRNA-encoded micropeptide ANCHOR promotes lateral root growth and drought tolerance in rice
items.abstract: Lateral roots (LRs) are important components of plant root systems, determining the robustness of root system architecture and influencing water uptake efficiency. Enhancing the phenotypic plasticity of LRs is key to improving crop production under fluctuating environmental conditions. In this study, we identified ANCHOR, a micropeptide encoded by a long noncoding RNA that is predominantly expressed in LR primordia and plumules. Overexpression of ANCHOR resulted in significantly longer and wider LRs, thereby altering root system architecture and enhancing drought tolerance; knockouts of ANCHOR produced the opposite phenotypes. Mechanistically, ANCHOR localized to plastids and directly interacted with the lysine biosynthetic enzyme LL-diaminopimelate aminotransferase 1 (LL-DAPAT). Our results indicate that ANCHOR functions as a “molecular glue” that enhances DAPAT dimerization. Through its influence on lysine metabolism, ANCHOR raises the levels of the auxin biosynthetic precursor tryptophan, thereby affecting auxin homeostasis. These findings show that lncRNA-derived micropeptides, like their precursor RNAs, can function as fine-tuning regulators. This function of micropeptides, together with their small molecular size, may make them suitable for application as bioeffectors to stimulate root growth and improve plant tolerance to abiotic stress without side effects for plants.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: piRNA loss unleashes episodic transposition bursts
items.abstract: In Metazoa, transposon expression is suppressed by the piRNA pathway, and disruption of this pathway leads to rampant transposon expression. However, it remains unclear whether increased transposon expression results in actual transposition, and if so, which and how frequently transposons mobilize upon piRNA loss. Here, we developed a framework to track transposon copy accumulation across generations on a single set of nonrecombining haploid genome in the Drosophila male germline, with or without the piRNA biogenesis factor HP1D/Rhino. Single-fly Nanopore DNA sequencing revealed that multiple transposon families mobilized after 10 to 45 generations of piRNA loss. Among them, the most prolific across all replicates was copia , producing dozens of new insertions that were distributed across chromosome arms. With genomic DNA collected at every generation, we validated and dated each copia insertion, revealing episodic bursts of transposition that deviated strongly from a Poisson process. Using phylogenetic analysis, we further showed that multiple copia loci—both autonomous and nonautonomous copies—can mobilize. Interestingly, two additional transposon families, mdg3 and invader3 , also mobilized episodically, but with distinct timing and magnitude, highlighting the stochastic nature of transposition bursts. Because we did not observe a single transposition event for these elements in controls, our results provide direct evidence that the piRNA pathway tightly suppresses germline transposition. More importantly, our findings argue that disruption of the piRNA pathway does not simply elevate transposition rates, but it instead unleashes punctuated and stochastic bursts of transposon movement that may radically reshape the timing and magnitude of mutational input during evolution.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Quantifying ancient architecture: Stone-level machine learning reveals architectural variation and settlement growth at Shivta
items.abstract: Built environments provide durable evidence for how ancient settlements were organized, expanded, and transformed over time. Yet quantitative approaches to documenting architectural variability are generally labor-intensive, limited to individual structures, or dependent on aggregate volumetric estimates. We present a scalable, machine-learning-based framework that shifts the unit of analysis to the individual building stone and combines two complementary datasets: low-altitude drone imagery of surface remains and close-range photographs of standing walls. Applied to the Late Antique settlement of Shivta in the Negev Desert, the method automatically digitized approximately 235,000 surface stones and 12,000 stones in 604 walls, quantifying stone size, shape regularity, and masonry arrangement across walls, households, insulae, and the settlement as a whole. Higher masonry scores cluster around churches and parts of the settlement boundary, while the spatial distribution of masonry variation reveals a previously unidentified earlier boundary and provides evidence for outward expansion from a southern core. Combined with architectural sequencing, these patterns indicate the use of larger and more regularly shaped stones during Shivta’s principal phase of growth. The framework combines analytical flexibility with demonstrated robustness, supporting broader application across diverse stone-built archaeological contexts while complementing architectural energetics and enabling settlement-wide and cross-site comparisons of construction practices and settlement change.

items.title: Profile of Barbara Sherwood Lollar
items.abstract: In a laboratory nearly 2.4 kilometers under the Canadian Shield, geochemist Barbara Sherwood Lollar has tracked the sustained release of enough hydrogen gas from Earth’s crust to produce 4.7 million kilowatt-hours of energy per year. Elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 2022, Sherwood Lollar revisited the Kidd Creek Mine in Ontario, Canada where, in 2013, her explorations found that waters flowing from deep fractures were 1.6 billion years old. Reported in her Inaugural Article, the findings, aided by studies of noble gases in the samples, pushed the age of Earth’s oldest waters back by hundreds of millions of years.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Synchronous end-Permian mass extinction zenith in marine and low–middle latitude terrestrial North China
items.abstract: The end-Permian mass extinction was the most severe biotic crisis of the Phanerozoic, yet temporal synchrony between marine and terrestrial extinctions remains debated due to correlation uncertainties. Here, we present an integrated magnetostratigraphic, cyclostratigraphic, and carbon-isotope and mercury (Hg) chemostratigraphic record from the fluvial Upper Shihhotse, Sunjiagou, and Liujiagou formations at the Sigou section, North China. We identify 14 magnetozones spanning the late Changhsingian to late Olenekian, constrained by a floating timescale based on gamma-ray cyclostratigraphy and subsequently anchored through magnetostratigraphic correlation. Our chronostratigraphy reveals a Hg peak at 252.4 Ma, aligning with the main eruptive phase of the Siberian Traps Large Igneous Province, while the carbon isotope excursion onset (252.1 Ma) and minimum (252.0 Ma) are synchronous with the Meishan Global Stratotype Section and Point. Furthermore, the Induan–Olenekian boundary is positioned below magnetozone SG4n, constraining the Induan Stage duration to 1.6 to 1.8 My. These findings establish a high-resolution chronostratigraphic framework for the Permian–Triassic boundary in North China, supporting a synchronous extinction zenith across marine and low–middle latitude terrestrial ecosystems, with latitudinal diachroneity relative to high-latitude and tropical landmasses.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

items.title: Septin binding restricts Shigella growth and triggers intracellular tolerance
items.abstract: Pathogen survival relies on their ability to adapt to changing environments, yet how intracellular bacteria tolerate cell-autonomous immunity remains unclear. Septins assemble into cage-like structures around cytoplasmic Shigella targeted by autophagy, but their antibacterial activity was unknown. Using advanced microscopy and cell-free reconstitution, we show that septins polymerize into circumferentially oriented filaments that inhibit bacterial growth. RNA-sequencing reveals that septin binding to Shigella upregulates type III secretion system (T3SS) effectors and triggers a stress response. Underlying this, septin-bound Shigella possess hyperpolarized membranes, but without lethally damaged cell envelope. We show that exposure to septin binding enhances the impact of the cell envelope-targeting antibiotic polymyxin B.
